en: Prosperity!
Now begins the tenth maṇḍala.
In the tenth Maṇḍala there are twelve Anuvākas.
In that [Maṇḍala], there are sixteen Sūktas in the first Anuvāka.
Among them, the first Sūkta, consisting of seven verses beginning with "agre bṛhan," is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Trita Āptya.
By the *anādeśaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding the absence of specific instruction), it is a *triṣṭubh* meter;
by the *maṇḍalādiparibhāṣā* (the rule concerning the [first] maṇḍala, etc.), Agni is the deity. Thus it is enumerated: “Agra, seven, Trita.”

In the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*, within the Agneya Ṛtu, one should exclude three verses from the eighth hymn among the eight hymns beginning with *idam*, namely those in the Maitrāvaruṇa meters.
For it is stated: “From the eight [verses] beginning with *agre naya agre bṛhan*, one should omit the last three of the last [hymn]; this is the Triṣṭubh” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).
And: “According to the rule of the *prātaranuvāka*, one should recite these [verses] from that very Saṃhitā until the thousandth [verse] is reached” (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 6.5).
When the Āhavanīya fire has been established for the sake of the *homa* and has become extinguished prior to the *homa*, a certain sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) dedicated to the deity Jyotiṣmat is performed.
Among these, the first is the *yājyā*.
It is stated in the Sūtra: ‘The *iṣṭi* is [for] Abhijyotiṣmat; “O Varuṇa, O Udame, thy purifiers... O Bṛhat, standing erect over the dawns, [protect] us”’ (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.12).
This same rule applies to the *upākaraṇa* and *utsarjana* rites, as well as to the *maṇḍala-homa* and other such offerings;
thus the Sūtra has been cited.
At the forefront of the dawns, the great one has stood erect; having swallowed the darkness, he has come with light.
Agni, the fair-limbed one, with his brilliant luster, has been born, overcoming all that is hostile.

In front, the great one has stood erect among the dawns; having emerged from the darkness, he has come with light. Agni, with his radiant luster and beautiful limbs, has been born and, as a companion to all, has filled the worlds.
This great Agni has risen high; at the time of the dawns, above the dawns, being kindled and standing upright, he remains in the form of flames. Then, from the darkness—this is a name for night.
Having consumed the night, he emerged from the forest.
The form [of the word] *gami* occurs when there is an absence of the suffix *kvip*.
That fire, having gone forth and emerged, being characterized by its own brilliance and luminous splendor, has come back;
being carried from the *gārhapatya* fire toward the *āhavanīya*, it returns.
Immediately thereafter, this fire—possessing beautiful flames as its limbs, born for the sake of the ritual—is radiant with a hundredfold light; such is its form as it blazes intensely.
By means of that which is shining;
or rather,
for the root *ruśati* has the meaning of "to injure."
With his light, which destroys darkness,
he fills all the worlds— or indeed all dwellings, that is, the sacrificial halls— with his splendor.
[The root] *prā* means "to fill."
Regarding the rule “tiṅām tiṅo bhavanti,” there is the substitution of *sip* for *tip*.
On this point, the Vājasaneyaka states: “The great one has risen erect from the lap of the dawns,” for indeed, he stands erect from the lap of the dawns;
“driving away the darkness with light,” for he drives away the darkness of the night with light.

"Agni, with his radiant glow, is well-limbed"—for indeed, he, with his radiant glow, is well-limbed when born. "He fills all the meeting places"—these worlds are indeed all the meeting places; having been born, he fills them. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.7.3.10).
Born as an embryo at the beginning of heaven and earth, you move beautifully among the plants;
as a brilliant infant, you have roared forth from your mothers, dispelling the darkness and the nights.
1. *ga-ta-ma-vam* (the first three syllables) are the highest; *ta-bha-ra-vam* (the last three syllables) are the highest of the high. 2.

O Agni, you whose limbs are beautiful, who have been born from the womb of the two worlds (*rodasī*), you are lovely, the sustainer of the people, the wondrous infant among the plants. You have dispelled the darkness all around; bellowing loudly, you have come forth from your mothers like a calf toward the cows. ||2||

O Agni, you who are born, arisen, and beautiful in form, you are specially churned among the plants—that is, among the products of plants and in the forests—or alternatively, you are "vibhṛta," being variously carried as the Āhavanīya fire; thus, existing within the plants, you are the embryo of the two worlds, Heaven and Earth. You exist as the embryo in the form of Agni and in the form of the Sun.

Furthermore, O Citra, you of variegated color—[you who are] like the tongues of fire described in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* as "Kālī, Karālī, and Manojava" (MU 1.2.4)—you are multiformed; or rather, you are the Child worthy of being sought after (*citrāyanīya*), like the infant of the plants. Like the night, you envelop the darkness and overcome the black enemies with your own splendor; you surpass them. Such as you are, [you act] for the sake of the Mothers, those who have become mothers.
[Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 1] Seventh Aṣṭaka, 273.

For the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering at the *Ātithyā* ceremony, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is "The Hotṛ" (*hotāram*). And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two *saṃyājyā* verses are 'The Hotṛ with the variegated chariot' and 'Of the sacrifice whose chariot is the path, the Agni of Bharata, we hear'. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.5).
Agni, the Hotṛ-priest with the variegated chariot, the bright banner of every sacrifice,
the counterpart of every god by virtue of his greatness— him, Agni, the guest of men, we honor with splendor.

The Hotṛ-priest with the variegated chariot, the banner of every sacrifice, the resplendent one who stands as the counterpart to every god by his greatness; Agni, through his glory, is indeed the leader of men. 5.

Go forth preeminently toward the Hotṛ—by name the officiating priest of the *adhvara* sacrifice, or rather the invoker of the gods; Citraratha, whose chariot has various forms; the banner, or the indicator, of the entire *adhvara* sacrifice that is unharmed by Rākṣasas; the white-colored one, shining with his own greatness; toward every god who desires [the sacrifice], go forth with excellence.
Immediately thereafter: O Agni, son of strength and majesty, bring hither—that is, cause to arrive—the gods, Indra and the others, here at this sacrifice of ours.
"Piprīhi" is the second hymn, consisting of seven verses.
The seer and other details are as before.
It is introduced with the words "Piprīhi."

The application of the *sūkta* is for the *prātaranuvāka*, the *abhilava-śastra*, and the *iṣṭi* offerings of the New and Full Moon sacrifices; it is also the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Now, for the Sviṣṭakṛt [offering], 'O most youthful one, satisfy the longing gods' is the invitatory verse" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.6).
Satisfy the longing gods, O youngest one; knowing the seasons, O Lord of the Seasons, sacrifice here.
With those who are the divine officiating priests, O Agni, you are the most skilled sacrificer among the hotṛ-priests, according to our desire.

Satisfy the longing gods, O youngest one; knowing the seasons, O Lord of Seasons, perform the sacrifice here. With those who are the divine officiating priests, O Agni, you are among the invokers the most skilled in sacrifice. 1.
O Agni, youngest one, please satisfy the gods who desire to hear our praises with oblations.

O Agni, Lord of the Seasons (*ṛtupati*), you who know the seasons—the times for the divine sacrifices—perform the worship of them here in this sacrifice. Furthermore, O Agni, together with those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who exist among the gods—such as the Adhvaryu, the Agnīdhra, the Neṣṭṛ, the Potṛ, and the Upavaktṛ mentioned in the *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* (3.1)—worship the gods.
Alternatively:
"Daivya" refers to the divine officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) mentioned by Āśvalāyana: "The Moon is the Brahman, the Sun is the Adhvaryu, and Parjanya is the Udgātṛ" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.23.8–9).
Perform the sacrifice together with them.
Because you are the most effective sacrificer (*bhāyajiṣṭhaḥ*)—that is, the one who most directly sacrifices to the gods—among all the *hotṛ* priests.
Thou performest the office of the Hotṛ and the Potṛ for the people; thou art the wise thinker, the giver of wealth, and the observer of Truth.
With the cry of Svāhā, let us prepare the oblations; may Agni, the god, worship the gods.

Thou art the Hotṛ and the Potṛ of the people; thou art Māndhātṛ, the giver of wealth, the observer of Truth (Ṛtāvā). Svāhā! Let us prepare the oblations. May Agni, the worthy god, sacrifice to the gods. 2.

O Agni, you desire (*veri*) the *hotra*, the office of the Hotṛ and the hymn performed by it, for the sake of the sacrificers among men; and furthermore (*uta*), you desire the *potrā*, the office of the Potṛ and the praise performed by it.
Moreover, as a wise one (*mandhātā*), as one who possesses truth (*ṛtavā*), you are the giver of wealth (*draviṇodāḥ*).
Now, regarding those performed out of sight:
"We shall offer oblations to the gods, svāhā! We shall perform the svāhā-call; we present them."
Therefore, let the shining god, the Arhat worthy of praise, or Agni fit for the sacrificer, worship the gods;
let him honor them with those oblations.
When there is an occasion such as the omission of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Pāthikṛtīṣṭi must be performed.
In that rite, "ā devānām" is the *yājyā* verse.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "vedhā hi vedho adhvana ā devānām panthāmagamma" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.10).
At the Prāyaṇīyā [offering], the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) for the offering to Agni is the same as the offering verse (*yājyā*) at the Udayanīyā;
and it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth; we have come upon the path of the gods" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.3).
And thus, the offering and invitatory verses are reversed.

1. *ga-ta* 1.24.5–56: go forth with excellence. 2. *ga-ta3-bha1.4.5.6.7*: to hear and to consume the oblations. 3. *ga-ta-bha2.4.7*: belonging to us. 4. *ga-ṛtāvā*; *ta1.24.5.7-ṛtavān*: truthful. 5. *ga-namasyo*; *ta-bha4.6-praśasyo*: worthy of homage; praiseworthy.

We have come even unto the path of the gods, that we may follow what we are able to perform. May Agni, the knowing one, offer the sacrifice; he indeed is the Hotṛ priest; he shall arrange the rites and the seasons. ā devānām api panthām aganma yat śaknavāma tad anu pra voḷham | agniḥ vidvān sa yajāt sa id u hotā sa adhvarān sa ṛtūn kalpayāti || 3 ||
May we go upon that path—the path belonging to the gods, which is their own and serves as the means for reaching the world of the gods and other realms—by which we may attain the gods.
Likewise, may we be able to perform that ritual action; may we be capable and competent to carry out that action in due order, to bring it to completion.
Thereafter, may Agni, the wise one who knows that path, sacrifice to the gods.
May he indeed be the *vhotr̥*, the performer of the oblation for human beings;
may he, as Agni, ordain—may he fashion and bring about—the *vadhvar* sacrifices and the *vr̥tu* seasons.

In the event of a transgression of a vow (*vrata*), the *Vratapatīṣṭi* sacrifice must be performed. Regarding this, "yad vo vayam" is the *yājyā* verse. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "tvam agne vratapā asi, yad vo vayaṃ pramināma vratāni" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.13). Whatever vows of yours we have violated, O gods, being more ignorant than the wise; may Agni, the knowing one, fulfill all that for us, by means of those seasons with which he ordains the gods. Whatever vows of yours we have violated, O gods, being more ignorant than the wise; may Agni, the knowing one, fulfill all that for us, by means of those seasons with which he ordains the gods. (4)

O gods, you who are most wise, we—being less wise, having known even less, and being utterly ignorant—have indeed violated (*pramināma*) your *vratas*, that is, your actions, you who are the knowers and possessors of knowledge. The meaning is:
while you were aware, we have omitted the obligatory and occasional rites.
May Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, knowing all this, fulfill (*āpṛṇāti*) this entire collection of ritual acts.

The meaning is: "May he make it endowed with fruit. By what means shall he fulfill it? To this he says: "By these seasons (*ṛtubhiḥ*)," that is, by the times suitable for sacrifice; "he ordains the gods" (*kalpayāti*), meaning he prepares them for the performance of ritual action—by those [seasons] may he fulfill it.

Whatever mortals, with minds of feeble skill, do not conceive of in their ignorance regarding the sacrifice—Agni, the Hotṛ, the knower of the seasons, discerning all, shall as the most excellent sacrificer worship the gods according to the proper times. || 5 ||

The mortals—the human officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—who are weak in skill due to constant sacrifice, or whose strength and enthusiasm are diminished, [are] at *pākatrā*; that is, by means of *pāka*. Because of the inclusion of the word *bahula*, the suffix *trā* is used here even in the sense of the instrumental case. By "by means of *pāka*" is meant by that which is to be cooked—that is, by those devoid of specialized knowledge.

Those who, being joined with a narrow mind, do not reflect upon—that is, do not understand—the ritual action connected with the sacrifice, let that Agni perform the sacrifice: he who is the Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods or the preparer of the oblation; the Knower of the Rite (kratuvit), the Knower of the Action (karmavit); the most excellent sacrificer (yajiṣṭha), the one who sacrifices pre-eminently among the gods; he is Sviṣṭakṛt. Let him sacrifice to the gods according to the seasons (ṛtuśaḥ) in the sacrificial fire at their respective times suitable for worship; let him honor them with oblations.
The progenitor has established you as the brilliant banner and the face of all sacrifices.
Therefore, perform the sacrifice for us; may the lands be favorable, and may there be desirable refreshments, rich in food and beneficial to all people.

For you, the father, has generated you as the face of all sacrifices, the wondrous banner and signal. Now, worship according to the lands that are responsive, the desirable refreshments accompanied by food, which belong to all people.

O Agni, you who are the face—the beginning, the principal, the wonderful (citra), the admirable, or the multiform—of all (viśveṣām) sacrifices (adhvarāṇām), you who are the banner (ketum), the indicator; you, the progenitor (janitā), Prajāpati or the sacrificer (yajamānaḥ), having performed sacrifice, brought you forth (ajanayat).
Having been thus produced, you [rule over] the *kṣāḥ*—this is a name for the earth (*pṛthivī*)—the lands endowed with gifts and other blessings.
For *kṣāḥ* means the earth (*bhūmiḥ*).
Sacrifice after [them]; bestow them one by one.
Or rather:

sacrifice and offer those desirable foods—characterized as oblations—which have been consecrated with the *nuvatī* verses, which follow the earth characterized as the altar (*vedi*) and have been placed upon the altar, which are full of food (*kṣumatī*), accompanied by the sounds of hymns and mantras, beneficial to all people (*viśvajanyā*) because they are the cause of rain and sacrifice; sacrifice these to the gods and present them.

O Agni, being kindled, shine forth brilliantly, knowing the path traveled by the fathers, you whom Heaven and Earth, you whom the Waters, you whom Tvaṣṭṛ, and you whom the well-born one have consecrated.

Thee whom Heaven and Earth, thee whom the Waters, thee whom Tvaṣṭṛ, the well-born, have generated—knowing the path well, O Agni, shining along the father’s way, being kindled, blaze forth with splendor! 7.
O Agni, you whom Heaven and Earth brought forth— either as the Self of the Ādityas or as another Self—
and likewise you whom the Waters, residing within the womb of the clouds, brought forth as the lightning; or else:
The waters are called the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
These three worlds—the two, heaven and earth, and the intermediate space—are those who have generated you.

Furthermore, Tvaṣṭṛ, the Lord of Progeny (*prajāpati*) of beautiful birth, has generated you through sacrifice, O Agni. Knowing well the path of the fathers—that path by which the ancestors go, the route for carrying the oblation—and being kindled, shining with splendor, blaze forth; that is, shine forth preeminently with light.
The third hymn is the mantra beginning with “Ino rājan. The seer and other details are as before. It is catalogued under the heading “Inaḥ.”
The application [of these verses] in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra has been stated.
This king, kindled in the assembly, the fierce one, has appeared for the sake of skill;
take heed, he shines with great luster; he strides forth, driving away the ruddy dawn.

The lord, O King, the glowing one, kindled, belonging to Rudra, for skill, well-formed—he has been seen. Be mindful; he shines with great luster. Without faltering, he goes toward the gleaming [dawn], driving away the darkness.

The paths of this great Agni, as he is kindled, are like the vast expanse of heaven; the radiant splendors of his friend, the auspicious, the worshipful, the bull-like, and the mighty, shine forth clearly upon his journey through the nights. asya yāmāsaḥ bṛhataḥ na vūman indhānāḥ agneḥ sakhyuḥ śivasya īḍyasya vṛṣṇaḥ bṛhataḥ svāsaḥ bhāmāsaḥ yāman aktavaḥ cikitre || 4 ||
The blazing rays of this great Agni—
those rays which go, that is, move—
are not obstructed by the people who offer praise.

Furthermore, O Agni, you who possess a beautiful face (*śvāsaḥ*), whose rays (*aktavaḥ*) are your own nature and dispel the darkness—you who have become a friend through a friendship characterized by the relationship of the praiser and the praised, the worshipper and the one to be worshipped; you who are auspicious (*śivasya*), the bringer of happiness to your devotees, worthy of praise (*īḍyasya*), the object of hymns (*stotavyasya*), the showerer of desires (*vṛṣṇaḥ*), the great (*bṛhataḥ*)—bring that greatness to us and sit down between Heaven and Earth, those two youthful maidens.
May Agni, the well-guiding, swift with his swift horses, impetuous with his impetuous steeds, come hither.

Do thou bring hither great wealth for us, and sit down as the messenger between the two youthful ones, Heaven and Earth. May Agni, the wise one, with his swift, impetuous horses, come here himself, being full of vigor. 7.
O Agni, you who are such a Vasu, you have grown; at our sacrifice, we shall worship you. You, the great one, bring the gods hither; carry them forward and cause them to arrive.

Furthermore, between the two youthful ones—the two that are mutually mingled, whether they be the young [gods] or heaven and earth—you, Agni, the mover, go as the soul of the sun; you dwell as a Vasu; sit down upon our sacrifice.
Likewise, you are the bestower of wealth (*vasutuka*).
The root *tug* has the sense of "going";
it is easy to understand [in this context].
[It is used] by the praisers.

You are the messenger for the wise ones and for men by means of conveying the oblations. Therefore, you are great; taking the offerings within the space between heaven and earth, you move—that is, you go—through the *rocana*, the intermediate region of the world.
"We praise you"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Like a noble infant, the mother, increasing thee, bears thee while seeking thy favor; from the dry land thou goest down the slope, longing for it, and like a beast let loose, thou desirest to conquer. 3. Like a child, thee, the noble one, the mother, increasing thee, bears thee, seeking thy companionship; from the height thou goest down the slope, longing, and like a beast set free, thou desirest to win. 3.

O Agni, the Mother—Pṛthivī—nurturing and nourishing you like a young child, desiring your company and seeking union with you, sustains and supports you, the noble and victorious one. Thus, longing for you, you abide upon the seven worlds;
"upon" (adhi) here indicates the locative sense.

From the intermediate space, you go by way of the downward slope, the inclined path; that is, you return toward the sacrifice. Furthermore, being released by the sacrificers, you desire to conquer—that is, you wish to go toward the gods. How so? Like a horse. Just as a horse, when let loose from its tether, desires to win the prize and wishes to go toward the goal, so do you. Thus, having been released by the sacrificers, you desire to conquer the gods and wish to go toward them. Therefore, O Agni, you are indeed a horse. Thus, having praised him with the horse-imagery, he now praises him with the imagery of a bull. Just as a bull, having been released from the enclosure, desires to conquer—that is, wishes to go toward the pasture—so do you. How so? Like a bull. Just as a bull, having been released from the enclosure, desires to conquer the pasture and wishes to go toward it, so do you. Therefore, you are indeed a bull. Having thus praised him with the imagery of a bull, he now praises him with the imagery of a goat. Like a beast;
just as a released beast returns to the pen, so it is.

O wise one, we are indeed deluded; O Agni, you alone truly know your own greatness. Vṛtra lies prostrate, yet he moves about devouring with his tongue; licking her repeatedly, he acts as the lord of the people, even while being a youth. murāḥ | amūra | na | vayam | cikitvaḥ | mahi-tvam | agne | tvam | aṅga | vitse | śaye | vṛtraḥ | carati | jihvayā | adan | rerihyate | yuvatiḥ | viś-patiḥ | san || 4 ||
O Agni, you who are unerring (*amūra*), undeluded (*amūḍha*), and therefore wise (*cikitvaḥ*), we, the deluded (*murāḥ*), do not know your greatness;
yet, O Agni, you indeed [know it].
The particle *aṅga* has the sense of "indeed.
You alone know—that is, you understand—your own greatness (*mahitvam*), that is, your majesty. Who else could possibly be capable of knowing it by himself?
Furthermore, *vattriḥ*— meaning "worn out"— refers to the collection of herbs (*oṣadhīsaṅgaḥ*) which lies, that is, remains or stays there. Alternatively,
*vattriḥ* is a name for form (*rūpa*), and by implication, the sense of "extremely" (*atyanta*) should be understood as being contained within it.
Possessing form through the form known as the Āhavanīya fire, he lies and moves;
then, with his tongue known as the flame, he moves about eating—that is, consuming—the oblations.
Due to the difference in the clauses, there is no elision of the accent (unighāta).

Furthermore, Agni, being the lord (*viśpati*) of the people (*viśām*), repeatedly licks—that is, he thoroughly tastes—the young maiden, his own mingling offering (*āhuti*), with his tongue, which is a flame extended far forward.
The root *lih* means "to taste.
Whether it be form (*rūpa*),
or else—
That fire consumes the youthful, fresh earth, which is like a young woman with her medicinal herbs withered.

He is born anew in the sacred songs; gray-haired and smoke-bannered, he has taken his stand in the forest. Like a bull that has not bathed, he does not enter the waters—he whom conscious mortals lead forth. kūrcin (smoke-bannered) | jāyate (is born) | sarṇayāsu (in the sacred songs) | navyaḥ (newly) | vanam (in the forest) | tasthau (he has stood) | palitaḥ (gray-haired) | dhūmaketuḥ (smoke-bannered) | asnātā (unbathed) | āpaḥ (waters) | vṛṣabhaḥ (bull) | na (like) | pra (forth) | veti (he enters) | sacetasaḥ (conscious) | yam (whom) | praṇayanta (they lead forth) | martāḥ (mortals) || 5 ||
The ever-new, more recent, or worthy of praise [Agni] is born by means of words in some place or other;
where? In the ancient, aged, and worn-out plants, that is, in the two kindling-sticks (araṇi).

Likewise, *palitaḥ* means a protector; *śvetavarṇaḥ* means white-colored. *Dhūmaketuḥ* is fire, known by its smoke (*dhūmaprajñāna*). [The phrase] "in the forest, he increases everything" does not exist [in this context]. [Regarding the variants: 2. *ta-ma6* reads *kāmanān*; 3. *ta1.4.5-ma6* read *jihvā*; *tara.4.7-mu* read *jihvayā jihvā*; 4. *ta* reads *prabhṛtayā*; 5. *ta1.2.6.7-ma6* read *jīrṇāsvadhikā*; *tara.5* reads *jīrṇoṣadhikāṃ*. He stood in the great forest (*simvaraṇye tasthau tiṣṭhati*).
Or alternatively:
he who abides in the forest (the sky) and in the water in the form of lightning;
and who, being unanointed (not requiring bathing), remains always pure even without performing ablutions—he is Agni, he is the Waters.
He is one whose expenditures are well-restrained. For the sake of peace, he goes forth toward the waters;
therein lies the illustration.
Or like a bull:
just as a bull goes toward the waters situated in the middle of the forest for the purpose of quenching its thirst,
so too do the mortals— the human officiants— being "sacetasaḥ," that is, of one mind and of equal wisdom, lead forth Agni, the sacrificial fire, and gratify him with oblations.
The two thieves, casting off their bodies, were bound by ten girdles of forest-creeper;
this is a newer hymn for you, O Agni: yoke your chariot as it were with your radiant limbs.

Like thieves who have cast off their garments, they have bound [thee] with ten girdles as if with forest-cords. This is a newer hymn for thee, O Agni; yoke thy chariot as it were with radiant limbs. 6.

O Agni, those two who are eager for the forest (*vanagū*), who go to the forest (*vanagāminau*), and who have abandoned their own bodies (*tanutyajau*)—having made a firm resolve, they are like two thieves (*taskarau*) who bind a helpless traveler with a rope, drag him away, and place him in some remote spot; so it is.

Thus Yāska says: "The two arms, which abandon the body (*tanutyak*), which go to the forest (*vanagū*), and which are the churners of fire (*vanagāminau*), he compares to two thieves" (Nirukta 3.14), and so forth.
[They] have studied.

In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense of the root *dadhāti*, because the *sic* suffix is elided and because the *tas* suffix is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule "in the Veda, both ways," it is *ṅit*; consequently, by the rule "ghu, mā, sthā, etc.," the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final *t*].
Then: O Agni, for you—this newest (*navyasī*) and most recent hymn of praise (*stuti*) is being performed by me, a mortal (*marta*).
Knowing this, with your pure (*śucayat*), all-illuminating limbs—that is, with your splendors (*tejas*)—yoke (*yukṣva*) yourself toward my sacrifice.
How so?
Like a chariot;
that is, just as they yoke a chariot with horses, so it is here.
In the Ukha-saṃbharaṇīya sacrifice, the invitatory verse for Agni accompanied by the Brahman is this one: "brahma ca te.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "brahma ca te jātavedo namaśca puruṇyame purudhā tvāyā" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.1).
O Jātavedas, may our prayer and our song of homage ever be an increaser for you;
O Agni, protect our children and our progeny, and guard our bodies with unceasing vigilance.
O Jātavedas, let this prayer and this song be for you always a source of increase; O Agni, protect our children and our progeny, and guard our bodies without ceasing. 7.

O Jātavedas, may this prayer (*brahma*) being offered by us for your sake, or this oblation (*havis*), or this food (*upama*), become a nourisher (*vardhanī*)—that is, a means of strengthening—for you. Likewise, let there be salutation (*namas*) to you. Furthermore, may this praise (*stuti*) being performed now be ever (*sadamit*) a strengthener (*vardhanī*) for you.
And therefore, O Agni, protect and guard our offspring— our sons and our grandsons— and furthermore,
being ever vigilant and never negligent, protect our very bodies and limbs.
‘Ekaḥ samudraḥ’ is the fifth hymn, consisting of seven verses. The seer and other details are as before. And [here follows] the ritual application (viniyoga).
The word "one" (ekaḥ) has been mentioned [in the preceding rule].
1. In *ta1.2.6* and *bha6*, it reads *tanutyaje*; in *ga*, it reads *tanutyaje*. 2. In *ga*, it reads *tadvat aṅgulibhirdaśabhiḥ mama bāhū tvām abadhnatām*.
3. In *ta1.2.6.7* and *mu*, it reads *ityādi raśanābhirdaśabhirgulibhiḥ kṛtvā rajjubhir abhyadhītām abhyadhāyi*.
4. Just as a charioteer yokes a chariot with horses, so too should you yoke [the senses] toward the sacrifice as the goal.
How? Not like a mere chariot. 5. The wondrous food in the form of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
The one ocean, the supporter of riches, born of many births from the heart of the stone, gazes abroad.
He moistens the heights and the depths; the bird’s footstep is set down in the midst of the spring.

One: The ocean, the supporter of riches, born from many sources, gazes out from our heart. He, the high one, unites [us] in the lap of the two secret ones; his station is placed in the midst of the spring. 1.

He is the one who flows toward the ocean, from which other waters flow; he is the sole supporter (*dhartṛ*) of the three kinds of wealth (*vrayīṇām dhanānām*); he is the peerless (*ekaḥ asahāyaḥ*) one; he is the one born in many ways (*bhūrijanmā*), being produced in various sacrifices through the form of the *āhavanīya* fire and others. That Agni, from him—from us—[he sees]; [here the sixth case ending is elided by the rule] *supāṃ suluk*. He clearly beholds (*vi caṣṭe*) our hearts (*hṛdaḥ*) and our desires.

And it has been said: "The gods indeed know the mind of a human being. Furthermore, at the two junctions—the morning and evening times—which are hidden and covered by light and darkness, the wise man dwells in their presence, near them; he attends to them and depends upon them for his livelihood.
Or alternatively:
it frequents the *modha*, the cloud, which exists near the *niṇya*, the hidden atmosphere.
Now, [the following is] direct observation (*pratyakṣa*).
O Agni, in the midst of the world that holds the waters of the ocean, your station—the place of the waters—is established.
Go to that middle speech;
or rather:
That which is called lightning, placed in the midst of the cloud—the ocean—go there as your own armor.
*ve*:
[This is] the form of the root *vī* in the sense of "motion" and so forth,
in the *laṅ* tense, with the suffix *sip*.
There is no loss of accent (anighāta) because of the difference in sentence structure.
Wearing their common dark-blue hue, the bulls have united with the mares;
the sages guard the station of Eternal Order and have established their supreme names in secret.

The same; the dark-blue; the bulls; clothed in [garments], they have come together; the mighty ones with the mares. The seers guard the station of *Ṛta*; they have established their secret, supreme names in the cave. || 2 ||

The stallions, worthy of honor through their oblations, though dwelling in one common place, the *nīḷa*, yet covering themselves according to the sacred formulas (*mantra*), the mighty bulls—the sacrificers—have come together with the swift mares;
they have united with them and become possessed of horses.
Or rather: [the text continues].
They have yoked the ruddy mares to come toward this very sacrifice of their own.
Likewise, the wise ones, possessing intelligence, guard the dwelling place—the abode—of the encompassing water;
that is to say, they honor it with oblations and hymns of praise.
Therefore, in the cave— the secret, hidden space within the atmosphere— they have held, that is, they maintain, the divine names, which are the waters;
or alternatively, in the cave— the concealed and enclosed heart— they assume, that is, they employ, the supreme names such as "Agni," "Jātavedas," and "Vaiśvānara."
The meaning is that they praise.
The two who uphold the truth and possess creative power have united; having measured him out, they brought forth the infant and nurtured him.
Moving toward the navel of the universe, the center of the firm, they follow with their mind the thread of the Sage’s thought.

The two, bestowing the truth-bringing and the illusion-possessing [powers], have together established the infant; they brought him forth as he grew, the navel of all that is firm. Moving about with their mind, they extend the thread even of the Sage. 3.
1. *ta-vinaśyati* (he perishes). 2. *ta-bhara-jānāti* (he knows how to carry it).

3. *ta3-bhara-udakadhārasya*; [variants: *bha1.4.7-udakādhārasya*, *lokadhārasya*; *bha6-udakādhārasya* (of the bearer of the water-stream; or: of the support of water, of the support of the world; or: of the support of water).

The Rigveda [Book 7, Chapter 5, Section 33]

The seers fashioned seven boundaries; of these, one alone the transgressor has approached. The pillar of Āyu stands in the dwelling-place of the highest, at the release of the paths, upon the foundations. The wise seers fashioned the seven boundaries—those consisting of lust-born and anger-born [vices]: drinking, gambling, women, hunting, violence, harshness, and false wagering—or as specified in the *Nirukta* (6.27): "theft, violating the teacher’s bed, killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, repeated performance of evil deeds, and falsehood regarding sin. Having established them, they fashioned them well, meaning they made them difficult to transgress. Of these boundaries, a transgressor—a sinful man—approaches only one. The sense is: he who acts thus becomes a sinner. Furthermore, the pillar—the restrainer and obstructer—of that man, namely Agni, stands in the dwelling-place of the highest Āyu, in the release of the paths, that is, in the midst of the atmosphere where his own rays, being of the nature of the sun, are released, standing in the form of lightning within the waters existing upon the foundations. By this, its presence throughout the three worlds is indicated.
In truth, he is the supreme truth in the highest heaven, born of Dakṣa in the lap of Aditi.
Here, Agni is our first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta), the bull and the cow in the earliest age.
Non-existent and existent.
And in the highest heaven.
The birth of Dakṣa from Aditi.
In the lap:
Agni indeed.
Of us, the first-born of Order.
The former:
in life,
the bull.
And: a cow.
The non-existent is the unmanifested, and the existent is the manifested.

According to the Śruti: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; that became existent; that grew. Thus, the entire world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, has always arisen within the supreme, highest *vyoman*—the causal ground endowed with knowledge.
From the beginning, in the lap—that is, the vicinity—of the Earth; or [in the lap] of Dakṣa Prajāpati.

Alternatively, it refers to Dakṣa himself, for according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (10.6.5.3), "He divided himself threefold: the Sun as one third, and Vāyu as one third"; thus, because the Sun is the presiding deity of the third realm, the celestial world (*dyuloka*).

In birth after birth—this being so—it follows that, prior to the creation of man, Agni alone was our first-born (*prathamajā*), born and arisen at the very beginning for us who are the enjoyers of the fruit of action (*ṛta*). This is because of the scriptural revelation: "Agni emerged as luster and essence" (*Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* 10.5.2; *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.2).

Later, in that same context, because the creation of humans is stated at the very beginning with the words "From that, humans were born," it follows that subsequently— in the earlier time relative to the later creation— this Agni alone was both the bull and the cow; that is to say, he existed as having the nature of both female and male, like a man and woman together.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may the Great Lord of the Holy Tīrtha bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the fifth chapter of the seventh book in the Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa, a commentary on the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial authority of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
1. Of *ṛta*, which has become truth; of that *ṛta*, which has become reality.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas.
Thus the wise one named Sāyaṇa has explained the fifth [section] of the seventh Aṣṭaka;
he now desires to explain the sixth chapter.
In the tenth Maṇḍala, the first Anuvāka contains sixteen Sūktas.
Among them, the sixth Sūkta, consisting of seven verses beginning with "Ayaṃ sa yasya," is addressed to Agni; it is composed by the seer Trita Āptya, is in the Triṣṭubh metre, and its deity is Agni.
This is indicated by the introductory statement "Ayam."
The application [of these verses] is in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra when they are joined.
This is he in whose protection the singer prospers through his ninefold praise;
surrounded by the most excellent rays of the seers, the radiant one pervades all.
This is he; under whose protection the singer prospers through the flames of Agni in his favor; he who, radiant and encompassed by the highest beams of light, moves around the seers.
The praiser, the singer, when the sacrifice has been performed, seeks the protection and shelter of that Agni through his guardianships;

he who rules over every feast for the gods, who possesses all life, at the dawning of the dawn—in whom the one with the unharmed chariot fixes his mind and his oblations within the fire with splendors. 3.

That Agni who rules—has mastery over—the entire feast for the gods, that is, over every sacrifice; and furthermore, he whose life is all-encompassing (*viśvāyuḥ*), whose movement is everywhere unimpeded, rules at the dawning of the dawn (*uṣasaḥ vyūṣṭau*) during the time of rising, for the sake of the oblation of the sacrificers. With his auspicious [powers] and the forces of his enemies, he whose chariot is unhurt (*ariṣṭarathaḥ*)—meaning whose sacrificial chariot is not harmed—is that very Agni in whom every sacrificer fixes (*skamnāti*) the thoughts (*manā*), that is, the offerings worthy of reflection, binding them with reverence and casting them [into the fire]. This Agni has been invoked for the purpose of the sacrifice by those who are not his equals.
Frequented by auspicious hymns like the moon, he hastens toward the gods with speed;
the joyous Hotṛ, the most skilled sacrificer, Agni, being well-mingled, sprinkles the gods with his ladle.
By means of auspicious things;
increasing; enjoying.
Arka 288: Rigveda [Maṇḍala 7, Anuvāka 6, Varga 2]

These [songs], O Agni, are for you; they celebrate you with cattle and horses for the sake of wealth. When, O Vasu, well-born one, your thought has attained its fulfillment according to our enjoyment, he who maintains it through his hymns. 2.

O Agni, these thoughts and praises of his—these hymns have arisen for you, for your sake, produced from the mouths of us, your reciters; this is the meaning. Together with cattle and horses, they celebrate—that is, they praise—the wealth consisting of gold and other riches being bestowed by you.
They praise you, saying, "This [gift] has been bestowed by you upon us, corresponding to our hymn of praise.

O *vaso*—O possessor of excellent wealth! O you who cover all with your own splendor! When a mortal, such as one among us, attains (*ānaṭ*), reaches, or obtains the enjoyment or wealth worthy of enjoyment being given by you, then [they praise you].
O well-born one, you who possess beautiful deeds, bestowing wealth upon us, may you spread yourself through our thoughts—this is the sense.
I honor Agni as my father, Agni as my kin, Agni as my brother, and ever as my friend.
I worship the face of the great Agni, the bright and worshipful radiance of Sūrya in heaven.
I honor Agni as my father; I honor Agni as my kinsman; I honor Agni as my brother and ever my friend. I venerate the face of the lofty Agni—the bright and worshipful splendor of Sūrya in heaven. 3.
I, the praiser, consider Agni alone to be my father; I know him as such. I consider Agni alone to be my kinsman and friend;
I consider Agni alone to be my brother.
I know Agni alone as a friend who is ever-present and never-failing;
I worship—that is, I attend upon—the face of the great Agni, known as the Āhavanīya fire.
In this context, it is an elliptical simile.

Just as someone might propitiate the radiant, shining orb of the sun—which resides in the sky, the celestial world, and is worthy of worship and adoration—in order to accomplish a desired object, so [is this].
O Agni, may our prayers be successful, you who are the eternal Hotṛ-priest protecting us in our home;
may he, the observer of Truth, whose horses are ruddy, be most bountiful to us with many food-providing days.

O Agni, may that wealth which wins for us our prayers—wealth which you, the eternal Hotṛ, the upholder of Ṛta, protect within our home—be ours through your many steeds and through the days; may it be most excellent for us. 4.
O Agni, you who are the winner (*sanutrī*), you who are to be shared with us (*asme*), our prayers (*dhiyaḥ*)—our hymns of praise—are successful (*sidhāḥ*), accomplished, and perfected;
that is to say, they have been performed by us for your sake.

O Agni, established according to the proper measure (*maryādayā*) within our sacrificial hall (*dame*), being the eternal offerer (*nityahotā*)—the constant performer of oblations—or the invoker of the gods, you protect me from the deficiency of ritual action (*karmaveguṇyāt*). Being thus protected, may I, through your grace, having attained union with you (*tvatsāyujyam*), become one who possesses the sacrifice (*ṛtavān*) or one who possesses truth (*satyavān*). This is the sense.
May I possess red horses—horses known as *rohitās*—and may I be rich in much food (*purukṣu*).
Furthermore, for you who are such as this, may there be desirable and praiseworthy oblations (*vāmaṃ vanīyaṃ haviḥ*) during these shining days (*yubhir dīpteṣv ahassu*).

1. *ta1.2.4.5*—“He uttered a hymn of praise (*stotra*)”; *ta2*—“produced from the mouth of the hymn (*stotra*)”; *ta6.7*—“produced from the mouth of the hymn (*stotramukha*)”; *bha6*—“produced from the mouth of the release of the hymn (*stotramocana*)”. 2. *ga*—“O Agni produced by ritual action (*karma*)”; *ta2.4.5*—“O Agni who goes forth from ritual action (*karma*)”; *ta3.7-bha*—“O Agni who has gone forth from ritual action (*karma*)”; *ta6*—“O Agni produced by ritual action (*karma*)”.
[He is] like a friend established by the days, the ancient officiant, the lover of the sacrifice (*adhvara*).
With their two arms, they generated Agni and Māyava; they established Viśvahotṛ.

With their arms, men have generated Agni, who is established by days, like a friend, like a well-employed ancient officiant; they have seated him, the lover of the sacrifice, the universal invoker. 5.

By means of the days, they have established him who is placed by the shining ones as a friend, like a friend, as one to whom an affectionate application should be directed—the ancient, the primordial Hotṛ-priest.
For the Śruti says: "Agni indeed was the Hotṛ of the gods" (AiB 2.7; 3.14).
Men, the sacrificers, with their arms generated Agni—such as he is—the lover (completer) of the *adhvara*, the sacrifice.
Furthermore, "among all men" means among the gods who possess that same form; they "seated the Hotṛ"— that is, they established him as the invoker according to the rule.
The meaning is that they have performed sacrifices for the gods.
O God, sacrifice yourself to the gods in heaven; what can a witless man accomplish for you by his cooking?
Just as you have sacrificed with the seasons, O God, so do you sacrifice to the gods and to your own body, O well-born one.

O Sacrifice, yourself, in heaven, O God, [bring] the gods. What has the ignorant one done for you as his work? Just as you, O God, have sacrificed to the gods according to the seasons, so, O well-born one, sacrifice to your own body. 6.

O radiant Agni, you yourself perform the sacrifice for the gods, Indra and the others, who abide in the sky, the heavenly world. What can a man—unripe, having completed his sacrifice but lacking higher wisdom—do for you? The meaning is that, without being presided over by you, he understands nothing at all.

Furthermore, O God, just as you have sacrificed to the gods with the *ṛtus*, the specific divisions of time, even so, O well-born Agni of auspicious birth, sacrifice yourself—your very self—as an offering.
Be for us, O Agni, a helper and a protector; be a maker of strength and a bestower of vigor upon us.
Grant us, O most glorious one, the gift of oblations, and protect our bodies with unswerving care.

O Agni, be our protector and our guardian; be the maker of our strength and the bestower of vitality upon us. O most glorious one, grant us the offering of oblations and protect our bodies with unwearied care.
O Agni, may you be our protector (*avitā*), the guardian who shields us from visible dangers;
and furthermore, may you be our shepherd (*gopā*), the protector who guards us from invisible dangers;
and furthermore, may you be the creator of food (*vayaskṛt*).
O bestower of vigor, become the giver of food!

O Agni, who art well to be honored, grant and bestow upon us our own rightful portion, the offering of the oblation. Moreover, without neglecting or being heedless, protect and preserve our own bodies.
The eighth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “pra ketunā,” is in the Triṣṭubh meter. Its seer is Triśiras, the son of Sraṣṭṛ.
The first six verses are addressed to Agni, and the subsequent ones are addressed to Indra.
And thus it has been enumerated: "With *pra ketunā*, [there are] nine; [the hymn] for Triśiras and for Aṣṭra belongs to Agni, while the other belongs to Indra.
Regarding these, the application of the first six in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra during the Āgneya sacrifice has already been stated.

He has reached even the highest ends of heaven; the buffalo has grown mighty in the place of sacrifice.
Agni goes forth with his lofty banner; the bull bellows unto the two worlds, heaven and earth. He has reached even the highest ends of heaven; the buffalo has grown strong in the lap of the waters.
Agni, joined with a great and lofty banner—that is, with supreme wisdom—now proceeds forth and goes toward the two worlds, heaven and earth.
Moreover, at the time of summoning the gods, he bellows like a bull, uttering a sound that transcends ordinary speech.
Even from the very ends and boundaries of heaven, reaching even to the nearby regions, he pervades upward by means of his nature as flame or as the sun.
In the lap, that is, the receptacle of the waters characterized by rain, in the intermediate space, the Great One (Mahiṣa) has grown, that is, he increases, in the form of lightning.
The bull, the peak-clinging embryo, rejoiced; the vigorous calf has bellowed.
Performing those deeds among the gods, he goes forth as the first in his own dwellings.

The embryo rejoices—the bull, the humped one, the tireless, the vigorous calf has bellowed. He goes forth as the first among his own dwellings, performing divine services for those who have raised him up.
The embryo situated within heaven and earth, the bull who rains down desires, Agni, the high-peaked one with exalted splendor, rejoices— indeed,
he delights. Furthermore, "asema" is a name of praise.

The praised calf—Agni, who has become a calf for Night and Dawn because he subsists on the evening and morning oblations; the vigorous one, possessing the activity of carrying the oblation and summoning the gods—is roaring; he utters the sound of summoning the gods and so forth.

That Agni, performing the uplifted and exalting deeds at the sacrifice among the gods, staying in his own dwellings—the places such as the Āhavanīya fire—goes forth as the first, the chief among the abodes of the gods.
He who established the head upon the two parents; they placed him as the flood of the sun.
At his flight, the wide ones, whose base is the horse, took pleasure in their bodies in the womb of Cosmic Order.

He who grasped the head of his parents at the sacrifice; they established him as the lord of the sun. In his flight, the ruddy ones, awakened by the horses, took pleasure in their bodies within the womb of the Eternal Order (Ṛta). 3.
The Agni who has grasped the head of his two parents— the heaven and earth acting as mother and father—
or rather,
the head-like, foremost region for churning within the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) acting as mother and father, by means of his own splendors.
In the sense of "beginning": it has begun; it destroys slightly. Even at the time of friction, it is capable of burning by means of heat.

The performers of the sacrifice have established, and by rule maintain, the flood-like, moving luster of the heroic and powerful Agni within the *adhvara*—the sacrificial rite. At the flight or movement of this Agni, his rays shine brightly in the womb—the place—of *ṛta*, the sacrifice; they are like horses with uplifted tails, or those whose roots are spread out, or whose bonds are food.
The meaning is that they are endowed with the consumption of oblations (*havir-āhāra*).
The sages (*kavayaḥ*) enjoy—that is, they resort to—their bodies (*tanvaḥ*), which are their own forms.
For at every dawn, O Vasu, you go forth as the first; be the radiant one between the two worlds.
For the sake of cosmic order, you have established the seven stations, engendering Mitra for your own person.

O Agni, you who are a vessel by your own splendor, the coverer of all, or the possessor of wealth (vasuman), or the praiseworthy one—you rise higher and higher; indeed, at every dawn, you go to the very forefront, you reach it first.

Moreover, between the two twins—the day and night which are coupled and never separated—you become, or are, radiant with light. Producing Mitra, the Sun, from your own body, you maintain the seven stations, such as the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, for the sake of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), that is, for the purpose of sacrifice.
You are the eye of the world, the guardian of the great Order; you become Varuṇa as you move toward that which is restrained.
You are the Son of the Waters, O Jātavedas; you become the messenger for him whose oblation you accept with joy.

Trita, by means of the *ṛtu*, chose for himself within [the waters], seeking the inspired thought (*dhīti*) through the ways of the Father; being pressed between his two parents, calling it kinship, he goes toward his weapons. 7.
In this *ṛc*, this meaning is expressed:

"O Trita, you who know all weapons, grant me your assistance for the sake of slaying the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ. Thus questioned by Indra himself, Trita chose a share in the sacrifice for the increase of his own power.
And Indra gave him water for washing his hands as well as a portion of the sacrifice.

By means of this sacrificial portion, the seer named Vṛtra—whose power had increased and who was intent on protecting himself through his own efforts—chose a share of the ritual thought (*dhīti*) in the midst of the sacrifice; and for the sake of Indra, the supreme protector of the entire world, he chose him as a friend by means of that rite which served as assistance for the purpose of slaying me, the three-headed one, at the proper season.

Furthermore, being seated in the *upastha*— the vicinity— of the sacrifice belonging to the two parents, namely Heaven and Earth (*mātā-pitṛ-bhūta-vāvāpṛṣṭhivya*), while being served by the officiating priests (*ṛtvigbhiḥ sevyamāna-sthitaḥ*), and uttering (*bruvāṇaḥ*) a hymn of praise (*jāmi*) that is appropriate (*yogya*) and worthy of Indra, chanting it for the sake of increasing Indra's strength,
he comes with his own weapons (*āyudhāni veti*) for the purpose of slaying me, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
Knowing the weapons of his fathers, Trita, impelled by Indra, went forth to battle;
he slew the three-headed, seven-rayed one and released the cows of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son.
He, the wise Āptya, impelled by Indra, fought against the paternal weapons; having slain the three-headed, seven-rayed [monster], Trita released the cows even from the son of Tvaṣṭṛ. 8.
Vāptya is the son of Āptya, or rather the son of the Waters (Apas);
the addition of the letter *t* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

He, Trita, knowing the ancestral weapons belonging to his own forefathers, being impelled by Indra—sent by Indra for the purpose of fighting with me, Triśiras—fought against [me], engaging in battle face-to-face.
Immediately after that, [he worships] Saptaraśmi for the purpose of subduing enemies, who has seven reins in his hands;
or alternatively,
Saptaraśmi is the Sun.
"Similar to that";

Furthermore, Trita even released—that is, he carried off—the cattle, the livestock, of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son. This is the meaning.
Indra looked down upon his great might; the Lord of the Good struck down him who deemed himself invincible.
Even of Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, he cut off the three heads that had proclaimed the cattle, and cast them away.

Indra, the lord of the virtuous, brought down his abundant power upon him who looked upward; the master of the host struck down him who deemed himself invincible. Seizing the cattle of Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, he tore off and cast away his three heads.

Vasu-patiḥ is the protector of the virtuous; Vindra is the lord of wealth; and Vbhūrī is his abundant, extensive, or even greater than before, Vojas—his “strength” which is Vudinakṣantam—pervasive and all-encompassing—and who is Vmanyamānam—a hero, considering himself such.
Alternatively, the root *man* has the sense of seeking or the sense of anger.
Whether blazing or raging,
he struck me— the son of Tvaṣṭṛ— with his thunderbolt; having split me open,

Viśvarūpa beheld such a future event with his own eye at the end of his life.

In this regard, the sequence is stated: “Now follows the dialogue between Yama and Yamī, the two children of Vivasvat, consisting of six sets of verses; there, Yamī spoke to Yama for the sake of union, but he, not desiring her, rejected her with nine sets of verses.
Therefore, in the first set of verses of the sixth [maṇḍala], the seer (ṛṣi) is Yamī, the daughter of Vivasvat, and the deity is Yama.
This is according to the rule: “He whose words [are recited] is the seer, and that which is spoken by him is the deity.”
Likewise, on the ninth [day], and on the second, fourth, and so forth, the seer is Vaivasvata Yama, the deity is Yamī,
and by the rule regarding unspecified meters, the meter is Triṣṭubh. The application has been explained.

Herein, in this hymn, the dialogue between Yama and Yamī, the two children of Vivasvat, is recounted. In this verse, Yamī spoke to Yama.

meaning a deserted place.

No; your friend does not desire this friendship, O Yamī, which consists of the characteristics of male and female. For you, though of the same womb (*sakṣmā*), are of a different form (*viṣurūpā*) because you are his sister. Therefore he does not desire it. Yama, having made himself invisible, replied to Yamī: "O Yamī, your friend—Yama, who became your companion through the experience of dwelling in the womb—does not desire this 'friendship' (*sakhya*) characterized by the traits of woman and man, which you have mentioned. This is an illustration; the meaning is that they are the sustainers of the bright worlds of immortality. 2. The immortals indeed desire this of you alone, the immortal one among mortals:
let your mind be placed within our mind; O husband, enter our body as a wife.

They indeed desire this: those immortals, even for the sake of one mortal, desire this kinship. Your mind has been fixed upon our mind; as a husband, you shall enter into the body of your wife. Again Yamī replied to Yama: The particle *gha* has the sense of "indeed. O Yama, those well-known immortals—Prajāpati and the other gods—even they desire this kinship (*tyajasaṃ*), which is to be understood through the scriptures: the class of women such as daughters, sisters, and so forth, who are called "kin" (*tyajasaṃ*) because they are given away (*tyajyate*) to another. They desire it even for "one," that is, even for the foremost of all the world, such as Prajāpati himself; the implication is that there exists a relationship with one's own daughters, sisters, and so on. For this reason, let your mind, your thought, be fixed upon our mind. As a husband, you shall enter into the body of your wife.

What we have never done before, how could we now speak untruth, claiming to be speakers of truth?

No; what have we done in the past? What now shall we speak, professing the Truth while uttering falsehood? The Gandharva in the waters and the watery maiden—she is our kin, she is our bond; that is our highest relationship. 4.
Yama speaks again to Yamī:

"In the past, when Prajāpati committed the act of approaching one who was not to be approached—doing so because he was possessed of immeasurable power—we have not done that; we have not performed it. Speaking the *ṛtas*, the truths, how indeed (*kad*) could we ever surely (*nūnam*) speak (*rapema*) what is false (*anṛtam*), the untruth?"
The meaning is "never at any time";
that is to say, we do not engage in approaching those who should not be approached.
Furthermore, [we do not approach] in water.
This is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

The meaning is "mother and father. Therefore, for that reason, our *jāmi*—our kinship—is declared [to be the cause]. This being so, since it would take the form of approaching one's mother and father, it is improper to perform; therefore, the intention is: "I do not do this."
In the womb, indeed, our progenitor made us a married couple—Tvaṣṭṛ, the impeller, whose forms are manifold. No one violates his ordinances; of this, both Earth and Heaven are aware.
In the womb, indeed, our progenitor made us a husband and wife—Tvaṣṭṛ, the god Savitṛ, the omniform. No one violates his ordinances; both Earth and Heaven know this of us. 5.

Tvaṣṭṛ, the fashioner of forms; Savitṛ, the impeller of all that is auspicious and inauspicious; Viśvarūpa, the god who is the soul of all and endowed with qualities such as generosity; Janitā, the progenitor Prajāpati—he, while we two, husband and wife, were still in the womb, made us dwell together in a single womb.

When you two came as if striving toward the sacrifice, the god-seeking men brought you forward;
sit down in your own place, you who know the world, and be well-disposed toward our Soma-juice.

Like twins, like Yama and Yamī; striving together—what they have brought forth for you both, the god-seeking men. Sit down in your own place, O you who know it! Be well-established in your own abode; be present for our Soma-juice. 2.

Just as two others move immediately toward the same goal, so when you two exert yourselves—engaged in your respective duties such as carrying the sacrificial oblation—the two carts that hold the oblation proceed; and whenever you both go toward this place of the oblation-holder (*havirdhāna*), then the human sacrificers, desiring the gods, bring forth offerings for you.
Furthermore, recognizing your own domain, the very place called *havirdhāna*, may you both take your seats.
Therefore, may there be a pleasant seat—a beautiful place of dwelling—for us, for our sake, for the sake of the Soma juice, for the Indu.
1. *ta-bha1.2.4.6-su* has "havirdhānam";

*2. tara2.5.6-stu* has "svāhutivān"; *ta4-bha6* has "sukhāvahā āhutirvān"; *ta3-bha1.4.7* has "sukhāvaha āhutirvā"; *bhara* has "sumāvaha āhutārvā". 3. *ta1.2.4.5.6-bha1.2.4.6* have "adhiṣṭhitavantaḥ".
4. *ta-bha* read *havirdhāne*; 5. *ta-bha6* read *yuvayoḥ*; 6.
*ta1.2.3.6.7-bha1.2.6* read *yadyadā etaṃ*; *ta4.5* read *yadyadā eta*; *bha8* read *yadyadā evaṃ*; *bha7* reads *yabdā yetaṃ*.

7. For those who have gone, sit down; for those who are sitting, sit down. 8. For those who have become [beings]. I have ascended after the five steps of form; I follow the four-footed one with my vow. By means of the syllable, I measure this out; I purify it completely upon the navel of Truth. 3. Five steps. Of form. After. I have ascended. The four-footed one. After. I go. With my vow. By the syllable. Against. I have measured. This. Upon the navel of Truth. I purify completely. 3. Five steps. Of form. After. I have ascended. The four-footed one. After. I go. With my vow. By the syllable. Against. I have measured. This. Upon the navel of Truth. I purify completely. 3.

I ascend after—following—the five-footed oblations, which consist of parched grains (*dhānā*), Soma, the animal cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and bones; these are the limbs of the sacrifice that lead the sacrificers to heaven, and as the Hotṛ, they move toward the gods.
Furthermore, I perform the act [of mounting] the wagon for you both after it has been established and harnessed;
moreover, by means of my vow (*vrata*), the ritual performance consisting of four feet, such as the *triṣṭubh* meter and so forth, I follow along.
The meaning is: "I employ [it] at the proper time.
By means of the *akṣara*, known as the *praṇava*, I have fashioned (*nirmame*) this present act of response (*pratigara*).
Furthermore, [I have done so] for the sake of *ṛta*, that is, the sacrifice (*yajña*).
The prefix *adhi* expresses the sense of the locative case.
In the navel—that is, in the place called the *vedi* which has become the navel—I purify, that is, I cleanse [the Soma].
The meaning is: "I prepare the Soma with the *daśāpavitra*."

For the sake of the gods, he chose death; for the sake of progeny, he did not choose immortality. They made Bṛhaspati their seer and their sacrifice; Yama relinquished his own dear body. 4. For the gods, he chose death; for the sake of progeny, he did not choose immortality. They made Bṛhaspati their sacrifice and their seer; Yama cast off his own beloved body. 4.
For the sake of the gods, whom did Yama choose—that is, request or employ—as his own servant who would slay death (mṛtyu)?

Furthermore, for the sake of progeny—meaning for the human and other offspring distinct from the gods—whom did he not choose as his own servant who would grant immortality (amṛta), that is, who would prevent their destruction?

The meaning is that since the maintenance of all those previously mentioned is certain once the act of offering oblations has commenced, Yama designates no one at all as his own servant who could cause destruction.

Moreover, those performing the sacrifice—the officiating priests—make Bṛhaspati the seer; he who is the protector of the great gods in the holding of oblations, or the lord of the great mantras, the beholder of everything, both seen and unseen results.
Furthermore, Yama has extended our dear and desired body;
for since the verbal roots have a single meaning, *ric* here functions in the sense of "to spare" or "to preserve."
It causes [the breath] to flow forth;
it wards off [death] from the presence of Mṛtyu.
The meaning is that, due to the absence of defects arising from the deficiency of ritual action (*karmavaiguṇya*), it does not take away our life.

Seven flow for the infant accompanied by the Maruts; the sons have further strengthened their father with the *ṛta*. Both of these belong to him; he rules over both. Both strive together; they nourish both. sapta | kṣaranti | śiśave | marutvate | pitre | putrāsaḥ | api | avīvatanvatam | ṛtam | ubhe | iti | asya | ubhayasya | rājataḥ | ubhe | iti | yatete | ubhayasya | puṣyataḥ ||5||

O singers, for the sake of the great one accompanied by the Maruts—for that father who is like a father to the officiating priests, for the infant Soma who sits comfortably upon the two sacrificial carts (havirdhāna-śakaṭa) that are to be praised—the seven meters flow; that is, they proceed as hymns of praise. Moreover:

1. *ta-bha4-dhanā*; 2. *ta-mu-padairyuktāṃ*; 3. *ta-bha-su- kriyā nāsti*; 4. *tara.2.7-bha1.2. 4.6-yaṃ kaṃ*; 5. *ta-bha-amārakaṃ vināśakaṃ*; 6. *ga-nivārayati*. The meaning is: for the sake of progeny, for the sake of men, he has taken up the immortal food (*amṛta*), and he does not ward off anyone; *ta* explains this; *bha1.2.4* says "he does not form" (*na rūpayati*). 7. *ta-rirecetra*; *bha-riricaratra*.
Even the sons—the priests who have become sons of Soma—have extended (*vavīvatan*) the praise that has become true (*vṛtaṃ satyabhūtaṃ*). They cause it to meet [with its object].
The meaning is that they offer praise by perceiving his true virtues.

Both, indeed, the two *havirdhāna* carts of that [sacrificer] rule over both these classes of beings—the divine class and the human class—as they proceed. Both carts alone exert effort in the performance of the ritual acts.
The meaning is that you cause nourishment for both classes, the divine and the human, as they flourish; that is, you effect their growth by means of the offering of oblations.
The fourteenth hymn, consisting of sixteen verses beginning with "pareyivāṃsam," is the seerly composition (*ārṣam*) of Yama, the son of Vivasvat.

The five verses beginning with "aṅgiraso naḥ pitaro navagvāḥ" have as their deities the Aṅgirases, the Pitṛs, and those characterized as Bhrigus, as indicated by their respective marks (*liṅgoktā devatāḥ*).
The three verses beginning with "prehi" have deities indicated by their marks, or else the Pitṛs as their deities.
The hymn beginning with "ati drava sārameyā~" has as its deity the two dogs, the sons of Saramā, who stand guarding the path to the other world;
the remaining verses have Yama as their deity.
The thirteen verses beginning with "yamāya somam" are in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
The verse beginning with "yāmāya madhumattamam" is a Bṛhatī; the first twelve verses are Triṣṭubhs.

Thus it has been enumerated: "In the hymn beginning with 'pareyivān', there are sixteen verses; [the first] is addressed to Yama, the sixth has its deity indicated by its internal marks (liṅga), the next three concern the Pitṛs, and the following three are to be recited softly; the last four are Anuṣṭubhs, while the others are Bṛhatīs."
The application of the hymns (*sūktaviniyoga*) has been concluded.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, the two verses beginning with "imaṃ yama prastaram ā hi sīda" and "pareyivāṃsaṃ pravato mahīr anu" are the *ājyā* and *yājyā* for the sacrifice to Yama.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "imaṃ yama prastaram ā hi sīdeti dve pareyivāṃsaṃ pravato mahīr anu" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).

Honor with an oblation Yama, the King, the son of Vivasvat, the assembler of people, who has departed along the great slopes and has spied out the path for those who are lofty. *pareyivāṃsam* (one who has departed), *pravataḥ* (from the slopes), *mahīḥ* (the great), *anu* (along), *bṛhadbhyaḥ* (for the lofty ones), *panthām* (the path), *anupaspaśānam* (having spied out), *vaivasvatam* (the son of Vivasvat), *saṃgamanam* (the assembler), *janānām* (of people), *yamam* (Yama), *rājānam* (the King), *haviṣā* (with an oblation), *duvasya* (honor). 1.
O my inner self, or you who are the sacrificer, worship with the oblation—the cake and other offerings—the lord of the ancestors, Vāja, who is the possessor of wealth.
Of what kind is he?

He has led upward, step by step after death, those men who have performed excellent deeds—having practiced merit (*puṇya*) which is the means for attaining enjoyments existing in the world of earth—and who have reached various specific regions of the land appropriate to their respective stations; likewise, he does not obstruct the path suitable for heaven for the many meritorious ones who are guests of the celestial realm, meaning that he causes only sinful men to reach hell by obstructing the path to heaven, but not those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Vaiivasvatam means the son of Vivasvat, the Sun; saṃgamanam means the place of assembly, which is the destination for sinful people.

Yama was the first to find the path for us; this pasture-land is not to be taken away from us, where our ancient fathers have passed away, along that path by which those born of old followed their own kin. Yama | for us | the path | the first | found | not | this | pasture-land | to be carried away | indeed | where | our | ancestors | the former | have departed | by this | having been born | the broad ones | after | their own (kin) || 2 ||
Yama, the first and foremost of all, knows— the term *vyama* meaning he discerns— the *gātu*, that is, the cause of good and evil for us, our progeny;
his pasture-ground (*gavyūti*) cannot be taken away or removed by anyone, because of his possession of extraordinary knowledge— this is the meaning.

On that path by which our ancient fathers departed—going by this very way—all those who were born, having come into existence, go toward their own respective paths, the courses of destiny consisting of their own actions.
1. *ta-bha-mu* read *prāpayati*.
2. *ta1.4.5.7-bha1.2.4.6-mā* read *viveda*; *tara.6-māṃ* read *viveda*. 3. *ta-ma6* do not have the word "pūrve."

4. In the manuscripts ta3 and bha1, there is space for a verbal form after the word "pareyuḥ"; [the reading would be] "bhara pareyuḥ pitrādayo gatāḥ" (on the following day, the father and others departed).
5. In manuscript bha1, there is space for a verbal form after the word "gacchantaḥ".
[Maṇḍala 1, Adhyāya 10, Sūkta 14] Seventh Aṣṭaka, 309.
In the Āgnimāruta [section], the verse "Mātalī kavyaiḥ" is the dhāyyā.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "imaṃ yama prastaramā hi sīda mātalī kavyairyamo aṅgirobhiradīratāmacara usarāsaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).
May Mātali with the Kavyas, Yama with the Aṅgirases, and Bṛhaspati, increasing through the Ṛks, [protect us].
Those whom the gods have strengthened, and those gods who [in turn] strengthen others—may they rejoice in the Svāhā-call and in the Svadhā-portion.

Mātali with the Kavyas, Yama with the Aṅgirases, Bṛhaspati with the Ṛks—having grown strong through these, and those gods who have strengthened him; some rejoice with *svāhā*, others with *svadhā*. 3.
Mātali: Mātali is the charioteer of Indra;
Indra, possessing him, is called Mātali.
And he, increasing together with the *kavyas*—the ancestors who partake of the *kavya* offerings—becomes great;
and he, increasing together with the *Vāṅgirases*, specific classes of ancestors, becomes great.

In that regard, the gods, Indra and the others, have increased and continue to increase the ancestors such as those who partake of the *kavya*; and those ancestors who partake of the *kavya* increase the gods, Indra and the others. Among them, some of these gods, Indra and the others, rejoice with the cry of "Svāhā," finding delight through the utterance of *svāhā*.
The ancestors in the forest rejoice with the *svadhā* offering through the utterance of *svadhā*.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, there are two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for Yama, beginning with "imaṃ yama" and so forth;
for it is stated in the Sūtra: "'imaṃ yama prastaramā hi sīda'—these two" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).
This same [verse] is also used as a *dhāyyā* in the Agnimāruta [Śastra].
The sūtra has already been cited previously.
Sit down upon this sacrificial grass-strewn seat, O Yama, in harmony with the Aṅgiras fathers;
may the mantras recited by the seers bring you here, O King, and rejoice in this oblation.
O Yama, sit down upon this sacrificial grass-stalk (prastara), being in full accord with the Aṅgiras ancestors; may the mantras recited by seers bring you hither; O King, rejoice in this oblation. 4.
In harmony with the Vyaṅgiras—the ancestors so named—having attained unanimity, sit down and take your place upon this wide sacrificial grass (*prastara*) or this specific sacrifice (*sava*).
For this reason, let the mantras recited by the learned officiating priests bring you here.
O Vena, moving through the air, being gratified by this oblation, rejoice and gladden the sacrificer.
Come with the Angirases who are worthy of sacrifice; rejoice here with the Vairūpas.
I invoke Vivasvat, who is your father, that he may sit upon the sacrificial grass at this sacrifice.

Come hither with the Angirases, who are worthy of sacrifice; O Yama, rejoice here with the Virūpas. I invoke Vivasvat, who is your father, that he may sit down upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) at this sacrifice. || 5 ||
Come with the Vairūpas—those endowed with various forms, or those who delight in the Vairūpa Sāman, or the Vaṅgiras who are worthy of sacrifice;
having come, rejoice here at this sacrifice and gladden the sacrificer.
I invoke that Vivasvat who is your father at this sacrifice.
And having sat down upon the strewn sacrificial grass, let him gladden the sacrificer.
1. By the names *ga*, *udgītha*, and *kavi*; 2. and by *ta*, *bha*, and *ya*;
3. and by *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, *mu*, and *prastara*—this [sequence] applies also in the *agnimāruta* [section].

The Aṅgirases, our fathers, the Navagvas, the Atharvans, and the Bhṛgus, who are worthy of Soma; may we abide in the good-will of those worshipful ones, and also in their auspicious favor. (6) Aṅgirasaḥ: those named Aṅgiras; atharvāṇaḥ: those named Atharvan; bhṛgavaḥ: those named Bhṛgu; naḥ: our; pitaraḥ: fathers; navagvāḥ: "possessing new movement"—meaning they are always as if newly joyful. And they are *somyāsaḥ*: "Soma-worthy," for they honor Soma. Of those *yajñiyānām*: worshipful ones, worthy of sacrifice; *teṣām*: of them; *sumatau*: in the benevolent mind [of grace]; *vayam*: we; *syāma*: may we ever abide. Moreover, *api*: and also; *bhadre*: in the auspicious; *saumanase*: in the cause of favor, in the fruit of goodwill; *syāma*: may we ever abide. In the midst of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), if the consecrated person (*dīkṣita*) dies, the Hotṛ priest should recite the five verses beginning with "Prehi" (RV 10.2.7), excluding the third. As it is stated in the Sūtra: "Of the five [verses] beginning with 'Prehi prehi pathibhiḥ pūvyairit,' one should omit the third" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.10).

Go forth, go forth by the ancient paths; there our ancestors have gone before us. Behold both kings, rejoicing in the *svadhā* offering—behold Yama and the god Varuṇa. (7) Go forth, go forth by the ancient paths; there our ancestors, the fathers and grandfathers, have gone before us. By those paths existing from former times—the meaning being those set in motion from beginningless time—go forth, O my father, proceed quickly to that place. And having gone, behold both the kings rejoicing and satiated with the *svadhā* food, the immortal nourishment: behold Yama and the radiant god Varuṇa. (7)

Unite with the ancestors, unite with Yama, and with the fruits of your sacrifices and good deeds in the highest heaven. Leaving behind all that is blameworthy, come back to your home; unite with a body, O you of radiant splendor. *saṃ gacchasva pitṛbhiḥ saṃ yamena iṣṭāpūrtena parame vyoman | hitvāyāvadyaṃ punarastamehi saṃ gacchasva tanvā suvarcāḥ || 8 ||* O my father, go forth to the highest, most excellent heaven (*parama-vyoman*), and join with the ancestors who are your own. Unite with the fruits of your *iṣṭāpūrta*—the results of Vedic sacrifices and worldly charitable acts. Having reached that state through your sacrifices and good deeds, leave behind all that is blameworthy (*avadya*) and sinful; come back to your own home (*asta*). Then, endowed with beautiful luster (*suvarcāḥ*), unite once more with your own body. In the *Paitṛmedhika* ritual, one sprinkles the cremation ground with the mantra "Come, depart" (*aveta vīta*). As it is stated in the Sūtra: "With water that has flowed away, while walking three times around the site from right to left with a *śamī* branch, one sprinkles it, saying: 'Come, depart, and move away from here. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 4.2.10).

1. *ta-bha1.2.4*—*tadā*; 2. *ga-ta3.4-bha5.6*—*pareyuḥ paretāḥ*; 3. *ta3.4-bha1.2.4.5*—*tatra gatvā*; *ta5*—*tāṃ gatvā*; 4. *ga*—*tvaṃ*; *ta-bha-mu*—*atastvaṃ*; 5. *ga-ta-bha*—the word ‘*suvarcāḥ*’ is not present; 6. *ta-bha*—*śākhayā*. "Depart, go away, and creep far from here; the ancestors have prepared this world for him.
May Yama grant him a resting place through days, waters, and nights."
Go away! Depart! Creep away from here! O Fathers, you have prepared this world for him; Yama grants him a resting place through days and nights that never fail. 9.
O Piśācas and others who previously dwelt in this cemetery, depart from here— from this place where the fire is being extinguished; go away, go forth specifically, and creep away!
The meaning is: "Leaving this place, go to a much more distant land by way of various states.
For the sake of this deceased sacrificer, the ancestors have prepared (*aknan*) this world, this cremation site;
they have made it so by the command of Yama.

Yama also gave— meaning he bestowed— the cremation ground (*avasāna*) for the sake of this deceased sacrificer; it was clearly joined with days (*ahobhiḥ*), days (*divasaiḥ*), waters (*adbhiḥ*) such as sprinkling-water, and nights (*naktabhiḥ*, *rātribhiḥ*), that is to say, purified by time, water, and other such means of purification.
Two wolves, shaped like dogs, are placed on the two sides [of the bier] with the *anumantraṇī* formulas.
Having lifted them up, he places them in the hands of the deceased with the two verses beginning, “Run past the two *sārameya*s.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “Having lifted the two wolves, he places them in the two hands [with the words] ‘Run past the two *sārameya*s, the two dogs’” (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* 4.3.20).
Pass quickly by the two dogs, the offspring of Saramā, four-eyed and brindled, along the righteous path;
then approach the benevolent fathers who rejoice in the company of Yama.
Run past the two dogs, the sons of Saramā, four-eyed and brindled; then go by the straight path to the benevolent Fathers who rejoice in their banquet together with Yama. 10.
O Agni, run past both dogs by the straight path, by the correct way; having bypassed them, go on.
The meaning is: leaving behind those two dogs belonging to Yama who harass the deceased, lead the deceased by the correct way.
Of what kind are the two dogs?
The two *sārameyas*:
there was a certain well-known divine dog named Saramā;
her two sons were four-eyed, meaning they possessed another pair of eyes on the upper part of their heads, as previously described.

Then, after traveling by the auspicious path, approach and go unto those well-disposed ancestors who, together with Yama, rejoice—that is, attain—joyful revelry; reach those ancestors who are easy to find.
O Yama, those two dogs of yours who are guardians, four-eyed, watchers of the path, and observers of men—to them entrust this person, O King; bestow upon him well-being and freedom from disease.
O Yama, those two dogs of yours who are the guardians, four-eyed, protectors of the path, and watchers of men—entrust him to them, O King; bestow upon him well-being and freedom from disease. 11.

O King Yama, those two dogs of yours that exist—O King Yama, entrust this deceased person to those two dogs for the sake of protection. What kind of dogs are they? They are the guardians, the protectors of the house of Yama; they have four eyes, being endowed with a set of four eyes; they are the protectors of the path, guarding the way; and they are the observers of men, pervading over human beings.
Persons well-versed in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas proclaim those two [dogs].
