Having given [the offering] to those two dogs, bestow—accomplish—for this deceased person well-being (svasti), security (kṣema), and freedom from disease (anamīva).

The two broad-nosed, life-sustaining, tawny dogs, the messengers of Yama, roam among the people. May they today grant us back auspicious life, so that we may behold the sun. (12) The two messengers belonging to Yama—dogs with long noses (*uruṇasau*), who satisfy themselves by taking the lives of others (*asutṛpau*), and who possess great strength (*udumbalau*)—roam everywhere, targeting living beings. May both those messengers, for the sake of beholding the sun (*sūryāya dṛśaye*), grant us back today, in this rite, auspicious and excellent life (*bhadram asum*).

For Yama press out the Soma; for Yama offer the oblation. To Yama indeed goes the sacrifice, with Agni as its messenger, well-prepared. O priests, for Yama—for the sake of the deity Yama—press out the Soma; that is, extract the juice from the plant. Likewise, for Yama’s sake, offer the oblation (*havis*). That sacrifice in which Agni is the messenger is called *agnidūtaḥ*. Regarding Agni’s role as messenger, it is stated elsewhere: "Agni was the messenger of the gods" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.5.8.5). *Araṃkṛtaḥ*: equipped with many materials in the form of ornaments; such a sacrifice indeed goes to Yama.

Offer to Yama an oblation accompanied by clarified butter, and stand forth; may he, possessing long life, lead us among the gods so that we may live on. O priests, offer to Yama an oblation—such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—joined with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). And stand forth; you should worship Yama. Among the gods, may that god Yama, being of long life, grant us long life so that we may live well.

Offer to King Yama the most honey-sweet oblation; let this homage be to the seers, the first-born, the ancients who prepared the paths. (15) O officiating priests, offer to King Yama the most honey-sweet oblation—the sacrificial offering such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and the like. Let this visible homage be to the seers, those born at the beginning of creation, and therefore ancient ones who existed before us, the makers of fair paths. (15)

1. *ta-bhara* 6. *amuṃ* | 2. *ta-bha1.2.4-pūrvajebhyaḥ* | 3. *ta-bha-śobhanamārgapathikāribhyaḥ* | 4. *ta-bha1.2.4.6-mu-ya idaṃ* | With the three *trikadruka* [sacrifices], he falls; the six wide [spaces], the one alone, the *bṛhat*—the *triṣṭubh*, the *gāyatrī*, and all the meters (*chandāṃsi*), they are all established in Yama. 16 With the three *trikadrukas*, he falls; the six, the wide ones, the one indeed, the *bṛhat*; the *triṣṭubh*, the *gāyatrī*, the meters—all those are placed in Yama. 16
With the *trikadruka*s;
the third case ending is used in the sense of the second case:
[the meaning is] "the *trikadruka*s."
The three specific sacrifices known as Jyotis, Gaura, and Āyus are called the *trikadrukas*.
He flies toward them for the sake of their manifestation and protection;
Yama reaches them.
There are six earths (*urvīḥ*);
he obtains them for the purpose of examining what has been done and what remains to be done.

And these are recited in another branch of the Veda with the following mantra: "May the six earths protect our secret: heaven and earth, the waters and the plants, and the one who is born and the one who is about to be born."
In him alone is contained the one, vast, and great universe, and he attains Yama as that which is to be protected.
Furthermore, all those meters—namely the *triṣṭubh*, *gāyatrī*, and so forth—which exist, have been placed within him; they are established by the officiating priests as objects of praise.
The fifteenth hymn consists of fourteen verses beginning with "udīratām.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: "udīratām; six [verses], Śaṅkha, addressed to the Pitṛs; the eleventh is a Jagatī.
According to the statement "the last five are by the Yāmāyanas," the seer (ṛṣi) of Śaṅkha is the son of Yama.
The verse beginning with "agniṣvāttāḥ" is a Jagatī; the remaining verses are Triṣṭubhs.
The Pitṛs (Fathers) are the deity. [The ritual application] has been explained.
The application of the hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*):
In the *Aṣṭakā* rite, the eight verses beginning with "udīratām avare" are for the purpose of the oblation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having offered with [the verses] 'udīratām avare' and 'utparāsaḥ'... (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.4.6).
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) for the mantra "The Pitṛs accompanied by Soma" is this verse beginning with "udīratām.

This is stated in the Sūtra: "The Pitṛs, the Agniṣvātta-s, Yama—may they rise up, those below and those above" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.19). This same verse is also used as a *dhāyyā* in the Abhimāra sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "May Mātali with the Kavyas, and Yama with the Aṅgirases, rise up—from those below and from those above" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).

May the lower, the higher, and the middle ancestors, those worthy of Soma, rise up—those who have gone to the life-breath, who are harmless and knowers of the Eternal Order (Ṛta). May those ancestors protect us in our invocations. 1. May they rise up—the lower ones, the higher ones, and the middle ones—the Soma-loving ancestors. Those who have gone to the life-force, who are free from malice and knowers of the Truth, may those ancestors protect us in our calls. 1.
The ancestors are of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
Those who attained the status of ancestors by performing the Vedic (śrauta) rites according to the rules are the superior;
those devoted solely to the Smārta rites are the middling.

In this regard as well, some inferior [souls] are deficient in certain purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). With this very intention, the mantra beginning with "those who were cremated and those who were not cremated" has been recited.
Among them, let the lowly ones be uplifted; let them attain the supreme oblation (*havis*).
May the highest ancestors rise up;
may the middle ancestors also rise up.
May they all, being *somyas*—that is, gentle and intent on bestowing grace—be so toward us.
Free from predatory intent—like wolves or wild horses—they have not harmed us; being cognizant of the sacrifice (*vṛtajñāḥ*) performed by us, they have come to protect our vital breath (*vasum*).
May those fathers protect and guard us during our invocations.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, "idaṃ pitṛbhyaḥ" is the second invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) for the verse "apitaro barhiṣadaḥ.
The Sūtra has already been cited previously (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19). In the Ābhimāra sacrifice, this "idaṃ pitṛbhyaḥ" is the *dhāyyā* verse.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "He recites the four [verses] beginning with 'I have summoned the benevolent fathers; sit down for the fathers; homage to the fathers; O Svadhā, this is indeed sweet' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20)."
1. These are specific sacrifices for the *ta-bha* [deities].
2. See the commentary on Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.5.1.22 and Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.47.3:
"Let this homage be today for the ancestors, those who have gone before and those who have followed after."
Those who have settled upon the earthly dust, or those who are now indeed among the well-fortified communities;
This [obeisance] be unto the fathers today: those who went before, those who followed after, those who are seated in the earthly realm, or those who are now among the well-fortified clans. 2.
Those who were "prior"—those born before the sacrificer’s birth, such as elder brothers, grandfathers, and so forth—who have "gone," having reached the world of the ancestors;
and those others who are "subsequent"—those born after the sacrificer’s birth, such as younger brothers, one’s own sons, and so forth—who have gone, having reached the world of the ancestors;
and those others who, in this earthly matter—that is, in this ritual action which is an effect of the quality of *rajas*—have "descended," having arrived and sat down to accept the oblation.

Or whoever else are our kinsmen in the form of ancestors, who have settled among the people as relatives among offspring, having come and sat down to accept the *śrāddha* offerings and the like—by what cause have they come? Come toward us; reach us face-to-face.
Then, immediately thereafter, grant us—bestow upon us—śam (happiness), yoh (freedom from suffering), and arapaḥ (freedom from evil).
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, the *yājyā* for the verse "The Pitṛs accompanied by Soma" is this [verse]: "The Pitṛs, worthy of Soma, have been invited.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'The Pitṛs, worthy of Soma, have been invited; O Soma, take note with your wisdom' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19)."
The Soma-loving ancestors have been invited to these beloved seats upon the sacred grass;
may they come, may they hear us here, may they speak for us, and may they protect us.
Invited are the Soma-loving Fathers, upon the sacred grass, upon their dear offerings. May they come; may they hear us here; may they speak for us; may they protect us. 5.

O gentle ones, the Pitṛs who are gracious toward us, intent on bestowing favor, or who prepare the Soma—when these oblations, which are like treasuries, pleasing, and satisfying, are present as the occasion for sacrifice upon the sacrificial grass (barhis), may those Pitṛs, having been invited by us, come hither. Having arrived, may they hear the hymns of praise employed by us in this rite;
and having heard them, may they speak in our favor.
May those such ancestors, saying with reverence, "Excellent is this sacrificer," protect and guard us.
Sitting down to the south with knees bent, may you all, O Fathers, graciously accept this sacrifice.
Do not harm us, O Fathers, for any offense whatsoever that we, in our human nature, may have committed.

Having come hither, having knelt, and having seated yourselves on the south, accept this sacrifice, O All-Gods. Do not harm us, O Fathers, for anything whatsoever, whatever offense we may commit against you through our human nature. 6.

This is the natural duty of the ancestors, according to the scriptural injunction: "The ancestors, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītinaḥ), having bent the right knee" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.4.2.2).
O all you ancestors, having bent the knee—that is, having placed it upon the ground—and having seated yourselves on the south, that is, on the right side, praise this our sacrifice;
that is to say, extol it with supreme delight, considering it to be endowed with excellent qualities through the application of distinguished praise.

Moreover, O fathers, whatever offense or transgression we have committed against you—arising from any deficiency in our actions—whether by reason of our manhood or our human nature, do not harm us on account of any such offense whatsoever.
Seated in the lap of the ruddy dawns, bestow wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations;
O Fathers, grant those riches to his sons, and bestow strength upon them here.
Seated in the lap of the ruddy ones, bestow wealth upon the mortal who offers oblations. O Fathers, grant a portion of that treasure to our sons; bestow strength here upon them.
Seated in the lap— the vicinity or the altar-house— of the rising Aruṇīs, whether they be flames or deities, you Pitṛs, bestow wealth (*rayi*) upon the mortal sacrificer who has offered the oblation.
O Pitṛs, grant riches (*vasu*) to the sons of that sacrificer.
O you who are not such [as others], bestow—that is, deposit—strength and wealth here in this work of ours.
Those ancestral fathers of ours who were worthy of Soma, the Vasiṣṭhas, who have followed after the drinking of Soma—
with them may Yama, being well-pleased, eat the offerings, desiring them along with those who desire, according to his wish.

Our ancestors of old, the Vasiṣṭhas, who were worthy of Soma and who followed the drinking of Soma—may Yama, rejoicing together with them, desiring the oblations, eat them according to his desire along with those who desire him. 8.

The Vasiṣṭhas are those who possess *soma*, that is, those who provide *soma*; they are the most excellent, well-sheltered, or most wealthy. Our ancient ancestors, O you [Vasiṣṭhas], attained the *somapītha*—the drinking of *soma*—in due succession, reaching it for both the gods and the *pitṛ*s;
that is to say, they bestowed it.

Desiring enjoyment together with the Pitṛs who desire [him], O Yama, lord of the Pitṛs; together with those [Pitṛs] who desire [him] along with Yama, rejoicing (*vrarāṇaḥ*) with them—our own Pitṛs—accept (*vattu*) the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) given by us according to our desire, that is, according to their desire.
The meaning is: let him eat whichever specific oblations he desires.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, for Agni Kavyavāhana, the verse beginning with "ye tātṛpuḥ" is the first invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ye tātṛpuḥ... devatrā jehamānāḥ... tvad agne kāvyā tvan manīṣāḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).

Those who have satisfied [the gods] among the gods, striving with fervor, knowing the priestly offices, fashioning hymns with their chants— O Agni, come hither with those well-disposed ones, with the truthful Kavya ancestors who sit at the Gharma-vessel.

O Agni, come toward us, facing us, together with those Pitṛs who have been satisfied—those who, being eager for the gods here, know the sacrificial call (hotrā), have fashioned the hymns (stoma-taṣṭāsaḥ), and are the perfecters of the chants (stomānām saṃyaktāraḥ). With what kind [of Pitṛs]? With those who are *suvidatra*—meaning true (*satyaiḥ*) and non-deceptive—and who are *kavya*, that is, connected to the oblation (*havis*) intended for the Pitṛ-gods; or alternatively, *kavya* means the wise ones (*kavibhiḥ medhāvibhiḥ*), the suffix *-ya* being used in its own sense (*svārthika*). And with those who abide in the sacred law (*dharmasadbhiḥ*), that is, those who establish the sacrifice (*yajña-sādbhiḥ*).

O Agni, come with the thousand truthful ones who eat the oblation, who drink the oblation, and who share the same chariot with Indra and the gods— with the ancient, supreme Fathers who sit at the Gharma.
Those who are truthful; the truthful ones.

O Agni, come with those Pitṛs— those who eat the oblation fit for consumption, who drink the oblation fit for drinking, and who, together with Indra and the gods, maintain a single common chariot (or one equal chariot)—
for they always hold it steady for their journey; come, O Agni, with those Pitṛs.
Of what kind? A thousand.
The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.

"By a thousand" means by many. "Accompanied by praises of the gods" means joined with hymns related to the deities. "By others" refers to those belonging to later times; "by former ones" refers to those belonging to earlier times—namely, by those who were established in *dharma*, such as the founders of sacrifice (*yajñasādi*), the founders of the *mahāvīra* vessel, or the founders of the *āditya* vessel.
1. *ta-bha-mu-kāmaṃ*. 2. *ta-bha1.2.4-mu-ā arvāṅ*.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, for the [verse] "O Agniṣvātta fathers," the first invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) is "O Agniṣvātta fathers."
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, come here; those Pitṛs who are here and those who are not here" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).

O Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, come hither; sit each upon his seat, O you who are excellent leaders. Eat the oblations presented upon the sacred grass (barhis), and bestow wealth consisting of all heroic sons. Agniṣvāttāḥ | Pitaraḥ | Ā | Iha | Gacchata | Sadassadaḥ | Sadata | Supraṇītayaḥ | Atta | Havīṃṣi | Prayatāni | Barhiṣi | Artha | Rayim | Sarvavīram | Dadhātana || 11 ||

"O *agniṣvāttāḥ*—the ancestors so named because they have been tasted by fire—come here to this ancestral rite (*pitṛkarman*). Having arrived, O *supraṇītayaḥ*—you who are led by superior knowledge—sit down in each respective place;
that is to say, sit down at those various locations as you please."
And having sat down, [say]: "Eat—consume—the offered oblations placed upon the sacrificial grass, which are pure and stainless;
then, thereafter, bestow upon us wealth consisting of all heroes, accompanied by sons, grandsons, and other descendants."
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, during the performance of the Vaṣaṭkāra, the verse "tvam agne īḷitaḥ" is the invitatory prayer (yājyā) for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two verses for the concluding offerings (saṃyājye) are 'yo agniḥ kavyavāhanaḥ' and 'tvam agne īḷito jātavedaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).

O Agni Jātavedas, being praised, you have carried the oblations; having made them fragrant, you have offered them to the ancestors. They have eaten them with the *svadhā* offering. O God, you [have accepted] these presented oblations. 12. O Agni, being praised, O Jātavedas, you have carried the oblations; having made them fragrant, you have offered them to the ancestors. They have eaten them with the *svadhā* offering. O God, you [have accepted] these presented oblations. 12.
O Jātavedas!
He who knows all that has been born is Jātavedas.

O Agni of such a nature, being *īḷitaḥ*—praised by us—you have made our *havyāni*—our oblations—*surabhīṇi*—fragrant—and having done so, you have *avāṭ*—performed the act of carrying them [to the gods].
And having done so, you gave [the oblation] to the ancestors;
and those ancestors ate—that is, consumed—the offered oblation with *svadhā*, by means of the utterance *svadhā*. O God, you too, consume the oblations prepared with effort by means of water.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, "aye ceha" is the second invitatory verse (anu-vākyā).
The Sūtra has already stated this.

Those ancestors who are here and those who are not here, those whom we know and those whom we do not know—you know how many they are, O Jātavedas; with the *svadhā* offerings, enjoy this well-prepared sacrifice. 13.

1. In the text of *ta*, "agniṣvāttāḥ" is not present. 2. Regarding "svasthānam": *ta*3, *bha*1.2.4, and *san* read "sanasthānam"; *bha*3 reads "svasthānam"; and *mu* reads "svasthānam". [The commentary states: "O fathers (*pitaraḥ*), you who are here (*viha*) in our presence, and you who are not here (*viha na santi*)."
O wise one, having drawn near those *vyas* who are the *pitṛs*, we recognize them; yet those *vyas* who are far away, we do not know because of their remoteness.

O *Jātavedas*, you—whose knowledge encompasses all produced objects—know all of them exactly as they are described. With the *svadhās*, characterized by oblations, graciously accept the well-performed sacrifice.
In the very sacrifice previously mentioned, "Those who were burnt by fire" (*ye agnidagdhāḥ*) is the *yājyā* verse.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] beginning with 'Those who were burnt by fire and those who were not burnt by fire, O Yama, sit down upon this sacrificial grass-stalk' (*imaṃ yama prastaramā hi sīda*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.19).

Those who have been consumed by fire and those who have not been consumed by fire, who rejoice in the self-offering (svadhā) in the midst of heaven—with them, O Sovereign Lord, fashion this body according to your will along this path of the life-force (asunīti). 14. Those who have been consumed by fire; those who have not been consumed by fire; in the midst; of heaven; with the self-offering; they rejoice; with them; O Self-Ruler; this path of the life-force; according to your desire; fashion the body. 14.
The ancestors who have been consumed by fire, reduced to ashes by the fire;
that is to say, those who have reached the cremation ground.

And let the ancestors who were not consumed by fire—those who did not undergo the cremation rite—rejoice and be satisfied with *svadhā*, that is, with food characterized as an oblation, in the midst of heaven, in the middle of the celestial world. O Agni, you who shine by virtue of your own actions (*svarāṭ*), being accompanied by those ancestors, fashion and perfect according to our will the body of this deity—that inner self of our fathers which leads the vital breaths (*vasunīti*) toward their objects.
In other words, cause it to eat. 6.
The sixteenth hymn, consisting of fourteen verses beginning with "menām," is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Daman, the son of Yama.
The first ten verses are Triṣṭubh, and the following four are Anuṣṭubh. Its deity is Agni.

And thus it is listed in the Anukramaṇī: "The *mema* [hymn] for Damana, addressed to Agni, ending in the *catuṣṭubh* meter. Upon the death of one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), these first five [verses] are to be recited.

This is also stated in the Sūtra: "'O Agni, burn him not; do not consume him with heat'—these six [verses], and 'May Pūṣan call him hither,' and 'May he, the wise one, lead him away'—these two verses" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.10).
These [verses] should also be recited when attending upon a deceased person who is being cremated.
O Agni, do not burn him up; do not consume him with heat; do not scorch his skin, nor his body. When you have made him cooked, O Jātavedas, then send him forth to the Fathers. || 1 ||
Do not burn Vena, who has departed; do not especially consume him so that he becomes ashes. Do not grieve for him; do not surround him with sorrow and torment.
Do not scatter his skin here and there;
do not scatter his body either.
O Jātavedas, Agni, when you have made him cooked, well-baked, and thoroughly burnt, then send this deceased one forth to the ancestors; send him into the presence of the Pitṛs.
O Jātavedas, when you have cooked him, then deliver him to the fathers;
when he goes along this path leading away from life, then he becomes subject to the will of the gods.

1. ta-bha6—*eṣām*; ta3-ma1.2.4—*tām*. 2. udgītha—*yānāpi*. 3. ta-bha6—*vāyantaste*. 4. ta—*jānāmi*. 5. ga—*vṛne vṛthayantu*; ta-bha—*tṛpyantu*. 6. ta-bha6—*grāmāyetyarthaḥ*; udgītha—*gāmayahavetyarthaḥ*. 7. tara2.3-7-ma—"*mā kuru*" is not present. 8. ga-bha—*tvaṃ yadā*.

It is heard: when you, O Jātavedas, have finished your work, then deliver him over to the Fathers; when he goes upon this journey to the world of spirits, then he shall become subject to the will of the gods.

O Jātavedas, when you have made the departed body cooked—that is, when you shall have prepared it—then, at that very moment, deliver him, the deceased, over to the fathers; grant him to them. When this deceased one attains this "leading of the breath" (asunīti)—the guidance of the vital breath, the impelling of life-force—effected by Agni, then, at that very moment, he becomes subject to the will of the gods, brought under the control of the gods.
Let the eye go to the sun, the breath to the wind; go to heaven and to earth according to the law.
Or go to the waters, if that is where your welfare lies; take your stand among the plants with your bodily parts.

Let the eye go to the sun; let the breath go to the wind. Go to heaven and to earth according to the cosmic law (dharman). Or go to the waters, if they are your appointed place there. Take your stand among the plants with your bodily parts. || 3 ||
O preta, may your eye-faculty go to and reach the sun;
may your self, your vital breath, go to the external wind.
Furthermore, by virtue of your righteous deeds (*dharma*), you too shall go to heaven to enjoy the fruit thereof.
And here the word *ca* has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*). Go to, that is, attain, either the heavenly world or the earth; or go to, that is, attain, the waters or the intermediate space.
There, in the intermediate space, your fruit of action has been placed and established;
settle within the medicinal plants with your bodies and the limbs of your body.
The unborn portion is yours; burn it with heat, let your flame burn it, let your radiance burn it.
O Jātavedas, with those bodies of yours that are auspicious, carry this man to the world of the righteous.

The Unborn One is the portion; burn him with fervor! Let your heat burn him, let your flame burn him, and let your radiance burn him. O Jātavedas, with those bodies of yours that are auspicious, carry him to the world of the righteous. 4.

The Unborn (*aja*) is one who is devoid of birth, characterized as the inner person (*antarapuruṣa*) distinct from the portions consisting of the body, senses, and so forth; O Agni, by means of your heat (*tapas*), that is, your burning power, do you heat—that is, make heated—that such portion.
Likewise, let your glow (*śocis*)—the specific flame that is the cause of heat—heat and purify that portion.
Furthermore, let your radiance (*arcis*)—the illuminating specific flame—heat and purify that portion.

There is a distinction among the words *tapas*, *śociḥ*, and *arcis* based on the degree of intensity of the heat. O Jātavedas, by those forms (*tanvaḥ*) of yours which are auspicious (*śivāḥ*), being causes of happiness and not givers of pain—with those forms, carry (*vaha*) this deceased person to the world (*loka*), the abode of those who have performed good deeds (*sukṛtām*).
The word *u* is an expletive used for metrical completion.
Release him again, O Agni, to the fathers—he who, offered as an oblation, moves by means of the *svadhā* offerings;
clothing himself in life, let him approach his offspring; let him be reunited with his body, O Jātavedas.

Release him again, O Agni, to the fathers—he who, offered as an oblation to you, moves according to his funeral offerings (svadhā). Clothed in life, let him approach his remnant; let him be united with a body, O Jātavedas! 5.

1. *ga-ta-bha* (6.7) *gacchati*; *bha1.2 4* *gacchati*; *su-gacchati gacchati*. 2. *su-bhavati*. 3. *ta-bha6* *prāpnuhi yāhi*. 4. *ta-bha-tapanaṃ*. 5. *ta4* *śokahetutvāt*; *ta5.6.7* *śokahetu*. 6. *ta-* “*api ca ... saṃskarotu*” does not exist.

O Agni, that deceased man who has been offered as an oblation and entrusted upon the funeral pyre with a mantra moves together with the *svadhās*—the offerings of water and other things presented with the utterance of *svadhā*. Release that deceased one again for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛbhyaḥ*), meaning for the purpose of reaching the world of the fathers; send him forth once more. Furthermore, let the deceased, clothing himself in *āyus*—meaning life, being endowed with life—proceed.
"Let the remainder—the remaining body characterized by bones, which is to be sacrificed—approach;
let it come near. O Jātavedas, by your grace, let it be united with its own form, that is, with the body."
Whatever the black bird has pecked at you, or the ant, the snake, or even the wild beast—
may Agni make that free from poison, and Soma too, who has entered into this non-Brahmin.
Whatever the black bird has pecked at you, or the ant, the serpent, or even the wild beast, may Agni make all that free from disease, and Soma, who has entered into the Brahmins. ||6||
That limb of yours, belonging to your deceased body, which a black bird—such as a crow or the like—pecked at;
the prefix *āṅ* here signifies "slightly":
it was slightly wounded.
Likewise, whether it be an ant, a female ant, a snake, or even a beast of prey— such as a dog, a jackal, or the like—
if any one of these has bitten [it], then Agni, the devourer of all, shall make that limb free from disease, that is, he shall render it devoid of affliction.
The meaning is "may he prepare.
Likewise, "may Soma—whether in the form of a deity or in the form of a plant—prepare [it].
That Soma which "has entered" (āviveśa) the Brāhmaṇas, such as the officiating priests and others.
One should cover the mouth of the deceased with the omentum of the *anustaraṇī* cow, using the verse, "The armor of Agni.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the omentum of the *anustaraṇī*, he should cover the head and face of the deceased with the verse, 'Do not hide us from the light, O Agni, with thy rays; protect us with thy bodies, O thou whose wealth is cows'" (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* 4.3.19).

Envelop Agni’s armor on all sides with cow-hides; cover it thoroughly with fat and marrow, so that the bold one, rushing forward with his heat and eager to strike, may not consume you while seeking to burn.

O Agni, clothe yourself all around with the armor of cattle; envelop yourself completely with fatness and marrow. Let not the bold one, seeking to strike, slay you with his fierce heat; he who intends to consume you is being led around. ||7||
O *preta*, clothe yourself all around with the cowhide used for the *anustaraṇa*—the armor consisting of flames that is Agni’s own nature.
Furthermore, completely cover yourself with fat and thick marrow.
When this is done, you shall be bold through your heat and splendor, eager to seize, and defiant, intending to take up what is false as an offering.

The word *ṛtvij* has been derived [from the root] *dṛś* (to see) by means of the rule beginning with "ṛtvig" etc. [Pāṇini 3.2.59]. [The phrase] "desiring to speak" (*vivakṣyan*) means "desiring to reduce to ashes in various ways"; such is the fire. "It does not spread around you" (*na tvā paryaṅkayāte*) means it does not extend itself all around you.
The augment *āṭ* is applied before the suffix *lyap* due to the sense of the fire.

One should consecrate the carrying forth of the *praṇītā* waters with this verse: “This very chalice [I do not let slip]. And it is stated in the Sūtra: “With the words, ‘This very chalice, do not let slip,’ one consecrates the carrying forth of the *praṇītā* waters” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.3.24).
Do not overturn this cup; it is dear to the gods and to those who offer Soma.
This is the cup from which the gods drink; in it the immortal gods rejoice.
1. In *ta-bha6*, *punaravāsujaḥ*; in *ta3-bha1.2.6.7*, *punaravāsuja*.
2. In *ta*, *soma aśva*. 3. In *ga-ta-bha1.2.4.5*, the phrase “*anustaraṇayā... iti*” is absent; in *bha6*, it reads “*agnervarma pari gobhiryyasyetīti*”.

4. *ga-ta-bha* 1.2.4.5. 7—“*imamame... iti*” does not exist [in this recension]. O Agni, do not overturn this cup; it is dear to the gods and to those worthy of Soma. This is the cup from which the gods drink; in it, the immortal gods rejoice. (8)
O Agni, do not tilt, do not move, this cup used for bringing forth the *praṇītā* waters.
This cup is dear to the gods, Indra and the others, and also dear to the Soma-worthies, the Pitṛs;
moreover, this cup is that which is the drinking-vessel of the gods.

"Because the gods drink in this [vessel], it becomes a place for the drinking of the gods. In that cup, the 'immortals'—the gods who are free from death—and the 'fathers' rejoice; they become exhilarated by the *havyas* (offerings to the gods) and the *kavyas* (offerings to the ancestors)."
I send forth the flesh-eating fire far away; let it go to the realm of Yama, carrying off impurities.
Let this other Jātavedas remain right here, conveying the oblation to the gods with full knowledge.
I send the flesh-eating Agni far away; let him go to the realm of King Yama, carrying off impurities. Here indeed is this other Jātavedas; may he, knowing well, carry the oblation to the gods. 9.

Regarding the death of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), these two verses beginning with "etadādikaṃ" are prescribed for use at the *aupāsana* fire-altar. Therein, with the first half-verse, he discards the *aupāsana* fire toward the southern direction at a crossroads or similar location; with the latter half, he takes it up for the sake of pacification (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.4.6).
The "flesh-eater" (*kravyād*):
flesh (*kravya*) is raw meat;
I send forth—that is, I drive away—to a distant place the fierce fire that devours it.
The root *hi* means "to go" and belongs to the *svādi* class;
*ripra* means "flow," and *ripra* means "evil."
The carrier of that [oblation] is Agni; let him go to—reach—those other regions whose king is Yama, those ruled by King Yama.

This one, distinct from the flesh-eater (kravyād), the Jātavedas—the knower of all born things or the possessor of innate wealth—is the Agni known by all; let him carry, let him deliver, the *havya*—the oblation fit for offering—to the gods (*devebhyaḥ*) right here in this very place, for the sake of the gods, as a means of propitiatory peace (*śāntikam*).

The flesh-eating Agni who has entered your house, beholding this other Jātavedas—him, the god, I carry away for the sacrifice to the ancestors; may he, impelling the sacrificial rite, go to the highest abode.

The flesh-eating Agni who has entered your house, seeing this other Jātavedas—him I bring for the sacrifice to the ancestors; may that god promote the Gharma-oblation in the highest abode of bliss. 10.
"The flesh-eating Agni, the deity who has entered the house of you householders—that flesh-eating deity I remove; that is to say, I cause him to go outside the house. For what purpose?
For the sake of the Pitṛyajña, for its purpose."
Doing what?
Beholding—that is, reflecting upon—this other Jātavedas, the bearer of oblations, distinct from that [first fire].
That being so, let the other fire, the consumer of raw flesh (kravyād), reach the *gharma*—the sacrifice—in the supreme, most excellent dwelling-place (*sadhastha*).
"With the ancestors who uphold dharma"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, during the performance of the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance, the verse beginning with “*yo agniḥ kavyavāhanaḥ*” serves as the *yājyā* for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “*yo agniḥ kavyavāhanaḥ svadhām* and *īlito jātavedaḥ* are the two *saṃyājyā* verses” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).
The Agni who is the bearer of the *kavya* offerings, who increases the sacrificial food for the fathers—
may he announce the oblations to the gods and to the fathers.
1. In the case of *ta* [the reading] ‘*tasmin...bhavanti*’ does not exist.
2. For *ta-bha6*, it begins with *atikramaṇe*; for *ta3*, it begins with *atimaraṇe*; for *bha1.2.4*, it begins with *atimaraṇaṃ*. 3.
For *ta1.7-bha6-mu*, [it is] *kavyavāhanaḥ*.
4. Taraṇi 7-bha2.6-mu-kavyavāhana | Ka.
4-21 yaḥ | Agni, the carrier of the *kavyas*, shall worship the Fathers who increase the *ṛta*; he shall indeed proclaim the oblations to the gods and to the Fathers. 11.

*Kavyavāhana*: the fire that carries the *kavya*, the oblations for the ancestors. He shall worship (*yakṣat*) the ancestors who increase the *ṛta*—the sacrifice, water, or truth—or the gods who have grown through truth. This may also be an epithet of the ancestors themselves. He worships them; in the *leṭ* tense of the root *yaj*, there is the augment *si* with the addition of *ṭ*. That Agni shall proclaim the *havya*, the oblations, saying at the ancestral sacrifice: "These have been brought by me for your sake. This [verse] is complete. For whom? For both the gods and the ancestors; the particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction. In the Mahāpitṛyajña, the verse beginning "uśantastvā" serves as the *sāmidhenī*. For it is stated in the Sūtra: "'uśantastvā ni dhīmahi'—this [verse] is recited three times without pausing; these are the *sāmidhenīs*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).

Desiring you, we set you down; desiring, we kindle you. Desiring, bring the ancestors here to eat the oblation. (12) Desiring, we set you down; desiring, we kindle you. Desiring, bring the desiring ancestors here to eat the oblation. (12)
O Agni, desiring and longing for you, we have established you here for the sake of the ritual;
desiring [you], we kindle you with fuel.
You too, desiring and longing for the oblations and other offerings, bring hither the Pitṛs who are desiring and approaching this sacrifice.
For what purpose?
For the sake of eating—the oblation given by us—to eat the oblation (*havis*). The suffix *tavena* is used in the sense of "in order to eat" (*aditum*).
"The term 'action' (kriyā) must be included [in the definition]"—thus, the object (karman) receives the designation of recipient (saṃpradāna).

O Agni, that which you have completely consumed, cause that to be extinguished once more; let the *kriyāmbu* grow here, and the *pākadūrvā* grass with its spreading stalks. 13. [That] which you, O Agni, have completely burned—*om*, extinguish that again! Let the *kriyāmbu* grow here, and the *pākadūrvā* grass with its spreading stalks. 13.
O Agni, that very place which you formerly completely burned at the time of cremating the ancestors—
[the word *sam* is unaccented by the rule *tiṅi codāttavati*]—
extinguish that very spot once again.
In this place, let there be a lotus pond or similar body of water containing sufficient water;
moreover, let there grow various stalks of *vyalkaśā* and ripe *dūrvā* grass.

At the collection of the bones, he sprinkles the cemetery site three times from right to left with milk and water using a branch of the *śamī* tree, with the verse: "O cool one, O thou who art possessed of coolness. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Wiping [the ground] three times from right to left with milk and water by means of a *śamī* branch, he sprinkles it with the words, 'O cool one, O thou who art possessed of coolness'" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.5.3).
O Śītikā, you who possess coolness; O Hārdikā, you who possess the heart’s delight! Come together well with the female frog and gladden this fire.
1. Tā1.2.7-mu: *udgītha-kavyavāhanaḥ* [is the deity] of the *kavya* offering.
2. Ga-ta4-bha1.2.4.5: *dhīmahi nidadhīmahi*; ta5: *dhīmahi nidhīmahi*. 3. Ta1-mu: *puṣkaraṇyādi* (beginning with the lotus-pond).
4. *ga-ta-bha- ‘with milk-water... does not exist. O Śītikā! O Śītikāvati! O Hrādikā! O Hrādikāvati! O Maṇḍūki! Come well; come together. Accept this most excellent [offering]. 14.

O *śītike*, you who possess coolness; O *śītikāvati*, you who are endowed with those cooling herbs (*oṣadhi*) called *śītikā*; O *hrādike*, you who gladden; O *hrādikāvati*, you who are endowed with trees that bear gladdening fruit; O Earth, unite well—*saṃ gamaḥ*—with the female frog (*maṇḍūkī*), who is fond of rain.
The root *gam* is used with the suffix *luṅ* in the active voice (*parasmaipada*) by way of transposition;
therefore, take pleasure in this fire most excellently.
In the second section (anuvāka), there are thirteen hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of fourteen verses beginning with "tvaṣṭā duhitre," has as its seer (ṛṣi) the son of Yama named Devaśravas.
The first twelve verses are *triṣṭubhs*;
the thirteenth and fourteenth are *anuṣṭubhs*.
Or alternatively:
The thirteenth [verse] is a *bṛhatī* with the *bṛhatī* at the beginning. In the first two, *Saraṇyū* is the deity;
the four beginning with "pūṣā tvetaḥ" have Pūṣan as their deity.
The three verses beginning with "sarasvatīṃ devayantaḥ" have Sarasvatī as their deity;
the five ṛcs beginning with "āpo asmān" have the Waters (Āpas) as their deity.
Among those, the three verses beginning with "drapsaścaskanda" have Soma as their deity.

And thus it has been enumerated: "Tvaṣṭṛ and Devaśravas [are the deities]; two [verses] have Saraṇyū as their deity; then three [verses] have Pūṣan as their deity; three [verses] have Sarasvatī as their deity; five [verses] have the Apsarases as their deity; three [verses] have Drapsa as their deity; or the others have Soma as their deity; the last two are Anuṣṭubhs, or the other is a Purastādbṛhatī. The application of the hymn is concluded.
Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend: there was a divine couple consisting of a man and a woman named Tvaṣṭṛ and Saraṇyū Triśiras.
Then Tvaṣṭṛ gave his daughter, named Saraṇyū, to Vivasvat.
From her and from Vivasvat, Yama and Yamī were born.
Then, on one occasion, having placed those two children near a woman created by himself who resembled his own self, he assumed his own form and departed for the Northern Kurus.
Then Vivasvat, thinking this woman was Saraṇyū, united with her.
From her was born the royal sage named Manu.
Then, realizing that Saraṇyū was no longer his wife, Vivasvat himself became a horse and approached her in the form of a horse.
While the two were sporting together, their own semen fell upon the earth.
Then she, out of a desire for offspring, gathered that fallen semen.
Then, from her, the two Aśvins were born, with the thought: "May the two Aśvins, preeminent in self-restraint, be born."

"Tvaṣṭṛ prepares the bridal procession for his daughter"—saying this, this entire world comes together. The mother of Yama, being carried away, the wife of the great Vivasvat, vanished. Tvaṣṭṛ; for his daughter; prepares; the bridal procession; saying; thus; this; entire; world; comes together; the mother; of Yama; being carried away; of the great; wife; of Vivasvat; vanished.

Tvaṣṭṛ—the deity bearing this name—for his daughter (the dative case used in the sense of the genitive); for the wedding, that is, the carrying away or marriage of the daughter named Saraṇyū; the suffix *catur* is applied to the root *vah* according to the rule "pṛthivyoṣṇaḥ" (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.79).
"He performs it; he makes it.
For this reason, all this entire world—the totality of living beings—comes together at that wedding.
While being carried away, Saraṇyū, the mother of Yami and the wife of the great Vivasvat, who was to be wed by him, vanished.
She vanished toward the Northern Kurus;
that is to say, she went to the Blessed One.

They concealed the immortal one from mortals; they gave the skillful Savarṇā to Vivasvat. And she bore the two Aśvins when that [child] was born; Saraṇyū abandoned the two pairs. apa | agūhan | amṛtām | martyebhyaḥ | kṛtnīm | savarṇām | adaduḥ | vivasvate | uta | aśvinau | abharat | yat | tat | āsīt | ajahāt | u | dvā | mithunā | saraṇyūḥ || 2 ||
1. [The gods were] like themselves; because of their likeness to themselves. 2.
Come!
For the sake of satisfying mortals—those who are subject to death—they concealed, that is, they hid away this Saraṇyū, who was immortal and free from the nature of death.
The meaning is that the gods brought her near.
Furthermore, having taken possession of the splendor of Saraṇyū, which was like unto hers, the gods gave and bestowed it upon Vivasvat.
Moreover, Saraṇyū, in the form of a mare, then bore the Aśvins.
She bore [the twins] as a fetus within her own womb.

When, at the time of sexual union, the seed had fallen from the horse-forms of the husband and wife, she then gave birth to the Aśvins; such is the meaning. Thus Saraṇyū, she who is named "The Swift One," abandoned the two pairs—the twin brothers and sisters.
The meaning is "she has generated.
Alternatively,
Saraṇyū— the deity of the middle station (madhyamasthāna) bearing this name— has generated the embryo of the middle region and the speech belonging to the middle region (mādhyamikīṃ vācam).
In the event of the death of one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), the four verses beginning with "Pūṣan, the white one" (*pūṣā śvetaḥ*) are to be recited for pacification.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "The four [verses] beginning with 'May Pūṣan, the white one, the wise, drive him away' (*pūṣā śvetaścyāvayatu pra vidvān*). (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.10).
May Pūṣan, the wise guardian of the world whose cattle are never lost, drive you forth from here.
May he entrust you to these Fathers and to Agni, who is well-disposed toward the gods.
May the Son, the wise guardian of the world who has not lost his cattle, lead you forth from here. May he, Agni, deliver you over to these Fathers and to the gods who are easy to find. (3)
May Pūṣan—the god of this name—cause you to swell; may he cause you to depart from this world, that is, may he lead you preeminently to the highest world.
Of what nature is he? He is *vidvān*, one who knows our devotion; he is *vanaṣṭapaśuḥ*, possessed of imperishable cattle.

The meaning is that in him all creatures abide and do not perish. He is the protector (*gopā*) of the world, that is, of the multitude of beings. Furthermore, may he, Pūṣan, having stepped forward, bestow you upon these ancestors.
Likewise, Agni [is praised] for those who are worthy of good gifts (*suvidatriya*). "Good gift" (*suvidatra*) means either knowledge or wealth;
those who deserve such are *suvidatriya*.
The suffix *gha* is used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
May he bestow you upon the gods who possess excellent knowledge or excellent wealth;
the meaning is that he should establish you in their world.
May Āyu, the life of all, protect you on every side; may Pūṣan protect you on the distant path ahead.
Where the doers of good deeds dwell, where those offerings are placed—there may the god Savitṛ establish you.
May Viśvāyu protect your life; may Pūṣan protect you on the distant path ahead. Where the doers of good deeds dwell, where your kinsmen are—there may the god Savitṛ place you. 4.
Vāyu is he who possesses all life, or he whose limbs are complete, or he whose nature is to move everywhere; the elision of the letter *va* is a Vedic archaism. Thus: *vāyuḥ*.
Alternatively,
the form is derived by applying the *uṇ* suffix according to the rule "chandasīnaḥ" and then performing the vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*);
thus, "gantā" means Vāyu.
Having approached you, may he protect you;
may Pūṣan, by his permission, guard you on all sides—
[the root] *pā* meaning "to protect."
May Pūṣan, who stands at the very beginning of the broad path— that is, in the wide way or in heaven— protect you, the measured sacrificer, by himself.

Wherever the doers of good deeds (the virtuous) dwell or abide, and wherever those doers of good have gone, there, in that place, may the radiant god Savitṛ— the impeller of all toward their respective duties— establish you.
For the animal sacrifice to Pūṣan belonging to the Ekādaśina set, the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) is "pūṣemāḥ";
for it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "pūṣemā āśā anu veda sarvāḥ śukraṃ te anyadyajataṃ te anyat" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).

1. According to Ta and Bha, [the reading is] *mu-°saṭaśāmanyāṃ*. 2. According to Ta and Bha, *retaḥ* does not exist. 3. According to Ga, *asmin*. 4. According to Ta³·⁴ and Bha¹·²·⁴, *sarvasya bhūtajātasya*. 5. According to Ta and Bha⁶, *chāndasīnaḥ*. 6. According to Ga, Ta¹·²·⁴, *prathamata eva*; according to Ta³, *prathama eva*. 7. According to Ta, *tasmistasmin*.

Puṣan knows all these quarters; may he lead us by the path most free from fear. Bestower of well-being, glowing, possessed of all heroes, may he go before us, watchful and knowing the way. 5. Puṣan | these | quarters | along | knows | all | he | us | most fearless | may he lead | bestower of well-being | glowing | possessing all heroes | without negligence | before | may he go | knowing. 5.
The god Pūṣan knows all these directions—the quarters beginning with the east—in their proper sequence;
that is to say, he knows them in order, whether they are to be traversed with ease or with difficulty.
This being so, when we have been measured out, the sacrificer speaks [to us] either through the mouth of his son or through the mouth of the officiating priest.
May he lead us by the most secure path, one that is entirely free from fear.
How so?

As the giver of well-being (*svastidā*), the bestower of prosperity; as the radiant one (*āghṛṇi*) endowed with approaching splendor; as the possessor of all heroes (*sarvavīra*), accompanied by officiating priests who are heroic and capable in their duties; being unwearied (*aprayucchan*), vigilant, and fully cognizant—knowing our merits and demerits—he shall go before us, proceeding ahead of us.
The meaning is: "May he go in such a way that no fear arises for us."
The invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) of the animal dedicated to Pūṣan in the *ekādaśina* set is: “On the far path of paths...
It is also stated in the Sūtra: “Pūṣan was born on the far path of paths; with eloquence, [I praise] the lord of all paths” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7).

On the far path among the paths Pūṣan was born; on the far path of heaven, on the far path of earth. Toward both most beloved meeting-places he moves, and hither and thither he goes, knowing all. On the far path among the paths Pūṣan was born; on the far path of heaven, on the far path of earth. Toward both most beloved meeting-places he moves, and hither and thither he goes, knowing all.

Among the paths that serve as the means for traveling through the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), Pūṣan was born—that is, he has become manifest—on the *prapatha*, which is the most excellent path among them; the sense is that he stands there for the purpose of leading those of meritorious deeds to the happy realms (*sugati*). Likewise, he was born on the *prapatha*, the most excellent path, among the paths of the sky (*divaḥ*), the celestial world.
Likewise, he has appeared upon the "far path" (*prapatha*) of the earth—that is, on the most excellent path for the purpose of inciting men toward their respective duties.

This very Pūṣan moves toward, that is, moves facing, both heaven and earth—the two most beloved (*priyatame*) and most desired (*sarvasyeṣṭame*) dwelling places (*sadhasthe*) where all beings reside together.
The meaning is that he moves in a manner favorable to those who perform good deeds, in order to manifest the fruits of their meritorious actions.
Likewise, he acts for the sake of others;
he proceeds in opposition to evil deeds.
What is he doing?
Knowing specifically that "by this [cause] this action was performed, and this is the fruit of that action."
In the *prauga-śastra* of the third *chandoma* of the ten-night *vyūha*, for the *sārasvata-nuṣṭhuka*, the first verse is "Sarasvatīm devayantaḥ.
For it is prescribed: "pra brahmaṇo agniraso nakṣanta sarasvatīm devayanto havante" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.11).

Those seeking the gods invoke Sarasvatī; they invoke Sarasvatī while the sacrifice is being performed. The doers of good deeds have turned toward Sarasvatī; may Sarasvatī grant what is desirable to the donor. 7. Sarasvatīm | devayantaḥ | havante | Sarasvatīm | adhvare | tāyamāne | Sarasvatīm | sukṛtaḥ | ahyanta | Sarasvatī | dāśuṣe | vāryam | dāt || 7 ||
1. *ga-ta3.4-asmān sa pūṣā*; *bha1-asmān pūṣā*. 2. *ta-narya*. 3. *ta-bha1.2.4.6-mu-prauge*.

The *devayantaḥ*—the sacrificers desiring to sacrifice to and praise the gods—invoke *Sarasvatī*, the deity of the intermediate region who bears this name, so that she may become a constituent part of the ritual; they call upon her. Likewise, while the *adhvara*—the sacrifice—is being extended through praises and oblations, they worship Sarasvatī (this is the ellipsis). The *sukṛtaḥ*—those of meritorious deeds—*ahyanta*: they strive toward Sarasvatī in order that she may grant the fruits [of their actions].
For this reason, therefore, may the goddess Sarasvatī bestow—that is, grant—the desirable fruit of ritual action to the sacrificer who has offered oblations.

O Sarasvatī, you who have come on the same chariot for our purpose, O Goddess, rejoicing with the *svadhā* offerings along with the Fathers—having seated yourself upon this sacred grass (*barhis*), rejoice; bestow upon us food free from disease.

O Sarasvatī, you who have come with your chariot for the sake of the sacrifice, rejoicing with the ancestral offerings along with the Pitṛs, O Goddess—having sat down upon this sacred grass (barhis), take your delight; bestow upon us food free from disease. 8.
O Sarasvatī, O Goddess, you who have come with your fathers upon a common chariot— meaning, having arrived at our sacrifice in such a way that you are joined with them on a single vehicle—
what were you doing?
The connection is as follows: "Together with the ancestors (pitṛbhiḥ), rejoicing (madantī) through the *svadhā* offerings characterized by oblations (*haviḥ*), you go to the sacrifice.
Having sat down—that is, having taken your seat—upon this sacred grass (*barhiṣi*) in this sacrifice consisting of the strewing of the altar, do you rejoice;
be satisfied by the oblations, or rather, satisfy yourself.
Then, being satisfied, grant us—unto us—plentiful food that is free from disease; "āmīvā" means disease, so grant us foods devoid of that, which produce health. Grant it to us in sufficient measure.
Sarasvatī, whom the ancestors invoke as they approach the southern sacrifice— bestow here a share of nourishment equal to a thousandfold, and grant abundance of wealth to the sacrificers.
O Sarasvatī, whom the ancestors invoke as they approach the sacrificial gift from the south—bestow here a thousandfold portion of nourishment and an increase of wealth upon the sacrificers. 9.

The ancestors invoke you, O Sarasvatī—how? As *dakṣiṇā*; [the suffix] *āc* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 5.3.36 (*dakṣiṇādāc*). They call upon you. Of what kind are they? [They are those who give] sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). The suffix *āc* is added [to *dakṣiṇā*] by the aforementioned rule.

Coming from the south (dakṣiṇā), approaching the sacrifice, moving around it on all sides, and pervading it—here, in this sacrifice, bestow and establish upon the sacrificers half of a thousand (sahasrārdham), which is to be honored and employed by many; the portion (bhāgam) of nourishment (iḷaḥ) consisting of food, and the increase (poṣam) of wealth (rāyaḥ).

In the place of the *adhva-sthāna*, this [verse] "āpo asmāt" is prescribed, and it is also stated in the Sūtra: "Then, having sipped water, they bathe with [the verse]: 'May the waters, our mothers, purify us'" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 6.13).
On the tenth day, during the cleansing of the omentum (*vapā-mārjana*), this same [verse] is used;
and it is stated in the Sūtra: "'idam āpaḥ pra vahata,' and at the place of the fire: 'may the waters, our mothers, purify us'" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 8.12).
May the waters, our mothers, purify us; may those who cleanse with ghee purify us with ghee. For the goddesses carry away every impurity; from them, having come forth, I emerge bright and pure.
May the Waters, our mothers, purify us; may they, whose essence is ghee, cleanse us with ghee. For these goddesses carry away every stain. From them I emerge bright and purified. 10.

1. *ga*—only for the purpose of sacrificing to or praising the gods; 2. *ga-ta-bhara.4-mu*—being expanded; 3. *bha*—making; 4. *ta*—of food (*iṣaḥ*); 5. *ta-bha6*—the phrase "‘sūtritaṃ...’pyeṣā” does not exist [here]. May the *mātaraḥ*, the waters who stand in the place of mothers of the world, purify (*śundhayantu*) us by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇena*); likewise, may those that are purified by clarified butter (*ghṛtapvaḥ*).
Ghee is water;
by means of that they purify others—
those waters are thus described.
Or else, they are "clarifiers of ghee" (*ghṛtapvaḥ*);
*ghṛtam* means "cow's butter";
by that, they purify.

Likewise, it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "O you who purify with ghee, purify us with ghee"—that which is purified by ghee is indeed sleep (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.1.2.11). May those waters purify us with ghee—that is, with manifest water—for since they are divine (*devīḥ*), meaning the goddesses whose nature is to shine, they carry away (*pravahanti*) all (*viśvam*) impurity (*riram*) from the person, driving it forth.
That is to say, "removing" [impurities]. Immediately thereafter, being purified—that is, cleansed—by means of the *aṅgyas* (the bodily parts), I, the praiser, rise up;
that is to say, I go upward to heaven.
On the day of the *sūrya* sacrifice, the two verses beginning with "drapsaścakanda" constitute the two *vimuḍḍhoma* offerings.
This is prescribed in the sūtra: "Having offered the two *vimuḍḍhoma* oblations with the two verses beginning 'drapsaścakanda'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 5.2).
Furthermore, this same verse, "drapsaḥ," is also used when touching the spilled sacrificial oblation (*skannahavis*).
If an oblation should fall outside the enclosing sticks (paridhi), then one should offer it with the *āghāra* formula.

Regarding the rule that "one should touch what has fallen," it is stated in the Sūtra: "'Drapsaś cakanda... [with this verse] one should offer the oblation if it has fallen outside the enclosing sticks" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.13).
The drop has throbbed following the first days, and that which follows the womb of the ancients;
I offer the drop as it moves along toward the common womb, following the seven Hotṛ-priests.
The drop has roared following the first days; I offer this drop into this womb, as it moves together with that which was in the former ones—into the common womb—following the seven Hotṛ-priests. 11.
The drop of Soma, as it is being poured out, has flowed—that is, it has scattered and moved—toward the first, pre-existing earthly worlds and toward the shining celestial worlds.
He explains this very point:
it has gone toward this visible womb, the world that serves as a place of origin, and also toward that which is prior to this one.

I offer in due order the *drapsa*—the Soma-essence characterized by the *vimuḍ*—which moves correctly toward its common, shared source, namely the place characterized by Heaven and Earth; [I offer it] along with the seven *hotrās*, that is, the seven officiating priests, beginning with the *hotṛ*, who are the performers of the *vimuḍ* oblation.
Or alternatively, [it refers to] the *hotrās*.
The sacrificial acts performed by the seven *hotṛ* priests are the *hotrās*. Following those, or after them, I, the *adhvaryu*, offer the oblation.
Or else:
*Drapsa*:
because of his swift movement, the Sun is called *adrapsa*.
That Sun goes to both the earth and the sky, aiming for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) as their common womb (*yoni*).
I offer oblations after that drop, the Sun, who moves correctly, directed toward him—that is, following the seven *hotrās*, the seven directions;
namely, the seven directions other than the one in which the Sun currently resides.
I offer them subsequently.
"Wherever that [power] resides, I bestow it as a substance in each respective direction;
the meaning is that I establish it there."

Regarding this, the Vājasaneyaka states: "That sun is indeed the *drapsa* (the drop), which leaps across both heaven and earth, over this womb and that which was before—meaning over this world and that [world], traversing this common womb; for he indeed traverses this common womb. And: "'I offer the *drapsa* according to the seven *hotṛ*s'—that sun is the *drapsa*, and the quarters are the seven *hotṛ*s; he thus establishes that sun in the quarters" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 7.4.1.20).
That drop of yours which falls, that stalk of yours which has slipped from the arms or from the lap of the *dhiṣaṇā* [pressing-board], or that which [falls] from the *adhvaryu* or from the filter—
to all that, fashioned by rain, I offer with my mind.

That drop of yours which falls, that stalk of yours shaken by the arms, from the lap of the Dhiṣaṇā vessel, or from the Adhvaryu priest, or from the filter—that, I offer for you with my mind, made into rain. 12.

1. *ta-bha* carries it away (*vahati*). 2. From the presence of the person (*puruṣakāśāt*) of *ta-bha*. 3. In *ta-bha*, the word "not" (*asa*) does not exist. 4. In *ta-bha*, there are seven directions (*sapta diśaḥ*). 5. In *ta-bha*, *saṃcarati* [occurs].
O Soma, that (*va*) drop (*drapsaḥ*) which is yours (*te*), your (*va*) essence (*rasaḥ*), spills over (*skandati*)—that is, goes elsewhere from the pressing-skin (*adhiṣavaṇacarmaṇaḥ*).
That (*va*) stalk (*aṃśuḥ*) of yours (*te*), being other than the essence (*rasād itaraḥ*), spills over (*skandati*).
Or it spills while being moved by the arms, having fallen from the two arms of the *adhvaryu*;
or rather,
the pressing-stones (*grāvan*) are the means for the action of the arms.
By means of those [stones], having been displaced from the *adhipūta* [vessel],
he [is placed] upon the *adhiṣavaṇā*, which is the name for the two pressing-boards (*adhiṣavaṇaphalaka*).
The singular number is used because each board is intended to be expressed individually.
It goes elsewhere than from the vicinity of the two pressing-boards;
likewise, it spills from the hand of the Adhvaryu who is pressing,
or it spills from the *daśāpavitra* strainer itself.

I offer all that—whether it be your drop (*drapsa*), or your essence (*rasa*), or with the mind (*manas*), or with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), or together with the ladle (*sruc*), or that which is consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* call (*vaṣaṭkṛta*), or that for which the *svāhā* call has been made—into the fire; I cast it therein.

That drop of yours which has been spilled, that stalk of yours which has fallen, and that which was [offered] before with the ladle—may this god Bṛhaspati pour it all together for the sake of prosperity. 13. That drop of yours; spilled; that stalk of yours; fallen; and that which was [offered] before; with the ladle; this god; Bṛhaspati; may he pour it together; for the sake of prosperity. 13.

O Soma, that which is yours—whether it be your drop (*drapsa*), your essence (*rasa*) that has fallen elsewhere, or that stalk (*aṃśu*) of yours which is your cause, distinct from the juice, or the Soma taken up with the *sruva* ladle—that Soma which spills below or overflows above, may this god named Bṛhaspati pour it together, may he sprinkle it properly.
For what purpose? For the sake of our prosperity (*rādhase*).
For when the Soma is spilled, offspring, cattle, and so forth indeed become spilled as well.

The plants are full of milk; my luster is full of milk. The milk of the waters is indeed full of milk; with that, purify me together. 14. Full of milk are the plants; full of milk is my luster. The milk of the waters is indeed full of milk; with that, purify me together. 14.

This is performed through direct perception: O Waters, you; O Plants, you—rich in milk (*payasvatīḥ*), meaning you possess essence by means of water characterized as rain. May my speech, my word—the speech that is a prayer for rain—be rich in milk, that is, full of essence.
What need is there for much?
Whatever essence there is here—whether of water (*ap*) or of milk (*payas*), like the cream that constitutes the quintessence—all that is full of milk, indeed full of essence.
With that essence of water, purify me; you, cleanse me.
"O Waters, today I have moved along with you; we have united with your essence"—this is another exit [from the body].
The second hymn, consisting of fourteen verses beginning with "paraṃ mṛtyo," is the seerly composition of Saṃkusuka, the son of Yama.
The eleventh verse is a *prastārapaṅkti*;
the first two are *jagatī*, followed by two *gāyatrī* verses.
‘The *prastārapaṅkti* is at the beginning’ (Piṅgala Sūtra 3.41).
The thirteenth [verse] is a *jagatī*, the fourteenth is an *anuṣṭubh*,
and the remaining ones are *triṣṭubhs*.
In that regard, first are the four deities of death;
the fifth is the deity of the elements;
and the sixth is the deity of Tvaṣṭṛ.
The remaining [verses], beginning with the seventh, designate the Pitṛmedha;
therefore, they have that as their deity. Others, because they are not specifically defined, belong to Prajāpati.

And thus it has been enumerated: "Beyond death, [the hymns] 'saṃkusuka', 'śata', 'mṛtyudevatāḥ', 'parā dhātrī', 'parā svāṣṭrī', 'parāḥ pitṛmedhāḥ'; the eleventh is a Prastārapaṅkti; the others are Jagatīs, Anuṣṭubhs, or Prājāpatyas; that which is without expressed meaning (anirukta) is accompanied by the Sāman."

1. *api vā* is not present in Ta1, Ta5, Ta6, and Ta7; it is *vā* in Ta2; it is *api ca* in Ta3 and Ta4; and it is *athavā* in Bha6. 2. According to Ga, Ta, Bha, and Sā, that which exists is the essential core (*sārabhūta*).

Go away, O Death, along your own path, which is distinct from the path of the gods. To you who have eyes and hear, I speak this: do not harm our progeny, nor our heroes. O Death, you whose nature is the slayer of all, go away (*parā ihi*) in succession (*anu*) along another (*param*) path, turning your face away from the sacrificer—this is the ellipsis. What is that path? It is the one belonging to you (*te svaḥ*), which is different (*itaraḥ*) from the path of the gods (*devayānāt*). The "path of the gods" is so called because the gods travel by this route; go toward that other path. Not only go away from here, but also [speak] to you who possess sight (*cakṣumate*) and who hear. Do not harm (*mā ririṣaḥ*) our offspring (*prajām*), nor (*uta*) our brave men (*vīrān*).

So be it! Therefore, we who are wise, facing the east, have gone or shall go—meaning we have turned back toward [the west]. For the sake of dancing—that is, for the activity of dancing, which involves the movement of the limbs; the sense is, for the performance of our own duties. For the sake of striking—that is, for playing with our sons and others. Of what sort are we? We are those who bestow a longer and more extended life.
I set up this boundary for the living, so that no other may now reach this goal. May they live a hundred long autumns, placing death beyond them with this mountain.
I set up this boundary for the living; let no other among them go to that goal. May they live a hundred abundant autumns, placing death beyond them with this mountain. 4.
With this [formula], they place a stone as a boundary (paridhi) for the protection of living beings.

May Sviṣṭṛ— the god of that name, who possesses beautiful offspring and is well-born— being in harmony with you, grant long and abundant life for the sake of living to you who have engaged in this ritual act, for the sake of those living sons and grandsons.
Let these women, the widows, well-supported, enter together with collyrium and clarified butter. Let the mothers, tearless, free from disease, and adorned with fine jewels, ascend first to the womb.

Let these women—widowless, with noble husbands—enter together with collyrium and clarified butter; tearless, free from disease, and possessing fine jewels, let the wives ascend first to the place of birth.
Avidhavā:
"dhava" means husband;
thus, one who has not lost her husband.
The meaning is "those whose husbands are living. *Supatnīḥ* means "having excellent husbands"; *imāḥ* means "these"; *nārīḥ* means "women."
Anointed with collyrium— a means for seeing everything— and with clarified butter (ghṛta), let the women enter their own homes, their eyes truly clear;
likewise, let them be tearless,
free from weeping, and free from disease (amīvā).
*tadrjitāḥ*:
meaning free from mental suffering (*mānasaduḥkha*).
*Suratnāḥ*: endowed with excellent wealth (*śobhanadhana*).
"Janayas" means wives, for they produce offspring;
let them ascend— that is, come first— to the womb, the home, at the very beginning of all things.
The officiant and others should raise the wife of the deceased from the presence of her husband with the verse, "Arise, O woman" (*udīrdhva nāri*).

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Her brother-in-law, one standing in the place of a husband, a pupil, or a barber should raise her with [the verse], 'Arise, O woman, toward the world of the living'" (*āśva. gṛ. 4. 2. 18*).
Arise, O woman, toward the world of the living; come to this one whose life has departed, for you lie here beside him.
You have attained the state of wifehood before this husband who once took your hand and desired you.
Arise, O woman, toward the world of the living! You lie beside this one whose life-breath has departed; come! This state of being a wife to your husband, who took your hand, has now come to you. 8.
O woman, having set your sights upon the world of the deceased husband—the world, place, or home of living beings such as sons and grandsons—arise from this place; rise up!
[The root] *īr* means "to go," belonging to the *adādi* class.
You lie beside this husband whose life has departed, whose breath has gone.

Therefore, come; come here, for you have become [a wife] by virtue of this relationship with this husband of yours—one who has grasped your hand, who takes your hand, who is your husband, and who is the depositor of the embryo—having set your sights upon this state of being born as a wife (*janitva*), that is, *jāyātva* (the status of a wife), and having resolved to follow him in death. Therefore, come.
For a Kṣatriya, one should strike with a bow using the verse "dhanurhastān.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Taking the bow from the hand of the deceased" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.2.20).
Taking the bow from the hand of the deceased for our sovereignty, splendor, and strength—
right here you are, and here we, possessing excellent heroes, shall conquer all rivals and adversaries.

Taking the bow from the hand of the deceased, for our sovereignty, for splendor, and for strength—right here you [remain], and we here, possessed of brave heroes, shall conquer all rivals and adversaries. 9.

1. In Ga-ta-bhara (4.7), the phrase "the brother-in-law should raise her up... is absent; in bha6, the officiant should mutter at the *vṛṣala*: "Arise, O woman, toward the world of the living. 2. In Ta, the phrase "of sons, grandsons, and so forth" is absent.
3. In Ta and Bha, it is *upakrānta*; in Uddītha, it is *utkrānta*.

4. Regarding the phrase "with bow in hand" (*dhanurhastā*) at [Gaṇapāṭha] 1.2.4.5.7: it does not exist [as a separate entry]. [The compound is formed as follows: taking the bow from the hand of a deceased Kṣatriya.
For what purpose?

Taking up my bow for our *kṣatra*—our power capable of protecting the subjects—for *varcas* (splendor), for *tejas* (vital energy), and for *bala* (strength) characterized by the army, I speak; this is the ellipsis. What do I say? "O you [bow], remain right here in this very place; and may we, being endowed with excellent heroes (*suvīrāḥ*)—that is, possessed of noble sons—conquer and overcome all *abhimātīs*, that is, all contending, rivaling, and obstructing enemies."
In the event of the death of one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), the four verses beginning with "Approach your mother" (*upa sarpa mātaram*) are to be recited.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The four [verses] beginning with 'Approach your mother, this earth,' [are used]; some [recite them] for the Soma [sacrifice]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.10).
With the verse "Approach," they should place the collected bones into a pit (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 4.5.5).
Approach this mother, the earth, the wide-extending, the very gracious;
the young maiden, soft as wool, belongs to the liberal giver.
May the earth stand firm; may a thousand [pillars] be set up around her. May these houses of yours be dripping with clarified butter; may they be a refuge for him here for all time. 12.

Having covered it with dust, they recite: "Breathing heavily, leaning upon a jar of bones, she goes upward; may the earth stand firm, may it be well-established. Furthermore: "A thousand"—meaning those numbering a thousand—"measured" (*mitaḥ*). [The form *mitaḥ* is derived from the root *mī* with the suffix *kvip* in the sense of the object, followed by the augment *tuk* and the nominative plural suffix *jas*. Alternatively: "A thousand" (*sahasram*) is used in the first case for the sense of the instrumental; "measured" (*mita*) is a form ending in the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*); the singular number is used for the plural by metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*), and the accentuation is to be understood as belonging to the class beginning with *vṛṣan*. "Measured by a thousand" means "of great number. May the earthly dust-particles "resort to" (*upa-śrayantām*) this—may they attend upon it; the meaning is that they should remain surrounding it on all sides. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis. Likewise, let those dust-particles become "houses" (*gṛhāsaḥ*) for him—becoming dwellings—dripping with clarity (*ghṛtaścut*).
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas.
Having appropriately explained the seventh section of the eighth book, Sāyaṇa, who is skilled in the sacred scriptures,
now desires to expound the seventh chapter.
Now, in the second anuvāka of the tenth maṇḍala, which consists of twelve anuvākas, there are thirteen hymns.
Among them, the third hymn, consisting of eight verses, begins with "ni vartadhvam. Its seer is Mathita, the son of Yama, or else Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, or Cyavana of the Bhṛgu lineage.
The sixth verse is a *gāyatrī*, and the remaining ones are *anuṣṭubh*s.
This [hymn] has either *ida* as its deity or *go* (cattle) as its deity.
The half-verse beginning with “*agnīṣomā punarvasū*” has *Agnīṣoma* as its deity.

And thus it has been enumerated: "Nivartadhvam consists of eight [verses]; [the seer is] either Mathita, Bhṛgu, Vāruṇi-Bhārgava, or Cyavana; [the metre is] prose or Anuṣṭubh; [the deity is] Agni-Soma; the second half-verse is [in] Gāyatrī.
The application [of the hymn] has been explained.
Turn back, do not go further away from us, O sevenfold Revatīs;
O Agni and Soma, you who possess the wealth of renewal, bestow riches upon us.
Turn back! Do not follow after us. O Agni and Soma, you two who are wealthy and possessors of renewed treasures—bestow upon us abundant riches once more. 1.
O cows, or O waters, you must turn back; come toward us.
Do not go away; do not go to a sacrificer other than us.
And having arrived, O wealthy ones—ye who possess riches—unite with us.
The meaning is: "Serve [them] by means of bathing, milking cows, drinking, and so forth.

O Punarvasū—those who are repeatedly established as the protectors and coverers of the singers and the sacrificers—O Agni and Soma, you two gods named Agni and Soma, "dhārayatam" (establish) "rayim" (wealth), characterized by rice and other grains, "asme" (among us).
Turn them back again, bring them back again;
may Indra restrain them, and may Agni drive them away.
Again, bring them back; again, settle them here. May Indra restrain them; may Agni drive them together. 2.
Here, the seer of the mantra speaks to himself:
"O my steed (arvan), turn back these cows—or these waters—that have gone elsewhere; bring them back again toward this place.
Thereafter, make these others yours once more and again, making them subject to your own control."
Furthermore, "May Indra, being your ally, restrain these—make them subject to you.
And may Agni "acquire" (upārjatu)—that is, bring near, or present—these cows or waters;
the meaning is that he should make them objects of enjoyment.
May these [cows] return again; may they thrive under this master of the herd.
O Agni, establish them right here; let whatever wealth there is remain right here.
O Indra, do you turn back; turn back toward us.
Then, bring back the cows that are going elsewhere; make them face toward us.
Having done this, O Indra, give the cows back to us once more; bestow them upon us.
May we enjoy ourselves with the cows given by you— cows that live long, or rather, that give life to all;
or else,
the root *bhuj* here has the causative sense implied within it.
Let us feast the gods and the ancestors.
I bestow upon you from every side strength, with clarified butter and with milk;
whatever gods there are who are worthy of sacrifice, may they endow us with wealth.
I bestow upon you from every side strength, clarified butter, and milk—those who are gods and whoever are worthy of sacrifice; may they endow us with wealth. 7.

O gods, I sustain you—who stand on every side—from all directions with strengthening food consisting of curds related to the cow, with clarified butter (ghṛta), and with milk; that is, I offer it to you by way of the oblation. The meaning is not merely that I nourish myself.

Knowing this, whatever gods there are who are worthy of sacrifice and entitled to the sacrifice—may those gods unite us with *rayi*, that is, with wealth characterized by cattle. May they join us with it.
O you who turn back, cause him to turn; O you who turn away, cause him to turn away.
From the four quarters of the earth, from those very directions, cause him to turn back.
O Nivartana, turn them back! O Nivartana, turn them back! From the four quarters of the earth, from those [quarters], turn these [beings] back! || 8 ||
The seer, the perceiver of the mantra, addresses himself and the cows, saying:
"O my self, do thou bring back the cows.
The prefix *ā-* is also connected with this [verb].
"Turn them toward me!"—
the meaning is that you should appease them with praise and sacrifice and bring them near. O cows, being thus appeased, turn back, come back!
"Come forward!
He spoke again:
"O my soul, turn back; drive away the cows that are departing from the grazing ground and bring them hither."
"O cows, you too, as you are returning, turn back!
Now the self speaks in response to its own limbs:
"O Seer, from where shall I turn back the cows, and from where shall we turn back? Being thus questioned by itself through the cows, it says:

From the four excellent directions—the four quarters belonging to the earth, the ground—bring these cows back; O Self, make them face toward me. By implication, it is understood that "O cows, you too must turn back from those directions. Or alternatively:
Even in the view that the deity is the water-element (ab), the construction of the meaning of the hymn must be made in such a way that it remains consistent.
The fourth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “bhadram,” has its first verse as a single-word *virāj* of ten syllables;
the verse “agnim īḷe bhujām” is an *anuṣṭubh*.
The ninth [verse] is Virāj, the tenth is Triṣṭubh, and there are six Gāyatrīs in the middle.
For these seven hymns beginning with this one, the seer is Vigada, the son of Agni or the son of Prajāpati; alternatively, he is the son of Vasukra or the descendant of Vasukradāsyu.
This and the following [hymn] are dedicated to Agni.

And thus it has been enumerated: "The *Sasottaraṇī* belongs to Indra or to Prajāpati; the *Vāsukra* is for the giver of wealth; the *Bhadra* is the tenth [verse] and is in the *Gāyatrī* metre; the first is a single-footed verse, or perhaps just a foot, intended for the purpose of pacification; the next is an *Anuṣṭubh*, and the last two are *Virāj* and *Triṣṭubh*.
The application [of these verses] has been explained.
1. Having covered the gods and ancestors with *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *deva*.
2. With *ta*, *bha*, *mu*, and clarified butter (*ājya*).
3. Facing toward me with *ta*, *bha*, *ra*, and *mad*; with *ta*, *mu*, and *madabhimukhī*; with *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *madabhimukhaṃ*.
May you also inspire our minds toward what is auspicious.
May you also inspire our minds toward what is auspicious.
O beloved one, cause our mind to be directed toward what is auspicious—that is, endowed with purity—and likewise bring it back [to that state].
Here, the particle *api* is used to reiterate the meaning of the verbal root.
Bring it back.
The meaning is: "Impel me to compose a hymn of praise concerning you."

I praise Agni, the youngest of the enjoyers [of oblations], the friend by his command, who is difficult to restrain; whose law the bright, swift ones honor as they approach the mother’s udder. I praise Agni, the youngest among the gods who enjoy the sacrificial offerings (*bhujām*), the most youthful because he is born day after day for the sake of the *agnihotra* and other rites. By his command (*śāsā*), he is a friend (*mitram*); the meaning is that since he instructs everything—“this must be done, this must not be done”—he is therefore a friend to all. He is one who is "difficult to restrain" (*durdharītum*), meaning he is impossible for enemies to hold back in battle. Such is the Agni whom I praise. Furthermore, at whose law (*dharman*)—that is, in the ritual acts such as the *agnihotra*—the "bright ones" (*svaḥ*), meaning the celestial world, the sun, or the entire host of gods, along with the "swift ones" (*enīḥ*), meaning the fragrant oblations and hymns of praise, "honor" (*saparyanti*), that is, attend upon, serve, and worship.
