Or rather, there is grammatical coordination between *svaḥ* and *saparyanti*. Here, *svaḥ* is a particle. All the gods honor—that is, they serve and subsist upon—the oblations and hymns that come toward them. This is the meaning. Therein lies a simile (with the comparative particle *iva* understood): just as calves subsist upon the udder of the mother cow, which is the place where milk is gathered, so it is here. "I praise him, that Agni"—this is the connection with the preceding verse.

Whom they, with their mouths, increase—the one whose dwelling is the sacrificial vessel, whose banner is light; he shines, bestowing rows [of blessings]. (3) Whom—*āmā* (with their mouths)—the praisers and the sacrificers increase through worship characterized by hymns and oblations; what kind of one? *Kṛpanīḷam*, whose dwelling is the place of action; that is to say, the gateway to ritual action. *Bhāsāketum*, whose banner is light—that is, having light as his mark, or the maker of radiance. Since the word "whom" (*yam*) is heard in the text, the word "he" (*saḥ*) must be supplied. That Agni, being such—*śreṇidan*, bestowing a multitude of desired fruits upon the praisers and sacrificers, or bestowing rows of flames upon enemies—shines and glows.

The noble one, the goal-seeker of the people, goes forth when he has reached the ends of heaven; the sage, the far-reaching, [pervades] the cloud. (4) The noble one (*aryaḥ*), the goal-seeker (*gātuḥ*)—Agni, who is by nature mobile—of the people (*viśām*), that is, of the human sacrificers; the far-reaching (*dīrghāṅgaḥ*), meaning the shining one; *when* (*yat*) he *goes forth* (*eti*), moving upwards, then that *sage* (*kaviḥ*), the wise Agni, *reaches* (*pra...ānaṭ*) with pre-eminence the *ends* (*antān*), the boundaries of *heaven* (*divaḥ*), the celestial world; and he also pervades the *cloud* (*abhram*), representing the intermediate space.
1. "This must not be done"; "this must be done. Kratu 4-22:

Taking pleasure in the oblations of man, standing upright and reaching upward, he goes before all, establishing everything at the sacrifice. He takes pleasure; in the oblations; of the human being; standing upright; he has stood; reaching upward; at the sacrifice; establishing; everything; he goes before. ||5||

In the sacrifice of a human sacrificer, at the worshipful rite, Agni—enjoying and partaking of the various oblations (*havyāni*)—standing tall, having flourished and become vast with many flames, rises up; that is to say, he blazes upward. Moreover, this Agni, starting from the *prāgvaṃśa* hall, marking out and delimiting his seat—the Soma-altar (*saumikī vedī*)—proceeds as he is being led forward from the front, from the *uttaravedi-śālāmukhīya* fire.

For he is the secure one; the oblation, the sacrifice—by his swift hearing, his path is open. To Agni, who wields the axe, the gods [come]. 6. He. For. Secure. Oblation. Sacrifice. By swift hearing. Truly. His. Path. Goes. To Agni. Gods. Wielding-the-axe. 6.
That fire which is most excellent and distinguished— indeed, the word "hi" (for) serves as an emphatic particle—
it is that very fire which is *kṣema*, the cause of well-being.
The meaning is that he is the cause of the preservation of everything.
He alone is the oblation, such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and so forth, because they have him as their cause.
He alone is also the sacrifice, the ritual offering (*yāga*), because that too has him as its cause.
Furthermore, by the swift impulse of this Agni, his moving and presiding self goes forth to invite the gods.
Having gone and returning, the gods also go toward Agni, who is "armed with the axe"—that is, endowed with speech characterized by praise; this is the sense of the remainder of the verse.

I have kindled Agni for the sake of the sacrifice, for the sake of food, and for the sake of ancient bliss. They call him the son of the rock, the long-lived one. (7) I have kindled Agni for the sake of the sacrifice, for the sake of food, and for the sake of ancient bliss. They call him the son of the rock, the long-lived one. (7)
Here, for the sake of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the words *yat* and *na* must be supplied.
The latter half-verse (*ardharca*) should be explained first:
they call that Agni the son of the rock (*adraḥ sūnum*), the offspring of the stone (*aśmanaḥ putram*), who goes as a messenger (*dūtyena*) to summon the gods.
Mantras such as "Thou art Agni, O Agni, [be] around me" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.1.1) and others declare this.
"Yajñasaham" means the bearer of the sacrifice;
that is to say, its supporter.
Aiming toward him, I desire service— that is, attendance—
for the sake of the former.

In this context, the word *pūrva* signifies "superior. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "for the sake of attaining the superior Śiva, whose nature is the bliss characterized by heaven and liberation (*svarga-apavarga*)."

Whatever men there may be who belong to our side, let all of them be in the village, increasing Agni with oblations. (8) Men—whatever they may be—from us, let all of them indeed be on your side; let them be so, increasing Agni with oblations. (8)
"Those who are our leaders, and whoever they may be—our sons, grandsons, and so forth—who belong to us (the word *asmat* being used for *asmākam*);
the vowel *ā* is a filler (*pūraka*).

May those sons, grandsons, and others be on our left—that is, in the desirable and worshipful [portion]—in all (the word *viśvet* meaning *viśvasmin*) of our wealth, including the cattle and so forth; may they be present on all sides."
We hope that they would sit down. Doing what?
Increasing—that is, causing to grow—the god Agni, who is distinguished by qualities such as being anointed, with the oblation consisting of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and other offerings.
Black, white, and ruddy are his paths; his jaws are straight and he is red, full of glory.
The progenitor begot him in a golden form.
1. According to *ta*, Pavamāna is Agni.
2. According to *ga*, *ta*, *bha* 5.6, [the gods] "are coming.
3. According to *ta* 1.2.3.4.5.6 and *bha*, the word "increasing" (*vardhantaḥ*) is not present.
Black, white, ruddy, tawny—his [color] is bright, straight, and even worn-out; glorious, the progenitor has brought forth him who is golden-hued. 9.
In this context, the word "going" (gacchat) should be supplied and joined [to the verb].
"Yāmaḥ": that in which one goes or moves is a *yāma*, a chariot fashioned by Prajāpati.

Of what kind? Black (kṛṣṇa), meaning dark-colored; white (śveta), meaning bright-colored; ruddy (aruṣa), meaning shining; bradhna, meaning great; ṛja, meaning moving straight; and also (uta) even śoṇa, meaning red-colored; and yaśasvān, meaning possessed of fame. Or alternatively:
*Yaśas* is a name for wealth;
[the chariot] is endowed with wealth characterized by the oblation.
*Hiraṇyarūpam*, meaning "having the form of gold," that chariot the *janitā*, the progenitor of the entire world, Prajāpati, *jajāna*, brought forth for this Agni.
The meaning is that he gave it to him.
If it is asked how it is possible for a single chariot to possess various forms such as Kṛṣṇa and others, the answer is that it is possible through the extraordinary power of Agni.
Or alternatively:

Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "having a golden form" (*hiraṇyarūpa*), which denotes a chariot, the words "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) and so forth are to be construed as being in the accusative case.
The meaning here is that Agni is being praised for possessing a chariot endowed with all these qualities.

Thus, O Agni, driver away of adversaries, may our prayer bring hither songs of praise, well-disposed and approaching, in harmony with the sons of Manu through the eternal laws; grant us food, vigor, a secure dwelling, and all that we desire.

Thus, O Agni, may Vimada bring to you his inspired thought, nourishment, and songs, being in harmony with the immortals; seeking your favor, may he obtain all—food, strength, and a secure dwelling. 10.

O *ūrjo napāt* (son of strength), grandson of Agni who has satisfied the plants and the ancestors—O *agne*, being in harmony (*sajoṣaḥ*) with the immortal oblations characterized as food, the seer named Vimada, desiring an exalted intellect (*manīṣām*), has addressed (*ā vakṣat*) these songs (*giraḥ*) consisting of hymns of praise to you (*te*).
[The form *vakṣat* is used for the subjunctive (*leṭ*) in the Vedic language.]

Therefore, having understood this, you— moving with *sumatibhiḥ*, that is, with auspicious insights (*buddhi*)— unite us with *iṣam* (food), *ūrjam* (the essence of milk and other nourishment), and *sukṣitim* (a beautiful dwelling). Alternatively, *kṣitayaḥ* refers to human beings.
Whatever there is to be given—such as handsome sons, grandsons, and so forth—that entire wealth and splendor, bring and give it to that Vimada.

The fifth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "āgniṃ na," is composed in the *astārapaṅkti* meter. It consists of two initial *gāyatrī* feet followed by two *jāgatī* feet; this is the *astārapaṅkti*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and deity (*devatā*) are as previously stated.
And thus it has been enumerated: "Having chanted 'āgniṃ na,' [one uses] the Āstārapaṅkti.

On the fourth day of the Pṛṣṭha [stoma], it is stated: "'āgniṃ na svavaktibhiḥ' is the Ājya [laud]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11). At the Mahāvrata, in the Ābhimāruta [laud], as many verses as they may chant with the Vichandasāman, so many verses are to be used as the Anurūpas.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "If they should praise with more verses than the *icchandas*, [they should do so] with the thought 'not Agni with his own words'; [therefore] they should recite that many *anuṣṭubh*s" (AiĀ 5.3.2).

We choose you as the Hotṛ priest with our unctuous offerings, like Agni for the sacrifice upon which the sacrificial grass is strewn—for your exhilaration—sharp and purifying in your luster; you wish to speak forth.

Like Agni, we choose you as the Hotṛ-priest with our invocations, for the sacrifice where the sacrificial grass is strewn—O Indra, in your exhilaration, [we praise] the one who is sharp and of purifying luster; you are waxing great. 1.
1. *buddhīḥ stāgamanay*; ta3-*buddhīstagamana*; ta5-*buddhīḥ stāgamanay*; ta7-*buddhīḥ tā-gamanay*; bha1.2.4.7-*buddhīstāḥ gamayan*; bha6-*buddhiḥ agamayat*.
O Agni, this praise has been offered by me to the seer named Vimada, who is your own (*svabhūta*).
The particle *na* is used here in the sense of "now" (*saṃprati*).

Therefore, we now choose you, Agni— the invoker of the gods or the performer of the oblation— with our own hymns of praise, which are self-composed and free from defects; we honor you face-to-face for the sake of the sacrifice upon which the sacrificial grass has been spread.
The dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (tādarthye).
[It means] for the sake of sacrifice. Of what kind?
[The fire] that lies latent everywhere within herbs and other substances, possessing the brilliance of a purifier, a cleansing light—
this is what you intend to speak of; this is food.
O Agni, you too are great;
or rather, it should be construed thus:
"O Vimada, for the sake of the exhilaration arising from drinking Soma related to the sacrifice, we choose you."

In these [flames] of yours, the self-existent ones, moving with wealth, shine forth. The oblation, worthy of being sprinkled, approaches you; O Agni, in this exhilaration of yours, the straight-flying offering desires to be proclaimed. 2.

To you—Om! To you—O you who are present in the sacrifice! They shine forth; they come from the unobstructed. You indeed, O Agni, are the one to be praised; the oblation, seeking you, goes toward you in the exhilaration of the Soma; it is straight-flying; you are about to proclaim it. 2.
O Agni, those sacrificers—self-existent, shining by their own radiance, possessing abundant wealth—beautify you alone;
that is to say, they illumine you with oblations in the sacrifice.
Furthermore, O Agni, the straight-moving oblation (*ṛjīti*), which flows toward you as it is poured, goes to you.
For what purpose?
For your sake—that is, for the sake of you who are intoxicated;
the meaning is: for the purpose of your satisfaction.
Moreover, you also intend to say that he is great.
In you, O Lord of Dharma, they sit with their ladles as if pouring out libations.
Black forms and white ones—indeed, all glories—you bestow upon us in your exhilaration; you desire to reveal them.
In thee, O Lord of Dharma, they take delight with their ladles as if pouring out dark and bright forms; in thy exhilaration, thou hast placed all glories upon us, for thou desirest to bestow them. 3.
The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), who maintain the sacrifice—the ocean of Dharma—sit near, worship, and serve you alone with ladles (*juhū*) filled with complete oblations and sacrificial vessels.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like those pouring [water]."

The waters, characterized by rain, drench the earth; they serve it as their own father, just as [the waters] do. According to the scriptural text, "From fire, water" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.5), fire is the father of those waters.
Or else:
Like oblations being poured forth as if from *juhū* ladles, the streams of *dharma* maintained by you—the rays—reside and remain fixed within you.

O Agni, you uphold all splendors (*śriyaḥ*), both those that are black (*kṛṣṇā*) and those that are white (*arjunā*), as well as the forms contained within the flames; you sustain them all so that they may be preeminent (*adhidhipe*). For what purpose?
O Vimaḍa, [this is] for the sake of the various intoxications arising from the drinking of soma for all you gods;
since you desire this, you become great.

O Agni, O powerful one, whatever wealth you deem fit for a mortal, bring that to us for the winning of booty; at our sacrifices, during the exhilaration of the Soma, bring the wondrous gift, for you desire to proclaim it aloud.

O Agni, O immortal one, possessor of power, whatever wealth you deem worthy, bring that to us for the winning of booty; at our exhilaration with Soma, bring that wonderful wealth to our sacrifices, for you desire to bestow it. 4.

1. *ta-va*: "It does not exist. 2. *ta1.2.4.5-vivakṣate*. 3. *ta-ahajñāmaitat*. 4. *ta-bha-dīptadhanāḥ*. 5. *ta-siṃcati*. 6. *ta3.4.5-bha1.2-āpaḥ ammān*; *ta1.2.6.7-āpa vṛṣṭyudakaṃ pṛthivīṃ amrīn*; *bhava-āpa iva ammān*.

O immortal Agni, you whose nature is deathless and who are powerful by force—such as you are, bring to us that chariot which you deem the most excellent among all riches, that wonderful and praiseworthy chariot, for our acquisition of food;
why?
For the sake of the sacrifice of you all, the gods, at the occasion of the various intoxications produced by the oblations of Soma and other offerings.
The meaning is: "for the sake of satiating you with various kinds of oblations in the sacrifices.
You too, "vivakṣase," become great.
Agni, born through the Ṛṣi Atharvan, has disclosed all poetic wisdom;
he became the messenger of Vivasvat. In your exhilaration, you, the beloved and desirable one of Yama, are being proclaimed aloud.
Agni was born by the Atharvan; he discovered all poetic wisdoms. He became the messenger of Vivasvat. In your exhilaration, you, the beloved and desirable one of Yama, are being proclaimed aloud. 5.
Agni was born—that is, generated—by the seer named Atharvan.
How is this known?
From another mantra: "O Agni, Atharvan churned you forth from the lotus-leaf" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.16.13).
He knows all the poetic hymns (*kāvya*) taken together;
he becomes the messenger for the sake of summoning the gods on behalf of the sacrificer, Vivasvat.
Furthermore, being dear to Yama, the controller—the sacrificer—he becomes desirable, that is to say, worthy of longing and prayer.
The remainder is clear.
They praise you, O Agni, at the sacrifices during the ritual proceedings;
you bestow all desirable treasures upon the donor for our exhilaration—you proclaim this in your song.
They invoke you, O Agni, at the sacrifices during the ritual proceedings. You bestow all desirable treasures upon the donor; in the exhilaration of the Soma, you proclaim this aloud. 6.

O Agni, when the sacrifice (adhvara)—the rite—is being performed with excellence, and when the oblations worthy of worship are placed upon the sacrificial seats, the officiating priests and the sacrificers praise you.

Moreover, O Agni, you bestow all desirable and lovely treasures (vasūni) upon the donor, the sacrificer who has offered the oblation; and when there is satisfaction born from the Soma and other offerings, you grant them to Vimada.
For this reason, you are celebrated as the Great One.
Men have established you, O Agni, as the beautiful priest at the sacrifices;
with your face anointed with ghee, you, the bright and most observant one, are kindled by the men for our exhilaration, and you speak aloud with your flames.

In sacrifices, men have established you, O Agni, as the beautiful officiating priest; with your face anointed with ghee, you shine forth—bright and most wise—with your eyes in the exhilaration of the Soma. 7.
O Agni, human beings who are sacrificers establish you in sacrifices— that is, they station you there by rule—

[you] who are the *ṛtvij* (the priest named Hotṛ), the lovely (*cāru*) and delightful, whose face is filled with oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛtapratīka*), the bright (*śukra*) and flaming, and the most perceptive (*cetiṣṭha*) among all knowers, pervaded by your rays of light (*akṣabhiḥ*).
For what purpose?
For the sake of various satisfactions produced by your Soma and other oblations in the state of exhilaration (*mada*).
Since this is so, you *vivakṣase*—you become great.
1. That sacrifice; 2. [the syllable] *ga* [is] *ta*; 3.7. Greatness (*bha-tvaṃ mahān*);
3. He becomes (*ta-bhavati*).

O Agni, with your bright flame you spread yourself out widely and loftily; thundering aloud, you bestow strength upon us. In your exhilaration, you place the germ within your kindred sisters; you desire to speak forth.

O Agni, with your brilliance and your flame, you spread yourself out widely and loftily. Roaring aloud, you act as a bull; in your exhilaration, you place the germ within the sisters. You desire to speak forth. 8.
O Agni, with your lofty, great, and white-hot brilliance, with your flaming luster and splendor, you spread yourself wide; you become expansive as it were.
Furthermore, roaring toward [the enemy] and challenging the foes for battle, you act like a bull (*vṛṣāyase*);
at the time of combat, you roar repeatedly like a proud bull—this is the meaning.

Being the central one (*mādhyamika*), you place, that is, maintain through the medium of rain, the seed-essence as a germ within the plants that are your sisters—that is, those who have become like sisters. They are metaphorically addressed as "sisters" because they have arisen from the same source, Prajāpati.
Under what condition?

In your exhilaration (*mada*), when the exhilaration produced by various oblations such as Soma has arisen—because you have acted thus—you are "vivakṣase," that is, you become great. *Vivakṣase* is a form derived from the root *vac*, *vah*, or the desiderative of *san*. It is a name for "great."
The sixth hymn, "Kuha," consisting of fifteen verses, is dedicated to Indra.
The fifteenth verse is a *triṣṭubh*; the fifth, seventh, and ninth are three *anuṣṭubhs*;
and the remaining verses are *purastādbṛhatīs*.
The first twelve-versed [hymn] consists of three *bṛhatī*s followed by one [verse];
the particle *api* is as before.
Thus it has been enumerated: "In *kuha*, there are five; the first is a *bṛhatī* ending in a *triṣṭubh*; in *tvaṃ syāḥ*, *cidā naḥ*, and *tvaṃ naḥ*, there are *anuṣṭubh*s."

Thus [it is said]. On the fourth day, this hymn is used for the Niṣkevalya [śastra]. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Niṣkevalya is 'Where has Indra been heard of? ... of you... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11).
Where has Indra been heard of? Among which people today is he renowned like Mitra—whether in the abode of the seers or in secret—who is celebrated with song?
Where has Indra been heard of? Among what people today is he renowned like Mitra—whether in the abode of the seers or in secret—who is celebrated with song? 1.
Today, on this very day, where—in what place—is Indra heard of, renowned, and celebrated?
Among which person is he heard of and proclaimed as one who is to be worshipped through sacrifice and praised?
In this regard, there is an illustration:

Like Mitra, like the sun, or like a friend—Indra is thus. He who, in the *kṣaya* (dwelling), *āśrama* (hermitage), or *guhā* (cave) of the *ṛṣis* such as Bhṛgu and others, or within the secret place (*guhāyām*), is intensely drawn toward by the word (*girā*) characterized as praise;
that is to say, he is excessively praised.
The phrase "Where is that Indra heard of? is to be connected with what precedes it.
Here has been heard [the cry]: "Indra belongs to us! Today let me praise the wielder of the thunderbolt, the peerless one, who like Mitra among the people has established incomparable glory."
Here, Indra has been heard of. Today I shall praise him, the wielder of the thunderbolt, who is worthy of hymns; he who, like Mitra among the people, has established incomparable glory for us. 2.
In this sacrifice here, Indra is renowned—that is, famous.
Today, on this very day, he is praised by us; how so? [The following describes him:]
The wielder of the thunderbolt, possessing the thunderbolt,
equal to the seers; even if there were a hundred earths for you, O Indra, a hundred times over, they would not suffice to contain you.
The meaning is that he possesses identical qualities through the praise beginning with "O Wielder of the Thunderbolt" (*vajrin*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.70.5).
That Indra, like Mitra or like the sun—meaning like one who is affectionate—bestows (*cakre*) upon the people, that is, among the people who are his worshippers, *yaśaḥ*, which means food or fame.
Of what kind?
"Unowned" means "unshared.
The connection with the preceding clause is: "That Indra is praised by us."
He is the lord of great glory, the peerless master of power; he is the swift bringer of great wealth, the bearer of the bold thunderbolt, like a father cherishing his beloved son.
He who is the lord of abundant strength, the impeller of great wealth, the bearer of the bold thunderbolt—like a father his beloved son—he is the Great One. 3.

He who is Indra, the lord (pati) and master (īśvara) of great (mahaḥ) and mighty (mahataḥ) strength (śavasaḥ), is incomparable (asāmyā). *Ā* is used here as a limitative particle (*maryādāyām*) or in the sense of inclusion (*samāse*).
The meaning is "possessing infinite qualities.
He is the "tūtujiḥ," the one who impels or bestows "mahaḥ," the great "numṇam," wealth, upon his worshippers.
Furthermore, he is the "bhartā," the sustainer or wielder, of the "vajra," his own weapon, which is "dhṛṣṇoḥ," the subduer of enemies.
The ellipsis is: "May that Indra protect us.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"as a father [protects] his dear son."
Just as a father protects his beloved son, so too does he [protect].
Yoking the two roaring horses of the wind, O god, wielder of the thunderbolt, may the two radiant ones flow forth; setting them in motion, you shall traverse the paths to be praised.

Yoking the two horses of the wind, O thunderbolt-wielding god, let the two roaring steeds of the god flow forth; spreading out with radiant splendor, as you release them, you shall praise the paths. 4.
"He is like a thunderbolt, as indestructible as a vajra.
The single meaning of the mantra is reiterative:
'O God, you who are radiant; of the god, the radiant Vāta, the wind, you are the impeller.'"
The meaning is that they are even swifter than the wind.
"Harnessing the two bay horses belonging to you"—that is, yoking them to your own chariot. Of what kind are they?
"By the shining, radiant path, you two who are moving along;
creating the paths of travel in battle, you are constantly praised."
You yourself have urged on even those swift horses of the wind to carry you; like a god among mortals, you go as one whose driver is no one to be found.
You have come even from those horses of the wind; you have come straightway to be harnessed by yourself. You have gone like a god, not like a mortal; no one can restrain you, O finder of wealth.
Because of its connection with the word *yat* ("which"), the latter half-verse is explained first:

"Of your two [paths], O Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), there is no one among the gods who is a controller, restrainer, or warder-off; nor is there anyone among mortals; indeed, there is no one at all who is a knower (*vidāvyaḥ*) of [your] speed or strength (the word *javyasya* or *balasya* being understood as the remainder)."
O Indra, those two swift-moving steeds of yours, yoked by the strength and speed of Vāta (the wind), even they— your own horses— carry [you] by their own self,
that is, independently of a driver,
for the purpose of carrying you.
The meaning is "for the sake of reaching the intended place. "Āgāḥ" means "you go towards [it]."

1. You go to that house; as you approach, one asks you both: "For what purpose have you come to our home? From afar, you have come from heaven and earth to this mortal man. 6. As you approach, desiring [us], one asks you both: "For what purpose, indeed, have you come to our home? From afar, from heaven and earth, you have come to this mortal man."
Now, after the completion of the sacrifice, the seer Uśanas Bhārgava asked you two, O Indra and Agni, as you were returning to your own abodes: "I ask you," or alternatively,
"Uśanā" is a case-ending substitution (vibhaktivyatyaya).
Every sacrificer asks you two—Uśanas, the descendant of Bhṛgu, who is a friend of Indra, and Indra himself—the question:
"What did he ask? It is said in response:
"Being what kind of stingy ones (vkadarthā), possessing what purpose (kiṃyojanavantau), do you two [act] toward us (naḥ)?"
The prefix *prati* has the sense of "toward" (*pratītya*). [In the example] *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut*, this is a term for distance (*dūra*).
It means "from afar" (*parākāt*).
Or from afar, you two have come;
that very thing has been said:
from heaven (*divaḥ*), from the celestial world, and from earth (*gmaḥ*), from the terrestrial world, you two have come toward me, a mortal human (*martyam*).
The meaning is that, by saying "Your arrival here is solely for the sake of favoring us, as you have already achieved your own purpose and not for your own ends," he honors them.

Come to us, O Indra; you shall be satisfied with our most exalted prayer. For that reason, we entreat you for great protection, so that you may slay Śuṣṇa, the non-human foe. 7. Come to us, O Indra; you shall be satisfied with our most exalted prayer. For that reason, we entreat you for great protection, so that you may slay Śuṣṇa, the non-human foe. 7.
"O Indra, you [are our protector]," here the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental; "vnaḥ" means by us, and "udyatam" means lifted up.
The meaning is "given. "Our" (*naḥ*) refers to our own; "brahman" refers to the food characterized by the oblation (*havis*).
The word *ā* is used here in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*).
The meaning is "unto the men.
You shall be joined with yourself;
this is a form of the root *pṛcī* in the sense of "contact."
The meaning is "consume.
Furthermore, we too have known you to be such;
that is to say, [we know] that there exists something superior—this is the ellipsis.
We pray for such food and its protection;
likewise, we pray for that supreme strength which slays *vṛśaṇa*—that is, non-human beings other than men, such as Rākṣasas and the like—or rather, [we pray for] that which slays them.
Or else:
O Indra, you slew that *śuṣṇa*—an asura, a non-human being whose mind is distinct from that of humans;
and having slain him, you protected the three worlds through sacrifice and guardianship. We pray to you that this same protection (*avaḥ*) may be ours as well; such is the meaning of the statement.

The Dasyu who performs no rites, who is mindless toward us, who follows other laws, and who is non-human—O slayer of enemies, O increaser, do thou subdue that Dāsa. akarmā | dasyuḥ | abhi | naḥ | amantuḥ | anyavrataḥ | armānuṣaḥ | tvam | tasya | amitrahan | vardhaḥ | dāsasya | dambhaya || 8 ||

The *vadasyu*— one who performs no rites such as sacrifices, a destroyer (*upakṣapayitṛ*)— may he, being unknown (*ajñāta*), drive us away (*vamantu*) from his very nature (*svarūpataḥ*) toward himself (*abhī*).
Or rather,
here the elision of the letter *va* of the prefix *ava* should be understood.

One who is contemptuous and prone to despising others is overcome [by his own arrogance]. Following the "forest-vow" (*vanyavrata*), performing actions outside the scope of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, he is "non-human" (*vamānuṣa*), meaning excluded from human social intercourse;
the sense is that he is of a demonic nature (*asuraprakṛti*).
O Vamitrahan, slayer of enemies, you who are such as this, O Indra, being the slayer (vadhah) of the Dāsa who is to be destroyed (upakṣapayitavya), terrify that enemy; strike him down!

O Indra, O hero, you [are] with heroes; and we, aided by you, through our greatness—your fulfillments are manifold, like men and like the peoples. 9. You, O Indra, O hero, [are] with heroes; and we, aided by you, through our greatness—your fulfillments are manifold, like men and like the peoples. 9.
O heroic and valiant Indra, you, being accompanied by the Maruts, your brave warriors, protect us—this is the ellipsis.
Moreover, protected by you (tvotāsaḥ), may we be capable in the destruction of enemies—that is, in the act of crushing them.
Furthermore, your fulfillments—the granting of desired objects that satisfy our wishes—reach out in many directions to various worshippers.
The earths;
this belongs to humans.
Just as humans pervade their own master for the sake of service, so it is here.
O Hero, wielder of the thunderbolt, impel those men toward the slaying of Vṛtra and toward the drawing of the sword; for you are hidden within the sages and among the people.
O Indra, O valiant hero, our own great and excellent aids are here—rich in wealth and worthy of worship in our presence.
Alternatively,
*abhīpsitaprārthanā* means a desire directed toward something desired;
*kutsyaka* means those who are contemptible.
The meaning is "fruitless.
Do not be so;
rather, O wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrin), by your grace, we—those who are performing the sacrifice—[shall be successful].
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the supreme excellence of the two-fold speech.

The meaning is: "May we abide in *sudhā*—that is, in happiness—belonging to these sacrifices or desires; may we quickly become endowed with the visible and invisible happiness resulting from our worship. This is what we pray for.
O Indra, may those [powers] of yours be true for us—those non-harming ones that touch upon [our needs].
May we partake of them, O wielder of the thunderbolt, as one enjoys the milk of cows.
O Indra, may those [powers] of yours be true and non-violent for us—those touches by which we may obtain enjoyment, O wielder of the thunderbolt, like that of a milch-cow. 13.
"Indra, they are ours"—that is, they belong to us.

"They are true": in both instances, the vowel *ā* is a Vedic (chāndasa) form of the nominative plural; this is because the word *san* is used as a specific qualifier in the grammatical rule (*nirdeśaviśeṣaṇatvāt*). "Tā" means those such [beings]; "upaspṛśaḥ" means those who touch.
"Upaspṛśaḥ" refers to praises that touch you by approaching you. "Te" means "by your grace. "Satyāḥ santu" means "may they be true," that is, may they be consistent with reality.
The meaning is: may they be perceivers of your excellent qualities.
Moreover, "ahimsantī" means: may they be non-violent toward us, and may they be free from hostility; that is to say, because of their praise, may they be free from causing agitation.
O Indra, may we obtain through those hymns of praise the enjoyments—both seen and unseen—that belong to you;
in this regard, there is an illustration:
"like milch-cows."
Just as the owner of cows receives the enjoyment of their milk and other products,
so too do those [virtues] become real through connection with the past.
When the handless and footless earth grew by the powers of the discerning ones, you,
turning to the right, struck down Śuṣṇa for every living being.
Though handless and footless, the Earth grew great through his powers; with the skillful acts of the wise, you struck down Śuṣṇa from every side for the sake of all living beings. 14.
O Indra, when the earth was handless— devoid of hands— and footless— devoid of feet—
the meaning being that it was devoid of human activity—
it grew and flourished through the *śacīs*, the deeds associated with the gods such as yourself who are worthy of praise (*vedyānām*).
The meaning is "prosperous with wealth, grain, and so forth.
At that time, you, having circumambulated—that is, having surrounded—the earth in such a manner so as to be moving clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*), [you struck] the Asura Śuṣṇa for the sake of Viśvāyu;
the dative case is used here in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).
O you who move unimpeded everywhere, for the sake of this king, the son of Urvaśī, you have struck him— *niśiśnathaḥ* means you have beaten him thoroughly—
or rather:

When a certain earth—devoid of hands and feet—was produced by the illusory forms and deeds of the Asuras to serve as a covering for Śuṣṇa, and having enveloped the Asura Śuṣṇa, it stood surrounding him in a clockwise direction and grew; then, you struck down that illusory earth for the sake of allowing entry to Viśvāyu, the all-pervading host of Maruts.
Drink, drink the Soma, O heroic Indra! Do not fail us, you who are the possessor of wealth among the Vasus.
Protect the singers and the patrons; bestow upon us great riches and make us prosperous.
Drink, drink, O Indra, hero, the Soma! Do not fail us, you who possess all wealth and are the giver of riches. Protect the singers and the patrons; O wealthy one, grant us great abundance. 15.

1. By means of *ta*-bandha (the suffix -ta). 2. Regarding *ta* in the sense of "for that purpose" (*tādarthye*)... [the form] *viśvāyave* does not exist. The repetition *piba-piba* is for the purpose of demonstrating an excessive frequency (*vīpsā*).
O heroic and brave Indra, drink this self-pressed Soma quickly;
that is to say, drink the Soma as swiftly as possible before the time for the sacrifice passes.
The word *ha* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).

O Vasavāna, you who possess the *vasu*s—meaning riches—you are the most excellent *vasu*; as such, may you not suffer harm. That is to say, do not injure us with the fault arising from the transgression of the time for sacrifice.

It is improper to harm you, who are so highly praised, by causing deficiency in your ritual performance. Furthermore, O Indra, protect the singers—those who praise you—and the liberal patrons—the sacrificers endowed with wealth in the form of oblations—preserving them from the defect of ritual deficiency born of negligence.
Furthermore, in both instances, the genitive case *mahaḥ* and *rāyaḥ* is used in the sense of the instrumental;
thus, with *mahaḥ* (meaning "with greatness") and *rāyaḥ* (meaning "with wealth"), make us (*naḥ*) *revataḥ*, that is, make us possessed of riches.
"Yajāmahe" is the seventh hymn, consisting of seven verses.
The first and seventh are *triṣṭubh* meters;
the fifth is an *abhimāriṇī*.
It is called *dvirdaśakavatībhisāriṇī* because it consists of two sets of twelve [syllables]. The remaining four are *jagatī* verses. The seers and deities are as before.
And thus it is introduced [in the Anukramaṇī]: "We worship Indra today... [and] others; these two are Triṣṭubhs, and the fifth is an Abhisāriṇī.
On the fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), by repeating the third and fifth [verses], the three Hotṛ-priests should each insert a triplet (*tṛca*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'We worship Indra, whose right hand holds the thunderbolt'—thus the second [verse] is exactly the same" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.11).
Let us worship Indra, who holds the thunderbolt in his right hand, the charioteer of the bay horses that range in various directions.
May he, the bearded one, brandishing his arms, come forth like a bull; may he, being invoked by our armies, appear with his bounty.

We worship Indra, who has the thunderbolt as his right hand, the charioteer of the bay steeds, the master of those who follow different paths. Let him raise his beard; let him stand erect; let him be manifest with his armies, displaying himself with his bounty. 1.
We worship Indra; we honor him with oblations characterized by Soma.
Of what sort?

O wielder of the thunderbolt in your right hand (*vajradakṣiṇa*), he whose right hand constantly holds the *vajra* for the slaying of enemies; the charioteer (*rathyam*) who brings forth the two horses named *harī*, those steeds of various actions such as drawing the chariot, belonging to those of diverse activities (*vivratānām*).
That Indra, immediately after drinking the Soma, shook his own beard again and again; while shaking it, he appeared aloft, rising upward.

Furthermore, with his armies—the hosts of the Maruts and others—he struck out in various ways against his enemies, destroying them with *rādhas* (wealth or bounty)—the instrumental case being used here in the sense of the accusative.
*Rādhaḥ* means wealth.
Because of the hearing of the prefix *vi-* [in the root], there is an ellipsis of the action of "joining" (*yoga*).
He bestows variously upon the praisers.
Indra, the Maghavan, the slayer of Vṛtra, finds his two bay steeds in the forest; he becomes the destroyer of enemies through his riches.
As Ṛbhu, Vāja, and Ṛbhukṣan, he rules over his might; I humble even the name of the Dāsa.

"O tawny steeds! Now indeed, that wealth which Indra finds in the wood, the bounteous Vṛtra-slayer has become the subduer through his strikes. As Ṛbhu, Vāja, and Ṛbhukṣan, he rules over power; I humble even the name of the Dāsa. (2)
The two bay horses (*harī*) belonging to this Indra—
[the word] *vana* refers to either the sacrifice (*yajña*), in which the gods take delight (*vanayante*), or the forest (*araṇya*)— in that [place],
he quickly (*nu*) finds (*vide*), that is, obtains, wealth (*vasu*) characterized by straightness (*ṛjīpa*) or consisting of fodder (*yavasa*).
Or rather: those two bay steeds (*harī*) of this Indra, which quickly become [ready] for the sake of enjoying the forest and for the acquisition of wealth (*vasu*),
by means of those two bay steeds, Indra— the possessor of wealth (*maghavān*)— becomes the slayer of Vṛtra (*vṛtrahā*), that is, the destroyer of the demon named Vṛtra or of the cloud.

Moreover, Ṛbhu is radiant, Vāja is powerful, and Ṛbhukṣan is the great Indra; [this is] through the power of power. [Notes: 1. *ta*: due to the deficiency of the ritual action (*karmavaiguṇya*). 2. *ta*: the word "and" (*ca*) is not present. 3. *tabha*: they resort to this (*saṃbhajante 'smin*). 4. *tamu*: characterized by the *ṛjīṣa*. 5. *tabha1.2.4*: the word "wealth" (*vasu*) is not present.

He looks upon or rules over strength or wealth; or rather, he looks toward—that is, encounters and advances against—the host (*dala*) of his enemies. By his grace, I too shall humble even the very name (*nāma*) of that enemy who is to be subdued by a servant. "Name" (*nāma*) is so called because it is bent down (*namyate*); that very head (*śiras*) I shall strike down—I destroy it. How much more so other limbs? Or else, I shall destroy even his designation (*nāmadheya*), let alone the enemy himself.

When the golden-hued thunderbolt is fixed upon the chariot that the two bay steeds of Yama draw, Maghavan, renowned from of old, mounts it along with the patrons; Indra, the lord of long-famed strength, arrives.

When the thunderbolt, the gold, and the chariot for which his two bay steeds draw come from here, Maghavan, renowned from of old, Indra—the lord of far-famed booty—ascends it together with the patrons.

When Indra takes up his own weapon, the golden and most beautiful vajra, for the purpose of slaying the enemy— the word "takes" being understood from the context; the word "han" (slays) serves as a filler— then at that time, his two bay horses, the *harī*, carry the chariot and bring it specifically to the destination to be reached.

Maghavā increases strength through gifts; likewise, by means of rain, he increases—the root *vṛdh* meaning "to increase"—the power (*vaśvaḥ*) and strength of the entire world. We praise that very same heroic strength of that Indra, each and every one of its qualities.
The meaning is: we praise each and every power by which Indra slays his enemies.
O Indra, Vimada has generated for you this ancient, most abundant storm for the sake of the bounteous giver;
knowing well his enjoyment of this food, he shall provide for the Great One as a herdsman provides for the cattle.

O Indra, those Vimadas have generated for you a never-before-seen and most abundant [offering] for the bounteous giver; for you, the wise one, know his enjoyment, so that you may make it great like a herdsman driving cattle.

O Indra, for you, the giver of beautiful gifts (*sudānu*), we, the Vimadas— those named Vimada— have generated (*vyañjanat*), that is, have performed, this particular hymn of praise (*stoma*) for the sake of your magnificent bounty.
Here, there is a shift in grammatical person between the preceding and following clauses.
Of what sort?

[Drink] this unprecedented Soma, Indra; drink this honeyed one, pressed in the ladle. Bestow wealth upon us; in your exhilaration, O Puruṣa, O possessor of many riches, you shall bestow thousands. You are waxing great. 1.
O Indra, you, drink this such soma. Of what kind?
Sweet, endowed with the nature of sweetness, pressed out—that is, filtered—within the *camū* vessels, the two pressing-boards.

Immediately after that, O *puruvaso*, O Indra, possessor of much wealth, when there is for you (*vaḥ*) a special exhilaration (*vimade*) born of Soma, bestow (*dhāraya*) riches (*rayim*) upon us (*asme*); establish them firmly within us. Of what kind? Thousandfold (*sahasriṇam*), meaning abundant in number.
The meaning is: "Since we shall perform the sacrifice for your sake once again with the wealth given by you yourself, therefore, bestow wealth upon us.
For this reason, you are "desirous of speaking" (vivakṣase); this is a great favor from you.
You are great.

We approach you with sacrifices, with hymns, and with oblations. O Lord of powers, of all powers, in your exhilaration, bestow upon us the most excellent treasure. You are waxing great. tvāṃ yajñebhirukthairupahavyebhirīmahe | śacīpate śacīnāṃ vi vo made śreṣṭhaṃ no dhehi vāryaṃ vivakṣase || 2 || We approach you with sacrifices, with hymns, and with oblations. O Lord of powers, of all powers, in your exhilaration, bestow upon us the most excellent treasure. You are waxing great.

O Indra, we— approaching you with sacrifices such as the Soma-offerings, with hymns characterized by the *śastra*-recitations, and with oblations such as the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*)— we entreat you; for the prefix *upa-* is heard, its connection implies simultaneity, and thus "approaching you" is supplied— we beg for the wealth we desire.
Therefore, O *śacīpate*, Lord of powers, it is not that you are the protector of only some actions; rather, the meaning is that you are the protector of all *śacīs*, that is, of all actions.
Being thus entreated, grant (*dhehi*) to us (*naḥ*) that which is desirable (*vārya*), to be chosen, most excellent, and most praiseworthy—namely, wealth consisting of horses and other such things.
The remainder is clear.

You who are the lord of desirable things, the impeller of wealth, O Indra, the protector of those who praise you—protect us from hatred and from distress in your exhilaration; you grow great. You are the lord of desirable things, the impeller of wealth, O Indra, the protector of those who praise you—in your exhilaration, protect us from hatred and from distress; you grow great.
O Indra, you who are the lord (*pati*)—the master—of desirable riches (*vāryāṇāṃ dhanānām*);

you are the instigator (*coditā*) of the benefactor (*radhasya*) and the singer of praise, impelling them through the granting of wealth. Furthermore, O Indra, since you are the protector (*avitā*) of those who praise you, do you protect (*pāhi*) us from our enemies (*dviṣaḥ*) during your various exhilarations (*made*) born of Soma.
Protect us from distress and from evil. Why is this said?
Because you, being *vivakṣase*, are great.

O powerful ones, you two, masters of wondrous power, churned forth the united pair when you were implored by Vimada, O Nāsatyas; indeed, you two churned them out. yuvaṃ śakrā māyāvinā samīcī niramanthatam | vimudena yadīḷitā nāsatyā niramanthatam || 4 || O powerful ones, you two, masters of wondrous power, churned forth the united pair when you were implored by Vimada, O Nāsatyas; indeed, you two churned them out.
1. By means of those characteristics of the treatise.
2. Ta1.7-bha6—most praiseworthy; Ta5—most praiseworthy.

O Śakra-s, you two who are capable in deeds such as the slaying of enemies, O Aśvins, you two who are possessed of *māyā*, i.e., wise or skilled in deceiving the enemy—you two, being *samīcī*, joined together with one another, churned out Agni, you produced Agni.

Because it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa, “The two Aśvins are the Adhvaryus” (AiB 1.18), the churning of the fire is appropriate for the two Aśvins. When were the two Aśvins invited? It is said: when, O Nāsatyas, you two were impelled—that is, praised—by me with the *Vimada* hymn, then and there you two, having come together, performed the churning; this is the meaning.
All the gods lamented for the two who were joined together and stretched out;
the gods said to the Nāsatyas, "Bring her back again!"
All the gods took pity on the two as they were falling from their chariot. The Nāsatyas said to the gods, "Bring them back! (5)

O Aśvins, when you two were being urged at the time of churning, while the two fire-sticks (*araṇī*) were joined together, facing one another, and emitting sparks as they were being rubbed—then all the gods, Indra and the others, took pity on you and praised you.
Furthermore, the gods spoke to you, O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins; what did they say?
"May you two carry [us] back again"— that is, may you two, standing face-to-face, repeatedly perform such actions as are the causes for the maintenance of the world. Or alternatively:
The gods said to the Nāsatyas: "The fire being produced by you two must, moreover, carry our oblations to its support."
Honey is my ancient source; honey is my renewed source.
O gods, by your divine power, may you two make this for us full of honey.
Sweet be my departure; sweet be my return. O Gods, by your divine power, make both of these for us sweet. 6.

O Aśvins, may my departure from home—my going away—be sweet (*madhumat*). Here, by the word *madhu*, which denotes a specific kind of essence, the joy residing therein is indicated. The ellipsis is: "By your grace, may it be filled with joy."
May the return journey, the coming back home, be full of sweetness—that is, endowed with joy.
Furthermore, O two gods, you two who are radiant, make us full of sweetness—endowed with joy. By what means? It is said: [as follows].
"By means of divinity" means by way of divinity; that is to say, through the possession of the lordly powers (aiśvarya) of the deities, such as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and so forth.
"Bhadram" is the eleventh hymn, the ninth [in this section]. According to the technical definition beginning with "tuṣṭādi," this is also an āstārapāṅkta; its deity is Soma.
By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "and a seer [is named] after another," the seer is Vimada Vāsukra, who is either Prājāpatya, Aindra, or both.
Thus it has been enumerated: "The eleven [hymns] beginning with *Bhadram* are dedicated to Soma.
The application (*viniyoga*) is concluded.
Bestow upon us a blessed mind, skill, and mental resolve.
Then, in the friendship of your juice, may we rejoice in its exhilaration like cattle in a pasture; you yourself are eager to bestow it.
Send to us a blessed mind, and skill, and mental power. Then, in the friendship of your juice, may we rejoice in its exhilaration like cattle in a pasture; you are about to speak forth.

1. *ta-nirmathitau* (those two rubbed out). 2. *ta-sutābhyām agniḥ*; *bha-yuvām agniḥ* (by those two sons, Agni [is produced]; O Bhaga, you two, Agni). 3. *ta-su-sthitvāvahatām* (having stood well, they two carried away). 4. *ta-vam abhi asmādīyāni* (O *v-am*, toward our [offerings]). O Soma, you, *naḥ*—our—*manaḥ*—mind—*bhadram*—auspicious, *dhātaya*—lead;
that is to say, make our mind possessed of virtuous intentions.
Likewise, [lead] Dakṣa, and even Dakṣa as well.
[The root] *dakṣ* means "to grow.
Lead even the grown, all-pervading Inner Self (*antarātman*) to auspiciousness, characterized by the performance of what is beneficial.
The meaning is: "Make our inner self a doer of auspicious deeds. Furthermore, "lead our *kratu*—that is, our wisdom—to what is auspicious," characterized by the resolve for the good;
the meaning is, "make us resolute toward the auspicious."

Now, O [Indra], let your praisers rejoice—that is, take delight—in that friendship characterized by the relationship of the one praised and the one praising, and of the worshipper and the worshipped; therein they shall find pleasure.
An illustration for this is:
"like cattle in a pasture."

Just as cows delight in fodder and take pleasure in it, so too [is it here]. Under what condition? When there is *vimada*—the exhilaration caused by various kinds of soma—which pertains to you and is connected to *andhas*, that is, to this food, namely soma.
Why is this so?
Because you wish to speak, you become great.
O Soma, they all abide within the heart, touching it during all ritual duties.
Now, these desires of mine, seeking wealth, spread abroad in your exhilaration; you wish to speak them out.
They dwell within my heart, O Soma, in all their laws. Now these desires of mine spread abroad for you, seeking wealth, as I am eager to speak in the exhilaration of the soma-juice. 2.

O Soma, the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), who touch your heart with their hymns of praise, sit in all stations—that is, they remain praising you in all places. Now, when this state of yours has come to be—namely, the various desires or longings arising from the occasion of your diverse exhilaration (*vi vo made*) caused by the drinking of Soma;
that is to say, for the purpose of the Soma sacrifice.
Desiring wealth, seeking riches, and longing for my fortune— from my heart, so it is understood—
they spread forth; they arise.
Why is this so?
Because you wish to speak, you become great.
Moreover, O Soma, I, being simple-minded, violate your sacred laws;
therefore, as a father is to his son, be gracious to us in your exhilaration—O you who are praised for your wondrous deeds, you wax great.

Moreover, O Soma, I, being simple-minded, violate your sacred laws; therefore, as a father toward his son, be gracious to us in your exhilaration. Even though you, a host of warriors, desire to speak against us.
Moreover, O Soma, I [have observed] your *vratāni*— the sacrificial rites and other duties— with *pākya*, that is, with fully ripened wisdom that perceives all objects;
or alternatively,
*pākya* is an adjective qualifying the *vrata*.
"Pākayāni" means fully matured or perfected;
"pra mināmi" means I cast away;
it means I perform [the action] with excellence.

Now, after the sacrifice (*yāga*), when there is various exhilaration (*vividha-mada*)—in that state, "be gracious" (*mṛḷa*) to us, that is, make us happy. "Bestowing wonderful [gifts]" (*abhi-citra-dhāt*), having stood before us, bestow [them] from the *śastra* and so forth; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "protect us.
Therein is an illustration.
"Like a father for his son":
just as a father brings happiness for the sake of his son and protects the son alone from everything, so too [is it here].
Since I, being made happy and protected, perform the Soma sacrifice again and again for your sake, therefore the meaning is: "make me happy and protect me."
Why is it said thus? Because you desire to speak; that is to say, you are great, and the great ones bring happiness to their devotees and protect them.
Our prayers go forth together like unrestrained floods;
O Soma, for our life, maintain our mental power as one maintains the cups—at your exhilarating outpouring, you desire to speak aloud.
Together, O Soma, our thoughts go forth like streams of those without vows; for our life, in your exhilaration, you desire to pour out our power like cups with your stream. 4.
1. The characteristic of performing that which is not auspicious;
2. These [are] the [verses]: "O Soma, be for us a protector from every side, one who cannot be deceived."
Repel them, O King; you have repelled them in your exhilaration. Let not the evil-minded master us; you speak forth [the truth].

O Soma, be our protector from every side, you who are inviolable. O King, drive away those who would harm us; in the exhilaration of the juice, let not the malevolent have power over us. You are about to speak forth. 7.
O Soma, you who are inviolable (*adābhya*)—unharmable by anyone—be our protector (*gopā*) from every side (*viśvataḥ*).
Furthermore, O King, O radiant Soma, drive away (*sedha*) those who would exhaust us; cast them far from us or utterly destroy them.
Let the one who speaks ill of us (*duḥśaṃsa*), the proclaimer of our existing or non-existing deeds, have no power over us (*mā īśata*).
The meaning is: "Through your grace, may there be no one at all who speaks against us.
For what purpose is all this being prayed for?
It is for the sake of your various exhilarations (*vi vo made*)—that is, for the satisfaction produced by the oblations during your various states of intoxication.
Therefore, since you wish to speak, you are great.
O Soma, you who are skilled in deeds, be watchful for us so that we may win the prize;
as one who knows the field better than man, in your exhilaration, protect us from the malevolent and from distress; you desire to speak forth.

O Soma, you who are well-disposed toward us, be watchful for our welfare; as one who knows the field better than man, protect us from the stingy and from distress in your exhilaration—you, O Virvākṣas, desire to speak forth.
O Soma, you who are skillful in action, possessed of beautiful wisdom, and the supreme obtainer of the field—be watchful for us, for the bestowing of vital strength and the granting of food.
Furthermore, protect us from the malicious man, from the one who seeks to do us harm;
protect us from distress and from sin.
For what purpose?
"In your exhilaration" (*vi vo made*); the meaning is: for the sake of generating satisfaction through your oblations, such as the *soma* and others.
If you wish to speak, you are great.
O Indu, you are our most excellent slayer of Vṛtra and the auspicious friend of Indra;
when they call upon you in the encounter, in the exhilaration of the soma-pressing, you, fighting for the sake of offspring, desire to bestow it abundantly.

O Indu, you are our most excellent slayer of Vṛtra; O Indu, you are the auspicious friend of Indra. When they invoke him in battle, in the exhilaration of the soma-juice, as they fight for the sake of offspring, may you be proclaimed aloud. 9.
O Vṛtrahantama, O Indu, O Soma, you who are the supreme slayer of enemies, you who are Indra’s auspicious, bliss-bestowing friend and ally—protect us; this is the ellipsis. When? It is said:
at the winning of offspring (tokasātau).
*Toka* is a name for offspring.
*Sāti* is a form derived from the verbal root *paṇu*, meaning "to give."
*Tokasāti* is a specific term for a battle, derived from the sense that "offspring (*apatyam*) is won (*sāti*) in this";
it means "in that [battle] which is exceedingly great."

In the encounter, in the battle, while fighting—that is, while waging war—when the enemy folk call upon us from all sides for the sake of combat, then [O Agni], become our protector; this is the meaning. On what occasion?
In your exhilaration (*vi-vakṣase*), caused by the joy of various oblations offered by men,
you become great;
for it is indeed fitting that the protection of the great should be so.
This indeed is the swift, exhilarating draught, the beloved of Indra; it increases his strength.
This is the swelling belly-full; in your exhilaration, O gods, may it increase the inspired thought of the sage as you proclaim it.
1. ta-bha6-ca | 2.

ga-ta-bha- 'yat yadā' is not present | This | gha | he | swift | crusher | of Indra | shall increase | beloved | this | of Kakṣīvat | the great | may it expand | for you | in exhilaration | the thought | of the sage | as you desire to speak aloud || 10 ||

This indeed is the most excellent Soma, renowned as Indra’s own, purified by us; it is swift in all undertakings, resonant by nature, intoxicating, exhilarating, dear to Indra, and a source of satisfaction. May this Soma increase our thought; he has increased it. This Soma, through the leaf of Kakṣīvat—of whom?—of the great sage (vipra), the wise one, has increased his thought, that is, his wisdom.
In the same way, it means that he should increase our understanding as well. The remainder has been explained.
This [Soma] sends forth strengths consisting of cattle for the liberal Brahmin;
this one, the most excellent for the seven [priests], has furthered the blind and the lame—so may you proclaim it in your exhilaration.

This one sends forth strengths for the liberal patron, the Brahmin; he brings cattle-wealth. This one has brought forth the hero for the seven [sisters]. For your exhilaration, may he further the blind and the lame. You desire to speak forth [this praise]. 11.

This Soma impels— that is, bestows— food-wealth consisting of cattle upon the wise, inspired, and liberal sacrificer who has offered oblations. Furthermore, this very Soma grants excellent, desirable wealth to the seven Hotṛ priests.
By granting sight to the blind, eyeless seer Dīrghatamas, and by granting a leg to the lame seer Śroṇa Parāvr̥j, he thus delivered both of them, having caused them to flourish preeminently.
The remainder is clear.
The tenth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "pra hi," is in the Anuṣṭubh meter and has Pūṣan as its deity.
The first and fourth verses are in the Uṣṇih meter.
The seer is the same as before.
And thus it has been introduced: “*Pra hi nava pauṣṇam ānuṣṭubham ādyā-caturthyā uṣṇihau*”;
the application [of these verses] has already been explained.
Toward him proceed these desirable prayers, like teams of horses;
may the mighty Pūṣan, whose chariot is drawn by teams, and the two Dāstṛs, protect us.
Forth indeed go our prayers; the desirable teams advance. May the two Dāstṛs, Pūṣan with his team-drawn chariot, and the mighty one protect us. 1.
For this reason, our inspired thoughts (*manīṣāḥ*), which consist of hymns of praise, go forth—meaning they proceed pre-eminently—to reach Pūṣan by means of perceiving his qualities.
Of what nature are they? They are desirable (*spārhāḥ*), being worthy of longing because they are endowed with all virtues, and they are numerous (*niyutaḥ*).
Or, because of its restriction (*niyamanāt*) or its application (*niyojanāt*), this is its form;
it means that we have restricted it, applied it, or uttered it.

Having understood this, in order to return the favor, the two *dastrau* (the destroyers/assailants) should show themselves; the one with the chariot of steeds (*niyudratha*), whose chariot is ever-fixed (*niyataratha*) or yoked (*niyukaratha*), the majestic (*māhinaḥ*) and great god Pūṣan, has entered among us—may he protect us preeminently.
Or rather:
*dastrau* means the two who strike down or diminish [enemies] through their deeds.
The two who bring [the sacrifice] to completion; the word *vitti* means "for the sake of wealth.
Thus, it should be construed as: "May Pūṣan protect the wife and the sacrificer who have become such."
Whose greatness indeed this person, the inspired singer, has attained through his thoughts;
may he take notice of our well-spoken hymns.
1. One whose nature is to hasten; one who is habitually quick. 2. Great and powerful steeds. 3. A great and noble chariot that is well-restrained.

May this wise person, this sacrificer, through his prayers (*dhītibhiḥ*), attain that celebrated greatness (*mahitvam*) of Pūṣan which belongs to him—that greatness consisting of the water gathered in the solar orb (*vātāpyam*). May that god take notice of these beautiful hymns of praise (*sustutīnām*).

He knows the nature of beautiful hymns; like Indu, he is Pūṣan, the bull. He sprinkles upon the citadels; he sprinkles toward our stall. He, who possesses the aforementioned qualities—Pūṣan, the bull—knows the nature of beautiful hymns (the word *svarūpam* is understood). Moreover, like Indu (Soma), this Pūṣan is a bull, the increaser of desires. Being handsome, he sprinkles (*pṛṣāyati*) upon us; likewise, he sprinkles toward (*ā pṛṣāyati*) our stall (*vraja*). The meaning is that he bestows upon us gold, cattle, and other riches.

May we honor you, O God Pūṣan; may we honor you who are the accomplisher of our thoughts and the steadfast supporter of the wise. (4) May we honor you—we, the singers—O radiant God Pūṣan. Of what sort? You who are the accomplisher (*sādhana*) of our own thoughts and desires, and the one who, through service, causes even the wise (*viprāṇām*) to tremble (*ādhravam*).

The seer of sacrifices, the sharer of their portions; the driver of horses for chariots; that seer who is well-disposed toward Manu, the friend who keeps the wise man at ease. (5) *Pratyardhiḥ*: the counterpart or sharer. *Yajñānām*: of sacrifices. *Aśvahayaḥ*: the driver of horses. *Rathānām*: of chariots. *Ṛṣiḥ*: the seer. *Saḥ*: he. *Yaḥ*: who. *Manuhitaḥ*: well-disposed toward Manu (or beneficial to humanity). *Viprasya*: of the wise one. *Yāvayatsukhaḥ*: the friend who drives away [enemies] and brings happiness. (5) The seer (*ṛṣi*) is the beholder of all. He, Pūṣan, is the *pratyardhi*, the sharer of half the portion, of sacrifices. Of chariots, he is the *aśvahaya*, the driver of horses. The root *hi* signifies the act of going. He is one whose nature is to move by means of horses connected to chariots; the meaning is that he is always a traveler by means of a horse-yoked chariot. *Manuhitaḥ* means beneficial to men. He who is the friend of the *vipra*, the wise singer, the one who separates the enemies and brings them happiness—he is such a person, as connected with the preceding verse. (13)
1. This wise person is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); this wise person is the class of sacrificers.
2. *ta1.2-bhava-ya tat*; *ta3.4.5.6.7-bhara-yat*; *bha1.4.6-yat tat*. 3. Sacrificial rites and so forth (*yāgādikarma*).

The lord of her who is longing, and of both the woman in sorrow and the man in sorrow; he, the protector of garments, thoroughly cleanses the woolen cloths of the sheep. 6. Of her who is longing, the lord; and of the woman in sorrow, and of the man in sorrow; the protector of garments; of the sheep; thoroughly; the garments; he cleansed. 6.

The meaning is: the lord and master not only of the *kṣīmat* (the one being milked), but also of the *ajā* (goat)—that is, of the one who is *ādhīṣamāṇā* (being impelled) for her own sake as she is being milked, and of the one who is *śucāyan* (shining/flaming) and *dīptā* (blazing). That is to say, he is the master of the goat as well as of the male animal (*puṃpaśu*) that is shining and blazing.

The god Pūṣan, being thus, driving forth the garments—the ten-fold filters and other cloths—belonging to the sheep (*avīnām*) and the rams (*uraṇānām*), by means of their woolly hairs (*romabhiḥ*), which act as a cloth (*vāsovāyaḥ*); he thoroughly cleanses (*ā marmṛjat*) those clothes that are to be washed by the dyer, purifying them on all sides with light and heat.

The lord of strengths, the lord of nourishments, the friend; the beloved one has vigorously shaken his beard at will—he who is invincible. 7. The lord of strengths, the lord of nourishments, the friend; the beloved one has vigorously shaken his beard at will—he who is invincible. 7.

He is the lord (*īśvara*), Pūṣan; he is the master (*pati*), the owner of all foods such as the *havis* offering and so forth; he is the powerful one (*inaḥ*), the lord (*prabhu*) over all nourishments (*puṣṭīnām*)—that is, over the acts of sustaining all living beings that belong to him—and he is the friend (*sakhā*), acting as a benefactor because he assists everyone. Furthermore, he drinks the Soma belonging to the desiring sacrificer (*haryataḥ*). (This is the ellipsis to be supplied.)

He who is Pūṣan, the invincible—meaning one who cannot be harmed by enemies—is that one who, without effort or exertion, vigorously and variously shakes out his beard; this is how it connects with what precedes.
O Pūṣan, may your goats turn the pole of your chariot hither; you are the friend of every seeker, born of old, and unshakable. 8.
O Pūṣan, O God, may the goats turn toward and draw the pole of your chariot;
that is to say, they carry it.

You, who are a friend to every supplicant—that is, to everyone who seeks—because you bestow the desired object upon them, who are "sanajāḥ" (born of old), who have existed for a long time, and who are "anapacyutaḥ" (unfallen), not having departed from your own office; such is the connection with the phrase "your chariot."

May the majestic Pūṣan protect our chariot with his vigor; may he be the awakener of spoils and hear this our invocation. 9. asmākam | ūrjā | ratham | pūṣā | aviṣṭu | māhinaḥ | bhuvat | vājānām | budhaḥ | imam | naḥ | śṛṇavat | havam || 9 ||
May the mighty Pūṣan, the great one, protect and guard our own chariot with vigor, strength, or food. Furthermore,
may he be the awakener and increaser of strengths— that is, of foods—
and may he hear this such-like invocation of ours.

1. In the protection of those who nourish [them]; in the making of those who nourish [them] well. 2. Of one who has not departed from supporting [them]; of one who has not fallen away from supporting [them]. 3. With sap and vigor; with sap and strength.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of twenty-four verses beginning with “*asatsu me*,” is the seerly work (*ārṣa*) of Vasukra, the son of Indra; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and addressed to Indra.
Thus it is recorded in the *Anukramaṇī*: “*asatsu* [consists of] twenty-four [verses]; it is addressed to Indra; the seer is Vasukra.
This hymn is employed in the *marutvatīya* recitation during the *mahāvrata* ritual.
Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "O singer, when these [senses] are absent, my impulse is directed toward you; drink the Soma, O fierce one, for that which you desire" (Ai. Ā. 5.1.1).
When I am enraged against the wicked, I am impetuous in my desire to help the one who presses the juice and performs sacrifice.
I am the slayer of him who offers no blessing, who is false to his vows, and who, being crooked, approaches with deceit.

It is not so, O singer; that impetuous onset of mine is for the sake of assisting the sacrificer who presses the soma. I am the slayer of him who gives no blessing, the destroyer of the one who is false to his vow, the crooked, and the arrogant.
In the *Vasukra* hymns, Indra is praised for the most part.
Now, Indra, wishing to praise Vasukra, addresses his own son and declares his own power, so that he, having come to know the form of the deity, may praise him with ease.
Or else:

Due to the metaphorical treatment of cause and effect as one—as in the statement, "The self, indeed, is named 'son'" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.15.11)—Vasukra, abiding in the form of Indra, praises himself; in some places, however, he praises Indra. O singer, O praiser: "my" (*me*) "good" (*mṛ*) "he" (*saḥ*), that such "impulse" (*abhivegaḥ*), meaning an approach or a particular modification of the mind, "exists" (*asat*), i.e., it is present.

"Whatever [gift] I bestow as a desired object for the sake of the *yajamāna*— the sacrificer who presses the Soma for my exhilaration with great zeal— I am also the giver of the *āśīr*. Here, *āśīr* elsewhere means a prayer, but by implication it refers to the offered oblation that has been prayed for."
He gave that to me, the person who does not give;
or rather,
"blessing" (āśīḥ) refers to the curd used as a mixing agent for the Soma.
"Of him"—
meaning of one who does not sacrifice with Soma—
"I am the slayer," that is, I become his thorough destroyer.
Of what kind? "Satyadhṛtam" means a destroyer of truth;
that is to say, one who speaks falsehoods.
‘Vṛjināyantam’ means one who desires to commit evil; ‘ābhum’ means pervading.
If today I were to lead forth for battle those who are eager for the gods and who have exerted themselves with their bodies—
for you, O Bull, I would now prepare the powerful, well-pressed fifteen-fold draught, the fierce one that delights the five tribes.

If I were to bring together for battle those godless ones who are harming their own bodies, then at home I shall cook for you a vigorous bull; I shall prepare the sharp pressed juice, the fifteenfold draught. 2.
"Whenever I shall bring together for battle those who do not desire the gods— that is, those non-sacrificers (ayajvanaḥ) who are unwilling to worship the gods—
how [shall I bring them]? [I shall bring them] "with their own bodies," that is, with their own persons, "glowing," endowed with a brilliance characterized by self-satisfaction.
The meaning is "well-nourished.
Then, O Indra, I—accompanied by the *ṛtvij* priests and others—"to thee" (*te*), "tumram," meaning impelling or powerful;
that is to say, "fat" (*pīvānam*).
"I cook for you a bull capable of sprinkling [the herd],

a male, and furthermore, the intense, intoxicating juice that has been pressed— the fifteenfold. From the first day onwards, throughout the fifteen lunar days of the bright fortnight, the leaves are produced by an increment of one."
But during the dark fortnight, they are withdrawn;
because it is of such a nature, the fifteenth [day] is called Soma. Him.
Alternatively,
it means that which is endowed with the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* *stomas*, namely the midday libation (*mādhyandina-savana*).
"I pour down" (*ni piṃśva*) means that I sprinkle or cast [the soma] into the *daśāpavitra* filter, the *droṇakalaśa* vat, the *camasa* cups, or into the fire.
1. There is no such thing as "ta-’tu”. 2. That which is being sought is "ta-prārthyamānam”. 3. For one who desires [it], there is "ayajanaḥ" (non-sacrificing).
4. In the case of *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, *pra*, and so forth; 5.

in the case of *ta*, *ca*, *ma*, *sa*, *pā*, *tre*, *ṇa*, and *m* [the rule applies] in the fire; *ta*, *ca*, *ma*, *sa*, *pā*, *tre*, *a*, *m*, and *va*; *ta*, *ca*, *ma*, *sa*, *pā*, *tre*, *tha*, *m*, and *a* [apply] in the fire, *ca*, and *mu*.
"I do not know him who, being godless, speaks thus when he has struck down [the foe] in the encounter."
When he, the fierce one, spoke of death as an obstacle, they proclaim to me, "The bulls have come."
"No," he said, "I do not know him who speaks thus, having struck down the godless in the encounter. When the fierce encounter has come here, then indeed my bulls will be heard abroad. (3)

I do not know—that is, I am not aware of—any person other than myself who can say, "In battle, I have slain those people who do not desire the gods and who hate the gods, such as the Rākṣasas and others.
The meaning is that there is no slayer of enemies in combat other than I. Furthermore, whenever I behold a battle being cast down or defeated [by me], [then I know it].
Of what kind? "Righāvat" means possessing mutual injury; that is to say, extremely cruel.
Then, indeed, [the wise] proclaim my own deeds, which are like those of a bull—deeds of prowess like that of a proud bull.
"The wise" is the ellipsis;
the two particles *it* and *it* are for filling the meter.
When I dwelt among unknown tribes, all the wealthy lords were mine;
whether I conquer one who is at ease or one who is striving, I crush him upon the mountain like a beast in a cave.
When I was among unknown tribes, all the wealthy lords were mine. Either I conquer the secure and prosperous man, or I destroy him on the mountain, he who dwells in a cave. 4.

Whenever I sit down for battle in unknown encounters—unrecognized by [my opponents] through their physical strength, weapons, missiles, or power—at that time all the *maghavans*, the seers possessing wealth characterized by oblations and ascetic heat, sit down in the presence of me, Indra, as I exist in this manner; that is to say, they praise me, who am the subduer of my enemies, and thus torment [their foes]. Moreover, [they sit] while I am present for the sake of *kṣema*, the protection of the world.
The suffix *ākāra* occurs in the sense of what is desired.
I shall indeed conquer—that is, utterly destroy—the great enemy who overcomes all;
there is no doubt regarding this destruction.
*It* is a filler particle. Having seized that great enemy by the feet (*pādagṛhya*), I cast him down (*pra kṣiṇāmi*)—I hurl or throw him—upon the mountain (*parvate*).
Neither the enclosure nor the mountains hold me back when I intend to act;
from my very vitals the one with quick ears shall flee in fear, and the scorner shall tremble.

No, indeed! "Om! they say; they hold me back in the struggle. Neither the mountains can restrain me when I set my mind upon it. When the vital point is pierced, the one with quick ears trembles in fear; even from here, the rays shall rush forth after the youth.
"Vai u" means "indeed.
In battle (*vṛjane*), when I have arrived for the sake of combat, no one restrains me; none are capable of restraining me.

Whatever deed I intend (*manasye*)—desiring to perform with my mind—even the mountains (*parvatāsaḥ*), such as the Himavat and others, which are incapable of yielding, are not able to withstand that deed intended by my mind. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, at the mere sound of my name, Indra, the asura named Krudhukarṇa—or indeed, Krudhukarṇa, meaning "short-eared," one with dull hearing or even a deaf creature such as a stationary ant—[fled].
[Note: 1. *ta*, *bhara*, *mu*, *deva*: those desiring the gods;
2. *ga*, *bha*, *pa*: they proclaim; *tā*, *bha*, *ha*: he proclaims.]

3. The reading "ta-vṛjaneṣu" does not exist [in this context]. 4. In the versions *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, it is "atitaraṇakṣamāḥ"; in the *udgītha* version, it is "atibhākṣamāḥ. *Bhayāte* means "he fears. Furthermore, *vevet* means "just so," like *krudhukarṇa*. *Vanu vyūnū* means "day after day. *Kiraṇaḥ*: this contains an implied meaning (*antarṇīta-artha*). It refers to the sun, which possesses rays (*kiraṇavān*) or beams (*raśmivān*). *Samejāt*: it moves properly or stirs; the meaning is that it proceeds according to its fixed law (*niyamena prayāti*). || 15 ||

May those who drink the cooked oblation, who are without Indra, who sit upon their arms, and who wander about for the sake of glory— those bold ones who have reviled our friendship— be turned back from among them by the ancient ones.

Behold now those here who drink what has been cooked, who are without Indra, whose arms are cut off, and who fall before the arrow—those who have boldly reviled you in their friendship; may the ancient ones now turn away from them! 6.

In this world, I, Indra, behold—swiftly—I the Asuras and others who, having seized the cooked offerings such as Soma and other oblations, drink them; who, deprived of Indra by me, weaken the sacrificers with their arms (*bāhukṣadaḥ*); and who, rushing forth for the sake of destruction (*śarave*), fall upon [the sacrificers]. Against such beings as these, my own weapons (*pavyaḥ*) turn upward and strike them down.
The word *ā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
They, acting like friends, revile me—who am great, a friend, dear like a comrade, and a doer of what is beneficial.
The particle *v* is used here as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).
Furthermore, my weapons swiftly descend upon them.
The days have come; life has extended. May the one who was first not be surpassed by the one who comes later.
Two garments encompass him who has clothed himself on the further shore of this world.

You have become. Om. You have grown strong. Apart. Om. Life has reached its full span. Let the former pride now depart; let the later pride now depart. Two are the garments at the further shore. He who entered the other side of this world-space was not born. || 7 ||
In this context, because Indra is addressed in the second person, Suka praises Indra.
The particle *vu* is used for emphasis.
O Indra, *vabhūḥ*: you alone manifest yourself.
The meaning is: "From time to time, you alone sprinkle the earth; no one else.

In all instances where there is an indirect reference (parokṣanirdeśa) at the beginning of a passage starting with *ānaḍ*, the word *bhavat*—which has the same meaning as the pronoun *yuṣmad*—should be supplied to bring about direct address (*pratyakṣakaraṇa*) through the middle person (*madhyamapuruṣa*), so that the context may form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*).
The particle *vi* signifies variety (*vaividhya*).
The particle *ca* is used here in the sense of "and.
*Āyus* is said to mean life. You are Indra; furthermore, you are variously the wind (*vāyu*), for you pervade (*vyāpnoti*) by means of speech (*vāc*).
The meaning is that he lives until the dissolution of all beings (*bhūtasaṃplava*).
Furthermore, you, Indra, are ancient (*purātana*) and have existed from before; *vnu* means quickly (*kṣipram*), and *vdarpa* is in the sense of "tearing apart" (*vidāraṇe*).
‘The suffix -si is frequently used in the subjunctive (leṭ). He shatters his enemies with the thunderbolt.
Another enemy, distinct from him, trembles.
The particle *nu* has the sense of negation.
It does not cause you, O Indra, to be pierced;
rather, the meaning is that you alone destroy the entire host of enemies.
Moreover, you, O Indra, are beyond (*pāre*) such a world (*vrajas*), that is to say, beyond the three worlds (*trailokya*).

Having remained within as the essence of the cause of creation in the form of the most subtle wind, [the Lord] entered—that is, pervaded—everywhere you, O Indra. By implication, "the two" refers to heaven and earth; they have not overcome (*paribhūta*) you, meaning they were not able to overcome you.
Of what kind?
*pavaste*. The root *pavi* signifies the act of moving.
From this [root] *āṅ*, the suffix *āṇ* is applied by the rule for the suffix *aṅ*.

Then, when the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 4.1.4 (*ajādyataṣṭāp*), this form arises in the nominative dual. They go along, overcoming everything by means of their greatness.

1. ga—ābhūtasaṃplavaṃ; ta—abhūtasaṃplavā; bha1.4—ābhūtasaṃpla; bha1(2)—udvītha-āmahābhūtasaṃplavā; bha2—abhūtasaṃpūrṇa; bha6—abhūtasaṃplavā; bha7—ābhūtaṃ saṃplavaṃ | 2. ta1.2.9—mu—tamindraṃ; ta4—taṃ bhadraṃ |

The cows, released in great numbers, have eaten the barley of the noble one; I saw them as they wandered together with their herdsman.
