The noble one’s calls came from all sides toward them; how much of the milk will the Lord of Light desire from them? The cows—the milch-cows—released in great numbers, mingled together in abundance, have eaten the barley, the fodder consisting of barley and other grains, which I beheld. Of what kind were they? Accompanied by their herdsman, they were wandering about, grazing on the grass. I behold them with supreme joy; such is the meaning. Furthermore, the noble one’s calls—meaning the calls for driving and milking—came from all sides toward those cows. "From all sides" (*abhitaḥ*) means in every direction. Having come together in a group, they approach. The word *hṛt* is a filler. When they have arrived, the Lord of Light—the master of his own cattle—desires to milk how much? He desires to milk [as much] as he wishes for my sake. This is because of the statement: "The cows yielded the mixture for the pressing" (RV 8.60.6).

When we are gathered together, when there is the destruction of men, I am the destroyer of grain within the wide field; here, being harnessed, he shall seek one who provides food, and then, seeking to win, he shall harness the unharnessed. saṃ yat vayaṃ yavārdo janānām ahaṃ yavārda urvajñe antar | atrā yukto 'vasātāram icchād atho ayuktaṃ yunajad vanvān || 9 || When we are gathered together, when there is the destruction of men, I am the destroyer of grain within the wide field; here, being harnessed, he shall seek one who provides food, and then, seeking to win, he shall harness the unharnessed.

In this matter, you shall consider what I have spoken to be the truth: that I shall create both the biped and the quadruped; and whoever here, through women, would fight against the Bull—though unarmed—I shall divide his wealth. In this matter (*atra*), you (*it*) shall consider (*ū~ iti me maṃsase*) what I have spoken (*uktam*) to be the truth (*satyam*); know it to be exactly as it is. The sense is that this is not a mere figurative exaggeration (*arthavāda*) nor an attribution of qualities not actually present. *U* is a filler particle. Furthermore, know that I shall create (*saṃsṛjāni*) both the bipeds (*dvipāt*), such as humans, and the quadrupeds (*catuṣpāt*), such as cattle—the entire world consisting of the moving and the stationary. In this world (*atra*), whoever (*yaḥ*), being like a woman (*strībhiḥ*)—that is, a man lacking strength and other virtues—would, out of pride in his own heroism, wish to fight (*pṛtnyāt*) against me, the showerer (*vṛṣaṇam*) of desired things (the word "having abandoned" is to be supplied), I shall divide (*vi bhajāni*) the wealth (*vedaḥ*) of such a person.

1. There is no [reading] *ta-* for *sarvataḥ*. 2. Regarding *tu-bhā* 1.2.4.6, it means "the milker" (*dogdhrī*). By this [*mu*-suffix], the seer proclaims his own universal sovereignty obtained through the grace of Indra.

Among people—that is, among the worlds—those who are "yavasādaḥ," meaning cattle that eat grass (*tṛṇa*), know us to be them; [note that because of the prefix *upa-*, the verb "to join" (*yuj*) is supplied as the action]. And those who are "yavādaḥ," meaning humans who eat food characterized by barley (*yava*), know us to be them as well.
In truth, I am that Brahman which exists within the vast and wide courtyard of the heart, in the form of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin).
O Indra, remain joined and concentrated within this space of the heart; you desire the equipment for yourself—that is, you wish to realize the Self as its discoverer.
Moreover, you seek out even the unjoined, the one who is not a yogi.
The nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
The meaning is: "He binds"—that is, he yokes—to saṃsāra the person who "desires," meaning one who excessively indulges in sense objects;
the implication is: "I myself am he who is capable of both cursing and bestowing grace, appearing in your very form."
The meaning is: "I know my own wealth; having fought with that man, being myself a fighter, I shall divide it by force and bestow it upon the singers and the sacrificers."

Whose daughter was ever without eyes? Who, knowing her, would think of her as blind? Which of the two would release their resentment against him: he who carries her away, or he who would woo her? Whose daughter was ever without eyes? Who, knowing her, would think of her as blind? Which of the two would release their resentment against him: he who carries her away, or he who would woo her? (11)
The daughter of that Indra—who exists in me as the causal form—was at one time "without dice," meaning devoid of dice (akṣa), or lacking vision;
the sense is that she was insentient.
Her name was Prakṛti. She existed for a time in that state.
This is a form of the root *as* meaning "to go" in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
By implication, having been dissolved into me alone during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*),
Indra— being a portion of that— is here praised in the form of the Sun.
Indra, in the form of the sun, having stepped forth, devours—that is, he swallows or takes up—the water characterized by its function through his feet known as the rays;
and having taken it, he eats—that is, he consumes—the water that has returned to himself limb by limb;
the meaning is that he establishes it within his orb.

Immediately thereafter, he places— meaning he directs— the desirable *varūtha*, which is water characterized by its function as a covering, toward the head, the summit of the entire world, by means of his net of rays that stands in the place of a head. Furthermore, sitting— that is, seated— in the lap, his own vicinity, namely the solar orb, he destroys— that is, he diminishes— his upward-rising radiance.
The meaning is that he casts [it] forth to produce light.
Being one who moves low, as a mass of downward-pointing rays, he follows—that is, he traverses—the outstretched, expansive earth.
The mother, of vast luster and leafless, stands near; she, the impotent one, devours the embryo.
Licking the calf of another, she has lowed; in what world has the cow deposited her udder?
Vast, shadowless, leafless; the mother stood erect. The impregnated embryo devours the offspring of another. Licking [the calf], she has lowed. In what world has the cow laid down her udder? 14.
He praises Indra, whose essence consists of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas:
"Bṛhat" means great, and "acchāyaḥ" means devoid of shadow;
that is to say, free from darkness.
*Apalāśaḥ* means devoid of leaves; *parāśadanavarjitaḥ* means free from destruction—this is the meaning. *Arvī*, meaning one who moves constantly, *tasthau* (stood) or remains.

Furthermore, the Mother, by means of bestowing rain, is the creator of the entire world; she is "virpita," meaning liberated, that is to say, independent. As the "garbha"—the womb-like essence of the three worlds—Indra, in his solar form, eats, that is, consumes the oblations.
Alternatively,
by this [word], destruction is indicated;
it destroys sins.

Furthermore, licking—that is, tasting, subsisting upon, and nourishing—the calf, namely the son Aditya, of another mother of the gods called Aditi, she has measured out (mimāya), that is, she brings him forth.
The meaning is that she produces him day after day in the eastern direction.
By what being (bhuvā)—that is, by what state or intention?
The meaning is "either out of devotion or out of fear.
The cow—the sky—because it is the support of water and because it flows, places the sun, which stands in the place of the udder, within itself;
or alternatively:
Just as the earth supports a cow that is grazing, so does the sky support the sun.
Seven heroes rose up from below; eight came together from above.
Nine came from behind with their broad backs; ten horses stretched across the ridge from the front.
Seven heroes have ascended from below; eight have come together from the high place. Nine have approached from behind toward the broad one; ten horses extend across the ridge from the front. 15.
By this [verse], Indra is praised in the form of Prajāpati.
Seven—that is, numbering seven—heroes, the sons of Prajāpati such as Viśvāmitra and others, *udāyan*, meaning they were born from the lower part, the lower body of Prajāpati.
Eight—that is, numbering eight—those well-known ones, such as the Vālakhilyas and others, *samajagmire*, meaning they were born from the upper part, the upper region of the body.

The nine Bhr̥gus, possessing greatness and possessing their own stations, came from behind— that is, they were born from the rear. Likewise, the ten Aṅgirases, being ten in number, having been born from the front, [reached] the ridge— the elevated region— of Akṣa, the world of heaven characterized by its movement.
1. In the *ta* recension, "he swallows" (*girati*) is absent; in the *bha* recension, it is "he goes" (*jigati*). 2. In the *ta* recension, "he takes" (*gṛhṇāti*) and "water" (*mudakaṃ*) are absent.
3. In the *ga* recension: "This Āditya praised—vast, great, shadowless, and leafless, meaning devoid of shadow and devoid of leaves."
4. Free from the color of the *parāśada* tree; free from the face of the *parāsada* tree; free from the face of the *palāśa* tree.

4. By the eating of the *udgītha*. 5. Destruction (*vināśa*); destruction of the *vilāśa* according to Ta1, Ta2, and Ta7; destruction of the *udgītha* according to Ta3, Ta5, and Bha; destruction according to Mu.
6. What is that? 7. It causes one to subsist upon the [milk] of the mother (bha1(2)).
8. *Ūdhaḥ*: that which stands in the place of the udder (*ūdhaḥ-sthānīya*).
9. He places it within his own belly; he deposits it in the interior of the *udgītha*.
They spread it out and expand it.
Another teacher says:
Seven in number, the heroic Maruts rose upward from Indra’s lower right side;
eight in number, those Maruts gathered from the northern side;
and nine in number, the established ones came from behind the back of the Great One.
Those ten, being "aśvāḥ" (possessing horses) and "aśanavantaḥ" (possessing food), stationed in the eastern region of Indra, spread forth the uplifted water or energy;
the meaning is that the Maruts, stationed in every direction, provide assistance to Indra.
Of ten, one tawny bull is common; they urge him on for the decisive rite.
The mother bears the well-placed embryo within her flanks, swelling as she nurtures him who is rushing toward the goal.

Of the ten, one is tawny; it is common to them all. They urge him forward for the decisive rite. The mother bears the well-placed embryo within her womb, while she, the cow, brings forth the one who does not stir. 16.

Among the ten aforementioned Aṅgirases, he [chose] one—the principal one, the famous seer named Kapila. Of what sort? Equal (samānam), that is, similar. To whom? By implication, to Prajāpati. "The shouting ones went forth; they cooked. Not half of Nemi did he cook. This god Savitṛ said to me: 'He who eats dregs shall indeed conquer; he whose food is ghee. 18.
Crying out, calling upon Prajāpati their father as they carried the sacrificial burden, the Aṅgirases—going in various directions or offering various forms of worship—came together;
that is to say, they were born from the presence of Prajāpati.
Among those Aṅgirases, one portion, being born from the lower part of Nemi, cooks the oblations for the sake of Prajāpati.
"The other half" means the remaining portion; "it does not cook" means it does not ripen.
How was all this known?
It is said: this such-like "god"—the shining one, the impeller of all, whether the Sun (Āditya) or Prajāpati—has told me all that as described.
Furthermore, Agni—who has ghee for his food and rice cooked in ghee, and who indeed desires the *brahman* as his food—desires and partakes of the progenitor (Prajāpati) by means of the oblation.
I saw a village being carried away from afar, moving by its own power upon a chariot;
he who is the head-ornament of men, the one who instantly bestows gifts, outstripping the generations as a newer one.

I beheld the village being carried away from afar, moving by its own inherent power without wheels; the noble one strikes down the yokes of the people, instantly bestowing gifts while diminishing the older generation as he renews them.
"I, Vasuka, saw Indra in the form of Prajāpati; I beheld him through perfect knowledge. Of what sort was he? He was carrying—that is, driving—the *grāma*, the multitude of beings."
The meaning is "creating. Why? Because [it says] "from afar" (ārāt), that is, from a distance.
The meaning is: "from the primordial nature which is the material cause.

"By means of a weaponless [weapon], that is, by a spear devoid of a discus and lacking a chariot; by a self-sustaining army, that is, one that maintains itself by its own power. The meaning is: "beholding him who is thus situated, as he approaches."

Furthermore, Indra, the noble lord (*aryaḥ*) of all, who is connected to the people—the sacrificers—by way of their duty, "prepares" (*pra mipakti*) or zealously attends to "the ages" (*yugā yugāni*), that is, the specific times of sacrifice.
Of what nature is he?
"Worthy of praise" (*madyaḥ*), he bestows gifts (*śikṣāni*) at that very moment.

According to the etymological derivation "he resorts to training" (*śikṣam śrayateḥ*, Nirukta 4.19), he is *kṣatritṛṇi*—the strikers—and *praminān*, meaning he is striking down or violently destroying the multitudes of Rākṣasas; he is *navīyān*, being newer or more recent in terms of his body, as well as in his strength, manliness, and valor.
These two oxen of Pramura are yoked for me; let them not indeed sit down and trample [the grain]. May his [rival's] cattle perish, failing their purpose; the Sūri has become superior to Marka.

These two bulls of mine are his masters; they are yoked. O wise one, let them truly settle well for me again and again. Even the waters go astray from his purpose; the fool and the madman have come near him. 20.

Because of the metaphorical identification of cause and effect, as stated in the scriptural passage, "Thou art indeed the self named son" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.15.11), these two horses of mine—belonging to me, who am Indra, the one who stands in the form of Indra and who slays enemies most effectively—being yoked to the chariot, highly honored, and moving toward the enemies and the sacrifices:
do not drive them away; by concluding this hymn of praise, remove my ignorance.

What then? "Muhur" means repeatedly; "mamandhi" means praise again and again—the sense is that they should constantly offer praise. Furthermore, even the waters characterized by rain "vi naśanti"—that is, they vanish—before the movement of this Indra.
[The root *naś* here carries the sense of "to pass away" or "to perish."]
They possess pervasiveness. Likewise, both Sūra and Sūrya pervade.
Of what kind?
"Markaḥ" means a cleanser, one who purifies everything; "uparaḥ" means cloud-like; "babhūvān" means becoming—meaning, being as swift-moving as a cloud.
1. Those possessing the power of *ta*; those possessing the power of *bha* and *ṣa*.

This thunderbolt, which has turned down from many places from the mass of the great Sun; there is indeed another glory beyond these fortresses. Without distress, the aged ones cross over that. This [is] the thunderbolt belonging to Indra, which has turned down from many places—from the *purīṣa*, the filling or orb, of the great, lofty Sun—from below, in the lower regions, for the sake of rain, having been set in motion and fallen. (The particle *avaḥ* also implies "even though"; because the word *tat* is heard, the word *yat* is to be supplied. Beyond, above the atmospheric world, situated in the solar orb—*enā* means this; *śravaḥ* is a name for food, and because it is the cause of that, water is called *śrava*. Even that water which exists other than the water within the belly of the clouds—the undistressed, active, aged ones, the singers such as the Maruts and others, cross over that; they cause such water to descend toward the atmospheric world.

Upon every tree, the cow, firmly fixed, lowed; from that [bow] the feathered arrows, devourers of many men, flew forth against those who fall. Then this entire world was struck with fear; it offered libations for Indra and gave gifts to the seer. **Word-by-word:** *vṛkṣe-vṛkṣe* (on every tree); *niyatā* (fixed/firmly attached); *mīmayat* (lowed/made sound); *gauḥ* (the cow); *tataḥ* (from that); *vayaḥ* (feathered/flighty); *pra* (forth); *pantān* (those who fall); *purupādaḥ* (devourers of many men); *atha* (then); *idam* (this); *viśvam* (entire); *bhuvanam* (world); *bhayāte* (was afraid); *indrāya* (for Indra); *sunvat* (pressing the Soma); *ṛṣaye* (to the seer); *ca* (and); *śikṣat* (gave/gifted). **Translation:** On every tree—meaning on every bow made of wood—the "cow," that is, the sinew-string belonging to the bow, lowed. The root *mīmayati* signifies making a sound; being drawn, it makes a noise. From that bow, the "vayas"—the feathered arrows that go to their final destination—fell forth toward those who fall, meaning the slayers of many men. Then, at that time, while pressing the Soma for the sake of Indra and performing the sacrifice for the seer (the observer of rites), the priest gave full sacrificial fees. This entire world, the totality of created beings, was struck with fear; it feared Indra. What else could it do? **Note:** The commentary explains that the "cow" is the bowstring (*maurvī*), which is made of sinew (*go-sambandhinī snāyu*). The "vayas" are the arrows. The "seer" (*ṛṣi*) is the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who witnesses the ritual acts. The "entire world" fears Indra because of his power. The verse describes the intensity of the battle and the devotion of the sacrificers.

At the measuring of the gods, the first ones stood; from their piercing, the others rose upward. Three, following the waters, heat the earth; two carry the *bṛbūka* moisture. At the measuring (*māne*)—that is, at the time of creation—of all the gods, these first ones stood; by Indra’s command, these former ones remained there. Who are they? They are the clouds. How is this known? Because they are mentioned in the subsequent quarter-verse. For it is said: "The intermediate host of gods are indeed the clouds" (Nirukta 2.22). From the piercing (*kuntatrāt*)—that is, the breaking open—of these such clouds, the others rose upward. This word *upara* refers to the water; the waters situated therein are called *upara*. The waters within the clouds rose upward; that is to say, they were cast down upon the earth in the form of rain. Once the waters have been cast down, by the command of Indra, three deities—Parjanya, Vāyu, and Āditya—heat the earth, meaning the plants situated there.

1. When the clouds have gathered (ga-ta³⁻⁴-bha⁶-sthiteṣu); 2. performing [the action] (ta-bha-kurvan); 3. that one alone (ta-ekā); 4. those situated there (ga-ataḥ tatrasthā; ta-tatra tatrasthā; ta³-bha⁵-atra tatrasthā); 5. raining down (ta-bha⁶-udārayan); 6. fallen (ga-ta³-bha⁶-nipatitā). They cause relief from the heat by means of the rain; the meaning is that they purify.
Of what kind? They are *vanūpāḥ*: those who dwell (*vasāraḥ*) in succession through the rainy season and so forth, that is, those who cause [the seasons] to manifest;
the meaning is "those who inhabit."

Or rather, the two—Vāyu and Āditya—carry the *purīṣa*, which is the water that has been cooked within the plants and which nourishes or fills everything; they carry it toward the solar orb as *vr̥būka*.
The meaning is that Vāyu dries it up while Āditya takes it up with his rays.
Know that to be your life-sustenance, and know it to belong to him; let such a one not be hidden from you in the assembly.
He makes it manifest by his own means, yet he hides the chaff; he is exposed, and his mantle does not conceal him.

She is your life-sustainer; know this of her. Do not hide such a one away in the assembly! Thus she makes herself manifest with her own [parts], yet she hides the chaff with her own; that foot of hers, stripped bare, is never released. 24.
Herein, Indra is praised as the inner self (*antarātman*).

O inner self, that bellowing bull with sharp horns has stood upon the height of the earth’s expanse. In all the assemblies, I protect him who, having pressed the Soma, fills my belly. He. Bellowing. Bull. Sharp-horned. Upon the height. He has stood. Upon the expanse. Of the earth. In all. Him. In the assemblies. I protect. Who. For me. In the belly. Having pressed the Soma. Fills. 2.

I am Indra, the bull who rains down desires, with sharp horns and fierce rays. Upon the height— the height— of the earth and the intermediate space (the word *varṣman* signifies "height" or "firmness"), being such as I am, I protect and guard this sacrificer, this wealthy one, in all battles and conflicts.

The connection is as follows: "I protect such a sacrificer"—one who has pressed the Soma (*sutasoma*), meaning one who has performed the soma-pressing, who fills both my flanks (*kukṣī ubhau pārśvau*) with the soma juice, sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), and other offerings. I protect him in this manner.

With the pressing-stone, O Indra, they press out the exhilarating Soma for you; you drink of these. They cook the bulls for you; through their nourishment, O Maghavan, you are summoned. With the pressing-stone, O Indra, they press out the exhilarating Soma for you; you drink of these. They cook the bulls for you; through their nourishment, O Maghavan, you are summoned. 3. With the pressing-stone, for you, the exhilarating one, O Indra, they quickly press the Somas; you drink of these. They cook the bulls for you; through their nourishment, O Maghavan, when you are being invoked. 3.
O Indra, for your sake, the sacrificers press out and extract with the stone—the pressing stones—the exhilarating, intoxicating, swift, and unhesitating Soma juices.
You drink these Somas belonging to us and other sacrificers.
Furthermore, you consume the sacrificial animals belonging to those sacrificers who cook bulls for your sake.

"O Maghavan, O wealthy Śakra, when you—being invoked as the cause by means of *pṛkṣa*, that is, the oblation consisting of food—are being offered by the sacrificers, then [you come]"—this is the connection with the preceding [verse].

Take this well to heart for me, O singer: the rivers carry curses against their currents. The hyena has devoured the lion; the jackal has eaten the horse; the wolf has driven the boar out from the thicket. This, indeed, do thou understand for me, O singer: the rivers carry curses back against themselves. The hyena has devoured the lion; the jackal has eaten the horse; the wolf has driven the boar out from the thicket.
O Indra, you who have aged [the world] and are the age-wearer of enemies, take full cognizance—know thoroughly and completely—this beautiful form and capability of mine.
Of what kind? The rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others, carry their waters against the current, that is, in opposition to the curse.
Moreover, the *lopāśa* is a beast that devours (*akṣāti*) the grass it is lusting for;
thus, being sent by me, it has driven away (*atsārita*) the lion that was coming toward it—that is, approaching the horse.
It goes directly face-to-face with it.
Likewise, the jackal (kroṣṭā), the śṛgāla, drives out even a powerful boar (varāha)—a pig—from its thicket (kakṣa), that is, from an extremely dense place.
Know that all this capability, though obtained by me, your son, through your grace, belongs to you as well. This is the meaning.
1. In *ta* and *bha6*, "somān" is absent. 2. Belonging to *ta*, *bha1.2.4.6*, and *saṃ*. 3. In *ga* and *bha2*, it is "te tvadartha". 4. Belonging to *ta*, *bha2.6*, and *saṃ*.
[Maṇḍala 10, Adhyāya 2, Sūtra 28] Seventh Aṣṭaka, 369.

How may I, an unripe one, fully comprehend this—the ripening of the thought of you, the wise and powerful? You, being the knower, declare it to us in due season: that portion of yours, O Maghavan, which is a secure burden. How? Of this. I. An unripe one (pāka). Fully (ā). May I comprehend (ciketam). The ripening (pārkaḥ) of the thought (manīṣām) of you, the wise (gṛtstas) and powerful (tavasaḥ). You (tvam). To us (naḥ). Being the knower (vidvān). In due season (ṛtuthā). Declare specifically (vi vocaḥ). That portion (yam ardham) of yours (te), O Maghavan, which is a secure burden (kṣemyā dhūḥ). O Indra, I—an unripe one, whose wisdom is immature—how can I fully comprehend this: the ripening of the thought of you, the wise and powerful, that is, your praise? This is the ellipsis. How, by what means, may I fully understand such power of yours? The meaning is: without your instruction, I do not know it. Therefore, you, being all-knowing, speak specifically to us from time to time. O Maghavan, wealthy Indra, that portion of you which we fashion as a part of praise—that praise—is a secure burden; it exists as something peaceful, free from distress, and capable of being borne. Since we are unable to fashion even a portion of your praise without effort due to our dull-wittedness, therefore, tell us yourself once more your own power and the manner of praising you.

For indeed, in this manner, the singers magnify me, the powerful one, with their hymns; even from the great heaven, my yoke-pole is higher. I hew down many thousands all at once, for my progenitor begot me without a foe. For indeed, because the singers, praising me with hymns, thus magnify me as the powerful and exalted one, therefore the praise (*dhūḥ*) of me, Indra—the great one—is loftier and more exalted than even the heavenly world (*divaḥ*). Moreover, I simultaneously (*sākam*) and all at once hew down (*ni śiṃśāmi*), that is, I utterly destroy, many thousands of enemies. For indeed, my progenitor (*janitā*), Prajāpati, the creator of all, begot me, Indra, as one who is without a foe (*aśatrum*). 1. *hi* (for): because of which reason. 2. *eva* (thus): in the manner already described. 3. *tavasam* (powerful): highly increased. 4. *mām* (me): me. 5. *vardhayanti* (magnify): they increase by means of valor. 6. *divaḥ* (from heaven): from the celestial world. 7. *cit* (even): also. 8. *me* (my): of me. 9. *bṛhataḥ* (great): of the vast. 10. *indrasya* (Indra): of Indra. 11. *dhūḥ* (yoke-pole/praise): the song of praise. 12. *uttarā* (higher): more elevated or superior. 13. *adhikatarā* (more abundant): exceeding. 14. *kiṃca* (furthermore): moreover. 15. *puru* (many): numerous. 16. *puruṇi* (many): plural of *puru*. 17. *bahūni* (many): numerous. 18. *sahasrā* (thousands): thousands. 19. *śatrūṇām* (of enemies): of foes. 20. *sākam* (simultaneously): together. 21. *yugapat* (all at once): at the same time. 22. *ni* (down): prefix indicating destruction. 23. *śiṃśāmi* (I hew down): I make thin or destroy. 24. *tanūkaromi* (I make thin): I diminish. 25. *hinasmītyarthaḥ* (the meaning is "I strike down"): the sense is "I kill. 26. *hi* (for): because of which reason. 27. *janitā* (progenitor): the creator of all. 28. *prajāpatiḥ* (Prajāpati): the Lord of Creatures. 29. *mā* (me): me. 30. *indram* (Indra): Indra. 31. *aśatrum* (without a foe): one whose enemy does not exist. 32. *aviyamānaśatrum* (one whose enemy is absent): one who has no adversary. 33. *jajāna* (begot): he brought into being. 34. *janitavān* (he begot): he produced. 20. [End of section]

For thus indeed have the gods known me, O Indra, as powerful, fierce, and virile in every deed; rejoicing, you slew Vṛtra with your thunderbolt, and by your greatness, you opened the enclosure for the donor. For indeed, O Indra, because the gods—the Maruts and others, or the officiating priests and the sacrificers—have known me, the son of Vasukra, as I abide in my own form, to be powerful, great, fierce, or irresistible, and as a showerer of oblations in every rite such as the slaying of Vṛtra or the Agnihotra; therefore, rejoicing, I slew Vṛtra—the cloud or the Asura—with my weapon, the thunderbolt. Furthermore, for the sake of the donor who has offered the oblation, I have, by means of my greatness and mighty roar, opened the enclosure, the mass of clouds, to release the rain.

1. At that time. 2. We perform that state of being (*tadbhava*). 3. Because of that; from that cause. 4. The word "not" (*na*) is absent in both *ta* and *bha*. 5. Many for me (*bahuni me*) in *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*; many for him (*bahuni se*) in *ta₅*. 6. It means it does not exist. 7. The phrase "one whose enemy is non-existent" (*aviyamānaśatru*) is absent in *ta* and *bha₆*. 8. Established in the state of defining your own nature (*tvadūpanirūpaṇāvasthitam*) in *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*.

The gods went forth, bearing axes; cleaving the clouds, they advanced with their hosts. Establishing a good flow within the channels, they burn up the dry wood wherever it lies. The gods, impelled by Indra, went forth; they bore axes—that is, they wielded thunderbolts—for the purpose of destroying the clouds. Thereafter, accompanied by their subjects such as the Maruts, they advanced toward the "woods"—meaning the waters characterized by rain—cleaving the clouds. Then, establishing a "good flow" (sudam)—the excellent moving water of rain—within the "channels" (vṛkṣaṇāsu), that is, the rivers, they burn up the "dry wood" (kṛpīṭam) wherever it exists in that mass of clouds.

Alternatively, it means for the purpose of drawing near. Having drawn near, Gāyatrī brought the Soma from its concealment; "without effort" (ayathám) means effortlessly—that is, by way of sport. She drew this collection of Soma, having pulled it forth; the meaning is that she brought it from the vicinity of heaven.
The lizard drags them away from their place, who obstruct the sacred formulation with their lack of insight.
Like bulls let loose, they devour everything, crushing their own bodies with their own strength.

To them [he says]: "The iguanas pull this loose joint apart—those who revile the sacred word (*brahman*) with their mouths, devouring even the bulls let loose, while they themselves crush the strength of their own bodies. 11.
The hosts of gods, beginning with the Maruts, [approached] Brahmā, who is protected by Indra and is their own source,
with offerings of Soma and garlands;
"being human-like," is the implied sense.
They are being pressed;
the root *pī* has the sense of harming (*hiṃsā*).

By the command of Indra, they harm the *visakas*; for their sake, for the benefit of those hosts of gods, the previously mentioned *godhā*, who is the *gāyatrī*, drew forth—without effort (*ayathena*)—this collection of *soma*, having drawn it out.
"He was placed in the forest.

As in a forest, like a bird in its own nest, he placed his own young son there—a chick whose wings had not yet grown. Once placed there, he was contented, looking about and gazing toward the quarters out of fear.
Or rather, he was longing for it with a mind eager for that [desire].

Thus, this pure (śuci)—that is, free from defect—hymn (stoma) of yours, which has become like a son of a bird dwelling in the nest of a tree among us, belongs to you both, O Bhuraṇūs—O Ashvins, who are swift or sustainers;
for *bhuraṇyu* is a name for "swift."

Furthermore, for which hymn (*stoma*) Indra becomes the invoker (*hotr̥*)—that is, Indra himself calls out—over many days, over many offerings, thinking, "May this hymn be equal [to me]"; what kind of Indra, moreover, is the invoker?
He who is the most manly among men, the most human even among humans.
The meaning is that he is the most heroic even among arrows;
he is *narya*, beneficial to men, and *kṣapāvān*, one who possesses nights as his paths.
(Maṇḍala 10, Adhyāya 2, Sūkta 29) [End of] the Seventh Aṣṭaka, 373.

He brought—that is, he obtained—the *mṛn*, meaning human beings, who had become his followers. Likewise, that chariot which was yours and Kutsa’s, shared simultaneously by both as a winner (*sasavān*), exists; that chariot was obtained by Kutsa—this is the ellipsis.
And so it is heard in another mantra: "Thou goest on the same chariot with Kutsa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.16.11).
Since this is so, the meaning is: "By your grace, may we become pre-eminent."
O crusher of the Kaste, O Indra, be joyful; fierce upon the mountain, run forth!
When shall my inspired thought come hither to me? O Agni, may I be able to bring you near with gifts of wealth.

Who is it for you? Your joy, O Indra, has become one that delights. O fierce one, run forth toward the doors and our songs! What brings you hither? Let my inspired thought draw you near; may I bring you hither with offerings and great bounty. 3.
O Indra, among those exhilarations of yours—born of Soma, consisting of the middle and highest [pressings]—which exhilaration is the most delightful (*rantiya*), that which brings pleasure?
This question is asked with the intention of obtaining a Soma-draught suitable for your own delight.
O powerful (*ugra*) one, you who possess might, run toward (*abhi vi dhāva*) the doors—the gates of the sacrificial hall—and toward the songs, the words characterized by praise.
Furthermore, what or when is this "vāh"?
"Vāh" refers to the Soma that has been offered toward Indra;
the sense is that such [Soma], through your grace, will turn "arvāk"—that is, it will become directed toward us for the sake of bestowing its fruit.

Moreover, when will my vision, which perceives all objects (*marṇāpā*), or my praise, which grasps all virtues, come to me through your grace? This is the ellipsis. When, O Indra, shall I [attain] you?
Since the preposition *ā* is heard, the verb "to reach" (*ā-yam*) is to be supplied from the context.
O Agni, may we win over the most excellent wealth along with the gift; I am able to bring it near.
Here, the root *śak* (to be able) has the sense of "going" (*gati*) with the causative meaning (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied:
"I would cause [it] to come together."

O Indra, what would you do for men such as we? With what thought would you act, and how have you come to us? O wide-striding one, true like Mitra, provide for our sustenance, O Agni, when our inspired thoughts meet together in assembly.

What? "Ūm!"—thus [you speak]. O Indra, for you who protect us, what deed shall we perform with what thought? What have you done for us? You have come like a true Mitra, O wide-striding one. O Agni, when the hymns were gathered together, the inspired thoughts were fulfilled. 4.

O Indra, when (*kadu*) or at what time (*kadā*)— having consumed our food characterized by oblations (*havir-lakṣaṇam*), the ellipsis being "our"— by what thought (*kayā dhiyā*) or by what deed (*kena karmaṇā*) will you make us (*nṝn*), our leaders, like yourself (*tvādṛśaḥ*)? When (*kat*) will you come (*āgan*) toward us (*naḥ*)?
"True" means blameless. "Like Mitra," that is, like a friend;
O Indra of wide renown (urugāya), you are [the one] for the sake of supporting and nourishing—this is the ellipsis.

When, O Agni, the cause of the world's stability, the thoughts—that is, the cognitions characterized by the desire for food—of "every" [being], such as ourselves and all the world, should arise in regard to food;
then the meaning is that you exist for the nourishment of all.

Like a hero who has reached the further shore of his goal, those who have fulfilled his desire go forth like wives to their husbands; and those men, O Indra born of many powers, who provide for you with abundant songs and food—[to them you grant your favor].

Having set forth toward the goal like the sun to the further shore, those who have come to fulfill his desire like wives to their husbands—those men, O Indra born of many powers, who with their songs and fires strive to win back thy many favors. 5.
1. In manuscripts *ta* and *bha*, the phrase "sasavān" does not exist.
2. In manuscript *ga*, *bha* 1.2.4.7 reads "evambhūtaḥ somaḥ"; in *ta* 1.2.4.5.1 it reads "evambhūmaḥ". 3. In *ta* and *bha* 1, the phrase "api ca ... śeṣaḥ" does not exist.

Just as the *sūra* (the sun), by favoring the *artha* (the goal-seeking) yogin who is like a traveler, leads him to the *pāram* (the further shore), that is, to the end of *saṃsāra*, which is liberation (*apavarga*), so too, O Indra, do you impel and lead the sacrificers to the end of *saṃsāra*.
Those sacrificers, ourselves and others, have gone toward—meaning they have fulfilled—the *kāmam* (desire), the wish for drinking Soma, of this Indra, O *gamin* (O goer);
here the prefix *vi-* should be understood as having the sense of "completely" (*antābhāvitavya*).
They cause [the enemies] to vanish; they remove them by means of a great drinking of Soma.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like women."
Just as husbands, who support their wives— the *janīs*— upon their couches at the time of sexual union, satisfy their desire for intercourse by providing abundant enjoyment,

so too [are you]. Furthermore, O *tuvijāta*, one of many forms— as it is said, "He became the counterpart to every form" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 6.47.18)— those leaders such as ourselves who are the sacrificers [approach you].

In every battle, O Indra, for you, the mighty one, Indra has prevailed over the hosts. Many [people] strive for friendship with him. Ascend his chariot in the battles, just as you would urge it on with your auspicious and gracious favor.
The self-born, possessed of beautiful strength, Indra pervades—that is, he encompasses—the *vṛtanāḥ*, the enemy armies;
the meaning is that Indra, being unassailable by anyone in battles, conquers his enemies.
Furthermore, [he overcomes] the *pūrvīḥ*...
In this context, the word *pūrva* signifies "superior.
The superior enemy armies, being powerless, immediately strive for the sake of friendship—meaning for an alliance characterized by peace—or for companionship with this Indra;
that is to say, they desire to make peace.
Another interpretation: because it is based on direct perception, this is the meaning of the verse.

O Indra, you impel your own chariot with auspicious, excellent, and beautiful benevolence—that is, with a mind intent on favoring others—and thus urge it toward the sacrifices; mount that chariot with great zeal to come to our sacrifice.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as one ascends a great chariot with great care in battles and conflicts, so do you [ascend] your own chariot;
the word *sma* is a filler (*padapūraṇa*).
In the third Anuvāka, there are thirteen hymns.

Among them, the first hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "pra devatrā," is the Ṛṣi-seer Kavaṣa, son of Ilūṣa; it is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to the All-gods (Viśvedevas) or to the Waters (Āpas).
And thus it has been introduced: "‘pra devatrā’ [is] five short of [ten]; [it belongs to] Kavaṣa Ailūṣa; [it is] addressed to Āpa or to Aponaptrīya.
Being addressed with the words ‘apa ipya hotar’, the Hotṛ should recite the nine verses beginning with ‘pra devatrā’.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘pra devatrā brahmā gātu-retu’ [are] nine; ‘hinotā no adhvaraṃ devayajyā’ is the tenth” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.1).

Let the path to the gods proceed for the sake of the sacred word (*brahman*), as if toward the waters by the impulse of the mind. May the great nourishment of Mitra and Varuṇa flow forth; O wide-ruling one, grant us a well-fashioned hymn of praise. 1. Let the way go forth toward the gods for the sake of the sacred word, as if toward the waters by the impulse of the mind. Grant the great nourishment of Mitra and Varuṇa; O you of broad dominion, bestow upon us a well-fashioned song of praise.
To Brahmā;
the dative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
By means of Brahmā, that is, by means of the hymn of praise.
The word "being praised" (*stūyamāna*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Soma, the *vāyu*—meaning either the one who moves among the gods or the one whose nature is to go toward them—should flow forth (*vaccha*) toward the deities (*devatrā*), that is, toward the divine celestial regions (*dyomānāḥ*). Let him go forth (*pra vetu*) with excellence toward the waters characterized by the *vasatīvarī*, the *ekadhana*, and so on.
Regarding this, there is an illustration:
It is not through the application of the mind alone;
rather, just as when the mind is applied, directed, and exerted, it moves swiftly, so too,

when the waters have entered the Soma, O my soul, or O Adhvaryu, you bestow a great vessel (*dhāsi*)— that is, food characterized by the great *stoma*— for the sake of Mitra and Varuṇa, who possess broad speed (*pṛthuñjyase*).
"For the sake of Indra of great course" means for the purpose of [Indra]. "Accomplish," that is, complete or prepare;
make him worthy of receiving gifts.
And offer a well-composed hymn of praise, perfectly free from all defects.

O Adhvaryus, become possessed of oblations; go toward the waters, you who desire them, desiring them yourselves. Cast down that wave which the ruddy, fair-winged one beholds; seize it, O dexterous-handed ones. O Adhvaryus! Be possessed of oblations! Indeed, go toward the waters, you who desire them, desiring them yourselves. That which the ruddy, fair-winged one beholds—cast it down; seize the wave, O dexterous-handed ones! 2.
O Adhvaryus, you indeed possess the oblation; that is, you are endowed with the oblation characterized by the Soma to be pressed.

Furthermore, O Adhvaryus, desiring—that is, longing to perform the pressing of the Soma—[you should press] for the sake of friendship, characterized by companionship (or, according to some, for the sake of connection); [that is], for the sake of friendship, characterized by the state of being a friend.
2. Like a charioteer;
3. he stands with great reverence;
4. of the great Indra.
5. "For your sake" means for the sake of the ritual purpose; "with vigor" means with energy.
Desiring the state [of being], go toward the waters, which are characterized by a single essence.

The ruddy, well-winged Soma beholds from below—that is, in the intermediate space—the waters that are contained within the womb of the clouds. O you of fair hands, because you perform the beautiful rites such as the pressing of Soma, you are adorned with golden strainers and other ornaments.
The *bhadrās* are those with beautiful hands.

You, these *adhvaryu*s, now (*atha*) at this very moment (*idānīm*), *asyadhvam*—standing face-to-face with great reverence, cast (*asyadhvam*) that such mass (*saṃghātam*) of Soma together with those waters into the *daśāpavitra* for the purpose of purification.
O Adhvaryu, go to the waters; worship the Son of the Waters with an oblation at the ocean.
May he grant you well-purified strength; for him, press out the honeyed Soma.
O Adhvaryus, go toward the waters, toward the ocean; worship the Son of the Waters with an oblation; he shall grant it to you.

Come hither to reach the reservoir; go toward it. Furthermore, when you sprinkle the Soma juices from all sides with those [waters] that have been brought, then purify both the waters and the Soma plants through the *daśāpavitra* filter. In this very way, let the young women bow down to the youth, for they, desiring him, come toward him. The two Adhvaryus, the *dhiṣaṇā* (the sacrificial vessel), and the divine waters agree in mind and are conscious together. Let the young women bow down to the youth, just as they bend low; even so do the waters called *vasatīvarī* and *ekadhanā* bend low for the sake of the Soma. Or rather, the young women—the waters about to be mixed with the Soma—bow down to the youth, the Adhvaryu who himself mixes them for the performance of the pressing rites. The word *it* is a filler. When? When, desiring them—that is, when Soma, desiring the *vasatīvarī* waters for the purpose of pressing, or the Adhvaryu, desiring to perform the Soma-pressing, goes toward these waters (*īm*) to obtain them while they themselves desire to be mixed with the Soma and to participate in the pressing rites. Then they submit. The Adhvaryus, the *dhiṣaṇā*—his speech characterized by praise—and the divine waters, agree in their minds through superior intellect; they are fully conscious and perceive with their eyes their respective duties and their mutual assistance. O Waters, send forth for that Indra your honey-sweet wave, which makes the gods rejoice, you who made a path for yourselves when obstructed, and who released yourselves from great calumny. O Rivers, send forth for this Indra your honey-sweet wave, which is the womb of yours and a spring of sweetness, whose back is sprinkled with clarified butter, and which is to be praised at the sacrifices. O wealthy Waters, hear my call! (Note: Here, due to the connection with the relative pronoun *yaḥ*, the second quarter-verse should be explained first. O flowing Rivers, that which is your womb—a spring of sweet juice—send forth that honeyed wave, the essence of the water, for the sake of this Indra. O wealthy Waters, hear my call! 1. *ta-āhatābhistābhiḥ* (Ta edition: "by those brought ones") 2. *ta-eva...prahībhavanti* (Ta edition: "in this very way... they bend low") does not exist. 3. *ta-pāda* (Ta edition: "quarter-verse") does not exist.
Drive it forth; send it forth; cause it to go forward.
Of what kind?
At the sacrifices where the bridegroom is present, [he is] one whose back is ghee—that is, whose back is smeared with clarified butter;
the meaning is that he is one who subsequently drinks the oblation.
He is "vīḍya," meaning worthy of praise.
Furthermore, O Vāpas, you who are wealthy—though you may seem poor in comparison to the riches that must be given to us—listen to my invocation.
O rivers, send forth that exhilarating wave for Indra’s drinking, which impels both worlds;
it distills intoxication, is eager, possesses nourishing food, and moves around the triple-stranded spring.

Send forth that wave, the exhilarating draught for Indra, the Sindhu’s own, which impels both worlds, the distilling, offspring of the waters, born of the clouds, wandering through the triple-stranded source.

O Sindhavas—those waters that flow swiftly—your essential mass, being the bestower of both seen and unseen fruits upon us, shall proceed toward the absence of ritual defects. O officiating priests (ṛtvijas), send it forth, dispatch it, cause it to go forward, and extend this sacrifice (adhvara) for the sake of the worship of the gods (devayajyā).
Furthermore, send forth the sacred prayer (brahma)—consisting of praise—in accordance with the sequence of the scriptures, for the sake of our acquisition of wealth.

Furthermore, regarding the "joining" (*yoga*)—that is, the connection—of the "Rite" (*ṛta*), namely the sacrifice: this refers to the hide used for pressing, which, when full of Soma, lies there as if it were a vessel.
Alternatively, because of its connection with the act of joining, the "chariot" (*śakaṭa*) is called *yoga*;
for that [chariot] is indeed yoked right there.
Thinking that it refers to the pressing-skin situated beneath the udder, the author of the *Nirukta* says: "Or, [it means] 'on the sacrificial cart'" (*Nirukta* 6.22).
This pressing-skin, which is either below or above the sacrificial cart—release it, let it go!
This "unloosening" of the pressing-skin from the udder is the pouring out of the Soma into the cups, bowls, jars, and so forth.
For when that Soma is being poured out, it becomes *śruthī*—that is, flowing or yielding—as other [streams] are from a cow being milked.
Having thus addressed the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he now speaks to the waters mixed with Soma:
"O waters, you too, being poured out by these priests, become *śruthīvarīḥ*—that is, be pleasant or full of comfort—for us."
Thus, because the meaning becomes even more manifest through the prefix *pra*, the commentator has supplied (*adhyāhṛta*) the prefix *pra*.
In the word *prahiṇata*,
the sense of motion for the root *vi* is justified by its connection with the word *adhvaram*.
The explanation of this ṛc has been set forth in the Nirukta-ṭīkā.
For the Prātaranuvāka, the opening verse is "āpo revatīḥ.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The hymn begins with 'āpo revatīḥ' and continues with the hymn 'upa prayantaḥ' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13)."
O wealthy Waters, for you indeed rule over riches; you sustain auspicious wisdom and immortality.
You are the mistresses of wealth consisting of noble offspring; may Sarasvatī bestow that vital strength upon the one who praises her.

O Waters, you are wealthy; for you indeed rule over riches. You bear auspicious wisdom and immortality. You are the mistresses of wealth and of noble offspring. May Sarasvatī bestow all that vitality upon the one who praises her. O wealthy Waters—rich in treasure—you truly possess dominion over riches. Furthermore, you sustain auspicious wisdom—that is, the ritual action characterized by the Soma sacrifice and the like—and immortality, which is the fruit resulting therefrom in the form of deathlessness. Or rather, you nourish them. Likewise, you are the mistresses and protectors of wealth and of noble progeny. Thus, may Sarasvatī—the deity presiding over her—grant all this vitality, characterized as food and wealth, to me who sings her praise.
The verse for the *apanodanī* is "When the waters come forward" (*prati yad āpo ahṛmāyatīḥ*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "When the waters are being brought forward, [the priest recites] 'prati yad āpo ahṛmāyatīḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.1).
When the waters, bearing ghee, milk, and honey, came forward—
being in mental accord with the Adhvaryu priests and bringing well-purified Soma for Indra.

When I behold you, O Waters, as you approach our sacrifice, carrying clarified butter, milk, and honey—being in mental accord with the Adhvaryu priests and bringing the well-pressed Soma for Indra. O Waters, when I behold you as you come toward us at this sacrifice (*ahram*), I look upon you who carry *ghṛtam* (clarified butter mixed with Soma), *payāṃsi* (milks), and *madhūni* (honey-like, sweet-flavored juices)—being in harmony of mind with the Adhvaryus and bearing the well-pressed Soma for Indra.
1. *Ta*, *Bha*: "Devayajyā" is not present.
2. *Ta*: "taddhi tarhi"; *Bha*: "su-taddhi tarhi".

3. Regarding "ta-bha-bravīte," it says "śakaṭa" (the cart). 4. From the commentary on the eleventh mantra found in the Ga manuscript: "hinota"—impel our *adhvara*, that is, the sacrifice for the purpose of the worship of the gods.

For the sacrifice is established in the waters; impel [it] for the sake of obtaining the wealth of sacred knowledge (*brahma*) and ritual action (*karman*). For the sake of the application of the sacrifice, "vi vyadhvam"—open wide, that is, make free, your own udder.
O Waters, you who are hearers of our call, become pleasant for us; [may it be so]—may the Lord grant this.

You, who at the time of sacrifice, having come together, bear and hold the waters (payāṃsi), and who, being in harmony with the Adhvaryus through mental application, converse with them, and furthermore, who carry and sustain the well-pressed Soma for Indra—for such as you, I implore you (the rest of the sentence).
In the Āponaptrīya rite, there are two verses beginning with "emā amanra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having recited the two verses 'emā amanravatīr jīvadhanyāḥ' and the Saptasūktarya, he should put on the garment" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.1).
O Adhvaryus, O friends, set down these wealthy ones, which bring life and prosperity;
place them upon the sacrificial grass, O Soma-offerers, in harmony with Apām Napāt.
O Adhvaryus, friends, place these wealthy ones, rich in life and prosperity, upon the sacrificial grass; O Soma-offerers, being in harmony with Apām Napāt, set them down here. 14.

The Revatīs—those who possess wealth, those who are rich in sustenance, the sustainers of life, and the protectors or gratifiers of living beings—these waters of such a nature have come toward us for our sake.

Knowing this, O friends—O Adhvaryus who are our companions—being in agreement and consulting together with the Son of Waters (Aponapāt), the deity presiding over the act of rain, set down these waters; establish them.
Where shall we set them down? It is said: [here].
O gentle ones, you Adhvaryu priests who prepare the Soma, place [the oblation] down—establish it by rule—upon the Barhis, the sacrificial grass spread upon the altar.
The longing, divine women have come here to this sacrifice and have seated themselves;
O Adhvaryus, press the Soma for Indra! Your devotion to the gods has now become easy to accomplish.

The longing waters have come; they have settled upon this sacred grass at the sacrifice, seeking the gods. O Adhvaryus, press the Soma for Indra! Your devotion to the gods has indeed become easy to perform. 15.

The waters, known as *vasatīvarī* and *ekadhana*, have come hither to this such-like sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and the strewing of the altar (*vedi*), desiring, that is, longing [for us]. Having arrived for our sake, they come to our sacrifice (*adhvara*), seeking the gods— that is to say, desiring the gods, wishing to satisfy them.
They have settled down, they have sat down. Knowing this, O Adhvaryus, press out and extract the Soma for Indra, for the sake of Indra.
Now, by the grace of the waters, your sacrificial rite directed toward the gods, Indra and the others, has indeed become easy to perform, capable of being well executed.

"Ā naḥ"—this second hymn, consisting of eleven verses, has Kaśyapa as its seer, is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to the Viśvedevas. It is thus enumerated: "Ā naḥ, eleven verses; addressed to the Viśvedevas.
The application of this hymn [in ritual] has been explained.
For the Vaiśvadeva animal sacrifice belonging to the Ekādaśina set, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the cake (*puroḍāśa*) is "ā naḥ.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "viśve atha maruto viśva ūtī no devānām upa vetu śaṃsaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7).
1. That [text] does not exist. 2. Ga: For all this is found in the Sarasvatī;
as it is said: "She milked out ghee and milk for Nahuṣa."
Likewise, having attained unanimity of mind with the *adhvaryu* priests, they carry the well-pressed *soma* for the sake of Indra;
"I beheld them in such a state"—this is the connection [of the sentence].
(Note: the reading "dhārayantīḥ" does not exist in the Ta-Bha manuscript).
3. [The variants] ta1.2.3.4.5.6 read *pāyayiṣya*; bha1.4 read *pāyayiṣya*; [the variant] udgītha reads *vardhayiṣya*. 4. [The variants] ga and bha5.6 read *vṛṣṭikarmaṇyadhikṛtena*.
5. ta5.7 and bha read *udgītha-amantr*.

6. Ga-nyaṣīdan; Ta-bha-mu-niṣīdan. May the praise of the gods come unto us for our protection, along with all the swift ones, O worshipful one! Through them may we become good friends; crossing over all difficulties, may we abide in prosperity. May the praise of the gods come unto us for our protection, along with all the swift ones, O worshipful one! Through them may we become good friends; crossing over all difficulties, may we abide in prosperity. (1)
May Indra—who is thus worthy of praise by us, his worshippers, and worthy of sacrifice—come hither for our protection along with all the great ones who are swift and resonant; may he approach us.
And may we, together with them, become excellent friends;
furthermore, may we be those who cross over all difficulties and all evils.

Even a mortal may win wealth; he should seek to acquire it through the wide expanse of Truth with reverence. Moreover, he should converse in accordance with his own proper season and grasp with his mind a more excellent skill. Even a mortal may win wealth; he should seek to acquire it through the wide expanse of Truth with reverence. Moreover, he should converse in accordance with his own proper season and grasp with his mind a more excellent skill. (2)
A mortal man, the sacrificer, should desire— *man* being a root meaning "to love"— to obtain wealth from all sides for the sake of the sacrifice to all the gods;
and having obtained that wealth, he should attend to it and offer it with reverence (*namas*) along the path of *ṛta*, that is, the way of sacrifice.
Moreover, he should converse with his own recognized season— that is, with his mind.
In this context, *saṃvāda* is said to mean "concentration" (*samādhāna*).
The meaning is that, having taken the oblation and being about to utter the *vaṣaṭ* call, one should meditate upon all the gods with the mind.

And after the sacrifice to all the gods, by their grace, one should—with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as the instrument of meditation—seize (*jagṛbhyāt*), that is, grasp, *dakṣa*, who is more excellent (*śreyāṃsam*), most highly praised (*atiśayena praśasyamānam*), increased (*pravṛddham*), and all-pervading (*sarvavyāpinam*).

The prayer has been offered, reaching the essence; the aids approach the wondrous one as if to a ford. We have come toward the splendor of well-being, even unto the presence of the immortals. It has been offered. The prayer. Reaching the essence. The portions. As at a ford. To the wondrous one. They approach. The aids. Toward. The enjoyment. Of well-being. Truly. We have become partakers. Of the immortals. 3.

The devotion— the performance of the sacrifice to the gods— has been established, placed, and set in motion by us. Immediately thereafter, the *ūmas*— the protectors, the gratifiers— the *aṃśas*, the portions of oblation given by us, [have reached] the *dasma*, the one worthy of being seen, or the destroyer of enemies, who is of incomparable creation (*asasragam*).
The meaning is "to those of superior birth.
They approach, that is, they go toward, such a host of gods.
In this regard, there is an illustration.

Just as portions of water released during the rite of libation (*tarpaṇa*) at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), such as the Gaṅgā and others, reach the assembly of gods, even so [may our offerings reach them].
Immediately thereafter, may we attain the auspicious happiness (*sukham*) of "well-gained" (*suvitasya*), that is, of that which is well-attained, such as heaven and other realms.
Furthermore, may we be knowers of the immortals, the gods.
In this sense, it is not "veda" (knowledge);

rather, it refers to 1. *taduritāni* (those evils), 2. *bha-viśvāni* (all [beings]—this word does not exist in *ta*), 3. *ṛtunā prajñātena* (by means of the well-known season—this phrase does not exist in *ta*), 4. *dakṣam* (skill—this word does not exist in *ta*), and 5. *su-uprajanmāna* (well-born).
The word *nabhrāṇapājvedā* is established as an irregular formation (*nipātita*).
"Not non-cutters, but cutters indeed"—
the meaning is that they are knowers by their very nature.
"May we become [beings] on this ground"— thus we pray.

The eternal Lord of Heaven, the subduer of enemies, has taken pleasure [in him], for whom the divine Savitṛ has bestowed [his favor]. Or rather, Bhaga with his cattle, or Aryaman, shall anoint him; may he appear beautiful to him and be gracious. nityaḥ | cākanyāt | svarpatiḥ | darmūnāḥ | yasmai | om iti | devaḥ | savitā | jujāna | bhagaḥ | vā | gobhiḥ | aryamā | īm | anajyāt | saḥ | asmai | cāruḥ | chadayat | uta | syāt ||4||
May the eternal Prajāpati, who abides throughout the eon, be pleased;
may he desire to grant him both visible and invisible fruits.
Of what nature is he?
The self-ruler, the lord of his own subjects or the master of wealth, is "darmūnāḥ," one whose mind is intent on giving.
For whom does he desire this? It is said:
moreover, for which sacrificer has the great Savitṛ, the impeller of all, brought forth [this gift], O God?
The meaning is that he has bestowed both seen and unseen fruits.
The word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Likewise, may *Bhaga*, the god, and *Aryaman*, the god, together with our own *gobhiḥ*—that is, with words consisting of praise—*anajyāt*: may they manifest such a fruit, both seen and unseen.
The meaning is "out of compassion.
Furthermore, whatever other host of gods there may be who is delightful—that host of gods also, we pray, "may it please" (chadayat) this sacrificer, desiring to grant him both seen and unseen fruits.

May this [song] become like the dwelling place of the dawns, since those who possess food have come together with power. Seeking the praise of this singer, may the gladdening strengths come unto us. 5. This; that; may it become; like the dawns'; the dwelling place; since; indeed; possessing food; with power; have come together; of this; the praise; of the singer; seeking; unto us; gladdening ones; may they come; the strengths. 5.

The word *kṣumantaḥ* contains the term *kṣu*, which signifies either food or sound; thus, it means "possessing food," "possessing praise," or "possessing fame. May this praise—which the gods, being such as they are, have come toward (*samāyan*) with their power (*śavasā*) and strength (*balena*) in response to our hymn—be attained by the gods; may it be so.
Like the dawns;
just as the earth is pervaded by the dawns and is attainable by all, so too [is he].
Moreover, [the gods] who are *śammāsaḥ* (givers of happiness), begging—that is, requesting—the hymn of this singer, of me, the praiser.
"Śam" is a name for happiness.
May the "vājas"—the sons of Sudhanvan, or alternatively, the Ṛbhus, who are themselves happiness and the bringers of happiness—come toward us, approach us.

His was this far-reaching benevolence; he became the ancient cow through his vastness. Dwelling together in the womb of the Asura, they were borne along in their common nourishment. His was this far-reaching benevolence; he became the ancient cow through his vastness. Dwelling together in the womb of the Asura, they were borne along in their common nourishment.

Now, this excellent hymn (*sumati*), consisting of a beautiful praise (*sustuti*) related to him and belonging to the host of gods, has become widespread (*paprathānā*); that is, it is being extended while being performed by us. Of what nature is it?
"Purvyā" means belonging to former times; "bhūmanā" implies being endowed with abundance. The meaning is that she is the most excellent among all that pertains to the gods.
"Gauḥ" means she who goes toward the gods.

Having understood this, may all the gods—belonging to me, who am powerful through the form of the progeny of the Asura—come together; being of common origin (*sanīḷāḥ*), sharing the same place, and dwelling in the sacrificial ground (*yajñaye sthāne*) which is the source of nourishment (*bharṇe*) common to all the gods and the means of their sustenance, they come, maintaining for our sake both seen and unseen fruits. (This is the ellipsis to be supplied.)
What was the forest, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned forth heaven and earth?
Upon those two standing together, undecaying and providing aid, the ancient seers have praised the many days.
What was the forest, what indeed was that tree from which they fashioned forth heaven and earth? Standing firm together, undecaying, with swift aid, they have celebrated many days and dawns. 7.

From which tree the gods fashioned heaven and earth—that tree, what indeed was it, and of what nature did it become? And what indeed was the forest or grove that produced it? [The two] stand well established, ageless and free from decay, with protection extending from these very teeth.
Moreover, all the days and many mornings—
the gods have fashioned them forth.
Praisers praise such gods as these with hymns of praise.
There is nothing else before him; as a bull, he supports heaven and earth.
The self-dependent one makes his skin a filter; like bay horses, they carry him to the light, as if to the sun.

Not by this much, nor by this alone; there is something else before him: he is the Bull who supports heaven and earth. Endowed with self-power (*svadhā*), he makes his skin a filter, when the tawny steeds carry him like the sun. ||8||
The form of the creation of heaven and earth is endowed with such power as this entire host of gods; however, beyond these gods, there exists another, superior being, namely Hiraṇyagarbha.
He is the bull, the shedder [of seed], for the purpose of creating progeny.

Hiraṇyagarbha—the supremely subtle one, whose form is wind and who is the self of the *liṅga*—having entered the waters, sustains and upholds heaven and earth. Furthermore, that Hiraṇyagarbha, being self-sustaining, powerful, or wise, makes his own body, which consists of purity, or his radiant mantra, into a purifier. When? It is said: [at the time of creation].
"When—indeed, at whatever time—the green horses do not carry, that is, do not bring forward this skin [of the world], it is as follows;
the meaning is: prior to creation."
The earth does not extend beyond its boundary, nor does the wind blow through the ground like mist;
where Mitra and Varuṇa are anointed, Agni has released his brilliance like fire among the forests.

He does not go to the earth, nor to the parched land, nor to distress; like the wind blowing away the mist over the ground, so Mitra and Varuṇa, being anointed, have released their brilliance like Agni among the forests. 9.

The root *sthā* means "to stand" and "to sound. The sun (*āditya*) is a mass of rays. It does not exceed—that is, it does not go beyond—the broad back of the earth, the expansive ground, by means of its brilliance.
The sun is praised because it remains within its fixed course (*maryādā*).
Likewise, the wind (*vāta*) is praised because, although it is capable, it does not blow excessively upon the earth (*bhūma*) nor does it scatter the rain (*miham*);
rather, it causes the rain to fall toward the earth with moderation. Thus, the wind is praised.
In which Prajāpati, when the god Mitra is being clarified— that is,
being manifested or brought into existence—
he emits his own radiance, casting it forth in all directions; likewise, Varuṇa, as he is being manifested, casts forth his own radiance.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as the god Agni, in a forest, radiates his own light in every direction amidst a mass of trees,
so too do I praise such a Prajāpati— this is the ellipsis.
1. ta1.2.6.7—“it rains”; ta3.4.5-bhad-mu—“the *udgītha* rains”; ma1.2.4—“he causes it to rain. 2.
ta—The phrase “being produced... becoming manifest” is absent. [The verse: “Like a swift arrow, being anointed at once, may the piercing one, like a leader of a herd, create a path for the cattle.”
When the son was born before his parents, when the cow swallowed the sacrificial pin, or whatever else they may ask.

When you, O Sūta, were suddenly being anointed, you, the protector of cattle, made the pain vanish; for when the son was born before his parents, the cow swallowed the sacrificial pin—this is what they ask. 10.
He figuratively represents the *śamī* tree, which is the cause of the two *araṇi*s, as a cow. A *stūrī* is a cow whose offspring has ceased.

When, being "immediately milked"—that is, quickly restrained from other activities—she brings forth her calf, then that cow, though she is a *vyathiḥ* (an affliction) that causes the pain of suffering, becomes one who possesses her own protector (*svagopā*) or whose protection is self-dependent; thus, she makes the offspring *anyathīḥ*, free from affliction.

When the *śamī* tree brings forth the *aśvattha* tree, which stands in the place of a son, then that *śamī*—the progenitor of such an *aśvattha*—becomes a cause of happiness for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are searching for that [wood] to carry it to the forest.
This is the meaning of the statement: "They churn fire from the womb of the *śamī*" (*Tai.
Brā.* 1.1.9). Furthermore, it is the "former," that is, the ancient, son.
He is the savior of our sons from hell;
or rather, Agni stands in the place of a son.

When he is born—that is, when he manifests through friction—from his two parents, the two kindling woods (araṇīs), then the Cow, the Earth, swallows that *śamī* tree—the mother of those two woods—which contains the Aśvattha within it;
here, the substitution of *jy* for the case-ending follows the rule "supāṃ suluk.
He vomits it up.
Or rather, when the officiating priests ask about that *śamī* tree, they inquire and search for it.
And they say that Kaṇva was the son of Nṛpada; moreover, the dark steed won the prize.
For Kṛṣṇa he caused the bright milk to swell; no one here could satisfy him when his task was half-finished.
And they say that Kaṇva was the son of Nṛpada; moreover, the bay steed brought back the wealth. For the dark one, the bright udder overflowed; here, no one else caused the Truth to flow for him. 11.
Moreover, those who speak the Vedas say that the seer Kaṇva was the son of Nṛpada;
furthermore, the vigorous Kaṇva, possessing a horse characterized by the oblation, received wealth from that Agni.
For the dark-complexioned Kaṇva, the bestower of wealth, he poured forth his shining, radiant udder.
In this regard, no deity whatsoever other than Agni has ever increased or furthered the *ṛta*—the sacrifice—for this Kaṇva;
as it is said: "You two gave the bright [cow] to Śyāva" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.117.8).

The third hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "pra su mantā," has its first five verses in the Jagatī meter; the remaining six are in the Triṣṭubh meter. These two [meters] were previously observed. Thus it is concluded: "pra su mantā: nine verses; the first five are Jagatīs. The application (viniyoga) has been explained.
May the two benevolent ones, who assist the one meditating on prayer, sit down with their choice gifts upon our choice offerings.
O Indra, may you enjoy both of these, when you take notice of the Soma juice.

Come forth, O you who are well-disposed, to aid the one who meditates; with your choicest gifts, sit down well upon our choice offerings. May Indra enjoy both of us, when he takes notice of the Soma juice. || 1 ||

Indra, for me—the sacrificer who is contemplating the arrival of Indra—well impels his two bay horses (*harī*) toward the *mantā* (the two who come) at the sacrifice, which is characterized by service (*sakṣaṇi*), accompanied by skill (*saguṇake*), and worthy of being honored (*sevye*).
Then that Indra [proceeds]. (Note: *maduṇake*; *taduṇake* are variants.)
May Indra come well toward the excellent and most desirable offerings and specific praises of the sacrificer who, through the most excellent and desirable paths,
has become gracious and has presented the oblation; having arrived, may he take pleasure in both that which belongs to us— the oblation and the praise—
and thus enjoy, consume, and listen to them.

Whenever [the god] perceives— that is, becomes aware of and recognizes with his tongue— the essence (rasa) of my *soma*, that is, the food-form (*andhas*) of the *soma* which produces *soma*; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The meaning is that he drinks the Soma;
then, "he enjoys it" is to be connected with the preceding clause.
O Indra, much-praised one, you traverse the divine luminous realms and the earthly regions with your splendor.
May those who repeatedly bring you to the sacrifices overcome the hostilities of the stingy ones.

O Indra, much-praised one, you traverse the celestial luminaries and the earthly realms through the mid-air. May those who repeatedly bring you to the sacrifices overcome the stingy ones who have failed to offer gifts.

O Indra, you pervade the celestial luminaries (*rocanā*) existing in heaven— those whose nature is light— or rather, the divine worlds; O Puruṣṭuta, you who are praised by many, O Indra, you pervade the earthly realms with your own radiance (*rajas*), characterized as the three worlds— or rather, [with your own light].
The vowel *ā* replaces the case-ending *śas* after the word *rajaḥ*.
You pervade the earthly worlds.

Those horses of yours which repeatedly—again and again—bring you near to our sacrificial rites (*adhvara*), may those horses, through their speech—that is, by means of praise—fully favor us, who are destitute of wealth (*arādhasaḥ*), so that they may grant us riches. May they truly bestow wealth upon us.
Then, at that time, the son, possessing a more beautiful form than his parents, recites the sacred hymns for them;
the wife leads her husband with her charm; and Indra is the well-adorned vehicle of the virtuous man.

This form of mine is more beautiful than the most beautiful, when the son is placed upon his parents. When the wife, well-disposed, leads her husband with her voice, then the auspicious marriage-procession of the man is fully adorned.
Of the body; "body" means form; that is perceived.
May Indra desire for me that sacrificial rite which is more beautiful than even the beautiful, exceedingly well-formed.
When the son—his own birth, his origin from his parents—reaches [the ritual] by way of being proclaimed;
at the time of the invocation of the *suvah* cry, he proclaims his own birth, saying, "The son of so-and-so Śarman sacrifices."
Alternatively:
let the son obtain from his parents that wealth which has come down through sacrifice;
and let the wife, the partner, by means of this auspicious speech in the form of sound, lead her husband, the sacrificer, to herself.
"Bhadraḥ" means auspicious; "pariṣkṛtaḥ" means well-prepared; "puṃsa it patyuḥ" means specifically for the husband.
It is to be given as a bridal gift to the wife. As it has been said: "O noble one, you bring forth excellent food" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.1.34).
Alternatively:

for the sake of the man, the exceedingly heroic Indra, that Soma—auspicious (*bhadra*), worthy of being honored (*bhajanīya*), and possessing the nature of a vehicle (*vāhavaḥ*) toward the gods—is prepared and consecrated (*pariṣkṛtaḥ saṃskṛtaḥ*).
The meaning is: "May Indra desire that."
I have meditated upon that beautiful place where they stand together, when the limbs of the cows direct their course like a bridal procession;
when the mother, the thought of the herd, is fulfilled by the people through the seven-toned song.

1. ta-bha1.2.4-mu- ‘su’ is not present; 2. ta-bha-mu-upā; 3. ta-bha1.2.4-mu- ‘su’ is not present; 4. ga-ta-bha2.5.6-mu-saṃskṛtaḥ; 5. ga ta-bha1.2.4-mu-it puṃsaḥ. Ka. 4-25: Thither I have directed my mind toward the beautiful common dwelling-place, where the cows, like lowing milch-cows, give their command for the journey. Where the ancient mother of the herd, the thinker, comes hither to the gathering of the singer who provides sustenance. (4)
That very same place is the common dwelling (*sadhastha*);
it is called *sadhastha* because they stand together there—a place, namely the sacrificial ground.
O Indra, contemplate it as beautiful and auspicious; shine forth upon it from all sides.

Wherever the "cows"—that is, the words characterized by praise, such as "O Indra, come! O Lord of the Bay Steeds, come!"—pray for your arrival toward one who does not know the ritual of instruction, there the illustration is: "like milch-cows toward their stall."
Just as cows that have recently calved long for the home that serves as the means of their arrival, so it is here. He states the reason why [the light] comes and shines forth:
"from which," that is, from what cause, "the thinker" (mantuḥ).

The root *man* means "to praise. My own mother, who is the worshipper, is indeed the goddess who brings about the qualities of the deities; she is the praise that belongs to the host, the first among the multitude of sacrificers. And because she consists of seven elements (*saptadhātu*).

The *dhātus* (elements) are so called because they are held (*dhāryante*) or because they perform actions (*kriyante*). Alternatively, they are the *chandāṃsi* (Vedic meters), which are not [material] elements. We, who possess seven meters, seven seasons, and consist of the seven officiating priests (*saptahotr*), are indeed the ones who direct the arrow—the word of praise—toward you.
Therefore, the sense is: "Come quickly!"
Or rather:
Grant us— that is, bestow upon us— that very auspicious place,
in which place you, as cows, shall delight us by providing milk for our journey.
A "vahatu" is a horse, so called because a person is carried by it;
it refers to milk, ghee, and so forth,
and does not have the sense of "at present."
Now they bestow [the gift].

Likewise, when the mother of the group of sons—who is to be praised, who is to be honored, and who approaches—approaches, or when the person of Vāṇa, the son of Vacas, endowed with the seven dhātus and the musical notes beginning with Nipāda, approaches; the meaning is that one should bestow [the gift] in a manner corresponding to that.
He has surpassed you all; seeking the gods, he goes alone with the Rudras to the place of victory.
Sing forth praise for those among the immortals who grant gifts; pour out the honeyed mead for them from the jars.

He who seeks the gods has surpassed you; alone among the Rudras, he goes forth victorious. Or rather, among those immortals in whom there is praise for the sake of giving, pour out the honey from the waves all around. 5.

He, the sacrificer, longing for the gods, has reached your station, the place of the Hotṛ, having become exhausted. Then, from among the Hotṛs, one— the principal Indra— going swiftly together with the Rudras, the sons of Rudra, the Maruts, goes to your sacrifice, or [he goes] with speed.
The word *vā* has the sense of *api* (also).
Even praise becomes capable of bestowing wealth (*dāvane*) upon those gods who are immortal (*amṛteṣu*), that is, free from the nature of death.
Therefore, *vaḥ* means "you."
The substitution of *vas* for *vaḥ* is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Pour out from all sides with water the honey—the exhilarating Soma—for the waves, for the rays, and for the gods.
While being deposited, hidden within the womb, the guardian of the gods’ ordinances spoke to me:
"Indra, the knower, has indeed looked after you; instructed by him, I have come here."
Being deposited, hidden away in the waters—Indra, the guardian of the gods’ laws, has declared this to me. For he, the knowing one, beheld you; instructed by him, O Agni, I have come here. 6.
1. In manuscript *ga*, "the cows" (*'dhenavaḥ*) is absent. 2.

In manuscripts *ta*1.2.5.6.7 and *bha*6, it reads "the mother of the qualities belonging to her own nature"; in *tā*3.4, "the qualities of various deities belonging to her own nature"; and in *bhā*1.2.4.7, "of the qualities belonging to her own nature of the deities.
3. In manuscripts *ta*, *bhā*1.2.4.6, it reads "auspicious" (*kalyāṇam*).
4. "Give the house to Ga-ta3-bhā2.6.
5. "He has become one who is superior to Ta.
6. "To those other than the Hotṛs; to those other than the Avyahotṛs, [to] Bhara2.4.6. (Bhā1.4)
In the sacrifice of Kuruśravaṇa, Agni is designated as "the one being deposited.

Indra, the protector of the gods' vows (vratapāḥ)—that is, the guardian of their ritual action—proclaimed to me, "to me," you who are being deposited by the Adhvaryu priest in the Āhavanīya fire, hidden and concealed within the waters that serve as your mothers. He spoke thus.
O Agni, you who are wise and knowing—Indra, having recognized his own authority, or rather, having looked back upon you, his own devotee, followed after you;
instructed by that Indra, being thus taught, "By this path you must go to heaven with him," I have come, and I shall go toward heaven.

One who does not know the field, having approached one who knows the field, goes forth instructed by the knower of the field. This indeed is the blessing of instruction; moreover, he finds the path of the Aṅgirasas. One who does not know the field, having approached one who knows the field, goes forth instructed by the knower of the field. This indeed is the blessing of instruction; moreover, he finds the path of the Aṅgirasas.
This is also a supplementary praise of the instruction.
"One who does not know the field":
[the root] *kṣi* is used in the senses of dwelling and going.
That by which one goes is a *kṣetra*, meaning a path.
