A man who does not know the path asked a *kṣetravit*, a knower of the field—that is, a person who knows the way. Being instructed by that knower of the field who understands the path, and having had the way shown to him, he proceeds; that is, he goes to the destination he desires.
This indeed—this very thing—is the auspicious, worshipful, and beneficial path of instruction in the form of guidance.
What is it?
Moreover, one who is thirsty finds—that is, obtains—the *suti*, the path to the waters that must be traversed by way of the straight limbs.
Alternatively,
"aṅgasīnām" is an adjective qualifying "suteḥ" (of the path). Indeed, one obtains a path that is straight, not crooked, and easy to traverse without effort.

Then indeed he was led forth from his mother’s udder; these days have come back to him. Old age has overtaken this youth; the benevolent one has become gracious in spirit. Then indeed he was led forth from his mother’s udder; these days have come back to him. Old age has overtaken this youth; the benevolent one has become gracious in spirit.
This Agni was exhausted by the fire on this day;
[the root] *śram* is used in the sense of "to breathe" (*prāṇana*) with the suffix *ana*.
At that very moment, he thought of leading these, these days of the Soma sacrifice.
In the case of *manas* and *jñāna*,
there is the substitution of *bhlu* by way of transposition; the subsequent *tiṅ* suffixes are unaccented (*anighāta*).
Moreover, enveloped by splendors and surrounded [by them], he drinks— that is, consumes— the oblation consisting of soma and other essences from the udder of his mother,

the Earth. Likewise, old age— *jarimā* (derived from the root *jṛ*, meaning "to praise," with the suffix *iman* added according to the *Uṇādi* rules)— wears out this Agni, who is eternally youthful and who mingles himself with the oblations of the gods.
The praise being performed by the singers reaches him directly;
*īm* is a filler particle.

Then, being without malice (*ahelan*)—that is, not angry toward the singers—the Vasu became a dweller (*vasuḥ*), one who covers all through the granting of wealth, or one who possesses wealth (*vasumān*) through his splendors against enemies; he became well-disposed (*sumanāḥ*), having a beautiful mind, through his words.
1. For him, there is no such thing as "heaven.
2. Because one who knows the path asks when he has not reached [his destination]; the root *praccha* is used in the sense of a desire to know.

And he says, "One must go by this path," [saying] "then" (*tataḥ*). Then the man asked that Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*); for it is because he asks one who knows the way—[the root] *praccha* being used in the sense of a desire to know—that he asks him.
And when [he asks], "When should one go by this path? then that man [replies]. [The reading] "kṣetrajñaṃ...saḥ" does not exist in Bha 1.2.4.7.
3. Of that which has the form of instruction for creation:
"O Bhadra Kalaśa, perform this rite; O Kṛśaśravas, bestow gifts. May there be abundance in giving for the Maghavans; and may this Soma, whom I bear in my heart, be present."
These [are they]: Bhadra, Kalaśa, Kriyām, Kuruśravaṇa, Dardataḥ, Maghāni, and Dānaḥ. O bounteous ones, may he be yours, and this Soma which I carry in my heart. 9.
He is the jar (kalaśa) who is full of all arts (kalā);
or rather,
the possessive suffix has been elided.

O Kuruśravaṇa, like a *droṇakalaśa* vessel, perform [the sacrifice]! O Indra, worthy of hearing the praises that belong to them—the priests—grant and bestow riches and wealth upon the singers and the sacrificers. For the sake of Indra, let us perform these auspicious oblations and hymns that are worthy of being partaken.
In the case of the root *kṛ* with the suffix *liṅ*, the substitution *riṅ* occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule *riṅ śayagliṅkṣu* (7.4.28).

Now, the one who praises speaks: O *maghavan*s—O you whose wealth consists of praiseworthy hymns—let that Indra be for you (*vaḥ*) a giver (*dānaḥ*), that is, a giver indeed of wealth and other such things.
And let this Soma, present at the sacrifice, be the giver within my own heart—that Soma which I drink and which I bear (dhārayāmi) [in me].
[The root] *ḍubhṛñ* means "to sustain" and "to nourish.
By the rule *bhṛtrāmit*, the substitution of *it* occurs for the reduplicated syllable.
And that which is the absence of distress when entering [the water].
Or rather:
O King Trasadasyu, son of Kuruśravaṇa—by name Kalaśakulajāta—while you bestow riches upon the officiating priests, we perform the rites for your sake.
"Maghavānaḥ Kuruśravaṇāḥ"—
the plural number is used for honor.
Thus, may Indra be the giver to you as you perform this sacrificial rite.
And may this Soma bestow riches upon us.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness within the heart,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the seventh chapter of the seventh book in the *Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa*, a commentary on the *Ṛgvedasaṃhitā* composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial throne of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the eighth chapter begins.
Therein, the fourth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "pra mā," is the work of Kavaṣa Ailūṣa;
its first verse is a Triṣṭubh, and it is dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
The second and third [stotras] consist of Bṛhatī verses for Indra as the object of praise. The following six are Gāyatrīs.
With two verses beginning "Kuruśravaṇāvṛṇi," he praised the gift of King Kuruśravaṇa, the son of Trasadasyu.
Therefore, they have those [deities] as their presiding deities.

Now, when King Mitrātithi had passed away, the seer Kavaṣa approached his son Upaśravas—who was overwhelmed by grief—out of affection and freed him from his sorrow by means of the four verses beginning with "yasya prasvādasaḥ.
Therefore, those [verses] have those [deities] as their presiding deities.

And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: "The *pragātha* beginning with 'pra māyā' belongs to the Viśvedevas; the [verse] beginning with 'indraḥ' is a *gāyatrī*; two [verses] belong to Kuruśravaṇa Trāsadasya as a praise of his gift; and by the following [verses], out of affection for King Mitrātithi who had died, [the poet] caused his son Adhipaśravas to forget his grief.
The application (*viniyoga*) has been explained.
The impulse of men has yoked me; I carry Pūṣan between [the worlds].
All the gods have protected me; the cry arose, "A wicked spirit has come!"
1. "The bountiful ones are not here!
Thus [he cried]. He yoked the steeds of men; I was indeed carrying Pūṣan between them. All the gods protected me; the ill-advised one has arrived—such was the cry that arose. 1.
The gods, the instigators (*prayuj*) of the people who perform the sacrifice, have directed me, the seer Kavaṇa, toward Kurūśravaṇa; they have yoked me for his sake.
Along the way, between [the two], I indeed carried—the friend Pūṣan, the lord of paths.

Thus it is heard in scripture: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni for one desiring offspring," and beginning thus, it continues, "One should subsequently offer a pap to Pūṣan" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.1.4).
Then, on the road, all the gods protected me, Kavaṇa;
and there was a cry and a sound on the road, saying, "This sage Duḥśāsu—this one who is difficult to subdue by anyone—is coming!"
The cattle, like wives with a common husband, burn me on every side;
the immortal [pain] oppresses me, the mortal am I, exhausted; my thought trembles in agitation.

My cattle on all sides distress me like rival wives; the immortal [affliction] oppresses me, and the emaciation of poverty; my mind trembles like that of a bird. May not the cattle—those things standing by my side—distress me on both sides like rival wives, as rival wives do, because of the lack of food, weakness, and lying on the ground. Furthermore, the "immortal" (amarti)—the ill-fortune arising from poverty concerning all matters—oppresses me; it afflicts me. And the "emaciation" (namratā) arising from the lack of clothing oppresses me. Moreover, the "wasting away" (jasuḥ), the exhaustion arising from the lack of food, also oppresses me. Furthermore, just as the mind of a bird (veḥ) trembles out of fear of hunters and the like, so too my mind trembles violently before the enemy.
The middle ones devour me like mice gnawing at their traps; O performer of a hundred sacrifices, they devour your praiser.
O Maghavan Indra, be gracious to us even once; then, be to us as a father.

The Rat: No; they gnaw at me from all sides. O Śatakratu, O Maghavan Indra, let not the devourers consume my praiser. O Indra, grant us mercy once for all; then, be to us like a father. O Śatakratu, you of many deeds, O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, O Indra: let not the devourers (*ādyaḥ*)—like rats (*mūṣaḥ na*) who gnaw at the threads of their own nests (*śikṣā*)—variously consume (*vyadanti*) me, your praiser. As Yāska says: "These desires (*ādyaḥ*) torment me on all sides like co-wives; they are like rats gnawing at the threads of their own nests. Or rather, it may refer to the limbs themselves: "they gnaw at the *śikṣās*. Thus [Yāska] says: "The desires torment me" (Nirukta 4.6). This being so, O Indra, grant us mercy (*mṛḷaya*) once for all by granting our desired objects, and thereby bring us complete happiness. Furthermore (*adha*), be our protector like a father.
I, the seer, have chosen King Kuruśravaṇa, the son of Trasadasyu,
the most generous among those who offer worship.
I, the seer, chose Kuruśravaṇa, the son of Trasadasyu, the king, the most bountiful patron of the priests. 4.

The seer (*ṛṣi*), who perceives objects beyond the senses, says: "I, Kavaṣa, [make] Trasadasyu’s son, Kurucravas—him who is most liberal in granting wealth—the object of my praise. The Kurus are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
I have chosen King Nanna, the listener of those praises and the glory of the Kurus, for the sake of the sacrificial priests (vāghat), that is, I pray for wealth.

I shall praise him whose three bay horses carry me straight in his chariot—he who bestows a thousandfold sacrificial fees. 5. Of whom my three bay steeds carry me straight in the chariot; I shall praise him, the giver of a thousand-fold dakṣiṇā. 5.

The three bay horses belonging to that king named Kuruśravaṇa carry me, Kavaṣa, swiftly and properly as I set out in the chariot; I praise and extol King Kuruśravaṇa at this sacrifice where a thousand-fold sacrificial fees are given.
Thus the seer prays, having taken hold of the chariot that lacks a firm foundation.
Following this, with the remainder of the hymn beginning with "yasya" (of whom), Kavaṣa approaches Upamaśravas, the son of King Mitratithi who has died, and out of affection dispels his grief.

Whose songs, sweet-tasting as those of his father Upamaśravas, were like a field spoken of for one who has praised it. 6. Whose; sweet-tasting; songs; of Upamaśravas; of the father; like a field; as it were; for one who has praised it. 6.
O King, you will cause the songs—the words—of your father Upamaśravas, son of Mitrātithi, to be exceedingly sweet.
Therein lies the illustration:
just as one does not find pleasure in a field that has been prepared for the sake of giving to a poor man who comes seeking, so too is the sense of [your father's] hymns.
The connection [is to be understood] with what follows.
Come hither, O son of Upamaśravas, grandson of Mitratithi! I am the one who honors your father. 7. adhi | putra | upama'śravaḥ | napāt | mitra'atithe | ihi | pituḥ | te | asmi | vanditā || 7 ||
O son Upamaśravas, grandson of Mitrātithi, look upon me with favor; come to me.
I am the one who honors and praises your father, that very Mitrātithi.
Knowing this, do not grieve.
If this substance exists, give it all to me.

If I were the master of immortality, or even of mortals, then my bountiful lord would surely live. (8) If I were the master of immortality, or even of mortals, then my bountiful lord would surely live. (8)

Moreover, if I were the lord—were I the master—over the causes of death for either the immortals, the gods, or mortals, the humans, then Maghavan, the wealthy King Mitratithi, who was the sacrificer of me, Kavaṣa, would still be living, that is, he would maintain his life-breaths.
Thus, since I am not the lord over the cause of death, the meaning is that this king has died.
No one, even one with a hundred lives, lives beyond the decree of the gods; he has been separated from his companion by that very [decree]. || 9 ||
Even one who has lived a hundred autumns—that is, for a hundred years—does not live beyond the *vrata*, the action characterized by the limits set by the gods beginning with Brahmā.
Likewise, knowing that one is separated from or becomes dissociated from a companion (*yuja*) such as a friend or relative, do not grieve. This is the meaning.

The fifth hymn, consisting of fourteen verses beginning with "prāvepāḥ," is the seer's work of Kaṣapa Ailūṣa, or of Akṣa, the son of Mujavan.
The seventh verse is a Jagatī; the remaining thirteen are Triṣṭubhs.
Here, the twelfth [verse] praises the dice, as do the seventh and those beginning with the ninth;
therefore, they have those as their deities.
The thirteenth praises agriculture.
Therefore, that deity belongs to her.
Thus, five [verses] have been accounted for.
With the remaining nine, the gambler and the dice are censured.
Therefore, those [verses] also have that very deity.

Thus it has been enumerated: "The *Prāvepas*, the five [verses], the *Maujavat*, the praise of agriculture, the censure of gambling, and the seventh is a *Jagatī*. Their application (*viniyoga*) has been explained.
The dangling ones, born in the wind, rolling upon the gaming board, exhilarate me like the draught of Soma from Mount Mujavat; the wakeful Vibhīdaka nut has brought me joy.
The dangling ones do not intoxicate me; born in the windy place, they roll about in the hollow. Like a draught of Soma from Mount Mujavat, the wakeful Vibhīdaka nut has pleased me. 1.

"The dice—belonging to the large *bṛhat* fruit of the *vibhītaka* tree, born in windy places, rolling on the parched expanse of the desert, trembling and shaking—intoxicate me, that is, they gladden me. Furthermore, the *vibhīdaka*, the die made from the *vibhītaka* fruit, which is wakeful—that is, the cause of the gamblers' staying awake through joy and grief at victory and defeat—has covered me; it exhilarates me.
In this regard, there is an illustration: [the text continues].
‘As of Soma’:

of that.
In that place, the most excellent Soma is born;
the meaning is that it exhilarates both the drinkers—the sacrificers—and the gods, just like that [Soma].
And so Yāska says: "The fruits of the great trembling Vibhītaka tree exhilarate me."

"Born in the wind, born on the slope, rolling in the hollow; the hollow is a crushing place, for it crushes; it becomes a place without water, for 'the plants have departed from him'—so they say. Like the draught of Soma from Mount Mujavat, [there is] the draught of the Mujavat plants; born on Mount Mujavat, Mujavat is a mountain; Mujavat is muñja grass, for it is released. *Iṣīkā* is so called because of its movement and crossing; this other *iṣīkā* is from the same root. *Vibhītaka* is so called because of its splitting; *jāgṛvi* is so called because of its wakefulness; *mahyam acchadat* (he covered me)—thus [it is said]. (Nirukta 9.8)
She did not scold me, nor was she angry; she was kind toward her friends and even toward me. Yet, for the sake of a single throw of the die, I have driven away my devoted wife.

No, she did not scold; she was not angry. She has been kind toward her friends and even toward me. For the sake of a single die, I have driven away my devoted wife. ‘This is my wife; she did not scold me, nor was she angry with me, the gambler; she did not despise me, nor was she ashamed.
She was kind—that is, she was pleasant—to our fellow-gamblers, and indeed, she was also kind to me.’

Thus, for the sake of—that is, on account of—the "eye" (akṣa) of that man for whom the Supreme (para) is the sole primary object, I abandoned—that is, I renounced—my wife who was devoted and compliant. This is the meaning.
My mother-in-law hates me, my wife holds me back, and when I seek help, I find no one to comfort me;
like the bladder of an aging horse, I find no enjoyment in this gambler.
The mother-in-law hates him; his wife holds him back. Seeking refuge, he finds no one to comfort him. Like the worn-out hide of an old horse, I find no use for this gambler.
1. *ta-mu-vimuñcatī-pīkam-īṣīkā-īpate*; *bha-vimucyate-ṣīkayā-pīkate*.
2. *ta-‘jāyā’ does not exist*. *Vśvaśrūḥ*: the mother-in-law hates—that is, reviles—the gambler who has gone home to his wife.

Furthermore, his wife (bhāryā) restrains (vṛṇaddhi) him—that is, she holds him back. Moreover, the gambler (kitava), when he has been supplanted (nāthitaḥ)—meaning when he is begging—does not find (na vindate), that is, does not obtain, one who would comfort (marḍitāram) him by giving wealth. Reflecting thus with my intellect, I [speak] of the old man (jarataḥ), the aged (vṛddhasya), the one who has perished (vastasya).
"Vasna" means price or value.
I do not find, nor do I obtain, the enjoyment of that wealth, like that of a gambler who has lost his stake.
Others embrace the wife of him whose eye was the swift steed at the place of sacrifice;
his father, mother, and brothers say of him, "We do not know him; lead him away bound."
Others caress the wife of him whose wealth the swift die has coveted; his father, mother, and brothers say of him, "We do not know him; lead him away bound. 4.
In the acquisition of the wealth of that gambler, the strong and vigorous one, the god, desiring [the prize], exerts himself; he creates a longing for that [wealth] of his.

The dice here are like goads, piercing, deceitful, burning, and causing torment. They bestow wealth upon children to the victor, yet they are mixed with honey through the destruction of the gambler. The dice—indeed, they are like goads (*aṅkuśinaḥ*), possessing hooks; they are piercing (*nitodinaḥ*) and deceitful (*nikṛtvānaḥ*), prone to cutting down the loser. They are burning (*tapanāḥ*), causing distress to the gambler upon defeat, and tormenting (*tāpayiṣṇavaḥ*), for by seizing all one's possessions, they have the nature of afflicting the entire household. Furthermore, to the victorious gambler, they are "bestowers of wealth upon children" (*kumāradeṣṇāḥ*), becoming givers to children through the granting of riches. Moreover, being mixed with honey (*madhvā saṃpṛktāḥ*), they become the "slayers again" (*punarhaṇaḥ*) of the gambler through the "destruction" (*barhaṇā*)—the increased seizure of all property—by his opponent.

The troop of fifty-three plays; like the god Savitṛ, whose laws are true. Even before the wrath of the fierce one, they do not bow down; even the king pays homage to them. The troop (*vrātaḥ*) of these dice, numbering fifty-three (*tripañcāśaḥ*), plays (*krīḍati*)—that is, it moves about in the gambling arena. For the dice generally play with the players as their counters. Therein lies the comparison: like the god Savitṛ, the impeller of the entire world, whose laws (*satyadharma*) are true; just as the god Savitṛ moves about in the world, so does the troop of dice move about in the gambling arena. Furthermore, even before the wrath (*manyave*) of the fierce (*ugra*) one—that is, even before the anger of a cruel person—they do not bow down (*na namante*); they do not submit to his will. Even the king (*rājā*), the lord of the world, performs homage (*namaḥ*) to them at the time of the game; he does not treat them with contempt.

Rolling low, yet flickering above, the handless dice overcome the man who has hands. Like divine coals cast upon a barren wasteland, though cold to the touch, they utterly consume the heart. Furthermore, these dice roll on the low ground; nevertheless, they flicker over the hearts of the gamblers who fear defeat. Though handless—devoid of hands—the dice overcome the gambler who possesses hands by bringing about his defeat. Like divine coals—that is, dice resembling coals cast upon a barren wasteland devoid of fuel—they, while being cold to the touch, utterly consume the heart, the inner organ of the gamblers, reducing it to ashes with the torment born of defeat.

"Who indeed is the wife of that gambler wandering [here and there], who, having been abandoned, suffers with the torment born of separation?
Even the mother, deprived of her connection to the son wandering [here and there], suffers;
she becomes distressed through grief for her son."

O gambler, you who are in debt from losing at dice, fearing on all sides and desiring wealth born of theft, do not play with dice against others, such as Brāhmaṇas and the like; go instead to their home. Do not gamble with dice; rather, practice agriculture. Delight in your own earnings, regarding them as much. There are cows there, O gambler; there is a wife there. This neighbor, having come, points this out to me. 13. ṛṇāvā akṣaparājayāhaṇavān kitavaḥ sarvato bibhyaddhanaṃ steyajanitam icchamānaḥ kāmayamānaḥ anyeṣāṃ brāhmaṇādīnām astaṃ gṛham | akṣaiḥ | mā | dīvyaḥ | kṛṣim | it | kṛṣasva | vitte | ramasva | bahu | manyamānaḥ | tatra | gāvaḥ | kitava | tatra | jāyā | tat | me | vi | caṣṭe | sritā | ayam | aryaḥ ||13||
O gambler, thinking highly of yourself and placing your trust in my words, play with dice; do not gamble [with me].
Practice agriculture alone; cultivate the land.
Once wealth has been acquired through farming, take delight in that riches.
In that [state], there are cows for cultivation;
in that, there is a wife.
Savitṛ—the author of the Śruti and Smṛti, the impeller of all, this visible noble Lord—discloses that very secret of Dharma, having declared it in various ways.
Make us your friend; indeed, have mercy on us. Do not approach us with your terrible and impetuous wrath. Let your anger and hostility now depart; let another now be the one to seize the brown ones.
Make us your friend; indeed, have mercy upon us! Do not approach us with your terrible, bold assault. Let your wrath and hostility now depart; let another fall into the snare of the tawny ones.
O dice, you must make us a friend; establish friendship toward us. The word "khalu" is a filler. And "naḥ" means "toward us"; have mercy upon us and grant us happiness.
Do not approach us, O bold one— with the bold, [here the nominative is used in the sense of the instrumental]— with your terrible and irresistible [nature]. Do not go toward us.
Furthermore, let your wrath—your anger—and our enemy, the adversary, settle among us; let it abide in our enemies.
Let some other enemy of ours quickly fall into the snare, that is, the binding, of you who are tawny-colored.
The sixth hymn, consisting of fourteen verses beginning with “*abudhram*,” is the seerly composition (*ārṣam*) of Luśa, the son of Dhanaka.
This [hymn] and the following one are dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
The thirteenth and fourteenth verses are *triṣṭubh*s; the remaining twelve are *jagatī*s.
And thus it has been listed: “*Abudhram*, [the hymn] of Luśa, [beginning with] *dhānākaḥ*, is dedicated to the Viśvedevas and ends with two *triṣṭubh* verses.
The application of the hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*) has been explained.
This verse, “*Viśve adya*,” is the invitatory prayer (*anuvākyā*) for the offering of the omentum (*vapā-yāga*) of the eleven-fold animal sacrifice dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "May all the Maruts today, may all [the gods] come to our aid; may the praise of the gods reach us" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
These foremost ones, accompanied by Indra, have awakened; bearing light at the dawning of the Uṣas, may the great Heaven and Earth be mindful of this. Today we choose the waters and the gods.

O Indra, those foremost ones, accompanied by you, have brought forth light at the dawning of the mornings; may the great Heaven and Earth take notice of this. Today we choose the waters of the gods. 1.

Accompanied by Indra—that is, belonging to Indra as the one to be worshipped—those fires, namely the Āhavanīya and others, at the dawning of the dawn, during the times when darkness is dispelled, bearing and maintaining light and splendor, have awakened. The two great ones, Heaven and Earth, performed their work (*apah*);
for *apaḥ* is listed among the names for "work" (*karman*) in the lexicon.
Let them know this:
now, on this day, we choose for ourselves the protection of the gods, Indra and the others, against the demons.
We choose for ourselves protection from heaven and earth; we seek the Mothers, the Sandhanvan mountains, and Śaryaṇāvat.
We pray to Sūrya and Uṣas for sinlessness; may the well-pressed Soma bring us auspiciousness today.
1. In *ta* and *bha*, ‘*abhi*’ is absent.
2. In *ta* 1.2.6 and *mu*, “*nosmākam anyaḥ*”; in *ta* 4.5.7, *bha* 6, and *nu*, “*nosmākaṃ*”.

From heaven and earth, from the waters, we choose for ourselves; from the mothers, the rivers, the mountains, and Śaryaṇāvat. We implore the Sun and the Dawns for sinlessness. May Soma, being pressed today, bring us what is auspicious. 2.

We choose for ourselves the protection (*avas*) of Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), who are related to us as our effects. Furthermore, we pray for sinlessness—the freedom from the evil produced by defects in ritual action—from the mothers who fashioned the world, from the rivers, from the lake Śaryaṇāvat, from the mountains and mountain peaks, and likewise from the Sun and the Dawn. Moreover, on this very day, may the pressed and celebrated Soma bring about for us what is auspicious and beneficial.
May Heaven and Earth, the two great mothers, today grant us freedom from sin for our well-being;
may the dawning Uṣas drive away evil. We pray for the auspicious blessing of the kindled Agni.
May Heaven and Earth, the two great mothers, deliver us today from sin for our well-being. May Dawn, shining forth, drive away evil. We pray to the kindled Agni for prosperity. 3.

May the two great Mothers, the Earth and Heaven—who are the mothers of all—protect us today on this day, making us free from sin and devoid of offense, for our well-being and prosperity. Furthermore, may the Dawn, shining forth and driving away the darkness, dispel and remove our evil and sin.
Moreover, we pray for well-being—the total absence of destruction—for Agni, who is being kindled and blazing brightly.
This is not the first dawn for Sudevi; may Revati shine forth with wealth for the Revatsus.
May we keep far away the wrath of the malicious one; we pray to the well-kindled Agni for well-being.
May this Dawn, the first among our goddesses, shine forth wealth upon the wealthy patrons. May she drive far away the wrath of the malicious man. We pray for well-being from Agni as he is kindled. 4.

Revatī, the wealthy one, the foremost and preeminent; this Dawn, the dispeller of evils, O auspicious goddess, may she shine forth for us—bestowing wealth and the excellence of the principal sacrifice upon those who partake of it. May she drive away the darkness.
Furthermore, let us cast far away, at a great distance, the wrath and anger of the man who possesses ill-wealth.
Thus they sing.
The Dawns, who stream forth with the rays of the sun, bringing light at their break—may they shine auspiciously upon us today for our renown; we pray for well-being from Agni as he is kindled.

The Dawns, who glide forth with the rays of the sun, bringing light at their breakings—may they shine upon us today with auspiciousness for our renown; we pray for well-being from the kindled Agni. 5.

Those Dawns which, with the rays and beams of the Sun, hasten forth—meeting together at the dawns, at the times of breaking through when the darkness is dispelled—and which bear their own light and splendor; may you, being auspicious and worthy of worship, shine for us today on this day for the sake of renown and food. Shine forth! Dispel the darkness! May they resound.

1. By that which is not to be done; 2. O you who have become like a mother to the letter *t*; 3. O you who protect the letters *ta* and *bha* well; 4. The darknesses; [and] 6. from the darkness, O *bha*.

May the Uṣas dawns come to us free from disease; may the foremost ones rise up with great light. May the Aśvins yoke their swift chariot. We pray for well-being from Agni as he is kindled. Free from disease, may the Uṣas dawns come toward us. May the foremost ones rise up with great light—that is, endowed with great splendor. May the Aśvins yoke their swift-moving chariot, yoked with she-mules, so that they may come toward us—according to the reading: "The bay horses belong to the Āditya, the she-mules to the Aśvins. The rest is self-evident.
O Savitṛ, impel for us today that most excellent and desirable portion, for you are the bestower of treasures.

I invoke the Mother of Wealth, the Dhiṣaṇā, on this day when the sacrificial grass is spread upon the altar. When the mind is fixed upon the attainment of the desired fruit, and when there is the separation from the drinking of water and the union with Soma, we, free from hatred, pray to the Ādityas for our desired goal.
O singer, you stand in the protection, the happiness, or the secure place of those Āditya gods;
you support—that is, you carry out or accomplish—the duties to be performed.
The rest is self-evident.
Upon our sacred grass at the shared feast in the high heaven, O Gods, I invoke you; seat yourselves, O seven Hotars!
We pray to Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga, and Agni—the foremost bringer of well-being—who is kindled with fuel.

Upon our great sacrificial grass at the communal feast, I invoke the gods in heaven; O Hotṛ, seat the seven! For the sake of success, we seek Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga, and Agni—him who is kindled—for our well-being. 10.

O Agni, seat upon the sacrificial grass at our great, vast, and radiant feast in heaven—wherein the gods rejoice—those seven Hotṛ-priests who utter the *vaṣaṭ* call: Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga, and the other gods worthy of sacrifice. You yourself, O Agni, must establish them there.
The act of turning toward the fire is understood from such mantras as, "O Vasu, seat the divine folk here today upon the sacrificial grass" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.45.9).
For in that context, I praise—the word *vīḷe* meaning "I laud"—those gods, such as Tvaṣṭṛ and others, who have been seated there for the sake of obtaining wealth;
the rest is self-evident.

O Ādityas, come hither for our complete well-being; with one accord, protect our sacrifice for our prosperity. We pray to Bṛhaspati, Pūṣan, the Aśvins, and Bhaga, and to Agni, the leader of well-being, as he is kindled.

O Ādityas, come hither for our complete well-being; protect our sacrifice for our prosperity, being of one accord. We pray to Bṛhaspati, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Bhaga; we seek the blessing of the kindled Agni. 11.
O Ādityas, you who have been summoned by us, come for our total well-being—that is, for the sake of the sacrifice.
Having arrived, O you who are of one mind and united, come toward our sacrifice for our prosperity.
And we pray for well-being—the non-destruction in every way—for Bṛhaspati, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, Bhaga the god, and the kindled, brightly shining Agni. We entreat them for auspiciousness.
O Gods, grant us that well-spoken shelter which is auspicious, well-sustained, and protective for men;
for our cattle, our children, and our progeny, we pray for well-being from the kindled Agni.

O Gods, Ādityas, grant us that well-praised shelter which is easy to maintain and provides protection for men; for our cattle, our children, and our progeny, so that we may live—svasti! We pray to Agni as he is kindled. 12.

O Ādityas, O gods, you—grant us that most praiseworthy, highly extolled, well-sustaining, and very great *nṛpāyya* (protection for men), that *chardiḥ* (abode) desired by us; grant it for every animal, for our offspring, for our sons, for our grandsons, and for the sake of life.
The rest is established.
May all the Maruts come today with every aid; may all of them be foremost when kindled.
May all the gods come to us with protection; may all wealth and strength be ours.
May all the Maruts come today with their aid; may all the fires be well-kindled. May all the gods come to us with protection; may all wealth and strength be ours. 13.
On this day, the principal day of sacrifice, may all the Viśvedevas, all the Maruts, and all the gods beginning with Rudra, together with their hosts, be present for our protection (*ūti*).
Furthermore, may all the fires—the Āhavanīya and others—be well-kindled and blazing.
Moreover, may all the gods beginning with Indra come to us with their protection (*avasā*).
Furthermore, may all wealth, all riches, and food be ours—may they be with us.
O Gods, whomsoever you favor in the winning of booty, whomsoever you protect and carry across the day;
he who knows no fear under your guardianship—may we be such as these for the feast of the gods, O swift ones!

O Gods, whomsoever you favor in the contest for booty, whomsoever you protect, whomsoever you deliver—may both Heaven and Earth, the wise and observers of cosmic order (*ṛtavarī*), guard us from distress and injury.

Let not the treacherous, threefold-turning pitfall prevail over us. Today we choose that blessing of the Gods. 2. O Gods, whomsoever you favor in the contest for booty, whomsoever you protect, whomsoever you deliver—may both Heaven and Earth, the wise and observers of cosmic order (*ṛtavarī*), guard us from distress and injury. Let not the treacherous, threefold-turning pitfall prevail over us. Today we choose that blessing of the Gods. 2.

May Pracetas, Subuddhi, Ṛtāvarī, Yajñavatī, Satyavatī, Uṣas, and Pṛthivī—both Heaven and Earth—protect us from injury, from harm, and from sin. Furthermore, may Nirṛti, the goddess of death who possesses base knowledge, have no power over us. Moreover, today, on this very day, we choose and pray for that unique protection belonging to the gods.
May Aditi, the mother of Mitra and of wealthy Varuṇa, protect us from all distress.
May we obtain that all-encompassing light; this, O gods, we choose from you today.

May Aditi protect us from all distress; she is the mother of Mitra and of wealthy Varuṇa. May we obtain that light which possesses the splendor of heaven. Today, O gods, we choose that which is the source of strength. 3.
May Aditi, the divine mother and progenitress of the wealthy Mitra and Varuṇa—of the two wealthy Mitra and Varuṇa—protect and guard us from all evil, from every distress.
Furthermore, may we attain the light and splendor of heaven that is free from predators—that is, devoid of harmers.
(The root *naś* here signifies the act of reaching or attaining.)
And "flight" means moving swiftly;
the sense is that we may reach [our goal] quickly. The rest is established.
May the sounding pressing-stone drive away the Rakṣasas, the evil-doers, Nirṛti, and every devouring fiend.
May we obtain the protection of the Ādityas and the Maruts; that we choose from the gods today.

May the pressing-stone, speaking aloud, drive away the Rākṣasas, evil dreams, and the pitfall; may we attain the protection of the Ādityas and the Maruts. That which is the refuge of the gods, that we choose today. 4.

May the pressing-stone (*grāvan*), the stone for crushing [the soma], while speaking—that is, making sound at the time of pressing—drive away the *rakṣases*, those who create obstacles to the sacrifice;
may it drive away the evil dream, our misfortune arising from bad dreams;
and may it drive away *Nirṛti*, the deity of death.
May he ward off the devouring, all-consuming Viśva, including the Piśācas and others.
Thus, when the sacrifice has been accomplished free from obstacles, may we attain and enjoy *śarma*, the happiness associated with the Ādityas and the Maruts. The rest is established.
May Bṛhaspati sit upon the sacred grass; may the nourishment swell; may the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants sing their praise.
Let us fashion a well-awakened prayer for life; this we choose from the gods for you today.

May Indra sit upon the sacred grass; may the sacrificial food swell; may Bṛhaspati chant the verses with the Sāman hymns. Let us fashion a prayer of clear vision for the sake of life. Today, we choose that which is the strength of the gods. ||5||
May Indra sit upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).
May Iḷā—the speech of the intermediate region characterized by thunder—also overflow and sprinkle us.
And may Bṛhaspati, praised with *sāman* chants and possessing the *ṛc*, also sing our praise and honor us.

1. *ta-bha-mu-satyavatyau ca* (and [the two verses] containing the word *satyavatī*). 2. *tara.6-hiṃsakamakāt*; *ta5-hiṃsakasakāśāt* (from the presence of the one who harms). 3. *ga-ta3-bha-pāpāt* (from evil). 4. *ga-cāvighnena*; *ta-bha-mu-nirvighnena* (without obstacle). 5. *ta1.2.3.4.5.7-bha-gīyamāne*; *ta6-mu-gāyamāne* (while being sung).
Furthermore, we place—that is, we set down—*supraketaṃ* (well-known), *suprajñānaṃ* (of excellent wisdom), *manma* (a thought, wealth, or hymn) for *jīvase* (for the sake of living).
The rest is established.

O Aśvins, perform our sacrifice with a double or triple touch; make the rite swift for the attainment of bliss. This oblation, offered with ghee toward the eastern direction—that we choose today from among the gods.

The touch of heaven, our sacrifice, O Aśvins—make our swift rite successful; grant us favor for the sacrifice. With ghee offered toward the east, that which belongs to the swift-moving host of the gods, we choose today. 6.
O Aśvins, you two make our sacrifice one that touches the sky, reaching unto heaven;
likewise, make our sacrifice swift and free from injury.
For the sake of the fulfillment of our desires, grant us happiness.
Furthermore, the meaning is: "with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), offer oblation to Agni, whose rays extend eastward, so as to turn him toward the gods.
The rest is self-evident.
I invoke the well-invoked host of Maruts, whose backs are bright with flame, who are auspicious for the noble man and bringers of well-being.
May we obtain abundance of wealth for the sake of high renown; this, O Gods, we choose today.

I invoke the host of Maruts, who are swift to hear, purifying, lofty, and bringing prosperity for our common welfare. May we obtain an increase of wealth for the sake of high renown. Today, we choose that which belongs to the swift-moving troop of the gods. 7.

I invoke for the sake of companionship the host of Maruts—easy to invoke, purifying, lofty, beautiful to behold, the source of happiness, the nourisher of wealth, and the assembly belonging to the Maruts.
Having approached them, I call upon that host for the sake of excellent food or great renown; we shall hold them in our thoughts.
The rest is self-evident.
We bring forth the protector of the waters, the life-sustaining wood, the one who favors the gods, the easily invoked, the glory of the sacrifice;
we choose today that Soma, the radiant, the power of Indra, which belongs to the gods.

We bring forth the supreme life-giving strength from the waters; we choose for ourselves today that which belongs to the gods—the divine, woolly fleece, the one easily invoked, the glory of the sacrifice, the well-reined Soma, the power of Indra. We choose that which is the swift course of the gods. 8.
We bring—that is, we hold—Soma, the protector of the waters, whose life-force is wealth (jīvadhanva);

he who is the nourisher of living beings is jīvadhanva. We bring him who gratifies the gods (devāvya), who is easy to invoke (suhava) or worthy of beautiful praise, the glory of the sacrifice (adhvaraśrī), the one with beautiful rays (suraśmi), the Soma.
Either we cause [the Soma] to reach the Havirdhāna from the Patnīśālā,
or we entreat that deceased Soma for *indriya*, that is, virile power.
The rest is established.
May we, being well-guided, press the Soma; may we live as those whose sons live, free from sin.
May the haters of sacred knowledge carry away our transgression with their feet. This, O Gods, we choose today.

May we, being well-disposed, well-bestowing, and pressing the Soma with our hymns—living ourselves and having living sons, free from sin—cast the guilt upon those who hate sacred prayer; that we choose today as the refuge of the gods. 9.
1. In Ta-bha6-mu, "kuṣata" does not exist.
2. Ta-śāsvāya. 3. Ta1.2.6.7-vīrya tat.

May we— living, with living sons, free from offense, and devoid of transgression— along with our wives, children, and grandchildren, through excellent worship and beautiful devotion, obtain that host of divine beings;
may we enjoy them through praise and the offering of oblations.
Furthermore: let the haters of Brahman—that is, those who hate us Brāhmaṇas—let them gather together from all sides; let the *venas* (envious ones) bear our sin within themselves;
let them nourish it.
The rest is self-evident.
O you who are present, you who are worthy of sacrifice, listen! O gods, grant us that which we implore.
Today we choose for ourselves victorious wisdom, wealth accompanied by heroes, and invincible power against the enemy.

O you who are worthy of sacrifice among men, listen! O gods, grant us that which we implore of you: a victorious will, wealth, and glory consisting of heroic sons. This we choose from the gods today. 10.

O gods, those who are the all-gods of Savitṛ, whose covenant is true—those gods who are in the ordinance of Mitra and Varuṇa—bestow upon us auspiciousness accompanied by heroes, abundance of cattle, and manifold wealth. ||13||

O all you gods, you who abide in the *vrata*—the act known as *prasava* (impulsion)—of Savitṛ, whose impulsion is true, and of Mitra and Varuṇa; do you grant to me prosperity (*saubhaga*), wealth consisting of heroes such as sons, wealth consisting of cattle, wonderful and praiseworthy riches, and the performance of sacred rites. Grant these to me!
Savitar from behind, Savitar from the front, Savitar from above, Savitar from below;
may Savitar impel us toward complete well-being, and may Savitar grant us long life as a gift.
Savitṛ from behind; Savitṛ from the front; Savitṛ from above; Savitṛ from below; may Savitṛ impel for us complete well-being; may Savitṛ grant us long life. 14.

Savitar stands behind us from the west; Savitar stands before us from the east; and Savitar stands above us from the north. May Savitar impel toward us *sarvatāti*, that is, all our desired wealth and possessions.
Furthermore, may Savitar himself grant us long-lasting protection.
The repeated mention of the word "Savitar" is for the sake of expressing extreme reverence.
‘Namo mitrasya’: this is the eighth hymn, consisting of twelve verses. The seer is Abhitapā, the son of Sūrya.
These first five hymns are composed in the Jagatī meter.
The tenth verse of this hymn is a Triṣṭubh;
its deity is Sūrya.
Thus it has been declared in the Anukramaṇī: “*Namo* consists of twelve verses; *Abhitapāḥ* is dedicated to Sūrya; it is in the Jāgata [meter], though the tenth is indeed a Triṣṭubh.”
In the *āśvina-śastra*, after sunrise, this hymn belongs to the section concerning the Sun (*saurya-kāṇḍa*).
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "‘citraṃ devānām’, ‘namo mitrasya’" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.5).
At the Viṣuvat day, it serves as the *anurūpa* for the first verse of the *niṣkevalya* chant.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Vibhrāḍ bṛhat pibatu somyaṃ madhu namo mitrasya varuṇasya cakṣase*—these are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.6).
When another person is sleeping at sunset, one should remain for the remainder of the night and worship the Sun in the morning with the five [verses] beginning with “*yena sūrya jyotiṣā*.”

And it is stated in the Sūtra: “If the sun should set while one is sleeping after having begun [the recitation], he should remain silent and not sit down; having remained thus for the remainder of the night, he should worship the sun with the five verses beginning, ‘With that light by which you dispel the darkness’” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 3.7.1).
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping, he should worship the sun with the four verses beginning, ‘Of whom all...

And it is stated in the Sūtra: “If the sun should rise while the ritual is incomplete due to an improper performance, he should remain silent; the procedure is the same, with worship performed using the following four verses” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 3.7.2).
This is the *yājyā* for the oblation of the eleven-fold animal sacrifice dedicated to Sūrya.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*śaṃ no bhava cakṣasā śaṃ no ahā vāyo bhūṣa śucipāḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).
For the Hotṛkā priests during the placing of the wood-shavings, the verse is “*yad vo devāḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.12).
At the wedding, when the bride is to be made to weep, this verse, "ajīvaṃ rudantī," is to be muttered (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.8.4).
Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa! Paying honor to that great god, proclaim this Truth to Sūrya, the far-seeing, the banner born of the gods, the son of Heaven.
Homage! To the gaze of Mitra and Varuṇa; do service to that great god, that *ṛta*. Proclaim it to Sūrya, the son of Heaven, the banner born of the gods, who is visible from afar. 1.

1. *Ga*-Savitṛ is thus situated above and to the south; *Ta3-bha*-Savitṛ is situated below and to the south, and Savitṛ is likewise situated above and to the south; *Ta4*—thus Savitṛ is situated above and to the south. (404) Ṛgveda.

O you priests, for the sake of Mitra and Varuṇa— for the sight, for the beholding of the great, shining god who is visible from afar (even from the seventh distance)— for him who is born among the gods, for the banner who makes all things known,
for the son of heaven (the designation "son" being used because he is born in heaven)—
having offered salutation to Sūrya, honor that ordained *ṛta*, the ritual act characterized by sacrifice and the like.
Praise him; offer hymns of praise as well.
May my truthful speech protect me on every side, as far as heaven and earth extend their vastnesses;
everything else that moves enters into it, for the waters flow everywhere and the sun goes everywhere.

May she, whose speech is truth, protect us on every side—she by whom heaven and earth are stretched out and the days are spread; wherein everything else that moves comes to rest, while the waters flow forever and the sun rises forever. 2.
May that truthful speech, that utterance of truth, protect me—preserve me—from all sides, from every direction.

By that truthful speech, in whatever place heaven and earth (dyāvāpṛthivī) and the days and nights stretched themselves out, there everything else—the entire multitude of beings—enters and finds rest.
This multitude of beings which moves and trembles at all times, forever.
The waters flow forever, at all times, and the sun rises;
may she, who possesses such true speech, protect us—this is the meaning.
No godless man from of old can hold you back when you, O Sūrya, drive forth on your chariot with your swift, dappled steeds;
one region follows after the eastern one, and you travel toward the ocean with your light.

No, they are not gods; from of old they have dwelt in darkness, while you, with your swift, dappled steeds, drive upon your chariot. One portion of the realm follows along the eastern direction; with the other light, O Sūrya, you rise upward. 3.
O Sūrya, in your presence, from time immemorial, no ancient or primordial godless being—whether an Asura or a Rākṣasa—dwells; he does not abide there.
When? To this he replies: when you, with your swift-moving Etaśas horses, desire to harness your chariot.
Furthermore, another ancient light of yours follows along with the dust and the waters;
by means of that other light, you go forth—you rise up.
Or else:
The other ancient realm, the abode of the moon, follows after you—that is to say, it shines together with another light.

O Sūrya, with that light by which you dispel the darkness and with that radiance by which you quicken the entire world, with that drive away from us all lack of food, lack of offerings, disease, and evil dreams.

O Sūrya, with that light by which you dispel the darkness and send forth the entire world with your radiance—with that [light], drive away from us all lack of nourishment, lack of offerings, disease, and evil dreams; send them far away! 4.

O Sūrya, by that light and splendor with which you dispel and ward off darkness and gloom, and by that radiance with which you cause the entire world— the whole moving universe— to rise up, by that light drive away from us (*asmat*) lack of luster,
lack of radiance, lack of offerings, lack of oblations, and the multitude of diseases.
Drive away bad dreams, that which arises from bad dreams, and whatever is undesirable.
For you have been sent forth as the guardian of the universe; you wander here according to your own nature, protecting the sacred law (*vrata*).
Whatever resolve we declare to you today, O Sūrya, may the gods favor that intention of ours.
For, impelled by all, you guard the sacred law; rising up without malice, you follow your own inherent powers. O Sūrya, since we address you today, may the gods favor this our purpose. 5.
O Sūrya, sent forth and impelled by us, you, being free from malice and anger, protect the *vrata*—the ritual act—of every sacrificer;
indeed, you guard it from the Rākṣasas who would destroy the sacrifice.
Following after the *svadhā* offerings, you rise up and ascend.
The meaning is that after the morning oblation has been completed, you rise up.
And so, when we address you today on this day, may the gods, Indra and the others, favor—that is, grant their approval to—that ritual act of ours.
May Heaven and Earth, may the Waters, Indra, and the Maruts hear this our invocation for splendor!
Let us not be empty in the sight of the Sun; living, may we reach old age in prosperity.

May Heaven and Earth hear this call of ours; may the Waters, Indra, and the Maruts hear our invocation. May we not be deprived of the splendor of the sun’s gaze; living auspiciously, may we reach old age. 6.
May Heaven and Earth—the two worlds—Agni, Indra, and the Maruts hear this our invocation, our call, and that speech of ours consisting of hymns of praise.
The repetition of "naḥ" (our) is for the sake of emphasis.
May they listen!

Furthermore, may we not come to exist in the sight—that is, in the vision—of the Sun for the sake of increased suffering; indeed, let it not be so. Rather, living long and sustaining our vital breaths, may we attain and reach auspiciousness, well-being, old age, and immortality.
May we, with benevolent minds, possessing good offspring, free from disease and sinless,
behold you every day as you rise, O Sūrya of Mitra-like splendor, living long and full of life.
May we, with good intentions, good eyesight, possessing offspring, free from disease, and sinless, behold you every day as you rise, O Sūrya, great as Mitra, living long through many days. 7.

O Sūrya, may we—possessing benevolent minds, having good eyesight, endowed with progeny, free from disease, and devoid of sin—worship you at all times; this is the sense of the remainder [of the verse]. Furthermore, O Sūrya, who possesses the greatness of friends, may we, living long, behold you day after day as you rise.
O far-seeing Sūrya, may we, living mortals, behold you as you ascend from the vast expanse of light— you who bear great radiance, the shining one, for the eye of every eye.
1. You are impelled by the praises of Ga, Ta, Bha, and Sa.
2. "Na" does not exist in Ta, Bha, Na, and A.

O far-seeing Sūrya, may we, living long, behold you day by day as you ascend—the one who bears the great light, who sustains it, the radiant one, the eye for every eye, the bringer of joy, the vast and powerful one, rising above the great and mighty waters. *Note: The term "pārjasaḥ" is interpreted here as "of the water" (from *pāja-* meaning water or strength), referring to the rising over the great expanse of the ocean.*

O Sūrya, O you of golden hair, by whose signal all beings go forth and by whose rays they enter [to rest] with the nights—by means of our sinlessness, rise up for us day after day with ever-increasing prosperity. O Sūrya, O you of golden hair, by whose signal (ketunā) all beings (viśvā bhuvanāni) go forth (pra īrate) and by whose rays (aktubhiḥ) they enter (ni viśante)—that is, they rest or sleep—rise up for us (naḥ) through our sinlessness (anāgāstvena), day after day (ahnā-ahnā), with ever-increasing (vasyasā-vasyasā) welfare or excellence.

Be auspicious to us with your sight, be auspicious to us by day, be auspicious with your radiance, be auspicious with cold, and be auspicious with heat. O Sūrya, bestow upon us that wonderful wealth by which there may be well-being on the road and well-being in our home. 10. Be auspicious to us with your sight; be auspicious to us by day; be auspicious with your radiance; be auspicious with cold; be auspicious with heat. Just as there may be well-being on the road and well-being in the home, so, O Sūrya, bestow upon us that wonderful wealth. O Sūrya, may you be a bringer of happiness (*śam*) to us (*naḥ*) with your sight (*cakṣasā*), your splendor; be a bringer of happiness to us by day (*ahnā*); be a bringer of happiness with your radiance (*bhānunā*); be a bringer of happiness with cold (*himā*); and be a bringer of happiness with heat (*ghṛṇena*). Just as there is happiness for us on the road (*adhvan*) and happiness (*śam*) within the home (*duroṇe*), so, O Sūrya, grant us that wonderful (*citram*) wealth (*draviṇam*).

O Gods, grant protection for the welfare of both our classes of beings—of the two-footed and the four-footed. Let them eat, let them drink, and let them thrive; bestow upon us that peace, security, and freedom from disease. O Gods, authorized by the Sun, do you grant *śarma* (protection and happiness) to both kinds of our progeny—the two-footed, consisting of humans, and the four-footed, consisting of animals. Furthermore, let [our offspring] eat what is to be eaten, let them drink their water, and let them be well-fed, acting with vigor as if they were full of strength. Bestow upon us that which is auspicious, secure, and free from affliction.

Grant that which is beneficial, as well as auspicious happiness characterized by the pacification of disease, and that which is sinless—the happiness born from union with the objects of the senses—and bestow it upon us.

O Vasus, O gods who provide shelter, whatever grievous offense against you we have committed with our tongue—that is, through speech—or through the activity of our mind, namely, an act of hostility toward the gods; and whoever, being an enemy, approaches us with ill-will and behaves wickedly or causes us agitation—upon that enemy of ours, O Vasus, place that sin. (12) [Note: The commentary explains that "Vasus" are the gods who cause all things to dwell (*vasayitāraḥ*). "Jihvayā" means by speech. "Manasaḥ prayutī" means by the application or activity of the mind. "Guru" means great. "Devheḷanam" means an offense against the gods. "Arāvā" refers to one who moves as an adversary. "Ducchunāyate" means he acts like a wicked person or agitates us. "Ni dhaitana" means "place [the sin]"; the sense is "establish it" by the command of Sūrya.]
The ninth hymn, "asmin naḥ," consists of five verses; it is in the Jagatī meter and is dedicated to Indra. Muṣkara is its seer (ṛṣi).
Thus it has been declared: "asmin naḥ [has] five [verses]; Muṣkara."
"Indra is the one who bestows sleep.
Thus ends the application [of the hymn].
However, others—the followers of the Tāṇḍya and Śākhyāyana schools—describe the deity of this hymn as Indra the bull-testicled, and Luśa as the seer.

In this glorious, impetuous, and tumultuous battle, O Indra, protect us for the sake of victory. Wherein, in the struggle for cattle among the bold combatants who devour one another, the celestial weapons fall on all sides upon those who overcome men. O Indra, in this glorious, impetuous battle that has arrived—characterized by mutual blows and tumultuous shouting—you let out a lion’s roar; protect us for the acquisition of wealth. Where? He says: in that battle which is for the winning of cattle (*gopātā*), where men are overcome (*nṛpāhye*), and where among the bold warriors who devour one another, the celestial weapons fall from every direction.

O Indra, disclose for us in our dwelling wealth accompanied by food, a flood of cattle, and renown. O Śakra, may we be sharers of your victory; O Vasu, do that which we desire. O Indra, you who are renowned as the benefactor of all, disclose for us—in our dwelling—wealth that is abundant in food (or resonant with sound), rich in a flood of cattle, and worthy of praise. Furthermore, O Vasu, O Śakra, through your grace, may we be victorious over our enemies and become possessed of fatness—that is, strong and vigorous. What need is there for much speaking? Whatever we desire, O Excellent One, make all that come to pass.
1. [The suffix *kta*] occurs in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) when it possesses the sense of "gone" (*gata*).

O Indra, much-invoked by many, whoever—whether a Dāsa or an Ārya, whether godless or a non-god—plots against us for battle, may those enemies be easily overcome by us through you; with you as our ally, may we conquer them in the encounter. (3) O Puruhūta, much-praised Indra, whoever—a Dāsa, a laborer, a Śūdra, or an Ārya, a member of the [upper] three castes, or a godless one, an Asura other than the gods—intends against us for the sake of war, let all those enemies be "easily overcome" (*susahāḥ*) by us through your grace; that is, let them be subdued by our own power. Furthermore, with you as our helper, may we slay those enemies in the *saṃgame*, the encounter or battle. (3)
Him who is to be invoked by the few and by the many, who finds room for us in the encounter,
that Indra— the famous hero, the friend of all people, the possessor of bay horses— we shall bring forth for our protection.
The tenth hymn, consisting of fourteen verses beginning with "yo vām," has as its seer the daughter of Kakṣīvat named Ghoṣā, a proclaimer of sacred knowledge (brahmavādinī).
The last [verse] is a Triṣṭubh;
the remaining ones are Jagatīs.
The Aśvins are the deities.
And thus it has been introduced: “*yo vām palunā kākṣīvatī ghoṣārdhinaṃ hi triṣṭubantam*.
These three hymns beginning with *idam* belong to the *jagatī* metre in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*yo vām parijmā... these three; then for Triśirghna*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.15).
O Aśvins, that well-rolling chariot of yours which travels all around, to be invoked at evening and at dawn by the one who offers oblations—
this very name of yours, ever-present in the soma-libations, we invoke as easily summoned as that of a father.

O Aśvins, that well-rolling chariot of yours which travels all around, to be invoked at evening and at dawn by the offerer of oblations—evermore, we here invoke that name of yours which is easy to call upon, as one calls the name of a father. 1.
O Aśvins, your chariot— which goes all around (*parijmā*), which moves well (*suvṛt*), and which travels about—
[comes] at evening (*doṣām*) and at dawn (*uṣasaḥ*);
that is to say, during both day and night.

He is to be invoked—that is, to be offered oblations—to you two by the sacrificer possessing the sacrificial offering (*haviṣmat*). That very chariot of yours, which is your own and easy to invoke (*suhava*)—meaning its invocation is auspicious—we, the most ancient ones (*śaśvattamāsaḥ*), call upon it, just as one calls upon a father; we invoke it with this name.
Urge on the pleasant truths; swell our inspired thoughts; send forth our prayers.
That very thing we desire from you: O Aśvins, make for us a glorious portion, and make us as dear to the patrons as Soma is.
Stir up the pleasant truths; swell our inspired thoughts; raise up our abundant wisdom. We desire that glorious portion from you; O Aśvins, make us as dear to the patrons as Soma is. ||2||
O Aśvins, you two, impel the pleasant words or the dawns;
nourish and fulfill our thoughts and our ritual acts;
and raise up and inspire many inspired insights.
The meaning is "producing.
We desire these three things;
furthermore, make for us a glorious, illustrious portion—wealth and the like that is worthy of being enjoyed.
Make us beautiful and auspicious, like Soma; make us among the wealthy and liberal givers, O you two who are like Soma.

O Nāsatyas, you two have helped even the decrepit and the lame; you are the protectors of the blind and the one who stumbles. Even for the weak and the emaciated, people call upon you as physicians, even for the sick.

Even though you are ageless, you become our portion; even for the one who has no food, you are the protectors. Even of the most distant draught, O Nāsatyas, and even for the emaciated man, they call you two alone the physicians of the sick.
O Nāsatyas, O Nāsatyas, you two—you became the fortune (bhaga) for Ghoṣā, who was aged before her time and growing old in the house of her father, even though she was unfortunate;
that is to say, having transformed yourselves into beautiful forms, you gave her a husband. And so there is another Vedic citation:
1. This [reading] does not exist in the *Dhanavatsu* manuscripts.

2. Regarding *jūryatām*: *ta¹·²·⁵·⁶·⁷* read *jūryatām*; *ta⁴* reads *jūryatām*. [The mantra is: “O Aśvins, you gave a husband to Ghoṣā, who was growing old in her own home at the chosen place” (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.110.7).
You two are the deliverers and protectors even of one who has taken refuge in the forest through fasting;
you two are the protectors even of a leper, though he be of a most lowly birth;
you two are the protectors even of a captive, though he be deprived of sight.
You two are the protectors even of one who is emaciated or weak;
moreover, the wise declare that you two alone are the physicians for the sacrifice when it has been injured.
You two fashioned Cyavāna anew for movement, making him young again like a well-guided chariot;
you carried away his decrepitude from the chariot—all these deeds of yours are to be proclaimed among all people.

Just as you fashioned Cyavāna anew, skillful and young again for the sake of movement, so did you carry Tarya away from there to these [people]. All these deeds of yours are indeed to be proclaimed among all men. 4.

O Aśvins, you two fashioned Cyavāna—the ancient, aged seer—once more young and vigorous for the purpose of moving, like an old chariot; that is to say, you restored him. Thus says Yāska: "You two fashioned Cyavāna, the ancient and aged, once more young for the purpose of moving, just as one fashions a chariot; the root *takṣ* signifies 'to impel,' and it is used in the sense of 'to act' or 'to do'" (Nirukta 4.19).
Moreover, you two indeed brought forth Bhujyu, the son of Tugra, from the midst of the ocean;
moreover, all those deeds of yours are to be proclaimed preeminently at the sacrifices and in the dwellings.
I shall proclaim your ancient heroic deeds among the people; then indeed you two acted as healing physicians, bringing delight.
Therefore, I shall now perform these new services for your great protection; O Nāsatyas, may this humble man place his trust in you.

O Vāma, proclaim your ancient heroic deeds among the people; for you have indeed been physicians who bring happiness. As such, may I now perform new acts for your great protection, so that this pious man, O Nāsatyas, may place his trust in you.
O Aśvins, I proclaim aloud your ancient heroic deeds in the world of men.
Furthermore, O Nāsatyas, you two have become physicians, healers who bring about well-being.
For our protection, we make you two worthy of praise and worthy of adoration.
May we go to the wide space; the sacrificer is the lord, who, through faith, establishes the truth by means of Aditi.
Listen to me here, O Aśvins; like two parents to their son, bestow great aid upon me.
We are without kin, without alliance, and devoid of wisdom; before that calamity strikes, protect us from it!

This [prayer] I have called upon you; hear me, O Aśvins! Bestow your favor upon me as parents do for their son. I am without kin, ignorant, without noble birth, and lacking in wisdom; save me from that curse before it reaches me.
O Aśvins, you two, I, Ghoṣā, call upon you;
hear this invocation of mine.
Having heard my call, come to me just as parents—mother and father—come to their son.

1. Even for one who is lowly by birth (ga-jāti); even for one who is lowly by birth such as ta-bha6-su; even for one who is high by birth such as ta3-bha1.2.4; even for one who is high by birth such as bha7.
2. Even for one belonging to the ta7-ha group. 3. The word "pra brava" does not exist in the ta-bha [recensions].
4. From that [he is] satisfied.
5. This sacrificer goes.

Teach me wealth and give it to me. Hostility, kinlessness, ignorance, ingratitude, ill-conceived thought, and blame unworthy of belief come upon me. Before that curse reaches me, deliver me from it. You two, with your chariot, carried away Śundhyū, the daughter of Purumitra, for Vimada. You two went to the call of Vadhimatī; you two brought forth fair praise for Puraṃdhi. O Aśvins, you two carried away Śundhyū by name—the daughter of Purumitra, who was called Purumitra—by means of a chariot surrounded by your own army, for Vimada, the seer named Vimada. You brought her to the house of Vimada. Thus says another Vedic text: "You two, with a chariot swift as an army, carried the wife to Bhaga for Vimada" (Ṛgveda 1.116.1). Furthermore, you two went to the call of Vadhimatī, whose hands had been severed by enemies in battle. Having arrived, you gave her a golden hand. Thus says another Vedic text: "Puraṃdhi called out to you both at the great journey, O you who enjoy much; hear that, O Aśvins, like the Āsurī, and give the golden-handed [gift] to Vadhimatī" (Ṛgveda 1.116.13). Moreover, you two brought forth fair praise—a beautiful horse or a fine flow—for Vadhimatī, who possessed great wisdom. You two restored the youthful vigor to the sage Kali, who had reached old age. You two raised Vandana up from the pit of the wolf. You two instantly made Viśpalā able to go. O Aśvins, O powerful ones, you two raised Rebha, who was hidden in a cave and was sinking in the water. You two made Ubīsa and Tṛsa full of spirit for the sake of Atri’s sevenfold slaughter. 1. *ta-bha6-mu- ‘ca’ is not present. 2. *ta-bha6-mu- to him. 3. *ta-bha6-mu- gave; *ta3-bha1.4- did not give; *bhara- did not give.
O Ashvins, you two showerers of benefits, you raised up Rebha—the sage named Rebha—who was hidden in a cave, placed there by the Asuras, and was dying.
Thus, there is another Vedic passage: "For ten nights they kept him hidden, slaying him for nine;
seeking him who had perished, they drew forth Rebha from the water, like Soma with beauty" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.24).
Moreover, you two made the scorching *ṛbīsa*—the cauldron—for Agni, for the sake of maintaining the fire;
you made it cooling, meaning you quenched it by raining down cold.
And so says another Vedic verse: "With snow you warded off the heat from Agni’s shoulder; you bestowed upon him nourishing strength."
"In the *ṛbīsa* [pit], O ye two who possess sweetness, ye churned out the clarified butter for Atri with all his company for his welfare" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.116.8).

Furthermore, for the sake of the seer named Sasavardhin—who had been placed in a wooden trap by a certain king, the performer of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) due to some offense—ye two "made him prosper" (*sasavardhayethām*).
The meaning is that ye two performed the opening of the mantra.
And likewise, another Vedic passage states: “O Lord of the Forest, open wide like the birthplace for the sun;
O Aśvins, hear my call, bestow prosperity, and release [me] from bondage” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.78.5).

O Aśvins, you bestowed upon Pedu a white horse, swift and full of vigor, accompanied by ninefold strength and ninety steeds—a praiseworthy gift, like fortune for men, to be invoked and bringing bliss. 10. O Aśvins, you bestowed upon Pedu a white horse, swift and full of vigor, accompanied by ninefold strength and ninety steeds—a praiseworthy gift, like fortune for men, to be invoked and bringing bliss. 10.

O Aśvins, you two gave to King Pedu—named Pedu—a white, powerful steed, accompanied by ninety-nine horses; a horse worthy of praise, the supreme achiever in battles, the conqueror of enemies, a driver-away of those who face the foe, one to be invoked, the bringer of happiness, and like a desirable treasure for men—you bestowed him as a gift.

Neither from any quarter, O Kings, Aditi, nor for a single day does distress reach him, nor any fear—him whom you, O Aśvins, easy to invoke, whose path is like that of Rudra, place in front with a chariot together with his wife. 11. Neither from any quarter, O Kings, Aditi, nor for a single day does distress reach him, nor any fear—him whom you, O Aśvins, easy to invoke, whose path is like that of Rudra, place in front with a chariot together with his wife. 11.

O two Kings, O Lords, O Aditi-like ones, O noble ones, O you who are easily invoked, O you who are well-invoked, O you whose paths follow the ways of Rudra, O Aśvins, you two—you who, for that person whose chariot is foremost (puroratha), make him one whose chariot is broken (bhagtoratha) through a self-choice marriage (svayaṃvara) together with his wife—that person is not reached by any distress (aṃhas) from anywhere;
neither is he reached by misfortune (durita) or calamity (durgati). Nor does he encounter any fear—the fear of saṃsāra. No one [can harm him].

Come hither with that chariot swifter than thought, which the Ṛbhus fashioned for you, O Aśvins—the chariot at whose harnessing the Daughter of Heaven is born, and both fair days of Vivasvat arise. 12. Come hither with that [chariot], swifter than thought, that chariot which the Ṛbhus made for you, O Aśvins; at the harnessing of which the Daughter of Heaven is born, and both days of Vivasvat, the two auspicious days. 12.
1. Of those who were his friends. 2. One who causes [them] to flee (according to Ta, Bha1.2.6; Bha4.7; Bha5 reads *abhidrāvayitārakam*). 3. Do not give [it] (according to Ta and Bha).

O Aśvins, that chariot of yours which the Ṛbhus fashioned—the chariot at the harnessing of which the daughter of heaven, Uṣas, is born, and at the harnessing of which both auspicious days, day and night, are born from the all-possessing Sun—with that chariot, swifter even than thought, come hither, you two.

With that victorious power, O Aśvins, you caused the mountain to gush forth milk for Śayu; even the quail, swallowed within the mouth of a wolf, you released by your mighty deeds. 13. Those two... with victory... the mountain... you made to flow... for Śayu... a milch-cow, O Aśvins... even from the mouth of a wolf... the quail... between [the jaws]... you two... by your powers.

O *narā*, leaders of deeds, O Aśvins, to whom does your *dyumantam*—the radiant, *prātaryāvāṇam*—the sacrifice that goes forth at dawn, *viśvam*—the all-pervading and omnipresent, which *vastor-vastoh*—day after day—*vahamānam*—brings wealth to every person, and which *yantam*—is moving along—that chariot belong? In what place, and who indeed, what sacrificer, with *dhiyā*—through the act of praise in the form of ritual—adorns it for the sake of *suvitāya*—prosperity and high fortune—within the *śami*—the work consisting of the sacrifice?
The intention is this: "In what country, at what sacrifice, did which other sacrificer worship you with hymns and oblations such that you have come late to our sacrifice?"

Where is the slumberer? Where do you dwell at night, O Aśvins? Where will you make your approach? Where do you stay? Or who, like a widow with her brother-in-law, or like a young woman with a suitor, brings you to your dwelling-place?

Where are you at night? Where at dawn, O Aśvins? Where do you bestow your protection? Where have you approached? Who has brought you to his dwelling, as a widow brings her brother-in-law, or as a young woman brings her bridegroom to the place of assembly?
O Aśvins, where are you two at night?—this is the sense of the question; where are you during the day? And where do you perform your arrival?—that is, where do you come?
Where, or from where,
have you come? Furthermore, which sacrificer brings you both to the common place— the site called the altar—
for the sake of service, turning you toward himself?
In this regard, an illustration is shown:
"Just as a widow (*vidhavā*)—a woman whose husband has died—at her bed (*śayutrā śayane*), turns toward her brother-in-law (*devara*, the husband's brother);
and just as every woman (*yoṣā*) turns toward every man (*marye*) at the time of sexual union; such is the meaning."

And thus Yāska says: "Who are you two at night? Who by day? What do you intend to attain? Where do you vomit [your heat]? Or who is it for whom you lie down, like a widow for her brother-in-law (*devara*)? Why is he called *devara*? He is called the second husband (*vara*).

A widow (*vidhavā*) is so called because she is deprived of her husband (*vidhātṛ*), or from 'shaking off' (*vidhavana*), or from 'running away' (*vidhāvana*). Alternatively, *dhava* is a name for a human being; she is a widow because of separation from him."
"The brother-in-law plays with the dice;
the mortal is a human being subject to death;
the woman (yoṣā) is so called because she unites (yauti) in the place of assembly" (Nirukta 3.15).
At dawn you go forth like two aged men, like two worn-out garments; from stall to stall, you go to the house unbound.
Whose steadfast ones do you become, or whose, O heroes? Like two princes, you go to the libations.

In the morning you come to the house of the one who offers worship, like two worn-out garments being cast off. Whose steadfast ones do you become? Or whose, O heroes, do you approach at the libations like two princes, turning hitherward? 3.
O *narā*, leaders, you two Aśvins are praised with hymns at every dawn;
there is an illustration for this:
like two kings who have grown old in power (*jaraṇā*), through their majesty (*kāpayā*).
The speech of the bard who awakens [the king] in the morning is of what kind?
It is praised in such a manner;
the meaning is "just like that."
Furthermore, day by day (*vastoḥ-vastoḥ*), you two go to and reach the house—the dwelling—of the sacrificer while performing the sacrifice.
As such, you two become the destroyers (*dhvasā*)—the annihilators—of whose [enemy's] sacrificial stake (*dopaḥ*)?
And to whose libations (*savanā*) do you two go down, as if to those of a prince (*rājaputreva*)?
1. *ta-mu-prati* is not delayed; 2. *ta-bhara* adorns; 3. *ta-ākurute* does not exist; 4. *ta-rājakumārīva*.
[Maṇḍala 10, Adhyāya 3, Sūtra 40] Seventh Aṣṭaka, 415.

Like two wild elephants, you who seek the deer, we invoke you with an oblation at evening and at dawn. O Lords of Splendor, you carry the sacrifice to the people at the proper time for those men who offer it. You two, like two wild elephants, seekers of the deer, we call down with an oblation at evening and at dawn. You two, O Heroes, Lords of Splendor, carry this sacrifice to the person among men who offers it at the appointed time.
O Aśvins, you two are like two bulls, like two tigers seeking deer, and like hunters seeking game; even so, we invoke you with oblations by rule, both at night and by day.
Moreover, O Heroes, O Aśvins, those who offer the *hotrā*—the sacrificial oblation—at the proper times, [the sacrificers] invoke you both.
(The word "sacrificers" is to be supplied.)
Furthermore, you two, being auspicious lords (svāminau) of the auspicious rain-water, bring and convey food (hvapam) for the sake of the people.
O Aśvins, Ghoṣā indeed called upon you both for aid;

she spoke of wealth. O Aśvins, you [aided] Bhujyu; you [aided] Yaśas; you approached Uśanas Śṛṅgāra. For you two, the nights sit around as their chief [treasure]; through your protection, I have sought favor. 7.

O Aśvins, you two indeed rescued Bhujyu, the son of Tugra, whose ship was wrecked in the midst of the ocean; you approached him in order to deliver him. Furthermore, you two rescued Vaśa, the king named Vaśa, who was being defeated by his enemies through the power of Hasti. Moreover, you two delivered Śṛṅgāra from the pit of Atri, and you brought Uśanā—the desirable one—so that she might hear your praise.
And so another mantra says: "O Aśvins, [you are] the ornament of Atri" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.5.25).
Furthermore, O Aśvins, by virtue of your favor, those men who weep for the sake of life—the living—for their wives, possess true friendship with you both.

The meaning is that even by their weeping, they desire only life. Those wives disperse and settle themselves at the *adhvara*, the sacrifice; moreover, they fix and bestow upon them a long and great extension, a reaching out of their arms.
And this desirable offspring for the fathers, they impel and send forth.
To those husbands, the wives—the women—embrace them; the ellipsis implies that they provide happiness (*mayaḥ*) for the sake of embracing.

That [secret] of his, let him proclaim well, since he, the youth, dwells according to the rite within the wombs; we would go to the house of the bull, the beloved of the woman, for the sake of his seed—O Aśvins, that is what we desire.

Not so! Of that, speak clearly and well: "O Aśvins, may we go to that house where the youth dwells within the wombs of the young woman—the house of the bull for the sake of the seed of the beloved cow. This we desire. 11.
We do not know that happiness of those two Aśvins, like a bird;
you, however, proclaim that happiness well—well indeed.
The plural number is used for the sake of honor.

My husband is indeed young and youthful; he dwells—that is, resides—in my wombs, that is, in my houses. Furthermore, let us go—to that house of my husband, the beloved of the woman, the bull, the shedder of seed, the possessor of virile power. We long for—that is, we desire—that house.
May your benevolence come to us, O possessors of wealth and horses; O Aśvins, desires have been directed toward our hearts.
You two have become our protectors, a pair, lords of splendor; as the beloved friends of Aryaman, we have entered your dwelling.

Your benevolence has come to us, O Lords of ample wealth; O Aśvins, our desires have been directed toward your hearts. You have become our protectors, a pair of lords of splendor. May we reach the dear dwellings of Aryaman. 12.
O Aśvins, possessors of wealth and food, lords of splendor, masters of the waters—O you two who are a pair, joined with one another, may your benevolence come to us.
May our desires and longings be restrained within our hearts.
Furthermore, may you both become my protectors.
Moreover, being beloved wives, may we reach—the word *aśīmahi* means "may we attain"—the dwellings, the houses of our noble husband Aryaman.

Rejoicing in the dwelling of man, bestow upon the eloquent singer wealth accompanied by heroic sons. O Lords of Splendor, provide a ford with good watering-places; strike down the obstacle standing in the path and destroy evil intent.
