O you two who take pride in yourselves, bestow wealth along with heroic sons within the dwelling of the man who praises you. O Lords of Splendor, provide a ford and a good place for drinking; strike down the obstacle that stands upon the path and destroy ill-will.

O Aśvins, rejoicing, rejoicing— you two, for the sake of the mortal man, the lord of my thought, in his dwelling, bestow upon me, who desires to praise you with eloquence, wealth consisting of heroic sons and the like. Furthermore, O Aśvins, lords of splendor and masters of water, you two have made a good watering-place for me to drink at the ford as I go to my husband's house.
Furthermore, you two must strike down and drive away that evil-minded one of wicked intellect, who stands as an obstacle on the path like a tree blocking the way of the seers.
Who indeed, and among whom, do you two, O all-seeing lords of splendor, take delight? Who has detained you, and whose house have you visited—that of a sage or of a sacrificer?
Where indeed today, on which [days], do the two Aśvins, the all-destroying lords of splendor, rejoice? Who has restrained them? To whose house have they gone—to that of a sage or of a sacrificer? 19.

O Aśvins, O Aśvins, you two wonder-workers (dastrā), beautiful to behold (darśanīyau), lords of splendor (śubhaspatī), masters of the waters (udakasya pātārau)—where indeed, where are you stationed? On which people (viśva) among the various tribes (prajāsu) do you rejoice today on this day, satisfying yourselves? Furthermore, which sacrificer (yajamānaḥ) restrains these two? And to whose house of which wise singer (vipraḥ) have you both gone, having arrived as protectors?
The twelfth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with “samānam,” is the seerical composition of Suhasta, the son of Gopā; it is composed in the Jagatī meter and is dedicated to the Aśvins.
This is indicated by the statement: “The triplet beginning with ‘samānam’ belongs to Suhasta, the son of Gopā.
Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.
We invoke that same one, the much-invoked, the praiseworthy, the three-wheeled chariot that brings all things and is well-known;
we call upon him as he moves around, worthy of the assembly, with beautiful hymns at the dawning of the dawn.

The same. Om! Him, the much-invoked, worthy of praise, the three-wheeled chariot, all-conquering, accompanied by the Ganimat, the one who encompasses the assembly, we invoke with well-spoken hymns at the dawning of the dawn. 1.

O Aśvins, we invoke with excellent hymns—praises free from blemish—at the break of dawn, that very chariot of yours which belongs to both of you equally and in common: that one which is invoked by many, worthy of praise, possessing three wheels, reaching out to every libation and sacrifice, moving everywhere, traversing all around, fit for the assembly, and established at the sacrifice. We call upon it with well-spoken words.

O Nāsatyas, you mount at dawn the chariot yoked at early morning, the swift steed that carries honey. By means of this, O Heroes, you go to the people who perform sacrifice, even to the house of the poor man where the priest is present, O Aśvins.

O Nāsatyas, you mount the chariot yoked at dawn, the early-faring vehicle that carries honey, by which you go to the pious people, O Heroes—yea, even to the sacrifice of the poor man that is attended by the Hotṛ, O Aśvins.

O Nāsatyas—those who have become true, or rather, the leaders of truth, the two men, the guides, the Aśvins—you both mount that chariot which is yoked at dawn, which moves at dawn, which travels at dawn, and which carries honey (or the bearer of nectar). "Mount" is the meaning. By means of that chariot, you go to the *viśaḥ*—the subjects, the people—who are devoted to sacrifice (*yajvarīḥ*).
And by which [path], even through a parrot who praises you, you both go to the sacrifice that possesses a Hotṛ priest and is joined by seers.

1. Having stood [there] (ga-ta³-sthitvā); they have stood (ma¹.⁴.⁷-sthitā). 2. To the house of the praiser or of the sacrificer (bha-mu-stotuḥ vā yajamānasya vā gṛham). 3. Truly present (ga-ta³-bha⁶-satyabhūtau). 4. You two stand, you two preside over (ga-ta³-bha-tiṣṭhathaḥ adhitiṣṭhataḥ). Whether it be the Adhvaryu with honeyed hands and skillful fingers, or Agni who is dexterous with clarified butter and domestic, or when you go to the libations of the sage—come from there, O Aśvins, to the drinking of the honey.

Whether you go to the Adhvaryu priest with honeyed hands and skillful fingers, or to Agni who is dexterous with clarified butter and dwells within the home, or to the libations of the inspired singer—O Aśvins, come from there to this drinking of the honeyed soma.

He [invokes] the two Aśvins—the youthful ones who drink honey, who drink Soma, and who are Adhvaryus—or me, who am "Suhastya" (of skillful hands), or Agni, the special officiating priest named Suhastya, who possesses the strength of clarified butter (*ghṛtadakṣa*) and whose mind is intent on giving (*damūnasa*).
He shows this very point:

even though you go to the *savanāni* (pressings) or sacrifices of another wise man (*vipra*), nevertheless, from those sacrifices, come hither, come after us, to our drink consisting of Soma which is to be drunk like honey.
"‘It exists indeed’—this is the thirteenth hymn, consisting of eleven verses, addressed to Agni.
O Maghavan, why do they call you a liberal giver? Sharpen me; I hear that you are one who sharpens.
O Śakra, let my prayer be effective; O Indra, bring us the fortune that finds wealth."
Why indeed, O Maghavan, do they call you the liberal giver? Sharpen me; I hear that you are one who sharpens. Let my prayer be effective, O Śakra. O Indra, bring us Bhaga, the finder of wealth. 3.
"O friend" (*aṅga*) is a general form of address.
"O friend, O Maghavan—possessor of wealth—O Śakra, O Indra! Why do all the wise ones call you *bhoja*, the one who satisfies the desires of those who praise him?
The phrase "if you do not give" is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
Therefore, the meaning is that you shall indeed bestow riches upon the two praisers.
This being so, "sharpen" (śiśīhi) the praiser with the gift of wealth;
I hear that you, O Śiśaya, are the one who brings together the praisers.
Furthermore, may my intellect (dhī) be *armasvatī*, that is, possessed of action;
furthermore, [grant] us (*naḥ*) fortune (*bhaga*) that finds wealth (*vasuvid*), the bringer of riches.

In that Indra we have placed our praise—Indra the bounteous who has directed his desire toward us—let his enemy, even though he be far away, tremble; let all human glories bow down before him. In whom we have placed our praise—in Indra—who, the bounteous one, has directed his desire toward us—though he be far away, let his enemy tremble; let all human glories bow down before him.
In that Indra, whom we—possessing skillful hands—would support, we place and offer our praise and hymn;
and that Maghavan Indra, the possessor of wealth, has fixed his desire and intent upon us.
May the enemy of this Indra be afraid, even though he remains far away.
Furthermore, may all the *yumnā*—that is, the foods belonging to the enemy peoples (*janyāni*) arising from hostile territories—bow down before this Indra;
that is to say, let them become his provisions for consumption.

Drive the enemy far away, O fierce one! With that *śamba* weapon, O you who are invoked by many, bestow upon us wealth consisting of barley and cattle, O Indra! Grant the singer a prayer rich in booty and jewels. ārāt | śatrum | apa | bādhasva | dūram | ugraḥ | yaḥ | śambaḥ | puru'hūta | tena | asme iti | dhehi | yava'mat | go'mat | indra | kṛdhi | dhiyam | jaritre | vājiratnām || 7 ||

O Puruhūta, Indra, you who are invoked by many, that which is your fierce, upward-turning *śamba*, the thunderbolt (*vajra*)—as Yāska has said: "The word *śamba* is a name for the thunderbolt; it is derived either from the root *śam* (to pacify) or from *śāt* (to cut)" (*Nirukta* 5.24)—with that thunderbolt, drive away, cause to depart, and cast far from our vicinity the enemy, our adversary.
Furthermore, bestow—that is, deposit—upon us wealth consisting of barley and wealth consisting of cattle.
Moreover, for me, the singer who praises you, perform—that is, accomplish—the work of bringing delightful thoughts and riches.

Into whom the strong-pressed Somas, with their abundant ends, have entered like bulls—Maghavan does not withhold his gift; he brings much wealth to the one who presses the juice. 8. Into whom the strong-pressed Somas, with their abundant ends, have entered like bulls—Maghavan does not withhold his gift; he brings much wealth to the one who presses the juice. 8.

The Somas—poured by those who rain down [the juice], purified by the strainers, intense and possessing intense flavor, with abundant ends (meaning those Soma juices which have an abundance of *amba* and so forth at their conclusion)—have gone forth, they proceed, toward Indra within the belly. That wealthy Indra, the giver, does not indeed restrain the liberal sacrificer;
rather, for the sacrificer who performs the pressing of Soma, he brings down and fully bestows abundant, desirable wealth.

And he wins by playing even when losing, provided that at the right time he gathers what has been made; he who loves the gods does not lament for his wealth, for the self-reliant one bestows upon him gathered riches. And he wins by playing even when losing, provided that at the right time he gathers what has been made; he who loves the gods does not lament for his wealth, for the self-reliant one bestows upon him gathered riches.
1. We place [it] in the *ga*-position; we arrange [it] in the *ta*, *bha*, *mu*, and *vi* positions.
2. In the *ta* and *bha* positions, the word "asme" (us) is not present.
Furthermore (*uta*), Indra [defeated] the gambler (*prahām*) by surpassing him at dice.
The root *at* occurs in the sense of "highly honored";
the root *divyati* occurs in the sense of "going.
Having caused [him] to go in a highly honored manner, he conquers (*jayāti*, *jayati*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase *yathā*:
here, the elision of the suffix denoting manner (*prakāra*) should be understood.

Just as a gambler (*kitavaḥ*), having played (*kṛtam*), examines (*vicinoti*) and selects (*gṛhṇāti*) a counter-gambler (*pratikitavam*) from among gamblers, so too Indra, at the proper time—that is, at the time of battle—examines a powerful enemy and seizes him for the purpose of slaying; such is the meaning.
Furthermore, for that man who is "devakāmaḥ"—one who desires the gods, wishing to sacrifice to or praise them—he does not "ruṇaddhi" or obstruct their "dhanā," their riches;
that is to say, he does not conceal them.
Rather, the self-reliant (svadhāvān) and powerful Indra unites ("saṃ sṛjati") that seeker of the gods with "rāyā," with wealth.
With hymns, O Indra, you drive away the ill-intentioned with your cattle, and with food, O Much-invoked One, you dispel every hunger.
May we, as the foremost, win riches through the kings; toward us [come] our thoughts!
Our thoughts, seeking the light of heaven, have all together cried out in longing for Indra. They encircle him as wives encircle their husband, like a pure bridegroom—Maghavan—for his protection.
O Āṅgirasa Kṛṣṇa, you shall cause me to obtain the light of heaven for all. All my converging, united, and far-reaching hymns—desiring [you]—have resounded toward Indra; they praise him.
Moreover, just as wives embrace their husband, or as rivers embrace a man who is bright, pure, free from blemish, and wealthy, so do my hymns embrace Indra for the sake of protection.
No one else indeed knows my mind as well as you do; O Puruhūta, you have fulfilled my desire.
Like a king, O wondrous one, sit down upon this sacred grass (barhis); let there be for you the drinking of the pressed Soma here today.
No; my mind turns away from you. O Puruhūta, I have fixed my desire upon you alone. Like a king, O Wondrous One, sit down upon the sacred grass. Let there be a good drinking of Soma for you here. 2.

O Puruhūta, invoked by many, O Dasma, wondrous Indra! My mind turns toward you, toward you alone; indeed, it does not turn away from you. Furthermore, I fix my desire and longing upon you alone. Moreover, like a king, O Lord, sit down upon the sacred grass.
Furthermore, let there be a drinking-place for you in this Soma.
Indra overcomes both hunger and thirst; that Maghavan Indra rules over wealth.
For him, these seven rivers flow down the slopes, increasing the vigor of the impetuous bull.
Indra turns away hunger and thirst; he alone, the bounteous lord, rules over wealth and treasure. For him these seven rivers flow down the slopes, increasing the vigor of the impetuous bull.

May Indra be the one who turns away from us the lack of understanding—that foolishness which robs one of wisdom—or the thirst that consumes; and may he also be the one who turns away from us hunger. Furthermore, he alone, the bountiful and wealthy Indra, rules over *vasu*, the wealth that provides dwelling, and over *rāyas*, riches.
Furthermore, these seven well-known rivers (sindhu), numbering seven, increase his strength—that is, they augment the vigor of this Indra, the showerer (vṛṣabha)—in the sloping region.
Like birds settling upon a tree with beautiful foliage, the exhilarating Soma drops, dwelling in the vessels, have settled within Indra.
Their onset flashes with power; they have found the light of heaven for man, the light of Aryaman.

Like birds upon a tree with beautiful foliage, the exhilarating Soma drops have settled within Indra, seated in the vessels. Their vanguard has flashed forth with splendor; it has found the sun and the Aryan light for mankind.
Just as birds settle upon a tree with beautiful foliage, even so the exhilarating Soma juices—those that dwell in the ladles and rest within the cups—have settled upon Indra;
that is, they take their place.
The foremost part of these Somas, which are taking their place upon Indra, flashes forth with power and speed.
1. O Indra, of him who has a good hand; O Ghoṣa, of him who has a good hand!
2. He sits down; he settles.
He flashes forth.
Furthermore, may this Indra, by his own self, bestow upon Manu—that is, upon human beings—the noble, beloved light known as Āditya, the splendor of the sun.

The stingy man does not discern what has been done in the gambling; when Maghavan wins the sun as his total prize, no other can equal that heroic deed of yours—neither any of the ancients, O Maghavan, nor any of the moderns.

It was done; not by Śraghnī did he win it at the gambling-match, when Maghavan won the sun as his prize. No other than you could equal that heroic deed—neither one of old, O Maghavan, nor yet one of today. ||5||
The gambler is a destroyer of the wealth of others; in the game of dice, he sifts through what has been won as if sifting through what has been made. In that same manner, Indra seeks the sun.
When? To this he says:
when Maghavan, the wealthy Indra, conquers the sun—the Āditya who is the "thorough restrainer" (*saṃvargam*)—that is, he conquers him by means of seizing its essence.
Now follows the direct praise:

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, that heroic power of yours, characterized by the conquest of the Sun—like a bull when enraged, it rushes through the realms of space—[that power] which made these waters have a noble lord;

that Maghavan found light for the one who presses the Soma, for the one who gives quickly, and for Manu who offers oblations. Like a bull when enraged, he rushed through the realms of space—he who made these waters have a noble lord. That Maghavan found light for the one who presses the Soma, for the one who gives quickly, and for Manu who offers oblations.

Just as a bull, being enraged, rushes toward a rival bull in the realms of space (*rajaḥsu*), so too Indra, being enraged, rushes forth to slay the clouds; and having slain the cloud, he brings these well-known waters—the rain-waters that are the wives of the noble one (*arya-patnīḥ*), meaning they are to be protected by Indra, the lord of the entire world—toward us. That wealthy (*maghavā*) Indra, for the sake of the man who presses the Soma, who possesses swift gifts (*jīradānave*), and who offers oblations (*haviṣmate*), acts thus for the benefit of humanity (*manave*).
The meaning is "for the sacrificer.
He found—that is, bestowed—*jyotis*, which means splendor or light.

May the axe arise together with light; may it become, as of old, a well-milking cow of *ṛta*. May the ruddy one shine forth with his radiance, pure; like the sun, may the lord of the world blaze with brilliant, white light. May the axe arise together with light; may it become, as of old, a well-milking cow of *ṛta*. May the ruddy one shine forth with his radiance, pure; like the sun, may the lord of the world blaze with brilliant, white light. (9)
May Indra’s axe, his thunderbolt, arise together with light and splendor;
that is to say, may it be active in the slaying of our enemies and the destruction of the clouds.
Furthermore, may the well-milking speech of the mid-region, pertaining to Truth, be as it was in ancient times.
There is a transposition of genders.

Furthermore, may Indra, the radiant one, shining with his luster, pure and blazing, shine forth and manifest his light. Moreover, may Indra, the lord of the virtuous, like the sun (svaḥ), glowing brightly, burn intensely and blaze forth.

O Much-invoked One, may we cross over this evil way by means of cattle; O Much-invoked One, may we overcome all hunger by means of barley. May we, as leaders with our kings, win riches through our own vigorous band. 10. By means of cattle, may we cross over distress caused by evil intent; by means of barley, [may we overcome] all hunger, O Much-invoked One. May we, being foremost with our kings, win riches through our own vigorous band. 10.

May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and from above, and from below, from the one who seeks to do us harm; may Indra, our friend, from the front and from the middle, grant wide space to us, his friends. 11. Bṛhaspati; us; protect; from behind; and; and from above; from below; from the malevolent one; Indra; from the front; and; from the middle; us; friend; for friends; wide space; may he create. 11.
This pair has already been explained previously.

The second hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "ā yātu," belongs to Kṛṣṇa Āṅgirasa and is dedicated to Indra Apām. The first three verses are in the Triṣṭubh meter; the next six are in the Jagatī meter; and the final two are in the Triṣṭubh meter. Thus it has been enumerated: "ā yātu [has] three [verses], beginning with Triṣṭubh.
This [hymn] belongs to Maghavān Indra.
It is for the purpose of insertion (āvāpa) by the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest during the increase of the Stoma in the Pluvika and Ekapathya rites.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [recites] 'May Indra, the lord of good sleep, come to this prayer' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.9)."

May Indra, the lord of himself, come for exhilaration—he who, by his inherent law, is strengthened, the all-pervading one, who has grown mighty beyond all powers through his boundless and great virility. May Indra, the lord of himself, come for exhilaration—he who, by his inherent law, is strengthened, the all-pervading one, who has grown mighty beyond all powers through his boundless and great virility.
Indra, who is truly powerful, truly swift, truly mighty, and truly grown great—truly overcoming all and every hostile force with his boundless, great, and superior virile strength;

he who, truly increasing himself, truly surpasses [all]—the Lord of Wealth, Indra, let him come toward our sacrifice for the sake of exhilaration, by means of his sustaining chariot, according to the Law (dharma).

Firmly established is your chariot; well-governed are your two bay steeds. O Lord of Men, the thunderbolt is firmly grasped in your hand. Come quickly, O King, by a fair path hitherward; we shall increase your manly powers as you drink. Firmly established is your chariot; well-governed are your two bay steeds. O Lord of Men, the thunderbolt is firmly grasped in your hand. Come quickly, O King, by a fair path hitherward; we shall increase your manly powers as you drink. 2.
O King, O lord of men, O protector of men, your chariot is well-established with a beautiful seat; your two bay horses are also well-yoked, meaning they are firmly harnessed.
Furthermore, the thunderbolt is firmly grasped within your two arms.
That being so, O King, O Lord of all, come quickly, come swiftly by the auspicious path, come hither toward us;
having arrived, we shall increase, we shall augment your manly powers, you who have drunk the Soma.

Let the steeds that carry Indra—the fierce one with the thunderbolt in his arm, the fierce and powerful—bring him hither to our joint revelry: him who is most active, the bull of true vigor. ā indravāhaḥ nṛpatim vajrabāhum ugram ugrāsaḥ tuviṣāsaḥ enam pratvakṣasam vṛṣabham satyaśuṣmam ā īm asmattrā sadhamādaḥ vahantu || 3 ||

*Pa*: the king, the protector of men; *pa*: the one with the thunderbolt-arm, the one with the thunderbolt in hand; *pa*: the fierce one, the most fierce; *pa*: the one who excessively thins [his enemies], the one who utterly destroys the forces of his foes; *pa*: the bull, the showerer of desires; *pa*: the one of true vigor, whose strength is unfailing—[this refers to] this Indra. *Pa ā pa īm*: these are mere expletives. *Pa ugrāsaḥ*: the fierce ones; *pa tuviṣāsaḥ*: the greatly increased ones.
May they, rejoicing together in the shared exhilaration, may they, the bearers of Indra, bring [the gods] hither toward us.
Thus you hasten toward your husband, who is accompanied by the *droṇakalaśa* and is conscious; you, a bull, strive for him who is the pillar of strength and the support of the world.
Produce strength, gather it within yourself, so that he may be for the increase of those who drink from the *kenipa*.
1. There is no inauspiciousness.

Thus [I address] the Lord, the companion of the Droṇa-vessel, the conscious one, the pillar of vigor, the supporter—for the sake of increase. Grasp together the power; may it be centered within you, so that you may be the lord for the growth of those who drink the soma. 4.
O Indra, you pour into your own belly—the sustainer, the protector, the one who partakes of the *droṇakalaśa*, the conscious, the renowned, the pillar of strength, the Soma—for your nourishment;
that is, you hold it there.
Furthermore, bestow vigor and power upon me.
O you, hold us fast; indeed, gather us together.
Furthermore, [hold] us who are wise, for "kenipas" and "uśijas" are listed among the names for the wise.
For the sake of increase, in every way and as it truly is, you become the lord, the master.
Bring us treasures; for I have praised you with a good blessing. Come to the bearer of the Soma-offering!
You are the master; sit upon this sacred grass (barhis), by which your vessels are inviolable according to the Law (dharman).

Come to us with riches, for I have praised you; come to the one who brings a good blessing, the possessor of Soma. You are the lord; therefore, sit down upon this sacred grass (barhis). Your vessels are inviolable according to the eternal law (dharman).
O Indra, may the treasures and the wealth that are yours to give come to us, to me;
for I have praised you, I have extolled you. Furthermore, O Soma-drinker, come and join my sacrifice, which possesses beautiful blessings.
Furthermore, you rule; you are the lord of wealth.
Being such as this, may you sit down upon this sacred grass (*barhis*) spread out upon our altar.
Moreover, your Soma-vessels are unassailable—incapable of being overcome—by *dharman*, that is, by the actions of the Rākṣasas.

The first invocations of the gods went forth separately; they performed deeds worthy of hearing and difficult to surpass. Those who were unable to board the sacrificial ship—those weaklings indeed settled down right here.

Apart they went forth; the first invocations of the gods were made. They performed deeds difficult to surpass. Those who were unable to board the sacrificial ship settled down right there in their own bodies. ||6||

O Indra, by your grace, those who were the first—the foremost or principal ones—those who are the invokers of the gods (*devahūti*), go forth separately to the worlds of the gods; they depart individually. Furthermore, they have achieved for themselves glorious deeds worthy of renown, which are difficult for others to surpass.

Furthermore, those people who, having been deprived of your grace, were unable— meaning they could not— to board the "sacrificial boat," that is, the boat consisting of sacrifice; those *kepayas*, people of contemptible and putrid deeds, sinful folk, sank down low, as if submerged by debt alone.

The meaning is that they have gone to a downward course. And thus says Yāska: "They went apart; [the word] *prathamāḥ* is from the root *prath*, 'to spread. They were the first invocations of the gods, those who called upon the gods and performed deeds worthy of renown, glorious acts difficult to emulate, by which they were able to ascend the ship of *iṣ* (prosperity). But those who were not able to ascend the ship of *iṣ*, they sank down; they sank down because of debt, or rather, into this very world" (Nirukta 5.25).
1. That [is] "in every way" non-existent. 2. Ta1.2.6.7—[it is] among us. 3. Ta1.2.6.7—“The remainder becomes impossible. 4. Ta—kṛṇvata (making).

Let those others be turned away, the evil-minded ones whose ill-yoked horses have been harnessed for the difficult sacrifice. Likewise, let those who are forward and superior remain for the giving, wherein there are many wise means of enjoyment. Let those others—the evil-minded (duḍhyaḥ), meaning those of wicked intellect—be turned away (apāk) and go downward; they are the others (apare), meaning those who do not perform sacrifice. Let their horses (aśvāḥ), which are ill-yoked (duryujaḥ), difficult to harness and powerful, be harnessed to their chariots. The sense is that those who, despite possessing the capacity, do not sacrifice, go to hell. Furthermore, "likewise" (itthā), those who are forward (prāk) and superior (upare)—the sacrificers—remain for the giving (dāvane), that is, for the offering of oblations to the gods even before death. And in them, among those performers of sacrifice, there exist many (purūṇi) wise means (vayunāni), whether beautiful or leading to knowledge, as well as abundant (puruṇi) enjoyments (bhojanā), meaning riches, for the purpose of giving to the gods.

He held fast the mountains here as they were trembling; the sky cried out, and he agitated the mid-air regions. He props apart the two joined worlds, the Dhiṣaṇās; having drunk of the bull’s [Soma], he proclaims hymns in his exhilaration. He held firm the mountains—the clouds, moving and trembling—and made them motionless. Furthermore, the sky, or the people dwelling therein, cried out, terrified by the Asuras and Rakṣasas, calling upon Indra for protection. Moreover, Indra agitated the mid-air regions; that is, he stirred them up. Furthermore, Indra props apart the two joined worlds, the Dhiṣaṇās—heaven and earth—supporting them with the mid-air; that is, he makes them stable. And furthermore, Indra, having drunk of the Soma juices clinging to his belly, the "bull's" [Soma], while in a state of exhilaration, utters and proclaims hymns, words worthy of praise.

I carry this well-fashioned goad for you, O Maghavan, with which you shall break the hoof-breakers. Let there be a place of rest for you in this sacrifice; at the pressed juice and in the rite, O Maghavan, be mindful and partake. I carry this well-fashioned goad for you, O Maghavan Indra. Here, by the word "goad" (aṅkuśa), praise is expressed because of its quality of being a stimulator; the meaning is that I maintain your praise. Being praised by means of this goad characterized as praise, you, O Maghavan, shall break the "hoof-breakers"—the elephants such as Airāvata and others who strike down the enemy forces before them.

1. For those performing sacrifice (ta1.2.6.7-bha1.2.4); for those performing the sacrifice (ta4.5). 2. ‘They become’ is not present in *ta*. 3. ‘Is possible’ (*saṃbhavati*) in *ta* and *bha6*. 4. ‘Indra sustained’ is not present in *ta*. 5. ‘Certainties’ (*niścitān*) in *ta*, *bha6*. 6. By means of a goad in the form of praise (*stutirūpeṇāṅkuśena*) in *ga*, *ta3*, *ma1.4.7*.

[Pa. 10. A. 4. Sū. 45] The Seventh Aṣṭaka, 429. You strike [them] face-to-face; that is to say, you afflict them. Furthermore, "in this libation of ours," let there be "your own" (*okyam*), meaning your dwelling place. Moreover, O "Maghavan," O wealthy Indra, "being one who shares" (*ābhagaḥ*), worthy of being partaken of, "be mindful" (*bodhi*) at the pressed Soma, at the joyful sacrifice; be aware of our hymns of praise. With cattle, O much-invoked one, drive away our poverty and ill-fortune; with barley, [drive away] all hunger. May we, as leaders, together with our kings and our own host, win the riches first. May Bṛhaspati protect us from behind, and also from above, from below, and from the malevolent one. May Indra, our friend, from the front and from the middle, grant wide space to us, his friends. This verse has already been explained. The third hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "divas pari," is the work of Vatsaprī, the son of Bhālanda. It is addressed to Agni and is in the Triṣṭubh meter. Thus it is announced: "divas pari, twelve verses; [this is] the Āgneya of Vatsaprī. These two initial hymns are used in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āgnimāruta Śastra, excluding the last verse of this [third] hymn. And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Of the two hymns beginning with 'divas pari,' one should omit the last verse of the former" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13). In the Kṣamavatī rite, the verse "akandad agniḥ" is the Yājyā. And it is prescribed: "O Agni, drive away our diseases... akandad agniḥ stanayanniva dyauḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.13). From heaven, Agni was first born; from us, the Jātavedas was born second. Thirdly, he of manly mind was born in the waters. Kindling him incessantly, the well-intentioned one praises him. Agni was first born from heaven, above, in the form of the Sun. The Jātavedas, whose wisdom or wealth is born, was born second from us, above, in the form of the terrestrial fire. He of manly mind, whose thoughts are fixed on men as their benefactor, was born third in the waters, in the intermediate region, in the form of lightning. Thus kindling this Agni incessantly, the one of good intent praises him. Or rather, the meaning of this mantra should be understood according to the manner stated in the Vājasaneyi [Brāhmaṇa]. As follows: "'From heaven, Agni was first born. The sky is indeed breath; from breath, indeed, he was first born. 'From us, the Jātavedas was born second'—when they generated him a second time in human form. 'Thirdly, in the waters'—when they generated him a third time from the waters. 'Manly mind, incessantly'—Prajāpati is indeed manly mind, and Agni is incessant. 'Kindling him, the well-intentioned one praises him'—whosoever kindles him, he generates him as one of good intent" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.7.4.3). All your three forms, O Agni, are threefold; all your stations are distributed in many places. All your names are in the highest secret, whether they be here or where you have come from. 1. Ta-Bha6-Mu: *supajño netā*; Bhā1.2.4.7: *supājño netā*. 2. Ta: The phrase "yo vā...iti" is not present.
O Agni, you bear threefold; we know your three stations in many places. We know your supreme name which is hidden in secret; we know that fountain from which you have come.

O Agni, we know those three forms of yours—namely fire, wind, and the sun—which abide in three places, that is, in the three locations of earth, the intermediate space, and the heavenly world. Furthermore, O Agni, we know your many stations (*dhāman*), such as the *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya*, *anvāhāryapacana*, and others, which you maintain in various ways.

Furthermore: "O You, we who know the Veda recognize that supreme, most excellent name of Yours which is hidden—that is, concealed and not understood by those ignorant of the Veda—and which is well-known in the Veda.
Moreover, from whence You have come (ājagantha)—that is to say, from whence You were born."
"We recognize him as the one who supports—that is, causes to flow forth and brings into being—the spring, namely, the causal self."

In the ocean, within the waters, the manly-minded one, the beholder of men, kindled thee at the udder of heaven’s summit. Standing in the third realm, in the lap of the waters, the mighty ones caused thee to grow. In the ocean, within the waters, the manly-minded one, the beholder of men, kindled thee at the udder of heaven’s summit. Standing in the third realm, in the lap of the waters, the mighty ones caused thee to grow.

O Agni, you who were being born in the ocean, the great receptacle of waters—Varuṇa, whose mind is intent on men (nṛmaṇāḥ), kindled you while you stood within the waters as the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni). Furthermore, Āditya, the beholder of men (nṛcakṣāḥ), kindled you in the udder of heaven—that is, in the solar orb which stands in the place of an udder, or in the sacrifice.

Furthermore: "In the third [region], filling the three; in the lap, that is, the place of the waters—the rainwaters—in the *rajas*, the intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*), you who abide there, established in the form of lightning—*mahiṣāḥ*, the great Maruts and other celestial hosts, the praisers, strengthened you with their hymns.
Or rather, the meaning should be understood according to the manner stated in the Vājasaneyaka.

"Namely: 'In the ocean, thee, O man-minded one, within the waters... Prajāpati is indeed the man-minded one; 'thee within the waters, Prajāpati'—this is what it means. 'The man-beholding one kindled [thee] at the summit of heaven, in the udder... Prajāpati is indeed the man-beholding one; the waters are the udder of heaven. 'Thee standing in the third realm... Heaven is indeed the third realm. 'The buffaloes increased thee in the lap of the waters... The vital breaths are indeed the buffaloes; 'in heaven, thine own vital breaths increased'—this is what it means. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.7.4.5)

Agni roared like the thundering sky; licking the earth, he anointed the plants. As soon as he was born, being kindled, he looked abroad; with his radiance, he shines between the two worlds. Agni roared like the thundering sky; licking the earth, he anointed the plants. As soon as he was born, being kindled, he looked abroad; with his radiance, he shines between the two worlds.
The fire in the form of a forest conflagration is praised:
"Agni is the forest fire. Just as the sky, like a thundering rain-cloud, being ignited and taking the form of lightning, produces a great sound, so too does he "roar," producing a great sound.
To the question "What is he doing?", the text says:

Wasting away the already wasted earth, licking it as if with his tongue, he consumes and devours the plants and herbs, making them dry up. He who is praised here [is Agni], who, like the waters, pervades the dust and the sky in his lap. (Note: *kṣāma* is repeated for emphasis; *rerihat* means licking; *vīrudhaḥ* refers to climbing plants and *oṣadhīḥ* to medicinal/herbal plants; *samaśnan* means eating/consuming; *ṛkṣayan* means making them withered/dry.)
The meaning is "tormenting.

Furthermore: *sadyas* (at that very moment), at the same time, *jajñānaḥ* (being born), *induḥ* (the shining one), *īm* (this), *svena dagdham vastujātam* (the collection of things burnt by himself), *cikaśyat*—he beholds it variously. *Hi* is a particle used for filling out the verse.
Furthermore, it shines— that is, it illuminates— between the two *rodasī*, heaven and earth, by means of its own radiance (*bhānunā*).
Alternatively,
the meaning should be understood as stated in the Vājasaneyaka.
For example: “Agni has cried out, like the thundering sky” (RV 10.88.1).

For Parjanya, as it were, cries out while thundering; “he licks the earth and consumes the plants” (RV 10.88.2)—for he who is licking the earth indeed anoints the plants; “as soon as born, O Indu, you have spread abroad” (RV 10.88.3)—for as soon as he is born, he causes all this to melt away; “with his light, he has filled the two worlds, heaven and earth” (RV 10.88.4)—the two worlds, heaven and earth, are indeed *rodasī*, and he fills them with his light. This is the praise of the lightning-fire (*vaidyuta*). Or else: [the following].
This is a hymn of praise to the forest fire.

The bestower of glories, the supporter of riches, the inspirer of thoughts, the guardian of Soma—the Vasu, the Son of Strength, the King in the waters—shines forth at the forefront of the dawns, being kindled. śrīṇām uttāraḥ, dharuṇaḥ rayīṇām, manīṣāṇām prārpaṇaḥ, somagopāḥ, vasuḥ, sūnuḥ sahasaḥ, apsu rājā, vi bhāti agre uṣasām idhānaḥ. 5. He is the upholder of splendors, the sustainer of riches, the impeller of inspired thoughts, the protector of Soma; the Vasu, the Son of Might, the King within the waters, he shines forth at the beginning of the dawns, being kindled.

The noble one, the instigator and giver of glorious prosperities; the supporter of riches and wealth; the bestower who brings about desired objects; the guardian of Soma; the dweller of all the world; the son of strength (Sahasas); the King who resides within the waters; like the fire being kindled at the break of dawn for the sake of the Agnihotra sacrifice—he shines forth in three ways.

The banner of the universe, the germ of the world, filling the two worlds as he was being born, shattered even the firm mountain as he went forth when men sacrificed to Agni for the sake of cattle. 6. Banner of the universe, germ of the world, he filled the two worlds (heaven and earth) while being born; even the solid rock he shattered as he went forth, when men sacrificed to Agni for the sake of obtaining cattle. 6.

7. The banner (ketu) of the entire universe (viśvasya), the indicator; the embryo (garbha) of the world (bhuvanasya)—that is, Agni existing as an embryo—being born (jāyamānaḥ), even as he manifests, fills (āpṇāt) both heaven and earth (rodasī).
Departing (parāyan), he shatters (abhinat) even the firm (vīḷu) cloud (adri).
When [does this happen]? To this he says:
7. When the five peoples—the human beings—worshiped and worship Agni.

Desirous, purifying, a messenger, most wise, Agni, the immortal, has been established among our thoughts. Bearing aloft the ruddy smoke, he stirs; with his bright flame, he gazes up toward heaven. Desirous, purifying, a messenger, most wise, Agni, the immortal, has been established among our thoughts. Bearing aloft the ruddy smoke, he stirs; with his bright flame, he gazes up toward heaven.

Of that same Agni: *uśik*, desiring the oblations; *pāvaka*, the purifier of the entire world; *aratiḥ*, a mover or one who impels beings; *sumedhāḥ*, possessed of excellent wisdom; *amṛtaḥ*, immortal, free from the nature of death; *agniḥ*, Agni; *marteṣu*, among mortals, among human beings; *ni dhāyi*, has been established.
This very Agni *iyarti*, sends forth or impels the *dhūmam*, smoke.

Moreover, bearing (*bharat*) and maintaining (*dhārayan*) a ruddy (*aruṣam*) and radiant form (*rūpam*), he reaches (*inakṣan*) that heaven by means of his various (*śukena śukena*) splendors (*śociṣā rociṣā*); the ellipsis is "he pervades and goes."
Visible like a golden ornament, he has shone far and wide, the one of beautiful form; resplendent for the sake of glory,
Agni became immortal through his vital powers, he by whom this heaven was generated with its noble seed.
Shining like gold, he has spread far and wide; resplendent for the sake of glory, Agni has become immortal through his vital powers, when Dyaus, rich in seed, begat him.
Being seen—that is, being perceived by direct perception—the shining *rukma* (the radiant fire) has widely (*urviyā*) and exceedingly (*uru*) expanded and flashed forth.
Furthermore, this Agni, the goer (*āyuḥ*), shines for the sake of glory (*śriye*) and for majesty (*vibhūtyai*), becoming resplendent in such a way as to be difficult to overcome (*durmarpam*).
This very Agni became immortal (*amṛtaḥ*), free from death, through the vital forces (*vayobhiḥ*), that is, through fires and trees.
For this reason, *suretāḥ*—possessing excellent seed—the sky, or the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or the sun (*āditya*), generates (*janayan*) this Agni.
O God of radiant light, whoever prepares for you today at the outset a cake rich in ghee,
lead him further toward greater wealth, toward well-being bestowed by the gods, O most youthful one.
O Agni of auspicious luster, whoever today prepares for you a cake rich in ghee, O God, lead him further toward greater wealth, O youngest one, toward the favor bestowed by the gods. 9.

Likewise, lead that sacrificer—who is devoted to the gods, a worshiper who honors the gods with hymns and oblations—toward happiness (*sumnam*). Lead him forth! Lead him back! Lead him forward! Grant him a share in glorious deeds as the foremost; grant him a share at every hymn being recited.
May he be dear to Sūrya, dear to Agni; may he pierce through with his offspring and with wealth.

O Agni, grant him a share in glorious deeds; at every hymn being recited, grant him a share. May he be dear to Sūrya, may he be dear to Agni; may he prevail with those already born and with those yet to be born.
O Agni, in those rites which possess *sauśravasa*— that is, those actions characterized by excellent renown (*śravaḥ*) or food (*anna*)—
while they are being performed, favor (*bhaja*) that sacrificer or the praiser by bestowing the desired fruits; attend to them.
Furthermore, while the *uktha* hymn is being recited—that is, while it is being chanted—favor him; serve him by bestowing his desired fruits.
This very person is the sacrificer, the praiser, the impeller of beings (or, according to another reading, the destroyer of beings).

Or let him be dear to the Sun;
likewise, let him be dear even to the Fire.
Furthermore, may he, by means of the son who has been born, utterly shatter—that is, tear asunder—the enemies.
Likewise, through sons already born and those yet to be born, he shall utterly crush his enemies.
