seeking wealth through you, the seekers have opened the cow-filled stall. 11 O Agni, following you, the sacrificers have shaken down all desirable riches; seeking
O Agni, facing you, the sacrificers shake [the oblations] day by day; they have secured, and continue to hold, all desirable treasures and riches.
Moreover, desiring wealth in the form of cattle that had been carried off by the Asuras, the wise Uśij gods, longing for it, opened the cow-pen—making its gates wide open.

Agni, the benevolent Vaiśvānara, the guardian of Soma, has been praised by the seers among men. We invoke the two non-hostile ones, Heaven and Earth; O gods, bestow upon us wealth consisting of heroic sons. 12. Agni has been praised; he who is most gracious to men, Vaiśvānara, the protector of Soma, by the seers. We invoke the two non-hostile ones, Heaven and Earth. O gods, grant us wealth with excellent heroes. 12.

In non-hatred, we invoke—heaven and earth—we shall call upon the two, heaven and earth. Furthermore, O gods, bestow upon us wealth consisting of a chariot accompanied by excellent sons; maintain it for us.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, may the Great Lord of Vidyātīrtha dispel the darkness within the heart and bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the eighth chapter in the seventh book of the Commentary on the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial throne of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious Emperor, Supreme Lord, promoter of the Vedic path, and sustainer of the kingdom.
O Agni, you have been praised by the seers and by us.
Of what nature [are you]?
Vaiśvānara, who is most gracious and pleasant-faced toward men, who is the protector of Soma and is guarded by Soma—we invoke the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, which are free from hatred.
O gods, bestow upon us wealth consisting of excellent sons; that is, grant us riches. Thus, by means of the mantras of the seers, the god Agni, endowed with such qualities as these, has been praised.
What kind of fire is it?
It is "suśevaḥ," meaning exceedingly pleasant or auspicious for men (narām). "Śeva" is a name for happiness, as it is listed among the synonyms for "śiva" (auspiciousness) in the lexicon.
Furthermore, of what nature is he? He is Vaiśvānara, existing within all men (viśveṣu nareṣu).
As it is stated in the Smṛti: "Becoming Vaiśvānara, I have entered the bodies of living beings."
Furthermore, who are they?
They are the "Soma-protectors," the guardians of Soma.
Therefore, we invoke—call upon—the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, which are free from hostility (*adveṣe*) and serve as the support for Agni.
The fact that these two serve as the substratum for one another is clearly stated in this Brāhmaṇa passage:

"O gods, you who are headed by Agni, bestow upon us—upon us, the worshippers—wealth (rayi) consisting of excellent sons and other blessings; [wealth] accompanied by good heroes. Vaiśvānara, who is most auspicious and pleasant to dwell with for noble men—the leaders of ritual acts—has been praised by the seers through their mantras.
Of what nature is he?
The guardians of Soma, the protectors of Soma—may we invoke the two, Heaven and Earth, who are free from malice; may we call them.
Furthermore, O gods, bestow upon us wealth consisting of excellent sons and progeny; maintain it for us.
Oṃ,
salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
After the seventh chapter was explained by Ācāryavaṃśaja,
Sāyaṇācārya now explains the first [verse] of the eighth chapter.
In the fourth anuvāka of the section beginning with “acchā mā,” there are eighteen hymns.
Among them, the fourth hymn, consisting of ten verses, begins with “pra hotā.
It is thus cataloged as “pra hotā daśa.”
The *vatsapraiṣa* belongs to Vālakhilya because it follows [his hymn]. The *vaiṣṭhabha āgeya* is [assigned] by the rule regarding the absence of specific instruction (*anādeśa-paribhāṣā*).
The application (*viniyoga*) is stated together with the preceding hymn.

Born as the great Hotṛ, pervasive in the sky, he has sat down upon the lap of the waters; he has been established as one who bestows strength. May he, the protector of the body, bestow upon you vital powers, wealth, and the means of union.

The Hotṛ, born great, the protector of homage, the one who dwells among men, has sat down in the lap of the waters—he who was established as our strength, the bestower of riches, the dispeller of distress, and the guardian of our bodies.
That Agni who is the lotus among men— this is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)—

who sat down in the lap, that is, the bosom, of the intermediate space in the form of lightning, has now become the *hotṛ*, the performer of the oblations for the sacrificers; he has appeared, great and worthy of worship through his qualities, the knower of the sky, that is, the intermediate space.
Since he was born therein, he is therefore its knower. *Nṛpadmā* means "sitting among men";
[the suffix] *kan* is added to the root *sad*, and there is vocalization (*kṛt-svara*).
He sits down upon the altar;
he sits down in the lap of the waters, in their vicinity—that is, upon the altar characterized as described above.
Or alternatively:

The fire which was hidden within the lap—that is, the midst—of the waters, unable to endure the smoke, was sought again by the gods; being of the aforementioned nature, it settles upon the sacrificial altar (*vedī*).

That fire which was established as the supporter of the sacrifice (*dhātā*) and placed upon the altar—may that fire, O Vatsapra, provide for you who serve him, may the vital strengths (*vayāṃsi*), foods, and riches (*vasūni*) be restrained and brought to you. Furthermore, he is the protector of your body; this is the sense of the ellipsis.
Worshipping him in the gathering place of the waters,
the wise Bhr̥gus, seeking with homages like one who tracks a lost animal by its footprints, found him as he moved in secret.

Worshipping him in the gathering place of the waters, the wise Bhr̥gus, longing for him as he moved in secret, followed his tracks like one who has lost a beast; seeking him with adorations, they found him.

The seers, honoring and attending upon this Agni who is hidden in the *sadhastha*—the common dwelling place—in the midst of the waters (*apām udakānām*), followed him with their steps, which were like paths for escape; they pursued him as one would track an animal stolen by thieves, using his footprints as signs of flight.

Among them, he was moving within the secret cave (*guhā*). *Note:* Regarding the verb *anugman*, the *luc* (aorist) ending is applied to the root *gam* in Vedic mantras according to the rule *mantre ghasa*. The term *guhācarantam* means "moving within the cave."
1. Because it is stated as "this belongs to Agni" (āgneyam), it is dedicated to Agni (āgneya).
2. In the manuscripts Ta1, Ta2, Ta3, and Ta7, the word *vidhamantaḥ* is hidden in the middle; in manuscript Bha, it is *vidhamantaḥ*. The root *ghatat-* is a verb meaning "to go."

The meaning is that [Agni] had dissolved in the waters. 1. *Uśijaḥ* means desiring; 2. *Namobhiḥ* means by means of salutations or hymns of praise; 3. *Icchantah* means desiring for themselves; 4. *Dhīrāḥ* means wise; 5. *Bhṛgavaḥ* [the Bhṛgus]; 6. *Avindan* means they found [him].

That Agni, being afraid of carrying the oblation, fled and entered the waters, and was subsequently sought out by the gods, is clearly stated in the Vedic text: "The waters were greater than Agni" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.6.6).

Regarding those who were searching, the discovery of the Bhṛgus is stated in the passage: "Seeking this [fire] in the gathering place of the waters, the Bhṛgus established it twice" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.4.2).
Trita found this [soma] with great effort through his skillful deeds at the head of Adhrigū’s daughter;
born as one who increases bliss in the dwellings, he becomes the youthful center of the luminous realm.
Trita found him while searching, on the summit of the Vaimuda mountain, in the highest place. Born as the increaser of bliss, he becomes the youthful navel of the luminous realm within the dwellings.
1 This 2 vast and great 3 Agni— 4 the son of Vibhvas 5 Trita, the seer (ṛṣi)— 6 desiring, that is, wishing to obtain [him] 7 from the *adhryā* 8— the earth; 9 from that 10 earth,
11 on its summit— that is to say, upon the earth.
Therein he found [it], he obtained it.

That Agni, the increaser of bliss (*śevṛdhaḥ*), born and manifested everywhere within the *man*—that is, in the houses of the sacrificers—is the navel, the central bond, of the shining (*rocanasya*) fruit known as heaven, or of the sacrifice characterized as such, or of the Sun.
With prostrations, the yearning ones have established the gentle Hotṛ, the leader of sacrifices who guides the rites forward;
they have made him the purifier and the bearer of oblations for the clans among men.
The eager ones have fashioned with their homages the low-voiced Hotṛ, the leader of the sacrifice, the guide of rites, the purifier, the bearer of oblations, and the steward among men. 4.

1. *Uśijaḥ*: desiring; 2. *Mandram*: delightful, worthy of exhilaration; 3. *Hotāram*: the invoker, the performer of the oblation; 4. *Prāñcam*: moving forward from the *gārhapatya* fire toward the *āhavanīya* fire; 5. *Yajñam*: the sacrifice, that which is to be worshipped; 6. *Adhvarāṇām*: of the sacrifices; 7. *Netāram*: the leader, the one who brings [the sacrifice] to completion; 8. *Aratim*: the one who goes, who is ever present in the sacrificial hall; 9. *Pāvakam*: the purifier; 10. *Havyavāham*: the carrier of the oblations; 11. *Mānuṣeṣu*: among men; 12. *Dadhataḥ*: bestowing, the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*); 13. *Viśām*: for the sake of the people, that is, the sacrificers. Or alternatively:
The delight of the people, that is, of living beings;
the meaning is "the lord. 14 With salutations, that is, with acts of homage.
The meaning is "with hymns of praise.
15 *akaṇvan* means they performed. 16 They have made [him] pleased.

They brought forward the most abundant one, the great bestower of inspired thought, the unerring shatterer of forts; leading him as the fruit of the woods, they placed the wise one upon their hymn—he who has a beard like a wild beast and whose wealth is song.

The wise ones, leading him forward, have established as the fruit of their devotion the great, victorious, and unerring one who destroys the fortresses—the source of inspired hymns—like a golden-bearded steed that wins the prize. 5.
O singer, you [should praise] him who conquers—the one who conquers the enemies who are to be conquered; the great—the mighty; the bestower of wisdom—the wise upholder, Agni.
Be pre-eminent—be capable.
"To praise" is the ellipsis.

Regarding the *udgītha*, however, considering "bhūr jayantam" as a single word, [the syllables] *bhūḥ* and so forth are to be approached as the worlds (*lokāḥ*). [Variants: 1. *ta-mu-vibhuvamaḥ*; 2. *ga-bhara.8-āgantavyāḥ*; *ta1.2.3-antyāḥ*; *ta7-mu-ahantavyāyā*. 3. *bha1.4.7-gomūrdhani*; 4. *bha1.6.7-prāpa tataḥ*; 5. *bha1.4.7-sukharūpaḥ*; 6. *ta-bha-sa ca*. 7. *ga-ta4-yuvā tejasā miśrayitā agniḥ rocanasya*; 8. *bha-ādityasya yajñasya*; 9. *ga-krāmanta*; 10. *bha-hotaḥ*. [Maṇḍala 10, Adhyāya 4, Sūkta 46] 437.
The word *atyantam* is explained as "absolutely.
Not only are you alone [thus], but all men, being *mūḥ*—that is, deluded (*mūḍhāḥ*)—[have failed to know] the *amūram*, the undeluded one, the ancient child (*purāṇa-dārakam*).
The suffix *man* is derived according to the *auṇādika* rules.
The accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*):
[the word *vanam*] is derived from *vana* with the suffix *ani*, meaning "that which is to be desired" (*vanīya*).
Due to the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*, Pāṇini 6.1.106–107), there is no substitution of the preceding vowel (*pūrvābhāva*) before the accusative singular ending *am*.
*Hiri-imaśru* means "not possessing a beard. The particle *na* here has the sense of a comparison (*upamārthīya*).
In this context, the word *imaśru* is a general term for body hair (*roma-sāmānya-vacana*).
Like a horse characterized by its death (maraṇa), it is endowed with flames that stand in place of greenish-yellow hair;
thus, the wealth is a source of delight and praise.
The single-substitute form [of *marāṇa*] occurs due to its inclusion in the *śakandhu*-class.
Bringing such a fire within themselves—that is, conveying it by means of oblations—they have brought forth, or attained, *dhiyam*: either ritual action or a hymn of praise.
(The *luk* elision of the suffix *sic* occurs according to Pāṇini 2.4.77: *gāti-sthā-*)
Trita, staying firm within the womb of the waters, sat in the midst of them;
having seized the people with his overwhelming power, he is restrained by the law that sustains all.

Trita, having propped up the firmaments, sat within the womb like the wind; he has moved across the mid-air. Seizing the wild beast, by his mastery over the people and by his sovereign law, he proceeds toward men with unrestrained power.

*Trita*, being extended—that is, being firmly established—in the three places, such as the *gārhapatya* and the others; desiring to stabilize the house of the sacrificer (the form is derived from the desiderative *kyac* added to the root *stabh*, followed by the suffix *śatṛ*). Being *pārvītaḥ*, completely enveloped on all sides by flames, he sits down (*nipīdati*) in the dwellings—the sacrificial houses—and in the womb, that is, within his own place, the altar-mound.

Therefore, from this place, having repeatedly gathered the oblations belonging to the *viś*—the subjects—and having accepted the offerings such as *caru* and *puroḍāśa* presented for Indra and the other gods; being *damnāḥ*, possessed of a mind intent on giving to the gods or a mind intent on bestowing what is desired upon the sacrificer; by *vidharmaṇā*, through their various activities as the cause for that giving-mind (or, in the sense of giving to the gods, through activity in the form of various movements); together with *yantraiḥ*, the restraints of enemies, he goes toward or approaches the *nṛn*, the gods.
His flames are like the days, his purifying fires like the half-months;
they are threefold, consuming, restless, bestowing forest wealth, and like the winds are the Soma-draughts.
Of this [Agni]: ageless; the oars of the houses; with rising smoke; the fires; purifying; moving along their paths; gladdening; restless; seated in the woods; like winds; like Soma juices. 7.
Here, [the hymn] is praised by means of its multiplicity.
In connection with this sacrificer: *ajarāsaḥ* means those who are free from old age; *damām* refers to those who are to be subdued, such as the Rākṣasas and others.
Regarding the word *dame*, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the case-ending is due to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*.

Their oars are the stars; their sails are the half-months; they are called "the radiant ones" (arcantaḥ), meaning those whose flames are characterized by smoke that is worthy of worship; they are "purifiers" (pāvakāḥ); and they are "immersed in whiteness" (śritīcayaḥ), meaning they are submerged in a state of being whitened.
*Śriti* means white; the suffix *hra* is according to the *Uṇādi* rules.

The *śrātrāsaḥ* are those who move swiftly; *kṣipra-nāmānaḥ*, meaning "those whose name is swift. *Kṣipa-dharmāṇaḥ* means "having the quality of moving quickly. *Bhuraṇyavaḥ* means "those whose nature is to carry" (*bharaṇa-śīlāḥ*). *Vanarṣadaḥ* means "sitting in the forests" (*vaneṣu sīdantaḥ*).
In the *saṃhitā*, the change to *hratvam* is a Vedic (*chāndasam*) anomaly.
Like winds, the Soma-libations are swift; like Somas, they quickly reach the sacrificer who offers the oblation.
1. Even before the *ga-bha* [mantra].
2. According to Bha 1.4.7, they cause nourishment (*puṣṭi*) to be attained. 3. In the *ga* and *ma* [recensions], "having grasped" (*saṃgṛbhya*) does not exist.
4. *bhara*. 5.6.8—*prattā prattāni*.

5. *ta6-vābhimataphalam*. 6. *bhara*: by the word *akāra*, the sense of "action" (*karman*) is expressed; thus the meaning is: performing the subduing of enemies together with their "yantras," that is, their means of restraint.
7. [The words] *ga-bhara*, *ṣaṣ-ṭha-aṣṭama-sṛ-nṛn*, *netṝn*; *ta-netṝn*; *bha1-nṛṇām netṝn*.
8. *bha-yasya*.
Agni bears forth his trembling with his tongue; he discerns the pathways of the earth with his mind.
The swift and pure ones have established him as the purifier, the delightful invoker, the most excellent sacrificer.

Agni bears forth the inspired song with his tongue; he proclaims the ordinances of the earth with his wisdom. Him, the radiant, the purifier, the delightful, the most excellent invoker, the Āyus have established as the priest. 8.

That Agni who, with his tongue—that is, his flame—performs the work (for *vepas* is a name for ritual action), and likewise that Agni who, with a mind endowed with grace, brings forth the *vayunāni*—that is, the acts of wisdom or hymns—for the protection of the earth; that Agni, the *āyavas*—the approaching men—maintain: him who is shining, the purifier, the cleanser, the pleasant one worthy of praise, the invoker (*hotṛ*), the performer of the oblation, or the most excellent sacrificer, the one most fit to be worshipped.
Heaven and Earth gave birth to Agni, as did the Waters, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the Bhr̥gus with their powers.
Mātariśvan and the gods fashioned him, the first one worthy of praise and fit for sacrifice, for the sake of man.

The Heaven and Earth brought forth that Agni, as did the Waters, Tvaṣṭṛ, and the Bhṛgus with their powers. Mātariśvan and the gods fashioned him, the first one worthy of praise and worship, for the sake of Manu. 9.
That Agni whom Heaven and Earth brought forth— *jan-iṣṭām* is from *jan*,
with the substitution of the active voice for the middle;

and whom the Waters generated in the form of lightning, and whom Tvaṣṭṛ begot, and whom the Bhṛgus obtained together with their powers (*sahobhiḥ*), that is, by means of hymns and other such instruments.
The statement "the Bhṛgus found him" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.46.2) is thus appropriate.

Furthermore, he is worthy of praise (*īḍenya*), the one whom Mātariśvan, Vāyu, brought forth, and whom other gods fashioned (*tatakṣuḥ*)—having produced him—as the worshipful (*yajatra*) Agni to be sacrificed to for Manu, the king, according to his desire.

You, whom the gods have established as the bearer of oblations, whom men, longing for much, have made worthy of sacrifice—O Agni, grant life to the one who praises you on his journey; for you bestow many glorious blessings upon those who seek the gods.

The gods have established you as the bearer of oblations, O Yama; men of many desires have established you, the worshipful one. On your path, O Agni, bestow vital strength upon the one who praises you; for the god-seeking and glorious ones gather together in great numbers. 10.

O Agni, you whom the gods have established as the bearer of oblations, and whom men—desiring many things and longing for much—have established as the one worthy of worship; O Agni, as such, at every journey, that is, at every sacrifice, bestow and grant food (*vayaḥ*) to me who praises you. O Agni, from you indeed the sacrificer who seeks the gods, desiring the divine, attains many, numerous, glorious honors.
(The verb *sam-prāpnoti* is to be supplied following the hearing of the prefix *sam-*)—he surely attains them.
The fifth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "jagubhmā te," is composed by Saptagu, a descendant of Aṅgiras; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
There was an Asura woman named Vikuṇṭhā who, desiring a son resembling the moon, performed austerities such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.

With the thought, "May no other like me be born," Indra himself was born as her son; for there is no one equal to him, Vaikuṇṭha Indra, the deity. Thus it is enumerated: "The eight [sages] sang; Saptavaikuṇṭha praised Indra," and so forth.
The application is concluded.
1. bha1.4.7—That which is to be exhilarated. 2. ta—The sacrificers should sacrifice, as if [to obtain] the primary element.
3. ta—A son has been born.

We have grasped your right hand, O Indra, we who desire wealth, O Lord of riches. For we know you, O Hero, as the master of cattle; grant us wonderful, showering wealth. We have grasped your right hand, O Indra, we who desire wealth, O Lord of riches. For we know you, O Hero, as the master of cattle; grant us wonderful, showering wealth. O Indra, Lord of riches—master of many treasures—we, desiring wealth, have grasped your right hand. Just as those seeking much from a generous giver grasp his hand, saying, "Do not depart without giving me," so do we. O valiant Indra, we know you to be the master of cattle—the protector of many cows, as indicated here by both the sense of "showering" (*vṛṣi*) and "lordship" (*pati*). Therefore, grant us wonderful, praiseworthy, and showering wealth.

O Indra, grant us wonderful, showering wealth—wealth that possesses excellent weapons, excellent protection, or easy passage; that has a good leader; that pervades the four oceans with its glory; that is the sustainer of riches; that is to be celebrated again and again, worthy of praise, and the warder-off of many sorrows, or that which is desired by many. Or rather: O Indra, grant us such wealth in the form of a son, characterized by these aforementioned qualities. *Svāyudham* (possessing excellent weapons): having beautiful thunderbolts and other arms. *Svarvasam* (having excellent protection): possessing beautiful preservation, or easy movement. *Sunītham* (having a good leader): having excellent guidance. *Catussamudram* (pervading the four oceans): that which pervades the four oceans with its fame. *Dharuṇam* (the sustainer): the supporter. *Rayīṇām* (of riches): of wealth. *Carkṛtyam* (to be celebrated repeatedly): to be performed again and again. *Śasyam* (worthy of praise): praiseworthy. *Bhūrivāram* (warder-off of many sorrows): the remover of many sufferings, or that which is desirable by many. *Asmabhyam* (to us): for us. *Citram* (wonderful): marvelous. *Vṛṣaṇam* (showering): pouring down [blessings]. *Rayim* (wealth): riches. *Dāḥ* (grant): give. Or alternatively: O Indra, grant us a son as wealth, distinguished by the qualities mentioned above.

O Indra, grant us wonderful, showering wealth—a son who possesses excellent prayer (*subrahmāṇam*), is accompanied by the gods (*devavantam*), is great (*bṛhantam*), vast (*urum*), deep (*gabhīram*), broad-based (*pṛthubudhnam*), whose seers are renowned (*śrutarṣim*), fierce (*ugram*), and a subduer of adversaries (*abhimātipāham*). Or rather, there is a relationship between the adjectives and the noun: grant us wealth in the form of a son characterized by these aforementioned qualities. *Subrahmāṇam*: "Possessing excellent prayer"; *brahma* here means the powerful act characterized by praise; thus, it means "one whose praise is beautiful. *Devavantam*: "Accompanied by the gods. *Bṛhantam*: "Great. *Urum*: "Vast" or wide-extending. *Gabhīram*: "Deep," meaning inaccessible to Asuras and others. *Pṛthubudhnam*: "Broad-based," having a wide foundation. *Śrutarṣim*: "One whose seers are renowned"—either the establisher of such seers or one whose knowledge is celebrated. *Ugram*: "Fierce," possessing surging strength. *Abhimātipāham*: "A subduer of adversaries"—the overcomer and slayer of enemies (*abhimātīn*). *Citram*: "Wonderful" or worthy of honor. *Vṛṣaṇam*: "Showering," i.e., bestowing. *Rayim*: "Wealth," or a son. *Dāḥ*: "Grant" or "give. Alternatively, the relationship is that of qualifier and qualified: grant us wealth known as a son, endowed with the characteristics described above.

1. O Lord of treasures! 2. *ta1.2.3*: requested by many seekers; *ta7*: many gifts for this seeker; *bha1.2.4.8*: many-footed for the seekers; *bha6.7*: many-giving for the seekers. 3. *ga-bha*: the four oceans.
4. ta-mu-teṣām | 5. ga-ta4-tādṛśas tvam asmabhyam; bha-tādṛśāya asmabhyam | 6. ta-mu-vitatamūlam |

7. O Indra, grant us true, wondrous, and bull-like wealth—wealth that is accompanied by heroes, that is heroic, victorious, a winner of riches, ever-sounding, highly skillful, a slayer of Dasyus, and a breaker of forts. (The word *bha* does not exist here.)

O Indra, grant us true, wonderful, and bull-like wealth—that which wins booty, has wise heroes, overcomes enemies, touches the bow, breathes like a hero, is most skillful, slays the Dasyus, and shatters fortresses. 4.
A son who wins cattle, who has acquired wealth, a hero among the wise, intelligent, a deliverer, a savior, a winner of riches—that is, one who fills or bestows wealth—or one who is clearly visible;
or "mṛga" (deer) at the end [of the compound] from the root *sṛj* (to release), with the latter member [meaning] "one who releases";

one who breathes strongly, one who is increasing, one who is very skillful, one who slays the Dasyus—that is, a destroyer of enemies—one who shatters the fortresses—that is, a breaker of the cities of enemies—and one who is true—that is, one whose actions are truthful.
The remainder has been stated.
O Indra, grant us wealth consisting of horses, chariots, and heroes—wealth in the hundreds and thousands;
grant us wonderful, bull-like riches that bring auspiciousness, heroic sons, and the attainment of heaven.

O Indra, grant us wonderful, bull-like wealth—wealth consisting of horses, chariots, heroes, and hundreds and thousands; wealth that brings auspiciousness, with wise men as its champions, which protects the light of heaven. || 5 ||

O Indra, [bestow] that strength (*vāja*) which is possessed of horses (*vaśvāvantam*), endowed with many steeds; possessed of chariots (*vrathinam*), provided with vehicles; possessed of heroes (*vīravantam*), attended by brave men; thousandfold (*sahasriṇam*), possessing a thousand; hundredfold (*śatinam*), possessing a hundred—meaning it is yoked with an innumerable number of horses and so forth; possessed of auspiciousness (*bhadrāvantam*), surrounded by a host of auspicious attendants; possessed of wise heroes (*vipravīram*), accompanied by heroic sages; and the winner of light (*svarpām*), the enjoyer of all things. O Indra!
The remainder has been stated.
The prayer goes forth toward Bṛhaspati, the wise one of true thought, who has been won over;
he, the descendant of Aṅgiras, who is to be approached with reverence—grant us wonderful, virile wealth.

My prayer goes forth toward Bṛhaspati, the wise one of true insight, who is accompanied by the Sāsaṅga; he, the descendant of Aṅgiras, who is to be approached with reverence—may he grant us wonderful, virile wealth. 6.
My mind—my speech directed toward the gods in the form of praise—goes forth;
that is, it approaches Bṛhaspati. Of what nature is he? He who possesses true resolve, whose actions are real, who is of excellent wisdom, and who is the lord of the great mantra.
The Vyaḥ-sasaguḥ, the Aṅgirasas— having been born into the lineage of Aṅgiras— I, having approached the gods with *namas* (reverence),
have come near them; or rather, [I am] one who is to be approached (*upasadaniya*) by means of *namas*.
The meaning is that he ought to favor us;
to such as we are—to us, to me—he has granted wonderful, virile wealth.
The yearning messengers, our hymns of praise, go forth toward Indra, seeking his favor;
touching the heart and uttered by the mind, O Bull, grant us wondrous wealth.
The yearning prayers, the messengers, the hymns of praise go forth to Indra, seeking his favor; touching the heart, uttered with the mind, grant us wonderful, virile wealth. 7.

The eager ones, the seekers of the vital point, the messengers—these hymns go forth toward Indra, accompanied by auspicious thoughts, moving with wisdom, touching the heart, uttered by the mind; grant us wonderful, manly wealth. 7.
1. *ga-ta-ma-mu-he indra sanadvājam* | 2. *bha-śatinam śatavantam* does not exist. 3. *ga4-ta3-mu-’vājam... he indra* does not exist. 4. It is to be approached according to *ta1.2.3.7*.
*Vanīvān:* possessing the desire to win (*vanana-vant*).
The suffix *vanip* is used here in the sense of possession, according to the rule *chandasīvanipau*.

My companions—the messengers, those like messengers who, just as they deliver what is desired by their master, bring forth the praiseworthy qualities; these hymns (*stomāḥ*), praises (*stavāḥ*), and excellent thoughts (*sumantīḥ*)—approaching (*iyānāḥ*) and entreating (*yācamānāḥ*), reach (*caranti*) Indra, attaining his favorable intentions toward us.
Furthermore, they are further characterized:
they are "heart-touching" (*hṛdispṛśaḥ*), touching the heart.
The meaning is "beloved by the one worthy of praise.
The absence of elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending is according to the rule *hṛdyubhyāṃ ḍerupasaṃkhyānam*.
They are being addressed—that is, spoken to—by the mind characterized by the quality of goodness (*sattva*).
The passage beginning with "asmabhyam" has already been explained.

And that which I ask of you, O Indra, grant that to us: a vast dwelling, unsurpassed among the people. May Heaven and Earth approve of that; grant us wonderful, virile wealth. That which I ask of you, O Indra, grant that to us: a vast dwelling, unsurpassed among the people. May Heaven and Earth approve of that; grant us wonderful, virile wealth. (8)

O Indra, that which I entreat of you—I ask for it (the elision of the *va* is Vedic)—grant that which is being requested. [The root] *dad* means "to give. In the imperative (*loṭ*), the *parasmaipada* ending is used by way of substitution; the *śap* suffix is dropped according to the rule "in the Veda, [suffixes are] frequently [elided]. He specifies that which was indicated generally by the word "that": grant a vast, great dwelling (*kṣaya*)—an abode for people, unequalled and unique. May Heaven and Earth approve what is to be given by you. The rest, beginning with "for us," has been explained. 4.

The sixth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "ahaṃ bhuvam," was seen by [the seer] when he had been praised by the previous hymn, the *masaguna*. Having seen it, he himself praised his own self with the triad of hymns beginning with *sañjigami*. Therefore, because these are the words of Vaikuṇṭha or Indra, according to the technical rule that "he whose words they are is the seer (*ṛṣi*"), Indra is the seer.

Since both Vaikuṇṭha and Indra possess the quality of being the end (*ṛtyamantatva*), Indra alone is the deity according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "That which is mentioned by him [the seer] is the deity. The tenth and eleventh verses constitute the *savyaṣṭaka*.
The remaining verses are *jagatī*s, according to the technical rule regarding the *agniṣṭut*.

And thus it is enumerated: "The hymn beginning with 'I am the first' is a praise of the self; having praised the self with the [first] three verses, [the seer] says 'I was the first' with the next eleven; the seventh and the last two are Triṣṭubhs.
This hymn belongs to the Hotṛ's recitation during the second round of the Antaryāma sacrifice.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'I was the first... for the exhilaration of the pressed soma-juice' is the Yājyā verse" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
This hymn is also used in the *niṣkevalya* śastra on the third *chandoma* day of the ten-night *samūḷha* sacrifice;
for it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The *niṣkevalya* consists of [the hymn] beginning with 'I have become that power of yours' (*ahaṃ bhuvam tad ta indriyam*)" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).

I have become the ancient lord of wealth; I win together all treasures forevermore. Living beings call upon me as they would a father; I distribute nourishment to the donor. I have become the ancient lord of wealth; I win together all treasures forevermore. Living beings call upon me as they would a father; I distribute nourishment to the donor.
I, O Indra, have become the foremost, the principal, and the exclusive lord and master of wealth and riches. [The form *bhuvaṃ* is derived from the root *bhū* in the *laṅ* tense;
the suffix *śap* is elided by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," and the substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs according to the rule "aci nudhātubhruvām," etc.]
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Likewise, *ahaṃ* is a name for "eternal" (*śaśvataḥ*),
ending in the suffix *-man*.

The wealth belonging to the enemy (*bahoḥ śatroḥ*)—[the forms] *vanavantaḥ* [are derived as follows]: *vaniḥ* is the act of winning (*vananam*); according to Pāṇini 1.2.3.5, *vanavantaḥ* [is formed with the suffix] *vanip*; according to 1.2.8, *vanavantaḥ* [is formed with the suffix] *vi*; and according to 7, *vanavantaḥ* [is formed with the suffix] *kanip*, as per the rule "in the Veda, *kanip* and *vanip* [are used after roots ending in long vowels].
2. *ta-mu-*, by way of the *guṇa* [substitution].
3. Ga, Ta, Bha: let them both follow with their minds; Ta: let him approve. 4. Ta, Mu: of the Indra named Vaikuṇṭha.
5. Ga, Ta, Bha: the phrase "that deity" is not present.
6. There is no "ga-ta-mu-'sa" (gone-to-measure); thus, in the sense of oneness, I conquer together with victory.
Moreover, living beings— creatures who perform sacrifices— invoke me alone,
just as sons invoke their father. To the donor, to the sacrificer who offers oblations, I distribute— that is, I bestow— the food that is nourishment.

I am Indra; the breast is my rampart, the source of wealth. For Trita’s sake, I brought forth the cows from the mountain-fastness. I seized the booty from the Dasyus, bestowing the cow-pens upon Dadhyañc Mātariśvan as a gift.
I am Indra,
the dam.
The chest;
the one with the meaningful sound;
for Trita.
I generated the cows from the serpent.
In half [of it],
I [am] for the Dasyus.
Around the praise.
Hither!
He gave;
he was of noble lineage;
he was training.
To Dadhyanc;
to Mātariśvan.
They relate the historical account of the first quarter:
Indra approached Dadhyañc, the descendant of Atharvan, who possessed the knowledge of honey (*madhu-vidyā*), and commanded him, "Do not teach the knowledge of honey to anyone.
He further declared, "If you should teach it, I shall strike off your head."
And that [knowledge] was told by Atharvan to the two Aśvins:

"This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa told to the two Aśvins" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 14.2.5.16); for the Śruti says, "With the head of a horse, he told it to them" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.12). And it is stated here that Indra, having arrived, took away the head of Dadhyañc.
I am Indra, the destroyer of the chest— meaning the head characterized by that chest— of Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan. I shall be its obstructer, its seizer, and its remover.
Likewise, for the sake of rescuing Trita—so named—who had fallen into a pit, I generated and produced the waters (*gāḥ*) from above (*adhi*) the cloud (*vaheḥ*).
The prayer of Trita, who had fallen into the pit, directed toward Indra for his rescue is set forth in the verse: “They burn me on all sides” (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.33.2).
Likewise, I have taken away *numnam*—wealth—from the *dasyus*, the plunderers, that is, from the enemies;
while doing what?
Training—that is, disciplining—the *gotrāḥ*, the clouds which are the protectors of the waters (cows).
For what purpose?
Desiring to cause this [mantra] to proceed for Mātariśvan—the son of Mātariśvan—namely Dadhyañc Āptya, who was desirous of rain.
Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for me the great iron thunderbolt; the gods bestowed wisdom upon me.
My mind is as difficult to overcome as that of the sun; they seek me with every deed and every act.

Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for me the great iron thunderbolt; the gods bestowed creative power (*kratu*) upon me. My host is as invincible as the splendor of the sun; they come to me with what has been done and with what is yet to be done. Tvaṣṭṛ, the god, fashioned for me—the great one—this iron (*āyasa*) weapon, the thunderbolt (*vajra*). The gods bestowed creative power (*kratu*), that is, the act of slaying adversaries, upon me. My host (*anīka*), my multitude of troops, is difficult to overcome (*duṣṭara*), like the host of the sun, impossible for another to cross. They come to me alone with what has been accomplished (*kṛtena*) and with what is to be done hereafter (*katvena*), such as the slaying of Vṛtra. The root *ā-yā* signifies "to go. Alternatively, they make me their lord (*artham īśvaram kurvanti*).
1. For the sake of rescuing one who has fallen into a well (*ga-ta-mu-kūpapatitāya*), for the purpose of her extraction (*taduddharaṇārtham*).
2. To those who cause destruction (*upakṣayitṛbhyas*) [of the *ga-bha*]; to those who observe (*upalakṣitṛbhyas*) [the *ta*].
3. *Ga-ta1. 2.4.6.7.8-bha*: He fashioned it well (*atakṣat sādhu*).

4. He has accomplished it. The gods perform the *kratu*, the sacrifice, directed toward me. My host—consisting of horses and so forth—is as difficult to cross and difficult to penetrate as that of the sun, Sūrya; he has accomplished this in the form of Vṛtra and others.

While I was performing this sacrifice, he produced for me a host consisting of horses and other forces— difficult to overcome and difficult to penetrate, like the sun in its form as Vṛtra and the rest— as if he had brought it about through his power.
Moreover, O gods, while I was performing this sacrifice, you generated within me the mental resolve (*kratu*) for the ritual.

"My army (*anīkam*) and my horses and so forth are as difficult to cross and difficult to fathom as the sun (*sūryasyeva kheḥ*); it is called 'the tearer' (*dārayin*) of enemies such as Vṛtra," according to the *Nirukta*.

Such a powerful one as myself, in the form of Vṛtra and others—the gods (*devāsaḥ*, i.e., the *devas*)—performed against me a ritual act (*kratum*) consisting of the slaying of those who opposed them. By means of that deed (*karmaṇā*), which was the supreme duty (*param kartavyam*) consisting of the slaying of Vṛtra and so forth, they approached my splendor (*tejasā*) and my army (*anīkam*), the multitude of troops, which is as difficult to cross as the host of the sun (*sūryānikamiva*) and impossible for another to overcome. Thus, by means of that deed, they came toward me.

I have won this swift, golden-hued beast, rich in vital essence, with my missile; I sharpen many thousands [of weapons] for the donor, since the Soma juices, accompanied by hymns, have exhilarated me. I have won this swift, golden-hued beast, rich in vital essence (purīṣin)—meaning that which contains water in the form of milk—with my weapon; I have conquered the host of enemies. I sharpen many thousands of weapons for the donor who offers oblations, that is, for the destruction of the foes. When? It is said: when the Soma juices, accompanied by hymns (ukthins)—or rather, the sacrificers equipped with Soma and hymns—have exhilarated me.

I am Indra; I have never lost my wealth. I have never at any time stood still before death. Pressing the Soma, ask me alone for wealth. O Pūrus, do not suffer harm in my friendship. I am Indra, the master of all wealth. I have never lost my own riches; the meaning is that my wealth is never diminished. Furthermore, I have never at any time remained subject to death—that is, I have never been stationed as prey for the slayer of all. Indeed, those devoted to Indra do not become the portion of death; how much more so must it be said of Indra himself that he is free from death? Therefore, O sacrificers, pressing the Soma, ask me alone for *vasu*—the wealth you desire. O Pūrus, men, do not suffer harm in my friendship; do not bring ruin upon yourselves. 5.

I [Indra], with my deadly blow, struck down these panting ones, two by two—those who made Indra, the shatterer of enemies, wield his thunderbolt for battle. As they were being driven forward, I struck them down with my weapon; speaking harshly, I, the one who does not bow, humbled those who sought to pay homage. I, Indra, [struck] these aforementioned, panting ones—those who breathe heavily, whose strength has greatly increased—the enemies, two by two; that is, in pairs. This is the connection: "I struck them. He states this in a fitting manner: "Those enemies who made Indra—the destroyer of foes (for *indra* is the destroyer of enemies, according to Nirukta 10.8)—wield his powerful thunderbolt (*vajra*), or rather, who made him possessed of the thunderbolt, for the sake of battle. Furthermore, of what kind were they? "Being driven forward"—come on! [They were being urged on].

1. This [is] that which has the characteristic of a stone, which is unendurable and makes [one] unendurable; 2. *taha* (for *tatra*), *bha4.5.6*: golden (*hiraṇyayam*) means made of gold (*hiraṇmayam*); 3. *ta*: to one who has given (*dattavate*); 4. *ta*: to me (*mahyam*) or else; 5. *ta-bha1.4.6.7*: from affection (*prītataḥ*); 6. *ta*: the meaning is "having become a pair" (*yugmabhūtau*); 7. *ta*: "these [are] the bringers" (*hānetān*); 8. *ga*: may [he] protect me, the possessor of the thunderbolt (*vajravantam*).

"Fight!"—thus I have challenged the enemies; having bowed down the powerful forces with my bowing [strength], being one who does not bow (*anamasyu*), I, the destroyer of the firm (*dṛḍhahā*), speaking firm and terrifying words, have slain them. Facing this one, alone I am; facing two, I am the crusher. What can three do? Like leaves upon a threshing floor, I strike them down in abundance. Why do these Indra-less enemies revile me? (7) I, even now, being alone and without a companion, overcome this single enemy. Furthermore, being a crusher, I overcome even two enemies who are without companions. The meaning is that they make him their donor and their friend.
Or rather:
for the seeking of cattle, they establish him in two ways—for friendship, both for bodily [friendship] and for military [friendship].
When is it said? When, for the sake of victory for this my associated praiser in battles—that is, in conflicts—I shall take up the *didyu*, meaning the weapon;
immediately thereafter (*ādit*), I have made, or I am making, this praiser worthy of praise (*śastya*), praiseworthy (*ukthya*), and one who utters hymns (*ukthāham*).

In one, the Soma is seen within as a guardian; in another, he makes himself manifest. Desiring to fight the sharp-horned bull, he stands amidst the many, awakened within the darkness. In one, the Soma is seen within as a guardian; in another, he makes himself manifest. Desiring to fight the sharp-horned bull, he stands amidst the many, awakened within.
"Neither. The word "neither" (nerma) is a synonym for "object" (artha).
Or else, it refers to these two persons fighting.
The meaning is that [the Soma] is in one of those two sacrificial posts.
Within it, the Soma is seen;
Indra, the protector, guards one half of it, and with his *nemi*—the *āstha*, the weapon used for hurling—he makes it manifest.
The meaning is that he makes [himself] unconquerable by enemies.

¹¹Where Soma is not seen, there ¹²he—desiring to fight (*yuyutsan*), wishing to battle against the sharp-horned (*tigmaśṛṅga*) bull who wields a sharp weapon and rains down arrows, and who is favored by Indra—being bound by his two jaws (*dauhḥ-drobhyā*), stands ¹⁷within the thick darkness (*bahule andhakāre*).
Or rather, it may be explained as follows.
In this one who is devoted to Indra, Soma is seen within;
in another, the protector of his own devotees, Indra reveals [the enemy] with his bone-like thunderbolt;
he makes him manifest.
The meaning is that he oppresses with the thunderbolt.
He who, desiring to fight, [approached] Indra—the bull with sharp horns—to whom be homage;
the rest is the same.

I do not violate the station of the Ādityas, the Vasus, or the Rudras—the God among gods. They have fashioned me for auspicious power, unconquered, unsubdued, and invincible. 11. Of the Ādityas; of the Vasus; of the Rudras; the God; of the gods; I; do not; violate; the station. They; me; for auspicious; power; have fashioned; unconquered; unsubdued; invincible. 11.
The god Indra does not diminish—that is, he does not harm—the abode or station of the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudriyas, the Rudras, or those who are the sons of Rudra, nor that of the great gods.
May those [gods], beginning with the Ādityas, fashion me for auspicious strength; may they favor me.
[May they grant] that which is unconquered, unsubdued, unhurt, and unassailable.
‘Ahaṃ dām’ is the seventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses. Vaikuṇṭha alone is both the subject matter and the deity.
The second and eleventh verses are in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The remaining verses are in the Jagatī meter.
And it has been enumerated: “I [saw] Dāman and Upāc.
This hymn belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa during the second round of the night.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "May Indra be the protector of this pressed Soma" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).
I have bestowed ancient wealth upon the singer; I have fashioned the sacred word as a great means of increase.
I have become the impeller for the sacrificer, and I am the witness for the non-sacrificer in every battle.

1. *Ta* and *Bha*: "the givers" (*dātāraḥ*) and "friends" (*sakhāyaḥ*). 2. *Ga*: "to the one whose body is composed of *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*. 3. *Bha*: The word *nema* is a synonym for the word *artha*. 4. *Ga*: "only the meaning" (*artham eva*); *Ta* 1.2.78 and *Bha*: "one [verse] for the meaning" (*artham ekaḥ*). 5. *Ta*: "'te' does not exist. 6. *Ga*, *Ta* 1.2.6.7.8, and *Bha*: "Vaikuṇṭha is Indra. 7. *Ga* and *Ta*: "The third and eleventh [verses]. 8. *Ga*: "In the second *paryāya* of the *atirātra*"; *Ta*, *Mu*, and *Bha*: "in the second *paryāya*."

I am the one who gives ancient wealth to the singer. I, making the sacred word (*brahman*) my own strengthener, have become the instigator for the sacrificer and the adversary of the non-sacrificer in every battle. 1.

I am Indra; to the singer who praises me, I, the ancient one, have given and continue to give the foremost wealth and treasure. I alone perform the great, sovereign rite—namely, the act characterized by praise—which is my own magnification. The meaning is that by bestowing wealth upon the hymn belonging to the singer, I effect my own increase.
Likewise, I become the impeller— the one who urges on— the sacrificer and the one who bestows wealth; [I am] not [the impeller] of the non-sacrificer— that is to say,
of one who does not sacrifice.
In every single burden and in every battle whatsoever, I shall witness and overcome him.
I am the one whom the gods call Dhuriṇdra, the lord of the yoke, who moves between heaven and earth.
I am the one who possesses the two bay steeds, the powerful and swift ones that follow different paths; I am the bold one who took up the thunderbolt for the sake of strength.

They called me Indra by name, the deity of heaven, earth, and the waters, the one who moves within them. I, the impetuous one, have taken for my strength the two vigorous, swift, and differently directed bay steeds, and I, the bold one, have seized the thunderbolt for power. 2.
Me, who am named Indra— among the gods— I have placed; in these worlds, namely the sky (dyu),
the earth (gmaḥ),
and the atmosphere (ap)— in these realms, all beings (jantavaḥ) that have been born sustain me alone with oblations and hymns of praise.
I yoke to the chariot the two bay horses, green in color, virile and full of manly vigor, performing various tasks, swift and fleet of foot, for the sake of sacrifice or for going into battle.
Likewise, I take up the bold thunderbolt weapon for the sake of strength.
I taught the minister to the sage with my blows; I protected Kutsa with my aids. I, the loosener of Śuṣṇa, caused him to grow weak—he who did not yield the Aryan name to the Dasyu.

I taught the sage Arka with my blows; I protected Kutsa with these aids. I am the one who weakened Śuṣṇa, increasing him whom no one had given as a friend to the Dasyu, nor had I surrendered my Āryan name to the barbarian. 3.

I, Indra, [struck] Arka, the son of the enemy and a coverer [of truth], for the sake of the seer Uśanas Kavi’s dwelling in happiness; with various kinds of blows, with weapons or missiles, I have struck him down, having loosened his various deeds.
Furthermore, I [protected] Kutsa, who bears this name, with my aids consisting of slaying and other such acts.
"‘For Kutsa, you struck down the swift Śuṣṇa’ (Ṛgveda Maṇḍala 4, Hymn 16, Verse 12)—this and other such mantras [are the reference].
Regarding protection: "I have protected you both. He reiterates that even those protections already performed in the past are as if performed right now.
The "shattering" (śrathitā) refers to the destruction of Śuṣṇa, the Asura of that name;
it means for the sake of slaying him. The "weapon" (vadhaḥ) is the thunderbolt (vajraṃ), which I have raised for the purpose of striking him.
Moreover, I am noble and related to the noble; the meaning is that I am one to whom gifts should be given by the noble ones— such indeed is my name.
This is not water; I have not given this mere name "water" to the robber, the enemy, the one who seeks to harm me.
Or rather:
I have not bestowed upon a robber the unique name "Noble" (*ārya*), meaning "worthy of worship.

In this regard, Indra’s self-praise—including his protection of Kutsa and the slaying of Śuṣṇa and others—is elaborated in many ways in such passages as: “O Indra, you protected Kutsa in whom you took delight” (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.33.14) and “O Indra, [you slew] Śuṣṇa, Pima, Kuyava, and Vṛtra” (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.102.8).
Therefore, for fear of excessive length, I shall not discuss them here.

Like a father, I subdued the Vetasus for my protection; I delivered Tugra and Smadibha to Kutsa. I became the sovereign of the sacrificer when, in the contest for the prize, I overcame those who were difficult to assail. I, like a father, [subdued] the Vetasus for the sake of assistance; I delivered Tugra and Smadibha to Kutsa. I became the ruler for the sacrificer when, in the struggle for the prize, I conquered those who were not easily assailed.

Like a father carrying his son on his hip, or as one leads a child to a desired place for his nourishment, so did I lead the fierce Smadibha—who was hostile to Kutsa, the great seer who desired the Vetasus (the people of that name)—into subjection for the sake of his protection.
And I became capable, O King, in the battle of the sacrificer;
"capable" is the sense intended.

Since I bring these dear things for him—just as a father brings them to his son—for that sacrificer who is invincible against his enemies, for the purpose of overcoming them; therefore, the connection is: "May I be present for the sake of the kingdom of that sacrificer."

I, Indra, subdued Vṛmigha, the Asura of that name, for Śrutarvan, the great seer of that name; I brought him under control. (*Radhyati* means "in the act of going toward subjection"; I brought him into submission. Because Śrutarvan came toward me—*ohāṅ* meaning "to go"—he approached. That very thing is stated: he became *anupak*, joined with *vayunā*, which means either through wisdom or through ritual purity. *Vcana* is a filler word. I made Vveśa, the one of that name, submissive and struck him down. (In the *luṅ* tense of the root *kṛ*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule *kṛmṛdṛhibhyaḥ*; the absence of the augment *aṭ* is archaic. I subdued Paḍbhi, the one of that name, for Savya, the one of that name; I brought him under control. || 7 ||

I am he who, like the slayer of Vṛtra, shattered the Dāsa Narvāstva and Bṛhadratha, as if crushing obstacles; I, the helper, made him grow and expand, creating luminous realms far across the distant reaches of the mid-air.
I, Indra, am the one who carries away; I have shattered Navavāstva and Bṛhadratha, like Vṛtra, like Dāsa, like an oppressor—Navavāstva and Bṛhadratha, the breaker of the stronghold (*varuja*).
[The root *ruj* means "to break.
When I, being closely joined against both enemies as they were increasing, spreading out, and breaking forth, I cast them far away to the distant limit of the luminous realm, of the world.
I go around the sun with the swift steeds, being carried forward by the coursers with might.
When the Soma-pressing of Manu calls me as my adornment, I drive away the Dāsa and the sorcerer with my blows.
1. *bha* lacks "janapadān". 2. *bha* reads "prabharāṇi". 3. *ta*, *bha1.4* read "akaram". 4. *ta1.2.7*, *bha* lack "saḥ asmi".

I go around with the swift [horses] of Sūrya, being carried forward by might with the Etaśas. When the man called me forth with his bright raiment, I, apart from [him], seized the Dāsa and the Kṛtya with my steeds. (7)

Being carried— being drawn up— by the swift-moving *etaśas*, the horses of the god Sūrya that are *etaśa*-colored, I travel around, encompassing [the world] with my own vigor and power in the form of the Sun. Furthermore, whenever the pressing of Soma by a human being calls out to me— that is, when it invites me.
For what purpose did he say "for cleansing" (*nirṇije*)?
*Nirṇij* is a name for form (*rūpa*).
The meaning is "to her whose nature is sacrifice.
At that time, [the enemy] must be acted upon;
the meaning is "he must be slain."
I separate the enemy who seeks to harm me from the horses—the instruments of slaughter—by means of *ṛdhak*;
here, *ṛdhak* has the sense of "separately."

I am the great Nahuṣa, more powerful than Nahuṣa; by my might I have made Turvaśa and Yadu famous. By my power I have subdued one [foe] who was more powerful than power itself, and I shall carry off Navavādhatas and Narvṛti. I am the great Nahuṣa, more powerful than Nahuṣa; by my might I have made Turvaśa and Yadu famous. By my power I have subdued another who was more powerful than power itself, and I shall carry off Navavādhatas and Narvṛti.
I am the slayer of seven cities along with their inhabitants;
as it is said: “O Sasa, [you who destroyed] the cities and the autumnal shelters” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.174.2).
Or alternatively:

He slew the seven, beginning with Namuci. Furthermore, I, who am more powerful (*nahuṣṭara*) than even Nahuṣa the binder (*bandhaka*), have by my might (*śavasā*) made Turvaśa and Yadu renowned; that is to say, I have caused them to be heard of through the bestowal of wealth and other honors associated with victory over enemies, so that they may become famous in the world as they ought to be.
Furthermore, by means of *sahas*, that is, by force, I have made both myself and another who praises us *sahas*, that is, powerful.
[In the formation of this word,] the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix of the root *kṛ* takes *aṅ* according to the rule "kṛmṛdṛhi," and there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*.
Furthermore, "nine" refers to the number nine, and "ninety" refers to the number ninety;
that is to say, ninety-nine.
Of what nature are they?
"Growing stronger, I shall carry away [them]; that is to say, I shall utterly destroy them."

I, the bull, have sustained the seven flowing rivers, the swift-moving streams upon the earth. I, of noble wisdom, spread out the floods through my power; by battle, I found a path for man to seek his goal. I, the bull, have sustained the seven flowing rivers, the swift-moving streams upon the earth. I, of noble wisdom, spread out the floods through my power; by battle, I found a path for man to seek his goal.
I, the bull, the showerer, held—indeed, sustained—the seven flowing rivers. Of what nature were they?
They were rushing, flowing waters.
In the phrase "vā chandāṃsi," there is an absence of the long vowel resulting from the homogeneous preceding sound (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*). "Sīrāḥ" means those characterized by flowing.
Where? On the earth.
I, the well-doer of beautiful deeds, cross over— that is, bestow— the waters. Furthermore,
for the sake of man, for his desire to go, I provide a path through battle, that is,
by means of overcoming obstructions.
"Vidam alambhayam" means "I gave. For the root *vid* in the sense of "obtaining," the substitution of *aṅ* for *cli* occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.1.55, beginning with "pupādi."

I then held that within them which not even the god Tvaṣṭṛ had fashioned—the bright, pervasive [milk] within the heights of the cows, in the trees; the honeyed sweetness, the Soma mixed with milk for the draught. 10. I. That. Within them. I held. Which. Within them. Not. Even. God. Tvaṣṭṛ. Fashioned. Bright. Pervasive. Of the cows. In the heights. In the trees. Hither. Of the honey. The honey. The prepared. Soma. The milk-mixture. 10.
1. With those [arrows] that have reached the enemies;
2. with those that slay [the foes].

I have held—that well-known milk—in these cows. [The root] *dhṛ* means "to hold"; this is the form of the causative (*ṇyanta*) in the imperfect (*laṅ*). That milk which even the divine artisan (the *śvaṣṭṛ*), or the Sun, the divine, was not able to hold—was unable to sustain. If it is asked what kind of milk I held, it is said: it was *raśat*, radiant; *spāham*, desirable. In what places? It is said: in the udders of the cows, those parts of the cows where the milk is held. Furthermore, I hold *madhu* (water) in the *vakṣaṇās*. This is a term for rivers; it is understood that I hold it in the flowing rivers. The limit for holding the river water is stated: *ā madhoḥ*, until the arising of water—that is, until the coming rainy season. Of what nature is that *madhu*? It is said: it is *śrādhyam*. *Śrātra* is a name for "quick"; it means having a swift course. Or rather, *śrādhyam* is connected with what follows: *śrādhyam* means bringing happiness; I held the *āśiram* (mixture) for the *soma*.
Thus have the gods been won over by Indra; now Maghavan, whose bounty is true, has moved forward with his mighty stride.
O Lord of Bay Steeds, O Mighty One, all these swift ones, self-glorious, sing praises unto you.

Indra has indeed established the gods; now Maghavan, the giver of true wealth, has moved forward with his power. All these deeds of yours, O Lord of Bay Horses, O Mighty One, the swift ones proclaim aloud as your own glory.
Then another Indra, having abandoned his state as Indra, speaks in the form of a seer:

"In this very manner," as described, "Indra, the god, has driven forth the gods and men. Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Therefore, offspring are driven forward; they are born facing backward" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.1.4).
Is this [done] by some other means? No;
he says it is by his own inherent power (*cyautnena*).
Of what nature is Indra?

The possessor of wealth (*maghavān*), the one whose bounty is true (*satyarādhāḥ*), that is, whose riches are real—now he speaks by way of direct address: O *harivaḥ*, possessor of the two bay steeds; O *śacīvaḥ*, possessor of power, that is, of action; O *svayaśaḥ*, possessor of self-dependent fame; O *indra*, possessor of wisdom—*tā tāni viśvā*, all those various deeds belonging to you, in which deeds the *turāsaḥ*, the swift priests, *abhi gṛṇanti*, praise aloud.
The eighth hymn, beginning with "pra vo mahe," consists of a collection of verses. The first two are *jagatī* meters;
the next two, beginning with "ke te naraḥ," are *abhisāriṇī* meters.
The first two [pādas] consist of ten syllables each, and the following two consist of twelve syllables; this is the *abhisāriṇī*.
As it has been said: "The *vairāja* and *jāgata* [pādas] constitute the *abhisāriṇī*" (Anuṣṭubh 9.4).
After that, there is one *triṣṭubh*.
Then follow two Jagatī verses; their deities are the same as before.
Thus it has been enumerated: “*Pra vo mahe*—seven [verses] beginning with two Jagatīs, ending with *ke ṛbhubhiḥ*, are *abhisāriṇī*s.”
In the Mahāvrata, this hymn is the locus for the *nivid* during the *niṣkevalya* recitation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘pra vo mahe mandamānāndhasaḥ’ is the locus for the *nivid*” (AiĀ 5.3.1).
Sing forth for the great Indra, who rejoices in the soma-juice, for him who belongs to all men and is the source of all existence—
he whose heroic might, great glory, and manly strength the two worlds, heaven and earth, revere.

Sing forth for your great one who rejoices in the soma-juice, for Viśvānara who is all-encompassing—Indra, whose victorious power is truly mighty, and whose fame and manly strength both heaven and earth revere.

O singer, [sing] for you [your own]. The plural number is used for the sake of honor. For the great *andhas*—the meaning is "for the soma-juice"—for him who rejoices (*mandamānāya*) in the soma, for the one who gladdens (*modamānāya*), for Viśvānara, the leader of all; the lengthening of the vowel is Vedic (based on *Pāṇini* 6.3.129: *nare saṃjñāyām*). For Viśvābhu, the nourisher of all—for the great Indra, sing forth! The root *arc* means "to praise"; utter it aloud! Of whom... me.
1. *ga-ta-bha-mu-dhṛ* | 2. *ga-madhurasaṃ*; *ta-bha-madhu madhuraṃ* | 3. *ta-bha-mu-tvam ity arthaḥ*; *bha1.4-tvarthaḥ*; *bhara-tvadarthaḥ* | 4. *ta1.2.3-bha-netre viśvābhuve*. (Rigveda 4.29)

The two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), honor and revere Indra’s fair-faced one, his well-compacted strength (*sahas*), his great majesty (*mahi śravas*), his food (*anna*), and his manly vigor (*nṛmṇa*) and happiness.
To that Indra, [the hymn] proceeds; such is the connection.
Thus has Indra, the lord of men, been praised by his friend as one worthy of song;
may he, for the sake of a man like me, take delight among all the yokes, in deeds that win the prize, O Lord of the Good, or against Vṛtra, or in the waters, O Hero.

He indeed, the heroic and powerful Indra, being praised and worthy of celebration, delights in the friendship of one like me—a man for men—in all tasks, in deeds for booty, O Lord of the Hundred, whether against Vṛtra or for the waters, O Hero.

He indeed is Indra, who—on account of friendship, that is, by reason of being a friend; who is *narya*, beneficial to men; who is *vinaḥ*, the lord of all; and who is *stutaḥ*, praised by all—or rather, the connection is "praised on account of friendship.
He is to be celebrated again and again (*carkṛtyaḥ*) for a man like me, a hero (*māvate nare*).
The meaning is "to be served. Now follows the discourse on direct perception (*pratyakṣavāda*).

O *satpate*, protector of the virtuous, O Indra, you—upon all *dhūḥ*s, that is, upon all burdens of duty to be borne, in deeds requiring vigor and deeds requiring strength, and with reference to the waters existing within the cloud during the battle against Vṛtra—O Hero, you are celebrated and praised.

Who are those men, O Indra, who strive for your refreshment and your wealth-bestowing favor? Who have urged you toward manly power and divine sovereignty? Who have impelled you toward the waters and toward the choice of the beautiful ones for heroic deeds?

Who are those men, O Indra, who for your refreshment, who for your benevolence that brings wealth, strive with vigor? Who have urged you toward divine power for the sake of booty? And who [have done so] for manly deeds in their own waters and in the fertile fields?
"O Indra, who are those men of yours?"—this is the question.
The intention is: "Those great ones must be known by me.
He states those who are to be questioned:

"O men, they are capable of [consuming] your poison for food"—this is the ellipsis. And those two go toward your *vsumnam* (bliss), which is *sukham* (happiness) belonging to you, and *vsadhanvyam* (wealthy), that is, possessed of riches; *iryakṣān* means "they go.
The root *iryakṣati* has the sense of motion.

Who are those great-souled ones who obtain this happiness and wealth of yours? Furthermore, for what purpose do they impel the oblation—such as Soma and other offerings—for *vāja*, meaning strength, on account of the slaying of those who belong to the Asuras (*asuryāya asurasaṃbandhane*)? Or rather, for what purpose do they impel the oblation for *pauṃsya*, meaning manly prowess, when the waters (*apsu*)—those waters required by themselves—and the fertile lands (*urvarāsu*) rich with all kinds of crops, serve as the instrumental causes? The phrase "they impel the oblation" is to be understood as continuing [from the previous clause].
The meaning is that such greatness, as described, is difficult to attain.
The verse beginning with "bhuvasvamindra" is the *yājyā* for the oblation to Mahendra in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "mahoṃ indro ya ojasā bhuvasvamindra brahmaṇā mahān" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.6).
It is also the *yājyā* for the eldest Indra among the oblations of the Devasū offerings.
“*Bhuvas tvam indra brahmaṇā mahān amīvāsa iḷayā*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.11); thus it is prescribed.
This very verse is the *sūktamukhīyā* for the *niṣkevalya* śastra on the *bhūnāmnyaikāha* day.
And it is prescribed: “The recitation has been stated [to be] by means of the Bṛhaspatisava: *śvaṃ bhuvaḥ pratimānaṃ pṛthivyā bhuvas tvam indra brahmaṇā mahān*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.5).
O Indra, through our prayer you have become great; you have become the one worthy of sacrifice among all and every person.
You have become the shaker of men in every battle, the most excellent counselor, O you who are seen by all people.

1. In *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, the word “*sukham*” does not exist; [in *mu*] it is “*dhanam*”. 2. In *ga*, [the reading is] “*jaṅgamāya*”; in *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, “*janāya*”. 3. In *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, “*carkṛtyaḥ*” is not present; [it is] “*kartavyaiḥ*”. 4. In *ta*, *bha*, and *bru*, [the reading is] “*oddhavyeṣu*”. 5. In *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, the word “*ke*” does not exist. 6. In *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *ke*, [the reading is] “*hinvire*”. 7. In *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, [the reading is] “*eteṣu*”; in *ta* (1, 2, 3) and *bha* (4, 8), [it is] “*etiṣu*”. 8. In *ga*, *ta* (1, 2), and *bha*, for *jyeṣṭhasya* it is exactly the same.

O Indra, you have become great through our prayer; you have become worthy of sacrifice among all people. You have become the light of men in every battle; you are the supreme counsel for all mankind. 4.
O Indra, you have become great through the powerful hymn composed by us;
you have become [great].
In the form *bhuvaḥ*, there is a prohibition of the *guṇa* substitution and the replacement with *uvaṅ* due to the *leṭ* suffix, according to the rule *bhūsuvostiṅi*.
Likewise, in all the *savanas* (soma-pressings), you became worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*), one to be honored in the rite.
Likewise, in every battle (*bhara*), you became the shaker (*dyotna*) of men—the leaders—of the enemies.
O Indra, observer of all (*viśvacarṣaṇi*), you have become the one to be addressed with hymns (*mantra*), and the eldest among all.
Now indeed, the people know the great protection of you, the superior one who loves sacrifice;
may you, the ageless, grow strong, and may you bring all these things to fulfillment for us.

Now indeed, O Sage, the people who perform the sacrifice have come to you for the sake of great protection; they have approached you when the Soma is pressed, O inspired one, to bestow both riches and treasures. May they attain the path of your favor through their mind, at the enjoyment of the pressed Soma juice. (7) O Sage, those who perform the sacred rite have come to you when the Soma is pressed, to receive both riches and treasures. May they attain the path of your favor through their mind, at the enjoyment of the pressed Soma juice. (7)

O wise sage, O Indra, those who have performed *brahman*—that is, the singers of hymns or preparers of oblations—who, having gathered together as a community (*sacā*) when the Soma has been pressed, attend upon you for the sake of giving (*dāvane*) both many riches (*vasūnām*) and that one wealth (*vasum*) which is worthy of being a dwelling; this is the remainder [of the verse].
Here, by the plural "riches" (*vasūnām*), the various means of worldly enjoyment are intended;
and by the singular ending, it should be understood that the wealth called heaven, which is worthy of being a dwelling, is intended.

Those performers, for the sake of obtaining "sumna," which is happiness or prosperity, have with their minds, O Jātavedas— O you whose wisdom is born— beheld all your bodies, that is, all your limbs, in many ways, as one God.

Who has seen me? Which god was it who beheld my forms in their many ways? Who am I, O Mitra and Varuṇa? They abide in Agni’s all-encompassing kindling-sticks that lead to the gods. Who? Me? Has seen? Which? That? God? Who? My? Bodies? In many ways? Beheld? Who? Am I? O Mitra and Varuṇa? They dwell? Of Agni? All? Kindling-sticks? Leading to the gods? 2.
This is the speech of Atri.
Having stated that "one god saw [it]," he asks: who (*kaḥ*) has seen (*mā*) me (*mām*)? Who has beheld me?

Which god, which one among them, has beheld my bodies—my forms existing in many ways and manifold manners? O Mitra and Varuṇa, Agni has said that all my kindled bodies, which are the means for the path of the gods (*devayānī*), have been seen. If they have indeed been seen, then where do they dwell, where do they reside? Thus Agni addresses Mitra and Varuṇa while standing before the gods.

We sought you, O Jātavedas, who had entered manifoldly into the waters and the plants, O Agni. Yama recognized you, O Agni of wondrous luster, shining forth as the ten-fingered one, O far-beaming one. We sought you, O Jātavedas, who had entered manifoldly into the waters and the plants, O Agni. Yama recognized you, O Agni of wondrous luster, shining forth as the ten-fingered one, O far-beaming one.
Thus questioned by Agni, the gods say to Agni:
"O Jātavedas, O Agni, we seek after you—
after you who have entered manifoldly into the waters and into the plants."
Having searched for such a place and found it unentered, the wise god perceived it—O Citrabhāno, O one of wonderful rays!
Where it was situated, he perceived—that is now told:
within the ten directions.
The "intermediate flower" (*antaruṣpa*) is the place of the house or dwelling, and that place consists of ten [units].
Having transcended such a place— which is exceedingly radiant and manifesting—
there are indeed ten hidden places of fire.
The three worlds beginning with earth, the deities named Abhivāta and others, water, herbs, trees, and the body of vital breath—these are the ten stations.

O Varuṇa, fearing the office of the *hotṛ*, I fled; let not the gods enjoin me to this task here. My bodies have entered into many forms; as Agni, I did not perceive this purpose. *Hotrāt*: from the office of the *hotṛ*. *Aham*: I. *Varuṇa*: O Varuṇa. *Bibhyat*: fearing. *Āyam*: I went away. *Na*: not. *It*: indeed. *Eva*: even. *Mā*: me. *Yunajan*: may they enjoin. *Attra*: here. *Devāḥ*: the gods. *Tasya*: of that. *Me*: my. *Tanvaḥ*: bodies. *Bahudhā*: in many ways. *Niviṣṭāḥ*: entered. *Etam*: this. *Artham*: purpose. *Na*: not. *Ciketa*: I perceived. *Aham*: I. *Agniḥ*: as Agni. || 4 ||
Having determined that "the gods have recognized me by means of this," he states the purpose of the *gahana* (the secret place):
"O God Varuṇa, I [come] from the *hotṛṣya*,
that is, from the *hotṛ* function consisting of the carrying of the oblation (*havis*)."
Therefore, being afraid, I have come here;
hence, let the gods not yoke me in this manner—as before—to this carrying of the oblation. Of that...

1. Let him fear such a one. Of me, who am thus afraid, my limbs have entered into the waters in many ways. Regarding this matter, this task of carrying [the oblation], Agni—I do not perceive it, I do not understand it, nor do I accept it.

Come here! Manu, seeking the gods and desiring sacrifice, has prepared [the oblation] and cast it into you, O Agni. Make the paths easy to traverse for those who go to the gods; being well-disposed, carry the offerings. 5 Come! Manu, seeker of the gods, desiring sacrifice, having prepared [it], has cast it into you, O Agni. Make the paths easy to traverse for those who go to the gods; being well-disposed, carry the offerings. 5
Thus addressed by Agni, the gods call upon Agni again:
"O Agni, come!
Manu—the human sacrificer, or the descendant of Manu, or the king—becomes one who desires the gods and yearns for sacrifice."
Therefore, come!
If it is asked what one should do to become desirous of sacrifice, it is said:
having marked [it], adorning it as nothing but a mass of splendor.
This is connected with what follows later:
"But you, adorning yourself, dwell even in the *tamas*, in the darkness that cannot be perceived by others;
O Agni, come and make the paths—the ways by which men go toward the gods—easy to traverse."
The root *kṛvī* is used in the sense of "harming" and "making. By the rule *dhinvikṛṇyor acca*, the suffix *u* is applied.
Having cleansed [us], they become excellent paths leading to the gods for the accomplishment of our sacrifice.
And, being well-disposed, carry our oblations; practice benevolence.

The elder brothers of Agni followed this purpose, just as a charioteer follows a path; out of fear of that, O Varuṇa, I have gone far away, like a wild ox fleeing from the swift arrow of a stronger man. 6. Of Agni. The elder. Brothers. This purpose. Like a charioteer. A path. Along. They turned toward. Therefore. Out of fear. O Varuṇa. I went far. Like a wild ox. From the swift. I fled from the stronger one. 6.
Another Agni speaks regarding the cause of his own flight:

"O gods, my 'brothers,' born before me—namely the three elder ones known as Bhūpati, Bhuvanapati, and Bhūtānām Pati—successively chose (*anvāvarītuḥ*) this purpose, namely the task of carrying the oblation (*havirvahanāya*). In this context, the form *anvāvarītuḥ* is derived from the root *vṛ* (to choose) in the yaṅ-luk (intensive) stem, in the aorist (*luṅ*), with the Vedic elision of the augment (*luk*).
It has been stated that "it is common in the Veda.
An example regarding concealment is:
*rathī gādhvānam*.
Just as a charioteer chooses his path, so it was with them;
those brothers were slain while standing there.
Out of fear of that death, O Varuṇa, we have fled to a distant place.
Furthermore, from the bowstring (*jyā*) of the archer who was secure (*kṣema*), [the chariot] trembled (*avije*) like a *gaura*—that is, like a *gaura* deer—as it fears or moves;
for the root *vij* means "to fear" or "to move.
It belongs to the *tud*-class and is marked with the *anudātta* accent.
His form is supreme among those of Laṅkā.

We grant you that ageless life, O Agni, so that being yoked, O Jātavedas, you may not be harmed; then, being well-disposed, O well-born one, you shall carry the portion of the oblation to the gods. 7. We grant; to you; life; ageless; which; O Agni; as; being yoked; O Jātavedas; may you not; be harmed; then; you shall carry; being well-disposed; the portion; to the gods; of the oblation; O well-born one. 7.
This is the speech of the gods:
"O Agni, that life (*āyuḥ*) which is life-providing and undecaying (*ajara*), free from old age—that we bestow upon you.

Endowed with that life, O Jātavedas, you who possess born wisdom, act so that you shall not perish, that you shall not die. (Note: Regarding the variants *āhata-vantaḥ* and *āśvata-vantaḥ*, the former is supported by manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 7, while the latter is supported by 4, 6, 8, b4, 5, and 8.)

We perform [the rite]. Now, carry [the oblation], carrying it with a well-disposed mind, bringing about favor while conveying that which is to be conveyed. He shows that very thing: the portion of the *havis* (oblation) belonging to the sacrificer; for whom? For the gods. O *sujāta*, O Agni of auspicious birth!
O gods, grant me the fore-sacrifices and the after-sacrifices in their entirety, a portion of the oblation rich in vigor;
grant me the fatness of the waters and the essence of the plants, and may there be long life from Agni.

O gods, grant me the fore-sacrifices and the after-sacrifices exclusively; grant me a portion of the oblation rich in nourishment, as well as the fatness of the waters and the essence of the plants. May there be long life for Agni! 8.
Having stated that these oblations are to be given by this [priest] on the fire that carries the sacrificial offerings, he declares:

"O gods, give me—grant to me—the *prayājas*, those portions of the offering named thus which are to be sacrificed at the beginning of the principal rite; likewise, the *anuyājas*, those named thus which are to be sacrificed after the principal rite; give them exclusively and not shared with others. Furthermore, give me a portion of the entire offering, such as the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa*, called the *sviṣṭakṛt*, which is full of strength (*ūrjasvant*) and enriched by the subsequent sprinkling of clarified butter."
Alternatively, it should be construed as: "Give me the vigorous portion of the oblation known as the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings.

Furthermore, give me *ghṛta* (clarified butter)—the essence of the waters or produced from them—which serves as the means for the *ājyabhāga* and other rites; and give me *puruṣa*, which is produced from plants (*oṣadhīnām*). Moreover, let there be long life for me.

The meaning is: "May there be no fear of being killed by the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call. To illustrate this with an ancient legend (*itihāsa*), the *Kaupītaki Brāhmaṇa* states: "Therefore they say: 'The *prayāja*s belong to Agni; the *anuyāja*s belong to Agni; the clarified butter belongs to Agni; the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) belongs to Agni. And the *Brāhmaṇa* says: "The fires are indeed the heirs to the body," and also: "For whom the human oblation is most dear."
May the fore-offerings and the after-offerings be yours alone; may they be portions of the oblation rich in nourishment.
O Agni, let this sacrifice be yours; let the four quarters bow down before you.

Let the fore-offerings and the after-offerings be yours alone; let the portions of the oblation be full of vigor. O Agni, let this entire sacrifice be yours; let the four quarters bow down before you. 9.
Thus addressed by Agni, the gods replied:
"O Agni, let the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s be yours alone, your exclusive portions of the oblation, full of vigor and strength.
O Agni, let this entire sacrifice also be yours."
Likewise, let the four principal directions—the preeminent quarters—bow down to you;
therefore, come, [to receive] the oblation—this is the ellipsis.
The tenth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “viśve devāḥ śāsatana,” belongs to Saucīka; it is addressed to Agni and has the Viśvedevas as its deities.
The application of this hymn has already been explained. It is employed for the silent recitation (japa) that occurs prior to the *sugādāpana* rite.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O All-Gods, instruct me so that I may here become a successful invoker and sit down as the most excellent sacrificer" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.4).
O All-Gods, instruct me so that, having been chosen as the Hotṛ priest and having sat down here, I may think upon what is to be done;
tell me clearly my portion, how it is for you, and by what means I may carry the oblation to you, O Pr̥thās.

O All-Gods, instruct me how, having been chosen as the Hotar-priest here, I may meditate; and having sat down, tell me my allotted portion, how I may bring to you the oblation with that which Pṛthā [the Earth] provides. || 1 ||
1. *ta-bha-kurvan*; 2. *ga-tān*; *ta* 1.2.3.4.5.8-*bha* 1.4.6-*vāti*; *ta* 6-*bha* 2.4.8-*cāti*; *mu-cāni*; 3. *bha* 1.2.7-*prayājākhyaṃ*.
4. [The hymn] beginning with "ta1.2.3.4.5.7.8-ma-evamamibhiḥ"—this hymn is addressed to Agni Kṛṣṇa. O Viśve Devas, you must instruct me; grant me permission.
Just as I have been chosen here at this sacrifice as the Hotṛ of the gods—chosen for the office of Hotṛ—I shall praise you.
