Since I praise you after having sat down, therefore declare my portion;
tell me my share, just as you have assigned your own portions. Tell me that portion.
And by whichever path you say, "I shall carry the oblation," I perform the act of carrying.
I have sat down as the Hotṛ, the most skilled in sacrifice; all the gods and the Maruts impel me.
Day after day, O Aśvins, the office of Adhvaryu belongs to you; the Brahman priest kindles the fire for you, and this is your oblation.

I, the Hotṛ, have sat down, the most skilled in sacrifice. All the gods, the Maruts, impel me. Day after day, O Aśvins, the office of the Adhvaryu is yours; the Brahman is present with the fuel; that is your oblation. 2.
The most excellent sacrificer, the best of those who sacrifice; being the Hotṛ priest, I have sat down—seated upon my seat.
All the Vyāsas [behold] him as he is seated there.
The Maruts, the gods, impel [the fire] to carry the oblation.
O Aśvins, your *ādhvaryava*—that which is to be performed day after day—is the remainder [of the sense];
the meaning is that your office as *adhvaryu*s must be authorized by you.
May he become Brahmā. Who?
The moon, fully kindled with fuel.
Let the moon be Brahmā.
Furthermore, what is "sa"? It means "he."

And that moon, being kindled and fully ignited, becomes for you two an oblation (*āhuti*) intended for your sacrifice—that is, an offering to be made for the sake of the *adhvaryu*-ritual performed by you two; this is in the sense of what is destined to be.
For the moon, consisting of Soma, is indeed offered as an oblation.
As the *Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa* states, beginning with "This is indeed King Soma," and concluding with "that becomes both."

Then the Atharvans spoke thus: "That oblation which is to be offered according to the procedure of the Adhvaryu—may it be for you both; may it belong to you two. This is an elaboration of the phrase "the office of the Adhvaryu belongs to you."
Who indeed is this Hotṛ of Yama? To whom do the gods offer [oblations] when they assemble?
Day by day he is born, month by month; thus have the gods established him as the bearer of oblations.

This one—what is he? He is the Hotṛ. What indeed? *Ūm*. He belongs to Yama. Whom does he honor? Him whom the gods anoint day by day; he is born month after month. Then the gods established him as the bearer of oblations. || 3 ||
Who is this Hotṛ? What is he?
Of what nature is he?
What is its function? This is the meaning. The answer to that is stated: "Of which death one is afraid"—this is the remainder [of the sentence].
He carries some oblation;
or rather, he is the sacrificer (yama), so called because he restrains the entire assembly of officiating priests.
He carries some oblation belonging to him toward the gods.
That which they assemble, that which the gods obtain as an oblation;
furthermore, Agni is born— that is, he manifests— day after day for the sake of the *agnihotra*,
and likewise month after month for the sake of the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*).
These two periods of time are indicative of others, such as the fortnight, the four-month period, the full moon, and the year.
Others, however, say:
"Day by day he is born in the form of the sun, and month by month in the form of the moon."
Then the gods established that Agni as the carrier of oblations and the bearer of their offerings;
thus Agni spoke of himself by his own accord.

1. *ga*, *ta*, and *bha* do not have "tathā". 2. *ta1.2.7*, *mu*: aśvināśvinau; *ga1*, *bha6*: soma; *ga4*, *ta1.2.3.7*, *mu*: sāmaṃ; *sā sa soma*. 3. *ta1.2.3.6.7.8*, *bha1.2.6.8*: "vām" does not exist. 4. *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, *mu*: mṛteḥ. 5. *ga*, *ta4.5*, *bha4*: "hotrādyartha". 6. *ga*, *ta4.5*, *bha4*: "yajñārtha". 7. *ta1.2.3.7*, *bha*: "aharahaḥ" does not exist. 8. *ta*, *bha*: "devā" does not exist.

The gods have established me as the bearer of oblations, though I was cast away and wandering through many hardships. May Agni, the wise one, arrange our sacrifice—fivefold in its course, threefold in its structure, and seven-threaded in its extension. māṃ devā dadhire havyavāhamapa'mluktam bahu kṛcchrā carantam | agnirvidvān yajñaṃ naḥ kalpayāti pañcayāmaṃ trivṛtaṃ saptatantum || 4 || Me the gods have established as the carrier of the sacrificial offering, who had been cast off and was moving through many difficulties. Agni, the knower, shall fashion for us the sacrifice: that which has five paths, is threefold, and possesses seven threads.
The gods have established me, Agni, as the carrier of oblations—the bearer of the sacrificial offerings.
Of what sort am I?
One who has come after having departed; one who moves through many difficult places, traversing numerous hardships.
By what intention do they maintain [this]?
It is said: this Agni, being wise and knowing all, shall arrange—indeed, he does arrange—for us our sacrifice.
What kind of sacrifice?

It has five watches and five divisions; for the sacrifice is fivefold. It is threefold by way of the distinction between the three pressings (*savana*); it has seven threads, being expanded by the seven praises consisting of the *chandas* meters.

I shall worship you for immortality and for heroic strength, O gods, so that I may provide you with wide space. May I place the thunderbolt of Indra within my arms, and thus may he conquer all these hostile armies. 5. I shall worship you for immortality and for heroic strength, O gods, so that I may provide you with wide space. May I place the thunderbolt of Indra within my arms, and thus may he conquer all these hostile armies. 5.
O gods, I entreat you—
what? For immortality, which is indestructibility, and for excellent heroic sons.

O gods, so that I may perform for you—*vaḥ*—your service (*varivaḥ*) or wealth in the form of oblations (*havīrūpaṃ dhanaṃ*), for that purpose; furthermore, I shall place the thunderbolt (*vajram*) within the two arms (*bāhvoḥ*) of Indra;
that is, it should be grasped.
In the absence of Agni’s role as Hotṛ-priest, Indra would lack the Soma; being thus weakened, his wielding of the thunderbolt (*vajra*) would not be possible.
Therefore, the meaning is that he seizes the thunderbolt by performing that [role].
This being so, he conquers—indeed, he conquers—all these *viśvāḥ pratanāḥ*, all the enemy armies.
Or may it be victorious!

Three hundred and three thousand gods, and thirty-nine, have worshipped Agni. They sprinkled him with clarified butter, they spread the sacrificial grass for him, and then they established him as the Hotṛ priest. 6. Three hundred. Three. Thousand. Agni. Thirty. And. Gods. Nine. And. Worshipped. Sprinkled. With clarified butter. Spread. The sacrificial grass. For him. Then. Indeed. Hotṛ priest. Down. Established. 6.

Three hundred and three thousand, and thirty-nine—deities of this number worshipped me, Agni; they attended upon me. The manner of their attendance is described: with clarified butter, dripping ghee, they sprinkled and moistened me.
For this Agni, for me, they have strewn the sacrificial grass (*barhis*);
immediately after its spreading, they have seated the invoker (*hotṛ*) in his appointed place.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses, begins with "yamaicchāma.
Since these are the words of the gods, the gods themselves are the seers (ṛṣis). Regarding the verse beginning with "tadya," Saucīka Abhi is the seer for the *kṛcchra* rite.
The verses beginning with "tantuṃ tanvan" are Jagatīs, excluding the eighth;
the eighth verse and the remaining ones are Triṣṭubhs.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "The verses beginning with 'tantuṃ' are Jagatīs, excluding the eighth."
The rest has been stated.
The application of the hymns (*sūkta*) is concluded.
1. *ga-ta-bha-mu-paricāra*; bha4 *paricaraṇa*.

We sought him with our mind; he has come here, the knower of the sacrifice, the wise one who understands its every limb. May he, the most excellent sacrificer, worship for us among the gods, for he sits as the innermost one, even before us. We sought him with our mind; he has come here, the knower of the sacrifice, the wise one who understands its every limb. May he, the most excellent sacrificer, worship for us among the gods, for he sits as the innermost one, even before us. (1)
"We sought Agni; we searched for him with our mind, meaning with the intention that 'may he bring the great oblation,' that is, with the thought that he should convey the offering.
This very Agni has come;
what kind of Agni is he?
Knowing the sacrifice of the sacrifice, and likewise understanding the joints of the joints that are to be joined together, he, being observant, approaches them.

That Agni, the most excellent sacrificer (*yajīyān*), let him sacrifice for us in the assembly of the gods (*devatātā*)—that is, in the sacrifice. He has indeed sat down; the ellipsis is "he has sat down upon the altar-ground (*vedyām*)."
Being what?
Moving among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the deities who are to be worshipped, he is "prior to us," meaning existing before us and before the gods;
for it is after Agni has been kindled that the gods are subsequently invoked.

At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, this verse beginning with "arādhi" is to be muttered; the Sūtra has cited it as follows: arā̭dhi hotā̭ ni॒ṣadā̭ yajī̭yān abhi prayā̭ṃsi su॒dhitā̭ni hi॒ kratuḥ | yajāma̭he ya॒jñiyā̭n ha॒nta de॒vān ī̭ḻāmahe ī̭ḍyān ā॒jyena̭ || 2 || The Hotṛ-priest has succeeded through his sitting [in office]; he is the most excellent sacrificer. Toward the well-placed sacrificial offerings, let him fulfill his purpose. Let us sacrifice to the gods worthy of sacrifice; come, let us praise with clarified butter those who are worthy of praise. || 2 ||
This Agni, the Hotṛ—the performer of the oblation—who is most excellent as both sacrificer and object of sacrifice, has attained success through his seating upon the sacrificial altar;
that is to say, he has become fit for the offerings.
Being thus, he moves toward and beholds from all sides the well-placed *prayāṃsi*—the foods such as the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa*.
The word *hi* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).

"With what understanding?"—the remainder [of the thought] is: "With the understanding: 'Come, let us quickly worship with clarified butter (*ājya*) the gods worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*), those who are to be worshipped and who partake of the oblations; likewise, let us praise with hymns the gods worthy of praise (*īḍya*), those who partake of eulogies.'"

When the word "dead" is uttered for a sacrificer while he is still living, the *Surabhimatī* sacrifice must be performed for him. "Sādhvīmakad devavīti no adya" is the *yajyā* verse used therein. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "He sat down as one more powerful than the Agnihotra; Sādhvīmakad devavīti no adya" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.13). Sādhvīmakad devavīti no adya | yajñasya jihvām avidaṃ guhām | sa āyur āgāt surabhir vasāno bhadrāmakad devahūtiṃ no adya || 3 || Today you have made our divine invocation auspicious. I have found the tongue of the sacrifice hidden in the secret place. He has come, fragrant and clothed in life-force. Today you have made our divine invocation auspicious. || 3 ||

This Agni has today made our sacrifice successful—that is, he has made it excellent, characterized by the arrival of the gods (*devavīti*) or endowed with the consumption of the oblation for the gods.
And we have found, that is, obtained, the tongue of the sacrifice, which is most secret and hidden;
for Agni is indeed the tongue of the sacrifice, and thus he is figuratively called the "tongue" because he is the means by which the gods drink.
Such a fire is fragrant, possessing a sweet scent, and enveloping.
1. "We worship with *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, *su*, and *yajāmahe*.
Vāyu, clothing himself—i.e., covering himself—in the long life bestowed by the gods, has come (*āgāt*).
And having come, he has made our sacrifice—which possesses an invocation of the gods (*devahūti*) for our sake—auspicious (*bhadrāmakaḥ*), that is, he has rendered it beautiful; and so now.
At the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, this verse beginning with "tad ya vācaḥ" is to be muttered by the Hotṛ priest when commissioned for the Sāmidhenī verses;
it is also to be muttered prior to the Sugādāpana.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The verse 'tad ya vācaḥ prathamam masīya' is completed [as the mantra]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.2).
Of those words, may I first meditate upon that by which we gods may overcome the Asuras.
O eaters of strength, worthy of sacrifice, you five peoples, graciously accept my oblation!
Today may I first understand that speech by which we gods may overcome the Asuras—both we who eat strength and those worthy of sacrifice; O five tribes, take pleasure in my office as Hotṛ. 4.
This has been stated as the subsequent statement in this very context;
how then is it now the first? This is its primary name.
May I utter, may I utter that which is the foremost of speech, the word, the expression of speech.
By means of that word, may we—the gods and I—overcome, may we prevail over the Vasus.
What is that first word? It is said: [the syllable] *Om*.

"O eaters of strength (*vūrjādaḥ*), that is, O consumers of food (*annādaḥ*), and furthermore, O you five classes of beings (*pañca janāḥ*)—gods, humans, and so forth—who are worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiyāsaḥ*), may you enjoy (*juṣadhvam*) and partake of my oblation (*hotram*).
The intention here is that when this is thus spoken, all the gods take their seats.
In this regard, the *Nirukta* passage beginning with "That which of speech... (*tad ya vācaḥ*, Nirukta 3.8) should be consulted.
May five classes of beings enjoy my oblation—those born of the cow and those who are worthy of sacrifice.
May the Earth protect us from earthly distress, and may the intermediate space protect us from celestial distress.

May five persons enjoy my office as Hotṛ: those born of the cow and those who are worthy of sacrifice. May the Earth protect us from earthly distress; may the Atmosphere protect us from celestial distress. ||5||
May the five classes of beings, beginning with the gods, enjoy—that is, attend to—my *hotra*, my invocation;
and furthermore, those born of the earth (*gojātāḥ*).
Or else: [the text continues...]

By the word "cow" (go), its products such as milk and so forth are meant; the meaning is that they have appeared for the purpose of the sacrificial oblation (havis). Those which are of such a nature [are referred to].
Moreover, O you who are worthy of sacrifice (*vyajñiyāsaḥ*), those who are fit for the sacrifice (*yajñārhāḥ*), may you enjoy my *hotra* (sacrificial offering).
Furthermore, may the Earth (*pṛthivī*), the deity of the earth, protect us (*naḥ*) from earthly (*pārthivāt*) distress (*vaṃhasaḥ*), that is, from sin;
likewise, may the intermediate space (*antarikṣam*), the deity of the atmosphere, protect us from celestial and atmospheric distress—that is, from sin.
Starting from the *gārhapatya* fire, he spreads the sacrificial grass continuously toward the *āhavanīya* and other fires with the verse beginning, “The thread” (*tantum*).

This is stated in the Sūtra: “Without shaking [the bundle], spreading it continuously, he goes from the *gārhapatya* to the *āhavanīya* with his left hand, saying: ‘Spreading the thread straight, follow the light’” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 1.11).
Furthermore, during the *agnihotra* oblation, this same continuous stream must be poured out.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “One should carry an unbroken stream of water from the Gārhapatya fire, saying: ‘Stretching the thread, follow quickly toward the light’” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.2).
If one passes through the intermediate space [without pouring], one should fill the area between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires with water and ashes.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “One should connect the space between the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya fires with a line of ashes and a line of water” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.10).
This is the *dhāyyā* verse for the *ābhimāra* [sacrifice].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*tantuṃ tanvan... iheva na indro maghavā virapśī*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).
1. For the gods who offer oblations (ga-ta1.2.8-bha6), for the gods who summon [the sacrifice] (bha7). 2. As before (ga4). 3. The gods worthy of sacrifice (ga-ta-bha4. mu).
4. May he accept and enjoy the invocation and the call of the *ta3-bha8-hotṛ*.
5. From the presence of *ga-ta4.5-bha4*; according to *ta1.2.6.7.8-bha1.6.7-mu*, from the presence of evil.
Stretching out the thread, follow the radiance of the luminous mid-region; protect with your wisdom those things fashioned by the intellect.
Weave it without unevenness; O reciter, be mindful and bring forth the divine race.

Stretching out the thread, follow the radiance of the mid-air; guard the luminous paths fashioned by wisdom. Weave the waters of the singers without flaw; become Manu and bring forth the divine race. 6.
O Agni, spreading out—that is, extending—the thread of the sacrifice, follow along the radiance of the world whose nature is protection, that is, the sun;
the meaning is: enter the solar orb by means of your rays. Furthermore, [follow] the paths of the journey of the luminous, radiant sacrifice.
Alternatively, protect— that is, guard— the paths of the gods, which are the ways to heaven characterized by light and radiance;
of what kind are these paths?
[He consumes] those [oblations] performed and accomplished through intellect and ritual action.
Furthermore, that Agni [drinks] the *apah*— that is, the ritual actions— of the *joguvān*, the praisers.
The object (*karman*) is that which is pervaded by the action; even other gods, desiring to go to the sacrifice, speak to one another in a gentle manner.
The river named Amanvatī flows—that is, it moves.
The root *ṛ* means "to go" or "to seek.
Rise up (*usiṣṭa*) to cross over that [river] with sacrificial intent;
having done so, cross over (*pratarata*), that is, traverse that river.
"O friends"—this is an address to the gods, meaning "those who have become friends to the sacrificer.
"In this [place]," that is, in this river, "we leave behind," that is, we abandon. What is it that is abandoned? It is said: [the following].
"Those who are unkind"— *śeva* is a name for happiness; "those who have become unhappy," meaning those who exist depending upon us— we abandon them.
Having done so, may we cross over toward the attainment of auspicious, pleasure-bestowing foods and sacrificial offerings.
Tvaṣṭṛ, the most excellent guardian of the possessors of inspired knowledge, bearing the most auspicious vessels for the drinking of the gods,
has surely sharpened his axe of fine steel, wherewith Vṛṣan Etaśa, the Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati), shall strike.

They placed the embryo of your great [sacrificial] cow within the skin of the dead cow— that is, they held some cow belonging to the dead cow— just as it is said: "The one who emerges led forth the cow by means of his insights" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.161.7).
Likewise, when she had died while sitting, they placed the calf at her mouth;
by what means? By the secret mind that longs for the divine wealth, and also by the tongue—this description is primarily intended to convey similarity.
The meaning is "by being as long as a tongue.
Alternatively,
the connection is "a woman endowed with a tongue."

That host of Ṛbhus, who are devoted to service and characterized by a disposition toward sharing, always—through all their vehicles and at all times—accepts with a gracious mind the appropriate and fitting hymns of praise.
And that host effects victory over enemies according to their desire, acting just like those who effect victory over enemies.

The hymn beginning with “tāṃ su te,” consisting of six verses, is the twelfth hymn; it is the seerly composition of Bṛhaduktha of the Vāmadeva lineage, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and addressed to Indra.

Thus it has been enumerated: “tāṃ su [te], six verses; Bṛhaduktha, of the Vāmadeva family. This hymn is used on the second Chandoma day of the Daśarātra sacrifice characterized by the *samūḷaha* arrangement.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Apūrvyā purutamāni tāṃ su te kīrtiṃ tvaṃ mahāṃ indra*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).
This hymn is recited at the Niṣkevalya of the Mahāvrata.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Tāṃ su te kīrtiṃ maghavanmahitvā bhūya idvāvṛdhe vīryāya*” (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.1.6).

That fame of yours, O Maghavan, through your greatness—when the two worlds, terrified, fled away, you protected the gods and extended the power of the Dāsa; for you, O Indra, bestowed strength upon this very progeny.

That fame of yours, O Maghavan, is great indeed through your majesty, since when the two worlds, Rodasī, were terrified, you protected the gods and overpowered the Dāsa with your might—when you, O Indra, exerted yourself for the sake of this very progeny. 1.

O Indra, Maghavan, possessor of wealth—your fame, which has arrived through your greatness (*mahitvā*), I proclaim well; this is the sense of the ellipsis. Furthermore, when both *rodasī* (Heaven and Earth) were terrified and fled from you upon encountering fear caused by the Asuras, then you protected the gods.
Likewise, you utterly destroyed the Dāsa, the Asura who causes the decay of the gods.

The meaning is: "Having slain the Asuras by protecting the gods, you removed the fear from heaven and earth; whatever strength you bestowed—that is, granted—to this single progeny, which is the form of the sacrificer, that very fame I proclaim."

Whatever you performed while increasing in body, O Indra, proclaiming your powers among the people—that was but a mere illusion of yours; for as for those battles of which they speak, did you not already know your enemy long ago?

When you, O Indra, grew strong in body and proclaimed your powers among the people, that was merely a deception of yours—those battles of which they speak. For did you not find your enemy long ago? || 2 ||

O Indra, having grown great— whether by your own body, by your physical form, or by your hymn of praise— increasing among living beings and proclaiming your powers, such as the slaying of Vṛtra and other such feats, that which you have done in moving about— that movement of yours— is merely *māyā*, it is indeed a creative illusion. Furthermore, those battles concerning enemies of which they speak...

1. *ga* and *ta*: *temī marutaḥ*; 2. *ga* and *ta*: *bhara- ‘apīcyena’ is not present*; 3. *ta*, *bha*, 4, 5, 8: *yadvā api ca*; 4. *ta*, 1, 3, 7: *mu-sarvair vyahaḥsu*; 5. *ta*, 1, 2, 3, 7: *sumanāḥ samamānā*; 6. *ga* and *ta*, 4, 5: *rakṣety abūtām*; *ta*, 1, 2, 3, 8: *bhara*, 4, 6, 8: *adety abūtām*; 7. *ta*, 1, 2, 3, 7: *mu-bhāram*; 8. *ta*, 1, 2, 7: *bha-tad balam*; *ta*, 3: *tad vanam*; 9. *ta*, *mu*: *vṛttyarthaḥ*.

The seers who know the past—those too are merely illusion. Why? He says: "Now," that is, at present, you do not find a foe to slay; nor do you obtain one. Furthermore, he says that it is not the case that you might say, "In the past, I have slain him. To the question, "Is it not so? the meaning is: "Did you not find a foe in the past? The sense is: "That too is not so."
Who indeed among those of great power, even the seers of old, have reached the limit of this [universe],
since you, together with your own body, brought forth both mother and father?
O Ke! Om! Indeed, even the ancient seers did not reach the limit of your entire greatness, since you brought forth both mother and father together from your own body. 3.
O Indra, those limits and boundaries of your entire greatness—of all your majesty—exist; you have established them all.
Since this is so, therefore, O Vasu, O possessor of wealth, O Indra, do not harm my desire, that which is longed for by me; protect it as one who bestows gifts.
*Vai* is a filler; *vardhaya* (increase) is the ellipsis. O Vaindra, you are the one who brings (*vadhama-jñātā*) and causes [us] to attain the desired wealth.
Likewise, O Indra, you are indeed a speaker of truth.
He who from half [of the world] produced light within the light, who with honey joined together honey—
he, the beloved and powerful one, has been proclaimed for Indra as a sublime hymn by Bṛhaduktha, a maker of sacred prayer.

He who from the half [of the world], within the light, created the light; he who with honey joined together the honey, the beloved, the nourishing [soma] for Indra—this great hymn has been spoken by the one who performs the sacred formulation (brahman) from the Bṛhaduktha. 6.
Indra, while the light of the *vajra*—the radiance of the Ādityas and other luminaries—was shining, blew that *vajra*-light;
that is to say, he sustained that splendor which exists in the Ādityas and others as being produced by Indra.
Furthermore, with sweet nectar (*madhu*), he released—that is, he joined together—the sweet substances such as Soma and the like.
Alternatively:
by "honey" (madhu). Here, by the word "honey," the sun, who is to be served by all, is denoted.
Together with him, they mixed waters with honey.

Now, for that Indra, a pleasing, joy-inducing, and strengthening hymn—capable of crushing enemies because it withers them, a hymn worthy of reflection—was uttered by the mantra-composer, the creator of sacred speech, from the one named Vṛhaduktha, who was endowed with abundant recitations. It was proclaimed.
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "dūre tat," has the same seer and other details as the preceding one.
It is introduced by the word "dūre."
The application of the hymn has been explained.
Far away is that secret; the two terrified ones fled far off from the one who bestows vital strength.
O Maghavan, you raised up the earth and the heavens with your splendor, and you seized the sons of your brother.

Far away is that secret name which was hidden from you, when the two worlds, trembling in fear, fled for the sake of their own protection. Yet, in the encounter, you propped up the earth and the sky; O Maghavan, you shone forth while gazing upon the sons of your brother.

By this [verse], the first name among those called "the four sunless ones" is praised. O Indra, that body (*vatat*) of yours, which is to be described—namely, the body (*vanāma*) common to all—is hidden (*vaguhya*), kept secret and unrevealed; it exists far away (*vadūre*), at a great distance from men who turn their faces away (*vaparācaiḥ*). This is the sense.
When you blew forth, the two worlds, heaven and earth, being terrified, trembled and became agitated.
For what purpose?
For the sake of providing a storehouse of food for the one who knows the sacrifice.
The meaning is: "the means for this world.
At that time, by means of that body, in the encounter.
This is a synonym for "near. Just here, near at hand, you have propped up the earth and the sky so that they remain separated from one another.
What were you doing?
O Vamagha, O Indra, O Lord of the thunderbolt, illuminating the sons of Parjanya—who stand in the place of sons and consist of water—shine forth with your lightning-spears.
The great, secret, and much-desired one whom all beings have brought forth— that anciently born light which is his beloved— into it the five beloved ones have entered together.
1. [The syllable] *ta* is conditioned by *bha*.
2. [The syllable] *ga* is conditioned by the vowel *u* and the consonant *ra*.
3. [The syllable] *ta* is conditioned by *bha*, *mu*, and the word *priyajanakaṃ*.
4. In the *Ga* and *Ta* manuscripts, the word "bha-’asūryāṇi" does not exist.
5. In the *Ga*, *Ta1.2.3*, and *Mu* manuscripts, it reads "dīpayan" (illuminating) [instead of "bhūvan"], which refers to Indra in the form of lightning;
for the *Vājasaneyaka* states: "The god Indra is lightning" (*Ta1.2.7*; *Mu*: "Indra in the form of lightning").
Or rather, he speaks of him in the form of Parjanya.
At that time, Vāyu is his brother; Indra’s brother must be honored.

That great, secret name is widely sought after, by which all that has been and all that is to be is touched. It is the anciently born light, which his beloved ones—the five tribes—have entered together as their dear one. 2.

O Indra, that secret (*guhya*)—meaning worthy of being guarded and unknown by others—of yours, which touches many (*puruspṛk*), meaning desirable by many who seek rain, and which is your *nāma* (body) consisting of space (*ākāśātmaka*), is *mahat*, exceedingly expanded; by means of which name you generated (*janayaḥ*) both what has been (*bhūta*) and what is to be (*bhavya*).
The word "by which" (*yena*) is repeated for the sake of connecting both the past and the future.
For from the nature of the Supreme Lord, which consists of space, the world consisting of the past and the future is produced.
This is according to the Vedic scripture: "From space, wind [arose]" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.1).

Furthermore, that which is "prātṇam" (ancient), "purāṇam" (primeval), belonging to former times, the "jyotiḥ" (light)—whether called the shining Sun or the Waters—which is the "priyam" (beloved) reality of this Indra, was born;
this very thing is the "mahāyāḥ" (greatness) of the "nava" (new), the "mahaḥ" (great), the exceedingly exalted, the "ekam" (one), the unique and singular "vasutvam" (wealth or preeminent power).
The meaning is: "It was accomplished by your power.
Regarding the *mahāyati* [chant] in the *niṣkevalya*, there is this verse: "vidhuṃ dadrāṇam. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ā yāhy arvāṅ upa vandhureṣṭhā vidhuṃ dadrāṇam" (Ai. Ā. 5.3.1).
The gray-haired one has swallowed the young moon as it fled in the assembly of many;
behold the poetic power of the god through his greatness! He who was here yesterday has died today.
The gray-haired one has swallowed the youth who was fleeing in the assembly of many. Behold the poetic wisdom of the god through his greatness! He died today; he breathed his last yesterday. 5.
By this verse, Indra, who is of the nature of time, is praised.

*Vidhum* means the creator (*vidhātāram*) of everything, the maker (*kartāram*) of all that is expanded (*vyuddha*). The root *dadhāti* preceded by the prefix *vi-* is used in the sense of "to do" (*karoti*).
Likewise, in the *Vṛtrasaṃhāna*:
"Breathing" (*ānanam*) means the act of living.

By Indra’s command, old age (*jarā*) has swallowed—that is, devoured—the man who possesses such power, who is endowed with perfect breath (*ānana*), and who causes many enemies to flee (*drāvaka*) in battle.
O people, behold the poetic power—the capacity endowed with greatness—of the god Indra, who is Time, possessing both the characteristics already described and those yet to be told.
Thus, one who has reached old age dies today;
yet that same person performs his activities perfectly tomorrow.
The meaning is that it manifests in another future birth.
Thus, having explained it in this way, the four names of the bodies have been stated.
By his own power, the mighty one is powerful, ruddy, fair-winged; he who is great, the hero, the loud-shouting, the unassailable.
Whatever he intends is indeed true and not in vain; he is the winner and giver of desirable wealth.

By his own power: the powerful one; the ruddy one; the fair-winged one; he who has come from the great; the hero; ancient; peerless; that which he has perceived is indeed truth, not in vain; he is the winner of desirable wealth and the giver. 6.
By his own power; "śata" indeed means power. By his own power, that is, by his strength, he is "śāka," meaning capable.
Regarding the root *śaklṛ* in the sense of "capacity":
the meaning is that he is capable of performing everything by his own power alone;
for Indra has no need for dependence on any other assistance, precisely because of his status as Indra.
Varuṇa is reddish-brown in color.
Suparṇa is a certain bird with beautiful feathers; "goes" is to be supplied as the verb.
Because of the hearing of the prefix (*upa-*), the appropriate action is to be supplied.
*Vyaḥ*: pervasive; *vmahaḥ*: great; *mahān*: the Great One; *vśūraḥ*: the hero; *vikrāntaḥ*: the valiant; *sanāt*: from of old; *purāṇaḥ*: the ancient; *vanīḷaḥ*:
without a nest (*anīḷaḥ*), one who makes no nest—that is, Indra never at any time makes a dwelling-place in a sacrifice.
Thus, he speaks of Indra by means of the metaphor of the *suparṇa* (the well-winged bird).

That lord of birds (*pakṣīndraḥ*) perceives—that is, he knows—what ought to be done; he considers it rightly, and it does not become *mogham*, that is, futile. He wins—meaning he conquers—from his enemies the desirable (*spārham*) wealth (*vasu*), and moreover, he bestows it upon his worshippers (*stotṛbhyaḥ*).
[In this construction,] the prohibition of the genitive case applies according to the rule beginning with *na lokāvyaya*.
Through these [powers] he bestowed manly strengths and virile powers, by which the wielder of the thunderbolt protected the slaying of Vṛtra;
those gods who were born before the deed was performed, through the greatness of the rite being enacted.

Through these [deeds] he bestowed manly powers and virile strengths, by which the wielder of the thunderbolt grew mighty for the slaying of Vṛtra. And those gods who were born great during the performance of the sacred rite, even before the rite was completed—they too were brought forth. 7.
1. *bha*-vidadhāti; 2. *ga-bha*—‘*jarā*’ is not present; 3. *ta-bha-mu*—‘*śaklṛ śaktau*’ is not present; 4. *ga-ta-bha*—‘*uta*’ is not present; 5. *ga-ta-bha-mu*—‘*api ca*’.

Indra, together with these Maruts, takes up (*ādade*)—that is, he seizes—the *vṛṣṇiyāni*, i.e., the virile, and the *pauṃsyāni*, i.e., the manly powers, by means of which Maruts he is accompanied for the slaying of Vṛtra.
Vṛtra is evil because he obstructs the rain that benefits living beings;
"for his slaughter" means for the sake of pacifying the afflictions of human beings.
For that purpose, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), Indra, the possessor of the *vajra*, rains (*aukṣat* = *varṣati*).

And those great gods who arise for the sake of assisting in the deed characterized by the bestowing of rain—which is being performed by the great Indra—arise spontaneously toward the "deed of truth" (*ṛtakarma*), namely the act of bestowing rain; thus the syntactical connection is: "by these [gods], he (Indra) gives."
Performing deeds with his companion, possessing all vigor, slayer of the ill-spoken, all-seeing, and swift-conquering;
having drunk of the Soma and increased from heaven, the hero has driven away the sunless ones in battle.

Joining with his companion, performing deeds, generating all power, the destroyer of the malevolent, the one whose mind is all-encompassing, the swift subduer—having drunk of the Soma and grown strong from heaven, the hero blew the Dasyus away by means of battle. 8.

That Indra, with the Maruts as his ally, performing deeds such as sending down rain and so forth, being all-powerful (*viśvaujāḥ*) with pervasive strength, the slayer of the accursed (*aśastihā*) and the slayer of demons (*rakṣohā*), possessing a universal mind (*viśvamanāḥ*)—that is, one whose mind is all-pervading and exceedingly wise—the swift-overcomer of enemies (*turāpāt*):

thus endowed with such qualities, Indra, having drunk the Soma of Soma, that is, having drunk the Soma come from the heavenly world (*divaḥ*), growing strong (*vṛdhānaḥ*), the hero, by means of battle (*yudhā*) or by the stroke of his weapon, blew the Dasyus—the enemies—away.
The meaning is that he drives away the Asuras with his strength.
"This is yours" (*idaṃ te*)—thus begins the fourteenth hymn.
Bṛhaduktha, the son of Vāmadeva, is the seer (*ṛṣi*).
The fourth, fifth, and sixth verses are in the Jagatī meter.
The first three verses and the seventh are *triṣṭubh*s;
the Viśvedevas are the deity.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "This [hymn] 'idaṃ te' consists of seven [verses] dedicated to the Viśvedevas; the three beginning with the fourth are *jagatī*s."

The application of the hymns (*sūktaviniyoga*) has been concluded. If the Āhavanīya fire, while being extinguished, goes out from its hearth due to some cause and is burning in a place closer than the distance of a *śamyā*-throw to the west, one should recite the mantra “*idaṃ ta ekaṃ para ū ta ekam*” over it and then pour it back into its original hearth. This is also prescribed in the Sūtra: “While the Āhavanīya is being extinguished, before it has gone beyond the distance of a *śamyā*-throw, one should pour it back with the words ‘*idaṃ ta ekaṃ para ū ta ekam*’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.10).
This is one, and yonder is one; enter into the third with light.
At the time of entering, be firm in your body, dear to the gods in the highest birthplace.
This is one for you; beyond this is another for you. Unite with the third light. Be gracious in the union of bodies; be beloved among the gods in the highest birthplace.
With these and other verses, Bṛhaduktha speaks to his deceased son named Vājina:
"O deceased son, this [is for] you.
Since it will be stated later, "above the light," the word *jyotis* (light) here refers to the sun.
This light, which has another as its abode, is one; you are one limb. Therefore, enter into—that is, unite with—the external darkness by means of a portion of your body.
Likewise, another [portion] of yours, a single portion of the enclosure of your breath, enter into that [darkness] by means of that portion of the enclosure of your breath.
The sense is that because the first two are one with the body and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they are "universal" (*vaiśva*).
Likewise, enter into union with the third light, the splendor known as the sun, by means of your own self;
for there is a state of non-difference between the consciousness-body residing in the sun and the consciousness-body residing in yourself.

Therefore, the entry of the Self into the Sun is logical, according to the Vedic revelation: "He who is I, he is that; he who is that, he is I; the Sun is the Self of the moving and the stationary" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.115.1).
[The words] *tanvaḥ* [and] *tanvāḥ* [occur] in the sense of "in the merging of the bodies.
[Note: *vṛṇyā* and *vṛṣṇayāni*; *mahatā taṃtreṇa*; *tu*; *tat*; *tanvāḥ* are variants found in various manuscript traditions.]
Having entered into that sun, move about; be auspicious!
What kind of person are you?
One who is dear, taking delight together with him.
Of what nature is He?
He is the supreme, most excellent *janitra*, the progenitor, of the gods.
For the Śruti declares: "The sun is indeed this supreme *janitra* of the gods."

Leading thy body, O powerful one, may she bestow upon us what is desirable; may she grant protection unto thee. Unconquered, for the sake of the great support of the gods, mayest thou measure out thine own light like a luminary in heaven. tanuḥ | te | vājin | tanvam | nayantī | vāmam | asmabhyam | dhātu | śarma | tubhyam | ahutaḥ | mahaḥ | dhuruṇāya | devān | divīva | jyotiḥ | svam | ā | mimīyāḥ || 2 ||
O Vājin, this earth—this body which leads your body, bringing it to her own self—is your own body, since both share the nature of earth.
Since your body has reached the earth, it is fitting that she should lead your body;
may such an earth bestow upon us desirable wealth (*vāma*), and may she bestow protection and happiness (*śarma*) upon you.

Being thus unoffered and unfallen, you, the great one, should measure out—that is, enter—those great gods who are your causes, as well as the light in heaven, like the sun abiding in the celestial realm;
for the word *iva* has the sense of "and," since particles have multiple meanings.
And that which is your own, existing there as your very nature, you should measure out.

You are a steed; with your vigor, go toward the well-guided ones, the well-guided hymn, the well-guided heaven. O well-guided one, follow the first true laws; O well-guided one, follow the gods along the path. 3. You are a steed; by means of your vigor, you are well-guided. Go toward the well-guided hymn, the well-guided heaven. O well-guided one, follow the first true laws; O well-guided one, follow the gods along the path. 3.
O son, you are "vājī"—you possess vigor through the essence of food, through strength, or through speed; thus you become one who possesses that.
Of what sort are you? You are *suvenīḥ*, meaning very lovely.
The root *vāṃ* is used in the sense of "going" and so forth.

O such one, you who are *suvṛtaḥ*—well-impelled—you have *anugāḥ*, that is, you have followed after, or go after, the *stomam*, the hymn of praise previously performed by you, [specifically] toward the deity presiding over it. Go after it.
Likewise, having been well-restrained, go to heaven;
likewise, having been well-restrained, follow the dharmas accomplished by you.
Of what kind are they?
The first [rays] are the primary ones, true and bearing true fruit;
likewise, they have well-enveloped the gods, Indra and the others.
Likewise, having well-enveloped them, they have followed the path—the light called the sun—that moves through the sky.

Even their fathers did not master their greatness; the gods placed their creative power (*kratu*) among the gods. They pierced through that [obscure part], and those [powers] which were in the *atri*s entered again into their bodies. (4) Of these, even the fathers did not master the greatness; the gods bestowed creative power even upon the gods. They pierced through that [which was] in the *atri*s, and those [powers] of theirs entered again into their bodies. (4)
The fathers—our own ancestors, the Aṅgirases—were masters, the lords, of the greatness and majesty of these gods.

Those Aṅgirases, having attained divinity, also established and maintained their resolve (*kratu*) among the gods, such as Indra and the others. Moreover, they gathered together those splendors which shine within the Atris.
They have entered into the bodies of these gods; the Aṅgiras ancestors enter [them] as well.
The meaning is: "O you who are capable, you too should act in that same way."
1. *ta-bha-mu-gaccha* | 2. *ta-bha-gacchan* | 3. *ga-ta-mu-śarīreṣu* again; [but] in *ta3.7-śarīreṣu*, it is not.

Not here, nor in the intermediate directions, nor upon the earth—with his auspicious protections, he who is praised with the great hymn has, by his greatness, placed all difficulties behind him and established his own progeny among both those who are near and those who are far.

Just as people cross over water by means of a boat—a vehicle for crossing water—just as they cross all difficult passages (*viśvā dugāni*), which must be traversed with hardship, safely and successfully; even so, Bṛhaduktha, by his own greatness (*mahitvā*), placed his own offspring, his deceased son Vājina, among the *arvareṣu* (the lower ones, such as the earth), and then placed him among the higher, celestial ones, such as the sun. Thus, having become one who drinks [the waters], he either placed himself there or [placed him] through a metaphorical designation of his own self.
The hymn beginning with “mā pra gāma” consists of six verses; it is the fifteenth hymn, composed in the Gāyatrī meter, and has Viṣṇu as its deity.
There was a king named Asamāti of the Aiṣvāka lineage, who had four family priests (purohitas): Bandhu, Subandhu, Śrutabandhu, and Viprabandhu.

May we reach—that is, attain—this very thread called Agni, which has been spread out in the form of the Āhavanīya fire and others, the accomplisher of the sacrifice through its excellence, extended among the gods, and spread across the sacrificial altar by the gods through hymns and mantras; may we reach it when it is offered, being sacrificed into from all sides.
The root *naś* signifies the act of pervading or reaching.

In the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, the ancestors presiding over the rice-balls (piṇḍas) are to be worshipped with the verse, "We invoke the mind hither" (RV 10.57.3). As it is stated in the Mūśrita: "With the verse 'We invoke the mind hither' and with three [others], he should then cause them to depart" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.7).
We invoke the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa Soma and with the hymns of the fathers.
Now we invoke the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa Soma and with the hymns of the Fathers. 3.
We—Bandhu, Śrutabandhu, and the others—quickly call upon, we summon, the mind of Subandhu which has been carried away by the masters of illusion (māyāvins). By what means? That is stated:
by means of the *nārāśaṃsa*, that is, by the Soma contained in the *narāśaṃsa* cup.
The *narāśaṃsas* are the ancestors who are praised by men;
the shaking of their cups is itself the oblation.
With such Soma, and with the "thoughts" (*manma*)—that is, the meditative hymns—of the *pitaras* and the *Aṅgirases*, [he offers].
May your mind return to you again for the sake of sacred order, for skill, and for life, so that you may long behold the sun.
O man, let your mind return to you again for the sake of sacred order, for skill, and for life, so that you may long behold the sun.
O Subandhu, let your mind come back again; let it return from the presence of those who roam about.
For what purpose? It is said:
for the sake of *ṛtu*—that is, for ritual action pertaining to both worldly and Vedic spheres—and for the sake of *dakṣa*, that is, for strength.
Or alternatively:
for *ṛtu* (ritual action), that is, for *apāna*; and for *dakṣa*, that is, for *prāṇa*.
For the Śruti declares: "Dakṣa is indeed *prāṇa*, and *ṛtu* is *apāna*."
"And for living"—that is, for the sake of life—"for long," meaning for a long time, "to see the sun"—that is, to behold the sun;
the sense is: for the sake of extremely long life.
May our fathers and the divine folk grant us back our mind;
may we be united with the company of the living.
Again: May our fathers, the divine folk, grant us the mind; may we be united with the company of the living. 5.

"May our fathers—the Aṅgirases who have become like fathers—[grant] us; that is to say, their assembly. And may they give back the living host, the collection of vital breaths and senses. Likewise, may the divine host—the word *jana* here denotes an assembly—may the assembly of the gods also grant the living host. And may we, both [of us], possess and attain those two."
O Soma, bearing our minds within our bodies according to your law, may we, possessing offspring, abide together in harmony.
O Soma, we, bearing our minds within our bodies under your law, may we abide together, possessed of progeny. 6.

O Soma, O God, we— your kinsmen and others— bearing our minds with focused intent upon your *vrata* (your ritual action)— *vrata* being a name for action— and upon your *tanūṣu* (your limbs), may we, being endowed with progeny (*prajāvantaḥ*) through sons, grandsons, and so forth, remain united with you.
The remainder is "the host of living beings."
The sixteenth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "yatte yamam," is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.

The seers are Bandhu and others; they "saw" (composed) this hymn for the purpose of re-entering that [body] the mind of Subandhu—along with its group of sensory faculties—which had departed from the body.
Therefore, they are the seers of this [hymn].
Because it is that which is to be attained, the mind itself is the deity as it revolves;
thus it has been enumerated: "They recited the twelve verses beginning with 'yat te' in the Anuṣṭubh meter as the revolving of the mind.
The application [of the mantra] is established.

1. According to Ga, Ta, Bha, Mu: prāpnumaḥ; according to Ta, Bha, Mu: prāpnuyāḥ; according to Bha, Mu: prāpnuyāmaḥ. 2. According to Ta, Bha, Mu: manaḥ; according to Mu: mano. 3. According to Bha, the word "ṛṣayaḥ" is absent. 4. According to Bha: having seen, one should recite (dṛṣṭvā japet). 5. According to Ta, Bha: mano.
Your mind that has gone far away to Yama, the son of Vivasvat—that we cause to return to you here, for dwelling and for living. 1.
When a man is dying, his great element called *manas* (mind) becomes shattered in many ways.
The re-collection of that [mind] is now declared:
O dying man, that mind of yours which has gone to Vaivasvata—the son of Vivasvat, Yama—to an extreme distance, even so far away as possible—that mind of yours we cause to return; we bring it back.
For what purpose? For destruction here, for dwelling in this world, and for living—that is, for a long life.
That mind of yours which has gone far away to heaven or to earth—that we cause to return to you here, for dwelling and for living. 2.
O Subandhu, that mind of yours which went to heaven and that which went far away to the earth—
"far away" being an adverbial modifier—
bring that back here for our dwelling and for our life.
That mind of yours which has gone far away to the four-cornered earth—we bring it back to you here, so that you may dwell and live. 3.
O Subandhu, that mind which went to the four-edged earth—
she whose portions extend in the four directions—
that we shall now cause to turn back.
That mind of yours which has gone far away to the four quarters—bring that back to you here, for dwelling and for living. 4.
O Subandhu, whatever direction—whether the intermediate points or the four great directions—your mind has gone to, we bring it back from there.
Your mind that has gone far away to the ocean, the surging sea—that we cause to return to you here, for dwelling and for living. ||5||
1. ta1.2.3.7-bha-bhavataḥ | 2.

ga-ta-bha4.6.8-mu—The word ‘yat’ is not present. O Subandhu, that mind of yours which has gone to the ocean, or to the waters of the ocean, or to its end, or to the sea, or to a cloud—that is what is understood [by the word *gatam*].
That ray of yours which has gone far away, following the course of the mind—that we cause to turn back for you, so that you may dwell here and live. 6.
O Subandhu, that which your mind has gone toward—the rays and splendors proceeding forth along the slopes—that is what is called "the gone."

That which has gone far away from you—your mind—to the waters or to the plants, that we cause to return to you here, for dwelling and for living. 7. That which has gone far away from you—your mind—to the waters or to the plants, that we cause to return to you here, for dwelling and for living. 7.
O Sūrya, that which has gone far away from you— to the Sun or to Dawn— within the mind,
that we cause to return for you, so that you may dwell here and live.
That which is yours, the sun.

That mind of yours which has gone far away, to distant realms—O Subandhu, we cause it to turn back here for you to dwell and live. (11) That mind of yours which has gone far away, to what has been and what is to be—O Subandhu, we cause it to turn back here for you to dwell and live. (12) [Note: Regarding verse 12, the commentary explains that by mentioning "what has been" (*bhūtam*) and "what is to be" (*bhavyam*), and because the present is not mentioned separately (as there is nothing existing apart from these two), the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is implied. Thus, we cause the mind that has gone everywhere to return for the sake of life and habitation. (21)
The hymn beginning with "pra tāri," consisting of ten verses, is the seventeenth hymn; it is the seerical composition (ārṣam) of three descendants of Gopāyana, Bandhu and the others.
Of these, the first seven are Triṣṭubh meters;
the eighth is a Paṅkti meter of five eight-syllable feet.
The ninth is the *ṣaḍaṣṭaka-mahāpaṅkti*;
the tenth is the *paṅktyuttarā*, because its characteristic is as stated [in Anuvāka 9.11]: "The first two are decasyllabic, and the others are octosyllabic."
The remaining merchandise, beginning with the *ekākṣara* [hymn] and the *Aṅgirasvat*, is to be understood [as follows]:
at the beginning of the *sūkta*, four [verses] concerning the body and vital breath were recited by Bandhu and the others for the sake of the cessation of *Nirṛti*.
With the fourth verse, "O Soma, do not [lead us] astray," they praised Soma specifically for the sake of the cessation of death.
Therefore, Nirṛti is the deity of the first four [verses], and Soma is the deity of the fourth.
With the two verses beginning "O Asunīti, [lead] the mind," they praised the goddess Asunīti; therefore, she is the deity of those two.
For the verse beginning "Return our life-breath," the deities are Earth and the others, as indicated by their respective marks (*liṅga*).
Then, with the three remaining verses—the *paṅkti*, *mahāpaṅkti*, and *paṅktyuttara*—the two deities are Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivyau*).

With the half-verse beginning "O Indra" (*samindra*), Indra is the deity. Thus it has been enumerated: "In the ten-verse hymn beginning with *pra tāri*, they recited four verses for the purpose of removing *Nirṛti*; they praised Soma with the *śruttyā* verses for the sake of approaching death; with the next two [verses], the divine guidance (*asunīti*); in the seventh, the deities indicated by the words themselves; and with the remaining *paṅkti*, *mahāpaṅkti*, and *paṅktyuttara* verses, Heaven and Earth; and with the half-verse *samindra*, Indra."
The application is concluded.

May life be further extended, renewed once more, like two skillful charioteers of a chariot. Now, having achieved his purpose, may Cyavāna rise up; let Destruction depart far away. May life be further extended, renewed once more, like two skillful charioteers of a chariot. Now, having achieved his purpose, may Cyavāna rise up; let Destruction depart far away.
May the life-span of Subandhu, his vitality, be extended; may it increase.
The root *tṛ* with the prefix *pra-* has the sense of increasing.
How is it said that "may it increase"? It is explained as follows.
"Ever more, ever more increased, ever newer"—
that is to say, endowed with youth.
May his lifespan increase in this way through the very grace of Nirṛti.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

it increases just as one standing in a chariot does when the chariot is driven by a skillful driver—one possessed of ritual knowledge (*kratumat*) and skilled in action (*karmavat*). Likewise, *cyavāna*, not falling away from life, attains—that is, increases—his desired goal, characterized by longevity.
May Nirṛti, the evil deity who seizes one's good kinsmen and protection, go far away—let her abandon us and depart to the utmost distance.
1. Precisely because they are mentioned separately from *bha*.
2. Because they belong to the category of *upasad* [sacrifices], as indicated by *ta1.2.3.7-bha1.2.4.9.8*.
3. The deities are those specified by the indicative marks (*liṅga*), according to *ta-bha-mu*.
4. The two worlds, heaven and earth (dyāvāpṛthivī), [are supported] by the eight *ga* syllables.

5. When situated on the four *ga*s, one, two, three, and seven [syllables], she grows; when situated on the *bha*, she is made to grow; when well-situated (*su-sthitā*), she grows as she should. 6. She is the seizer of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) from the *bha*.
7. [The section] on the avoidance of the *ta*, *taḥ*, *ti*, *taḥ*, *tām*, *taḥ*, *taḥ*, *ma*, *pari*, and *jihīta*.

Now, while the *sāman* is being sung, we prepare for wealth a treasure-store and food; and may we truly produce manifold glories. May all these things of ours be enjoyed by the singer; may Nirṛti depart far away. Now, while the *sāman* is being sung, we prepare for wealth—a treasure-store and food. Here too, *nu* has the sense of "and. The meaning is: we perform both praise and oblation for Nirṛti. He says that very thing: "truly" (*su*), "in many ways" (*purudhā*), we prepare "glories"—that is, foods and oblations. May "all" (*viśvāni*) those oblations belonging to "us" (*naḥ*) be "enjoyed" (*mamantu*) by the "singer" (*jaritā*)—for *jaritā* means "one who has grown old" or "one who praises" (*jarā stutiḥ*). And having tasted them, may "Nirṛti" "depart far away" (*parātaram*) to another place.

Furthermore, place us within the cavity of the sun, where he is no longer visible;

O Asunīti, give back to us our sight; O Anumati, bestow upon us again our breath and our enjoyment here.
May we long behold the rising sun; be gracious to us for our well-being.
O Asunīti, give back to us our sight; give back our breath here to us. May we long behold the rising sun. O Anumati, be gracious to us; may it be well with us. 6.
O Goddess, bestower of life upon us;
the meaning is that you have restored our own state of being well-bound [to existence].
Furthermore, "eye" refers to the organ of sight that provides illumination.
The meaning is "the capacity for seeing.
Furthermore, O Prāṇa, place [this] within us again;
and may we long behold the rising, ascending sun.
O Goddess Anumati, grant us well-being—that is, non-destruction—and so, in such a way, be gracious to us and bring us happiness.
May the earth give him back again; may the goddess [heaven] and the mid-air give him back again.

Again let the earth grant us our breath; again let the goddess heaven, again the mid-air grant it. Again let Soma grant us our body; again let Pūṣan grant the path that is well-being. 7.
May the goddess Earth grant us vital breath;
may the deity Heaven likewise grant us vital breath; and may the intermediate space—the deity of the intermediate space—grant us vital breath.
Likewise, may Soma restore our body; and likewise, may Pūṣan—the deity presiding over nourishment—[restore] the path. "The path is the intermediate space" (Nirukta 11.45).
In that regard, let your honor speak.
For sound, whose essence is speech, arises from space;
let him give that back.
Furthermore, may Pūṣan grant that well-being (*svasti*) which is recited in the world and in the Veda;
or rather,
may Pūṣan bestow [the opposite of] evil.
May that goddess Svasti who is wise bestow upon us wholesome speech;
for "Wholesome speech is indeed Svasti," so says the Brāhmaṇa (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.2.3.8).
May Heaven and Earth, the two young mothers of Truth, bring well-being to Subandhu;
may they carry away his defilement, O Heaven and Earth, and may not even a trace of it remain within you.

May Rodasī—the two, Heaven and Earth—bestow well-being (śam) upon Subandhu. Of what nature are they?

"May he forgive and remove [the offense].

Two [plants] come down from heaven as healing remedies; one moves about upon the earth. May they both together drive away whatever malady there is. O Heaven and Earth, may no affliction whatsoever cause you pain.
From the sky, the two medicines and the three medicines descend.
Here, the Aśvins descend as the pair;
Iḷā, Sarasvatī, and Bhāratī descend as the triad.
"Patient" (kṣamā) [means] in the state of patience; "moving about" (cariṣṇu) means it moves; "single" (ekaka) refers to the intention that there is but one remedy.
The ellipsis is: "may all those protect the life of Subandhu."
I have uttered this curse upon him who brought [the sin] from the land of the Uśīnaras;
may Heaven and Earth bear away that blemish and the defilement, and let nothing whatsoever of yours be harmed.
O Indra, drive hither the ox that belongs to Uśīnarāṇī; let her bring us wealth and away whatever sin there is. O Heaven and Earth, forgive our transgression; may nothing at all cause you pain. 10.

O Indra, drive together, drive forth! What? The ox, the goer, capable of drawing the cart. That ox which brought, which carried, toward those who were equal [to him]. What? The cart (*anas*). Whose? Of *Uśīnarāṇī*, a plant of that name, with which they anoint the body; she is called *Uśīnarāṇī*. "May they bring," and so forth, is explained. || 23 ||
The eighteenth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "ā janam," has the Gaupāyanas, Bandhu and others, as its seers; the sixth verse is by Agastya’s sister, Mamatā.
The first five verses are *gāyatrīs*;
the eighth and ninth are *paṅktis*;
the remaining verses are *anuṣṭubhs*.
Since the King named Asṛṇāmasamāmnas is being praised from the beginning, he alone is the deity;
Indra is the deity of the fifth [verse],
and Apyasamāti is the deity of the sixth.
Then, for the five [verses], the deity is the one who restored Subandhu’s life.
For Subandhu, who had regained consciousness, the deity was the cause of the touch expressed in the words "This is my hand.

Accordingly, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: "The twelve-verse hymn beginning with 'ā janam' is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; with four verses he praised Agni, with the fifth Indra, and with the sixth Aṅgiras’s sister Mātali praised the King (Varuṇa). With the following [verses] she touched Subandhu, who had been deprived of life and then regained consciousness. The first five are *gāyatrīs*; the eighth and the first of the last two are *paṅktis*."

We have approached the people who gaze with brilliance, who are praised by the Māhīnas, bearing our homage. || 1 || To the people who gaze with brilliance, who are praised by the Māhīnas, we have gone, bearing our homage. || 1 ||
With these three [verses] beginning with *idam*, they praise the king:

"We, Bandhu and the others, have gone to—have approached—the people (*janam*), that is, the territory (*janapadam*), which is our own by nature. The root *gam* (to go) takes the *luṅ* tense; according to the rule *mantre ghasa*, the *cli* suffix is elided.
In the word *svośva*, the letter *s* becomes *n*.
What kind of person?
One who has a blazing appearance (*tvepasamdarśam*), and one who is praised by the great (*māhīnānām*) as having approached with praise (*upastutam*).
In the rule "tādau ca," the word *gati* takes its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
Of what sort are we?
We are those who "bear" (*bibhrataḥ*)—that is, maintain or perform—homage (*namaḥ*), namely, respectful salutation.
Alternatively,
it means "the destruction of the people.
The rest is the same.
"Salutation to those who bear [the burden]," meaning those who maintain the homage performed for the sake of the King.

I invoke the peerless, bountiful, radiant, and ever-advancing chariot of Bhajeratha, the lord of the virtuous. || 2 || Peerless; bountiful; radiant; ever-advancing; chariot; of Bhajeratha; lord of the virtuous. || 2 ||
To the king of incomparable measure, the destroyer of enemies—
the term *nitośana* denotes the act of slaying—
to him who is brilliant and radiant.
The expression "the well-guided chariot" (*ninyayinaṃ rathaṃ*) is a designation in which the simile is primary.
It means that which, like a chariot, is the means for attaining all desired goals; [it was born] in the lineage of King Bhajeratha, who bore this name.
Or else:
A certain person of such-and-such a name was his enemy;
[the word] *ninyāyinam* [is used] for him. [The compound is formed] with the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.3.9: *haladantāt*.
The lord of the good, the protector of those who possess wisdom.

He who has surpassed men like buffaloes—possessing praise through song, and moreover possessing the strength of heroes in battle. 3. He who [has surpassed] men, like buffaloes; possessing praise; and moreover, possessing the vigor of heroes through combat. 3.

He who is peerless (*asamāti*) stands surpassing (*atitasthau*), having transcended those people whose power is opposed to his own; the meaning is that he brings them to ruin. Who is he? He is *Ka*. Who is *Hva*? [He is *Ka*].
Like a lion [attacking] buffaloes;
what am I like?
One who possesses arrows.
*Pavīraḥ* means *paviḥ*,

The meaning is that he never even required the assistance of weapons.
What was he doing?
By means of *yudhā*, that is, by fighting.
The meaning is "it is logical."

This being the case, the remaining sense is that the five classes residing in that region—the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth—become happy, just as those who have their desires fulfilled in heaven (dyuloka) become happy.

This is the mother, this is the father, this is the life-giver; he has come hither. This is your path of approach; O Subandhu, come hither, go forth! 7.

"Let us pursue this very Subandhu again," they said.
"I shall take him within the enclosing sticks," she replied.
He spoke against that.
"This one is my mother, this one is my father. And Śaunaka said: "Praised thus, the king stood there, well-pleased, facing the Gaupāyanas."
They praised you with a hymn in two parts, as [they did] for the three [soma-pressings];
then, through these [verses], they drove them away and passed beyond the enclosing-sticks.
Desiring his welfare, the Fire-god gave life to this Subandhu, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, and having bestowed it upon him, said, "Live! to Subandhu.
Praised by the Gaupāyanas, he departed for the third heaven in delight;
exultant, they called out to Subandhu, "This is our mother!"
Having pointed out Subandhu’s body fallen upon the earth, they sang the remainder of his hymn: "O you who possess the concentration of the mind... (Bṛhaddevatā 7.97.101).
This Agni is the mother;
he alone is the father;
he is the life-sustainer, the one who gives life; he has come, he has arrived.
Therefore, O Subandhu, while you abide within the enclosure of the vital breath (*jīva-paridhi*), this body of yours is the means for your excellent movement (*prasarpaṇa*).
Therefore, come toward this; enter it! Go forth, depart from the enclosure!
Others explain it thus:
"O Subandhu, whose life has departed" (*nirgataprāṇa subandho*); here *ayam* is an indeclinable used as a case-ending.
"This is the mother, this is the father, and here has come the son, the sustainer of life, who is the very fruit of living"—thus it is connected.
All have come home in a state of suffering.
The rest is the same.

Just as they bind and fasten a yoke with a triple-stranded rope for support— that is, for the purpose of supporting the chariot and so forth; the word *kam* is a filler for the verse-quarter—
in that very same way, the *paridhāvamis* have held your mind.
For what purpose? For the sake of life—that is, for living—and not for death—that is, not for dying; and furthermore, for the sake of well-being—that is, for non-perishing.
The suffix *tāti* is used here in its own sense (as a nominal derivative).

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The final hymn is the *ukthya*; [one should recite] *grīṇīdaṃ raudramithā*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.1).

In this regard, the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* states: "The brothers excluded Nābhānediṣṭha Mānava while he was living as a religious student (*brahmacarya*). Having returned, he said: 'Why have you not assigned me a share? They replied: 'This very [share] has been allotted to you—the one who reviles us. (AiB 5.14), and so forth.

In that passage, Nābhānediṣṭha, having been deprived of his share by his brothers, approached his father and asked: "Why have you not assigned a share to me? And the father replied: "What is the use of this share?"

The Aṅgirases, having performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) for the sake of heaven for as long as six days, became bewildered. While they were reciting the hymn "Idamithā," Vasiṣṭha—having been sent by his father with the message that they would go to heaven and give him a thousand cows—approached the Aṅgirases. He explained to them the completion of the sacrificial session and the greatness of the gift of cattle, and had them recite these two hymns on the sixth day. By the power of those hymns, they brought the sacrifice to its conclusion and went to heaven; then, at the very source of the waters, they presented the thousand cows.
As he was taking possession of those six thousand cows, a certain man named Kṛṣṇasvāmin rose up from the north and said, "O Brāhmaṇa, do not take my portion of the sacrificial remnant.
He replied, "It has come to me from Aṅgiras.

Then [Kṛṣṇasvāmin] said, "In that case, O Brāhmaṇa, ask your father himself to whom the portion should go. Being thus addressed, he went near his father; having been told by him, "This belongs rightly to Rudra," he returned and replied, "My father said that this portion belongs to him exactly so."
It is stated that the man, being satisfied by the truthful narration, gave his own portion to Nābhānediṣṭha alone.

Likewise, this same matter is expressed in the *Adhvaryubrāhmaṇa* in the passage beginning, "The sons divided the inheritance among themselves; they [excluded] Nābhānediṣṭha" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 3.1.9.4).
All of that should be kept in mind here.
Having fashioned this formidable prayer with skillful speech, O you of mighty words, he has by his power overcome the two rival kings;
when he, the most bountiful, made his parents the instruments of his greatness, he carried the Hotṛ-priests across on the day of the cooked oblation.

This [is] thus: the praise of the Raudra [god], the one whose speech is laudable; having performed the sacred prayer (*brahman*) with power, he is the sovereign within the realm. When his two parents were most liberal in bestowing gifts, he, the performer of deeds, carried the Hotṛ-priests across on the day of the cooked oblation. 1.

The *gartavacāḥ* (one who speaks from the pit) and the *unnatavacanaḥ* (one who speaks from the height), namely Nābhānediṣṭha—having performed this praise (*stotra*) dedicated to Rudra, which is a description of the heart (*hṛdavarṇana*), in this manner (*itthā*) and in this way (*ittham*) at present, having produced it through wisdom (*prajñānena*)—performs the praise within the ritual action (*śacyām antaḥ karmaṇi*) during the sacrificial session (*satra*) in the battle (*ājau*) among the assembly of the Aṅgirases; this is the ellipsis.

As for that praise, the two parents (*pitarau*) of this [sacrificer], making their portion (*krāṇā bhāgam*) and bestowing gifts (*maṃhaneṣṭhāḥ*) in the act of giving, arrange it as a means for the lineage of the Aṅgirases to obtain cattle; this is the ellipsis.
Therefore, the *Nābhānediṣṭa* [is recited] at the *paktha*, that is, on the *pakthya* day;

the meaning is "on the sixth day. For it has been stated: "On the sixth day, they indeed come for food and become bewildered; recite these two hymns for them on the sixth day" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 5.14).
The meaning is that he saw all around, as far as the limit, the Hotṛ-priests, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and the others through their praise of the Hotṛ;
thus, by means of the two hymns beginning with "idam itthā," he caused the sacrifice to reach its completion.

Now, seeking to win for himself what is unassailable, the victorious one has measured out the altar with joy. Most eloquent in his praise, he, like a flood, has poured forth the seed for our protection.

He, Cyavāna, seeking to win through his gifts for the sake of the one who can be deceived, approached the altar with fair hymns; most eloquent in praise, he, the overcomer, poured forth the seed like a rushing flood for immediate aid.

May that man clad in black, the son of Rudra, come for the sake of giving to the singers—that is, for the bestowal of wealth upon those who praise him—and for the destruction of enemies; may he, winning over the singers and honoring them with well-aimed, sharp weapons that strike down the wicked, drive away the demons from the sacrificial altar.

1. *Ta* and *Ma*: extracted from that. 2. *Ta*, *Ma*, and *Mu*: the word "iti" is not present. 3. *Ta*, *Ma*: the word "gāḥ" is not present. 4. *Ga*, *Ta*, *Bha* 1.2.4.6.8, and *Mu*: our own. 5. *Ga*, *Ta*, *Bha* 1.2.4.6.8: the *Nābhānediṣṭha* of Mānava. 6. *Ga*, *Ta*, and *Mu*: the propitiation of Rudra. 7. *Bha*: proceeding. 8. *Ma*: acquisition of debt (*ṛṇalābha*). 9. *Ta*, *Ma*, and *Mu*: indeed the sixth. 10. *Ta*, *Ma*, and *Mu*: they are deluded. 11. *Ga*, *Ta*, *Bha* 4.6.8: harmful; *Bha* 1.2.7: by destroyers (*sūdakaiḥ*). *Ṛgveda* 4.31: he measured out (*vamimīta*), i.e., he has delimited.

The meaning is that he presided over the sacrificial site (*yajñavāstu*). The *Brāhmaṇa* states: "Kṛṣṇa Śava, having approached from the north, said to him: 'This is mine; indeed, it is my dwelling-place (*vāstu*)'" (AiB 5.14).
He says that very thing [here].

Like water (*kṣodaḥ*)—just as a cloud pours down water—so Rudra, who is swift-moving (*tūryathāṇas*), whose speech is most exalted (*vūrtavacastamaḥ*), and who is exceedingly eloquent (*vūrtavacas*), poured forth his own power (*vretaḥ*). "Vitaūti" means he poured it out so that it might go forth from here; the sense is that he impelled it. Or alternatively: [The verse continues: "He who is swift-moving, whose speech is most exalted, and who is exceedingly eloquent, like water—just as a cloud pours down water—so Rudra poured forth his own power. 'Vitaūti' means he poured it out so that it might go forth from here. Or alternatively: [the rest of the verse].
By this subsequent verse and the following two, a eulogy of the Aśvins is offered as a digression.

*Turvayāṇaḥ* means "one who moves swiftly" or "one whose speech is exceedingly energetic," namely Rudra. Like *kṣodaḥ*, water, he is the producer of semen; having cast the semen into the midst [of the waters], he poured it forth with *it-ūti* (this aid) and generated the Aśvins.
Since the name *it-ūti* is applied elsewhere to the Aśvins, and because their status as the sons of Rudra is established in other places, this meaning is obtained.
You two, with your sharp [weapons], by your power, swiftly conquer the songs of praise in those battles where the mind is intent;
he who, crushing many with his arrows, has mixed the direction in his hand.
Not in those invocations where you two, with power, win the sharp inspired songs while rushing forward; he who, crushing many with his arrows, has sharpened his bolt toward the target in his hand. 3.

O Aśvins, you two—just as the mind (*manas*) runs swiftly toward its own object, so too, at these invocations of the singer, you two, running with speed, enjoy the inspired hymns (*vipaḥ*) through the power of wisdom (*śacyā*), that is, with the understanding that they must be approached. That Adhvaryu priest, who possesses abundant wealth in the form of oblations (*tuvimṛṇaḥ*), mixes the offering with his fingers (*śaryābhiḥ*) during my ritual performance; having done what? Having [performed] this.
Having grasped the *vigarbha* in his hand and having indicated the eastern direction—
meaning, having pointed it out with the words "this [is the direction]"—
the connection with what follows is: "O you two, in those oblations at which you partake of such a my Adhvaryu, I invoke you both."
Since Kṛṣṇā sits upon the arms of Varuṇī, I invoke you two, Aśvins, sons of Dyaus;
come to my sacrifice, come to my food, having won the prize, O you who do not forget your promise.
Kṛṣṇā: Since you sit among the ruddy cows, O Aśvins, sons of Heaven, I invoke you both. Accept my sacrifice; come to my food, you who have won nourishment for us, O you whose resolve is unfailing. 4.
When the dark night has passed away among the ruddy-colored cows, she sits;
that is to say, Uṣas mounts her chariot for the sake of shining forth.
"The ruddy cows are the comparison," according to the Nirukta.
O Aśvins, sons of Dyaus—protectors of the shining, luminous heaven or of the sacrifice—at the time of dawn, I invoke you.
Desire my food, characterized by the oblation;
for that purpose, come to my sacrifice.
Having consumed the poison like two horses not sharing their fodder,
you have come here. Of what sort are you two?
Those two, who do not forget and who do not harbor malice, remembering no offense against me.
He whose heroic deed was celebrated when the manly one struck down the established [obstacle];
he then made firm again that which had been enjoyed by the maiden, the daughter of Anu.

He who has performed the sacrifice, whose heroic deed is impelling, who has now followed the established path—let him lead us forward. He has driven away that which was brought hither from the maiden’s daughter; the unassailable one has pulled it back again. ||5||

Just as the Lord Rudra, by means of his own portion, created Prajāpati Vāstoṣpati Rudra, so too does he [the sacrificer] divide him with these initial *ṛc* verses. Of that Prajāpati, this [portion] is characterized by desire (*dṛṣṇat*) and heroic deeds (*eṣaṇavat*).
There is a change of gender [in the grammatical forms].
"Vīrakarma" means semen;

that semen by which heroes become hot (virile) was spread out (*pradhiṣṭa*) and extended (*prathitam*). That semen, performed (*anuṣṭhitam*) by Prajāpati for the sake of offspring, was poured out (*niṣiktam*). Rudra, who is beneficial to men (*narebhyaḥ hitaḥ*), or rather beneficial to the leaders—the gods—drives it away (*apohat*, *apohati*).
That very [seed] again draws up— that is, it extracts from all sides and causes to emerge— that semen, having itself arisen in the form of a person.
Of what kind is that semen?
The meaning is: that semen which was experienced by Prajāpati in the maiden, the beloved daughter, his own daughter—there, in her;
[this is formed] from the root *as* with the suffix *sip*.
Of what nature is Rudra?
He is *anarvā*, meaning not displaced by another.
Regarding this, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: “Prajāpati indeed meditated upon his own daughter—some say she was Aditi, others say she was the Waters” (AiB 3.33).
When there was a task to be done in the encounter, as the father made love to the young maiden, the two who were mindful first left him;
they poured out upon the ridge in the womb of the well-performed deed.

When the middle one became a male in the encounter, the father, acting according to desire toward the young woman, abandoned his seed; they two, moving together, deposited it upon the ridge in the womb of the well-fashioned one. 6.
While their father Prajāpati was acting according to his desire— whether with a young woman, even with his own daughter,
or in heaven (the Brāhmaṇa cites, "Some say 'in heaven'")—
whatever act occurred between them, in the midst of them, or in the intermediate space (antarikṣa), namely that act known as copulation, at that time they both discharged a small amount of semen.
Regarding what they were doing, he says: "Moving apart," meaning approaching one another;
"at the height," meaning on the elevated place of Prajāpati, the womb of the well-performed sacrifice; the sense is that [the seed] was poured out there.
The meaning is that Rudra was born from that.
When the father, uniting with the earth, spilled his seed upon his own daughter,
the gods generated from their own sacred power and fashioned Vāstoṣpati, the guardian of vows.

When the father spilled his seed upon his own daughter, having united with her upon the earth, he smeared it. The gods, being well-disposed, generated the sacred word (*brahman*); they fashioned Vāstoṣpati, the guardian of the dwelling and protector of vows, from that [seed]. (7)

When Prajāpati, the father, mounted—whether it was *div* or *uṣas*, his own daughter—at that very moment, uniting with *kṣmā*, the earth, Prajāpati, having become a *rohita* deer in this world, deposited his seed; he performed the act of impregnation.
Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa states: "Having become a *ṛśya* [antelope], he approached her who had become a *rohita* [deer]" (AiB 3.33).
At that time, the gods—possessing good meditation (*svādhyas*) or performing good deeds (*sukarmāṇas*)—generated and brought forth the *brahman*.
"What is that Brahman? To this he says:

they have fashioned (*niratakṣan*), that is, produced, Vāstoṣpati—the lord of the sacrificial site (*yajñavāstu*) and the guardian of the vow (*vratapāṃ*), the protector of the ritual act (*vrata*) from Rākṣasas and other obstructors. The meaning is that, having granted him sovereignty over the sacrificial site, they created him as the protector of the rite.
