Like a bull, he cast foam in the battle; with us, he went forth, driving away those of feeble mind. Like a gift following the footsteps, he turned away; indeed, he has not seized those dappled cows of mine. (8) At the conclusion of the Aṅgirases’ sacrificial session, Nābhānediṣṭha, having been assigned the task of recovering the cattle, speaks upon seeing Vāstoṣpati approaching before him: "He—this very one—is like a bull, like Indra, who in the battle for the sake of slaying Namuci cast foam; following that casting, Vāstoṣpati now says, 'This portion of the dwelling is yours. After this statement of the truth, [the bull] goes away from us, having departed. Any person of feeble mind (*dubhracetāḥ*), having turned away from the cows intended as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), does not follow their tracks toward us. Indeed, he has not seized those dappled (*pṛśnyaḥ*) cows of mine, which belong to me and were given by the Aṅgirases—just as Rudra, skilled in seizing, has not seized the dappled ones. Thus he hopes.

Swiftly the bearer [of oblations] does not approach; like one who oppresses his own offspring, he does not sit down with reverence. He has won the fuel, and he has won the prize; he was born as the sustainer, overcoming by force those who seek to obstruct. In this sacrifice protected by Rudra, the Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstoṣpati*), the "bearer"—the burner, such as a Rākṣasa—does not swiftly approach. That bearer who would be an oppressor of "offspring" (the priests and participants) does not come for the purpose of destroying the sacrifice. By day, he causes no pain to the "offspring" in the form of the officiants and others. Likewise, at night—*ūrdhaḥ* being a name for night—even during the night, while Agni is blazing, the "reverent one" (the destroyer), such as a Rākṣasa, does not sit down. Thus, while Rudra is the protector, this Agni was born as the winner of "fuel" (*idhama*). Moreover, he was born as the winner of "prize" (*vāja*), that is, food or the oblation. He was born as the "sustainer," the upholder of the sacrifice or its fruit; that Agni was born as the warrior against those who seek to obstruct the sacrifice by force, such as the Rākṣasas.

Swiftly the Navagvas, speaking the Truth and joined with the *ṛta*, have gone to the manifestation of the lovely *kunāyī*. Those twice-swans who have come to the protector, the Adṛśriṇas, have desired to milk the unshakable [cows]. **Navagvas**: The Aṅgirases; those among the Aṅgirases who, having performed the *sattra* of the Gavāmayana, rose after obtaining cows in nine months are the Navagvas. Speaking the *ṛta*, they swiftly (*makṣu*) went to the manifestation of the lovely (*kunāyāḥ*) praise—prompted by Bhanandiṣṭha—from which the *ṛta-yukti* (the completion of the stated yoga) was reached. Or rather, the construction is: "The Aṅgirases, speaking the immortal sound—the praise endowed with the application of sacrifice (*yajña-yoga*)—went to the truth of *kunāyī*, the speckled cow (*pṛśni*). **Twice-swans**: [They are so called] because they go twice to the protector. They are the Adṛśriṇas. They desired to milk the unshakable [cows]. *** (Note: The provided Sanskrit text contains some orthographic variations and minor errors, such as "makṣu" for "makṣū," "ṛtayuktim" for "ṛtayukti," and "dudukṣan" for "duduhre. In two places—on the earth and in the sky—the masters, those who are the *Aṅgirases*, approached Indra, the protector (*gopa*) who is designated as the navel; they approached him while being "without sacrificial fees" (*adakṣiṇāḥ*), for there is a scriptural statement: "Those who are the sacrificers are the officiating priests," and they were "without fees.
And they desired to milk the "unfallen" waters or the inexhaustible fruits.
Swiftly the new song brings happiness, like wealth or seed, as the *ṛta* flows on.
That pure gift which they bestowed upon you, O Rekanas, from the milch-cow, from the cow of the Aryan.
Swiftly [comes] the newest gift of Kunāyā, like seed, like truth, hastening here. When they offered to you your pure wealth, he [came] from around the milch-cow, the cow of the dawn. 11.

"Quickly, swiftly"— the attendants, the rays of light, moving all around that Indra, the "desirable one" (*kanāyāḥ*) who "milks the dharma" (*dharmadogdhī*), went there immediately for the sake of illumination.

The many artificial *asuras*, sitting in their dwellings (*sadanāt*), desired to shatter— that is, to destroy— the "son of the man-seated ones" (*nṛṣadaḥ putraḥ*), the one who belongs to the noble ones (*nāryadam*).
Furthermore, this Indra, knowing the vital point (*marman*) of the Asura named Vṛṣṇa—who was of many births and manifold manifestations—pierces it;
he knows that which is difficult for the Asura to discern, hidden deep within the secret cave.

Bharga indeed is his name, and he whose gods sit like the sun upon the threefold seat; Agni indeed is his name, and Jātavedas. O Hotṛ of the Ṛta, hear us, you who are the guileless invoker. 14. Bharga, indeed, is the name; and he whose gods, like the sun, have sat down upon the threefold seat. Agni, indeed, is the name; and Jātavedas. Hear us, O Hotṛ, you who are the guileless invoker of the Ṛta! 14.

Moreover, *bharga* is indeed its name; it is well known as *tejas* (splendor). In that sacrificial grass (*barhis*) situated upon the three worlds, which is connected to this fiery *tejas*, all those gods who dwell there sit down in the very same manner as they do in heaven (*svar*). Furthermore, *agni* is indeed its name;
and furthermore, *jātavedas*—meaning "one whose wisdom is born" or "the knower of all beings"—is also a name for that *tejas*.

The meaning is that "Agni's splendor," "Agni," and "Jātavedas" are three names. Now follows the direct address: O Hotṛ—so named because you perform the oblation—you who are the invoker of the gods connected with the sacrifice, being free from malice (*avadhrak*), hear (*śrudhi*) our invocation.

And also those two Raudras, the radiant Nāsatyas, O Indra, I would worship for my praise; they who, being joyful and granting gifts to the man who has trimmed the sacrificial grass, are worshipped by all as they bestow well-prepared nourishment. 15. And also | those | me | the two Raudras | the radiant | the Nāsatyas | O Indra | for my praise | to worship | like men | for him who has trimmed the sacrificial grass | granting | the joyful ones | with well-placed nourishment | all | worthy of sacrifice. 15.
Moreover, O Vindra, let those two well-known Vr̥tra-slayers, the sons of Rudra—for their sonship to Rudra is stated in the Ṛgveda (10.61.2):
"Sprinkle the seed like a torrent"—let those two radiant Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, be present for our praise and for the sacrifice; this is the sense of the ellipsis.

Furthermore, O two who delight in praise (vmanu), just as you did at the sacrifice of my father and mother, so likewise, taking pleasure and being exhilarated, for me whose sacrificial grass is trimmed and whose grass is strewn—O two who are praised, who possess exhilarating power, whose wealth is impelled [by us]—you two should be sacrificed to among all our priests; this is the sense of the remainder.

This king, praised, lauded, and a creator, the sage, crosses the waters by his own bridge; he makes Kukṣīvat tremble, he [makes] Agni [tremble], like the swiftly running wheel of a steed [shakes] its rim. 16. This one, praised, the king, the one worthy of homage, the creator, and the inspired singer, crosses the waters by means of his own bridge. He caused Kukṣīvat to tremble; he [caused] Agni to tremble, as the swiftly running wheel [shakes] the rim of a horse. 16.
We are the *vvedhāḥ*, the ordainer of all; Soma is the *vrājā*, praised by all, and he is *vandī*, being extolled by us.

Furthermore, he is the *vipraḥ*, the special fulfiller, or like a sage (*vipravat*), the pure one, whose own rays are the light-bringers for the world. That Soma daily traverses and crosses both the earth (*vapah*) and the intermediate space (*antarikṣam*).
That Soma [resides] with Kakṣīvat, the seer, amidst the mountains.

Agni, the sacrificer and priest of the gods, made the cow— who yields milk like nectar— yield her milk for Śayu, though she was *aprasūtā*,
meaning one whose flow had ceased. When that Śayu thoroughly praised Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman with the most excellent,
praiseworthy, and desirable hymns (*ukthas*), then by their command, he caused that cow, whose flow had ceased, to yield milk in the waters.

His kinsman, the sage Nābhānediṣṭha, who bestows wisdom upon you in heaven, proclaims this aloud. This is our highest kinship with him; indeed, I myself was once his very self—what [other] person could have been there?
That kinsman, the wise one, in heaven—may he establish our thought. Nābhānediṣṭa speaks forth; may he protect us. That is our highest kinship, or indeed, "I am so-and-so many steps from him. 18.
*Tadvandhu*: That very earth is his *bandhu* (kinsman/support) by virtue of being his substratum; thus he is *tadvandhu*. The meaning is that he has that as his mother (*tanmātṛka*).
The word *sūri* means "praiser" or "impeller. The phrase "of you who dwells in heaven" implies that [the praiser] is your own being;
that is to say, he is your offspring.
Through this, a general relationship characterized by extreme intimacy is perceived.
And that [sage] is Manu, the son of Āditya; Manu’s son is Nābhānediṣṭa—thus it culminates in the state of being a descendant of Sūrya.
The relationship between Sūrya and Nābhānediṣṭa will be explained in the final verse and in the subsequent mantra.
And Nābhānediṣṭa, the supporter of the intellect (*dhiyaṃdhāḥ*), the sustainer of ritual acts, desiring (*venan*) the thousand cows given by Aṅgiras, "pralapati"—he speaks out or proclaims.
The meaning is "it leaps" (*sauti*).
Or rather, the meaning is "also" (*api ca*).
That heaven (*dyauḥ*) is our supreme, most excellent navel—that which binds—and it serves as the foundation for this Sun.

The word *gha* is a filler (*pūraṇa*). "I was that"—meaning immediately after that Sun, as the *katitha*, the filler of a certain number of [steps]—I became [so]. By this, it is stated that my relationship with the Sun, in the form of the relation between the born and the progenitor, is very close.
This is my navel; here is my dwelling place; these are my gods; here I am, the All.
I am the twice-born, the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta); this cow, being milked, is the doubly-born Āryaman.

This is my navel; here is my dwelling place; these are my gods; this am I in my entirety. I am the twice-born, the first-born of Cosmic Order (Ṛta). As soon as I was born, this cow milked it out for me. 19.

these, my shining rays, are my own, belonging to me.
"I am this All.

The twice-born ones are the Brahmins; they are the first-born of *ṛta*, the first-born of truth, the first-born of the Brahman that has become reality. The dappled cow is the Veda, the speech of the intermediate region (*mādhyamikī vāk*); being born, she milked—meaning she produced—all this. "She milked" signifies that she brought it forth.

Now the delightful messenger, the radiant one, the master of two paths, the protector, has moved across. When the child [Agni] has quickly grown strong, his mother has brought forth the firm, ever-increasing [flame] that rises up like a row of birds.

Now, when the two kings, seeking cattle, flow forth for the singer—flowing swiftly, worthy of praise—the inspired poet becomes their most beloved; he shall carry them across and bring them safely over.

Now, when the two Kings, eager for cattle, have sped forth—the swift one speeding for the singer, the inspired one most dear to them—he indeed has become their leader; he shall carry them away and also bring them across. 23.

The two kings, the resplendent Mitra and Varuṇa—now, at the conclusion of the sacrificial session—because Yama, the swift-moving one, goes toward Gaviṣṭha when the contest for cattle has begun; [he goes] for the sake of the singer performing the ritual for the host of Aṅgirases.
Desiring what?
Desiring praise for that host of Aṅgirases.
Therefore, he, the wise one, became the most beloved (*preṣṭha*) and dearest (*priyatama*) among these Aṅgirases; *nābhanediṣṭa* [is his name].
The particle *hi* serves as a filler.
He carried away (*vakṣat*), that is, bore away, their duty (*kartavya*).
"Moreover, O Aṅgirases, may you carry them across; may you cause them to cross over"—thus he prays for himself alone.
Now, indeed, for the prosperity of this noble one, we, the singers, implore that very thing in vain.
O you who are swift, the son of the horse, the one with wise horses—you are such in the winning of glory.
Now indeed, for the prosperity of this noble one, we, chanting freely, implore that [favor]. Truly, his son is swift; he is both a sage and [present] for the winning of glory. 24.

With this [verse], he praises Varuṇa individually: 1. *Adha* (then/now); 2. *atha* (furthermore); 3. *nu* (quickly); 4. through the praise of *jenyasya*, meaning "of the victorious one," or *janavyasya*, "of the one belonging to the people"; 5. that wealth consisting of cattle and so forth which is his own; 6. when there is a cause for nourishment or for the sake of his nourishment (*pāṃye*); 7. *vṛthā* (without effort/easily); 8. *rebhantaḥ* (praising/singing); 9. *nu* (quickly); 10. *īmahe* (we beg/solicit); 11. *saraṇyuḥ* (swift-moving by nature); 12. *aśvaḥ* (the horse); 13. *asya* (his), namely the son (*sūnuḥ*) of this Varuṇa.
Varuṇāṅgaśva was born;
now, [the verse] is made manifest: "O Varuṇa, you are a *vipra*, that is, worthy of worship like a sage, or you are pure."
And you are engaged for the sake of the hearing of the Veda (śravasaḥ), for the winning of food (annasya sātau), and for our acquisition of food (asmākam annalābhāya). || 15–17 ||
If you two, for our sake, have accepted this hymn with reverence for your friendship and for our host—
[the hymn] in which all our songs are gathered together, and which, like ancient doors, has been opened wide for the sake of true prosperity.
O you two, if you have graciously accepted our hymn for friendship—for our host who offers homage—in whom all songs are united, he is like a beautiful path toward abundance and truth. 25.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, [be present] for your powerful host, for our friendship;
or rather,
for your friendship and for our host and strength.
5 If the Adhvaryu priest is possessed of reverence, provided with food, and the Hotṛ priest is possessed of hymns; 7 if he has delighted in or partaken of the Stoma;

9 when that friendship has been established, 10 then everywhere—in every land—11 the songs of the Aṅgirases [resound]. O Lord of Men, O Indra, protector of men! 1. Ga4. He! (O King! 4. O Protector of Men, O Indra!
2. One whose burden has been cast off (gatabhara); 4.6.8. The action of the *muk* [suffix];
3. *tā* [suffixes] 1.2.4.5.6.7.8; *bha*. Desiring praise, the one who is weary (*jaraṇyu*);
4. *ga* [suffix] 4. He causes to reach (*prāpayat*); *ta* [suffix], *bha*, *mu*: he causes to cross over (*pārayati*).
5. *ga-ta*—thus he prays for himself; *tā-bha*—thus he prays for himself alone.
6. *ta-bha*—he becomes.
The relatives, coming together from all sides, approach him; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The meaning is that such sounds as "Take this! and "Take that! are heard in the houses of the noble;
or alternatively, that the songs of praise from those performing sacrifices come [to them].

Like the ancient path, like the eastern quarter— just as these provide ease to those who travel, so does it; or rather, like the ancient, well-known, primordial path— just as that provides ease to those who travel, so does it.
May he bestow—that is, grant—to Sūnṛtā, who is of the nature of what is dear, speech in the form of praise.
Being praised as "the stone that favors the gods," may Subandhu increase his strength with reverence and hymns;
for now, through the words of the Atharvan, he shall indeed swell with the milk of the ruddy cow.

He, being praised with waters, accompanied by the gods, well-allied through homage and well-spoken hymns, should be strengthened by lauds and splendors; for now indeed the path of the radiant milk-cow has been disclosed. 26.

May he—accompanied by the gods (*devavat*), having good kinsmen (*subandhu*), and being the most excellent (*vama*) Varuṇa—prosper (*vardhan*) while being praised (*gṛṇānaḥ*) with salutations (*namasā*) and hymns (*sūktaiḥ*) in this manner.
May he come now (*nūnam*) through the recited words (*ukthaiḥ*) or the praiseworthy words of praise; "hi" is used as a filler. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "may he come."
For the sake of his sacrifice, the path—the way—of the cow's milk is opened;
that is to say, the tips of her udders flow.
O worshipful gods, be truly great for our protection, being of one mind; you who, moving abroad, have brought us strength, and you who stand as unfailing discerners.

O you who are worthy of worship, O great gods, be well-disposed toward us for our protection; may you, being of one mind, who brought forth strengths while moving in three ways, and who are the unerring discerners, [be present]. 27.
Anayārañjara Āśāsate says: O *yajatrāḥ*, gods worthy of sacrifice, you—*u* being a filler particle—be united (*sajoṣaḥ*) for our great protection (*mahas ūtaye*). Be present for our preservation.
And you, O Aṅgirases, who have brought—that is, caused us to attain—the great *vājās*, the foods; who, going forth (*viyantaḥ*), have won various hymns (*mukthāni*) for our praise;
and who are unerring (*amūrāḥ*), meaning free from confusion in the performance of the recitation (*paṭha*).
"Be such judges, you who are the discriminators of cows"— this is the syntactic connection, meaning "you shall become possessed of the *sajaūpa*."
May Vidyātīrthamaheśvara, dispelling the darkness by illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the first chapter of the eighth book in the *Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa*, a commentary on the *Ṛgvedasaṃhitā* composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial throne of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the supreme sovereign of kings, the highest lord, and the promoter of the Vedic path.
1. In the case of *gaṃ4-tara.2.3.1-bha1.2.6.8*, it is related to [the preceding]. 2. Regarding the example (*ta-udāharaṇa*). 3. In *ga-ta-bha1.2.4.6.8*, the term ‘*tadvat*’ does not exist.

4. *ga-ta-bha-purā* means "formerly. 5. *ga-ta-bhara*. 4.6.8—The reading “*dāśat prayacchatu*” (let him give) is absent; it is *bhava-dāśat*; *mu-dāśat* means "let him grant happiness. 6. *ga4-satatamudhāya*; *ta1.2.3-bha1.2.4.6.8-sā* [is] for the sake of the hymn (*ukthāya*).
Bha 1: Always rising [from sleep].
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Having first explained the eighth chapter of the eighth book, the learned minister Sāyaṇa now desires to explain the second chapter.

In this regard, the hymn beginning with "ye yajñena," consisting of eleven verses, is the second hymn with respect to the *anuvāka*; it is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Nābhānediṣṭha, the son of Manu.
The first three verses are in the *jagatī* meter; the fifth verse is an *anuṣṭubh*.
The sixth is the Bṛhatī;
the seventh is the Satobṛhatī;
the eighth and ninth are Anuṣṭubhs.
The tenth [verse] is a *gāyatrī*;
the eleventh is a *triṣṭubh*.
For the first six, the deities are either the Viśve Devās or the Āṅgirasas.
The seventh [verse] belongs to the Viśvedevas.
In the four verses beginning with the eighth, the gift of the great king Sāvarṇi is praised;
these [verses], not being exhausted, have those same deities.

And so it is enumerated: “Those [verses] beginning with *ye yajñena* belong to Ekādaśa Āṅgirasa; they are a praise (*stuti*), or else a *triṣṭubh*, an *anuṣṭubh*, a *pragātha*, two *anuṣṭubhs*, four *gāyatrīs*, and others are a praise of the gift of Sāvarṇi.
This hymn belongs to the *vaiśvadeva-śastra* on the fifth day.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “With *idamithā raudram* and *ye yajñena*, one approaches [the recitation] prior to the penultimate verse” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.1).
Those who, anointed by sacrifice and the sacrificial fee, attained the friendship of Indra and immortality—to them, O Aṅgirases, may there be prosperity; O wise ones, accept this gift from Manu.
O Aṅgirases, you who, anointed by sacrifice and by sacrificial gifts, attained the friendship of Indra and immortality—to you, O wise ones, may there be prosperity; accept this human offering. 1.

Nābhānediṣṭha, having been authorized by his father Manu, approached the Aṅgirases who were performing a sacrificial session and said, "Accept me; I shall provide you with the sacrifice. This is what is being stated here. As for the historical narrative, it has been explained in detail in accordance with the Brāhmaṇa passage from the preceding hymn, "He recites the Nābhānediṣṭha; [for] the Nābhānediṣṭha is indeed Mānava" (AiB 5.14), as well as in accordance with the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa passage, "Manu divided his inheritance among his sons" (TS 3.1.9.4).
And thus is the meaning of this *ṛc*:

"O you who, being united (*samaktāḥ*)—that is, joined together—with the sacrifice (*yajñena*), that which is worthy of sacrifice, namely the oblation (*haviṣā*), and with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇayā*) to be given to the officiating priests (*ṛtvigbhyaḥ*), performing the *ahīna*, *ekāha*, and *satra* sacrifices, have attained (*ānaśa*) the friendship (*sakhyam*) of Indra—that is, the work of a friend—and thereby immortality (*amṛtatvam*), the state of divinity characterized by non-death. [The form] *ānaśa* is the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *aś* (to reach/attain), used in the middle voice with a plural ending by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
By the rule "aśnoteśca," the augment *ju* is added. Due to its connection with a word ending in a case-suffix (*yadvṛttayoga*), it does not undergo the *anighāta* (non-suppression of accent).
O Aṅgirases! May there be auspicious, beneficial action for you—*vaḥ*, meaning for you.
O you of sevenfold wisdom, O you of excellent insight, O Angirases, do you now accept me, the son of Manu, who has arrived here; do you accept me!
Since the sacrifice will be properly performed once I have been accepted, accept me for that purpose.

The Aṅgirases, who in the course of a year split Vala with their wealth and found the two parents and Soma in the high place—may long life be yours; O wise ones, accept the gift from the descendant of Manu.
O Utarjana, O Fathers, with the cow-dung, with wealth, and by means of Truth, you shattered Vala in the year’s course. May long life be yours, O Aṅgirases; O wise ones, accept this gift from Manu. 2.
1. Bha-Sāyaṇācārya: 2. Ga4-Ta1.2.7-Ma1—*ahernaika-sahasrāṇi*; Ta3—*ahainaika-sahasrāṇi*; Bha2—*ahainaikahika-sahasrāṇi*; Bha4.6.7.8-Mu—*ahīnaika-sahasrāṇi*.

O *aṅgirasaḥ*, you who are our *pitaraḥ* (fathers) by virtue of being our ancestors, you who *udājan*—that is, caused to emerge from the mountain—the *gomayam* (cow-made), i.e., the *vasu* (wealth) consisting of cattle that had been carried off by the Paṇis. [Those [cows] were presided over by them.]

Furthermore: when the year has fully elapsed—that is, when the year has come around—by means of the sacrifice that is *ṛta*, which is the nature of truth, they destroyed Vala, the Asura named Vala who had carried off the cows; may there be for you long life, an abundant lifespan. The rest is as before.
They who by the *ṛta* caused the sun to ascend to heaven and spread out the mother earth;
may you, O Aṅgirases, possess good progeny—O wise ones, accept this offering from the descendant of Manu.
They who by means of cosmic order caused the sun to ascend to heaven, and spread out the earth, the mother; may you, O Aṅgirases, possess good progeny. O wise ones, receive the human [offering]. 3.

O Aṅgirases, you who by means of *ṛta*—the sacrifice that has become truth—caused the Sun, the impeller of all, to ascend and establish himself in the sky, the celestial world; and furthermore, who spread out the Mother Earth, the creator of all, making her manifest through the performance of sacrificial sessions (*satra*) and other rites—to you, may there be excellent offspring, that is, the state of having noble sons. [The suffix] *amic* is applied according to the rule "nityamasic ca prajāmedhayoḥ," and from that, the *vapan* suffix is added.
This Nābha speaks sweetly in your dwelling; O sons of the gods, O sages, listen to that!
Let there be the Subrahmaṇyā hymn for you, O Aṅgirases; O wise ones, accept the man from the lineage of Manu.
This navel speaks sweetly to you both in your home; O sons of gods, sages, listen to that! May there be for you, O Aṅgirases, the excellence of sacred prayer. O wise ones, accept this man. 4.

O sons of the gods (*devaputrāḥ*), sons of the gods, sons of Agni, O seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*) who perceive objects beyond the senses, O Aṅgirases: this person here before you, Nābhānediṣṭa—this *nābhā*—speaks auspicious and pleasant words to you in the sacrifice, which is as your home.
Listen to those words with great respect; listen!
[The root] *śru* means "to hear."
By the rule "na-śana-sa-na-tha-nāś-ca," the substitution of *tana* occurs. To you—those [beings]—let there be excellent *subrahmaṇya*, that is, splendid spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
Now, accept me, this human being who has arrived. Accept me!
They who are of diverse forms, whose deeds are desired, and whose works are formidable—
those Aṅgiras, the sons of Agni, were born from him.
The Virūpas were indeed seers; they were of profound inspiration. They were the sons of Aṅgiras; they were born from Agni. 5.
The seer spoke from beyond the senses:

"These seers are the beholders of actions; these seers are 'of diverse forms,' meaning they are of various appearances and complexions among one another. And thus, these Aṅgirases are 'of profound power.'"
*Vepa* is a name for ritual action (*karman*).
They possess profound ritual actions;
indeed, these are the sons, the progeny, of the *Aṅgirases*.
He says that very thing:
"These Aṅgirasas were born from Agni," meaning they were produced and manifested from all sides.
The Brāhmaṇa states: "Those which were the glowing coals became the Aṅgirasas" (AiB 3.34).
In this regard, the Nirukta should also be consulted (Nirukta 3.17).
1. *ga-ta-bha-* ‘*nābhā*’ does not exist.
2. *ga-ta-bha-mu-* ‘*prati gṛbhīta*’ does not exist. 3. *ga-ta4.5-* [omitted]; *ta1.2.6.7.8-bha1.2.4.6.8-* read *praṇato*.
4. These are they who have been born from Agni, the multiform ones from heaven. Navagva and Daśagva, the best of the Aṅgirases, together with the gods, exults.
Those who were born from Agni, the multiform ones from heaven—the Navagvas and the Daśagvas; he, the best of the Aṅgirases, together with the gods, exults. || 6 ||
Those Aṅgirases of diverse forms, who were born from the sky— that is, from the world of heaven— and from Agni; or alternatively, *divas pari* (from the sky),
where *pari* indicates the ablative sense.
They were born from the fire blazing with its own splendor.
Among them, Navagva and Daśagva were the most eminent Aṅgiras, the best of the Aṅgirases.

Among the Aṅgirases who follow the path of the sacrificial session (*satra*), some performed the rite for nine months and praised *Aditi*, while others did so for ten months; thus has the *Aṅgirasām Ayana* been described.
Among them, Agni— both the ninefold and the tenfold—
is established as such among the gods; that Agni bestows great wealth,
for *maṃhati* is a verb meaning "to give."
With Indra as their ally, the worshippers have opened the stall rich in cattle and horses.
Giving a thousand to me, the sons of Aṣṭakarṇī have won glory among the gods.
With Indra as their ally, the worshippers have released the stall rich in cattle and horses. Those who gave me a thousand [cows] with eight-eared ears have won glory among the gods.

The *vāghats*— the performers of the rite, the bearers [of the sacrifice], whether they be the *viśve devāḥ* or the *aṅgirasaḥ*— together with Indra as their ally and great support, released and drove out the pen (*vraja*) filled with cattle,
accompanied by cows and horses, which had been seized by the *paṇis*.

They [gave] to me, toward me, a thousandfold—thousandfold is the wealth worthy of this [sacrifice], consisting of the distribution at the *sattra* sacrifice. "Aṣṭakarṇyaḥ": *aṣṭa* is a form derived from the root *aṣṭa* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) with the suffix *niṣṭhā*;
it means those whose ears are wide-spreading.
This is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
By means of their wide-extending bodies, while bestowing a dwelling, they have made for the gods—Indra and the others—*śravaḥ*, which signifies food characterized by oblations or fame.
Regarding the root *kṛ* (to make), in the *luṅ* tense, the suffix *cli* is elided according to the rule "in a mantra, [the *cli* of] *ghas* [is elided]."
Thus, when the Aṅgirases were praised by Nābhānediṣṭha, they declared wealth to him.
This has been stated by Śaunaka: "The Ṛṣis, the Aṅgirases, being pleased, [bestowed it] upon Yadu and Turvaśa;
and those who proclaimed their deeds in the sacrifice for the sake of Tapuṇatha."

With the hundred *uttarā* verses, Śaunaka [spoke] for this descendant of Manu, the seer Mārvāṇi, regarding that food which he does not consume: "That food which was spoken by Mārvāṇi for the descendant of Manu, as a great delight—
that has been declared in the hymn named *pra nūnaṃ jānatām*."
Now let this Manu be procreated; let him grow like a young sprout, he who bestows a thousand [cattle] and a hundred horses upon the supplicant as a gift.
Now let this man indeed be born; let him grow like a young sprout—he who bestows a thousand and a hundred horses as a gift upon us, overcoming our adversaries.
May this Sāvarṇa Manu truly and quickly become a progenitor of offspring;
may he flourish and manifest through wealth and the like, as well as through sons and the like.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as a seed produces a sprout, so may that man, joined with the fruit of his actions, flourish through sons and other descendants.
This very man, who at that very moment bestows for the sake of giving a thousand cows accompanied by many horses and cattle— this man impels the stone to give to the seer.
1. *ga-ta1.2.3-ma1.2.4.6-teṣām eṣām*; *ta6.8-ma7-teṣām yeṣām*.
2. *ta-bha-sthitaḥ saha*. 3. *ta-bha1.6.8-yajñeneti kīrtayat*; *bha2.7-mu-yajñeneti kīrtayat*.
No one can grasp it, as if reaching for the ridges of heaven; the sacrificial fee of Sāvarṇya flows like a river upon its course.
No one at all reaches him, as if grasping the ridge of heaven; the sacrificial fee of Sāvarṇi has spread out like a river upon its course. 9.
"No one at all" (*kaścana*) "is able to undertake" (*ārabham*), that is, to engage in, "that" Sāvarṇa Manu's own task by means of his own action;
the meaning is that he is unable to give it away to another in the manner that Manu bestows it. How is this established?
"Even by day, it stands like the sun—the lofty summit of the celestial realm (*dyuloka*), unapproachable by anyone due to its splendor.
[He] undertook [it].
The suffix *kamul* is used here according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.4.12: *śaki ṇamulkamulau*."
This sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of cows and other items belonging to that Manu Sāvarṇa spreads out upon the earth along the open path, like a river flowing toward the ocean;
it becomes extensive.
And may the two Dāsas, with their offerings and their wealth of cattle,
grant us Turvaśa as a gift.
And Dāsa Parivipra, Smadiṣṭi, and Goparīṇasa—Yadu and Turvaṣa have honored [thee]. || 10 ||

Moreover, in our sacrifice, the two Yadu and Turvaśa—named kings and seers who perceive auspiciousness, who are "goparīṇasā," that is, surrounded by cattle and possessed of many cows and other livestock, and who stand like servants (dāsā) or attendants under his command—are bestowing [wealth] for the enjoyment of this Sāvarṇa Manu; they look upon him and grant it.
The singular number is used because the reference applies to each one individually.
May the village-leader, the giver of thousands, not come to harm; may Manu’s sacrificial fee, striving together with the sun, reach its goal.
O gods, may you extend our life-span; for him, the unwearied ones have brought forth strength and nourishment.

May the giver of thousands, the leader of the people, bestow wealth; may Manu’s sacrificial fee, striving in unison with the Sun, proceed. O Gods, may Sāvarṇi prolong our life, in which we, unwearied, have won the prize of strength.

"Sahasradāḥ" means a giver of a thousand [cows] and so forth; "grāmaṇīḥ" is a leader or organizer of villages; "manuḥ" refers to this progenitor of the people. May he "mā ripat"—may he not be harmed by anyone at all.
Alternatively, may he not strike us who lead the ritual actions, but rather honor us with gifts of wealth and the like.
"May his sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), as it proceeds while being bestowed, go and unite with the Sun;
may it become renowned throughout the three worlds—this is the meaning.
May the gods, Indra and the others, prolong and increase the life of this Sāvarṇi, the son of Savarṇā, the Manu."

"Unwearied in our tasks, tireless, performing every work—under that patron (*manu*) with whom we have won (*amanāma*), that is, shared, food characterized by cattle, may I be the one who obtains it most closely;
thus he hopes."
The third hymn, consisting of seventeen verses beginning with "parāvato ye," is the *ārṣa* (seer's composition) of Gaya, the son of Plati.
The sixteenth and seventeenth verses are *triṣṭubh*;
the fifteenth is either a *triṣṭubh* or a *jagatī*.
The two verses beginning with "svasti naḥ pathāsu" have Pathyā-Svastidevatā as their deity;
the remaining ones are addressed to the Viśvedevas.

Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "From *parāvataścyūnā* to *gayaḥ pvātaḥ*, ending with two Triṣṭubhs; however, the verse *svasti naḥ* is a Triṣṭubh together with the following one, both having Pathyā-Svastidevatā as their deity."

On the third day of the *pṛṣṭhya-abhiplava* [six-day] period: 1. In the manuscripts *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, the phrase "giver of a thousand" (*sahasradāḥ*) is absent. 2. In the manuscripts *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *karma*, it appears as "in the rites" (*karmasu*). 3. In the manuscripts *ga*, *ta*, *ra*, *2.3.4.5.6*, and *bha*, it reads "not equal" (*analsamānāḥ*). 4. In the manuscripts *ta*, *bha*, *6.8*, and *mu*, it reads "in this" (*asmin*). [Aṣṭaka 8, Adhyāya 10, Adhyāya 5, Sūtra 63] 495.
This hymn is the insertion for the Vaiśvadeva Śastra; it belongs to the Viśvedevas.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Vaiśvadeva [Śastra] begins with 'anaśvo jātaḥ parāvato yaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.7).
Those who from afar desire kinship, who, beloved by Manu, belong to the lineage of Vivasvat—those gods who sit upon the sacred grass of Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa; may they speak in our favor.
Those who from afar desire kinship, who, pleased by Manu, belong to the lineage of Vivasvat; those gods who sit upon the sacred grass of Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa—may they speak for us. 1.
O gods, having come from afar, from a distant land, you establish— that is, maintain— kinship with men; or rather,
you call out to one another, "Let us form a friendship with those men who offer oblations."
"May Heaven and Earth pour forth nectar"—
the meaning is that Heaven and Earth cause the oblation to flow.
The Ṛṣi, addressing himself, says:
"The bulls (*vṛṣabhān*)—those possessing the power of hymns (*uktha-śuṣmān*), that is, those endowed with praise—and bringers of rain (*vṛṣṭer āhartṝn*).
[The form] *hyahobhaiḥ* contains the substitution of *bha* [for *dha*]."

Praise after praise those sons of Aditi, the gods of faultless deeds, for their divine [powers], for our well-being—that is, for our non-destruction. [The form] *anumada* is derived from the root *mad* (to rejoice) in the imperative mood with a substitution of the *śap* affix; or it may be derived from the root *mand*, meaning "to praise," where the absence of the augment *num* is due to the rule "the rules regarding augments are not always obligatory."
The gods, who are compassionate toward men, unwinking, and worthy of worship, have attained great immortality;
with chariots of light, possessing the power of serpents and free from sin, they clothe themselves in the strength of heaven for our well-being.

The gods, who are like men and free from malice, who never close their eyes, have attained great immortality through their worthy worship. Having light for their chariot, possessing the power of serpents in their magic, and being sinless, they clothe themselves in the strength of heaven for their well-being. 4.
O Ṛkṣasas,
you who take pleasure in— that is, you serve— the singer who praises you; [the root] *jup* means "to love" and "to serve."
The suffix *bhlu* is substituted for the imperative (*leṭ*) after the root *śap*. There is the augment *aṭ*.
Furthermore, O *manuṣaḥ*, O thinkers and knowers, O *viśve devāḥ*, O all you gods, you who are *yati*, of whatever number you may be.
The form *yacchabdāt* should also be understood as a Vedic anomaly (*chandasaḥ*).

O *dvijātāḥ*, those born from many [parts] through the portions of Dhātṛ and the other gods, O *devāḥ*, which *kaḥ*—what sacrificer indeed—would *aram karat*, fully prepare or adorn the *adhvaram*, the sacrifice, for your sake with hymns and oblations?
The meaning is: "There is no one other than me."
Who indeed adorns that sacrifice which carries us across the mountain—the path of sin, non-Vedic in nature—beyond destruction, unto our own end?

To whom Manu first offered the oblation with kindled fire and with his mind through the seven Hotṛ-priests—O Ādityas, grant us fearless protection; make for us easy paths and fair ways for our well-being.

To whom Manu offered the first oblation when the fire was kindled with his mind by the seven priests—O Ādityas, grant us fearless protection; make our paths easy to traverse and our ways fair for our well-being. ||7||

With the fire kindled by oblations—that is, with the fire properly ignited—Manu Vaivasvata, the first of human beings, through this mind of faith, together with the seven *hotṛ*s (the officiating priests who utter the *vaṣaṭ* call), [performs] for you that which is the first—the primary, or alternatively, the original because it is performed before all other men—the *hotrā*.
*Hotrā* refers to the sacrifice (*yajña*), so called because sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) are poured therein. That [sacrifice].
Or alternatively:
"the gods are summoned here by hymns of praise"— that sacrifice he "āyaje," meaning he sacrificed toward it with direct intent.
The form is from the periphrastic perfect (liṭ);
or else,
it is from the present indicative (laṭ), with the loss of the suffix *ta* according to the rule “lopasta ātmanepadeṣu.”

By the rule "yajivapyoḥ likhthevaṃ vaktavyam" (Kātyāyana 6.4.120.4), the vowel *e* is substituted. O Ādityas—O sons of Aditi—O Gods, you grant us (*naḥ*) fearlessness (*abhayam*) and protection (*śarma*), that is, happiness.
Furthermore, for our well-being (*svastaye*) and security, make the paths easy to traverse (*sugāni*); that is, make the excellent Vedic paths (*supathāni*) accessible.
In the imperative (loṭ) of the root *kṛ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the suffixal augment (*vikaraṇa*) by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi"; [then] the substitution of *ta* [for *hi*].
Those wise ones who rule over the world, the thinkers of all that is stationary and moving— they, the gods, having performed their work for us, protect us on every side for our well-being.
Those who rule over the world, the wise ones, the thinkers of all that is stationary and all that moves—O gods, deliver us from committed and uncommitted sin, and protect us for our well-being. 8.

Those gods who are *pracetasaḥ*—possessing supreme knowledge—and *mantavaḥ*—the knowers of all—who are the lords (*īśire*) of *sthānuḥ*—the stationary—and of *jagataḥ*—the moving—and of *viśvasya bhuvanasya*—of the entire world;

now directly addressed: O *devāḥ*, you gods who possess the aforementioned qualities, do you today, for our well-being (*svastaye*), for the sake of non-destruction and the increase of our lifespan, carry us across (*piprata*) from *kṛtān*—committed physical sins—and from *akṛtāt enasaḥ*—uncommitted [sins] such as those of the hands and feet, as well as mental sins.
The meaning is: "Make them free from evil."
In battles we invoke Indra, who is easily invoked, the deliverer from distress, the well-doing divine host;
we call upon Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga, Heaven and Earth, and the Maruts for gain and for our well-being.

In battles, we invoke Indra, who is easily invoked; the divine folk who release from distress and perform good deeds; Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga, Heaven and Earth, and the Maruts, for the sake of gain and for our well-being. 9.

In battles, we invoke Indra, who is easy to call upon; the divine host that releases from distress and performs good deeds; Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga, Heaven and Earth, and the Maruts, for the sake of gain and for our well-being. 9.
1. This [substitution] of *ta* for *bha* does not exist.
2. *ga*: there is the substitution of *ta* for that [which follows *t*]. (Pāṇini 8.4.31)
Rigveda 498: Indra, the deliverer from distress— that is, the liberator from sin— and the one who is easily invoked, [we call upon] in the burdens.
"Bhara" refers to battles, so called because they "bear," "consume," or "destroy" enemies;
in these we invoke [the gods] for protection.
Furthermore, we invoke another person, the divine one—belonging to the gods—who is of good deeds and noble actions.
He intends that person:
we invoke Agni, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga—the god worthy of worship by name—Heaven and Earth, and the Maruts, for our nourishment, for well-being, for safety, and for protection.
For the animal sacrifice dedicated to the deity Aditi, the verse beginning with "sutrāmāṇam" serves as the *yājyā* for the offering of the omentum (*vapā*).
This is stated in the ritual manual: "aditiṃ ha jan-iṣṭa sutrāmāṇaṃ pṛthivīṃ dhāmanehasam" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
In the *prāyaṇīya* sacrifice, this same verse is the *anuvākyā* for the oblation to Aditi; in the *udayanīya* sacrifice, it is the *yājyā*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Sutrāmāṇaṃ pṛthivīṃ dhāmanehasaṃ mahīm u mātaraṃ sutrāmāṇam" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.3).
At the time of departure, one should not board a boat by any other means.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the mantra 'Sutrāmāṇaṃ pṛthivīṃ dhāmanehasam,' [one boards] the boat" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.6.8).
May we ascend for our well-being the Sutrāman, the Earth, the faultless Dhāman, the good refuge Aditi, the excellent guide, the divine ship with fair oars, sinless and leakless.
May we ascend for our well-being the Sutrāman, the Earth, the peerless, the good refuge, Aditi, the excellent guide, the divine ship with beautiful oars—sinless and leakless. 10.

The celestial realm (dyuloka) is praised by way of its resemblance to a boat: may we ascend—that is, may we mount—for our well-being, for non-destruction, and for the attainment of divinity, this heaven which stands like a ship; a well-protecting (*sutrāmāṇam*) vessel that protects well; the broad earth (*pṛthivīm*), free from blemish (*anehasam*), devoid of evil; providing excellent shelter (*suśarmāṇam*), endowed with beautiful happiness; Aditi, the non-deficient; possessing good guidance (*supraṇītim*), a good leader who leads excellently; divine (*daivīm*), belonging to the gods; having beautiful oars (*svaritrām*), equipped with wood capable of carrying water; sinless (*anāgasam*), free from fault; not flowing away (*asravantīm*), not going—indestructible; [this] heaven, which exists like a boat. May we ascend it for our safety and for the attainment of the state of a deity.
In the case of *roherliṅ*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied by the rule "liṅy āśiṣy aṅ."
O all you worthy of sacrifice, speak in our favor for our protection; save us from the evil-minded who would strike us down.
With our true invocation of the gods, we call upon you, O hearing deities, for aid and for well-being.

O all you who are worthy of worship, speak in our favor for our protection; save us from the evil-minded one who assails us. May we truly invoke you with a prayer to the gods. O gods, who hear us, grant us your aid for our well-being. 11.
O you who are worthy of sacrifice, O all you gods, speak for our protection; speak out for our sake.
And having been invoked, protect us from those who are malevolent and intent on harming us.
If you do this, then, O gods, hear the hymns spoken by us, and [protect us] with that true invocation of the gods which accords with reality.
*Devahūtiḥ* is praise, because by it the gods are invoked; with that we would invoke— that is, call them— what for?
For protection against enemies, for well-being, for security, and for the increase of one's livelihood.

Drive away disease, drive away every lack of invocation, and drive away the stinginess of the ill-intentioned who offer no gifts. O Gods, cast our enemies far from us; grant us wide protection for our well-being. 12. Drive away disease, drive away every lack of invocation, and drive away the stinginess of the ill-intentioned who offer no gifts. O Gods, cast our enemies far from us; grant us wide protection for our well-being. 12.
O gods, drive away—cast far off and separate—from us *amīvā*, that is, disease and the like, or the enemy who increases disease.
Likewise, separate from us *viśvām anāhutim*, the lack of invocation toward the gods, or the great enemy of the gods.
Furthermore, cause *arātim*—the stingy one, the mind of greed, or the enemy who does not give oblations to the gods—to depart.

Moreover, O you who possess great power, drive far away from us—the enemy who intends evil and desires harm—his wicked intellect that is difficult to perceive and hard to understand; likewise, drive away all hatred.
In this way, grant us wide protection and well-being for our welfare.

That mortal man, O gods, becomes entirely unharmed—uninjured by anything—and prospers in mind, increasing through cattle and other possessions.
Likewise, after the performance of his sustaining ritual acts (*dharman*), that man is born forth preeminently through offspring, such as sons and others.

O Ādityas, O divine Ādityas, that man whom you lead across all difficulties and evils—whether they be misfortunes or enemies—by means of your guidance and auspicious paths, for his well-being and security, leading him safely upon the right path;
he is the one who prospers. This is the connection of the thought.

O Gods, that chariot which you protect in the winning of booty, which you, O Maruts, protect in the winning of heroes when the prize is set—O Indra, may we mount for our well-being that early-faring chariot, the ridge-piercing, the uninjured. O Gods, that chariot which you protect in the winning of booty, which you, O Maruts, protect in the winning of heroes when the prize is set—O Indra, may we mount for our well-being that early-faring chariot, the ridge-piercing, the uninjured.

O gods, O deities, that chariot which you protect and guard at the winning of booty—whether it be the acquisition of food or the attainment of nourishment—and which you protect, O Maruts, in the contest for heroes; for "śūrasātau" is a name for battle, where heroes are exhausted (sīyante) or where heroes are destroyed by the combatants; in that battle, when wealth is placed and staked, for the sake of that prize.
The locative case is used according to Pāṇini’s rule *nimittātkarmasaṃyoge* (2.3.36).
"Protect [him] with reference to that.
Because Indra is the foremost among all the gods, the subsequent verse speaks specifically with reference to him alone.
O Indra, [bring] that foremost of all, who sets out at dawn for battle, who is victorious, worthy of worship, and unassailable by anyone;
or rather,
one who does not obstruct the Maruts who have Indra as their ally.
May we ascend that chariot for our well-being and for our protection.
1. Ga: "are split here"; Ta-Bha: "are broken here.
2. Ga-Ta-Bha: "of the interior.
3. Ta-Ma: "by the upper part of the salutation."
In the Prāyaṇīya sacrifice, for the limb consisting of the Pathyā-svastī offering, "svasti naḥ padhyām" is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā), and the following verse is the offering verse (yājyā).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'svasti naḥ padhyāsu dhanvasu' and 'agne naya supathā rāye asmān'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.3).
At the *udayanīyā* [offering], these same *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are reversed;
and it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are also reversed."

May there be well-being for us on our paths and in the desert wastes; may there be well-being in the waters and in the assembly rich in light. May there be well-being for us in the wombs that bring forth sons; O Maruts, bestow well-being upon us for the sake of wealth. (15) O Maruts, gods who are the destroyers of enemies, grant us well-being—auspiciousness—in our *padhyas*, that is, in regions suitable for travel and delightful to reach. Likewise, grant us well-being in the *dhanvas*, waterless desert lands, characterized by the production of water. Similarly, grant us well-being in the *apsu* (waters). Furthermore, grant us well-being in the *vṛjana*, the force of the enemy’s army equipped with weapons (*svarvat*), which bends or overcomes us. Grant us well-being in our *putrakṛthas*, the wombs of women that produce sons, so that there may be security such that the embryos do not fall. Moreover, O Maruts, bestow (*dadhātana*) well-being and security upon us for the sake of *rāyaḥ* (wealth), characterized by cattle and other possessions.

May Svasti (Welfare) indeed be our supreme guide on the distant path—she who is rich in wealth and who approaches the desirable. May she protect us at home and in the wilderness; may she, guarded by the gods, be easy of access for us. For Svasti is indeed the most excellent bringer of well-being on the far path; she is the one who possesses riches and approaches the desirable sacrifice. May that Earth protect us at home—that is, in our house—and likewise in the wilderness, in the place to be traversed, or in the forest and such regions. Furthermore, may that Earth, whose guardians are the gods, be a source of pleasant dwelling for us.

Thus, O Viśve Ādityās—O all you gods—and O Aditi, goddess mother of the gods, the wise singer, Pṛthī by name, has magnified you; and Sūnu, the son of that Pṛthī, namely Gaya, has likewise magnified you, O lords, O heroes, with this immortal hymn. Thus has the divine Gaya praised the people. *eva pte muniḥ avīvṛdhat vo viśve ādityā adite manīṣī | īśānāso naro amartyenāstāvi jano divyo gayena || 17 ||* "Thus, O Viśve Ādityās—all you gods—and O Aditi, goddess mother of the gods, *manīṣī* (the wise one), the singer, *pte*—he who bears this name—the son *sūnuḥ* named *gayaḥ*, has *evā* (in this manner) *avīvṛdhat* (magnified)."

1. And in the places [marked] ga, ta, bha, and ṇa; 2. in the body [marked] ga, ta, bha, ṇa, ma, ya, ra, la, va, and śa, [the word] "of us" (naḥ) is used for "our" (asmākam); 3. in the place [marked] ga, ta, bha, and ṇa, [the verb] "may it be" (bhavatu) is used; 4. in the place [marked] ga, ta, and ṇa, [the pronoun] "us" (asmān) is used; 5. in the place [marked] ta, [the word] "in the house" (gṛhe) is used; 6. in the place [marked] ga, ta, ṇa, ma, ya, ra, la, va, and śa, [the vocative] "O you who are like a mother" (mātṛbhūte) followed by a name is used.
He caused to increase by means of praises. This is the form of the root *vṛdh* (to increase) in the *luṅ* tense.

By that immortal host of gods, free from human attributes, who—when praised—cause men to become lords and masters of wealth, that divine host dwelling in heaven has been extolled by me, Gaya, by name. [The form *astāvi* is the aorist (luṅ) of the root *stu* in the passive voice with the suffix *caṅ*.]
The fourth hymn, consisting of seventeen verses beginning with "kathā," is the seer's own composition by Gaya Jñāta and is dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
The twelfth verse, "yāṃ me dhiyam," is a Triṣṭubh similar to the Ṣoḍaśī, while the others are Jagatīs.
Thus it has been enumerated: "kathā yāṃ me triṣṭup."
The application is concluded.

How [is it] among the gods? At whose path? We shall meditate upon the one named Sumantu so that he may hear us. Who will be gracious? Which one will perform a human service for us? Which one will turn toward us with aid? 1. How? Among the gods? Of which one? At the path? O Sumantu! By name! May he hear! We meditate.
The seer, addressing himself, says: Narāśaṃsa.

The dual form "ubhe" (both) retains the original accent of its constituent parts according to the rule "vanaspatyādiṣu yugapat. The separation [of words] in the *saṃhitā* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). Praise with song this one named *Pūṣan*, who is to be praised by men and who nourishes the singers by bestowing wealth; likewise, praise with song this one named *Agnā-iḍa*, who is most difficult to attain (*agādham*), kindled by the gods (*deveddham*)—that is, ignited by seers such as Vāmadeva and others—and who is Agni. Praise him with your hymn.
Likewise, "with Sūryā and Māma Candramas. *Mā* is an epithet of Candramas; since he measures (*māti*) the fortnight (*pakṣa*), Candramas is called *Mā*.

One should praise these deities with hymns characterized by their respective attributes: Sūrya and Candramas; Yama, who dwells in the *div* (heavenly world); Trita, who is extended (*tata*) and vast (*tripula*) among the *keśu* (rays or hair), spread out by his own majesty, or occupying three stations; Indra; Vāta (the wind); Upama (the time of dawn); Aktu (the night); and the Aśvins.

With what speech does Bṛhaspati, the possessor of many heroes, grow great through well-fashioned hymns? May Aja Ekapād hear these invocations with his auspicious calls and chants; may Ahi Budhnya hear these offerings.
The sage, the wise one—by what song does Bṛhaspati grow great through well-fashioned hymns? May Aja Ekapād hear these invocations with his many songs of praise; may Ahi Budhnya hear them. 4.
How—in what manner or by what means—does Agni, the seer of far-reaching wisdom, become possessed of many praises?
There is a repetition of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*).
Alternatively,
the letter *r* is a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) applied to the word *nu*.
He becomes endowed with abundance and accompanied by gods.
By what song or hymn of praise does he become highly honored?
Bṛhaspati, the god so named, is magnified by beautiful hymns (*suvṛktibhiḥ*);
likewise is Ekapād.

The *ekapāt*—so called because he moves falling alone without a companion—and likewise the *aja*, the god of that name who sustains heaven, both increase through hymns (*arkas*) consisting of beautiful invocations; these three gods grow great. The plural number is used here with reference to the triad.
The root *vṛdh* means "to increase.
By grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*), the suffix *śap* is replaced by *ilu*.
And may *Ahibudhnya*, the deity so named, hear our invocations as we offer these oblations.
At the birth of Dakṣa, when the rite is recited, O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two kings are invoked;
Aryaman, whose paths are unfailing and who possesses many riches, is the sevenfold invoker among the births that have the forms of Viṣṇu.

Of Dakṣa, or of Aditi, at birth, in the sacred law, you seek to win over the two kings, Mitra and Varuṇa. Aryaman, whose path is unassailable and who possesses many riches, is the sevenfold invoker among the births that have the form of Viṣṇu. 5.
O unshaken Earth, at the birth of the skillful Sun—when he was born, during his sacred observance, that is, in his sacrificial rite—you serve Mitra and Varuṇa, the two shining Kings.
The word *vā* has the sense of comparison:
"Just as you, having become the altar (*vedi*), attended upon them, so may you do now also in our sacrifice"—thus does he pray to the Earth.
He, Aryaman, the restrainer and controller of the enemies—the darknesses—is Sūrya. Among births and actions of manifold forms, he is the one who releases [them] day after day;
he is the one in whom the seven *hotṛ*s—meaning the seven rays—offer and pour forth the essences. He is the one whose path is not false, being devoid of untruthful light.
For one who is moving with haste because his path is restricted becomes one whose path is unrestricted.
Pururatha:
a chariot speeds along.
Every day, due to the difference in the time of eating, it becomes difficult to discern.
Or rather:
O Aditi, O morning twilight, at the birth of Dakṣa—that is, at the rite known as the rising of the Sun.
The meaning is "standing at the beginning of the word *ucyatu*.
By the force of the Vedic text, the word *vā* means either "at the birth of Dakṣa" or "from you at your own birth," [the phrase being] "from Dakṣa.
The two kings are "radiant."

According to the Vedic scripture, “Mitra and Varuṇa are day and night” (Ai. Brā. 4.10), Mitra and Varuṇa are said to be day and night.
You attend upon them;
how so?
Regarding its entry:
for the purpose of the twilight, it enters the night, [and] the lowest part of the day.
The latter half [of the verse] is as before.

The *saptahotṛ* [formula]. This is a form derived from the root *van*, meaning "to choose. It signifies that Bharadvāja and others are the *hotṛ*s—meaning the officiating priests or chanters—at my joints (*parvan*).
Alternatively, he is the *saptahotṛ*. He is one whose seven priests (*hotṛ*) are accompanied by *malimlu* and *Aṃhasaspati*.
Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "In the birth of Dakṣa, in his action, or in his vow, [there are] two kings," and so forth (*Nirukta* 11.23).

May they all, the swift ones who hear our invocation, come running at our call; may the prize-winners, whose speed is measured by the thousand, hear us—those who by their own nature were born for great booty in the battles.

May they, the swift ones who hear our invocation, all come running at our call; may the prize-winners, who run measured courses, win a thousandfold like the very act of winning the sacrifice itself—those great ones who by their own nature have been born for the spoils in battles. 6.

Hearing our invocation, the swift ones, the powerful, those of measured pace who traverse the path, all the well-known coursers—the steeds such as the bay horses (*harya*) and others that serve as the vehicles for Indra and the other gods—let them hear our call. Of what sort are they? At the *medhasāti*—the sacrifice where praises (*medhāḥ*) are shared and enjoyed—they, being themselves great givers of thousands, let them hear. Those who are present in the *samithas*—a name for battle, so called because warriors meet there—in those battles, they have brought forth great wealth; they seize it from the enemies. *Hagra* means "to seize."
With hymns of praise, bring Vāyu, who yokes his chariot, Puraṃdhi, and Pūṣan for your friendship;
for they, being well-disposed and of one mind, follow the will of the god Savitṛ in his impulse.

With hymns of praise, bring Vāyu, who yokes his chariot, and Puraṃdhi, and Pūṣan, for the sake of friendship; for they, being well-disposed and wise, follow the will of the divine Savitṛ in his impulse. 7.

O you praisers, do you—by means of hymns characterized by the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, and other such meters—bring forward for friendship and for joint ritual action Vāyu, who yokes the chariot (the harnesser of the chariot), the *puraṃdhri* (the one of many deeds), Indra, Pūṣan, and him who bears this name as well.
Act so that they become our friends through the bestowing of wealth and other gifts.

For indeed, because those gods are mindful, endowed with knowledge, and possessed of consciousness, being of one mind with one another, they attend to and perform the sacrifice (kratu) within the impulse (savīman) of Savitṛ—the god Āditya, the impeller of all; therefore, you too should perform it.
We invoke for our prosperity the three times seven flowing rivers, the great waters, the forest trees, and the mountains;
we call upon Agni, Kṛśānu, Tiṣya, and Rudra—the divine one among the Rudras—to their common dwelling place.

We invoke for our protection the three, the seven, the flowing rivers, the great waters, the lords of the forest, the mountains, Agni, Kṛśānu, the archers, Tiṣya at his station, and Rudra, the son of Rudra, among the Rudras. 8.

"Triḥ": thrice. "Sapta": numbering seven. "Sasrāḥ": flowing. "Nadyaḥ": rivers. Sarasvatī, Sarayū, and Sindhu are the principal ones among the groups of rivers; [the term refers to] those rivers beginning with them. "Mahīḥ": great. "Apaḥ": their waters, for the purpose of the Soma-consecration (in the ritual act).
[Note: 1. ta-mu-vrate karmaṇi; 2. na4.5.6.8-bhava-pravṛddhā].

The trees—the wooden vessels such as the *camasa* cups; the mountains—the pressing-stones (*grāvan*) used for the extraction of Soma; Agni, the performer of the oblation; *Kṛśānu*, the Gandharva by name who drinks the Soma; the *Vastṛs*, the Gandharvas who are his followers and discharge arrows; *Tippa*, the constellation; and *Rudriya*, Rudra by name, the recipient of the sacrificial portion, or Rudra, the lord of the remnants of the sacrifice—I invoke all these at the *sadhastha*.
That which they stand upon together is the *sadhastha*, namely, the sacrifice.
While those Rudras are performing hymns of praise, we invoke them for that purpose; that is, we call upon them as objects of praise.

May Sarasvatī, Sarayu, and Sindhu come with their waves, great and mighty, with their protection, they who carry us along. O divine Waters, Mothers, furtherers of our work, praise us with milk rich in ghee and honey-sweet. 9. Sarasvatī, Sarayu, Sindhu—with their waves, great, mighty, with their protection—may they come, they who carry us along. O divine Waters, Mothers, furtherers [of our work], [with] milk rich in ghee, honey-sweet—for us, sing [this praise]. 9.

May these twenty-one rivers—the Sarasvatī, the Sarayū, the Sindhu, and others—great (*mahīḥ*), exceedingly vast (*mahīḥ*) even among the great (*mahaḥ*), accompanied by waves (*ūrmi-bhiḥ*), come with their protection (*vasā*) for the sake of our sacrifice; may they approach. Then may the divine (*devīḥ*), playful (*devana-śīlāḥ*), motherly (*mātaraḥ*), and impelling (*sūdayitnvaḥ*) Waters grant us milk (*payaḥ*) rich in ghee (*ghṛtavat*) and honeyed (*madhumat*) for our own sake. May they bestow it upon us.

And may the Mother, Bṛhaddivā, hear us; and Tvaṣṭṛ, the Father, with the divine Jartṛs, [grant] splendor. May Ṛbhukṣan, Vāja, Rathaspati, and Bhaga—the delightful one—protect us, the praise of him who exerts himself in worship. 10. And may the Mother, Bṛhaddivā, hear us; and Tvaṣṭṛ, the Father, with the divine Jartṛs, [grant] splendor. May Ṛbhukṣan, Vāja, Rathaspati, and Bhaga—the delightful one—protect us, the praise of him who exerts himself in worship. 10.

She whose great (*mahatī*) *divā*—that is, light—is [her own], she, the Mother, the Mother of the Gods (*devamātā*), may she hear our prayer (*āmantraṇa*).

Likewise, may Tvaṣṭṛ—by name, the father of all, along with the gods (devāḥ) such as Indra and others, and the divine wives (janayaḥ), the consorts of the gods—hear our speech. Also, may Ṛbhukṣan (Indra), Vāja (the younger Saudhanvana brother who assists him), Rathaspati (the lord of the chariot), Bhaga, the delightful (raṇvaḥ) and praiseworthy (śaṃsaḥ) host of Maruts, and thereafter protect (pātu)—that is, guard us—the singer who praises and extols us.

Delightful to behold like a food-filled dwelling, auspicious is the praise of the Rudras, the Maruts. May we, glorious with cattle among the people, O Gods, ever be united with nourishment. 11 Delightful; at the sight; like one possessing food; a dwelling; auspicious; of the Rudras; of the Maruts; the praise; with cattle; may we be; glorious; among the people; hither; always; O Gods; with nourishment; may we be united. 11
In their manifestation and appearance, the host of Maruts is delightful; like a dwelling-place rich in food, it becomes the abode of the singers.
The praise of those Maruts, the sons of Rudra, is auspicious and brings about a benevolent disposition.
It is excellent and auspicious.
1. [The hymns] of the Rudras; [Taraṇi 6.7.8–Bha 1.2.6: the Rudras are the hymns].
Therefore, among the people (*vrajeṣu*), in the midst of men, may we be glorious (*yaśasaḥ*) through cattle (*gobhiḥ*).
And immediately thereafter, O gods (*devāsaḥ*), may we always (*sadā*) attend upon you (*sacemahi*) with fuel (*viḷayā*) characterized by oblations (*havir-lakṣaṇena*).
O Maruts, O Indra, O gods, O Varuṇa, O Mitra—whatever thought you have granted to me, cause that to swell like a cow for the sake of milk; will you not, O heroes, carry us upon your chariot?
O Maruts, O Indra, O Gods, O Varuṇa, O Mitra—whatever prayer you have granted me, cause that to swell like a cow in her pasture; will you not carry my songs upon your chariot? 12.
O Maruts, O Indra, O Gods, O Varuṇa, O Mitra—since you have indeed bestowed this wisdom (*dhī*) upon me, having granted it to me.
In the word *marutaḥ*, there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) due to the division of the sentence;

Swell this prayer with its fruit; cause it to flow forth, as one causes a cow to swell with milk for milking.

Just as they nourish a cow that has recently calved with milk, so [do we nourish you].
Furthermore, O Vājas, do you carry our praises many times upon your own chariot;

O Maruts, will you not surely take notice of us, your kinsmen, as we approach?
Wherein we first gathered together at the navel [of the earth], there may Aditi establish our kinship.
Perhaps, O Maruts, you will indeed take notice of this our kinship; where at the first encounter we are joined together in common purpose, there may Aditi establish our bond of kinship. 13.
The word *vaṅga* is used in the vocative case.
O Maruts, may you awaken us—that is, wake us up—many times (*kuvit*). Thus, may you attend to us.
Because of its connection with the word *kuvit*, the first syllable is not subject to the rule of anudātta (unaccented).
Do not cause us distress by making us objects of hostility for our own kinsmen and relatives; know this.

Therefore, on the navel of the earth—that place characterized as the *uttaravedi* where we may first come together with the oblation—there let Aditi, the mother of the gods, establish for us kinship and alliance with men.
For those two, Heaven and Earth, the great divine mothers, have brought the gods here by their birth, O worthy ones of sacrifice.

Both of them, the two great divine Mothers, Heaven and Earth, worthy of sacrifice by virtue of their birth, sustain both [worlds] with their supports; together with the Fathers, they pour forth abundant seeds.

These two, indeed, Heaven and Earth, the two great goddesses, worthy of sacrifice through their origin, sustain both from here with their nourishments; together with the Fathers, they sprinkle many seeds. 14.

O Mothers, the two fashioners of the entire world, therefore great and vast, worthy of divine praise, deserving of sacrifice—those two, Heaven and Earth, by their very birth, have indeed reached the gods, Indra and the others;
for they truly encompass them. We come together; we shall unite. (Note: *sacema* is understood as "we may join" or "we may associate.")

A seer (kavi) is one of expansive wisdom; one who possesses powerful strength;
one whose activity consists in the expansion of the meaning of the mantras;
one endowed with abundant praise; a knower of Truth (ṛtajñā), a perceiver of sacrifice; and one desiring wealth (draviṇasyu).
The augment *suk* is added by the rule "after all nominal stems [the suffix *kyac* is applied] in the sense of longing. A clear statement of this very point is found in the word *draviṇasaccakānaḥ*,
which means "desiring wealth such as that beginning with *pad* (foot-wealth)."

The wise sage, Gaya, the seer, in the manner thus described, has in this hymn caused the divine births—the gods born in heaven—to swell and increase by means of *ukthas*, that is, words and prayers of praise. This is the meaning: he has praised them.
Thus, the son of Pluti, the wise one, O Ādityas, O Aditi, has magnified the whole world.
The lords, the heroes, have been praised by the immortal; the divine folk have been extolled by Gaya.
Thus, O Ādityas, O Aditi, the wise son has increased your strength. The lords, the heroes, have been praised by the immortal; the divine folk have been extolled by Gaya. 17.
Thus, from the flood, the son has increased for you, O all Ādityas, O Aditi, the wise one. The lords, the heroes, have been praised by the immortal; the divine folk have been extolled by Gaya. 17.
