O wise ones, you two, at this sacrifice, bestow wealth and riches;
the root *yaj* here has the sense of giving—
grant them to us with favor.
O three goddesses, sit upon this wide sacrificial grass; we have prepared a pleasant seat for you.
May the goddess Ilā, whose path is ghee, enjoy this well-placed human sacrifice and these oblations.

O three goddesses, sit upon this wide sacrificial grass; we have prepared for you a pleasant seat. May the goddess Ilā, whose path is ghee, enjoy the sacrifice performed by man and the well-placed oblations. 8.
O three goddesses, beginning with Ilā— yea, the three goddesses— sit down upon this most spacious (*varīyaḥ*) sacrificial grass (*barhiḥ*).
The accusative case is used here according to the rule *kālādhvanoḥ* [Pāṇini 2.3.5],
meaning "sit down for an exceedingly long duration" upon it.
Why is this so? To that he says:
"O you, for your sake we have made this wide-spreading wheel (*cakram*) comfortable (*syonam*).
There is no *nighāta* (elision of the accent) because of the difference in sentence structure.

May these goddesses—*Iḷā*, so named; *Sarasvatī*, the radiant one; *Ghṛtapadī*, whose feet are dripping with clarified butter; and *Bhāratī*, endowed with the power of consecration (*dīkṣā*)—just as they partook of the oblations in the sacrifice of Manu, so may they graciously accept and enjoy our sacrifice and the well-placed offerings.
The *yājyā* for the sacrifice of the animal dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ is "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ...
The ritual manual (*sūtra*) also states: "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, that beautiful form which has attained [beauty], golden-hued, well-supported, bestowing vigor" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).
O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, since you have attained beauty, you have become a companion to the Aṅgirases;
as one who knows the way, do you worship the gods at their path, O giver of wealth, possessor of beautiful jewels, according to our desire.

O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, since you have attained beauty, since you became the companion of the Aṅgirases, do you, the wise one, desiring it, sacrifice at the path of the gods as the giver of wealth, possessing beautiful jewels. 9.

O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, that beauty—which is to say, the state of having an auspicious form—that you have attained through the oblations; and that you have become our companion, the one who exists together with us as an ally, O Aṅgiras. (Note: In the word *ānaṭ*, the suffix *tap* of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) has been elided after the root *aj*.)

O giver of wealth (*draviṇodaḥ*), giver of riches, and therefore possessor of excellent jewels (*suratnaḥ*) and great treasure (*sudhanaḥ*), you—desiring the oblations (*uśan haviṃṣi*), being wise (*vidvān*) and knowing "this is his, this is his"—approach (*upa yakṣi*) the food (*pāthaḥ*) of the gods;
offer it to them.
In the Niṣkevalya [Śastra] dedicated to Vanaspati, the verse beginning with "O Vanaspati, with the cord" is the opening hymn.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "To the gods, O Vanaspati, the oblations; O Vanaspati, with the cord, bind [the victim]"—these are the opening hymns (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.5).

1. The two Hotṛ-priests have gone; O Vanaspati, being wise, lead [the offerings] along the cord to the path of the gods. May the god make them savory and prepare the oblations for the swift steeds; O Heaven and Earth, hear my call! 10. O Vanaspati, with the cord, having led [them] along, you who are wise, bring [the offerings] to the path of the gods. May the god make [them] savory; may he prepare the oblations for the swift steeds. O Heaven and Earth, hear my invocation! 10.

O Vanaspati, you who know the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) as a modification of the forest tree, having led it with its own rope—having bound and fastened it—bring near, that is, convey, the food (*anna*) for the gods, Indra and the others, to their path.
Then may the divine Vanaspati make it palatable by the offering of the oblation;
thus, making the oblations offered by us, may he prepare them for the gods.
Likewise, may Heaven and Earth—the two worlds—protect and guard my invocation, which is my call directed toward the gods.

O Agni, bring Varuṇa for our sacrifice; bring Indra from heaven and the Maruts from the mid-air. May all the worshipful ones sit upon the sacred grass. Svāhā! May the immortal gods rejoice. 11. O Agni, bring Varuṇa for our sacrifice; bring Indra from heaven and the Maruts from the mid-air. May all the worshipful ones sit upon the sacred grass. Svāhā! May the immortal gods rejoice. 11.
O Agni, for our sacrifice, bring hither from the heavenly world and from the intermediate space Indra, Varuṇa, and the Maruts to our offering.
Let all those adorable gods worthy of worship sit upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) there.
Then let the immortal gods, free from the law of death, rejoice in the oblations offered with the cry of "Svāhā! and gladden themselves.
The third hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "bṛhaspate," is the seerage of Bṛhaspati, the descendant of Aṅgiras. The ninth verse is a Jagatī, while the remaining ten are Triṣṭubhs.
With this hymn, the seeker has praised the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman, which is the means for achieving the supreme human goal.
Therefore, this hymn is dedicated to that very deity.
For it is stated in the *Bṛhaddevatā*: "Then Bṛhaspati praised with this hymn that knowledge through which one attains the supreme Brahman, the excellent light" (*Bṛhaddevatā* 7.109).
And it has been enumerated: "The ninth [verse], a Jagatī, 'O Bṛhaspati,' praised the knowledge of Bṛhaspati.
The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn (*sūkta*) has been explained.
Among the oblations of the Devasū offerings, the first invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) belongs to the mantra beginning with "Bṛhaspati, the Lord of Speech" (*vācaspati*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Bṛhaspati, the first beginning of speech, like swans with their companions, uttering cries" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.11).

O Bṛhaspati, that which was the first beginning of speech, when they sent it forth while bestowing names—that which was their most excellent and stainless essence, hidden in the secret cave, has now been revealed through their love. O Bṛhaspati! First! Of speech! The beginning! That! Which! Forth! They sent! Bestowing names! That! Of them! Most excellent! That! Stainless! Was! Through love! That! Of them! Hidden! In the secret cave! Manifest! 1.
Having seen children who had understood the meaning of the Vedas through this hymn, Bṛhaspati, smiling, spoke to himself as a self-awakening:
"O Bṛhaspati, O inner self! Those who, immediately after being born and even before the utterance of other speech, bestow a name—that is, a designation.
(Note: Ga, Ta, Mu read *vismayamānaḥ*.)

Whatever objects children place upon things, and whatever they have been prompted to do, that becomes the "first part" of their speech. Since they first utter words such as "Daddy" and so forth, and afterwards speak other words, it is therefore called the "first part" of speech.
Behold the children situated in this state!

Likewise, now that which was their best, most praiseworthy, and sinless knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas— that knowledge of theirs was hidden in the cave (guhā), meaning it was concealed; through *preṇā*— the elision of the letter *m* being Vedic—
the [knowledge] manifests through love (*premṇā*).
The meaning is that during the time of Vedic study, Sarasvatī reveals [the truth] from her own purposes.
In this way, one should reflect upon the Āraṇyaka passage beginning with, "O Bṛhaspati, at the time of wonder, the first point of speech" (Ai. Ā. 1.3.6).
Where the wise have fashioned speech with their mind, purifying it like groats through a sieve—there friends recognize their friendships; a blessed splendor is deposited within their speech.
Like sifting grain through a sieve, purifying it—there where the wise have fashioned speech with their mind; there friends recognize their friendships. An auspicious mark is set upon their speech. 2.
It is called *titaūnā* because one is purified by means of it;
or alternatively:

The word *titauḥ* means "sieve" (*natā vistṛtā bhṛṣṭayavā aneti*). The suffix *ḍa* is applied according to *Uṇādisūtra* 5.22: *tanoter ḍaḥ sanvac ca*, which prescribes the suffix *ḍa* after the root *tan* and causes it to behave like the desiderative (*sanvadbhāva*).
Due to this *sanvadbhāva*, the reduplication occurs.

By means of the Sun, whose etymology has been stated, just as someone purifies groats that are difficult to cleanse, so too do the wise—the intelligent and learned—purifying that which is the suffix from its base and the word from that [suffix], when—at which time—in the assembly of the learned, they fashion speech with the mind joined to wisdom.
This is the form of the root *kṛ* in the *luṅ* tense.

At that time, those who are friends (*sakhāyaḥ*), having the same renown, possessing knowledge of two or three branches of the Veda, recognize—their friends being those things arising within them—the knowledges belonging to those friendships. They come to know them.
Alternatively: friends sit with their speech bound; they know the friendships of each respective speech. The meaning is that they obtain prosperity through the proper application of speech.
Therefore, auspicious and beautiful fortune is established in their speech.
The prefix *adhi* indicates the sense of the locative case;
the meaning is that we perceive the knowledge of the meaning within their speech.

The *titau* is a winnowing fan; one should reflect upon the *Nirukta* passage beginning with, "It is like a stretched [cloth], or like chaff, or as fine as a sesame seed, or like flour through a sieve" (*Nirukta* 4.10).
The two verses beginning with "By sacrifice, they [attained] the track of speech" (*yajñena vācaḥ*) are, respectively, the *yājyās* for the animal sacrifice and the *puroḍāśa* offering to Vāgdevī.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "'By sacrifice, they [attained] the track of speech'—these two [verses]; 'The gods generated divine speech'" (*āśva. śrau. 3. 8*).

By means of sacrifice they followed the track of speech; they found it entered among the seers. Having brought it forth, they distributed it in many places; the seven singers chant toward it together.

By means of sacrifice, they followed the track of Speech; they found her entered into the seers. Having brought her forth, they distributed her in many places. The seven singers celebrate her together.
The wise say that this word *padavīya* is derived from the root *i* (to go) with the suffix *yat* added after *pada*, which has already been understood [as a prior member].
There is an absence of *guṇa* substitution because a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not invariably applicable.
A path that is to be traversed by means of a footstep is called *padavīya*.
They reached that path of speech by means of sacrifice;
they found and obtained that speech which had entered into the seers (*ṛṣis*), those who perceive objects beyond the senses.
Thereafter, having brought and gathered that speech, they distributed it in many places, throughout various regions.
The meaning is that they caused all human beings to study [the Vedas].
Birds (rebhāḥ), uttering such speech, sing together toward and gather around the seven meters (chandāṃsi), such as the Gāyatrī and others, which have taken the form of birds.
1. That speech which has gone forth—[it is] sevenfold (according to T1, T2, T3, T7).
And one, though seeing, has not seen this speech; and one, though hearing, does not hear it.
But to another she has revealed her body, like a longing, well-dressed wife to her husband.

And yet, one man, though seeing, has not perceived Speech; and another, though hearing, does not hear her. But to another she has revealed her body, as a lovingly-desiring, well-robed wife to her husband.
The word *va* signifies "one"; it means "a single one.
The word *uta* has the sense of "also" (*api*).
Even while seeing and even while reflecting with the mind, he does not see this speech; for he sees it only because there is no fruit in mere seeing.
Even while hearing, he does not hear this speech, because there is no fruit in mere hearing. He alone is such.
By this meaning, the ignorant person is described.
With the third quarter [of the verse], he speaks of one who has known the meaning of the Vedas:
"To him alone (*asmai ekasmai*), even though he is but one, she has extended (*visasre*) her own body (*tanvam*); that is, Speech herself causes herself to go forth in various ways."
The meaning is that she discloses herself, that is, she makes herself manifest.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

just as a loving wife, desiring union, beautifully clothed in fine garments, reveals herself of her own accord to her husband for the sake of sexual enjoyment at the end of her fertile period; so too does she reveal herself.

"Likewise, he sees her and hears her"—this is a praise of one who has known the meaning of the Vedas. The *Nirukta* passage beginning with "Even a single person, seeing, sees Speech" (Nirukta 1.19) should be consulted here.
Moreover, they say that in friendship he drinks deeply; they do not urge him on even in contests for prizes.
He moves about with the illusion of one who has no cow; having heard the word, he follows that which is fruitless and flowerless.

But they say that he has drunk deeply in friendship; they do not urge him on even in the contests for booty. He moves about with the power of a barren cow; though he has heard the voice, it is without fruit and without flower. 5.
Furthermore, even a single [verse] in the assembly of the learned is called *sragdharā* (the wreath) because it sustains the meaning;
and that is produced by speech.
Therefore, because of its connection with speech, the *vākasasya* is "firmly drunk" (*sthirapīta*).
That is, the honey remains firmly within one's heart;
or alternatively, *sthirapīta* means "having attained firmness."
They say; or rather,
they say it for the sake of making that known.

In the world, people speak of a man who has understood a matter as one who has "drunk" that matter. Furthermore, regarding this person who has understood the matter, [the text says] "among the *vājinas*.
Those for whom speech (*vāk*) is the lord (*inā*, *īśvara*) are the *vājinas*; indeed, matters are dependent upon speech.
They do not even impel [others] toward objects that are to be known through speech;
the word "even" (api) indicates a lack of purpose.
Some do not even follow [them].

The meaning is that he alone is pre-eminently wise. Alternatively, they do not drive him away— that is, they do not exclude him— from the *vājinaḥ*, which are the essential matters to be investigated.
The meaning is that they investigate the entire meaning of the Vedas by placing this very [work] at their forefront.
Thus, one who knows the meaning is praised.
Immediately thereafter, the latter half [of the verse] censures one who merely recites the words.

This person of unknown purpose wanders through the realms of gods and men by means of a deceptive illusion (*māyā*)—which, like a barren cow, is devoid of the capacity to yield milk—that takes the form of speech and fulfills desires.
What is he doing?
He is [producing] that which is fruitless and flowerless.
The meaning of speech is its flower and fruit.
[One should avoid] that which is devoid of meaning.
Or alternatively:
The meaning of the speech concerns sacrifice and the deities. Knowledge pertaining to sacrifice is *yājña*; knowledge pertaining to the deities is *daivata*.
He heard speech that was devoid of these—that is, speech devoid of knowledge concerning the objects of action and so forth.
He behaves as one who has merely heard through the recitation alone;

the meaning is that he conducts himself by uttering the text with authority, just as a barren cow, though fat, moves about creating an illusion by asking, "Does she yield a *droṇa* measure of milk?", or just as a barren tree stands creating the delusion that it blossoms and bears fruit out of season.
In this regard, the *Nirukta* passage beginning with "Even a single grain of the crop of speech, firmly drunk" (*Nirukta* 1.20) should be reflected upon.
He who has abandoned the wise friend—of him there is no share even in speech;
though he may hear, he hears in vain, for he does not know the path of righteous action.
1. *Ta* means "that" (*tat*) which has been drunk by the firm one (*sthirapītam*).
2. *Ga* refers to those things (*yeṣām arthānām*).
3. *Ta*, *4.5.6.8-bha*, *1.2.6.8*: this is the meaning (*ity arthaḥ*).
He who abandons a companion who knows the truth—there is no share for him even in speech; what he hears, he hears in vain, for he does not know the path of righteous action. 6.
*sacividam*.
The word *saci* signifies "friend.
Thus, it means "one who finds a friend."

He who is a student is a friend of the Veda, because he benefits the Veda by preventing the interruption of its tradition. One who knows such a benefactor is "one who knows" (*savit*). That person who abandons—that is, completely forsakes—such a friend, the Veda, which has become a companion to students by assisting them in understanding its own meaning; that person who abandons it by employing it for the sake of another purpose.
The word *tyajati* is derived as a nipātana (irregular formation) according to the rule beginning with *apaspṛdhethām ānucuḥ*.
For that person, there is no portion—no meaningful subject—to be partaken of (*bhajanīya*) in any speech whatsoever, whether worldly or scriptural.
Indeed, whatever this person hears apart from the Veda, he hears it as *alakam*—that is, false and utterly useless.

Because he does not know the path of good deeds—that is, due to a lack of faith, he does not know the path of practice—therefore even his hearing [of the Veda] is fruitless; this is the meaning. The intention behind the second and fourth quarters [of the verse] is shown in the *Āraṇyaka* by the passage beginning with, "He has no share in what is recited" (*Ai. Ā. 3.2.4*).

Likewise, [it is said] by the Adhvaryus: "He who abandons that [sacrifice] has no share in speech; he certainly has a share in the heavenly vault. Regarding this, the following verse is recited. (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15.5)
Friends possessed of eyes and ears have become swift as thought;
some are like water reaching to the mouth, others to the armpits, while others appear as if they have bathed, [piercing] with their hearts.

Some have eyes; some have ears; they are friends. In the swiftness of thought, they have become unequal. Some reach only to the mouth; others reach to the armpits. Some appear as if bathed; others appear as if seen with the heart. //7//

"Having eyes" (*akṣṇavantaḥ*) means possessing eyes. The suffix *anaṅ* is applied to the word *akṣi* [in the plural] according to the rule "it is seen even in the Veda" (*chandasyapi dṛśyate*). The augment *nuṭ* is added by the rule "ano nuṭ. It is called "eye" (*akṣi*) because everything is seen by it. Alternatively, because of its luminous nature (*taijasatva*), it is more distinct than other [senses]. Thus it is heard in scripture: "Therefore, these two are as if more distinct. They are not [merely] endowed with such eyes; they are "having ears" (*karṇavantaḥ*). "Ears" (*karṇau*) are the lower openings; the meaning is that they have cavities fashioned by someone while still in the state of the embryo. Alternatively, they are situated high, having reached the head of the body. They possess the space characterized as the ear. And thus it is recited: "As if reaching, let them rise up in the sky. Such are the "companions" (*sakhāyaḥ*). They are "companions" because they share the same place or knowledge. The meaning is that among those external senses, they possess equal knowledge. Among those "swift as thought" (*manojaveṣu*)—they are "swift as thought" because they are understood or known by the mind, namely, the powers of discernment (*prajñā*)—among them they were "unequal" (*asamāḥ*), i.e., incomparable. Among them, some were "mouth-deep" (*ādaghnāsaḥ*). By the rule for words beginning with *pṛṣodara*, there is the substitution of the vowel *ā*. "Mouth-deep" means lakes whose water has the measure of the mouth; this refers to those of middling discernment. Now, "but some" (*atha tve eke*). Because it is a pronoun, the substitution of *śī* occurs. "Under-the-arm-deep" (*upakakṣāsaḥ*) means lakes whose water has the measure of the vicinity of the armpits; the meaning is that they have little water. By this, he refers to those of little discernment. Likewise, "but some" (*tve eke*)—"worthy" (*sttvā*). The suffix *tvan* is used in the sense of a gerundive (Pāṇini 3.4.14), and that occurs in the sense of "worthiness" (*arha*) by the rule "the gerundives and *tṛc* are also used in the sense of worthiness" (Pāṇini 3.2.169). Worthy of knowledge, like lakes with unshakeable water, they "were seen" (*dadṛśre*), i.e., they appear. By this, he refers to those of great discernment. The syllable *uḥ* is a filler. For the etymological explanation of "having eyes, having ears, companions" (*akṣimantaḥ karṇavantaḥ sakhāyaḥ*), one should look here at the Nirukta (1.9): "The eye is from the root *cakṣ*" (*akṣi cakṣeḥ*), and so forth.
When the horses are well-pleased and swift in their course, when the Brahmins, as friends, perform the sacrifice together—then indeed you distribute [the offerings] by means of the sacrificial paths;
the priests move about, ascending toward the sacred formulation (*brahman*).

When the gods are pleased and the impulses of the mind are swift, when the Brahmins, as companions, perform the sacrifice together here, then you indeed abandon them through their ritual knowledge; those who have forsaken sacred prayer wander away from you.

1. *ga*—From others, from two [classes]: the *sakhāyaḥ* (companions), those of similar lineage, the *brāhmaṇāḥ* (brahmins). In their hearts—that is, within the heart of the wise—when the *taṣṭheṣu* (polished/refined) matters have been determined and conceived, regarding the *manaso javeṣu* (swift movements of the mind), that is, concerning the meanings of the Vedas to be reached through the discernment of merits and defects; *yat* (*yadā*) when they *saṃyajante*, they come together. Here, the root *yaj* signifies the act of bringing about a union.

In this assembly of Brahmins, they completely abandon—that is, they utterly cast aside—a single man whose meaning is unknown, by means of the sciences (*vidyā*) that are to be known, or by their activities;
"oha" is used for the sake of certainty. O Brahmins!
Those for whom Brahman—characterized by knowledge, sacred revelation, truth, and intellect—is being inferred are described as such.
Being of that nature, some wise ones "move about" (*vicaranti*), meaning they proceed according to their desire for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion regarding the meanings of the Vedas.
The particle *u* is used for emphasis.
The Nirukta passage beginning with "hṛdā taṣṭeṣu manasāṃ prajaveṣu" (Nirukta 13.13) should be consulted.
These who do not move forward with the boat, neither as brahmins nor as pourers of the libation— they,
having failed to grasp speech, weave a web of prosperity like those who lack discernment.

These who move neither hither nor thither, who are neither Brahmins nor performers at the Soma-pressing—they, having seized speech with evil intent, weave their web of prosperity like those devoid of understanding. 9.
By this [verse], those ignorant of the meaning of the Vedas are censured:

"Those who are unlearned (*avidvāṃsaḥ*), who do not move with the Brāhmaṇas in this world here below (*arvāk*), and who do not move with the gods in the world beyond (*paraḥ*), they—though called Brāhmaṇas—are not truly Brāhmaṇas devoted to the meaning of the Vedas;
likewise, they are not true performers of sacrifices (*sutekarāsaḥ*)."
The *sutekaras* are the officiating priests (*ṛtvijas*) who prepare the pressed and purified Soma;
they too do not exist, for they are "unborn" (*aprajajñayaḥ*).

They know: "The *kvip* suffix is applied after the roots *ā-hṛ*, *gam*, and *han*. These ignorant men, having reached worldly speech—that is, having attained common discourse—and being joined with that evil, sin-producing speech, are "sinful" (*siri*).
The suffix *vanip* is used here according to the rule "in Vedic meters, *vanip* and *iṣ* [are applied]."
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the suffix *jas* is replaced by *su*.
Having become ploughmen (*sīrin*), they "stretch out" (*tanvate*) the "system" (*tantra*) characterized by agriculture;
that is to say, they carry it out.
The intention is that the meaning of the Vedas must be understood in every respect.

In the *somapravahaṇa* [rite], the verse is "all rejoice" (*sarve nandanti*). And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The three verses beginning with 'O Soma, those [streams] of yours which are bliss-bestowing,' and 'all rejoice when he has arrived with glory'" (*āśva. śrau. 4. 4*).
All friends rejoice in their friend who has arrived with glory, victorious in the assembly;
for him, the one who wipes away sin and is eager for the fathers, he becomes a helpful ally for the sake of the prize-winning steed.

All friends rejoice at the arrival of their friend, who is glorious, peerless in the assembly, and the dispeller of evil. For he becomes one who wins the father’s wealth and is well-prepared for the prize-winning contest. 10.

The companions—those of equal lineage, equal knowledge, all members of the assembly (*sabhyāḥ*)—rejoice, being delighted by means of the glorious Soma, who has come to the sacrifice as a friend of the officiating priests (*ṛtvijām sakhibhūtena*), capable of enduring the assembly (*sabhāsahena*). For that very Soma is the remover of the sin (*kilbiṣaspṛt*) of these people;
for whatever other person than oneself attains excellence (*śraiṣṭhyam aśnute*), he becomes a "sin" (*kilbiṣam*) by virtue of being an object of obstruction.
Just as evil is to be countered by virtuous conduct,
so too is he the counteractor of the enemy, the personification of evil.
Or alternatively:
The sin that arises for these [priests] due to their failure to properly perform the recitation during the sacrifice—that which he wards off is the "remover of sin" (*kilbiṣaspṛt*).
Likewise, you are the "winner of food" (*pitupaṇiḥ*); *pitu* is a name for food, or it refers to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

By that Soma: 1. *ta-bha-mu-yathā*; 2. *ga-bha-mu* [the word] expressing the act of bringing together (*saṃgatakaraṇa*); 3. *ga4-ta1.2.4.6.8-jñāteḥ*; 4. *ga4-ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha-mu-somapravaṇe*; *ta4-somapravāhaṇe*; *ta5-somapravāhā*; 5. *ga4-ta-bhara.6.8-mu-sabhāsāhena*; 6. *ga4-yaḥ śreṣṭhavamaśrute*; *ta-bha-yaḥ śreṣṭhāmaśrute*; 7. *ga-bādhitaṃ*; 8. *ga-ta-bha-taṃ yo*:
he who obtains it, the sacrificer, partakes of it—such is he.
The meaning is that he is the giver of food and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to them.
Furthermore, Soma, who is beneficial and placed within the vessels, is for the sake of *vājina*;
*vājina* refers to sensory power (*indriya*) and vigor (*vīrya*).

He becomes capable, able, sufficient, and competent to perform that for their sake through his vigor (*vīrya*). One should here keep in mind the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with, “All rejoice at the arrival of glory; King Soma is indeed glory,” and ending with, “Vigor is indeed power (*indriya*); for him there is never a lack of vigorous, ageless power” (AiB 1.12).
One, having nourished them, sits chanting the growth of the *ṛc*s; another sings the *gāyatra* song upon the *śakvarī* verses;
one speaks as a *brahmán* the knowledge of all that has been born; and yet another measures out the dimensions of the sacrifice.

One sits nourishing the growth of the *ṛc* verses; another sings the *gāyatra* chant upon the *śakvarī* meters; one speaks the wisdom born of sacred knowledge as a *brahman* priest; and another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice—*oṃ*. 11.

By this [verse], he explains the application of the priestly functions, beginning with the *hotṛ*. One alone is the *hotṛ*, having nourished (*pupuṣvān*) the abundance of the *ṛc*s—that is, their employment in the ritual according to the rule.
The particle *ekaḥ* (one) is for the purpose of emphasis.
One sits reciting many *ṛc*s while nourishing; another alone is the *udgātṛ* priest among the *śakvarī*s;
the *ṛc*s are within the *śakvarī*s.
Indra became capable of striking down the Agniṣṭoma with these [verses]; thus they are called *śakya*.
Upon them he sings the Gāyatra Sāman.

"One alone" refers to the Brahman priest; regarding each thing that has arisen—such as the expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth—he utters the Vedic wisdom or speech concerning what must be done.
For Brahmā indeed is truly capable of knowing everything;
[the absence of the *nighāta* accent here is due to the rule] "there is optionally no *nighāta* when *ca* and other particles are elided.

And one, namely the *adhvaryu*, measures out—that is, he constructs with great precision—the measure (*mātrā*) of the sacrifice, which is the body of the sacrifice, by means of the ritual actions such as the drawing of the cups (*graha*). He fashions it to its full extent.

The meaning was explained in accordance with the Nirukta passage beginning with, “One, having nourished [the sacrifice], sits nourishing through the Ṛc as the Hotṛ, the one worthy of praise” (Nirukta 1.8).
Thus Bṛhaspati praised him who had understood the meaning of the Vedas.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human existence.

Thus ends the second chapter of the eighth Aṣṭaka in the Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa, a commentary on the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious King of Kings, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
The wise Śrī Sāyaṇācārya, through his commentary on the final Aṣṭaka,
is now prepared to clearly explain the second and third chapters.

In this context, the hymn beginning with "devānām" (of the gods) is the fourth hymn in view of the section; it consists of nine verses, is composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter, and has the gods as its deity.
Bṛhaspati, the son of Lokanāman, or indeed Bṛhaspati himself of the lineage of Aṅgiras, is the seer (ṛṣi).
Alternatively, Aditi, the daughter of Dakṣa, is the seer.
And thus it has been enumerated: "Of the gods there are nine; Bṛhaspati, whether worldly or the son of Dakṣa, or Aditi [is the deity]; it is the Daiva-Anuṣṭubh.
The application of the hymn (sūkta) is concluded.
May we proclaim with inspired speech the births of the gods,
so that he may behold them in a later age while the hymns are being recited.
1. The *ga-ta-mu* [verses] are *śakvarī* *ṛc*s.

2. O Gods, we shall now proclaim for you that knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas; we shall speak it forth with inspired praise while the hymns are being recited, so that he who sees may see it in a later age. 1.
He states how Aditi herself gave birth to the Ādityas by means of the Dākṣāyaṇa hymn. In the Bṛhaspatisūkta, that seer describes the manner of the birth of the Ādityas from Aditi:
"We proclaim—the births of the gods, the Ādityas—we declare them forth."
"With *vipaṇyayā*, that is, with clear speech.
In both instances, the plural number is used for honorific purposes; then he speaks as a singular.

That host of gods which was produced in the former age beholds—the present stotṛ who praises them in the later age, while the *ukthas* are being recited and the sacrificial *śastras* are being performed.
The meaning is that even though many ages have passed, he continues to exist, being praised throughout the ritual acts.
From *brahma* was born *vṛttānapada*,
and from that tree *vāśā* were born from *bhuvaḥ*.
Thus, Aditi was born from Dakṣa; she was produced from Dakṣa.
Furthermore, Dakṣa was born from Aditi.
It should not be argued that it is contradictory for an effect produced from something to also be its own cause.
Master Yāska, citing this very passage and raising an objection regarding its contradiction, resolved it as follows:

“‘Dakṣa was born from Aditi, and from Dakṣa, Aditi was born. How can this be possible? They would seem to have been born simultaneously. Or rather, according to the nature of the gods, they may have been born from one another and serve as each other’s material cause” (Nirukta 11.23).
In the sacrifice dedicated to Aditi as the deity, the verse beginning with "Aditirha jajñiṣṭa" is the invitatory prayer (anuvākyā) for the oblation.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "Aditirha jajñiṣṭa sutrāmāṇaṃ pṛthivīṃ dhāmanehasam" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.8).
Aditi was born as she who is your daughter, O Dakṣa;
after her the gods were born, the auspicious ones whose kinship is with immortality.
For Aditi was born from Dakṣa; she who is your daughter—the auspicious ones, whose kinsmen are immortal, the gods were born after her. || 5 ||
Your daughter, O Dakṣa, became Aditi; she indeed gave birth to the Ādityas as her sons.
Regarding this, it is said:
from her the gods were born—auspicious, worthy of praise and worship, and having immortality as their bond.
When she stood there, well-composed in that water,
then, as if from dancers, a thick cloud of dust rose up from you.
O gods, when you stood there in the waters, firmly grasping one another, a thick cloud of dust rose up from that place as if from dancers. 6.
By this subsequent verse, the Ādityas are praised:
O gods, when you stood—well-supported, having perfectly attained your own nature—in that water;
for the Śruti and Smṛti declare: "The waters indeed are all this" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.22), and "In the beginning, he created the waters alone" (Manusmṛti 1.8).
In this water, as if among those dancing, one part of you—intense, unbearable, and consisting of a single ray—departed;
it went toward heaven, with reference to the Sun.
As he will say later: "He cast Mārtaṇḍa away."
As soon as the ascetics, according to their nature, caused the worlds to swell,
you brought forth the sun that was hidden within the ocean.
O gods, just as the *yatis* caused the worlds to overflow, so did you bring forth the sun that was hidden within the ocean. || 7 ||

1. *ta-bha-bhūḥ*—thus [is] *uttānapadaḥ*. 2. *ga₁-mām eva*; *gara-ta₁.₂.₃.₆.₇.₈-ma-amum eva*. 3. *ga-ta-bhara*. 4.1.8—*samānadharmāṇau*. 4. *ga-ta-mu-yā tava*. *yat* means *yadā*. O gods (*devāḥ*), like the *yatayaḥ*.
Or, they are called *yatayaḥ* because they restrain by rain (*vṛṣṭyā niyamayanti*), or because they cause to proceed by raining (*varṣaṇena yātayanti*); thus, the *yatayaḥ* are the clouds (*meghāḥ*).

Just as the waters purify the worlds and the universe, so too did they cause [the sun] to swell and fill it with their own splendors. Here, within the ocean, in the waters, they brought forth and drew out the sun that was hidden away for its morning rising.
Eight sons were born to Aditi from her own body;
with seven she approached the gods, but she cast Mārtāṇḍa away.
Eight were the sons born to Aditi from her own body; with seven she went forth toward the gods, but she cast Mārtāṇḍa away. || 8 ||
The eight sons, beginning with Mitra, belong to Aditi—those who were born and produced from the very body of Aditi. These eight sons of Aditi are enumerated in the *Adhvaryu-brāhmaṇa* as follows:
"We shall enumerate them in order: Mitra, Varuṇa, Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Vivasvat, and Āditya" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 1.13.3).

Likewise, in another section of that same [text], having introduced Aditi, it is recorded: "They gave her the scrapings; she conceived them as seed; from her the four Ādityas were born; she cooked a second [offering]," and so forth, describing the birth of the eight Ādityas (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.6.1).
That Aditi approached the gods with seven sons;
she cast away the eighth son, Mārtaṇḍa—the Sun—meaning she threw him upward.
With seven sons Aditi entered upon a holy age; but for the sake of progeny and death, she brought forth Mārtāṇḍa, who was yet incomplete.
With seven sons, Aditi went forth toward the auspicious age; for the sake of progeny, she brought back Mārtāṇḍa from death. 9.
The very same matter previously stated in the mantra is now repeated:
Aditi approached the ancient age (yuga) together with the seven [sons], Mitrā and the others, excluding Mārtāṇḍa.
Then, for the sake of progeny—the birth of living beings—and for their death, she brought back, that is, recovered, Mārtāṇḍa, the sun named Mārtāṇḍa, who was born from the egg produced by rain.
He established [the world] in the celestial realm.
The occurrence of the birth and death of living beings is clearly dependent upon the rising and setting of the sun;
thus says the Brāhmaṇa: “From him, rain was produced as an egg” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.6.1), and so forth.

The fifth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “*janiṣṭhāḥ*,” belongs to Gaurivīti, the son of Śakti; it is addressed to the Maruts, is in the *triṣṭubh* meter, and is an *ārṣa* (seer’s) composition.
Thus it is recorded in the *Anukramaṇī*: “*janiṣṭhāḥ*: eleven verses by Gaurivīti.
In the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, this hymn serves as the insertion (*nividānam*) for the *marutvatīya* recitation.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘Having recited the [hymn] beginning with “janiṣṭhā ugraḥ,” which consists of more than one verse, one should place the Marutvatīya Nivid’ (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.14).
Among the Saumika Cāturmāsya sacrifices, this same Marutvatīya Nivid is also used in the Vaiśvadeva parvan.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘“janiṣṭhā ugraḥ,” “ugro jajñe,” etc., is the Mādhyandina [Śastra]’ (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.2).
This hymn is also [recited] in the Niṣkevalya section of the Mahāvrata;
likewise, it is prescribed in the fifth Āraṇyaka: "janiṣṭhā ugraḥ sahase turāyati nividānam" (Ai. Ā. 5.1.1).
1. By Ga-varṣa; by Ta-bha-mu-varṣa.
2. "Ga-ta-bha-bhuvanāni" does not exist.
3. Gabha-ta-bhara. 4.1—He protected those who were wicked from pride.
4. ta-bha4.7-mārtaṇḍa | 5. ga1-vā sūrya; ta1-bha2.8-mā sūrya;

ga4-ta7- ā sūrya | Thou hast been born fierce for victorious power, exhilarating, most mighty, with abundant pride. Even the Maruts strengthened Indra on that occasion, when the Mother bore the Hero as the most excellent giver. janiṣṭhāḥ | ugraḥ | sahase | turāya | mandraḥ | ojiṣṭhaḥ | bahulābhimānaḥ | avardhan | indram | marutaḥ | cit | atra | mātā | yat | vīram | dadhnat | dhaniṣṭhā || 1 ||
O Indra, you were born—indeed, you have arisen—as one fierce with overwhelming power, for the sake of conquering force and for the slaying of enemies.
Of what nature are you?
You are the delightful one, worthy of praise, and most mighty.
Ojas is bodily strength; one who possesses it in excess is "ojaḥ-pradhānaḥ.
One who has abundant conceit is "bahulābhimānaḥ," meaning one whose pride is most excessive.
The Maruts even—indeed the Maruts—increased this Indra of such great majesty here at the slaying of Vṛtra, either through praise or by providing assistance;
for when Dhaniṣṭhā, the sustainer and mother of Indra, bore the hero.

The two milch-cows, even though dappled, have sat down with the gods; they have strengthened Indra with much praise. Like embryos enclosed within a covering, those [calves] have emerged from the darkness through the great opening at the time of delivery. duhaḥ | ni-sattā | pṛśanī | cit | evaiḥ | puru | śaṃsena | vavṛdhuḥ | te | indram | abhi-vṛtā-iva | tā | mahā-pūdena | dhvāntāt | pra-pitvāt | ud | aranta | garbhāḥ || 2 ||

Even the army of the malicious Druhu, though it was "touching" (pṛśanī)—that is, seated in close proximity to Indra—was defeated. The connection is that it was defeated along with Indra by the Maruts, who are "goers" (evaiḥ).
Those Maruts also strengthened Indra—who desired to slay Vṛtra—with abundant praise and hymns (śaṃsena).

Then, just as cattle and other animals surrounded by a great herd or a large flock emerge when their enclosure is opened, so too did those waters—which were like embryos—issue forth from the darkness, that is, from the nearness of the palace-like gloom.

Lofty are your feet when you go forth; the strengths have increased, as well as those who were here. O Indra, you held a thousand hyenas in your mouth; may you turn back the two Aśvins. Lofty are your feet when you go forth; the strengths have increased, as well as those who were here. O Indra, you held a thousand hyenas in your mouth; may you turn back the two Aśvins.
O Indra, your two feet are lofty and great.
When you, being such as you are, go forth, then the Vājas and the Ṛbhus strengthened you;
and moreover, whatever gods there may be, they too strengthened you.
O Indra, you held a thousand hyenas in your mouth;
at that time, you also turned back the two Aśvins.
O Nāsatyas, you come swiftly and silently to the sacrifice; bring a fair chariot for the noble one.
O Indra, you have maintained the Vasāvyas; the Aśvins, O hero, have bestowed thousands of gifts.
1. *ga-tara*. 3. *bhara-mu-śārī°*. | 2. *ga4-mātā taṃ* | 3. *ga4-tā tānyadukāni* | 4. *ga-āvartaya*;

*ta4.5-avartayaḥ* | O you who are equal, swift, and approaching, you come to the sacrifice. O Nāsatyas, bring [the chariot] for Sūryā. O Indra, bestow garments; O Hero Aśvins, grant thousands of riches. || 4 ||
O Indra, you who are swift, even while sounding forth in the assembly of battle, you approach the sacrifice;
at that time, you carry the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, for friendship.
O Indra, you hold for our sake treasures in abundance—a multitude of thousands of riches.
O heroic Aśvins, even you two, as his followers, have bestowed riches; grant us wealth.

Rejoicing according to the cosmic order (*ṛta*), Indra, together with his vigorous friends, [attained] his purpose for the sake of progeny. For with these [powers], he approached the Dasyu through his creative illusions; he struck him down and cast away the darknesses.
Rejoicing—from the cosmic order—for the sake of the purposeful, manly sage, making it free from the Āryas (or, making it manifest to the Āryas);
and furthermore, among the gods, you have made pleasant paths for the sake of man, for the seer, or for humanity in general.
Alternatively, the connection may be "the paths to be traversed among the gods (vdevatrā).
He explains what was already stated as "syonāṃścarthā" by saying "vajñaseva vyānān."
The particle *iva* has the sense of *eva* (only).

[The meaning is: You made the paths for those going by means of nothing other than the crookedness of serving the ignorant; or rather, you made the goers travel by means of a path that was not crooked at all.

Just as in the world one speaks of a path as "one who has gone easily" or "a path that has gone to Kāñcī," employing the metaphorical designation of "going" for the path, so too here the state of being a "goer" (*yātṛtva*) should be understood.

O Indra, Lord, you have assumed these names; as the Sovereign, you hold them in your hand. The gods rejoice after you because of your power; you have made us like a boat that crosses over the waters. 8. You. These. You have encompassed. Apart. Name. As Lord. O Indra. You hold. In your hand. After you. The gods. With power. They rejoice. Like a boat crossing over. You have made us. 8.
O Indra, you indeed encompass these various names—the waters known as *nāmaka*;
O Indra, as the sovereign (*īśāna*) of all, you hold in your hand the thunderbolt (*vajra*) or wealth.
Furthermore, all the gods, having approached you with power (*śavas*), praise and celebrate you.
As such, you have made the water-bearing clouds, or the rays of light, with their tops turned upward and their roots downward—that is, you have turned them upside down.

That wheel of his which was set down within the waters—may that indeed yield him honey. That udder of his which is established upon the earth, the milk which is in the cows and in the plants. That wheel of his which was set down within the waters—may that indeed yield him honey. That udder of his which is established upon the earth, the milk which is in the cows and in the plants. 9.
I think that he whom they call the steed and so forth is known from his vigor;
he has gone forth from the two sages and has taken his stand among the invokers, for Indra knows his wisdom.
This wheel, the weapon of this Indra, which is seated within the waters and in the intermediate space—indeed, that too he has brought; for Indra, the honey flows, and he brings it under his control.

That sign which is not established upon the earth—the udder—from that cloud (*ūdhas*) you have placed that water, the milk, within cows and plants; [or: that udder, the belly, which is released and not established upon the earth, that you have placed within cows and plants. O Indra, you have indeed struck down the enemy; furthermore, even for this [Indra], the honeyed water flows toward the desires. That which is not established upon the earth and is released—the udder, the water—is indeed the waters placed within the cow-pens and other places. O Indra, that wheel of yours, which is of the nature of the sun and possesses rays, is seated (*niṣatta*) all around within the waters at night; immediately thereafter, that ray-bearing [wheel] offers the honey-water to you. Moreover, that wheel which, being of the form of night, is exceedingly bound and not established upon the earth—by means of that wheel, you have held the milk and the water within the cows and the plants.
The meaning of this is clarified in the mantra *kṛṣṇaṃ niyānam* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.164.47).
Thus says Pūraṇa.

A commentary on this mantra is found in Sāyaṇa’s Bhāṣya on the Sāmaveda Saṃhitā (1.4.1.4.9), which is as follows: "The wheel—the weapon—of this Indra was seated, that is, stationed, everywhere within the waters—that is, in the intermediate space—for the purpose of slaying the clouds; and moreover, he (Indra) brings even that [wheel] under his control, making it subject to his will."
Whatever water exists on earth that is unestablished and liberated, he places that milk below in the cows and in the plants.

"From the horse it has gone forth," so they say; "born of vigor, I consider him. From *manas* (mind) it has gone forth; it has stayed in the dwellings. Since Indra knows its origin, [he knows] this. 10.

Having observed Indra’s power, some say of him: "He went forth (iyāya) from the horse (aśvāt), that is, from the sun (ādityāt). Even though (*yat*) this may be so, nevertheless (*uta*), I consider (*manye*) and know (*jānāmi*) him to have been born (*jātam*) from *ojas* (vital force).
Having seen his brilliance, their opinion is that he was produced from the sun;
however, I believe he was born from the substance of *ojas*, because he has slain Vṛtra and the others.
Alternatively, this one "went forth" (iyāya) from the wrath of Manyu;
therefore, he "stands" (tasthau) in battles involving the enemies' mansions, or indeed within the mansions themselves.
Since he was born from Prajñā, Indra alone is his [lord].
The meaning is "of himself.
His capacity consists in knowing [it], for no one else is able to know it.
The Suparṇas, the Priyamedha seers, have approached Indra with their supplication.
Dispel the darkness, fill our vision, and release us like those bound in a snare.
The birds of beautiful wings, the Priyamedhas, the seers, have sat near Indra, imploring him. Dispel the darkness; fill our eyes with light; release us like those bound in a snare. 11.
The "goers through the air," the "fair-winged ones" (suparṇāḥ) who fly well—the rays of the sun—approached Indra; they became seated near him.
Of what sort were they?
They were the "Priyamedhas," those whose sacrifice is dear, the "seers" (ṛṣayaḥ), the perceivers, who were "beseeching," supplicating for wisdom.
The manner of the prayer is stated: O Indra, "apōrṇuhi"—remove "adhvāntam"—the darkness; "pūrdhi"—fill, that is, bestow "cakṣuḥ"—sight or luster;
and "mumugdhi"—release "asmān"—us, who are bound as if by a snare.
The *nidhā* becomes the *pāśyā*.
A *pāśyā* is a collection of nooses (*pāśa*).
Just as they release those bound by a collection of nooses, so it is here.
In this regard, the Nirukta passage beginning with "avayo vībahuvacanam" (Nirukta 4.3) should be consulted.
The sixth hymn consists of six verses beginning with "vasūnām.
The seer and other details are as before.
It is listed in the index as "vasūnāṃ ṣaṭ."
The application is concluded.
Whether it be for the praise of the Vasus, or for desiring to worship with sacrifices, or for the two worlds;
or for those who possess wealth in the acquisition of booty, or for those who, being well-heard, have granted a famous boon.

Whether you celebrate the Vasus with prayer, or with sacrifices, O seekers of wealth; or those who are eager for the two worlds, or those who possess riches in the winning of booty; or those who, being renowned, have established a wide-sounding fame—[to all these] [I offer praise]. 1.
Desiring to sacrifice—that is, wishing to give wealth—or for the sake of obtaining wealth (*vasūnām*), Indra is drawn forth;
or he is drawn forth by *dhī*.
*Dhī* is action (*karman*), because it is that which is held fast.
Or one is impelled by actions such as warfare which serve as the cause; or one is impelled by sacrifices that have become the cause. By what means? It is said:
The meaning is: "by the gods belonging to the two worlds, heaven and earth," that is, by both gods and men.

When there is a battle to be won, even those who come from afar (*arvāñcaḥ*) and possess wealth are drawn toward him. Furthermore, Indra is drawn toward those who, being renowned (*suśrutaḥ*), achieve great fame (*suśravasaḥ*)—that is, well-known and preeminent glory—whether it be through the winning of cattle (*vunam*) or through the infliction of injury (*hiṃsām*). Thus, even by them, Indra is drawn.
1. In the manuscripts ta, bha1, 6, 7, and 8, the word "yat" is absent.
2. In the manuscripts ga, ta, and bha, it says that the sun arose.

The cry of these [Aṅgirases] reached the sky; the Asura, with a mind desiring glory, settled upon the earth. There, where the gods saw the cattle stolen by the Paṇis, they, like the sun (Dhauḥ), made light for their own welfare through their desirable offerings. Of these performers, the Aṅgirases, *harvaḥ* is the sound of invocation. *Asuraḥ*, the impeller of Indra, *nakṣata*—reached—*dyām*, the heaven. The gods belonging to Indra there, with *śravasyatā manasā*, a mind desiring food (*anna*), *nisat*—settled—upon *kṣām*, the earth. *Yatra*, on which earth, seeing the *kṣoṇāḥ*—the cattle carried off by the Paṇis—the *devāḥ*, for *suvitārya*, for their own well-being and prosperity, like *dhauḥ* the sun, with *vārebhiḥ*, through desirable things, that is, through oblations or splendors, *kuṇvanta*—they made light. The ellipsis is "to dispel the darkness caused by the withholding of the cows. Or alternatively: the *havaḥ* of these sacrificers who had been robbed of their cattle, being the *asuraḥ*, the impeller of Indra, *nakṣata*. Impelled by Indra, the Aṅgirases, with a mind desiring food or fame (*śravasyatā*), *nisat* the earth. The meaning is: "to show the cattle to the performers. The rest is common.

This is the song of these immortals; may they, who bestow jewels in the fulfillment of all things, grant us our prayer and the sacrifice, and may they bestow upon us an abundance of wealth that is complete and undivided. *iyam eṣām amṛtānāṃ gīḥ sarvatātā ye kṛpaṇvantu ratnam | dhiyaṃ ca yajñaṃ ca sādhantaḥ te naḥ dhāntu vasuvyam asāmi || 3 ||* This is the song (*gīḥ*)—the hymn of praise—is being offered to these immortals (*amṛtānām*), that is, to the gods whose thoughts are fixed on sacrifice. Those gods who, in the fulfillment of all things (*sarvatātā*)—that is, in the sacrifice (*yajñe*)—bestow (*kṛpaṇvanti*) or are entreated for (*yācyante*) jewels (*ratnam*), which is delightful wealth; and who, perfecting (*sādhantaḥ*) both our prayer (*dhiyam*) and our sacrifice (*yajñam*), may they grant (*dhāntu*) to us (*naḥ*) a collection of riches (*vasuvyam*) that is complete (*asāmi*)—meaning either not small or not shared by others.

4. O Indra, those Āyavanas praised that [deed] of yours; they who desired to overcome the stall full of cattle, those Āṅgirases who wished to milk the great, lofty earth—once-born, possessing many sons, with a thousand streams. O Indra, those Āyavanas—the human Aṅgirases—then praised that [exploit]; they were praised from all sides. Those Aṅgirases who desired to overcome (*tirtṛtsān*) the stall (*ūrva*) full of cattle, which had been carried off by the Paṇis. [The form *tirtṛtsān* is derived from the desiderative of the root *hiṃs* ("to injure"), with the suffix *san* and the augment *āṭ*. Due to the presence of *yaṅ*, there is no *nighāta* (suppression of accent); the accent is that of the reduplicated stem. And those Aṅgirases [milked] the "once-born" (*sakṛtsvam*): she who gives birth once is "once-born"; her, the once-procreated, possessing many sons (*puruputrām*)—sons in the form of plants and trees—yielding a thousand streams (*sahasradhārām*), producing abundant desires, the "great" (*mahīm*) earth, which is widely praised (*bṛhatīm*). Or rather: [they milked] the one with many sons in the form of plants and trees, yielding a thousand streams—that is, raining down many desires—the "great" (*mahīm*) earth, or the "lofty" (*bṛhatīm*) heaven, which is immeasurable or worthy of worship. They milked it. Thus connects with "they praised. As it is said: "Once indeed the thief was born" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 6.48.22).
1. ta1.2.3.7-priyaṃti; bha-prayaṃti | 2. ga-ta-bha-mu- the word "ye" is not present | 3. ga-bhara-vṛṣṭilakṣaṇa- [she] is endowed with many sons characterized by rain.
O Śacīs, bring Indra here for our protection— him who subdues the limitless and tames those who fight in battle;
the lord of the Ṛbhus, the bounteous one, worthy of perfect praise, who as the possessor of the thunderbolt brings strength to men and abounds in food.

O you who possess power, bring Indra here for our protection—the infinite one, the subduer of enemies, the lord of the *ṛbhus*, the bounteous giver, the one worthy of well-fashioned hymns; he who, possessing abundant food, is the bearer of the manly thunderbolt. 5.

O you who possess power, O performers of ritual acts, O sacrificers— using the singular number by way of grammatical substitution— make Indra the god your protector for aid, that is, for protection; do so!
What kind of Indra?

The infinite one, who is never bowed down by others; the subduer of those seeking battle, bringing enemies under his control; the lord of the *Ṛbhus*, the great one, the possessor of wealth, the one worthy of excellent praise.
He, Indra, who is rich in food and many-sounding, [bestows] that which is beneficial for men.
Because of the destruction of the Asuras, the bearer carries such a vajra; therefore, "make that Indra your helper."
The verse "yadvāvāna" is used as a continuous stream (*dhārā*) for the *nikkevalya* [stotra].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *sāmapragātha* is 'yadvāvāna' with the stream, and 'pibā sutasya rasinaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.15).
This [verse] is also used in the Mahāvrata.
Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "That which comes with a stream, the Sūdadohas" (Ai. Ā. 5.2.2).

Whatever most abundant food Indra, the Vṛtra-slayer, the protector from of old, has filled with his names—the mighty Lord of the Multitude approaches it; whatever we desire him to do, may he perform that.

Whatever he has won most abundantly in ancient times, Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, has filled with his names; the lord of overwhelming power, the mighty one, comes forth. Whatever we desire him to do, may he perform that. 6.

When Indra—who is the destroyer of cities, the overcomer of enemy fortresses—slew Vṛtra, who was most numerous and exceedingly powerful, then immediately thereafter, Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, filled (*aprāḥ*) the names, that is, the waters.
[The middle voice is used here by way of grammatical substitution. This very Indra is *prāsahaḥ*, the preeminent overcomer of enemies, the lord and master of all, and the mighty one.
*Tuviti* is a name for "much"; by its force, "forest" (*vana*) is understood here, meaning "one who possesses much wealth.
Being such, he was perceived (*aceti*) and recognized (*prajñāta*) by mortals.
That great Indra—whatever this deed we desire, whatever we long for, he indeed performs it; he does exactly that.
"Let this be, let this be"—whatever we desire, he performs that very thing at that very moment; the meaning is that he does not neglect it.
The Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with, "He attained this very [power]: 'As much as he has encompassed, most widely, from of old'" (AiB 3.22), should be consulted here.
The seventh hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "pra su vaḥ," is the ṛṣi-seer Sindhuksita, son of Priyamedha; it is composed in the Jagatī meter and has the rivers as its deity.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Pra su [vaḥ], nine verses; Sindhuksita-Priyamedha; a praise of the rivers; in the Jagatī [meter].
The application (viniyoga) has been explained.
O Waters, the poet shall proclaim your supreme greatness at the dwelling-place of Vivasvat;
for you have moved forth in thrice-seven streams, and the river Sindhu has surpassed the seven rivers by her might.
O Waters, the poet shall proclaim your supreme greatness at the dwelling-place of Vivasvat. For you have moved forth three times sevenfold; the Sindhu has surpassed the seven rivers by her might.
1. Because of the destruction of the Asuras by Ga, Ta, Bha, Ra, Mu, and Asura; because of the destruction of the Asuras by Bha, Ra, Sa, Va, Ra, Ya, La, and Sa.
2. Ga and Ta: Āpāḥ. 3. Ga: ajñāyi.
O Waters, I, the singer dwelling by the rivers, shall proclaim your supreme greatness—the most excellent hymn of praise—well within the sacrificial hall of Vivasvat, the patron who performs the rite.
Those rivers, becoming seven times seven, have flowed forth in three ways: in threefold manner, they have moved across the earth, the mid-air, and the sky.
Among these most excellent rivers, the river named Sindhu, by her own power (*ojas*), flows forth, having surpassed all other rivers—this is the sense to be supplied.

Varuṇa dug out your path for you to flow, O Sindhu, when you rushed toward the prizes. You travel along the slope and over the ridges of the earth; you stir the vanguard of these moving creatures. Varuṇa dug out your path, O Sindhu, as the lowing rivers—like mothers toward their young—flow toward you with their voices. They approach you like milch-cows yielding milk, like cows newly calved.

Furthermore, like a king who fights, you lead your two banks—which are being eroded—along with the flood of water; for whenever you reach the very front of these downward-sloping streams that flow along with you, you extend yourself ahead and go at the head of them all.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, and Paruṣṇī, accept this hymn of praise along with the Asiknī, Marudvṛdhā, Vitastā, Arjīkīyā, and the beautiful Suṣomā. Listen!
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, Paruṣṇī—accept this hymn of praise! O Marutvṛdh, listen with the Asiknī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjakīyā along with the Susomā! 5.
Here, seven principal rivers and three rivers that constitute their branches are praised:
O Gaṅgā, O Yamunā, O Sarasvatī, O Śutudrī, O Paruṣṇī;
O Marudvṛdhā, accompanied by your branch Asiknī; and O Ārjīkīyā, accompanied by both the Vitastā and the Suṣomā—may you seven rivers thus attend to and favor our hymn of praise.

Listen and listen! Regarding the association of the Ārjakīyā with the Vitastā and the Supomā, the Nirukta states: “O Ārjakīyā, listen along with the Vitastā and the Supomā. In this regard, the Nirukta passage beginning with “Because of going to the Gaṅgā” (Nirukta 9.26) should be consulted.
I have first gratified the Tuṣṭā, the Sajūḥ, the Sustarvā, the Rasā, and the Śvetyā, so that you may go;
O Sindhu, with these you travel on a single chariot to the Kubhā, the Gomatī, the Krumu, and the Mehatnu.

Satisfied with me, first for the journey, in harmony with the well-praising Rasā and Śvetyā—O Sindhu, you [go] with those [waters] along with the Kubhā, the Gomatī, the Krumu, and the Mehatnu, by which you travel on a single chariot.
O Sindhu, you have descended from the mountain to flow toward the river Gomati, which is prone to movement; first, you were united with that satisfied river.
Afterwards, become united with Sustarva, Rasa, Śvetyā, Tyā, Kubhā, and Mehantī—those with whom you travel, proceeding upon a common chariot.
Moving straight on, dappled and brilliant in her majesty, she carries across the regions and the realms;
unassailable, the most active of the waters, she is like a wonderful mare, beautiful to behold in her form.

Straight-moving, dark-hued, and radiant in her greatness, she encompasses the vast spaces and the regions of the air. The Sindhu, the most active of the active, is inviolable; like a dappled mare, she is wondrous and beautiful to behold.
The *ṛjītī* (straight-moving), the *enī* (white-colored), the *ruśatī* (shining) Sindhu carries forth, brings forward, the *jyāyāṃsi* (mighty) *rajāṃsi* (waters).
Such an *adabdhā* (unassailable, unharmed) Sindhu becomes the most active (*apastamā*) among the *apasaḥ* (active ones), possessing the activity known as speed.
Like a mare (*aśvā na*), she is *citrá* (wonderful, admirable), *vapuṣī* (beautiful), and like a woman, she is *darśatā* (lovely to behold).
1. *ta-mu-tisraḥ* | 2. *ta-bha- ‘yātave’ is not present*.

She with good horses, the Sindhu, with good chariots, well-clothed, golden-hued, well-fashioned, rich in swift steeds; the young woman, woolly-haired and adorned with *sīlamā* plants—blessed, she puts on her garment that increases sweetness. (8) She with good horses, the Sindhu, with good chariots, well-clothed, golden-hued, well-fashioned, rich in swift steeds, woolly-haired, the young woman, adorned with *sīlamā* plants—also, the blessed one, she puts on her garment that increases sweetness. (8)

This Sindhu is possessed of beautiful horses (*svaśvā*), beautiful chariots (*surathā*), beautiful garments (*suvāsāḥ*), golden ornaments (*hiraṇyayī*), well-fashioned, rich in food (*vājinīvatī*), and rich in wool (*ūrṇāvatī*).
Indeed, in the region near her there is wool from which blankets are made.
She is ever-youthful (*yuvatiḥ*), eternally young, and always possessing water (*sīlamāvatī*).
That which is called *sīlamā* by farmers is that by which the furrows (*sīrāṇi*) are bound with a medicinal plant serving as a rope;
she is possessed of such a medicinal plant.
Moreover, the fortunate river clothes herself in *madhuvṛdh*, that is, *madhuvardhaka* (the honey-increasing plant), such as *nirguṇḍī* and others.
On its bank there are many [trees], such as the nirguṇḍī and others.

He has yoked his easy-moving chariot drawn by the horses of the Sindhu; with it, may he win the prize in this contest. For great indeed is the majesty of this unassailable one, of him who possesses celestial glory and is overflowing with power—his greatness is celebrated. He has yoked the easy chariot, the Sindhu with its steeds; with that, may he win the prize in this battle. For great is his majesty, which is praised—the majesty of the unassailable one, of him whose glory is heavenly and who is overflowing with strength.
The divine Sindhu has yoked his chariot—chariot that brings happiness, possesses beautiful doors, and is drawn by horses. With that chariot, may he bestow food and strength;
for in this battle or sacrifice, the greatness of this Sindhu-chariot is indeed praised and extolled.
Of what sort is he?
Of one who is *adabdha*, unassailable by others; who possesses his own glory (*svayaśas*), having fame dependent upon himself;
and who is *virapśin*.
This is a name for "great":
[it refers to] that which is great.
The hymn consisting of eight verses beginning with "ā vaḥ" has Jaratkarṇa,
a son of Irāvat and a member of the serpent race, as its seer;
it is composed in the Jāgata metre and is addressed to the pressing-stones used for the purpose of pressing Soma.
And thus it has been listed: "Ā vo'ṣṭau, Sarpa, Airāvata, Jaratkarṇa, Grāvṇo'ṣṭau.
This hymn belongs to the *grāvastotra*.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The two hymns 'Ā va ṛñje' and 'Pra vo grāvāṇaḥ' [are recited] either between, above, or before [the *grāvastotra*]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.12).

I implore you for strength at the dawning of the days; O Maruts, anoint Indra and the two worlds—heaven and earth—so that both day and night may be our companions, and that those who sit in the assembly may grant us wide space through their victorious power. 1. I implore you for strength at the dawning of the days; O Maruts, anoint Indra and the two worlds—heaven and earth—so that both day and night may be our companions, and that those who sit in the assembly may grant us wide space through their victorious power.
O pressing-stones, at the dawning of the *uṣas*—the nourishing ones, full of essence—I impel you toward Indra.
O Maruts, anoint Indra and the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, with Soma.
May both the days and nights, born together and existing in union, honor us in every sacrificial hall.
"May they be filled with wealth that is increasing and ever-increasing."

1. In *tam* (ma1.2.4.6.8), it is *mūsīramāvatī*; in *ga4*, it is *vibhāveṣu*; in *tam* (ma1.2.4.1.8) and *mu*, it is *vibhāgeṣu*; in *ga4*, *ta*, and *ma*, it is *sahotpanne*; in *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, it is *pūrayatam iti*.

Press that most excellent [Soma] out from all sides; the pressing-stone is guided by the hand like a steed. For the presser finds the noble power of victory, so that he may cross over toward great wealth and the swift horse. Press that most excellent [Soma] out from all sides; the pressing-stone is guided by the hand like a steed. For the presser finds the noble power of victory, so that he may cross over toward great wealth and the swift horse.
O pressing-stones, you must press out—that is, extract—that very same most excellent and praiseworthy Soma for the libation; that is, pour it out.
Now he speaks of them as a singular entity:
the pressing-stone, held by the hands—that is, grasped by the two hands—of the *sotṛ*, the Adhvaryu who performs the pressing, becomes like a horse held by its reins.

Just as one who is firmly grasped by both hands still struggles, so it is with him. This sacrificer, the impeller for the pressing of the stones, truly obtains from the gods *pausya*—that is, the conquering power that overcomes enemies.
Or rather:
Urged on by the officiating priests and others for the sake of the pressing, the pressing-stone bestows victorious manly power for the benefit of the sacrificer;
moreover, for the sake of great wealth, that stone which overcomes, extends, and bestows swift horses.

Truly, that all-pervading power of his has opened the waters, just as he established the path for Manu in ancient times. In the watery flood of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, in the cleansing of the horse, they have set him forward at the sacrifices as the master of the rite. For truly, that all-pervading power of his has opened the waters, just as he established the path for Manu in ancient times. In the watery flood of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, in the cleansing of the horse, they have set him forward at the sacrifices as the master of the rite.
The word *it* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).
May this pressing (*savana*) of the stone—consisting of our own work involving the extraction [of Soma] and called the *somagāthā*—penetrate (*viveḥ*), that is, pervade;
for the root *vi-vi* takes *luṅ*, and because it belongs to the *ad-ādi* class, there is the elision of *śap*.

Because there is doubt as to whether the root *vi* preceded by *pra* takes the *ślau* doubling according to Vedic usage or whether it undergoes the "subsequent form" (*apara-rūpa*) sandhi, there is no *avagraha*.
It has the accent of a compound.
Just as in the past [the path] came—that is, arrived—for King Manu, so may it pervade [the sacrifice].
Furthermore, [he dwells] in the water of the cow, in the form of the cow, surrounded by waters that have been driven away; likewise, in the "nirṇij" of the horse.
*Nirṇij* is a name for form;
thus, [it means] in the form of the horse.
The meaning is that he was surrounded by horses that had been struck down.

The fault [in the argument] is that such a son of Tvaṣṭṛ (Tvāṣṭra) ought to have been slain. "īm" refers to these; ancient sacrificers established (*aśiśrayuḥ*) these stones—which are either the performers of the sacrifice (*adhvara-sādhaka*) or the place of the Asuras—in the sacrifices (*adhvareṣu*). They take their stand there.

Strike down the demons who possess deceptive power; prop up the firm foundation and drive away destruction and mental darkness. Press out for us wealth consisting of all heroic sons; O stones, bring forth the divine song of praise! 4 Strike down the demons who possess deceptive power; prop up the firm foundation and drive away destruction and mental darkness. Press out for us wealth consisting of all heroic sons; O stones, bring forth the divine song of praise! 4.
O you stones, drive away and destroy the Rākṣasas, the demons—
of what sort?
Those possessed of crooked deeds.

Likewise, obstruct her from afar; keep away Nirṛti, the goddess of evil, so that she does not come to this sacrifice. Furthermore, ward off, restrain, and drive away Amati—malice—and the Rākṣasas and other such harmful beings.
Furthermore, press out for us wealth consisting of all heroes, endowed with many sons and so forth;
this is said because of the attainment of sons, wealth, and the like through the act of pressing.
Moreover, bring forth—that is, accomplish—the hymn that pleases the gods (*devāvya*).

1. That very same [thing]. 2. For the sake of pressing, beginning with the Adhvaryu priest. 3. *ga*: *ta* 1.2.3.4.5.7—*bhara* (the impeller); *ta* 6.8—*bha* 1.4.6—*preritā* (the impelled). 4. *ta-bha*: *tat*. 5. *ta* 6.8—*bha*: The phrase "Furthermore... beginning with the Rakṣas" is absent. 6. *ga*: O stones (*adrayaḥ*), sing this verse!
Even from heaven, sing for you who are more powerful; even from the forest, for you who possess greater speed than horses;
even from Vāyu, for you who hold the Soma in your hands; even from Agni, sing for you who have prepared the food.

Even from heaven, sing for you who are more powerful; even from the woods, for you who possess more excellent horses; even from Vāyu, for you who are greater drinkers of Soma; even from Agni, sing for those who provide more abundant nourishment. ||5||
I have praised you with a song of praise, even more than from the sun in heaven, for you who are exceedingly powerful;
or rather, O Adhvaryus and others, you should praise from all sides the pressing-stones characterized as being described here— thus the response should be applied to each sentence.
Vivana too—
Vivvan was the son of Sudhanvan;
by him [it was given] to those who are swift in action, meaning those who are most rapid in their deeds.
The rapid action of the three [deities] beginning with Agni, such as the preparation of the *camasa* cups and so forth, is well known.
Even from Vāyu—from Vāyu himself, who possesses extreme velocity for the purpose of pressing the Soma from the *barhis* grass—[the stones derive their speed];
for even the pressing-stones (*grāvan*) become possessed of velocity for the sake of pressing the Soma.
"O you, worship the pressing-stones for the sake of gratification— stones that are like Indra, who have acted as fathers even to Agni, and who are the ultimate providers of food."
May the glorious pressing-stones resound for us as they press out the exhilarating juice, with a heavenly voice that reaches the heavens,
while the men milk the desirable honey, shouting aloud to one another in their mutual rivalry.

May they resound for us as we press the glorious juice—the pressing-stones with our voice, heavenly and full of celestial light—wherein the men milk the desirable honey, making their voices ring out on every side, each striving against the other.
May the glorious, renowned pressing-stones bring forth, bear, and provide for us the pressed juice of the soma plant.
(The *u* is a Vedic [sandhi] form.
Moreover, with that which is radiant and luminous.
There is a change of gender.
By means of *vāc*, that is, by words of praise, may they make us *divitā*, that is, radiant or possessing splendor (*dīsimatā*) in heaven (*divi*);
the meaning is that they should establish us in the Soma sacrifice.
How is it said that "he possesses vision"?
In this sacrifice, men—the leaders and officiating priests—milk the desirable honey, which is the essence of Soma.
What are they doing?
Proclaiming aloud on all sides, making sounds in the form of hymns, recitations, and so forth;
on every side, hastening toward one another—
that [light] is possessed of splendor.
The chariot-borne stones press out the Soma; seeking the kine, they milk forth its juice.
They milk it for the sake of pouring; like men, they cleanse themselves with their mouths as if preparing offerings.

The chariot-borne stones press out the Soma; they milk its juice, which seeks the cattle. They milk the udder for the purpose of pouring it out; like men, they cleanse themselves with their mouths for the oblations.
The pressing-stones, swift as charioteers, possessing chariots and possessing speed, press out the Soma.
These stones milk out the essence of this Soma completely;
they are seekers of the cow, desiring the voice of praise.
They milk the udder for the essence connected with Soma.
For what purpose?
For the sprinkling of the fire.
*Kam* is a word used for metrical completion.

*Naraḥ* refers to the leaders, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who perform the pressing. Like *havyā*, the oblations, they cleanse themselves with their own mouths immediately after the pouring of the libations;
that is, they perform purification by consuming the remnants.
Or alternatively:
they purify Agni by means of the stotras, characterized by the *hotṛ*, the *daśāpavitra*, and the *apara-sabhi-rāsya*.

These men have become skillful workers, O stones, you who press the Soma for Indra. May every most desirable thing of yours go to the divine abode; may wealth come to you from the earthly one for the sake of the presser. 8. These | men | skillful-workers | have become | who | for Indra | press | the Soma | O stones | every-desirable-thing | of-you | to the | divine | abode | O wealth-giver | of-you | to the | earthly | for the presser. 8.
O men, O leaders, O stones, you have become well-skilled in the excellent work of pressing;
you who press the Soma for Indra—make each and every desirable wealth that exists for the sake of the divine splendor (*divyaṃ dhāman*).
Likewise, whatever wealth is fit for dwelling (*vasu*), make that for the earthly sacrificer who presses the juice.
The ninth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "aśrapruṣaḥ," is the work of Syūmaraśmi of the Bhṛgu lineage; it is addressed to the Maruts and is in the Āṣa meter.
The fifth verse is a Jagatī, while the remaining seven are Triṣṭubhs.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "aśrapruṣaḥ; [the seer] Syūmaraśmi, son of Bhr̥gu; it is addressed to the Maruts, but the fifth verse is a Jagatī."
The application is concluded.

Like drops of ghee, [I praise] you with speech; like the offerings of the wealthy, the sacrifices of the wise; like the priest of the well-accompanied Maruts, I am worthy of the host; I shall praise them, for you shine among them. Like drops of ghee, not [otherwise], with speech, the impellent calls, the wealth, the oblations of those possessing the sacrificial food, like the sacrifices of the discerning one; like the priest accompanied by the Maruts, you are worthy; I shall praise the host of these, for you shine forth.
Like drops of water falling from clouds, the Maruts—pleased by our hymns of praise—sprinkle down wealth (*vasu*).
(The plural number is used here by grammatical substitution. Furthermore, like sacrifices provided with oblations, they become the progenitors of the world.
Now, he speaks by way of a summary:
"Of these very Maruts, the excellent ones, I have not praised—that is, I did not praise—the great host of Brahmans for the sake of worship;
I have not offered praise to them previously."
Thus you shine; yet for the sake of beauty, you did not praise even the host of Maruts.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Now I praise you with a new hymn."

For the sake of glory, the youths have prepared their ornaments, like the many nights of the well-blown Maruts. The sons of Dyaus have extended themselves like coursers; those Ādityas have grown strong like bulls. śriye | maryāsaḥ | añjīn | akṛṇvata | sumārutam | na | pūrvīḥ | ati | kṣapaḥ | divaḥ | putrāsaḥ | etāḥ | na | yetire | ādityāsaḥ | te | akrāḥ | na | vavṛdhuḥ || 2 ||
"For the sake of glory—that is, for the purpose of beauty—the *maryās*: either the Maruts who are killers, or the Maruts in human form.
Having previously been humans, they later became immortals (*amaras*) through their particular excellence of merit. They made, that is, they fashioned, *añjīs*—ornaments to be anointed with."
For what purpose?
For glory—that is, for the sake of the beauty of his own body.
He [does not] overcome or defeat the "fair-winded" one—the host of the beautiful Maruts—through many nights, that is, through numerous armies; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Furthermore, these sons of Dyu, the goddess of heaven—these goers do not stay back; they go forth.
Those Ādityas, the sons of Aditi, like the Maruts who are prone to advancing, have not grown, nor do they grow, because they have not been praised by us; such is the sense.
