They who by their own greatness have surpassed heaven and earth, as the sun surpasses the cloud; like powerful heroes, they are worthy of praise; like men who destroy the foe, they are impetuous in their onset. They, the Maruts, have surpassed both heaven and earth through their own greatness, even as the sun emerges from the cloud. Furthermore, like powerful heroes, they are seekers of glory; and like men who destroy the enemy, they possess a blazing radiance.

In your gathering, O Maruts, like the course of waters, the great earth neither trembles nor is it loosened. This all-nourishing sacrifice goes well toward you; come hither, like those who provide food, moving together as a troop. O Maruts, in your gathering (*budhe*), which is like the flow of waters (*apām na yāmani*), the great earth (*mahī*) does not waver (*na vithuryati*) nor is it shattered (*na śratharyati*). The meaning is: even though you move with such speed, you do not cause this earth to suffer. This all-nourishing (*viśvapsuḥ*) sacrifice—the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) used as the means of worship—goes well (*su*) toward you (*arvāk*). Like those who provide food (*prayasvanto na*), being givers of happiness like skilled preparers, come hither (*ā gata*) moving together as a troop (*satrācaḥ*). The sense is: "Come in a body," for the Śruti says, "The Maruts are indeed accompanied by their hosts" (*sasagaṇā vai marutaḥ*).

O Maruts, you are like horses yoked with reins upon bold chariots, moving all around; like luminous bodies such as the sun, you are endowed with splendor at the break of dawn. Like hawks, you possess your own glory and are destroyers of enemies; like travelers on a journey, you are well-known and far-reaching. (5) O Maruts, you are like horses yoked with reins upon bold chariots—meaning you are bound and driven like steeds—moving all around. Likewise, like luminous bodies such as the sun and others, you are possessed of brilliance through your splendor when the dawns have broken. Furthermore, like hawks, you possess your own glory, being independent in your fame, and like those hawks, you are "riśadasaḥ," meaning destroyers of those who harm. Moreover, like travelers on a journey, you are "prasitāsaḥ," meaning renowned for your movement. Thus, O Maruts, possessing the aforementioned qualities, you are "parimṛpaḥ," meaning those who move everywhere. (5)
O Maruts, you who come forth from afar with that wondrous wealth of the hidden treasury—
being wise regarding the riches that are to be won, drive away all hostility far off.
1. From *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *abhra* comes *sūryaḥ*.
2. From *bha*, [the reading] "like the sun from the clouds" (*abhrādiva sūryaḥ*) does not exist. 3. From *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, moreover, [it is like] *iva*.

When you, O Maruts, come from afar, you who know of the great treasure that is well-concealed and worthy of attainment—O Vasus, drive away even from a distance the hatred of those who hide themselves, who are concealed; for *sanutaḥ* is a name for what is hidden. O great ones, when you come from the farthest distance, then, O Vasus, bestowing the great, well-concealed, and attainable wealth, drive away even from afar the hatred of those who are hidden, meaning those who are concealed. *Sanutaḥ* is a term for the hidden.

The mortal man who, seated at the sacrifice during the ritual rites when the hymn has been raised, offers gifts as if to the Maruts—he indeed possesses abundant wealth and food accompanied by noble heroes; may he also be present at the drinking of the Soma among the gods. He, the mortal sacrificer, seated at the *adhvara* (sacrificial rite) when the *udarcis* (the rising flame or the chanted hymn) is present—here the word *ṛk* implies the hymn of praise; when the sacrifice is complete with its full laudation—offers gifts (*dadāśat*) as if to the Maruts, or rather, to others such as the Adhvaryus and priests. Or alternatively, "when the sacrifice has begun" (*udaci*). In that sacrifice, he gives as if to the Maruts, or to another, Indra. That sacrificer maintains (*dadhate*) abundant wealth (*revat*) and food (*vayas*) accompanied by excellent sons and progeny (*suvīram*). [Note: the singular verb is used for the plural by grammatical substitution. May he also be included in the protection (*gopīthe*) and the drinking of Soma among the gods, such as Indra and the others.

For they are indeed the ones worthy of sacrifice at the rites, the helpers, most beneficent by the name of Āditya. May they protect us—those who speed the chariot, who delight in our prayer, and who long for the great journey and the sacrifice. (8) For they are indeed those worthy of sacrifice at the sacrifices, the protectors, most beneficent through the name of Āditya—that is, through the water associated with the Ādityas; or rather, most beneficent together with the deity named Āditya. May those Maruts protect us. Speeding the chariot—that is, being the accelerators of the chariot which is the means of proceeding to the sacrifice—they protect and guard our prayer, our hymn of praise. Of what sort are they? Those who, on the journey to the sacrifice, long for the great [deeds] during the performance of the rite.

Like kings, they are brilliant and beautiful to behold; like blameless youths among the people, they are stainless.

The wise ones, with their prayers, are well-intentioned; they are devoted to the gods through sacrifices and possess beautiful rites. Like kings, they are brilliant and fair to behold; like the young men of the people, they are stainless. || 1 ||

Like inspired poets—just as Brahmins, through their *manmabhiḥ* (thoughts) or hymns of praise, become *svādhyaḥ* (possessed of beautiful meditation)—even so the Maruts, through our *manmabhiḥ*, that is, through meditative hymns worthy of reflection, become *svādhyaḥ*, meaning well-disposed or benevolent.

Alternatively, joined with *manmabhiḥ* (hymns), they are like *viprāsaḥ* (inspired ones), that is, like wise singers; the meaning is that they are *svādhyaḥ*, meaning possessing excellent meditation, either at the sacrifice or toward the sacrificer.

Likewise, through sacrifices—that is, through offerings—the ones called "gods" (devāḥ), like sacrificers who satisfy the gods, are "svamasas": *agram* is a name for ritual action; thus, they are those whose actions are excellent.
The meaning is that they are engaged in activities such as bestowing rain just as those [kings] are engaged in their duties;
like "kings," that is, consecrated lords of the earth, they are "wondrous" (citrāḥ),
meaning they are worthy of admiration and worthy of worship.
Or rather, they have variegated ornaments;
likewise, they are *susaṃdṛśaḥ*, very beautiful to behold;
and likewise, as lords of *kṣitīnām*, of the dwellings, they are like *maryaḥ*, men, yet *arepasaḥ*, stainless and free from sin.

The meaning is that they are like those who, having received a loan, do not go elsewhere but remain in their own home and fulfill their obligations, and thus become faultless; such people are the ones who shine.

Those who [serve] Agni with straightforwardness, whose chests are adorned with golden ornaments, who are like winds self-yoked, providing immediate aid; who are like the eldest among those who know, providing good guidance; and who are like Soma-libations providing excellent protection for the one who walks the path of Truth (ṛta). Agni, indeed, those who with straightforwardness, whose chests are adorned with golden ornaments, who are like winds self-yoked, providing immediate aid; who are like the eldest among those who know, providing good guidance; and who are like Soma-libations providing excellent protection for the one who walks the path of Truth (ṛta). 2. O Maruts, like Agni, you shine with vigor (*ārjasā*); indeed, you are endowed with that vigor. Furthermore, with golden ornaments upon your chests (*rukmavakṣasaḥ*), like manifest winds (*vātāso na*), you are self-yoked (*svayujaḥ*) and swift-moving (*sadyaūtayaḥ*). Like those who possess superior knowledge (*prajñātāro na*), you are the eldest (*jyeṣṭhāḥ*), worthy of honor, and well-guided (*sunītayaḥ*). Like Soma juices that provide excellent protection (*suśarmāṇo na somāḥ*), you are most blissful; thus, come to the sacrifice of the one who goes toward *ṛta*, the sacrificer!

Like winds, they are shakers and swift; like the tongues of fires, they are radiant; like armored warriors, they are vigorous; like the praises of the fathers, they are bounteous givers. 3. Like winds, those who are shakers, swift, like the tongues of fires, widely spreading, like armored warriors, powerful, like the praises of the fathers, they are givers of good gifts. 3.
Those Maruts who are like winds (*vātāsaḥ na vāyavaḥ*), roaring (*dhunayaḥ*)—shakers of enemies—and swift-moving (*jiglavaḥ*).

In this hymn to the Maruts, it is not contradictory to describe them using the wind as a metaphor, given the distinction between the physical element of air, characterized by its nature of movement, and the deities presiding over it.
Likewise, they are radiant (*virokiṇaḥ*) with faces that shine like the tongues (*jihvāḥ na*) or flames of fires (*agnīnām*).
Likewise, like warriors clad in armor—fighters wearing their mail—and like those possessed of heroic deeds, being full of valor;
and like the praises of the fathers—the words of their progenitors—being excellent givers;
may these Maruts of such great majesty come to our sacrifice.

Like the spokes of chariots, which share a common hub; like victorious heroes, who are full of luster; like men seeking a bride, who are steadfast; like sprinklers of clarified butter, who are well-disposed; like those who have sung the hymn of praise beautifully—[they are] thus. Like the spokes of chariots (*rathānām na arāḥ*): just as the spokes of chariot wheels, though many, possess a common hub (*sanābhayaḥ*)—that is, they share a single center—so too these [Maruts] are "having a common bond" (*sanābhayaḥ*), meaning they are bound together by kinship, existing together in the same intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). The sense is that they are mutual kinsmen. "Like victorious heroes, who are full of luster" (*jigīvāṃso na śūrā abhidharvaḥ*): like heroes characterized by victory, they are "possessing approached brilliance" (*abhidharvaḥ*), meaning their splendor has spread forth. Furthermore, "like men seeking a bride, who are steadfast" (*vareyavo na maryāḥ*): like men desiring to give a chosen gift (*vara*) to another, they are "sprinklers of water" (*ghṛtapṛṣaḥ*). For gifts are invariably bestowed preceded by water; thus, the meaning is "bestowers of rain-water. And furthermore: "like those who have sung the hymn of praise beautifully" (*arkaṃ na suṣṭumbhaḥ*). They are like singers who have perfectly chanted the *arkam*. 4. In the secret cave, the head is placed apart; with unwearied tongue he eats the woods. For him they bring all foods together with their feet, stretching out their hands in reverence below. 2.79.2.
The head of this Agni is placed in secret—that is, within the secret cavity—in the bellies of men.
His two eyes are placed separately; that is to say, they exist in the form of the moon and the sun. This is the meaning.

Such is this Agni who, "insatiable" (*asinvan*), "with his teeth," does not merely chew but "eats" (*atti*) the "woods"—that is, he consumes the pieces of wood as fire. For this Agni, the "sacrificial attendants" (*adhvaravāṇaḥ*), having approached with their "feet," "bring together" (*saṃ bharanti*) and prepare the "foods"—the oblations (*havīṃṣi*).
Of what nature are they? They have "uplifted hands" (*uttānahastāḥ*), with hands raised for the purpose of holding the vessels, and are endowed with "reverence" (*namasā*), that is, with salutation.
Where?
Above all creatures, in the midst of the entire creation.
Seeking his mother’s secret place further within, like a child desiring heroic strength, he has crept forth; like a well-cooked, glowing snake, he has been found licking the raw flesh within her lap.
Seeking his mother’s secret place more deeply than before, the boy creeps like one seeking a dwelling; he has found the ripe food glowing within her lap, licking away the impurities.
This Agni, desiring the many wide-spreading plants belonging to his mother, the Earth, and likewise desiring their most excellent and secret root, creeps forward;
he glides forth like a young boy.
Just as one crawling on his knees knows how to drink milk,

so [Agni] finds (*avidat*) him who is shining (*śucantam*), like ripe food that has been cooked, within the lap— that is, the interior— of the earth (*ripaḥ upasthe*), even though he is a sapless tree.
Furthermore, of what sort is he?
Licking the sky— that is, tasting it—
or else licking the earth from its very root.
I proclaim that nectar to Heaven and Earth: as soon as he is born, the embryo devours his two parents.
I, a mortal, do not understand the god; Agni is the one who understands, he who possesses true insight.

That truth of yours, O Heaven and Earth, I proclaim: as soon as he is born, the embryo devours his two parents. I, a mortal, do not understand the god; Agni alone is the perceiver—he indeed is the one who perceives. 4.
O you two, Rodasī, Heaven and Earth, I proclaim that truth to you both: that the *garbha*—the fire arising as an embryo from the two kindling woods (*araṇī*)—consumes his two mothers.
And I, a mortal, do not understand the path of the divine Agni, who possesses the qualities of luminosity and the rest.
O Aṅga Vaiśvānara, that fire produced from the two kindling woods is possessed of manifold knowledge (*vicetāḥ*), and he is possessed of supreme wisdom (*pracetāḥ*).
Therefore, the meaning is "I do not know.
Alternatively, addressing myself by means of my own limbs, I say:
Agni alone is the one who perceives; he who knows in many ways is *pracetāḥ*; he alone knows.
The meaning is that I am not capable of praising my own greatness or power.

He who bestows food upon us with longing, who offers oblations with clarified butter and sustains us—for him you stand facing every direction from all sides with a thousand eyes. You are he who turns toward us from every quarter.

1. *ga-ta-bha* have no *atrāṇi*. 2. *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha4.6.8-mu* read "of Agni, who possesses qualities such as *cotamāna*"; *ta4.5* read "of Agni, who is *cotamāna*"; *bha1.2.7* read "of Agni, who possesses qualities such as *dāna*. 3. *ga-ta* read "he himself is *pracetāḥ*."
4. [The one] who possesses exalted knowledge... [is] Pracetas.
He who offers food to him quickly, who sacrifices with clarified butter and ghee, and nourishes him—to him, O Agni, you look out with a thousand eyes; you face every direction from all sides. 5.

he beholds clearly with a thousandfold flames acting as eyes, seeing him with infinite vision.
Now, [the verse] beginning with *pratyakṣakṛtaḥ*: O Agni, you are *pratyak*—that is, you are turned toward (*pratyaṅ*) from all sides (*viśvataḥ*), you are facing us;
you proceed in a manner that is favorable to us.
"Did you abandon it among the gods? What have you done? I ask you, for I am ignorant:
while not playing, or while playing, O tawny one, did you eat it, or did you cut it into joints like a butcher's knife?"

What [wrong] among the gods, O Agni, have you committed? I ask you now, being ignorant; whether playing or not playing, you, the tawny one, have cut yourself for eating, limb by limb, like a knife cutting a cow. 6.
I ask you, knowing this: "Why did you abandon the gods so suddenly and quickly? Why did you harbor anger and commit such evil?

He who, as a seer and a Hotṛ-priest, sat down offering up all these worlds—our father—he, seeking wealth through his prayer, first covering himself, entered into the lower ones. (1)

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: “Viśvakarman offered all beings as oblations in the Sarvamedha sacrifice; at the end, he even offered himself as an oblation. This is what is meant by the statement: ‘He who, offering all these worlds... (Nirukta 10.26).
Here, the seer (*ṛṣi*) named Viśvakarman, the son of Bhuvana, acting as the *hotṛ* priest—the performer of the oblation—while offering (*juhvat*) all (*viśvā*) the worlds (*bhuvanāni*).
The meaning is that first the entire world came into being;
afterwards, the father— the progenitor— sat down,
because the production of the body occurs through action performed by the self.
Nor is the relationship of producer and produced contradictory for a single being, because he assumes two bodies through the power of austerity;
as stated in the Śruti: "He becomes one-fold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).

That seer (*ṛṣi*), desiring—yearning for—*draviṇa*, wealth known as heaven, by means of *āśis*, that is, by the *sūktavāka* and other hymns which express such wishes, first covered the worlds with fire; he entered—the meaning of which has already been explained—the lower, more distant beings offered up as his own self, having entered them; this is stated again with a further qualification.
In the same manner, this should be applied hereafter with reference to the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*).
Now, this is also stated with reference to the self (*adhyātma*):

He who is the All-maker (*viśvakarmā*), the Supreme Lord, offering up all these worlds—these seven worlds beginning with the earth—at the time of reabsorption, like the casting of oblations into his own self; he who is the witness of that, the omniscient Hotṛ-priest, the performer of the oblation in the form of reabsorption, our father, the progenitor, has sat down, having established himself.
This is the meaning:
when the time of dissolution arrived, the omniscient Supreme Lord—who, having withdrawn all the worlds, was the destroyer and again the creator even of us—remained alone by Himself.
For thus say the Śruti texts: "In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone" (Ai. Ā. 2.4.1); "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chā. U. 6.2.1), and so forth.

That Supreme Lord, desiring through His blessing to become "much"—that is, with the repeated longing expressed as "May I be many, may I procreate"—and seeking wealth, that is, yearning for the enjoyment of the world characterized by material riches, first veiled His primary, principal, and ultimate form which is free from phenomenal expansion, and entered into the lower regions of the hearts of the beings He Himself had created, having entered them in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*).

And thus it is heard in scripture: "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he created all this, whatever exists here. Having created it, he entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.6).
In this manner, other Upaniṣads as well may be cited.

In the preceding mantra, it was stated that at the time of the dissolution of the universe, the Creator, having withdrawn everything, subsequently entered into it out of a desire to create.
Here, an objection is raised: since a second locus—an underlying material cause for the universe—is impossible, creation is logically untenable.

For in the world, a potter desiring to make a jar does so by occupying a certain place such as a workshop, gathering materials in the form of clay, and producing the jar with instruments such as a wheel.
In the same way, since the Lord is the substratum of the world, what was the support at the time of the earth's creation? What indeed existed [as its basis]?
The meaning is: nothing at all. Likewise, what was their "origin" (ārambhaṇa)? What indeed was it?
"Commencement" (*ārambhaṇa*) refers to that which is commenced, namely the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).
What could that possibly be? The meaning is: "That too does not exist."
Even if an undertaking were possible— [the question being] how it was, or how it came to be;

Because the partless Supreme Lord has no physical form apart from His manifestation as speech, and because the scriptures—such as "He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3)—reveal that it is the Supreme Lord alone who becomes manifold through the distinctions of gods and others.

it means of the lights, that is, of the rays.

And he, being free from dejection and having cast off a distracted mind, is in reality the Great One; specifically, he is the support, the sustainer, and the ordainer of the fruits of good and evil deeds, and he is the supreme seer of the senses.

With those seven seers—the senses—their desired forms rejoice and take delight together with the Knower (Īśvara) in that Self. The knowers of reality call that Self the one Supreme Self, which is beyond the seven—those whose nature is to move—and which transcends the senses and all else.

They made him equal, they honored him perfectly with clouds and so forth.
Now, this is the meaning:

those who, through their splendor, made these living beings existing in the world—consisting of both the stationary and the moving—equal, those ancient seers, the beholders, the rays, offered up wealth, that is, splendor, to this Viśvakarman whose nature is the Sun.
Before heaven, before this earth, before that which exists with the gods and the asuras—
what indeed was that first embryo which the waters received, wherein all the gods beheld one another?
Before heaven, before earth, before the gods and the asuras—what indeed was that first embryo which the waters received, wherein all the gods beheld one another? ||5||

That which exists beyond the realm of horses by day, even further than the world of heaven; likewise, that which exists beyond this earth, and that which exists beyond the gods, and that which exists beyond the Vasus—what indeed is that embryo, the reality that takes on the state of being an embryo, which the Waters first held fast?
In which womb all the gods, beginning with Indra, together behold one another;
thus does some knower of reality, a field of knowledge, pose a question.
The waters first held that kindled embryo where all the gods assembled;
it was fixed upon the navel of the Unborn, in which all worlds abide.
The waters first received that embryo, wherein all the gods came together; it was fixed upon the navel of the Unborn, in which all worlds abide. 6.
By this verse, the answer to the question stated in the preceding mantra is declared:
the waters (āpaḥ) held fast (dadhre) that very Viśvakarman as the embryo (garbham)—standing in the place of an embryo—first, prior to the other creation;
therein, in that embryo, all (viśve) the gods (devāḥ), Indra and the others, came together (samagacchanta), becoming united.
"Upon the navel of that Vaja"—
the word *adhi* here restates the sense of the locative case.
It is said that "it was placed upon the *veka*" with the intention of referring to the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*).
For before creation, the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) stood as my abode; within this egg all beings (*viśvāni bhuvanāni*), that is, all classes of living creatures, have stood—meaning they remain.
Or else:

In the navel of the unborn (*aja*), the Brahman who is devoid of birth and reclining upon the waters He Himself created, a single cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) was placed and established within the water that binds the entire world.
The rest is the same.
Now, regarding this matter, there is a traditional text (*smṛti*): "In the beginning, He created the waters alone; upon them, He cast His seed."
"Then that golden egg came into being, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns" (Manu 1.8–9).
You do not perceive him who generated these [worlds]; something else has come between you.
Enveloped by mist and prattling, the reciters of hymns wander about, seeking only their own sustenance.
No! You do not know him who generated these [worlds]; something else has come between you. Enveloped in mist, prattling, and greedy for life, they move about as mere reciters of hymns. 7.

O men, you do not know—that is, you do not perceive—that Viśvakarman, who brought these beings into existence, who produced them.

The nature of the Universal Architect, the Supreme Lord, is not the individual soul-form (jīvarūpa) accessible through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*); rather, there exists within you—a distinction, something other than the individual souls accessible through the notion of "I," namely the state of being the ultimate reality (*arthātmatva*) known by all the Vedāntas.
