"Enveloped by mist"—you are covered by ignorance which is like mist;
therefore, you do not know.

Just as mist is neither absolutely non-existent because it obstructs vision, nor is it absolutely existent because it is incapable of being identified with other forms such as wood or stone, so too ignorance is neither absolutely non-existent because it veils the Lord, nor is it existent because it is removable by knowledge alone.
All you living beings are enveloped by such ignorance.
Not only are you enveloped, but you are also covered by the false chatter of "I am a god" or "I am a human," and so forth.
Furthermore, you are "thirsting for life," seeking to satisfy your vital breaths by whatever means possible.
The meaning is "those who merely fill their bellies.
They have not, however, investigated the supreme reality of the Lord.

Not only are they satisfied with the enjoyments of this world alone, but as "reciters of hymns" (*ukthaśāsaḥ*)—chanting the *ukthas*, such as the *prauga* and *niṣkavalya*, in various sacrifices—they "move about," that is, they exist upon the earth.
The meaning is that those who are solely intent upon enjoyments pertaining to this world and the next do not know the divine Viśvakarman.
The hymn beginning with “*yaste manyo*” consists of seventeen verses; it is the fifteenth hymn. Manyu, the son of Tapas, is the seer (*ṛṣi*).
The first verse is in the *jagatī* meter, and the remaining verses are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
And this [hymn] is dedicated to Manyu;
thus it is enumerated: "yaste manyo manyus tapasaḥ... mānyavaṃ tu jagatyādi.
In the sacrifice that accomplishes non-deviation from the goal, this hymn is the insertion (nivid-vāna).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Manyu, that which is yours, O Manyu" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 9.7).
O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt and the arrow, you who nourish all-encompassing power and strength;
with you as our ally—victorious, thousandfold in action, and possessed of overwhelming force—may we achieve victory over the enemy.

O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, O arrow, he who has worshipped you nourishes all conquering power and strength; with you as his ally, through the overcoming force that is itself powerful, he overcomes both the Dāsa and the Ārya.
O *manyu*, god who presides over wrath— [as the *Nirukta* (10.29) states: "The word *manyu* comes from the root *man*, signifying brilliance, or anger, or even the act of slaying"—

that sacrificer who *avidhat* (worships/attends upon) *te* (you), O *vajra* (thunderbolt-like essence), O *sāyaka* (destroyer of enemies like an arrow)— that man, through your favor, nourishes *sahaḥ* (victory/strength) and *ojaḥ* (bodily vigor) *bhānuṣak* (in close connection) in battle.

Since this is so, therefore we would overcome—by what means? It is said: by you as an ally, with you as our companion—the *dāsa*, the oppressor, and the *ārya*, the enemy superior to us; both kinds of enemies. By what instrument? That is stated:
by you as an ally (*yujā*), with you as a helper.
The companion is distinguished:
by one who has performed a thousand deeds, who has produced strength, who overcomes others with force, and who is powerful—
this is the meaning of "with such a companion as you."
Indra is fury; fury indeed was the god. Fury is the Hotṛ, Varuṇa, and Jātavedas. The human tribes that exist offer praise to fury. O Manyu, well-pleased by our fervor, protect us!
Manyu is Indra; Manyu indeed was the god. Manyu is the Hotṛ, Varuṇa, and Jātavedas. The human tribes worship Manyu. O Manyu, well-pleased by our fervor, protect us with your heat! 2.
Then Indra became Manyu; indeed, Manyu alone became the god; even everything became Manyu alone.
Manyu himself was the Hotṛ—the Agni who accomplishes the oblation—and likewise Manyu was Varuṇa, as well as Jātavedas, Varuṇa who possesses born wisdom.
1. Among all those who possess splendor, [you are] great by your own nature (svabhāva); or rather, you are so regarded by us. 2. The meaning is: "we shall overcome [them] with you as our companion."
Because of the existence of Manyu:
those human clans—that is, the offspring descended from Manu—who exist, they praise and extol Manyu himself as a god.
O Manyu, being of one mind (*sajoṣāḥ*) with him through this [sacrificial] heat (*tapas*) known by that name, protect and guard us.
Attack, O Manyu, you who are more powerful than the powerful; with fervor as your ally, strike down the enemies.
You are the slayer of foes, the slayer of Vṛtra, and the slayer of Dasyus; bring to us all desirable riches.

Come hither, O Manyu; you who are more powerful than power, with fervor as your ally, strike down our enemies. You are the slayer of foes, the slayer of Vṛtra, and the slayer of Dasyus; bring to us all treasures. You alone are for us. 3.
O Manyu, do you come toward us; approach our sacrifice.
Of what nature are you? You are *tavasaḥ*, powerful, yet *tavīyān*, exceedingly more powerful.
As such, through your ascetic power, together with us as your consorts and allies, strike down the enemies; moreover,
you are the slayer of foes—
*amitra* meaning one who is unaffectionate or hostile.
Likewise, he is the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of obstructing enemies, and likewise of the Dasyu.

This person here am I for you; come toward me, O Conqueror, all-sustaining one! O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, turn toward me! Together we two shall slay the Dasyus; and take heed of me as your kinsman. This person here am I for you; come toward me, O Conqueror, all-sustaining one! O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, turn toward me! Together we two shall slay the Dasyus; and take heed of me as your kinsman. O Conqueror, you who are accustomed to overcoming enemies, O All-sustainer, O Manyu—this person here, I, am yours, performing your work. Since this is so, therefore, coming toward me, facing us, come near to me! O Manyu, wielder of the thunderbolt, turn back toward me! If it is asked for what purpose you come, it is said: together we two shall slay the Dasyus, the enemies. And furthermore, take heed of me, recognize me as your kinsman.

Come forward; be on my right side, and then we two shall slay many Vṛtras together. I offer for you, O Supporter, the honeyed first portion; let us both drink the *upāṃśu* draught first. 7. Come forward; be on my right side.

Like fire, O Manyu, blaze forth; be victorious! O conqueror, being invoked, be our army-leader. Having slain the enemies, distribute their wealth; displaying your power, drive away those who oppose us. Like fire, O Manyu, blazing, be victorious! O conqueror, being invoked, be our army-leader. Having slain the enemies, distribute their wealth; displaying your power, drive away those who oppose us.
O Manyu, blazing like fire, be victorious; overcome the enemies.
O Sahasvan, you who are capable of enduring, be our commander in battle when you are invoked.
Furthermore, having slain the enemies again and again, bestow upon us their wealth—the riches belonging to the foe.
Furthermore, "Ojas," meaning pride, "making our strength," "drive away" (vi nudasva) the "mr̥dhaḥ," that is, the enemies; the sense is "slay them."

Overpower, O Manyu, the adversary against us; breaking, crushing, and utterly destroying, go forth against the enemies! Your fierce power has indeed been let loose; you, O Sole-born, bring them under your control at will. 3. Overpower, O Manyu, the adversary against us; breaking, crushing, and utterly destroying, go forth against the enemies! Your fierce power has indeed been let loose; you, O Sole-born, bring them under your control at will. 3.
O Manin, overcome—that is, subdue—the enemy who is our assailant;
breaking, injuring, crushing, and utterly destroying him so that he may not live again, go forth against the foes.
For who indeed can obstruct or restrain your fierce and uplifted power?
O Ekaja, it is not possible that you, being without a companion and self-controlled, would bring [your enemies] under your power—that is, you cause them to fall into subjection.

You alone, O Manyu, are praised as the one among the many; sharpen every tribe for battle. With you as our ally, O you who grant unearned glory, we raise a resonant shout for victory. 4. You are the one among the many, O Manyu, the one invoked with praise. Sharpen every tribe for combat. With you as our ally, O you whose radiance is uncreated [by others], we raise a mighty shout for the sake of conquest. 4.
O Manyu, being invoked and praised, you alone, without a second, are sufficient to slay many enemies.
Therefore, sharpen thoroughly for battle each and every one of those subjects who oppose us.

Furthermore, O Akṛtavr̥k, whose brilliance is unassailable, with you as our ally and companion, we produce a resounding roar, full of splendor and like the lion’s roar, for the sake of supreme victory.
O Manyu, like Indra who grants victory, be our invincible protector here;
we celebrate your beloved name, O Conqueror, for we know that spring from which you have arisen.
1. *ta* = killing; *bha* = not killing.
2. *ga*, *ta*, *bha* = performing (the actions numbered) 1, 2, 4, 6, 8. 3. *ta*, *bha* = we perform (the actions numbered) 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8.
Victorious, like Indra, you have spoken; O Manyu, be our sovereign protector here. We celebrate your beloved name, O Conqueror, that universal spring from which you have arisen.
He is like Indra, the *manya*, the maker of victory;
likewise, he is *anavabravaḥ*, one whose speech is beyond reproach.
Regarding this, Yāska states: "Anavagrābhaḥ means one whose speech is not obstructed" (Nirukta 6.29).
"O Lord of the ten steeds, be our supreme protector and guardian here in this sacrifice.

O Conqueror, you who are capable of enduring enemies, we sing—that is, we praise—your beloved name. For from that hymn of praise, you have become manifest; we know you, the one who stirs up strength, the one who is all-pervading."
The two verses beginning with "ābhūtyā sahajā" and "saṃsparśanindayiṣyau" are for the sake of well-being.
The verse beginning with "ye vadhrvaśragmam" destroys consumption (kṣaya) for a married couple.
Therefore, that [verse] has those [deities] as its deities.
For the remaining sixteen [verses], the Sun is the deity.
Thus it has been enumerated: "With 'Satyena,' forty-seven [verses]. Everything has been enumerated.
The application of the hymn is based on its indicative marks.
The earth is supported by truth; the sky is supported by the sun.
By cosmic order (ṛta) the Ādityas stand firm; Soma is established in heaven.
By truth the earth is supported; by the sun the sky is supported. By cosmic order (ṛta) the Ādityas stand firm in heaven; Soma is established therein. 1.
By means of truth, which is the infinite self of Brahman—
Brahmā, indeed, being the embodiment of truth among the gods—
the earth, situated below, is supported and held aloft by him.
It was established in such a way that it would not fall downward.
Or rather,
the meaning is that by means of *satya*— the dharma which is the opposite of falsehood— the earth is supported, covered, and made fruitful.

Just as crops and other plants do not bear fruit when the earth lacks truth, so too is the sky supported by the divine Sun; for the Sun, by virtue of his abiding in the celestial realm, bestows heaven.
By means of the *ṛta* sacrifice, the Ādityas—the gods who are the sons of Aditi—stand firm.

Indeed, through the oblation offered by the sacrificer in the sacrifice, the gods subsist. In heaven, in the celestial world, Soma—which nourishes the gods, which is of the nature of strength (*valī*), and which is divine—is established and resides there.
Thus Sūryā praises her husband Soma.
By means of Soma the Ādityas are strong; by means of Soma the earth is great.
Furthermore, Soma is placed in the lap of these constellations.
By Soma the Ādityas are strong; by Soma the earth is great. Moreover, in the lap of these stars, Soma is established. || 2 ||
By means of Soma, the Ādityas—the sons of Aditi, Indra and the others—become powerful;
the sense is that this occurs through their taking possession of the cups dedicated to Indra, Vāyu, and so forth.
Likewise, by means of Soma offered as an oblation, the earth becomes great (mahī).
Through the oblation, by means of rain, crops and other things come into being;
moreover, this Soma belongs to these *nakṣatras*.
They are called *nakṣatras* because they do not perish (*na kṣiyante*) and because they provide a place of rest (*prachchhamasadayaḥ*).
Within their lap, Soma, whose essence is sap,
is placed; or rather,
in the lap— that is, the station— of these very well-known constellations, in the heavenly world, Soma is placed.
"From this world, Soma was in the third heaven; they brought him down by means of the Gāyatrī," according to such scriptural passages (*Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* 3.2.1.1).
This refers to the position that Soma is the deity. By means of Soma, the Ādityas, the gods, become powerful through the tasting of each of his digits (*kalā*).
According to the Smṛti passage beginning with, "The Fire drinks the first [portion], the Sun drinks the second," the earth becomes great through Soma; that is,
the earth's strength arises from the growth of plants and other vegetation through the sprinkling of nectar.
The moon's stationing within the lap of the lunar mansions is well known.
One thinks he has drunk Soma when they crush the plant;
but no one at all eats that Soma which the Brahmins truly know.
He who has drunk [of it] thinks he has drunk Soma when they drink the plant; but of that Soma which the Brahmins know, no one at all eats. 3.
1. Those [mantras] have as their deities the [syllables] *ta*, *bha*, and *a*.
2. The complete reading is provided in the manuscripts Ga4, Ta1, Ta2, and Ta7. 3. In the manuscripts Ta and Bha, it is written as *stabhitā*.

4. For the deities [of the verses] *ta*, *bha*, *1.4.6.7.8*. 5. According to *ga1.2*: "because of the drinking by the planets"; according to *ga4*: "because of the movement of the planets"; according to *ta*, *bha1.2.4.6.8*: "because of the transgression of the planets. 6. In the two *bhinu* [verses], according to *ta*, *bha1.2.4.6.8*.
He considers that Soma;
who? He who has drunk it.

By whom Soma was drunk for the sake of increasing [vitality] and for the purpose of medical treatment and so forth— *yat* here has the sense of *yam* (whom)— that Soma, who is of the nature of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*), they seek to consume (*sarpiṣanti*) for the sake of strength (*rāsāya*).
And yet, he is not Soma directly.
Then who is he? It is said:
For he considers that [person] to be a *soma*-drinker who is a *brahman*.

This is because the word *brahman* is a synonym for the word *brāhmaṇa*, as seen in such usages as “From where do you come, O *brahman*? and “O *brahman*, speak to him who is a guardian of the treasure.”
The meaning is "the Brahmins.
They—the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)—know, that is, they understand, the *aṃśa* (portion) of that which has been consecrated as the means for the sacrifice.
Or else:
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi ṣaṣṭhī*).
"No one whatsoever shall consume that Soma"—
the ellipsis being "no one who is not a sacrificer."
The meaning is that only a performer of sacrifice (yajvan) deserves to consume this, and no one else. Thus ends the section concerning the herb. Now, the section concerning the moon is stated:

The sacrificer thinks that he has drunk that *soma*—that is, he has drunk it—if the officiant and the sacrificer [have consumed] the clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) which has the form of the plant, [pressed] by means of the pressing-stones. But that is not *soma*. What then is it?

That which the Brahmins who possess higher knowledge (*abhijñā*) and those who know the divine (*daivajña*) recognize and describe as the Moon—no one other than a god shines like that, whether among the gods or among humans and others.
Here, "gods" refers either to Agni and the other deities or to the rays of light.
One should understand that the Moon’s lack of *soma*-ness (its non-liquidity) is not intended as a censure, but rather for the purpose of praising something else.
Just as in the passage, “Other animals are indeed not animals [in the true sense] compared to cows and horses” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.9.4), so here the terms *somyāḥ* should be applied in both ways.
O Soma, you stand protected by the various coverings of the Bṛhatī meters;
hearing the sounds of the vessels, the earthly king does not consume them.
Guarded by the ordinances, protected by the Bṛhatī verses, O Soma, you stand listening to the sounds of the vessels; no earthly being consumes you. 4.
He is protected by those who possess "concealing arrangements" (ācchadvidhāna);
that is, those for whom there exist arrangements that conceal—
by them he is guarded.

Likewise, you are protected by the seven Soma-guardians, such as Svāna, Ājñā, and Jñāya, who are associated with the Bṛhatī meters; for the Brāhmaṇa states: "These indeed guarded the Soma in yonder world" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.1.10.5). You stand there, listening to the *grāṇā* sounds—that is, hearing the very noise of the pressing-stones.
The earthly person does not consume you;
for Soma, who possesses the form of the moon, does not become fit for drinking through falsehoods.
As the Vājasaneyaka states: "Soma is indeed the moon, the food of the gods; they press it on the full-moon day" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.1.5.3).
O God, that which they drink from you, you cause to swell again;
Vāyu is the protector of the Soma, and the month is the form of the year.
When the gods drink you up, from that you swell again; Vāyu is the protector of the Soma, the month is the form of the year. 5.

O divine Soma, whenever they drink you—when you have assumed the form of the plants during the three pressings—at that very moment, you swell once again. You swell at the morning pressing with the words, “Swell up completely” (RV 1.91.16), and at the two subsequent pressings with the words, “May your milks unite” (RV 1.91.18). Furthermore, Vāyu [is yours], O Soma...
1. ga4–śrāmānakaḥ; ta1.2.3.6.7–nyaḥ nakaḥ; ta8–nyanekaḥ; bha1–nyanaḥ ka; bhara–nya nakaḥ; bha4.6.8–nyanakaḥ | 2. ta-bhara.8–yajamānāśca | 3. ga–yajvaiva tat; ta-bha–yajvaitat |
4. ga4—pītavān pātā; ta1.2.3.6.7—pītavān pītasomaḥ; bha—pītavān pīta | 5. ta-bha1.2.4.6—yajamānāśca | 6. ta-bha—svanājñādhārādibhiḥ |
The eighth book: the protector;
in such a way that it does not dry up.
Vāyu is well known in the world as that which dries up. Furthermore, there is *māsa*: [the root] *mas* means "to measure."
It is called *māsa* because it is measured (*masyate*) or delimited; it refers to Soma.
Furthermore, it constitutes the form (*ākṛti*) of the years (*samānām saṃvatsarāṇām*), serving as their defining characteristic.
This is because [the sacrifice] is performed every year during the seasons beginning with spring, according to the Vedic revelation: "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring."
Alternatively,
by way of the cups (graha) which are modifications of the tree that serves as the support for the Soma, Vāyu becomes the protector of the Soma juice;
for there is a Vedic revelation stating, "The trees have Vāyu as their guardian."
Thus is the application [of the verse] in the interpretation of Soma as the year.
In the interpretation of Soma as the moon, however: O divine Soma, whenever the rays drink you during the dark fortnight, immediately thereafter you swell again during the bright fortnight.
And Vāyu is the protector of your Soma,
because the movement of the moon is dependent upon Vāyu.
Furthermore, he is the month of equal years.
This is in the singular number.
You are both the creator and the form of the month;
for it is by the decrease and increase of each individual digit that the month is completed, and by those [months] the year is formed.

Raibhī was the bride’s companion; the hymns were the attendants; the meters were the head-ornaments; the *opaśa* was the headdress; the Aśvins were the wooers of Sūryā; Agni was the leader of the procession. || 8 ||

The hymns (*stoma*s), such as the *trivṛt* and others, were the *pratidhi*s (cross-bars) of Sūryā’s chariot; for they are called *pratidhi*s because they are fixed across [the pole]. Likewise, the *kurīra* metre was the head-ornament (*opaśa*) of the cart.
That by which one is adorned is an *opaśa* (head-ornament).
For such a *Sūryā*, the two *Aśvins* were the suitors (*varau*).
In her marriage, Agni was the leader (*purogavaḥ*), the one who goes before, the one who goes in front, acting as the precursor for the commencement of the ceremony.

"Prajāpati indeed gave his daughter Sūryā Sāvitrī to King Soma; all the gods came as suitors for her," and so forth is the Brāhmaṇa (Ai. Brā. 4.7). Herein is the intended meaning: Prajāpati Savitṛ gave his own daughter to Soma.
He formed the intention, "I shall give [this] to Soma.
At that time, the Puṣya constellation was present for the purpose of the offering.
And so, the two powerful Adhvaryus, having gone before the horse, obtained it.
Later on as well, this same meaning will become clear through such passages as “Soma became the suitor for the bride” (RV 10.85.40).
Furthermore, the verse beginning with “The maiden chose him as her lord” (RV 1.119.5) has already been cited.
Soma was the suitor for the bride; both Aśvins were the wooers. When Sūryā declared her intention to her husband, Savitṛ gave her away with his mind.
Soma became the suitor for the bride; the Aśvins were both the suitors when Savitṛ gave Sūryā to her husband, as she was consenting in her mind. 9.
Soma became the suitor, desiring the bride;
at that time, both the Aśvins were the two suitors.
When Sūryā, desiring a husband, was being proclaimed as a wife for her husband.
The meaning is "one whose youth has passed.
Savitṛ, her father, gave—indeed, intended to give—to Soma Varu, who was accompanied by Sūryā with her mind.
The mind was its axle; the sky was its canopy.
The two bright draft-oxen were they when Sūryā went to her husband’s home.
The mind was her cart; the sky was the canopy. Two bright oxen were there when Sūryā went to her husband's house. 10.

The chariot (*anas*) was the mind (*manas*) of this Sūryā as she went to her husband’s house; she who had the thought, "I shall go to my husband’s house by means of you," became the chariot. Moreover, the sky (*dyauḥ*), the celestial world, was the covering (*chadiḥ*), the upper lid, of that chariot.
The two bright ones, the radiant sun and moon, were the two draft-oxen, the bearers of the chariot,
when Sūryā went to the house of Soma.
Your two oxen were fashioned from the Ṛg and Sāma Vedas; your two wheels were the Sāmans, and your path was in the sky, encompassing all that moves and is stationary.
The two cows were designated by the *Ṛg* and *Sāman*; they were the two *Sāmans*. Your two ears were the wheels; thus they were. The path was in heaven, moving and unmoving. 11.

1. *ga-ta-bha* read as *gantāsīt*. 2. *ta-bha* read as *prajāpatiḥ*. 3. *ta-bha* lacks the phrase “*somāya prāyacchat*”. 4. In *ta* 1.2.6.7.8 and *ma* 1.2.4.6.8, *prabala* and *sabala* are [read]. 5. *ta* 4.5 read as *sahitā*. O Goddess Sūryā, your two oxen—standing in place of the *ṛk* and *sāman*, and thus designated by them—are the Sun and Moon, who serve as the two oxen of the chariot; being yoked together (*sāmanau*), they go from here toward the house of the husband, like draft animals drawing a wagon.
Your two ears were made for the purpose of hearing;
indeed, your two ears were fashioned as the recipients of the qualities of a bridegroom.
The meaning is that the two ears became the wheels of the chariot whose form was the mind (manas).
In heaven, there was a path—both moving and unmoving, a means for reaching the end—which served as the locus for the movement of the chariot;
that is, the celestial realm (dyuloka) became the region where the chariot travels.
Pure were your two wheels as you went; the axle was struck by the wind.
O Sūryā, mounting your chariot made of clay, you have set out toward your husband.
"Pure," they said; "two wheels," they said; "three-naveled," they said; "the axle is unshakable"; "the chariot is fashioned by Manu. Sūryā ascended it as she went forth to her husband. 12.
As you were moving along, the two bright ears became the two wheels—the parts of the chariot characterized by constant motion—of your cart;
the pervasive breath (vyāna) was your axle;
and that wooden pole which passes through the holes of both chariot wheels carries the entire burden of the vehicle.

That axle became the *vyāna* breath. As Sūryā, proceeding toward her husband Soma, mounted the mind-made chariot, her two ears—conveying the qualities of the husband—became the wheels, and the *vyāna*, the sustaining wind, became the axle; such is the meaning.
The bridal procession of Sūryā has gone forth, which Savitṛ sent away;
on the Aghā days the cattle are slain, and on the two Arjunī days the bride is led away.

The bridal procession of Sūryā has set forth; he whom [the gods] created here in the Aghā constellations will be her husband. In the Arjunī constellations cows are slaughtered; she is being led around. 13.
The bridal procession (*vahatu*) of Sūryā, who had been sent forth for Soma;
the *vahatu* consists of items such as cattle that must be given for the sake of pleasing the maiden;
and that [procession] *prāgāt*, meaning it went before her as well.
The vehicle which Savitṛ, her father, has sent forth—
meaning he has bestowed it—
is described here by stating both times: when she went and when she shall carry [the bridegroom].
"In the *aghā* stars"—
that is, in the *maghā* stars;
during the *maghā* constellations, the cows given by Savitṛ are "driven," meaning they are struck with sticks and urged forward toward the Soma-hall.
"Of the two Arjunyas"— that is, of the two Phalgunīs.
By means of those two constellations, the Soma is "carried," that is, led by chariot, from the presence of Savitṛ toward the Soma-hall.
When you two, O Aśvins, were asked and came as the vehicle for Sūryā on your three-wheeled chariot, all the gods recognized that deed of yours; Pūṣan, the son, chose you as his parents.

When you two, O Aśvins, were asked and came with the three-wheeled chariot to the wedding procession of Sūryā, all the gods recognized that deed of yours; Pūṣan, as a son, chose you as his parents. 14.
1. The two *g* sounds are restricted. 2. In *ga-ta1.2.3.4.5.7-bha7*, the term "not common" (*asāmāna*) does not exist.
3. In *ga-ta1.2.3.6.7-bhara.8*, [the reading] is *anovodhā*; in *ta4.5*, it is *anovopā*; in *bha4.6.7*, it is *anovodhā*.

4. *ta-bha-sūryāḥ* [are] *prati*. 5. *ga-ta-bha1.2.4.6.8-vāyuḥ* and so on constitute the *aṣṭaka*; in *ga1.2*, there is a house [beginning with] "one reaches the *maghā* stars by means of a chariot" (*rathena prāpyate maghābhir gāvaḥ*), etc.; in the manuscripts *ga4-ta4.5-bha1.2.6*, there is some space following the word "*rathena*".
O Aśvins, when you two went to Savitṛ to ask him—
by what means did you go? That is now stated.
With what [purpose], asking with a three-wheeled chariot— that is, one equipped with three wheels— [did they ask] for the bridal procession of Sūryā?
The meaning is "marriage.
At that time, all the gods recognized and authorized you two as you were going toward Savitṛ;
likewise, Pūṣan—the son of the Aśvins—chose [you] as his parents.
When you two, O Lords of Splendor, went toward Sūryā to choose her as your bride,
where was one of your wheels, and where did you stand while being seen?
When you two, O Lords of Splendor, came hither to Sūryā at this choice-marriage, where was the one wheel of yours? Where did you stand for the sake of the one who points out the way? || 15 ||
O lords of splendor (śubhaspatī), masters of the waters, you two went (ayātam) toward that which was to be chosen (vareyam)—
namely,
the bridegroom (vara) belonging to Sūryā, who is herself worthy of being sought (vareyā).
The meaning is "Savitṛ.
For what purpose?
To approach Sūryā.

"O you two, this single wheel which is now seen belonging to you—where was it before? Or where did you two stand when intent upon giving for the sake of bestowing [gifts]?"—thus he asks about the dwelling place of the Aśvins.
O Brahmans, you know two wheels of the sun according to the seasons;
but as for that one wheel which is hidden, even the wind does not know it.
"Two," they say; "two wheels," they say. The Brahmins know them according to the seasons. But that one wheel which is hidden—that the Adhvaryus do not know. 16.
Then, as it were, the Sun himself speaks to his own self:
"O Sun, your two wheels—the two consisting of the Moon and the Sun—which were known and seen of old, are designated as such in their respective seasons; these two wheels the Brāhmaṇas know.
But that third wheel, which consists of the year and is placed in secret, do you alone perceive."
This word is listed among the names for the wise (Ni. 3.15.21). Only those who are wise (*medhāvin*)—that is, the learned (*vidvas*)—know [this].
To Sūryā, to the gods, to Mitra, and to Varuṇa— to those who are the wise perceivers of all that exists— I have offered this salutation.
To Sūryā; to the gods; to Mitra and Varuṇa; and to those who are the wise perceivers of all that has come into being—to them I have paid this homage. 17.

To Sūryā, the wife of Sūrya; to the gods, beginning with Agni; to Mitra and Varuṇa; and to those who are the wise ones (pracetasaḥ) who bestow desired gifts upon all created beings (bhūtasya)—to all of them, I offer this salutation (namas), I perform this act of homage.
Moving by means of their creative power (*māyā*) from east to west, these two go around the sacrifice like playing children;
one surveys all beings, while the other, ordaining the seasons, is born again.

East and west they move by means of their creative power; these two, as if playing with children, go around the sacrifice. One of them surveys all beings; the other, ordaining the seasons, is born again. 18.
One goes before, the sun;
the other follows it, the moon.
Thus, "before and after," by way of succession, "through *māyā*," that is, through their own wisdom, "these two," the sun and the moon, "move," they travel, in the sky.
Those two are "infants" (śiśū);
or they are called infants because they are produced by wandering like infants.
Being infants, playing and sporting in the intermediate space, they go around the *adhvara*, that is, they proceed toward the sacrifice.
Of these two, one—the Sun—overlooks, that is, beholds, all beings;
the other—the Moon—is born again, ordaining the seasons such as spring and the rest, and creating the months and half-months.
Although both possess rebirth, nevertheless, because the Sun is ever-increasing, its "rebirth" is not intended here.
But because of the existence of the moon’s waning and waxing, the statement that it is born again and again is logical;

for the Śruti says, “The moon, indeed, is born again” (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.9.5.4). Therefore, O Lord, I praise with reverence and songs this husband who possesses all wealth. Seek another wife, one distinct from the assembly of ancestors. This is your portion by birth; know it as such. 21.
The marriage of the *ābhīna* [women] is praised.

O Viśvāvasu, "arise" (*udīṣva*) from this place, that is, from the vicinity of the maiden; or rather, since "this maiden has indeed become possessed of a husband," one should supply the word *antaḥ* (within) after "arise. Thus it means: "Arise from within [her]."

"I praise with reverence—that is, with salutation—and with songs—that is, with hymns—the Gandharva named Viśvāvasu. If you say, "Having abandoned her, whom else shall I accept? then [I reply]: "Another woman, situated in the father's house (*pitṛpada*), who is *vyaktā*—meaning clearly manifest as one not yet married—or *vigatānāṃ*, meaning immature due to the absence of breasts and so forth."
"That such an object is imagined as 'your own' portion—
know, understand, that portion of it by birth;
that is, obtain it."

Rise up from here, O Viśvāvasu; we honor you with reverence. Seek another woman who is fertile; unite your wife with her husband. 22. Rise up! From here! O Viśvāvasu! With reverence, we praise you. Seek another! One who is prolific! Unite the wife with the husband! 22.
"Therefore, from this piling, O Viśvāvasu—O Gandharva, master of maidens—arise, go forth!
[The root] *īr* means 'to go'; it belongs to the Ādādi class."
It is *anudātta*. Its form in the *loṭ* [imperative] is as follows:
"The Gandharva named Viśvāvasu is the lord of maidens."
"For by that [means] I obtain a maiden"—such is the mantra.
O God, we praise you with such reverence, with salutation;
as such, do you seek another, a great and exuberant maiden.
Unite me again with my wife and children.

May the paths be smooth-flowing and straight, by which our friends go to choose a bride for us. May Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; O Gods, may the lordship over the household be well-governed. May the paths be smooth-flowing and straight, by which our friends go to choose a bride for us. May Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; O Gods, may the lordship over the household be well-governed. (23)
O gods, may the paths—the ways and roads—be smooth-flowing.
"Ṛkṣara" is said to mean a thorn;
may they be free from thorns, straight, and not crooked. May those paths by which our friends, sent by the bridegroom, go toward the bridegroom—the father who is to be chosen—be such paths.
Furthermore, may the god Aryaman lead us—us, "naḥ"—together, that is, may he bring us properly [to our goal].
Likewise, may the god Bhaga lead us together.
O gods, may there be union; the word "patikula" (the husband's family) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Likewise, may this pair consisting of husband and wife be well-yoked and a harmonious couple.
When the wife releases the yoke-halter, the verse "I release you" (*apra tvā muñcāmi*) is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Then she unties his yoke-halter with the words, 'Now I release you from the noose of Varuṇa'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 1.11).
I release you from the bond of Varuṇa, with which Savitṛ, the most auspicious, bound you.
In the womb of Cosmic Order, in the world of well-performed deeds, I establish you, unharmed, together with your husband.
1. *ta-bha-te* | 2.
*ga-ta-ma- 'bṛhantam vāṃ'* does not exist [in these recensions].
3. *ta-bha-devorthamān*.

I release you from the bond of Varuṇa, with which Savitṛ, the benevolent, bound you. In the womb of Cosmic Order, in the world of well-performed deeds, I place you unharmed together with your husband. 24.
Once born, the living being is impelled by Savitṛ; then Varuṇa binds him with raw snares.
Therefore, O bride, I release you from that snare of Varuṇa, with which snare Savitṛ—the impeller of Varuṇa—bound you, being *suśeva*, most auspicious.
(In the context of the application to the sacrifice, he binds the wife with the *yoktra* cord.)
Varuṇa is the presiding deity of bondage;
therefore, I release you from the noose and yoke of Varuṇa—that yoke with which the divine Savitṛ, authorized by the ritual acts, bound you through the fetters of the officiating priests.

Having released you from that, I establish you, unharmed and uninjured, together with your husband for the sake of sons and other blessings, in the place of the sacrifice—the sacrificial ground—within the world of good deeds, the field of action, and the earthly realm.
As one who is immortal, I release from death this well-bound thief;
O bounteous Indra, so that she may become possessed of good sons and good fortune.
From here I release her; I, the immortal, loosen the well-bound bond. O Indra, Bounteous One, so that she may become possessed of good sons and be fortunate. 25.
I release you from here, from the house of your father; I do not release you from there, from the house of your husband.
I bind you firmly in the house of your husband with immortality.
O Indra, the bounteous one, act so that this maiden may be well-protected, possessed of good sons, fortunate, and blessed with good fortune.
At the departure occurring immediately after the wedding, he should cause her to mount a vehicle such as a chariot with the verse, "May Pūṣan lead you from here" (*apūṣā tveto nayatu*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With [the words] 'May Pūṣan lead you from here, taking you by the hand,' he should cause her to mount the vehicle" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.8.1).
May Pūṣan lead you from here, taking you by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot.
Go to the house so that you may become the mistress of the household; being self-possessed, speak what is beneficial.

May Pūṣan lead you from here by the hand; may the Aśvins carry you away on their chariot. Go to the house so that you may become a mistress of the household; as one who has power, you shall speak with authority over the distribution of goods. 26.
May Pūṣan, seizing you by the hand with his own crocodile-like grasp, lead you from here—that is, cause you to reach [your destination].
May the two Aśvins carry you forward on their chariot.
Go to the house related to your husband; may you become the mistress of the household, that is, the sovereign lady of your own home.
O Vaśinī, you who bring all those within the house under your control, whether you abide under the power of your husband or you command the husband's household—you speak to them;
you address the servants and others residing in the home.
The verse beginning with "iha priyam" is for the bride's entry into the house.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the words, 'May what is dear to you flourish here through offspring,' he should cause her to enter the house" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.8.8).

May what is dear to you prosper here through offspring; in this house, remain watchful for the status of the householder. Unite your body with this husband; thus, growing old together, may you both speak your words.

1. He bound [them] under the pretext of being officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); according to Tāṇḍya Mahābrāhmaṇa 1.2.3.5.6.8 and Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.6, he bound [them] under the pretext of being officiating priests.
2. In Ga, Ta, Bha1, 2, 4, 6, and 8, the word "they" (*te*) is absent.
3. In Ta and Bha, it says "just as you" (*tvaṃ yathā*).

582. Here too, the disparagement of touching the bride’s garment is expressed: the body belonging to the groom becomes *aśrīrā*, that is, devoid of beauty (*aśrīkā*). How might this be? It is said: *haśatī*. *Ruśat* is a name for color; it means "shining. If the body is joined with *amuyā*—that is, with *anayā*, this—sinful, evil-formed *kṛtyā* (magical spell), then he says just that: *patiyaṃta*, if the bride, with her garment, desires to clothe herself—that is, wishes to wrap her own limb—with it. || 25 ||
The consumptive diseases that follow the bride from among the people as she carries the moon— may the worshipful gods lead them back to the place from which they came.
The consumption-diseases that follow the bride from her people as she carries the splendor away—may the worshipful gods lead them back to the place from which they came. 31.
May those wasting diseases and ailments that follow and reach the bride— who bears the golden-hued moon— from us, her obstructors, or from the people;
or rather,
from the people among themselves.
Furthermore, let the *devas*—those worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*), such as Indra and others—lead them back;
that is, let them bring them to the place from which they came, from which those wasting diseases (*yakṣma*) originated.
At the departure of the bride, the mantra "May they not find us" (amā vidan) is to be muttered.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "At auspicious places, trees, and crossroads, one should mutter with the prayer, 'May no waylayers find us'" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.8.6).
May those who lie in wait as adversaries not find us;
may the enemies be confounded as we pass through the difficult terrain by easy paths.
May no adversaries find us—those who lie in wait for the couple with pride. By easy paths, may they pass over the difficult road; let the enemies be driven away. 32.
May those who lie in wait, the obsessors, the enemies—those who lie in wait and approach the husband and wife—not find them, may they not reach them.
By easy paths, by roads that are easy to travel, may they pass beyond the difficult terrain, the inaccessible region that can only be traversed with great hardship.
May the adversaries, the non-givers, the enemies, be driven away; may they depart.
This bride is most auspicious; come together and behold her!
Having bestowed good fortune upon her, depart and go back to your homes.
Most auspicious is this bride; look well upon her. Bestowing good fortune upon her, now depart and go back to your homes. 33.
This bride is auspicious, possessing beautiful blessings;
therefore, all you who bestow blessings, assemble and come together here.
Behold her!

Having seen her united [with him], and having bestowed good fortune upon her who has been wedded, now—*astaṃ* is a name for the house; go away in various ways to your respective relatives. *Vi pareta* means "go forth."

1. If [the syllables] *ga*, *ta*, *bha* occur in the *kṛtyā* [meter], [it portends death]. 2. If *ta*, *bha*, and *ya* occur, it portends the death of the bride. 3. If *ga*, *ta*, and *tān* occur, it portends consumption (*yakṣman*).
4. "May they depart. In every dwelling, she gazes at the men who have arrived at night with the verse beginning "sumaṅgalīḥ" (the auspicious one).
And so it is stated in the Sūtra: "In every dwelling, she should gaze at them with the words 'This bride is auspicious'" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.8.7).

This is satisfied; this is pungent; this is without a horse, three-peaked; not this for the sake of the sun. He who, as a Brahmin, should know Sūryā—he indeed deserves to ascend here. 34. This is satisfied; this is pungent; this is without a horse, three-peaked; not this for the sake of the sun. He who, as a Brahmin, should know Sūryā—he indeed deserves to ascend here. 34.
By this [verse] as well, the casting off of the bride's garment is established.
"This garment" is [described as] "pleasing yet causing a burning sensation," and likewise, "this is bitter."
Likewise, like *apāṣṭa*. *Apāṣṭa* means situated near;
it is just like that.
Likewise,
it is not right that this garment should be eaten;
it is unfit for consumption.
Only that Brahmin who would know—that is, correctly understand—the goddess Sūryā now being celebrated here, he alone is worthy of the *vādhya*, the garment of the bride.

The carving, the cutting apart, and furthermore the slicing—behold these forms of Sūryā; the Brahman, however, purifies them. (35) The carving (*āśasanam*), the cutting apart (*viśasanam*), and furthermore (*atho*) the slicing (*adhivikartanam*). Behold (*paśya*) these forms (*rūpāṇi*) of Sūryā (*sūryāyāḥ*); the Brahman (*brahmā*), however (*tu*), purifies (*śundhati*) them (*tāni*). (35)
The *āśasana* is the placing [of the head];
it is of a different color.
The *viśasana* is that which is placed upon the head.

Such things, being placed at the end of the ten [days], are the "cutters" (*adhivikartana*) by which they cut the garment of the woman; those garments, such as the *āśasana* and others, which remain there, become the forms of Sūryā— behold them!
Such inauspicious items as the āśasanā and others, which formerly resided upon the body of Sūryā, he (the groom) puts on as garments;
Brahmā, who is indeed a Brāhmaṇa, purifies—that is, removes—those forms from those garments.
At the wedding, during the grasping of the bride’s hand, this verse beginning with “I grasp” (*gṛbhṇāmi*) is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “With the words ‘I grasp your hand for the sake of good fortune,’ he should grasp only the thumb” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.7.3).

I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the state of a householder. I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the state of a householder.
O bride, I take your hand; I take it for the sake of good fortune, for the sake of prosperity.
May you, through me as your husband, attain such long life that you reach old age.
Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, Purandhi, and Pūṣan—these gods have given you to me.
For what purpose?
For the sake of the householder's fire: "May I become a master of the household."
O Pūṣan, bestow upon me that most auspicious [vagina], in which men sow the seed;
that which spreads its thighs wide for us with longing, and into which we, desiring, insert the phallus.
1. He is not entitled [to it].
But another, accepting [it], having violated his vow, gives the bride’s garment to one who knows the Sūryā hymn. 2. These two... [are] such.
O Pūṣan, send forth that most auspicious [vagina], into which men sow the seed, which, longing for us, spreads its thighs apart, and into which we, longing, may deposit our semen. 37.
O Pūṣan, impel, drive forth from all sides that goddess named Popakka, who is most auspicious (śivatamām), exceedingly blessed;
she upon whose thighs men sow—that is, deposit—the seed characterized as semen;
she who, longing for us, spreads her thighs wide.
"Upon whose thigh we, desiring—that is, longing—shall deposit the *śeṣa*, the male generative organ fit for contact;
that is to say, we shall effect the union of the penis with the thigh."
For you, O Agni, they have brought Sūryā away with her bridal procession;
O Agni, give the wife back to her husbands along with offspring.
To you, O Agni, they have brought Sūryā back with her bridal procession; give the wife back to her husbands, O Agni, together with offspring. 38.

O Agni, the Gandharvas brought [her] for you; that is to say, they presented her. Whom? Sūryā. With what? Together with the bridal procession (*vahatu*). And you, O Agni, gave that Sūryā together with the bridal procession to Soma. In the same way, even now, O Agni, give us back our wife again, along with offspring.
Again may Agni take back his wife together with life-force and splendor;
may he who is her husband live for a hundred autumns as one of long life.
Again: Agni has given back the wife together with life and splendor; may he who is her husband live a long life for a hundred autumns. 39.
Furthermore, Agni gave back her own wife together with life-span and together with splendor;
may the man who is the husband of this woman given by Agni live for a hundred autumns—that is, for a hundred years—possessing long life.
Soma first obtained you; Gandharva obtained you next;
Agni was your third husband; and human beings are your fourth.
Soma first obtained her; Gandharva obtained her next; Agni was your third husband; your fourth is born of man.
When the girl was born, Soma, being the first, obtained her;
Gandharva, being the next, obtained her;
Agni is your third husband.
Afterwards, the fourth, the one born of Manu, is the lord.
Soma gave [her] to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave [her] to Agni;
and Agni has given me both wealth and sons, as well as this woman.
1. From that, the thighs; 2.

gone together with life-span and luster; together with life-span and luster, Soma gave to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave to Agni; he gave wealth and sons; Agni gave them to me, and also this [woman]. 41.
Soma first gave her to the Gandharva;
the Gandharva gave her to Agni;
and then Agni has given this maiden, as well as wealth and sons, to me.
Stay right here; do not be parted until you have lived out your full span of life, playing with your sons and grandsons, rejoicing in your own home.
Stay right here; do not go apart. May you exhaust the full span of life, playing with your sons and grandsons, rejoicing in your own home. 42.
Stay right here; remain in this very world. Do not part; do not become separated.
May you both attain a full lifespan.
Furthermore, the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "May you both rejoice in your own home together with sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons."
Upon entering the house, there are four [verses] beginning with "May Prajāpati produce offspring for us," intended for the purpose of oblations.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having offered oblations with each of the four verses beginning with 'May Prajāpati produce offspring for us' one by one" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.8.9).

May Prajāpati generate offspring for us; may Aryaman anoint us for long life. Enter the world of your husband with auspicious fortune; be a source of well-being to our bipeds and well-being to our quadrupeds.
May Prajāpati engender offspring for us; may Aryaman anoint us for long life. Free from ill omen, enter the world of your husband. Be auspicious to our bipeds, be auspicious to our quadrupeds. 43.
May the divine Prajāpati procreate offspring for us;
and may Aryaman unite us with long life, until old age.
As such, may you be free from ill fortune—indeed, possessed of auspiciousness.
Alternatively:
she who vitiates auspicious customs is *durmaṅgalī* (inauspicious);
one other than her is *adurmaṅgalī* (not inauspicious).
Being such as this, enter and reach the world of your husband, that is, go near your husband.
Be auspicious for our two-footed beings; likewise, be auspicious for our four-footed beings.
With eyes that are not terrible, do thou be one who does not strike down our offspring; be auspicious to our cattle, well-disposed and full of luster.
A mother of heroes, desiring the gods, and pleasant—be a source of peace to us, peace to our bipeds and peace to our quadrupeds.

With eyes that are not terrible; do not be a slayer of your husband; be auspicious toward our livestock; be well-disposed, full of luster, a mother of heroes, and devoted to the gods; be pleasant; be a source of peace for us bipeds and peace for our quadrupeds. 44.

O bride, be one whose eyes are not terrible; though your eyes may be fearsome due to anger, be so. Likewise, be one who does not kill her husband. Likewise, be auspicious—that is, beneficial—to the livestock. Be well-disposed and full of luster.
O mother of heroes, may you be the progenitor of sons alone; O goddess-loving one, be gracious and a bringer of happiness.
1. Furthermore, playing; 2. the wife (according to Ga, Ta, Bha);
3. with eyes terrifying due to anger (according to Ta, Bha).
O bounteous Indra, make this woman rich in sons and fortunate;
bestow ten sons upon her, and make her husband the eleventh.
O bounteous Indra, make this woman one who has good sons and is fortunate; bestow ten sons upon her, and make her husband the eleventh. 45.
O Indra, you make this bride possessed of good sons and fortunate; grant her this.
Bestow ten sons upon this bride;
make her husband the eleventh.
Act so that there may be ten sons and the husband as the eleventh; do this, perform it!
Be a sovereign queen over your father-in-law; be a sovereign queen over your mother-in-law;
be a sovereign queen over your husband's sister; be a sovereign queen over your brothers-in-law.
Be a sovereign queen over your father-in-law; be a sovereign queen over your mother-in-law; be a sovereign queen over your husband’s sister; be a sovereign queen over your brothers-in-law. 46.
"O bride, may you be a sovereign queen over your father-in-law and the others; 'over the brothers-in-law' means over the gods."
The verse beginning with "samañjantu" is employed for the bridegroom's tasting of curd or for the touching of the hearts of the bride and bridegroom.

Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having tasted the curd with [the verse] 'May all the gods anoint,' he should hand it back; or he anoints their hearts with the remainder of the clarified butter" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.8.9).
May all the gods unite us; may the waters unite our hearts.
May Mātariśvan unite us, may Dhātṛ unite us, and may the goddess Sarasvatī unite us both.
May all the gods unite our hearts; may the waters unite our hearts; may Mātariśvan unite them, may Dhātṛ unite them, and may the goddess Sarasvatī unite us two. 47.
May all the gods, every deity, anoint our hearts—that is, our minds—thoroughly;
that is to say, having removed the afflictions such as suffering, may they make them endowed with clarity regarding both worldly and Vedic matters.
And may the waters also anoint them thoroughly.
Likewise, may Mātariśvan unite our hearts;
that is to say, may he make our intellects mutually concordant.
And may Dhātṛ also unite them.
The one who bestows and gives fruits;
that is to say, Sarasvatī. And may she "saṃ dadhātu," meaning may she effect a union.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the third chapter in the eighth book of the *Ṛgvedasaṃhitā-bhāṣya*, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial throne of the illustrious King Vīrabuka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
1. ga1.2-ta-bha1.2.4.7.8-yogurt | Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa!
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
The fourth chapter of the eighth Aṣṭaka begins.
Therein, the second hymn consists of twenty-three verses beginning with "vi hi.
Its author is Vṛṣākapi, the son of Indra.
Regarding those three—Indrāṇī, Indra, and [the speaker]—who were united and engaged in a dialogue:
therein, the nine verses consisting of "vi hi sotora-sṛkṣata," "kiṃ subāho svaṅgure," "indrāṇīmāsu nāriṣu" (two verses), "ukṣṇo hi me," and "ayamemi" (four verses) are the words of Indra.
Indra is the seer (*ṛṣi*) of these.

The five verses beginning with "parā hīndra," the two beginning with "avīrām," and the four beginning with "vṛṣabho na tigmaśṛṅgaḥ" are the statements of Indrāṇī; Indrāṇī is the seer (ṛṣi) of these. The three verses "uve amba," "vṛṣākapāyi revati," and "paśurnāma" are the statements of Vṛṣākapi.
Vṛṣākapi is the seer (ṛṣi) of these [verses].
The entire hymn is dedicated to Indra and consists of *padapaṅkti* meters.
Thus it has been enumerated: "In the *vi hi* [hymn], there are more than two; [it is] Indra's; Vṛṣākapi, Indrāṇī, and Indra rejoiced together; it is in the *paṅkti* [meter]."
On the sixth day, this hymn is the *uktha* recitation (*śastra*) of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "Now, they should chant the *vṛṣākapi* on the fourth day of the *hotravyāyā*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.3).

Furthermore, if on the sixth day the *uktha-stotras* were not chanted in three-footed verses, or if the *māmagāḥ* [were not performed], or if the day were an *iṣṭoma*, then at that time the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, after the *ārambhaṇīyās* in the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*), should chant this hymn; thus it is also said: "you should chant this hymn."
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin [recites] the Sukīrti and the Vṛṣākapi, praising them verse by verse" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.4).

For they have poured out the soma-pressing, yet they did not regard Indra as a god—at that place where Vṛṣākapi, the noble one, took delight among the well-fed [cattle], intoxicated with me as his companion; Indra is superior to all.

They have indeed poured out the Soma; they did not consider Indra to be a god. Where Vṛṣākapi, sharing the revelry with his noble kinsman, rejoiced in the nourishments of the enemy—Indra is superior to all. 1.
The chanters— those who perform the sacrifice for Vṛṣākapi and have been released and authorized by me toward the sacrifice— have "unleashed" (visṛkṣata) the pressing of the Soma.
The word "hi" is a filler.
In this regard, they did not recognize me as "Indra," the shining god.
Although impelled by me, those singers did not praise me;
rather, they praised my son, Vṛṣākapi, alone.
"In those sacrifices which have been nourished and increased by Soma, my son Vṛṣākapi—the noble lord—being my companion and my friend, has rejoiced, being delighted by the drinking of Soma.
Even though this is so, I, Indra, am superior and more excellent than all that is known.
Mādhava Bhaṭṭa, however, considers this to be the speech of Indrāṇī, who is about to cross over.
And so it has been said:
a certain animal, Vṛṣākapi, while dwelling in the sacrificial oblation prepared for Indra, stepped upon the limb of Indra’s son.
Therein, Indrāṇī speaks to Indra.
In that interpretation, the meaning of this verse of one's own [Ṛgveda] is as follows:
"vi" (apart) was said in order to perform the pressing of Soma;
the meaning is that the sacrificers had ceased the pressing of Soma.
Furthermore, the singers do not honor—that is, they do not praise—my husband, the god named Indra.
Where? To this he says:
in whatever prosperous region the lord (*arya*), the bull-like Vṛṣākapi, has rejoiced amidst abundant riches.
Indra, who is dear to me, is superior to—more excellent than—the entire world, that is, everything that exists.
"O Indra, you run away from the Vṛṣākapi," such is the distress [of the poet].
"Do not find pleasure elsewhere than for the drinking of Soma; O Indra, you are superior to all!"

1. From *ta4.5.8* onwards, these [verses] belong to Indra. 2. In *ta1.2.3*, they are called *ukthaśastra*; in *ta7-bha*, they are called *ukthaśastra*. 3. In *ta-bha*, they are [recited] at the *ārabhaṇīyā*. 4. *ta-bha*: For thus it is said:
For, O Indra, you have indeed sped away from Vṛṣākapi with your swift movements. Yet, for me, you find yourself elsewhere than for the drinking of Soma. Indra is superior to all. (RV 10.86.2)
O Indra, you are excessively agitated; you run away from Vṛṣākapi and go toward him.
Yet, for the sake of drinking the Soma—indeed, not even for that—you do not find your way forward [to us].
This very Indra is superior to all.
What has this Vṛṣākapi done to you, he the tawny wild beast, that you now feel resentment toward him?
Whether it be a noble man or one who possesses prosperity—O Indra, you are superior to all of them.
What has this tawny beast, Vṛṣākapi, done to you, that you are so envious of him? Whether he be a noble or one with abundant wealth, Indra is superior to all. (3)
O Indra, toward you this Vṛṣākapi— this deer-like being, of the color of a tawny horse,
belonging to the species of deer— what pleasing thing has he done? What has he performed?
To whomsoever, even as a noble or a generous man, you quickly bestow wealth consisting of nourishment and abundance for Vṛṣākapi—
Indra, who is superior to all.
O Indra, you who protect this dear Vṛṣākapi—may the dog gnaw his foot;
may the boar-hunter bite his ear. Indra is superior to all.
This Vṛṣākapi whom you, O Indra, protect as a dear friend—now let the dog gnaw at his ear, even though he is eager for the boar; Indra is superior to all. ||4||
O Indra, this dear, beloved son whom you protect and preserve— this Vṛṣākapi— let the dog,
seeking the boar (*varāhayuḥ*), quickly seize and devour him; the genitive case here is used in the sense of the accusative.
Moreover, the ellipsis "let him seize by the ear" is to be supplied;
for dogs indeed desire a boar.
The rest is established.
The dear, well-fashioned things of mine the monkey has disfigured and marred.
May I rend his head; may I not be easy prey for the evildoer. Indra is superior to all.
The dear, well-fashioned [limbs] of mine—Kapi, the bird-marked one, has torn them apart. Now I shall rend his head; may I not find an easy path for the evildoer. Indra is superior to all. ||5||

Someone—a monkey (kapi) acting in the domain of Vṛṣākapi—has defiled the oblations: those which were fashioned for me by Indra, prepared by the sacrificers, dear and most beloved, distinct and clearly manifested, and especially anointed with clarified butter (ājya).
Therefore, I shall quickly rend the head of this Vṛṣākapi, the lord of that monkey.
May I not find happiness (sugaṃ) in the presence of this Vṛṣākapi, the performer of evil deeds (duṣkṛte).
The meaning is: "I am not one who bestows happiness upon him.
Her husband, Indra, is superior to all.
1. There is no "ta-bha-ati". 2. Ta = tasmai. 3. Ga = yasyāḥ (as found in [texts] 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, and bha).

There is no woman more fortunate than I, nor one who brings greater joy; none is more devoted to me, nor more skilled at raising her thighs. Indra is superior to all. No woman other than I is more *subhasattarā*—that is, exceedingly blessed or fortunate. Nor is there any other woman who is *suyāśutarā*—meaning she who possesses greater happiness or better offspring. To this effect, another mantra states: "The generous woman gives me hundreds of swift horses to enjoy" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.126.6). Furthermore, no woman other than I is *praticyavīyasī*—one who causes the body to move excessively toward a man. Nor is there any other woman who is *sakthyudyamīyasī*—one who raises her thighs most effectively during sexual union. The meaning is that no other woman raises her thighs so favorably for intercourse. My husband, Indra, is *uttaraḥ*—superior to all.

O Mother, O you of easy attainment, just as you have said, so indeed, O dear one, shall it come to pass. Let your vulva, O Mother, and let my thigh be enjoyed; let my head, as it were, rejoice for Indra, who is supreme over all. O Mother, O you of easy attainment—just as you have spoken, so indeed, O dear one, shall it quickly come to pass. What need have I for this seizure that merely pleases you? Moreover, let your vulva be enjoyed by my father; let your thigh also be enjoyed by my father. Furthermore, let my father Indra rejoice with your head through pleasant conversation, just as a bird such as a cuckoo does; for my father is Indra, supreme over all.

Why, O Subāhu, why, O fair-armed one, O fair-fingered one, O broad-chested one, O broad-hipped one? Why, O wife of a hero, do you threaten our Vṛṣākapi? Indra is superior to all. (8) Indra pacifies her who is angry: "O Subāhu, O fair-armed one; O Svadaṅguri, O fair-fingered one; O Pṛthuṣṭi, O you with a thick mass of hair; O Pṛthujaghana, O broad-hipped one; O Śūrapali, O wife of a hero! O Indrāṇī, for what reason (*kam*) do you (*tvam*) threaten (*abhyamīṣi*), that is, become angry at (*abhikupyasi*) our Vṛṣākapi? One *kim* is used as a filler. He whose father is Indra—I am superior (*uttaraḥ*) to all."
1. *ga4*: A woman other than [me]. 2. *ga.ta4*: From the angry one, Indra’s consort; *ta3.5.6.7*: From the angry one, Indra’s consort, Indra.

“This cruel man regards me as if I were childless; yet I am the mother of heroes, the wife of Indra, with the Maruts as my kin. Indra is superior to all. (9) “He,” the cruel one, “regards” me “as if I were childless. “Yet” I “am” the mother of heroes, “the wife of Indra,” with the Maruts as my friends. “Indra” is “superior” to “all. (9)
Again, Indrāṇī says to Indra:
"This Vṛṣākapi is a predatory, murderous beast."

Indra’s consort thinks of me, Indrāṇī, as if I were childless; yet she knows well that I, Indrāṇī, am the wife of Indra, possessed of heroic sons, and have the Maruts as my companions, being joined with the Maruts. My husband is Indra, who is supreme over all.

In ancient times, a woman used to go to the common sacrificial feast or indeed to the assembly. Now, as the wise one, the mother of heroes, the consort of Indra, she is glorified. Indra is superior to all. 10. In ancient times, a woman used to go to the common sacrificial feast or indeed to the assembly. Now, as the wise one, the mother of heroes, the consort of Indra, she is glorified. Indra is superior to all. 10.

The woman (*nārī*) is the female creator (*vedhāḥ*), the ordainer (*vidhātrī*) of *ṛta*—that is, of truth; she is the mother of heroes (*vīriṇī*) and possessed of sons (*putravatī*). She is the wife of Indra (*indrāṇī*), the consort of Indra. She indeed goes toward the *saṃhotra*, which is the sacrifice (*yajña*), the assembly (*samana*), or the battle (*saṃgrāma*)—for "assembly" (*samitiḥ*) and "gathering" (*samana") are listed among the names for battle.
She goes forward against [the enemy] from of old.
He is magnified by his praisers and is praised;
my husband, Indra, is superior to all.

Among these women, I have heard that Indrāṇī is most fortunate; for her husband shall never die of old age, nor at any other time. Indra is superior to all. 11. Indrāṇī | among these | women | most fortunate | I | have heard | for not | of her | even later | by old age | shall the husband | die | than all | Indra | is superior. 11.
Then Indra praises Indrāṇī:

"Among these women who are renowned for their auspiciousness, I, Indra, have heard that Indrāṇī is the most fortunate, the possessor of supreme good fortune. Furthermore, her husband, the protector, Indra, is superior to all; moreover, he does not at all die through old age—that is, through the decay of vitality—just like other beings."
Alternatively,
this is the speech of Vṛṣākapi;
in that case, however, the word "I" (aham) must be interpreted as referring to Vṛṣākapi.
The rest is the same.

O Indrāṇī, I have no pleasure apart from my friend Vṛṣākapi, whose dear oblation, consisting of water, goes to the gods; Indra is superior to all. 12. I, O Indrāṇī, have not taken delight apart from my friend Vṛṣākapi, whose this watery oblation, so dear, goes among the gods; Indra is higher than all. 12.

1. Furthermore, Indrāṇī speaks. 2. In the versions *ga*, *ta*, and *bha*, the word "ghātuka" does not exist. 3. In the versions *ta*, *bha* 1.2.4, the word "strīṣu" does not exist. 4. In the versions *ta* and *bha*, it is "utkṛṣṭaḥ". 5. In the versions *ta*, *bha* 1.2.4.6.8, it is "yasmin". O Indrāṇī, I am Indra; because of my friend Vṛṣākapi—without this dear Vṛṣākapi—I do not rejoice, I do not take delight. Even this dear, pleasing oblation (*havis*), prepared with mantras from within the waters (*apām apyām*), which is presented here, goes toward me, Indra, among the gods, into the presence of me, that Indra.
And as for me, O Indra, who am superior to all—
this is the meaning: O Indrāṇī, I do not take pleasure (*rarāṇa*), that is, I do not delight, in Vṛṣākapi, the friend of Indra.
The rest is a compound.
O Vṛṣākapāyī, O wealthy one, you who have good sons and a good daughter-in-law! May Indra eat the oxen; may he eat the dear, all-pleasing oblation. Indra is supreme over all.
O Vṛṣākapāyī! O wealthy one! O mother of noble sons! And indeed, O you with noble daughters-in-law! Indra shall eat your oxen and your dear, most effective oblation. Indra is superior to all. 13.
O Vṛṣākapāyī!
Because he rains down desires, Indra—who wishes to go to his desired destination—is Vṛṣākapi;
you are his wife.

Or alternatively, the meaning is: "O Vṛṣākapi, my mother. O wealthy one (revati), O you who possess riches; O you with a noble son (suputre); O you with a beautiful daughter-in-law (susnuṣe); O Indrāṇī, this Indra of yours—immediately after (ādu) [the sacrifice]—[is] the bulls (ukṣarṇaḥ), capable of sprinkling [rain].
The meaning is "very quickly.
He devoured the animals until dawn.
Furthermore, it was something that produced some effect.
*Kam* means happiness (*sukham*). *Tasya* refers to that [happiness]. *Saṃghaḥ* means a collection (*cit*) thereof.
The remainder of the sense is: "Make the oblation (*haviḥ*) which produces that [happiness] dear (*priyam*), that is, desired (*iṣṭam*)."
Moreover, your husband Indra is superior to all;

thus says Yāska: "O Vṛṣākapi’s wife, O wealthy one, you who have good sons, O you with a good daughter-in-law through the intermediate [voice]—for the daughter-in-law is speech belonging to the intermediate region (mādhyamikā vāc); she is so called because she brings what is beneficial (sādhusādinī), or perhaps because she acquires what is excellent (sādhusāninī)."
"Perform what is dear, which brings about a mass of happiness; O Indra, you are superior to all" (Nirukta 12.9).
For fifteen oxen they cook for me at once, even twenty;
and with water they fill both my sides full of fatness; Indra is superior to all.
For they cook for me at once fifteen oxen and twenty more; moreover, they fill both my flanks with water and fat. Indra is superior to all. 14.
Then Indra says:
"For my sake, the sacrificers, impelled by my wife Indrāṇī, cook together fifteen—that is, fifteen in number—and twenty—that is, twenty in number—of bulls (ukṣan).
Moreover, I devour them."
"Having eaten, I become fat—that is, stout—this is the sense.
Furthermore, O Rāma, both my two sides (kukṣī) are filled—that is, the sacrificers fill them with Soma. Such as I am, I am Indra, superior to all."
Like a sharp-horned bull bellowing within the herds, this churning-drink is for your heart's delight, O Indra, which the pious one presses for you; Indra is supreme over all.

Beholding and discerning the Dāsa and the Ārya, here I go; I drink the Soma of the simple sacrificer; I look upon the wise one. Indra is superior to all. (19) Now Indra speaks: "Beholding (*vicārśat*)—that is, seeing—the sacrificers, and discerning (*vicinvan*)—that is, distinguishing—the *Dāsa*, the Asura who oppresses, as well as the *Ārya*, I, this very Indra, *emi*—I go toward the sacrifice. Having gone to the sacrifice, I drink the Soma of the *pākasutvan*. *Pāka* means 'one who cooks' (*pacati*), and *sutvan* means 'one who presses' (*sunoti*). Thus, I drink the Soma belonging to the sacrificer who has cooked the oblation and pressed the juice, and whose mind is matured (*pākena vipakvena manasā*). Likewise, I look upon (*abhyacākaśam*) the wise (*dhīram*) sacrificer. I, who am Indra, am superior (*uttaraḥ*) to all. (19)

The desert and the forest—how many leagues lie between them? O Vṛṣākapi, come from that place nearest to our home; come to our house. Indra is superior to all. *dhánva* is a waterless region devoid of forests. *Kuntatram* is a forest to be cut down. "Whatever desert and whatever forest there may be"—such is the forest inhabited by wild beasts, not an impenetrable wilderness. Between that abode of the enemy and our own home, how many *yojanas* (leagues) are situated? It is not very far away. Therefore, O Vṛṣākapi, from that place which is exceedingly near, come to our home (*astam*); having arrived, go specifically to our houses, the sacrificial halls. For I am Indra, the most excellent of all.

Come back again, O Vṛṣākapi; let us two perform auspicious deeds. You, who are this destroyer of sleep, go to your home by the path; Indra is superior to all. "Come back again, O Vṛṣākapi; let us two perform auspicious deeds. Having returned, Indra speaks to the departed Vṛṣākapi: "O Vṛṣākapi, come back to us. When you have arrived, let us two—both I and Indrāṇī—deliberate and perform auspicious deeds, those actions which bring about well-being and satisfy your mind. Furthermore, you, who are this 'destroyer of sleep' (svapnanaṃśana)—the Sun who, through his rising, destroys the sleep of every living being—go by the path to your own abode once more. For I, Indra, am superior to all. And thus Yāska says: "Let us two perform for you well-initiated deeds; you, who are this destroyer of sleep—the Sun who destroys sleep through his rising—he goes to his setting by the path once more" (Nirukta 12.28).

When Vṛṣākapi had gone and returned again, Indra asks him: "O Indra, possessor of supreme sovereignty; O Vṛṣākapi, you who are *udaśvaḥ*—meaning those who go upward—have you come to my house? The plural number is used for even a single person for the sake of honor.

In this matter, your relative Pulvagha—*pulvaghaḥ* being derived from *bahūnām* (many) and *bhaumarasānām* (earthly juices)—was intoxicated; where did that deer, the delighter of people (*janayopanaḥ*), go? To what region did he depart?
I am that very Indra, superior to all.

Regarding this, Yāska says: “O Vṛṣākapi, when you came to the house of Udaśva, where was that beast with many wounds? Where was that beast with many scars? ‘Beast’ (*mṛga*) [is so called] from the root *mṛg* meaning ‘to move. To what place did he go, leading the people? (Nirukta 13.3).

The third hymn, consisting of twenty-five verses, begins with "rakṣohaṇam.

Of the twenty-two verses, four are *anuṣṭubh* meters.
The remaining twenty-one verses are *triṣṭubh*s. Their deity is the slayer of demons (*rakṣohāgni*).

Thus it is stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: "The *rakṣohaṇam* [section] consists of five more [verses]; the *pāyu* [section] is for the removal of disease; the *rakṣohaṇam* [section] consists of four *ṛc*s ending in *nṛpūn*."
The application of the hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*) has been concluded.

O Jātavedas, being well-kindled, with iron fangs and with your flame, touch the Yātudhānas. Seize the fools who worship false gods with your tongue; having torn apart the flesh-eaters, place them within your mouth. O Jātavedas—O you whose wealth or wisdom is born—you, being well-kindled and blazing brightly, possessing iron fangs—that is, sharp fangs—touch the Yātudhānas, the Rākṣasas, with your flame, meaning "burn them. Furthermore, seize with your tongue—that is, with your flame—the Mūradevas, the fools who worship false gods, the Rākṣasas engaged in murderous activities; the sense is "slay them. Having slain them, tear apart the flesh-eaters, the Rākṣasas, and place them within your mouth; that is, cover them with it.

O you who possess both [fangs], set your fangs upon the destroyers; sharpening them, [set them] on the lower and the higher. And, O King, travel through the mid-air; with your jaws, seize and crush the sorcerers! O Ubhayāvin (you who possess both), you who are the destroyer of demons, sharpening both your fangs, set them down as the cause of destruction upon the demons. Furthermore, protect the world, both the lower and the higher. Moreover, O Radiant One, traverse the mid-air, encompassing the demons stationed there; having encompassed them, join them with your jaws—those teeth intended for devouring—and crush those sorcerers. The meaning is: "Devour them."

With those [arrows] with which, bending the shafts at the tip with our speech and smearing the points with thunderbolts, pierce the sorcerers in the heart with them; break their arms that are turned toward you. O Agni, with our sacrificial offerings—our own ritual acts—and with our speech—our own hymns of praise—you, bending the arrows that are curved and directing the shafts, smearing the points with thunderbolts—that is, sharpening them with your blazing rays—with those arrows, pierce the sorcerers, the Rākṣasas, in the heart. Then, break—that is, crush—their arms that are turned back toward you, having come against you for battle.

O Agni, rend the skin of the sorcerer (yātudhāna); let the destructive thunderbolt (aśani) strike him with its heat (haras). O Jātavedas, crush his joints (parvāṇi); let the flesh-eater (kravyād), seeking raw flesh (kraviṣṇu), tear apart (vi cinotu) the mangled (vṛkṇa) one. O Agni, O Jātavedas—whether "born of wealth" or "possessing born wisdom"—you must rend and split the skin of the sorcerer, that is, the Rākṣasa. Let the destructive thunderbolt, characterized by its habit of slaying, strike this sorcerer whose skin has been torn, piercing him with its heat. Once the Rākṣasa is slain, crush his joints—that is, sever the joints of his body. When the articulations of the body have been severed, let the flesh-eating wolf or similar beast, desiring raw meat, tear apart and devour this mangled sorcerer.

O Jātavedas, O most youthful Agni, whichever *yātudhāna*— a Rākṣasa who creates obstacles for our sacrifice— or whoever else, such as a Piśāca, performs this desecation of the sacrifice while standing here, you see him now;
"whichever" (*yatamaḥ*) is used for the purpose of specification.
"Speak forth to me who am engaged here in this sacrificial rite directed toward you;
seize—that evildoer—with your own fuel, that is, with your own splendor;
then subject this most wicked one to the sight, that is, to the power, of you who behold men."
The meaning is that he should burn them with his splendor.
With your sharp eye, O Agni, protect the sacrifice; lead it forward toward the Vasus, O wise one.
Blazing against the destructive Rākṣasas, let not the sorcerers deceive you, O watcher of men.

O Agni, with your sharp, piercing eye—that is, with your splendor—protect and preserve our sacrifice.

O you who watch over men, behold the Rakṣas on every side; crush its three points with your jaws.

O you who watch over men, look around at the demon! Tear out his three tips. O Agni, crush his ribs with your heat; rend the root of the sorcerer in three ways, like a tree.
O Agni, you who have the gaze of a hero (*nṛcakṣas*), look all around at the *rakṣas*, the demon, who dwells among men as a bringer of harm;
look upon him. And sever—the meaning is "cut off"—the three points, that is, the three heads, of that *rakṣas*.
Then, with your own heat (*haras*), your fiery energy, crush—that is, slay—the ribs of that *rakṣas* and the demons situated at his sides.
Thus, cut off the root—the foot—of that threefold demon, the *yātudhāna*, as one would a tree.
Let the threefold curse of the sorcerers fall upon him who, O Agni, strikes with falsehood against the truth.
O Jātavedas, strike him down from the sacrifice with your thunderbolt; destroy him openly before his very eyes as he utters his boast.

Three times! Let the sorcerer go to his own snare. O Agni Jātavedas, you who are born of the Truth, with your flame, strike down and crush him who destroys with falsehood—him who praises you while being present before your eyes. 11.
O Agni Jātavedas, whose wisdom is born, let the Yātudhāna—the Rākṣasa—enter your *prasiti*, the continuous series of your flames, three times over;
for that which is bound becomes triple-bound.
Furthermore, let him who is the Yātudhāna, the Rākṣasa, who destroys the *ṛta* (truth) with *anṛta* (untruth), be struck down by your own *arcis* (flame), flashing forth with your own splendor.

having seized him, strike him down with a wolf.

O Agni, place—that is, cast—that eye, that splendor, upon the shouting Rākṣasa, by means of which eye I may behold the Yātudhāna Rākṣasa who tears with his hooves (śaphārujam)—tearing with hooves or with claws resembling hooves—and who devours the virtuous face-to-face.
Furthermore, burn utterly like Atharvan with divine celestial light and splendor the one who injures the truth, who harms in the sacrifice, and who is devoid of consciousness through ignorance.
It was stated previously that Dadhyañc Atharvan is the slayer of the Rākṣasas.

O Agni, whatever curse the pair utters today, or whatever harshness the singers produce in their speech—whatever arrow is born from the fury of the mind—with that, pierce the sorcerers in the heart. 13. Whatever curse the pair utters today, or whatever harshness the singers produce in their speech—whatever arrow is born from the fury of the mind—with that, pierce the sorcerers in the heart. 13.

O Agni, whenever on this day a pair— a man and a woman— should curse one another, reviling each other; or whenever the *rebhas*, the singers, produce a harsh, bitter, and base speech characterized by mutual abuse—
that is, when they revile one another— then [act] there against that blazing wrath or evil spirit.
And thus Yāska says: "Manyu [is derived] from the root *man*, meaning 'to shine,' or 'to be angry,' or 'to kill'" (Nirukta 10.29).
From the mind (*manas*), that arrow (*iṣu*) which is the *śaravyā* is born; with that *śaravyā*, pierce—that is, strike—the *yātudhānas*, the Rākṣasas, in the heart;
the meaning is "slay them."
