O Agni, crush and slay the sorcerers (*yātudhāna*) with your heat and burning power;

furthermore, crush the demons (*rakṣas*) with your *haras*—your own fiery heat; and furthermore, crush the fools who worship false deities—the Rākṣasas engaged in murderous activities—with your own radiance and splendor.
Moreover, the meaning is: "Furthermore, crush those who are insatiable, who are satisfied by the lives of men."

May the gods today strike down the wicked man; may piercing curses return upon him. May the arrows of his own speech reach the thief in his vital organ; may the sorcerer go to the snare of everyone. May the gods today strike down the crooked one. May harsh curses return against him. May the arrows of his own speech reach the thief in his vital organ. May the sorcerer go to the snare of every living being.

1. In the *Ta-bha-ātharvaṇa* recension, [the name is] Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa. 2. In *ta¹·²·³·⁶·⁷·⁸*, *ma*, and *mu*: "on this day"; in *ta⁴*: "if on this day"; in *ta⁵*: "if indeed on this day. 3. In *ga*, *ta¹·²·³·⁶·⁷·⁸*, and *ma*, the word "yātudhānān" does not occur.

O gods, on this day, may all the gods, with Agni at their head, drive away the *yātudhāna* who deprives living beings of their breath; let them hear his evil words. Furthermore, as this approaching *rākṣasa* comes, let our harsh and bitter curses follow him back. Moreover, let the arrows of speech—words of falsehood—strike this *yātudhāna* in his vital organs and pierce his very vitals.
Let the snare—the net—of Agni Vyāsa, the pervader of all, [be cast].
And thus Yāska says: "Prasiti means either a spreading cord or a net" (Nirukta 6.12).
Let that net go to the sorcerer; let it pass him.
The sorcerer who anoints himself with human flesh, who with the flesh of a horse,
who first takes the milk of the cow— tear off their heads with your fiery heat!

O Agni, with your fiery heat, strike off the heads of those sorcerers who smear themselves with human flesh, who [smear themselves] with the flesh of horses, who [smear themselves] with the flesh of cattle, and who bring the milk of the cow. 16.
O Vaya, O Atudhana, O Rakshasa: with the flesh of men—belonging to man—consisting of crooked poison, you smear yourself; that is, you besmear your own body.
And with the flesh of horses—that is, with the flesh belonging to the multitude of horses—[you besmear yourself].
He unites himself;
or whatever sorcerer unites himself with another sacrificial animal;
or the sorcerer carries away and takes the milk from the cow that is to be slaughtered.
O Vaḍavāgni, by your own splendor, carry away—meaning, cut off—the heads of all these Rākṣasas; sever them!
O Agni, you who behold men, let no sorcerer consume the year-long milk of the cow;
whatever cream he may seek to devour, shatter him with your flame as he turns toward you at his vital spot.
The annual [milk] of the cow—let no sorcerer, O Agni, look upon its cream. Whosoever seeks to satisfy himself with it, shatter him from behind with your flame at his vital organ! 17.
O Agni, you who have eyes that see men, look upon our cow, the *usriyā*.
Since "the *usriyā* is a cow" is read among the names for cattle, [look upon her].
Whatever milk exists, produced within a year (*saṃvatsarīṇam*), which you purify—that let no *yātudhāna*, no demon, consume. Let him not drink that milk.

Furthermore, O Vāta (Wind), strike with your own radiance—that is, with your heat—the vital organ (*marman*), the seat of life, of that Rākṣasa who, desiring to satisfy himself, wishes to satiate his hunger with the milk of our cow using nectar instead of milk. [Note: *vata* is a variant of *vāta*; *vapīyūṣam* is a corruption of *amṛtena* due to metathesis; *vatarpritsāt* is a corruption of *tarpitum icchati*; *vapratiñcam* is a corruption of *pratyañcam*; *vamarman* is a corruption of *marmaṇi*; *vaviddhi* is a corruption of *viddhi*.]
The meaning is "kill."
Let the sorcerers drink poison; let the evil-doers be cut off from Aditi.
May the divine Savitṛ deliver them over; let them be deprived of their share of the plants. May they perish.
Poison! Of the cows! Let the sorcerers drink it! Let the evil-doers be cut off for Aditi! May the god Savitṛ deliver them over! May they lose their share of the plants; may they be defeated! 18.
O Agni, let the *yātudhānas*, the Rākṣasas, drink up the strength residing in the cattle, the livestock, within the house.
Furthermore, for the sake of Aditi, let the *yātudhānas* who are like trees be cut down—let them be severed by your weapons.
Moreover, O Savitṛ, let the divine one deliver those Rākṣasas over to the destroyers; let him hand them over to the injurers.
Moreover, these Rākṣasas shall obtain their own portion of the herbs—that is to say, they shall receive the food that is their rightful share.

1. *ga-ta-bha* 1.2.4.6.8: "śṛṇtu" means "let them hear" or "let them listen. 2. *ta-pratyayena*: "may they come hither. 3. *ga-ta4*: "and furthermore, of the universe. 4. *ga-ta-bha*: "from the overcoming [of enemies], [they shall] cross over. 5. *ga4*: "the meaning is 'may they not obtain'."

From of old, O Agni, you crush the sorcerers; the Rakṣasas have never conquered you in battles. Burn up the flesh-eaters along with their roots; let none escape your divine missile. From of old, O Agni, you crush the sorcerers; the Rakṣasas have never conquered you in battles. Burn up the flesh-eaters along with their roots; let none escape your divine missile.
O Agni, from of old, beginning from ancient times, you have crushed and oppressed the *yātudhānas*, the Rākṣasas.
Nevertheless, even in battles and conflicts, the Rākṣasas have not conquered, nor have they ever won over you.
Furthermore, may you now, in due order, burn with your splendor and reduce to ashes the flesh-eating Rākṣasas who are possessed of murderous intent along with their very roots.
Furthermore, let those sorcerers not be released—let them not be set free—from the ninefold bond, nor from the divine curse, nor from the divine weapon.
O Agni, protect us from below and from above; protect us from behind and from the front. May those unaging and most satiating flames of thine ward off the evil.
O victorious Agni, we set thee—the wise one—before us as our fortress, O subduer; thee of bold hue, day by day, the slayer of the treacherous.

O Agni, born for the greatness of the Great One, we—the Bhāradvājas known by the name Pāyu—surround you on every side for the slaying of the Rākṣasas: you who are the filler of the stronghold, the wise sage, of bold appearance, the daily destroyer and injurer of those Rākṣasas possessed of treacherous deeds.
With your song, burn away the deceptive Rākṣasas; O Agni, with your sharp flame and with your heat-tipped rays! || 23 ||

With poison! Against the treacherous Rākṣasas! Burn them, O Agni, with thy sharp flame and with thy spears whose points are glowing hot. O Agni, you, burn up—the treacherous Rākṣasas, those possessed of the act of breaking—with your spreading, sharp flame and with your spears whose tips are of a scorching nature. Spears (*ṛṣṭi*) are a particular kind of weapon; with those as well, burn them up.
O Agni, burn up the pairs of *yātudhānas* and *kimīdins*. I sharpen you, the undeceivable one; O sage, guard yourself with your vital parts. || 24 ||

O Agni, burn against the pairs of *kimīdins*, those sorcerers (*yātudhānas*) who wander about as *kimīdins*. Regarding this, Yāska says: “*Kimīdin* [is so called] because they move about as *kimīdins*; or perhaps it means ‘what is this? what is this? (Nirukta 6.11). Furthermore, O wise (*vipra*) Agni, I sharpen you—that is, I praise you—with hymns (*manmabhiḥ*), you who are unassailable (*adabdha*) by anyone. Therefore, be watchful; do not sleep; wake up.
O Agni, with your flame, O burner, crush him on every side! Break asunder the strength and the heroic power of the *yātudhāna*, of the demon! || 25 ||

O Agni, with your own heat (*haras*), crush the seizing power (*haraḥ*) of the *yātudhāna* demon from every side; shatter the strength and the heroic might of the *rākṣasa*. Regarding this, Yāska says: "Heat (*haraḥ*) is so called because it seizes (*harati*); light is called *hara*. O Agni, with your own brilliance, destroy—that is, annihilate—the seizing power of the *yātudhāna* demon. Likewise, break asunder the heroic vigor of the *rākṣasa*.
1. The strength of the *ga*-rakṣasa. 2. In *ta*, *bha* 1.2.4.6.8, ‘*haraḥ*’ is not present.
The fourth hymn, consisting of nineteen verses beginning with ‘*haviṣpāntam*’, is in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
The seer is Mūrdhanvat;
he belongs to the lineage of Aṅgiras or Vāmadeva.
The deity is Sūrya, characterized by Vaiśvānara, unmingled and manifest as a whole.

And thus it has been listed: “The *havir* [verse], the one less than nine [verses] of the Āṅgirasas, the *mūrdhanvat* [verse], the *nāmadheya* [verse], the *vāmadevya* [verse], or the *sauryavaiśvānarīya* [verse].
This *vaiśvānarīya-nivid* placement occurs on the fifth day of the expanded (*vyūḍha*) ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), in the *ābhimāruta* [section].
And it has been aphorized: “*haviṣpāntam agnir hotā gṛhapatiḥ sa rājā*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.8).
The imperishable drink of the oblation, reaching the light of heaven, touching the sky, offered and beloved in Agni—
for its maintenance and for the world’s upholding, the gods have proceeded according to their own inherent power.

The oblation—protecting, undecaying, the light-finder—is offered into Agni, who touches the heavens, as a welcome gift. For its maintenance, for the sake of the world, and for the sake of the cosmic law, the gods have set forth according to their own inherent power.

The water poured out is of the nature of Soma; it is ageless, free from decay, and beloved by the gods. This oblation, offered into the fire that reaches the sun, knows the light of heaven, touches the sky, and pervades the heavens—into this fire has it been poured. For the support and sustenance of that oblation which is of the nature of Soma, for the nourishment and maintenance of the world, and for the preservation of all, the gods extend and spread this Agni, who brings happiness to all, through *svadhā*, the food of the ancestors.

And thus Yāska says: “The oblation, which is to be taken up, which is undecaying, which finds the sun, which touches the sky, and is offered as a welcome offering—to him, for his support, for his nourishment, and for his maintenance, the gods approached with this intention” (Nirukta 7.25).
When Agni was born, the world that had been swallowed and enveloped by darkness became manifest through his own power;
the gods, the earth, the sky, the waters, and the plants were in his friendship.

Swallowed was the world, concealed by darkness; when Agni was born, the sun became manifest. At his birth, the gods, the earth, the sky, and the waters—yea, even the forest trees and the plants—were in his friendship. 2.

When Vaiśvānara Agni was born—having arisen, he made manifest that light (*svaḥ*) which had previously been vomited forth, then swallowed, hidden by darkness (*tamas*), and covered—the gods, beginning with Indra, as well as the earth, the sky, the waters, the intermediate space, the plants, and the forests, all took delight in his friendship;
that is to say, they found joy in the act of being his friends.
Impelled by the gods and by these sacrifices, I shall praise Agni, the undecaying and vast one,
who with his radiance has spread across this earth and heaven, and has pervaded both the worlds and the intermediate space.

Now, impelled by the gods with these sacrifices, I shall praise Agni, the undecaying and the great, who with his radiance has stretched across this earth and heaven, and the two worlds and the mid-air. ||3||
With these gods worthy of sacrifice—Indra and the other deities—I have quickly been released. I shall praise that Vaiśvānara Agni, the ancient, ageless, and great one.
That Vaiśvānara Agni, with his radiance and splendor, has stretched out and pervades both the earth and this sky.
He demonstrates this very point: [he extends across them].
He has stretched out, that is, he extends, the two worlds, heaven and earth; the meaning is that he causes them to expand.
1. *ta-bhuvanam* was swallowed; *bha1.2.7-pūrṇa* [variant] was swallowed. 2. *ga-iṣitaḥ* means sent forth. 3. *ga-mu-staumi*. 4. *ga-ta4.5-antarikṣam ca*; *ta1.2.3-mu-cāntarikṣam ca*.
He who was the first Hotṛ, beloved by the gods, whom they chose as they anointed him with clarified butter—he, Agni Jātavedas, made the moving world and the stationary firmament to be swift-winged.

He who was the first invoker, beloved by the gods, whom they anointed with clarified butter while choosing him—whatever is winged, whatever stands, whatever moves, and whatever breathes, all that Agni Jātavedas has brought forth. 4.

That Vaiśvānara Agni, who was the first and principal Hotṛ chosen and served by the gods—him, the Vaiśvānara, whom the sacrificers, choosing him, anoint thoroughly with clarified butter—that Jātavedas (he whose wisdom is born, or whose wealth is born), that Vaiśvānara Agni, quickly brought forth the world: the winged (that which flies), the crawling (such as reptiles and the like), and the stationary (in the form of trees and so on); that is to say, he generated the entire world of both the stationary and the moving, making it swift and vigorous.
And thus Yāska says: "The fire Jātavedas made that which is winged, swift, stationary, and moving all quickly" (Nirukta 5.3).

O Jātavedas, since you stood at the head of the world in the beginning together with the realm of light, I honor you with prayers, songs, and hymns; thus, worthy of sacrifice, you have filled both heaven and earth.

O Jātavedas, when you stood at the head of the world in the beginning together with the realm of light, you, being worthy of sacrifice, filled the two worlds—him, you, I honor with prayers, songs, and hymns; thus you have become the one who pervades heaven and earth. 5.

O Jātavedas, O Agni of born wisdom, since you have stood upon the head of the universe—the three worlds—along with the radiant Āditya, we approach you, that Vaiśvānara, with meditations worthy of worship, with songs, praises, and hymns.
(The root *hi* means "to go"). You, as Vaiśvānara, are the fulfiller of heaven and earth (*rodasī*), the one worthy of sacrifice, and you are indeed the one who deserves the sacrifice.
Agni becomes the head of the earth at night; from him, the sun is born as he rises in the morning.
He moves swiftly through these waters of the worshipful ones, knowing their illusory power (māyā).

The summit; of the earth; he becomes manifest. By night; Agni; from that; Sūrya; is born at dawn. At his rising, he indeed moves swiftly through this wondrous power of the worshipful ones, knowing the waters. ||6||

Agni Vaiśvānara is Agni; by night, he becomes the head—the preeminent part like a head—of *bhū*, the multitude of beings, because at night he provides light for all living creatures and they are dependent upon him. Then, immediately after that night, the Sun is born as it rises in the morning.

The meaning is that during the day, Agni Vaiśvānara indeed becomes the Sun. Furthermore, the wise consider this to be the supreme power (*māyā*) of the gods who are worthy of sacrifice and possess sacrificial vessels—
the Sun, being perceived and clearly manifest, moving swiftly and resonantly, traverses the waters, the intermediate space, or his own activity.

And thus Yāska says: “The *mūrdhan* is so called because it is placed (*dhīyate*) in this [world] as a formed entity (*mūrta*). It is the head of all beings; delighting in the night, it is born as the sun when rising in the morning—it is that very same one.

But the wise consider this to be the intelligence of the sacrificial gods who accomplish the sacrifice: knowing the water, he performs its work, and moving through all places, he travels about while sounding forth” (Nirukta 7.27).
The greatness that is visible, kindled, and has shone forth from its celestial source—
that Agni, the radiant one, into him all the gods, protectors of the body, have offered oblations with hymns of praise.

1. He who, by his greatness, shone forth together with all his limbs, he of the two-fold birth, the radiant one—into that Agni all the gods, the protectors of bodies, have offered oblation with the hymn of praise. 7.

That Vaiśvānara Agni, who by his greatness—that is, his vastness—is visible and worthy of being seen by all, who is well-kindled and perfectly radiant, who has two wombs and resides in heaven (*dyusthāna*), and who is full of splendor (*vibhāvā*), shone and continues to shine. Into that Vaiśvānara Agni, all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*)—the protectors of bodies—offered oblations (*havis*) directly with the *sūktavāka*, namely with the words beginning "O Heaven and Earth" (*idaṃ dyāvāpṛthivī*), or by means of the utterance of hymns of praise.
The gods first generated Agni from the Sūktavāka;
he became their protector of the sacrifice. Him the sky knows, him the earth, and him the waters.

First indeed they generated the *sūktavāka*, and then Agni, and then the oblation—the gods produced them. He became their sacrifice, the protector of their bodies; him Dyaus knows, him Pṛthivī knows, him the Waters know. (8)

First, they mentally recite the *sūktavāka*—the formula beginning with "idaṃ dyāvāpṛthivī"—and immediately thereafter, they produce fire by friction; immediately after that, the gods generate the oblation (*havis*). That Agni Vaiśvānara becomes, and is, the sacrifice of these gods—that which is to be sacrificed—and he also becomes the protector of their bodies (*tanū-pāḥ*).
Dyaus, the heavenly world, knows that Agni;
Pṛthivī, the earth, also knows that Agni;
and Āpas, the waters, as well as the intermediate space (antarikṣa), know that Agni.
The gods who generated this Agni, in whom they offered oblations and all the worlds— he,
being purified, heated this earth and this heaven with his flame through his greatness.
The gods generated that Agni, in whom they offered up all worlds. With his flame, he heated this earth and heaven with his greatness, advancing uprightly. ||9||

That Vaiśvānara Agni whom the gods generated— having brought him into existence— and when that Vaiśvānara Agni had arisen, into whom all beings offered oblations face-to-face in the Sarvamedha sacrifice; that Vaiśvānara Agni, with his radiance (*arcis*), by means of his splendor (*tejas*), heating the earth, the intermediate space (for "āpaḥ pṛthivī" is read among the names of the intermediate space),
and the sky, as well as this earth, moving straight forward (*ṛjuyamānaḥ*) and by his greatness (*mahitvā*), heats— that is, he burns— all things.
For by means of praise, the gods generated Agni in heaven; with their powers, he filled the two worlds. They made him threefold for the sake of existence; he ripens the plants of every form.
For by means of praise, the gods generated Agni in heaven with their powers, he who fills the two worlds. They made him threefold for the sake of existence; he ripens the plants of every form. ||10||
1. ga4-ta1.2.5.6—they invoked him with directness; ta4—they invoked him with directness; bha1.4.6—they offered oblations with directness; bha7—they offered oblations with directness.

The gods, by means of their powers—that is, their ritual acts—generated Agni, who is of the nature of the Sun and the fulfiller of heaven and earth (rodasaprāṃ), in the sky (divi) through praise (stomena hi).
Moreover, they make that very same one, the source of happiness (kam), threefold for the sake of his threefold manifestation within the sacrifice (yajñe tredhā bhuve).
Existing upon the earth, he ripens the plants of all forms—that is, rice and other crops—by means of various beneficial services.

Regarding this, Yāska says: "The gods, having generated him in heaven by means of hymns (*stoma*) or by their powers (*śakti*), or by means of ritual acts (*karman*), made him the filler of both heaven and earth; Śākapūṇi [says] that for the sake of his threefold existence, [they placed him] on earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven.
For the Brāhmaṇa states: 'That which is his third part in heaven, that is yonder Āditya'" (Nirukta 7.28).
When the worshipful gods placed him, Sūrya Āditya, in heaven;
when the moving pair had come into being, they beheld all the worlds through Āditya.
When the worshipful gods placed him there in heaven as Sūrya Āditya, and when the two moving ones became a pair, then indeed all beings beheld him. 11.
When, at dawn, the gods worthy of sacrifice (yajñiyāsaḥ) established in heaven the son of Aditi, Sūrya, the beloved (venam), and Agni; and when these two,
the ever-moving Sūrya and Vaiśvānara, became a pair and appeared,
immediately thereafter all beings (viśvā bhuvanāni) beheld them.

On this point Yāska says: “When all the gods worthy of sacrifice placed him, Sūrya, the son of Aditi, in heaven; when the two moving pairs appeared, ever-moving together—the Upāṃśu and the Āditya. Why ‘mithunau’? [The root] *math* means ‘to support’ (*śrayati-karman*), or the letter *tha* in the formation of the name [is used], or [the root] *nī* [is used]. They are joined together (*samāśritau*), they lead one another, or they desire one another (*vanutaḥ*). Even human couples are derived from this very [root]: they strive against each other (*methantau*) or they desire one another (*vanutaḥ*)” (Nirukta 7.29).
For the sake of the entire world, the gods established Agni Vaiśvānara as their banner;
he who has extended himself over the radiant dawns, spreading out the darkness with his flame as he moves.

For all the world, for the universe, the gods have made Agni Vaiśvānara their banner, the light of days; he who has stretched out the shining dawns, and as he moves, he unrolls the darkness with his flame. 12.
The gods, Indra and the others, made Vaiśvānara—the Agni who belongs to all men, the banner (sign) of the days, the one who makes things known—for the entire world.
That Vaiśvānara Agni, shining forth in various ways at the dawning of the day, has spread [himself] out.
Moreover, as he goes, he drives away the darkness with his luster, removing it with his brilliance.
The wise, worshipful gods generated Vaiśvānara Agni,
the ageless one— the ancient, moving star, the powerful and vast overseer of the sacrifice.
The wise, worthy of sacrifice, the gods generated Vaiśvānara Agni—the undecaying, the ancient star, the all-pervading, the overseer of the spirit, the powerful, the great. 13.

1. ta1.3-ma-hi yaṃ | 2. ma-‘śaktibhi: is not present | 3. ta1.2.7-āpūraṇaṃ | 4. ga-ta2.7- the son of Sūrya Āditya Aditi; ta1.6-Sūrya Āditya, the son of Aditi | 5. ga-ta-for Viśvasmai, for all; 6. ta-bha-for havanāya | The *kavayaḥ*, the wise ones, the *yajñiyāsaḥ*, those worthy of sacrifice or the performers of sacrifice, the *devāḥ*, the gods, generated—brought forth—*Agni Vaiśvānara*, who is *ajuryam*, free from decay or inviolable, belonging to all men (*viśvanarahitam*), and whose essence is the Sun.

And that fire, kindled by the gods, [knows] the constellation beginning with Kṛttikā, the ancient question, and that which is "cariṣṇu"— meaning having the habit of moving— of the Yakṣa. The root *yakṣ* has the sense of worship,
as seen in such passages as *pratyakṣam* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.5.1).

He has indeed harmed— that is, overcome with his splendor— the Yakṣa, the worshipful deity, the overseer (adhyakṣa), the manifest one (pratyakṣa), the lord (svāmin), the powerful (taviṣa), the ancient (vṛddha), the vast (bṛhant), and the great (mahānt).
We address with our hymns Vaiśvānara, who shines forever, the one who is manifest through his power—
he who by his greatness has encompassed the two wide worlds, the god who is from below and also from the front.
Vaiśvānara,
shining forever.
The two united, coming together, heaven and earth, [behold] him who moves and goes, born from the head, produced from the head.
And thus there is another Vedic citation: "Moreover, I think of him as born in the morning from the head of Manyu.
Or alternatively:
The meaning is that it was born from the Sun, who is the head of all; [it was done] "with the mind" (*manasā*),
where the root *man* signifies the act of praising.

Bearing—that is, maintaining—the fire which has been cleansed, purified, and consecrated by worshipful praise, that Agni, unwearied and vigilant, swift-acting, and shining brightly, stands facing all beings, directed toward every world. Thus it is heard in scripture: "Therefore, everyone thinks, 'It has risen up toward me'" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.4.2).

Where the lower and the higher speak, which of us two, the two knowers of sacrifice, knows [the truth]? Let them come together to the common feast; let the friends reach the sacrifice. Who will declare this? Where the lower and the higher speak, which of us two, the two knowers of sacrifice, knows [the truth]? Let them come together to the common feast; let the friends reach the sacrifice. Who will declare this? (17)

At whatever time the lower terrestrial fire and the divine Hotṛ, as well as the higher and intermediate Vāyu—both of them speak, that is, engage in dispute regarding the two leaders of the sacrifice—between the two of us, which one knows best the sacrifice? Therein, O friends, the officiating priests of equal renown are able to perform the shared feast of the sacrifice.

Likewise, among those learned ones who approach the sacrifice, recite the hymns, and perform the rites—whoever among these learned performers might speak forth this sentence, which is the form of a decision for this dispute?
He speaks of this central fire (mādhyamika).

And thus Yāska says: "Where the two divine Hotṛ-priests, Vyaghrabhūti and Agnimāt, dispute with the middle one, saying, 'Which of us knows more regarding the sacrifice? they perform that together as a source of exhilaration; those officiating priests who share the same narrative, while following the sacrifice, [ask] 'Who among us will declare this? (Nirukta 7.30).

How many fires? How many suns? How many dawns? How many waters, O women? I do not speak to you in jest, O fathers; I ask you, O seers, for the sake of knowledge. 18. How many are the fires? How many are the suns? How many are the dawns? How many, indeed, are the waters, O women? I do not speak to you in jest, O fathers; I ask you, O seers, for the sake of understanding. 18.
When they were thus disputing, they approached their ancestors with a question;
there, the middle one asked them: "How many fires are there?"
How many are the fires? How many are the suns? How many are the dawns? And how many are the waters?
The particle *u* is for filling out the meter.
The word *strit* here has the sense of deliberation (*vicāraṇā*).
O fathers, [I offer] your *upaspija*.
"Upaspijam"—this is said as a statement of rivalry.
This is not the previously mentioned question;
rather, [the meaning is: "O wise ones (*kavayaḥ*), being ignorant, I ask you for the sake of knowledge (*vidmane*)—for what pleasure (*kam*)—without the hardship of reflecting upon its true nature."
In this regard, the subsequent verses are shown in the Vālakhilya-saṃhitā: "The one fire alone is kindled in many ways; the one sun has spread throughout the universe.
The one dawn alone illumines all this; indeed, the One has become all this" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.58.2).

As much as the two fair-winged ones clothe themselves in the face of the Dawn, O Mātariśvan, so much does the Brahmin, approaching the sacrifice and sitting down below the Hotṛ, bestow. 19. As much as the two fair-winged ones [the Aśvins] clothe themselves in the face of the Dawn, O Mātariśvan, so much does the Brahmin, coming toward the sacrifice and sitting down lower than the Hotṛ, bestow. 19.
1. *ga* reads *bhuvanā bhuvanāni*. 2. *ta* reads *vidhānasya*. 3. *ga*, *ta1.2.6.8*, and *ma2.8* read *vadāmi na vakṣyāmi* (I say, I shall not speak).
[Maṇḍala 10, Anuvāka 7, Sūkta 89] Regarding the subject of Vaiśvānara under discussion, they declare the determination of his power through this [verse]:

O Mātariśvan— O Mātariśvan, the intermediate wind blowing within the mother, the atmosphere— however much, however great, is the face, the light, or the manifestation of the well-flying Suparṇīs, that is, the nights or the dawns.

"Na" is a filler word. "Vasate" means they cover or clothe. Just so, the Brāhmaṇa Hotṛ—the lower or inferior one—sitting down (*niṣīdan*) in this very place of the divine Vaiśvānara Hotṛ, approaching (*āyan*) the sacrifice in order to perform the duties of the Hotṛ (*hautram karma*), brings it near (*upa dadhāti*);
that is, he holds the duties of the Hotṛ within his own mind.

And thus Yāska says: “In the sense of ‘as much as,’ there is the usage of *upa* in the sense of comparison, as in ‘it is turned toward the dawn,’ or ‘it is seen again’; and in the sense of ‘presently,’ as in ‘here indeed is the prohibition’; and in the sense of ‘just like,’ as in ‘these nights dwell like well-flying birds (*suparṇyaḥ*); O Mātariśvan, he lays down [bricks] for as long as the color of light [is visible]; when approaching the sacrifice, the Brāhmaṇa Hotṛ sits down here, lower than the Hotṛ; and it belongs to the Hotṛ and Vaiśvānara. (Nirukta 7.31).
The fifth hymn, consisting of eighteen verses beginning with "I praise Indra" (*indraṃ stava*), belongs to Reṇu, the son of Viśvāmitra; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to Indra.
It is cataloged thus: "Indraṃ stava dyūnā reṇuḥ.
However, Sūryatviṣṭa declared that this hymn is to be recited as a Nividdhāna at the Niṣkevalya Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The midday [pressing] belongs to him who desires glory, with the verses 'Praise the Sun' and 'Drink the Soma, Indra,' and 'Exalt Indra'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.8).

I shall praise Indra, the most heroic, by whose greatness he forced asunder the luminous realms and the ends of the earth—he who, upholding the people, has surpassed the two broad expanses and the rivers with his might. I shall praise Indra, the most heroic, by whose greatness he forced asunder the luminous realms and the ends of the earth—he who, upholding the people, has surpassed the two broad expanses and the rivers with his might.
O singer, praise, indeed, Indra—the most heroic, the best leader—of whom the greatness is immense. (Note:
There is a shift in case endings [vibhaktivyatyaya].)
Shining brightly, she overcomes the splendors of others;
"overcomes" means she surpasses them.
She also surpasses the ends—the boundaries—of the earth.

And that Indra, the sustainer of the people, the upholder of human beings—who, by his greatness, has surpassed and continues to increase beyond the rivers and the oceans—fills both heaven and earth with his rays of light, which ward off the darkness.

May that Indra turn the sun toward the wide expanses, as a charioteer turns the wheels; he has struck down the black darkness with his splendor, like a flood of water that does not stand still. He, the sun—may Indra turn him toward the wide expanses, like a charioteer turning wheels; [he struck] the dark darkness with his brilliance, like a stream of water that does not stand still. 2.
Sūrya, the possessor of great heroism—he is well-known as Indra—shall turn back, that is, he causes to revolve, many *varāṃsi*, which means vast splendors.
Therein lies the illustration:
just as a charioteer, belonging to the chariot, turns back the wheels associated with the chariot, so it is for the sake of the sacrifice.

Furthermore, she beheld this steed—this "sarga" (from the root *sṛj*, meaning that which is let loose)—which was not standing still but moving swiftly, appearing as if it were not subject to ordinary action.

Kṛṣṇā struck, indeed strikes, with her brilliance—that is, her luster—the "kṛṣṇas," meaning the dark shadows. (Note: *Sarga* here refers to the horse; the word is derived from the root *sṛj* "to emit" or "let loose," signifying the one who is set forth.)
1. He was inferior to the one who had gone to the fire.

2. Ga1.2: sitting as the Hotṛ-priest; Ta-Bh4.8: sitting with the knowledge of the Hotṛ-priest; Bha1: the birth of the Hotṛ-priest; BhaRa: sitting as the best of Hotṛ-priests; Bha6-Mu: sitting with the knowledge of the Hotṛ-priest. 3. They approached.
4. *ga-ta-bha-mu* refers to the Mādhyandina school.
5. *ga-bha* is like a charioteer; *ta-sārathī* is the charioteer.
(Kārikā 4.39)
For him, I have opened up the floods; I sing a new prayer, peerless upon earth and in heaven.
Indra, who has distinguished the generations like ridges, seeks no friend for his own desire.

The same [is true] for him. O unobstructed one, sing forth! With the earth, [sing] of heaven; [sing] a new prayer that is never-ending. Indra, who has distinguished the births of the noble one like ridges, does not seek a friend for himself. 3.
O singer, you and I together [shall praise] that which is unrestrained (*anapāvṛt*), free from obstacles, and unsurpassed by earth or heaven— that is, exceedingly great,
in the sense of being vast. Recite this new, never before performed prayer (*brahman*) for this Indra.

Indra, who at the sacrifices distinguishes between the various beings born—just as one discerns the "backs" (pṛṣṭha) known as the hymns—and who separates the enemies from his friends, does not desire those who are hostile.
For Indra, I send forth unrestrained streams of songs like flowing waters,
from the fullness of my inspiration— he who, with his powers, has propped apart the earth and heaven on all sides, as if with two wheels by means of an axle.

For Indra, I send forth my songs with unrestrained flow like waters, from the source of the stream. He who, by his powers, has propped apart the earth and heaven on all sides, as if with an axle between two wheels. 4.

For Indra—that is, for the sake of Indra—I shall impel the waters from the region of the *bubhā* by means of those songs of praise (*giraḥ*) which proceed higher and higher with unrestrained emission, having abandoned the cause of fear;
for "Sagara" is read among the names of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), as in the phrase "Sagara is the ocean.
I shall send forth the waters from that place.
Indra, by his powers and deeds, has firmly propped up the earth and even the sky—he who fashioned the heavens like chariot wheels, supporting them on every side as if with a single axle.

The one who brings the waters near, the impetuous shatterer, the roaring, the powerful, the consumer of the dregs—Soma has overcome all forests and obstacles; no rivals have stood against Indra with their might.

With his wrath reaching to the end, impetuous in his onset, roaring, full of vigor, armed with arrows, the consumer of the dregs—Soma [is he]. All the trees, even the thorny bushes, have not stood as a match for Indra; they have not held him back. ||5||

Āpāṃtamanyuḥ—his wrath brought near; *tṛpalaprabharmā*—one whose onset is impetuous; *prāvabhiḥ*—striking swiftly with his weapons; *dhuniḥ*—the shaker of enemies; *śimīvān*—active; *śarumān*—possessing arrows; *āyudhavān*—armed with weapons; *ṛjīṣī*—possessing the *ṛjīṣa* (the dregs of Soma); [Soma] increases all the *atasā*, that is, the thorny woods and forests.
The meaning is that the various objects of comparison (*pratimānāni*), the things that serve as standards of comparison, do not surpass Indra.
The root *dabh* has the sense of "attracting.
When weighed on a scale, they do not attract [the balance] toward themselves;
the meaning is that they become light.
When heavy objects are substituted elsewhere, they pull toward themselves; Indra does not act in this way.
The meaning is that Indra is greater than all.
Three quarters are Soma’s, while the fourth belongs to Indra.

And thus says Yāska: "Āpādita-manyu (one who has attained fury), tṛpa-prahārī (striking with thirst), kṣipra-prahārī (striking swiftly)—is he Soma or Indra? Dhuni (the shaker) from the root *dhū* (to shake). Śimī is a name for action, derived either from *śam* (to pacify) or *śak* (to be able). Arjīṣī: that which remains over of the Soma while it is being purified is the *arjīṣa*; it is what is cast away (*apārjita*). Because of that [cast-off part], Soma is called *arjīṣī*. Now, there is a Vedic text concerning Indra: 'The *arjīṣī* [Indra] roars. Soma [conquers] all forests."

1. *ta-bha* read *antarikṣaṃ ca*. 2. *ga1.2-ta-bha-mu* do not have ‘*uyaḥ*’. 3. *tara.7-bha* read *rathākṣeṇeva*. 4. *gara* reads *āpādita0*. 5. *ta-bha* read *pratinidhāyamānāni*. 6. *ta1.2.7-mu* read *kṣipraprahārī kṣapraprahārī*. [The Nirukta states: "The boats do not deceive Indra, nor do those things by which they measure him deceive him" (*Nirukta* 5.12).

Neither heaven and earth, nor the desert, nor the mid-air, nor the mountains have contained him when Soma flowed. When his wrath is being aroused, it shatters the firm and breaks even the solid things. Neither heaven and earth, nor the desert, nor the mid-air, nor the mountains have contained him when Soma flowed. When his wrath is being aroused, it shatters the firm and breaks even the solid things.
Neither heaven and earth—those two, heaven and earth—are a match for Indra;
nor is the water in the ocean a match for him;
nor is the intermediate space—a match for him either.
Neither forests nor mountains serve as a defense for him;
Indra’s *soma* flows from his chest.
Moreover, when Indra’s wrath (*manyu*) is being raised against his enemies, then this Indra shatters—that is, destroys—the firm (*vīḷu*).
It crushes and shatters even firm things.

He struck down Vṛtra as an axe fells the woods; he shattered the fortresses and dug out the rivers. He split the mountain like a new jar; Indra brought forth the cows with his own companions. 7. He struck down Vṛtra; like an axe, [he struck] the woods; he shattered the fortresses; he dug out the rivers; he split the mountain like a new jar; Indra brought forth the cows with his own companions. 7.
Indra struck down Vṛtra, the Asura; moreover,
like an axe or a hatchet, he shattered— as one breaks through forests—
the citadels, that is, the cities of his enemies, and with the waters of the rivers, he dug out the streams.
The word *vna* is used here in the sense of "now. Furthermore, he (*indra*) shattered—indeed, he shattered like one breaking—a new jar, that is, a water-jar, which was like a cloud upon the mountain.
Moreover, Indra, with his self-yoked Maruts (those who join him of their own accord), brought forth the waters, or the rays of light, toward us.

O Indra, you, the wise one, truly shatter those crooked ones with your bolt as an axe cleaves wood; those people who violate the law of Mitra and Varuṇa, like those who harm a friend. 8. You, indeed, O Indra, [shatter] that [host]; you, the wise one, [shatter] the crooked ones like an axe [cleaving] wood; those people who violate the abode of Mitra and Varuṇa, like those who harm a friend. 8.
O Indra, you are indeed wise and discerning; you shall surely bring about that which is to be done. You are the one who causes the debts incurred by those who praise you to reach their fulfillment.
Furthermore, like a sharp weapon, you shatter—the word *parva* meaning joints—as you crush the crookedness, that is, the calamities of your worshippers.

Moreover, O Mitra, you destroy even those cruel men who violently injure the work that sustains the domain of Mitra and Varuṇa, just as one breaks the bonds of a chariot-yoke. The sense is that you utterly annihilate them as well.
Those of evil intent who violate the beloved Mitra, the *saṃgir* (oaths), and Varuṇa— O Indra,
sharpen here for our friends the increasing, powerful, manly, and ruddy bull.

1. It does not exist as one that has become a counterpart (pratimāna) to *ta*; it does not exist as one that has become a counterpart to *bha*. 2. In *ta* and *bha*, the syllable *na* is absent. 3. In *ta* and *bha*, there is *antarikṣam*. 4. In *ta* and *bha*, there are *adrayaḥ*. 5. In *ta*, *bha*, 1, 2, 4, and 6, there is *m upadravāṇām*; in *bha* 8, there is *m upadravyāṇām*.

pra ye mitram pra aryamaṇam duḥ’evāḥ pra sum’gireḥ pra varuṇam minanti | ni amitreṣu vadham indra tubhram vṛṣan vṛṣāgam arutram śiśīhi || 9 || Those of evil conduct who violate Mitra, Aryaman, the one well-disposed to speech, and Varuṇa—upon those enemies, O Indra, O bull, sharpen your fierce, bull-like, unyielding weapon! 9.

Those people of evil course, who violate Mitra, the god; who violate Arthaman, the god; who violate the Maruts, who possess harmonious praise; and who violate Varuna, the god—against those enemies, O *vṛṣan* (showerer of desires), O Indra, you [wield] the *tubhram* (swift-moving), the *vṛṣāṇam* (showerer of desires), the *arutram* (shining) weapon, the *vadhám* (thunderbolt).
Because "vadhaḥ vajraḥ" (the blow is the thunderbolt) is read among the names of the thunderbolt,
[the word] "ni śiśīhi" means "sharpen it."

Indra rules over heaven; Indra rules over the earth; Indra [rules] over the waters; Indra indeed [rules] over the mountains. Indra [rules] over those who prosper; Indra indeed [rules] over the wise. Indra is to be invoked in times of peace and in times of exertion. 10. Indra. Of heaven. Indra. Rules. Of the earth. Indra. Of the waters. Indra. Indeed. Of the mountains. Indra. Of those who prosper. Indra. Indeed. Of the wise. Indra. In peace. In exertion. To be invoked. Indra. 10.
Indra rules over heaven; Indra is the lord of the earth as well;
Indra is the lord of the waters;
and Indra is the lord of the mountains—that is, of the clouds.
Indra alone is the lord even of those who have grown great;
Indra alone is the lord even of the wise.
Furthermore, Indra is to be invoked for *kṣema*, the preservation of wealth already acquired, and Indra alone is to be invoked for *yoga*, the acquisition of wealth not yet obtained.

Indra has surpassed the waters, surpassed the days, surpassed the mid-air, and surpassed the reservoir of the ocean; he has surpassed the expanse of the wind, surpassed the limit of the earth, surpassed the rivers, and surpassed all inhabited lands. 11. Indra has surpassed the waters, surpassed the days, surpassed the mid-air, and surpassed the reservoir of the ocean; he has surpassed the expanse of the wind, surpassed the limit of the earth, surpassed the rivers, and surpassed all inhabited lands. 11.
Indra is more increased than the nights;
he is more increased, even superior, than the days;
he is increased beyond even the intermediate space.
He has grown even beyond the reservoir of the ocean, the holder of waters;
he has grown even beyond the vastness of the wind;
he has grown even beyond the limit of the earth.
He has surpassed the Sindhus, that is, the rivers;
the meaning is that he has become great.
He has also surpassed the kṣitis, that is, the human beings.

Like the gleaming banner of the dawning day, let your insatiable missile fly forth, O Indra. Like a stone hurled from heaven, shatter the deceitful enemies with your most parching fury. pra śoṣucatyāḥ upasaḥ na ketuḥ asinvā te vartatām indra hetiḥ | aśmāiva vidhva divaḥ ā sṛjñānaḥ tarpiṣṭena hepasā droghamitrān || 12 || Let your insatiable missile fly forth, O Indra, like the gleaming banner of the dawning day. Shattering them like a stone hurled from heaven, strike down the deceitful enemies with your most parching fury.
O Indra, let your unyielding weapon, the thunderbolt known as *heti*, like the banner-like ray of the blazing dawn, be hurled forth against the enemies.
Furthermore, with that most scorching [weapon]—
[which is] indeed powerful.

2. Free from the breaking of the *ga* and *mu* [syllables]; free from the breaking of the *ta* and *bha* [syllables]. Exceedingly to be tormented by the enemies through the weapon (*hetī*) that makes sound (*heṣasā*). "Those whose friends have been milked" are the *drohamitrāḥ*. (They are those whose friends have been exploited.)
Strike those enemies; pierce them.
Therein lies the illustration:
like Agni, emitting the light of heaven.
The meaning is that it is just as a thunderbolt fells trees.
Day after day the months followed, the treasures followed, the plants followed, and the mountains;
both worlds, crying out, followed Indra as he was being born, and the waters followed him.

The days follow him; the months follow him; the forests follow him; the plants follow him; the mountains follow him; the two worlds, crying out in longing, follow Indra; the waters followed him as he was being born.
The months, beginning with Caitra, followed after Indra as he was being born and manifested;
"aha" is a filler particle.
Even the forests and the wildernesses followed after Indra.
*It* is a filler [particle]. Even the *oṣadhīḥ*, the plants, follow after Indra; even the *parvatāsaḥ*, the mountains, follow after Indra.
Even Rodasī, Heaven and Earth, lowing—that is, desiring—follow after Indra;
the waters also follow after Indra. The meaning is that the presiding deities of the months follow Indra as he manifests.
Where indeed was that thought of yours, O Indra, when the devouring Rakṣas sought to strike?
When the friend-making [Indra], like a bull at the hurling of the bolt, lay upon the earth like a serpent in the waters?

Where indeed was that wisdom of yours, O Indra, when you shattered the demon who approached with evil? When you shattered the non-existent ones like calves at the slaughter, they lay scattered there upon the earth.

O Indra, that weapon of yours—whether it be the *ripu* (striking) or the *cetiyā* (to be thought upon), the one to be dwelt upon by the enemy—is it indeed (*kvit*) where? Or when (*kadā*) will it come to be (*asat*)?
By which weapon [is] your own [destruction], the genitive being used in the sense of the accusative (*aghasya*).
He shattered the *rakṣas* as it came rushing toward him for battle;

and with that spear (*śakti*) by which the *mitrakuvas*—those people who perform cruel deeds against their friends—were struck down like cattle in the slaughter-ground belonging to the earth, they lay there, joined with this earth in battle, having been slain.

O Indra, let those who seek to harm us, who swell with great pride against us, and those enemies who are devoid of virtue—let them be overtaken by blinding darkness; may the nights of thick gloom fall upon them.

Those enemies who, swelling with great pride, have assailed us from every side—O Indra, let those blind foes be overtaken by blinding darkness; may they be swallowed up by the nights as they flee toward the brilliant light. 15.
O Indra, those enemies who are hostile toward us, swelling with great pride and oppressing us, being devoid of virtue and gathered in a host—

those foes who stretch out against us and cast us down, let those enemies be joined with blinding darkness, with a vast gloom. Furthermore, may the days and nights, possessing excellent light, overcome those enemies.

4. Those who desire enmity from their enemies—many indeed are the libations of men for you, and the sacred prayers (*brahmāṇi*) of the praising ṛṣis delight you.
Hearing this joint invocation with favor, come hither across all those who sing your praises.
For many indeed are the libations of men; may the sacred prayers of the chanting seers delight you. Hearing this joint invocation with favor, come hither, passing beyond all who sing your praise. 16.
O Indra, these many *savanā*—the libations—and the *brahmāṇi*, the hymns of praise belonging to the people, gladden you; they cause you joy.

Hearing this joint invocation (*sahūti*) of the praising seers, saying, "Great and beautiful indeed is this praise," do thou come toward us (*arvāṅ*), with thy protection (*avasā*), passing over all others who are likewise praising and worshipping.
Thus, O Indra, may we find for ourselves new and enjoyable favors from you.
May we, the Viśvāmitras, finding delight, obtain all things through your protection at the break of dawn.
Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet. Having pervaded the earth on every side, he extended beyond it by ten fingers' breadth.
That Puruṣa known as Virāj, whose body is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and who consists of the collective totality of all living beings—
he is the one with a thousand heads.
Because the word "thousand" is used figuratively (*upalakṣaṇa*), the meaning is that he is endowed with infinite heads.
All the heads of all living beings are indeed known as His [the Puruṣa’s] own, because they are contained within His body; thus He possesses a thousand heads.
Likewise, He possesses a thousand eyes and a thousand feet.
That Puruṣa, having encompassed the earth—the cosmic egg—from all sides, remained transcending it by a space of ten fingers' breadth, that is, by a distance measured at ten *aṅgulas*.
The phrase "ten fingers" is an illustration;
the meaning is that he remains pervading everything, even outside the cosmic egg.
The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be;
moreover, he is the lord of immortality, which surpasses [all] through food.
The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be—and he is the lord of immortality, that which grows beyond by means of food. 2.
All this present world is indeed the Puruṣa;
and that which was the past world, and that which is yet to be—the future world—that too is indeed the Puruṣa.
The intention is that just as all the bodies of living beings existing in this present kalpa are the limbs of the Virāj-Puruṣa, so it should be understood for the past and future kalpas as well.

Moreover, he is the lord and master of immortality—that is, of the state of divinity—for this reason: by means of food, which serves as the object of enjoyment for living beings, he "surpasses," meaning that having transcended his own causal state, he attains the manifest state of the world; therefore, the meaning is that his true nature consists in the assumption of the state of the world for the sake of living beings' experience of the fruits of their actions.
Such is His greatness, and the Puruṣa is even greater than this;
one quarter of Him consists of all beings, while His three quarters are the immortal in heaven.
Such is his greatness; yet the Puruṣa is even greater than this. All beings constitute one quarter of him; his three quarters are the immortal in heaven. 3.
Whatever form the world takes—past, future, or present—all this is merely the majesty (*mahiman*) of this Puruṣa, his own particular power;
it is not, however, his true essential nature (*vāstava-svarūpa*).
Since the Puruṣa is the real entity (*vāstavavastu*), he is greater than even that majesty, being exceedingly superior to it.
Both of these points are now made explicit:
of this Puruṣa, all beings—all classes of living creatures existing throughout the three periods of time—constitute one quarter, the fourth part.
Of this Puruṣa, the remaining three-quarters, His true nature, which is immortal and indestructible, abide in heaven—that is to say, in the luminous realm of His own self-luminous nature.

Although it is impossible to define four quarters for the Supreme Brahman—of whom it is said, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.1; Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1)—nevertheless, the presentation of "quarters" is made because this world is intended to be shown as small in comparison to the nature of Brahman.

4. By means of the *ta*, *ta*, *ra*, *bha*, *mu*, and *nimitta* [meters].
