"The Puruṣa rose up three-quarters above; one quarter of him was here again.
Thence he spread out in all directions, over that which eats and that which does not eat. (RV 10.90.3)
With three quarters the Puruṣa rose upward; one quarter of him was here again. From there he strode out in all directions toward what is eaten and what is not eaten. || 4 ||

This Puruṣa, who has three feet, is free from saṃsāra and is of the nature of Brahman; He rose upward, having emerged from this saṃsāra which is the product of ignorance, remaining in a state of excellence, unassailed by the qualities and defects found here. Of Him, this one foot—a mere fraction—is that which has come again into this world of Māyā, returning repeatedly through the processes of creation and dissolution.
That this entire universe is but a fraction of the Supreme Self was also stated by the Blessed Lord: "Pervading all this, I remain with but one part, supporting the world" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.42).

12. Then, immediately after [the Lord] had entered into Māyā, 13 being manifold (vividha) in the form of gods, humans, animals, and so forth—meaning, existing as Viṣvaṅ—he 14 pervaded (vyakrāmat), that is, he extended throughout [the universe].
Having done what?
16 Having aimed at both the eating and the non-eating [beings].

The meaning is that He Himself, having become manifold, pervaded both the animate world—consisting of living beings endowed with the activities of eating and so forth—and the inanimate world—devoid of those activities, such as mountains, rivers, and the like.
Thus, He became diverse in accordance with both of these.
From him Virāj was born; from Virāj, Puruṣa was born.
Once born, he extended beyond the earth, both behind and before.
From him Virāj was born; from Virāj the Puruṣa arose. Once born, he extended beyond the earth on all sides, both behind and before. 5.
What was stated in the verse "He strode forth in all directions" is here elaborated upon.

From that *ādipuruṣa* (the Primordial Person), the *virāṭ*—whose body is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)—was born, i.e., produced. It is called *virāṭ* because various resplendent things (*vastu*) shine forth within it.

From Virāj, upon the body of Virāj—making that very body the substratum—a Puruṣa was born: a certain person possessing the conceit of that body. He, the Supreme Self who is known by all the Vedāntas, having himself created the body of Virāj in the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) through his own Māyā, entered it in the form of a living soul (jīva) and became the deity Ātman, the presiding soul of the cosmic egg.

And the followers of the Atharva Veda state this very clearly in the *Uttaratāpanīya*: “Having created the elements, the senses, the Virāj, the deities, and the sheaths, he, having entered them, remains undeluded, yet as if deluded, acting through Māyā alone” (*Nṛsiṃhatāpanīya* 2.1.9).
That Virāj Puruṣa who was born became *ayariyata*, i.e., exceeded [his original form];
he became that which is distinct from the Virāj, appearing in the forms of gods, animals, humans, and so forth.
12. Afterwards, after the state of existence as gods and other beings, Śeṣa created the earth (13).

Then, immediately after the earth, he created their 14 *purah*—that is, bodies (*śarīrāṇi*)—which are filled (*pūryante*) with the seven constituent elements (*dhātavaḥ*). 15. Thus, he created their bodies.
When the gods performed the sacrifice with man as the oblation,
spring was its clarified butter, summer the fuel, and autumn the offering.
When the gods performed the sacrifice with man as the oblation, spring was its clarified butter, summer the fuel, and autumn the oblation. 6.

1. *ga*-ta-bha-mu: Free from contact with saṃsāra. 2. *ga*-ta-1.2.3.6.7.8-bha: Whose essential nature is manifold. 3. *ga*-tasya yo 'yam; *ta*-bha4.7: Of him, this is that. 4. *ta*-bha: In the form of gods, animals, and so forth. 5. *ta*-mu: The multitude of living beings is perceived. 6. *ga*-ta4.5-bha: Diverse. 7. *ta6-bha8*: Elsewhere. 8. *ta*-bha: That very same one.

"When, in the manner previously described, bodies had come into existence, the gods—since external substances had not yet arisen and thus no other sacrificial offering was possible for the sake of accomplishing the subsequent creation—conceived the very form of Puruṣa as the mental oblation and performed, that is, carried out, a "mental sacrifice" with "Puruṣa," meaning the one called Puruṣa, as the "oblation. At that time, "of this sacrifice," "Spring" alone "was the clarified butter"; they conceived of that very season as the clarified butter. Likewise, "Summer was the fuel."

The meaning is that they resolved to regard her as the fuel (*idhma*). Likewise, "Śraddhā was the oblation (*havis*)," meaning they resolved to regard her as the sacrificial oblations such as the *puroḍāśa*.

It should be understood that first there is the mental resolve regarding the person as having the general form of the oblation, and subsequently there is the mental resolve regarding spring and the other seasons as having the specific forms of the clarified butter and so forth.
They sprinkled that sacrifice upon the sacrificial grass—the Puruṣa who was born in the beginning;
with him, the gods, the Sādhyas, and the Ṛṣis performed the sacrifice.
They sprinkled that sacrifice, the Puruṣa, upon the sacrificial grass.

From that sacrifice, the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born; from that sacrifice, the meters such as the Gāyatrī and others were born; and from that sacrifice, the Yajus-formulas also arose. From it were born horses, and whatever animals have two rows of teeth; from it indeed were born cows; and from it were born goats and sheep. (10) From that [sacrifice], horses were born; and whatever [animals] have two rows of teeth; cows indeed were born from that; and from that were born goats and sheep. (10)

From that aforementioned sacrifice, horses were born; likewise, goats and sheep—those with teeth in both the upper and lower rows—were also born. Furthermore, from that sacrifice, cattle were produced, and goats and sheep were also born. When they divided the Puruṣa, into how many parts did they arrange him? What was his mouth, what were his two arms, and what are his thighs and feet called? 11 When they divided the Puruṣa, into how many ways did they arrange him? What was his mouth, what were his two arms, and what are his thighs and feet called? 11

In the form of questions and answers, the questions of the seekers of Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*) are stated in order to explain the creation of the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes. When the gods, who are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of Prajāpati, fashioned—that is, produced by means of volition—the Person (*puruṣa*) in the form of the Virāj, then in how many ways (*katidhā*), that is, by how many modes, did they fashion him diversely?
What was the mouth of that Person?
What became the two arms? What the two thighs? And what are called the two feet?
First is a question regarding the general form, followed by specific questions such as "What is the mouth? and so forth.

The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) was made from his two arms; that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; and from his two feet the Śūdra was born. 12. Brāhmaṇaḥ | asya | mukham | āsīt | bāhū iti | rājanyaḥ | kṛtaḥ | ūrū iti | tat | asya | yat | vaiśyaḥ | pād'bhyām | śūdraḥ | ajāyata || 12 ||
Now he shows the answers to the questions previously stated:

Of that Prajāpati, the Brāhmaṇa—the person characterized by the Brāhmaṇa caste—was the mouth; the meaning is that he was produced from the mouth. Furthermore, the Rājanya—the person possessing the Kṣatriya caste—was made the arms; he was brought forth as the arms.
The meaning is that he was produced from the two arms.
At that time, the Vaiśya came into being in the form of Prajāpati’s two thighs;
the meaning is that he was produced from the two thighs.
Likewise, from his two feet—that is, from his two *pāda*s—a Śūdra, a person belonging to the Śūdra caste, was born.

Furthermore, this origin of the Brāhmaṇas and others from the mouth and other parts is clearly recorded in the seventh book (*kāṇḍa*) of the Yajurveda Saṃhitā, in passages such as: "He fashioned the Trivṛt [stoma] from his mouth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.1.4).
Therefore, both the question and the answer should be interpreted as being directed toward that very point.
1. From that, too, they were born; 2. by Time, they caused [them] to be produced; 3. "What... face? does not exist.

4. *ta-mu*: distinguished by the caste of Kṣatriya. 5. *ga-bhara*: by that very intentness; *ta1.3.4.5.6*: by that very intentness; *ta7-mu*: by the state of being intent on that. The moon was born from the mind; from the eye the sun was born. From the mouth Indra and Agni were born; from the breath Vāyu was born. || 13 || The moon. From the mind. Was born. From the eye. The sun. Was born. From the mouth. Indra. And. Agni. And. From the breath. Vāyu. Was born. || 13 ||

Just as substances such as curd and clarified butter, animals such as cows, the Vedas such as the Ṛgveda, and humans such as Brāhmaṇas were produced from him, so too the gods, beginning with the Moon, were produced from that very source; thus he says:
from the mind of Prajāpati the Moon was born, and from his eye the Sun also arose.
From his mouth, the two gods Indra and Agni were born;
from his breath, Vāyu was born.

From his navel the intermediate space arose; from his head the sky evolved; from his feet the earth, and from his ears the quarters; thus they fashioned the worlds. (14) From the navel there was the intermediate space; from the head the sky evolved; from the two feet the earth, and from the ears the directions; thus they fashioned the worlds. (14)

Just as they fashioned the moon and other celestial bodies from the mind and other organs of Prajāpati, so too did the gods fashion—that is, produce—the worlds such as the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) from the navel and other parts of Prajāpati.
This very point he demonstrates:
"From the navel of Prajāpati, the intermediate space arose."
From his head, the sky evolved;
from his feet, the earth was produced;
from his ears, the quarters were produced.

Seven were its enclosing sticks; thrice seven were the fuel-sticks prepared. When the gods, performing the sacrifice, bound Puruṣa as the victim. 15. Seven. Of him. Were. The enclosing sticks. Thrice seven. Fuel-sticks. Made. The gods. When. The sacrifice. Extending. Bound. Puruṣa. As the victim. 15.
In this sacrifice performed through mere resolve (*saṃkalpa-yajña*), the seven meters beginning with *gāyatrī* served as the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
For the sacrificial fire of the *iṣṭi*, there were three enclosing sticks and the *uttaravedi*; the sun was the seventh, serving as a substitute for an enclosing stick.
Therefore it is declared in the scripture: "One should not place an enclosing stick to the east, for the sun itself protects him from the front" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.6.6.3).
Thus, these seven enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) accompanied by the Ādityas are here in the form of the seven meters (*chandas*).
Likewise, the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) are three times seven—that is, twenty-one—having been multiplied by three.

As stated in the Śruti: “The twelve months, the five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun make the twenty-first” (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.1.10.3), these entities mentioned therein are conceived as the kindling-wood consisting of twenty-one pieces.

The gods—who are of the nature of Prajāpati, the vital breaths, and the senses—performing the sacrifice, that is, performing the mental sacrifice, bound that Puruṣa as the victim; they conceived the Virāj-Puruṣa himself as the sacrificial animal.
It is with this very intention that it was stated previously: "With the Puruṣa as the oblation..."

1. According to Ta, Bha, and Bhāṣya 4.6.8: [the deities] beginning with the mind of Prajāpati; according to Bha 7: [the deities] beginning with the mind of Prajāpati. 2. According to Ta 1–2–6: the deities beginning with the navel are the limbs; according to Ta 3–7: the limbs beginning with the navel; according to Ta 8 and Bha: the deities beginning with the navel. 3. According to Ta: of the sacrifice consisting of mental resolve (*sāṃkalpika*).
By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances.
These great ones attained the height of heaven, where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
By means of sacrifice, the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances. Those great ones attained the heavenly world where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide. 16.
The author here briefly demonstrates the meaning stated previously:

the gods, who are of the nature of Prajāpati’s vital breaths (prāṇas), worshipped—meaning they honored—the sacrifice, which is Prajāpati himself whose essential form is as described, by means of the sacrifice, that is, through the aforementioned mental resolve (saṃkalpa). From that act of worship, those well-known *dharmas*—the sustainers of the modifications that constitute the world—became the first, that is, the primary ones.
By this much, the meaning of the portion of the hymn that sets forth the creation has been summarized.
Now, the meaning of the portion that restates the fruits of meditation is summarized:

"In that heaven"—in that celestial realm consisting of the attainment of Virāj—"where the ancient Sādhyas," the gods who were practitioners having meditated upon Virāj, "dwell and abide," that heaven consisting of the attainment of Virāj, "those glorious ones"—the meditators of great majesty—"accompany it," that is, they come together with it and attain it.

In the eighth section (anuvāka), there are nine hymns (sūktas). The first hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "saṃ jāguvadbhiḥ," is the seerly work (ārṣa) of one named Āruṇa, the son of Vītahavya; its deity is Agni. The final verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter, while the remaining verses are in the Jagatī meter.
And thus it has been introduced: “*Saṃ jāguvadbhiḥ* [is] by Pañcona Āruṇa; *Vainahavya* [composed] an *Āgneya* [hymn].
This hymn belongs to the two meters used in the *Prātaranuvāka* and the *Āśvina-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Saṃ jāguvadbhiḥ*, *tri ṣṭubhaḥ*, *vasuṃ na citramahasam*—this is the *Jāgata* [hymn]” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
Kindled by those who wake with him, he, the domestic lord, is enkindled in the home, providing nourishment for the one who delights in the wind.
The Hotṛ of every oblation, most excellent, pervasive, far-shining, he is a good friend to him who seeks his friendship.

Awakened by those who keep watch, the domestic lord is kindled in the house; bestowing nourishment at the place of *iḷ*, the Hotṛ of every oblation, most desirable, pervasive, far-shining, and a good friend to him who seeks his friendship. 1.

O Agni, being praised by wakeful worshippers who are habituated to vigilance, you—being a *damūnā* (a domestic lord, or one whose mind is subdued through self-restraint)—dwelling at the place of *ilā* (the sacrificial food), namely upon the high altar (*uttaravedī*), seeking nourishment (*iṣayann*), as the invoker (*hotṛ*) of every oblation (*havis*), the most excellent (*vareṇya*), the all-pervading (*vibhu*), the radiant (*vibhāvā*), and the good friend (*susakhā*), you are thoroughly kindled (*sam idhyase*) for the sake of the sacrificer who desires friendship (*sakhīyate*).
He, the one of visible glory, is a guest in every house; he has taken refuge in forest after forest like a swift hero.
As one who belongs to all people, he does not disdain any person; as one who belongs to the clans, he dwells among the clans, entering every clan.

He of beautiful splendor, the guest in every house, has taken refuge in every forest like a swift bird. Like a stranger among people, he is not disregarded; as one belonging to the clans, he dwells among the clans, from clan to clan.
He of visible splendor, whose manifestation is beautiful to behold, he the guest who has become a guest—that Agni rests in every house among the sacrificers, and in every forest among all the trees.
Furthermore, he the friend of men, that Agni, [rests] among every person—among all people, [that is,] among the principal beings.
1. *ta-* omits *mukhyāni*. 2. *ga-* and *ta-* omit *atithiḥ*. 3. *ga-* and *ta-* read *vṛkṣeṣu*; *ta1, 2, 3, 5, 6* and *bhara2, 4, 8* read *vṛkṣeṣu*. 4. *ga*, *ta*, and *bhara2, 4, 8* read *jātam*.
Like a swift steed as it goes, he does not think too much [of himself]; the meaning is that he does not depart after having abandoned [his followers].
He demonstrates this very point:
being *viśyaḥ*, beneficial to the people (*viś*), he approaches and reaches the people, that is, human beings.
Furthermore, the ellipsis is: "He presides over every single clan, that is, over all subjects."
You are most skillful through skill, a good performer through the sacred rite, and a seer through poetic wisdom, knowing all things.
As the Vasu among the Vasus, you alone rule over them; both Heaven and Earth flourish because of you.

O Agni, you are most skillful through your skills; through the *ṛtu* (sacrificial season) you are possessed of good wisdom. You are a seer through your poetic insight, and you are the knower of all. As the Vasu, you alone rule over all treasures—those things which both Heaven and Earth nourish. 3.
O Agni, through your skillful powers you are very skillful and very strong;
moreover, through the seasonal rite you are one of excellent intellect and beautiful action;
furthermore, O Agni, through your poetic wisdom you are a seer and a sage.
Furthermore, you are the knower of all, the omniscient one.

Moreover, having been sent forth—that is, dispatched—to burn the forests, the groves of wealth (vasūnām vanāni), you yourself, by your own self, gather together and cast into your mouth the food characterized by stationary things (sthāvara). This is the meaning. 2.
The plants received him as their timely embryo; the waters, the mothers, brought forth that Agni.
Him the trees and the herbs bear within themselves, and they bring him forth perpetually.

The plants received him as their seasonal embryo; the waters, the mothers, brought forth that Agni. Him alone do the trees and the herbs alike embrace; within him they swell and bring forth perpetually.
The plants sustain that Agni, the slayer, who has arrived in due season as the embryo within them.

And the waters, acting as mothers by virtue of their capacity to bear him, bring forth that very Agni. Furthermore, the trees, through entering into a common state of embryonic existence, likewise bring forth that same Agni as one equal to themselves.

Moreover, even the plants (*vīrudhaḥ*) and herbs (*oṣadhayaḥ*), being pregnant (*antarvatīḥ*)—that is, containing him within as their embryo—give birth (*suvate*) to that very Agni at all times (*viśvahā*).
Stirred and impelled by the wind, you fly swiftly through the openings according to your will;
as you consume your food, your undecaying flames spread forth like chariot-horses racing apart.

The wind has fanned thee; impelled, thou rushest along thy desires. When thou, devouring the food, spreadest thyself swiftly, thy never-aging flames, O Agni, strive to burn it apart like charioteers racing toward their goals. || 7 ||

O Agni, when you, shaken by the wind (vāta-upadhūtaḥ), impelled and hastening along the lovely trees (vaśān vanaspatīn), quickly pervading and consuming (vevipat) the foods—the stationary things such as the trees—you spread yourself out here and there; then, as you burn the wood, your undecaying hosts (śardhāṃsi)—your flames—proceed separately, just like chariot-warriors (rathyaḥ).

To Agni, the maker of wisdom, the accomplisher of the assembly, the invoker, the all-pervading one, and the thought—him indeed we magnify with this common oblation; they choose him, and no other than you.

The source of wisdom, the accomplisher of the assembly, Agni the Hotṛ-priest who encompasses the thought—him alone, even with a small oblation, do men choose; him alone for a great purpose they choose, and no other than you. 8.

We choose you, O Agni—who are the maker of wisdom (*medhākāram*), the accomplisher of insight (*prajñāyāḥ kartāram*), the perfecter (*prasādhanam*) of the sacrifice (*vidathasya yajñasya*), the invoker (*hotāram*) of the gods, the one who utterly overcomes (*paribhūtam*) enemies, and the thinker (*matim*)—this is the ellipsis.
That very same Agni, even when there is only a small oblation (*arbhe haviṣi*) such as clarified butter or a sacrificial cake, the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*) choose him together;
and that very same Agni they choose even for a great oblation (*mahe*) consisting of Soma.
They do not choose any other god as superior to their own.

1. *ga*-satataṃ; *ta*-bhara.4.6.8-san taṃ | 2. The meaning is "you throw" (*prakṣipasi*); *ga4*-ta3.4.5-the meaning is "you throw" (*prakṣipasi*); *ta1.7*-the meaning is "I throw" (*prakṣepāmi*); *ta2.6*-the meaning is "for the purpose of throwing" (*prakṣepamārthaḥ*); *ta8*-the meaning is "I throw" (*pakṣipāmi*); *bha*-the meaning is "you throw" (*pakṣipasi*) | 3. *ga4*-yadyadā; *ta1.2.6.8-bha*-you, whenever you (*tvaṃ yadyadā tvaṃ*); *ta3.4.5.7-mu*-you, whenever you (*tvaṃ yadyadā*).
4. Ga, Ta, Mu: And sent by Bha;
5. Ga, Ta, Mu: Separately, separately; 6. Ta, Mu: He comes.
7. That which accomplishes it. 8. O Agni, you who are indeed the most excellent; you, the wise ones, seeking you, choose you here as the Hotṛ-priest at the sacrificial assemblies, O Agni.
Whatever offerings the god-seeking men, bearing oblations and having trimmed the sacrificial grass, present unto you;

Thee alone do they choose here, those who long for thee, O Agni, as their Hotṛ-priest at the assemblies—those wise ones, when, seeking the gods, the men bring forth offerings for thee with sacrificial gifts and trimmed sacred grass. 9.

O Agni, the gods choose you alone as their *hotṛ*, the invoker; you, the seekers of you—the wise ones (*vedhasaḥ*), the performers of rites (*karmaṇām kartāraḥ*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*)—desiring you, choose you here in this world at the sacrificial assemblies (*vidatheṣu*).

When? He says: when the men, the officiating priests, desiring the gods, having spread the sacred grass (*vṛktabarhiṣaḥ*), possessing oblations (*haviṣmantaḥ*), and having prepared the offerings, present to you the *prayāṃsi* (fore-offerings) and the oblations.
The meaning is that they bestow [it].
To you, O Agni, belongs the office of the Hotṛ; yours is the seasonal office of the Potṛ; yours is the office of the Neṣṭṛ; you are the Agnidh according to the Truth.
Yours is the office of the Praśāstṛ; you perform the duties of the Adhvaryu; you are both the Brahman and the Lord of the House within our home.

Thine, O Agni, is the office of the Hotṛ; thine is the office of the Potṛ at the appointed time; thine is the office of the Neṣṭṛ; thou art the Agnīdh. Thine is the office of the Praśāstṛ; thou art the Adhvaryu; thou art the Brahman and the Lord of the House in our home. 10.

O Agni, your *hotra* is the office of the *hotṛ*; for without you, that [office] would not exist. Furthermore, your very own *ṛtviya*—that which pertains to the proper season (*ṛtu*)—is the *potrīya*, the office of the *potṛ*, at the time of its performance.
Because even he would not exist without you. Furthermore, the office of the Neṣṭṛ priest and the duties of the Neṣṭṛ belong to you alone.
Moreover, for the sacrificer who desires to perform the *ṛta*, the sacrifice, you alone are the Agnidh priest, and no one else.
Furthermore, the office of the *praśāstṛ* priest belongs to you alone;
moreover, O Agni, you yourself desire to perform the *adhvara*,
the sacrifice— because you are the cause, you are the agent.
Furthermore, you alone are Brahmā, for without you he would not exist. Moreover, in our home (*dame*), you are the master of the house (*gṛhapati*), the sacrificer.
Because, without you, we lack the status of being sacrificers.

O Agni, that mortal who offers to you, the immortal, with fuel and the performance of oblations according to the *ṛta*, for him you become the Hotṛ; you go on his mission as messenger, you speak in his behalf, you sacrifice, and you conduct the ritual.

O Agni, to that mortal who offers to you, the immortal, with fuel or with the preparation of an oblation—to him you become the Hotṛ; you go on his mission as messenger, you speak for him, you sacrifice, and you are the officiant at the rite. 11.
O Agni, that mortal man who offers fuel— here the accusative form *samidham* becomes *samidhā* by the rule *supāṃ suluk*— to you, the immortal one who is free from the nature of death,
or even if he offers the oblation (*haviṣkṛti*).
The *haviṣkṛt* is one who performs the preparation of the oblations;
in that sacrifice, he offers the oblations—this is the ellipsis.
You become the *hotṛ*, the invoker of the gods, for that man.

Furthermore, you go—that is, you proceed—to perform the work of a messenger (*dūtya*) toward the gods. Moreover, having become Brahmā, you address them in this rite, saying, "These oblations (*havīṃṣi*) have been sent to you by the sacrificer. Furthermore, becoming the sacrificer, you sacrifice—that is, you give the oblations to the gods.
Furthermore, in that manner, according to the previously mentioned method, you act like an *adhvaryu* priest;
or rather, you desire to perform another sacrifice.
1. In the *ta* manuscript, "hotāram" is absent.
2. In the *ta* and *mu* manuscripts, "evam" is absent.
3. *Ta*: samiddhaḥ; *bhā.2*: samidha; *bha4.6.8*: samidhaḥ.

4. "He bestows that" (*tam u dadāti*) refers to the consecrated [fire] in which one performs that sacrifice; "he bestows fortune" (*bham dadāti*) refers to the consecrated [fire] in which one performs that sacrifice. 5. *Ta-prathā*.
6. *Ga-*: "In such a manner as that."
7. Not otherwise.

These vital breaths, these words, these *ṛc*-verses, these songs, these beautiful hymns, have come together unto him—from us. Seeking wealth for the wealthy Jātavedas, he who increases even those things that have increased, and in whom he has taken delight. *imāḥ* | *asmai* | *mṛtayaḥ* | *vācaḥ* | *asmad* | *ā* | *ṛcaḥ* | *giraḥ* | *su-stutayaḥ* | *sam* | *agmat* | *vasu-yavaḥ* | *vasave* | *jātavedase* | *vṛddhāsu* | *cit* | *vardhanaḥ* | *yāsu* | *cākanat* || 12 ||

To this Jātavedas, whose wisdom is born, to this Vasu, the dweller, to this Agni, let these thoughts—these words seeking wealth and desiring riches for our sake—truly go forth from us and come together toward him; that is to say, let them meet him face-to-face so as to please this very Agni. And what are they?
The *suṣṭutayaḥ* are hymns consisting of beautiful praises; the *ṛcaḥ* are verses composed in the *ṛg* meter; and the *giraḥ* are words.

Furthermore, even among those [verses] which are already *vṛddhāsu cit*—that is, naturally increased—he, being himself the *vardhanaḥ*, the one who causes further increase, the conscious *sañjñiḥ*, *cākanat*: he desires the worshippers.
This is the syntactical connection with the words "these thoughts" (*imā matayaḥ*).

May I utter this newest, well-fashioned hymn of praise for him, the Ancient One who desires it; may he hear us. May it dwell within his heart to touch it, like a longing, well-adorned wife for her husband. 13. May I utter this newest, well-fashioned hymn of praise for him, the Ancient One who desires it; may he hear us. May it dwell within his heart to touch it, like a longing, well-adorned wife for her husband. 13.
For this ancient, primordial Agni who desires the hymn, I shall utter a newer, more recent, and beautiful praise—a laud never before made by others. May that Agni hear our hymn;
furthermore, may I touch his heart, even within its very center, for the sake of intimate union.
The meaning is: "for the sake of winning over people through my virtues.
*Bhūyāḥ* means "may I become";
the second person is used here by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
The meaning is: "May we be objects of Agni's desire. Alternatively, it may be construed as: "Become one who enters into my excellent praise.
The rest is the same.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as a wife, well-adorned with beautiful garments and the like, being loving and desirous, becomes most beloved in the very center of her husband's heart—such is the meaning.

In whom horses, bulls, oxen, barren cows, and rams have been released and offered as oblations—to that Agni, the drinker of the sweet draught, whose back is laden with Soma, the Ordainer—I generate a beautiful hymn from my heart. 14. In whom: horses; bulls; oxen; barren cows; rams; released; offered as oblations; O drinker of the sweet draught; to him whose back is laden with Soma; to the Ordainer; from the heart; a hymn; I generate; beautiful; for Agni. 14.
In that fire into which bulls (*ukṣaṇaḥ*—

the lengthening is optional according to the rule *vā pūrvasya nigame*) and horses (*aśvāsaḥ*), capable of impregnation, as well as bulls (*ṛṣabhāsaḥ*), barren cows (*vaśāḥ*— those naturally sterile), and rams (*meṣāḥ*), having been released for the sake of the deities and abandoned, are offered as oblations (*āhutāḥ*) in the Aśvamedha; [this applies] to the drinker of *kīlāla*, that is, one who drinks the *surā* in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
Since "kīlālam" is listed among the names for water,

[the phrase] "to him who drinks water"— that is, to *Somapṛṣṭha*, whose upper portion (*pṛṣṭha*) or surface is joined with *soma*— to that *Vedhas*, the ordainer, to that *Agni*, I generate— that is, I produce— with my heart, a beautiful and auspicious *mati*, a hymn of praise. I bring it forth.

1. *Bha*: the meaning is "having worshipped. 2. *Ta*: even when they have increased (*pravṛddhāsu*). 3. *Ga*: well entered into the mind (*manasi suṣṭhu anupraviṣṭo*). 4. *Ta*: in this (*asmin*). 5. *Ta*: and those who are barren of their own nature (*svabhāvatavaṃdhyāśca*). 6. *Ga*: the word "water" (*udakam*) is not present. [Maṇḍala 10, Adhyāya 8, Sūkta 92] Eighth Aṣṭaka, 625.

The oblation has been offered into your mouth, O Agni, like clarified butter into a ladle, like Soma into a beaker. Bestow upon us wealth that wins booty, accompanied by brave sons, highly praised, glorious, and vast. 15. ahāvi | agne | haviḥ | āsyè | te | srucau'iva | ghṛtam | camvau'iva | somaḥ | vājasaṇim | rayim | asme iti | suvīram | praśastam | dhehi | yaśasam | bṛhantam || 15 ||
O Agni, into your mouth—that is, your face—the oblation, such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and other offerings, has been continuously poured by us.
Regarding this, there are two similes:
"like clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in the *sruk* ladle," just as [butter is poured] into the *sruk*.
"Like Soma in the cup"—the meaning is that it is just as Soma is in the *camasa* vessel.

In that same way, bestow upon us (*asme*) wealth (*rathiṃ*) that is delightful, a winner of booty (*vājasani*), accompanied by excellent heroes (*suvīra*), praised, consisting of gold and other riches, glorious (*yaśasaṃ*), renowned, vast (*bṛhantam*), and immeasurable. Grant it to us!
The second hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "yajñasya," belongs to Śaryāta, the son of Manu; it is composed in the Jāgata meter and is addressed to multiple deities.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "yajñasya: Śaryāta, the son of Manu; [this is] a Vaiśvadeva hymn in the Jāgata meter.
In the Cāturviṃśika ritual, on the Ārambhaṇīya day, this hymn serves as the *nirvid* (concluding verse) for the Vaiśvadeva Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "For they [are] heaven and earth; yours is the chariot-path of the sacrifice" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).

This [verse] is also the concluding verse for the Vaiśvadeva at the second day of both the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava ṣaḍahas, because the author of the Sūtra has extended its application by stating, "The third pressing is according to the Caturviṃśa [rite]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.6).

I praise for you the charioteer of the sacrifice, the lord of the people, the invoker of the clans, the guest of the night, the one rich in light—blazing among the dry woods, crackling among the green plants, the bull, the banner of the worshipper, who has settled in his place. Of the sacrifice, your charioteer, the lord of the people, the invoker of the clans, the guest of the night, the one rich in light—blazing among the dry woods, crackling among the green plants, the bull, the banner of the worshipper, who has settled in his place.

O gods, serve that Agni—who is the charioteer, the leader of your sacrifice; the lord or master who protects men; the invoker (hotṛ) of the clans (viś), that is, of the gods; the guest of the night; and the one whose wealth is manifold light. (This is the ellipsis to be supplied.)

In the dry plants that have become withered, he burns while grieving; in the green, moist plants, the bull—the showerer of desires, the banner, the indicator, the worshipful Agni—*jarbhrat*, consuming or moving crookedly, has settled upon *ghām*, the heaven.

Both [gods and men] have established this Agni as the upholder of the cosmic order (*dharman*) and the accomplisher of the ritual service. Like the night before the dawn, they have set him down as the domestic priest (*purohita*), the son of himself (*tanūnapāt*), for the radiant one to dwell within. 2. Both [gods and men] have established this Agni as the upholder of the cosmic order and the accomplisher of the ritual service. Like the night before the dawn, they have set him down as the domestic priest, the son of himself, for the radiant one to dwell within.
Both gods and men made this Agni—the protector who knows all things, the upholder of the *dharma*, and the accomplisher of the *vidatha* (the sacrifice)—their achiever.

Furthermore, they kiss—that is, they take refuge in—the son of the radiant Vāyu, Tanūnapāt, the great one, the domestic priest (*purohita*), as the rays of the dawn kiss the Sun when he is colored by his own beams. "Kiss" here means "they resort to."
1. [The sequence] *praṣṭyābhilava* consists of the *tṛca*s [of the verses] numbered 1.2.6.8 and 1.2.4.6.8.
2. The reading "vā" does not exist in the *ta* and *bha* manuscripts.
3. In the *ga*, *ta*, and *mu* manuscripts, it reads "purohitam imam agnim."

We contemplate the ways of Bala and of Paṇi; his branches were offered up for consumption. When the terrible ones attained immortality, they then began to celebrate the wretchedness of the people. *baṭ asya nīthā vi paṇeśca manmahe vayā asya prahutā āsurattave | yadā ghorāso amṛtatvamāśatādijjanasya dainyasya carkiran || 3 ||* Truly, we discern the paths of this [Bala] and of Paṇi; his branches were cast forth for devouring. When the formidable ones reached the state of immortality, from that time on they have proclaimed the misery of the people.

We desire that our various hymns (*nīthā*)—the songs directed toward Agni, who is to be praised and whose goods are to be bartered in the market—may indeed be true; this is what we think and long for.

Furthermore, we desire that our own branches (*vayāḥ*)—those offerings made by us without being known [to others]—may become food (*vasu*) for him to consume when he is offered to; this is what we long for. Moreover, at that time when the terrible flames of Agni roar and attain immortality (*amṛtatva*), immediately thereafter, may our priests [attain] the state of being free from distress.

The active Rudras, the Maruts, who belong to all people, the falcons of heaven, the dwellings of the Asura—with them Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and Indra look on, together with the gods who are free from blemish and possess swift horses. 6.

The dark-blue clouds of the Asura are the dwellings; the falcons belonging to the sky—the intermediate space—are those whose flight is to be praised, who belong to all people, and who are the Rudras, the sons of Rudra. Of those Maruts, who remain performing their respective duties—[the rest of the sentence is] to be supplied—Indra, together with those swift-moving gods who possess horses and Soma, looks upon [the world], being himself possessed of horses and Soma.
Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman, together with the Soma-drinking Maruts, behold.

Those who strive have obtained enjoyment from Indra; they have attained the sight of the Sun and the manly power of the Bull, those singers who, through his worship, fashioned for themselves the companion thunderbolt for the raids.

Those who strive have attained enjoyment from Indra, in the sight of the Sun and in the manly power of the Bull—those singers who, by his honor, fashioned for him the companion thunderbolt for the raids. 7.
Those who have exerted themselves, those striving worshippers, when Indra has been praised, obtain *bhujam*, that is, protection;
when the Sun (*sūraḥ*) has been praised, they obtain *dṛśīke*, that is, vision regarding all objects;
and when the Bull (*vṛṣaṇaḥ*), the showerer of benefits, Indra, has been praised, they obtain *pausyám*, that is, manly strength.

Furthermore, those artisans who are the praisers of this Indra, who have swiftly fashioned—meaning they perform—the excellent acts of worship for him; those praisers, as men who sit—that is, stand—as the agents within the *nusardana* sacrifices, obtain the *vajra*, the companion and ally of Indra.
Even the sun was wearied by his bay steeds; everyone fears Indra, the mightiest one.
From the belly of the terrifying bull comes the thundering breath; day after day, the victorious one lies low, unoppressed.

The hero indeed lets his bay steeds rest; everyone fears Indra, the mightier one—from the belly of the terrifying bull, as he breathes forth. Day after day, the unconquered victor strikes down the enemy.

Even the heroic Sūrya, considering it his duty to fulfill the command of this Indra—the Supreme Lord, the Paramātman—urges on his bay horses (the ellipsis being understood). While urging them along the path, he brings them to rest; that is, he causes them to delight in facing their course.
Whatever deity even fears within creation, that deity fears only out of dread of the more powerful Indra, the Paramātman.

And thus it is recited in the Taittirīya: "From fear of Him the wind blows," and so forth. Moreover, from the belly—the interior space—of the Paramātman, the Supreme Lord, who is *vṛṣṇi* (the showerer of desires), *bhīma* (the terrifying one who causes all fear), and *divedive* (day after day, every day), as He breathes forth (*abhiśvasaḥ*) toward [all things], there thunders—that is, makes sound—the *sahuri* (the victorious, enduring one), who is *abādha* (unobstructed, free from hindrance).
Today I desire to offer a hymn of praise to you, to Rudra, the lord of heroes; present it with reverence.
With those auspicious, self-possessed, and swift steeds, he who is self-glorious comes from heaven to us according to our desires.

1. *ga*-ta4.5-śaṃsamānāḥ | ta1.2.3.6.7-śaṃsamānāḥ | 2. *ga*-iha; ta1.2.3.6.7-dṛṣṭī; ta4.5-dṛṣṭī | 3. ta-mu-sahanaśīlaḥ san | [O you who] praise [him]; O Rudras, being of a patient nature, [offer] your hymn of praise (*stoma*) to Rudra. Then, for him whose heroes perish, point out [the way] with homage (*namas*). By means of those auspicious, self-strong, and desirable [powers], he, possessing noble glory, descends from heaven with his eager [attendants]. (9)

Accompanied by those Maruts who come with swift horses and flowing waters—[the Lord] who possesses cattle, whose fame is known, whose glory is inherent, who is the source of happiness, and the Supreme Lord—he attends to those dwelling in the heavenly world. O priests, in this sacrifice, together with the Maruts who possess heroes and have subdued their enemies, offer a hymn of praise (*stoma*) along with food, obeisance, and the fulfillment of desired objects to the Protector, the powerful Rudra, who is the refuge. Grant it; let it be directed toward him.
The meaning is "he causes to go."
For they indeed desired glory among their offspring; Bṛhaspati, the bull, [and] the Soma-born ones [did so].
Through sacrifices, Dhruva first established [the order]; the Bhṛgus, through their skills, became fully conscious of the gods.

For they were worthy of progeny; Bṛhaspati, the bull, [and] the kinsmen of Soma, through sacrifices, first established wide renown. The gods and the Bhṛgus, with their skills, attained full consciousness.

For this reason—that *pavṛṣabhaḥ* (the showerer) is *pabṛhaspatiḥ* (the lord of the expansive), and that other *somajāmayaḥ* (born of Soma) are *somabandhavaḥ* (kinsmen of Soma)—all these *viśve devāḥ* (universal gods), being *paśravaḥ* (hearers/protectors), *pavi* (purely) *pabharanta* (bring forth) or *vibharanti* (sustain) *annaṃ* (food) for the sake of *prajāyāḥ* (progeny), nourishing them through the medium of rain; therefore, among those *prajānāṃ* (progenies), the seer named *patharvā* (*paprathamaḥ*), being the very first (*prathamameva*) while the sacrifices (*yajñaiḥ*) were being performed, *pavi* (purely) *padhārayat* (upheld) the gods or the paths of action (*karmamārgān*), making them extensive (*vistṛtanakarot*).
On this point there is a Vedic citation: "Atharvan first laid out the paths with sacrifices" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.83.5).
Then, together with their foot-soldiers and forces, all the gods, the Bhṛgus, and the sages went to the sacrifice performed by Atharvan and, having arrived, recognized the sacrificial animals.
For they— Heaven and Earth of abundant seed, Narāśaṃsa, the four-limbed Yama,
Aditi, the divine Tvaṣṭṛ, Draviṇodas, the Ṛbhukṣans, the two worlds, the Maruts, and Viṣṇu— have been invoked.
These two, Heaven and Earth, rich in seed; Narāśaṃsa; the four-limbed one; Yama; Aditi; the god Tvaṣṭṛ; the giver of wealth; the Ṛbhukṣans; the two worlds; the Maruts; Viṣṇu; and the serpent. 11.

Pabhūri-retasā (the two possessing abundant seed), Bahudaka (the two with much water), Dyāvāpṛthivī (Heaven and Earth), Payas (the divine milk), Aditi, Tvaṣṭṛ, Deva (the god), Draviṇodā (the giver of wealth), Agni, the Ṛbhukṣans and the Ṛbhus, Rodasī (Heaven and Earth) and the wife of Rudra, the Maruts, the gods, and Viṣṇu—these are all the Viśvedevas.

Pacaturaṅga (the four-horsed chariot) joined with four horses, in that [chariot], Narāśaṃsa—by name Narāśaṃsa—in the sacrifice, Pra (the filler)—we have brought forth; they are honored by us, the praisers.
And may he, the far-reaching sage, the foundation of the earth, hear our invocation, even as we yearn for him.
O Sun and Moon, who move apart and dwell in heaven, and you two, O Heaven and Earth, through your wisdom, take heed of this man’s praise.

1. [The syllables] *ta*, *bha*, *la*, *ya*, *va*, *ra*, *sa*, *ja* are innate (*sahaja*). 2. [The syllables] *ta*, *bha*, *la*, *ya*, *va*, *ra*, *sa*, *ja* either lead one to the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), or the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) arises from the heavenly world.
3. [The syllables] *ta*, *bha* are fixed by their desired objects.
4. *ga*—*kṣapitaśatrave*; *ta*1.2.7—*rakṣitaśatrave*; *ta*3—*kṣataśatrave*; *bha*1.2—*bhakṣitaśatrave*. 5. *ga*-*bha*—*somabandhakāḥ*; *ta*-*su*—*somabandhukāḥ*. 6. *ga*-*ta*-*bha*1.4.5—*teṣām*.
7. In Ga and Bha, "the first" does not exist.
8. In Ta, "right from the beginning" does not exist.
9. In Ta, by means of those being modified.

10. He is joined with *ta*, *su*, and the four [syllables]. 11. By us, the Viṣṇu-like worshippers (*stotṛbhiḥ*), the serpent (*ahiḥ*) is being honored. And may he, the sage (*kaviḥ*), the serpent of the deep (*budhnyaḥ*), hear our call (*havīmani*). May Sūryā and Māsā, moving apart, the two who dwell in the double-folded [world], who sustain the *śamī* and *nahuṣī* plants—may they take heed of this! 12. *ta-su-caturbhir-yukto-'miṃ| 11. ta-su-viṣṇusmābhiḥ stotṛbhir-ahir-e-prapūjyate | uta | syaḥ | naḥ | uśijām | urviyā | kaviḥ | ahiḥ | śṛṇotu | budhnyaḥ | havīmani | sūryāmāsā | vi'carantā | dvi'dvikṣātā | dhriyā | śamīnahuṣī iti | asya | bodhatam ||12||* [Note: The provided text contains a mix of transliterated Vedic fragments and commentary. The translation above renders the meaningful Vedic portions.]

And also, may he—he who is the wise seer (*kavi*), the one dwelling in the depths (*budhnya*) within the foundation of the mid-air—listen to our wide and extensive praise, we who are yearning priests (*uśij*). May the divine Dragon (*ahi*), at this invocation where oblations are poured for the gods, hear us in that assembly.
May the Sun and Moon, who dwell in heaven, who move about and travel through the sky, perceive with their intelligence this hymn of his.
And may the Earth, active in her work, [be favorable].
Because "śamī" is listed among the names of ritual acts (*karmanāman*). Nahuṣī is the sky.
Regarding this, the Vājasaneyaka states: "The sky is Nahuṣī; this śamī is indeed that [sky], and this [fire] is its embryo."
O Heaven and Earth, you two— the seer named Aṅgiras, chosen for victory, praises the gods with his own inspired thought through this hymn of praise.
In this sacrifice, the ancient seer named Aṅgiras, by virtue of his very birth, utters praise to the gods.
And the pressing-stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*), standing upright and raised up, gaze toward Soma, the bridegroom and the means of sacrifice.
Through these stones—by the sounds associated with the pressing—the wise and far-seeing Indra became *vihāyāḥ*, that is, he became great;
the meaning is that he was filled with joy.

This axe of Indra, the thunderbolt, has cleared the path through the forested and watery region; it has brought forth the means of food and the beautiful, well-established water—this is the sense of the remainder.
The third hymn, consisting of fifteen verses, begins with "mahi.
Its seer is Tānva, the son of Pṛthu.
The second, third, and thirteenth verses are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
The *paṅkti* has nine syllables per line;
the *nyaṅkusāriṇī* consists of eleven, eight, twelve, and two [syllables];
the *purastādbṛhatī* consists of fifteen [syllables].

O you who are all-protecting, lords of all beings, and endowed with qualities such as luminosity—O gods—grant us your great, desirable wealth (*vāraṇīyaṃ dhanaṃ*), which is to be distributed; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, may you all be possessors of universal splendor (*viśvamahasaḥ*).
Furthermore, you all are worthy of sacrifice (yajñiya) and are to be worshipped (yajñya) at the sacrifices (yajñeṣu).
These are the kings of immortality, the delightful ones: Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Parijman;
and Rudra praised by men, the Maruts, Pūṣan, and Bhaga.
They are the kings of immortality, the joyous ones: Aryaman, Mitra, Varuṇa, Parjanya, and the praised Rudra among men; the Maruts, Pūṣan, and Bhaga. 4.

May the divine Aryaman, Mitra, and Varuṇa— the all-pervading one whose movement is everywhere unimpeded— and the other host of gods, praised by the seers, be gracious to us. (Ṛgveda 8.4.27) Furthermore, may the Rudras, the Aśvins, the Viśve Devās, Rathaspati, and Bhaga be favorable to us.
Ṛbhu, Vāja, and Ṛbhukṣan, you who travel everywhere, possessors of all wealth!
And may even the Rudras be gracious to us, the Aśvins, all the gods, Bhaga the lord of the chariot, Ṛbhu, Vāja, and the Ṛbhukṣans, the all-knowing ones who travel everywhere. 7.
Moreover, O Rudras, the two Aśvins—the sons of Rudra—may they favor us and grant us happiness.

Furthermore, may Rathaspati, the lord of the chariot; Pūṣan; Ṛbhu; Vāja, the possessor of horses; Bhaga; and Parijman, the one who moves everywhere, namely Vāyu—and all the gods (viśve devāsaḥ) grant us happiness.
O Viśvavedas, you who possess all knowledge or all wealth, O Ṛbhukṣans, great gods such as Brahmā and the others, may you grant us happiness!

R̥bhu, R̥bhukṣan, and R̥bhu are the exhilaration of the worshiper; may your two bay steeds, O swift one, hasten hither—steeds whose Sāman is difficult to overcome, like a human sacrifice that attains its goal.

O R̥bhu, O R̥bhukṣan, O Āyu, establish among these men, O Heaven and Earth, great glory for us, O you who belong to all people— glory that brings nourishment for the winning of strength, and nourishment through wealth for our overcoming of enemies. || 10 ||

O Heaven and Earth, you two—bestow upon these our kinsmen, upon these heroes, our sons, great glory and fame that encompasses all people, O Viśvacarṣaṇī. Furthermore, grant us nourishment for the attainment of strength;
and also, for the overcoming of enemies, grant us nourishing food along with wealth.
O Indra, you who are fond of us, protect this praise for our aid—wheresoever it may be—O victorious one, always protect it for our aid; let it be nourished and known, O Vasu.
O Indra, being well-disposed toward us, you have seen this praise wherever it may be.
Your manly powers (*pausyā*) are like those who rest in the midst of battle (*nemadhitā na nemadhitau*), or like a series of water-clocks (*vṛthāiva*)— that is to say, they flow forth spontaneously.
I have proclaimed this before Tahuḥśīma, Pṛthavāna, Vena, Rāma, and the Asura Maghavan—
those who, for me, have harnessed four hundred cattle so that their fame may spread far and wide.

I have proclaimed this before Duḥśīma, Pṛthavāna, Vena, Rāma, Asura, and the Maghavan-s: that for those who were intent on harnessing the cattle, a hundred head of livestock were bestowed upon them; their fame has resounded far and wide. 14.

Those gods, five hundred in number, who, having yoked their chariots with horses, proceed along the path of sacrifice desiring us—they, these very gods, possess this hymn which is renowned in the world of the gods or among the people, endowed with the quality of being heard.
Let these pressing-stones, the *upala* stones, resound; let them produce the sound of the soma-pressing.
We, the sacrificers, for the sake of the pressing-stones, utter our speech, making it resound as we perform the pressing.
Furthermore, O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), you too must speak—that is, recite—the speech characterized by praise.

When all of you—the *adrayaḥ*, meaning the worthy, firm, and swift pressing-stones (*grāvan*) that act quickly for the purpose of pressing Soma—and the mountains, together (*sākam*) for the sake of Indra (*indrāya*), produce (*bharatha*) and nourish (*poṣatha*) the *ślokam*, the sound worthy of being heard, namely the noise of the pressing—then at that time, as possessors of Soma (*sominaḥ*), you shall be filled with Soma.
These speak out as if a hundredfold, they cry aloud with their green-colored mouths;
the pressing-stones, well-fashioned by skillful workmanship, have reached the food of the oblation that is to be eaten by the Hotṛs.

These speak out; they cry aloud with their golden mouths like a hundred, like a thousand. The pressing-stones, well-fashioned by skillful workmanship, have reached the first food-eating of the Hotṛ-priest. ||2||
Just as hundreds and thousands—that is, as many humans as are countless—speak, so too do these pressing-stones speak; they produce sound.
Furthermore, with their green mouths—their mouths being green-hued from contact with the *soma*—they cry out toward [the sacrifice];
that is to say, they call upon the gods, aiming toward the *soma*.

Furthermore, the well-fashioned pressing-stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*), performing beautiful deeds, having reached the sacrifice as the *viṣṭrī* (the supporting hands), have already attained—the very first thing to be eaten today—the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) intended for the Hotṛ, the exhilarating one who delights the gods.
These roaring ones speak honey; they are gathered upon the cooked skin.
As they chew upon the branch of the ruddy tree, those bulls have bellowed loudly like the sun.

These speak; they have found the honey. They are carried down upon the ripe [soma-plant]. Even upon the branch of the tree, as they devour the shoot of the ruddy one, those sun-seeking bulls have roared aloud. 3.
Eating the branch of the red, crimson-colored tree, those well-formed, excellent-eating bulls have bellowed loudly;
just as flesh-eaters, devourers of meat, utter specific sounds over raw or cooked meat when they are being served, even so do these pressing-stones speak, making a sound.
Moreover, with their mouths, they have found the honey-sweet, intoxicating Soma.
They speak aloud with exhilarating, intoxicating [Soma]; crying out, they have found Indra as their honeyed food.
Seizing themselves, the wise ones have danced with their own wives, making the earth resound with their resonant songs.

They speak aloud; with the intoxicating, gladdening [Soma], they call out to Indra. Having found the honeyed food, the wise ones, having taken hold together, have danced with their sisters, making the earth resound with their low-toned songs. 4.
Calling out to Indra with the exhilarating, intoxicating Soma as it is being pressed, these pressing-stones speak—nay, they roar—loudly.
Moreover, with their mouths, they have found the honeyed, intoxicating Soma.
Furthermore, having exerted themselves and become bold, these wise ones fill the earth with their resonant sounds; together with their sisters—the fingers—they dance.
1. *ta-bha*: For the purpose of pressing the Soma.

2. *ga-bha5*: They became desirous; *ta*: They became satisfied; *bha1.6.8*: You two become desirous; *bhara*: You two become desirous; *bha4.7*: You two become desirous. 3. *ta*: The word "pressing-stones" (*prāvāṇaḥ*) does not exist.
4. Madhura (the sweet). Bha 1.2.7.

The well-winged ones have made their voice heard near the sky; the swift, dark ones have danced in the lair. They go downward toward the prepared place of the upper stone; the sun-sustained drops have deposited abundant seed. The well-winged pressing-stones (*suparṇāḥ*) make their sound near the sky (*dyavi*). Furthermore, like swift, black antelopes in a lair (*akhare*), the sun-sustained drops (*sūryadhṛtaḥ*), possessing the color of the sun, have danced (*anartiṣuḥ*). Having been pressed by the stones, they flow downward (*nyaṅk*) toward the prepared place (*niṣkṛtam*) of the upper stone (*uparasya*). Moreover, they hold (*dadhire*) the abundant (*puru*) seed, which is the Soma-water.

Like fierce, galloping horses, they have harnessed themselves together; yoked as bulls, they bear the pole. When, praising and swallowing [the Soma], they have roared, their snorting is heard like that of racing steeds. Like fierce ones drawing along, they have harnessed themselves together. Yoked as bulls, bearing the pole, when—praising and swallowing—they have roared, their snorting is heard like that of racing steeds. "Vṛṣan" means one who rains down fruit; thus, the sacrifice is the "bull. Bearing its "pole"—that is, maintaining its burden—these pressing-stones, being "yoked" together with the Soma, "drawing along" as they pull the chariot forward, "like fierce, spirited horses," have "harnessed themselves"; that is to say, they become taut. "When," while "praising"—meaning the stones, which at the time of pressing seem to be panting from the exertion of rising and falling—and "swallowing" the Soma, "have roared," then the "snorting" (the sound from the mouth) of these stones is "heard. Therein is the comparison: "like that of racing steeds"—just as the sound comes from the region of the mouths of horses.

Sing praise to those who possess ten fingers, ten girths, ten rings, and ten [fingers] for the joining; to those with ten reins, the unwasting ones, who carry ten yokes, ten yoked [parts], and ten pairs of bearers. (7) To those with ten fingers (*daśāvanibhyaḥ*): "Fingers" (*avanayaḥ*) are so called because they go toward the ritual acts (*karmāṇi*). Those stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*) which have a connection as the graspers of the ten fingers are "those with ten fingers. The dative case is used here in the sense of the accusative. To those with ten girths (*daśakakṣyebhyaḥ*): "Girths" (*kakṣyāḥ*) are the fingers that manifest [the sound]; those [stones] are "those with ten girths. To those with ten rings (*daśoktrebhyaḥ*): Those whose ten fingers serve as the means for binding the yoke (*yoktra*) are "those with ten rings. To those with ten [fingers] for the joining (*daśojanebhyaḥ*): Those whose ten fingers serve as the means for the joining (*yojana*) with Soma are "those with ten for the joining. To those with ten reins (*daśābhīśubhyaḥ*): "Reins" (*abhīśavaḥ*) are the ten fingers through which the ritual acts pervade [the stones]. Those [stones] are "those with ten reins. To the unwasting ones (*ajerebhyaḥ*): Those who are devoid of decay (*jarā*). Ten by ten, with ten yokes (*dhuraḥ*)—here the nominative is used in the sense of the instrumental—meaning "by the ten destroyers" (*dhūbhiḥ hiṃsitṛbhiḥ*). Yoked (*yuktāḥ*): Here the nominative is used in the sense of the accusative. Carriers (*vahadvayaḥ*): Those engaged in the act known as pressing (*abhiṣava*). "Sing praise" (*arcata*): O priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*), this is the ellipsis. In this context...
1. Ta: *urvīvarṇā*.
2. Ga, Ta, Bha: "ten fingers" (*daśāṅgulayaḥ*) is absent.

Yāska:—"The *avanayaḥ* are the fingers; they protect (*avanti*) the ritual acts. The *kakṣyāḥ* reveal the ritual acts. The *yoktrāṇi* are explained as 'bindings. The *abhīśavaḥ* are so called because they overcome (*abhyabhnuvate*) the ritual acts. The ten *dhuraḥ* are the ten yoked ones that carry [the burden]. *Dhūr* comes from the root *dhurv*, meaning 'to strike'; this other [meaning] of *dhūr* is derived from the same, for it strikes away [the weight], or it comes from the root *dhṛ*, 'to hold,' because it holds the burden" (Nirukta 3.9). They, the non-deceptive, showing their mechanisms, swift, their placing goes around the desirable one. They indeed have partaken of the first nectar of the pressed Soma-plant, of the stalk. (8) They, the non-deceptive (*advayaḥ*): worthy of respect. Showing their mechanisms (*darśayantrāsaḥ*): having visible mechanisms. Swift (*āśavaḥ*): acting quickly. These aforementioned pressing-stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*). Their (*teṣām*), belonging to these stones, the placing (*ādhānam*): the act of throwing down during the pressing. The desirable (*haryatam*): longed-for. Goes around (*paryaiti*): moves all around. They, these very stones, of the pressed (*sutasya*), the Soma-related (*somyasya*), the plant (*andhasaḥ*), of the stalk (*aṃśoḥ*)—of the nature of a fragment—the nectar (*pīyūṣam*), the immortality, the first (*prathamasya*), have partaken (*bhejire*). (8) Worthy of respect (*advayaḥ*): to be honored. Swift (*āśavaḥ*): acting quickly. They, these aforementioned pressing-stones, showing their mechanisms (*darśayantrāsaḥ*): having visible mechanisms. Belonging to these stones (*teṣām*), that which is the placing (*ādhānam*): the act of throwing down during the pressing. The desirable (*haryatam*): longed-for. Goes around (*paryaiti*): moves all around. They, these very stones, of the pressed (*sutasya*), the Soma-related (*somyasya*), the plant (*andhasaḥ*), of the stalk (*aṃśoḥ*)—of the nature of a fragment—the nectar (*pīyūṣam*), the immortality, the first (*prathamam*), have partaken (*bhejire*). (8) Eaters of Soma, they kiss Indra’s two bay horses; milking the stalk, they sit upon the ox-hide. Having drunk the Soma-mead milked by them, Indra grows, spreads, and acts like a bull. (9) Eaters of Soma (*somādaḥ*): consumers of Soma. They, these aforementioned stones, Indra’s two bay horses (*harī*), they kiss (*niṣante*): they reach; they attain—this is the sense. Moreover, upon the ox-hide (*gavi*), while milking the stalk (*aṃśum*), the Soma, they sit (*āsate*). Moreover, Indra, having drunk (*papivān*) the Soma-mead (*somyam madhu*), the nectar, milked by them (*tebhiḥ dugdham*), grows (*vardhate*): his body becomes large. He spreads (*prathate*): his body becomes broad. He acts like a bull (*vṛṣāyate*): he behaves like a bull. (9) O bulls, you surely do not harm the stalk; full of food, you are always satisfied. Like wealthy men, you are beautiful in your greatness, O stones, whose sacrifice you enjoy. (10) The stalk (*aṃśuḥ*): the Soma. For you (*vaḥ*), O bulls (*vṛṣā*): it will be the showerer in the sacrifice. You also (*na*) surely (*kila*) do not harm (*ripāthana*): you do not injure; you do not become exhausted. Moreover, like those possessing food (*iḷāvantaḥ*), you are always (*sadamit*) satisfied (*āśitāḥ*): you are fed. Moreover, like wealthy men (*raivatyeva*), who are endowed with splendor, you are endowed with greatness (*mahasā*) and are beautiful (*cāravaḥ*): you are auspicious. O stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*), you [enjoy] the sacrifice (*adhvaram*) of whichever sacrificer (*yasya*) you attend (*arjuṣadhvam*). (10) O bulls, you surely do not harm the stalk; full of food, you are always satisfied. Like wealthy men, you are beautiful in your greatness, O stones, whose sacrifice you enjoy. (10) The stalk (*aṃśuḥ*): the Soma. For you (*vaḥ*), O bulls (*vṛṣā*): it will be the showerer in the sacrifice. You also (*na*) surely (*kila*) do not harm (*ripāthana*): you do not injure; you do not become exhausted. Moreover, like those possessing food (*iḷāvantaḥ*), you are always (*sadamit*) satisfied (*āśitāḥ*): you are fed. Moreover, like wealthy men (*raivatyeva*), who are endowed with splendor, you are endowed with greatness (*mahasā*) and are beautiful (*cāravaḥ*): you are auspicious. O stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*), you [enjoy] the sacrifice (*adhvaram*) of whichever sacrificer (*yasya*) you attend (*arjuṣadhvam*). (10) [End of Section 30]

1. *te u te* (they indeed are those). 2. *ga-ta-mu-somasaṃbandhinaḥ*: connected with Soma. 3. *ta1.2.3.7-mu-amṛtaṃ prathamasya*; *bha-prathamamamṛtaṃ*: the first nectar. 4. *ta-bhejire bhajanta iti*: they partook, that is, they enjoyed. 5. *bha-prakṛtā*: the subject under discussion. 6. *ta-mu-‘ete’ nāsti*: the word "these" is not present. 7. *ta-bha1.2.4.6.8-adhiṣavaṇakarmaṇi*: in the act of pressing [Soma]. 8. *bha7-adhyāsate*: they sit upon. 9. *ga-viśīrṇā*; *bha-vistīrṇā*: scattered; extensive. 10. *ta-mu-bhojayitāraḥ*: those who cause to enjoy.

Piercing, yet not pierced; stones, free from weariness, unattached, immortal, free from disease, ageless—you stand firm, possessing great power, well-nourished, unsatiated, and without desire for grass. O stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*): you are piercing (*tudilāḥ*), meaning you break others [the Soma stalks], yet you are not pierced (*atudilāsaḥ*) by anything else. You are free from fatigue (*aśramaṇāḥ*), not loosened by others (*aśritāḥ*), immortal (*amṛtyavaḥ*), free from disease (*anāturāḥ*), and ageless (*ajarāḥ*). You exist (*sthā*) as those endowed with great power (*amaviṣṇavaḥ*), meaning possessed of the capacity for lifting and lowering. Furthermore, O stones, you are well-nourished (*supīvasaḥ*), meaning very strong; unsatiated (*atṛpitāḥ*), meaning devoid of thirst for grass (*atṛṇāḥ*), and without longing (*atṛṇajaḥ*). 1. *Aśramaṇāḥ*: free from weariness. 2. *Amaviṣṇavaḥ*: endowed with the power of throwing upward and downward. 3. *Atudilāḥ*: not pierced by another. 4. *Supīvasaḥ*: very powerful. 5. *Atṛpitāḥ*: without thirst for grass. 6. *Atṛṇajaḥ*: without desire.

Firm indeed are your fathers, age after age; desiring security, they do not stir from their seat. Undecaying, companions of the tawny [Soma], flowing with golden speed, they have made heaven and earth resound with their roar. O pressing-stones, in every age your fathers—the mountains—remain truly firm and immovable. Desiring security, they do not join themselves to the assembly. Free from decay, partakers of the tawny Soma, flowing with golden speed through contact with the Soma, they have caused both heaven and earth to resound with their roar of pressing.

That indeed the stones proclaim at the loosening [of the Soma], on their journey, like the bleating of goats; sowing as it were seed, the grain-makers cry out for the Soma; devouring, they do not diminish it. The stones—the venerable pressing-stones—on their journey, in their course, like the bleating of goats (ajaspāḥ)—those who protect by their own power—they proclaim that very process of pressing at the moment of releasing the Soma-juice. Moreover, devouring the Soma, the pressing-stones, sowing as it were, cry out; though they consume it, they do not diminish it.

1. [The atoms] are devoid of motion (*gati*), weight (*gurutva*), fluidity (*dravatva*), and effort (*prayatna*); they are devoid of sound (*śabda*) and fatigue (*śrama*). 2. According to *Ga* 1.2, they are endowed with upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) and downward throwing (*apakṣepaṇa*); according to *Ga* 4 and *Ta* 1.2.6, they are produced from non-grass (*atṛṇaja*) by means of upward throwing, downward throwing, and motion (*gati*); according to *Ta* 4.5, they are produced from non-grass in upward throwing, downward throwing, and motion; according to *Ta* 7.8 and *Bha* 1.2.4.6, they are produced from non-grass by means of upward throwing, downward throwing, and motion (the word "tā" is absent in *Bha* 4; *Bha* 8 reads "atujaḥ"); according to *Bha* 7, they are endowed with upward throwing, downward throwing, and motion. 3. According to *Bha* 1.2.7, they are themselves mutually undifferentiated (*anyonyābhinnāḥ*).
4. *ga*-ta-*bha*1.2.4.6- *supīvasaḥ* “does not exist.

5. *ta*- *bha*- *kṣemakāmāḥ sadaso na kāmāḥ*. 6. *ga*4-*bha*5- *sadamiṣo na yuñjate ajuryāso hariṣāco haridravaḥ ā dyāṃ raveṇa sadāṃsi ātmanā na yuñjate na saṃyojayanti*; *ta*- *bha*1.2.4.6.7.8- “*sadāṃsyātmanā...saṃyojayanti*” does not exist.
7. To her who goes, who is going; to her who goes, who is going; to her who goes, who is going.
8. This is to be meditated upon; this is to be meditated upon. Just as grain-dealers, that is, farmers, moisten the seed, so do they moisten the Soma.
The meaning is "they compete.
"They do not measure him" means "they do not harm him."
When the sacrifice was pressed, they raised their voices, striking like playful children their mother;
let the thoughts of the one who has performed the libation be scattered abroad, and let the pressing-stones roll away as they are being held fast.

At the pressed sacrifice, they have raised their voices; like playful children nipping at their mother, they have well brought forth the inspired thought of the one who has pressed the juice. Let the pressing-stones turn around, being watched with care. 14.

Being struck and being honored, the pressing-stones—the venerable grāvan stones—upon the sacrifice, when the Soma has been pressed, strike their mother with the hand; like playful children who make a sound while playing, they produce that sound, the voice.
Of the pressing-stones that have pressed out the Soma, [the] inspired thought...

From Tadelā was born King Purūravas, the son of Soma. Urvaśī fell in love with him as he resided in the city of Pratiṣṭhāna. (8) She made this agreement: "If I see you naked anywhere other than on your bed, I shall depart just as I came. But if you have sons, and if you fulfill my vow, [I shall remain]. (9) Having made this pact, she took pleasure with that king. When four years had passed, two divine *haraṇaka* birds were killed at night. (10) Hearing the sound of their being slain, the king rose up while still naked; having defeated them, he called out from another direction, "Come here! (11) He revealed himself to her while still naked, and Purūravas was shaken [by shame]. Then Urvaśī, who was like a tree, departed for heaven. (12) Thereafter, like a madman, the king wandered here and there, desiring to see her. On the shore of Lake Mānasa, he made her his goal. (13) Purūravas saw her sporting with the Apsarases. Again, Purūravas desired to enjoy Urvaśī. (14) Tearful, she looked at him and, being addressed, she rejected him, saying, "Go away! This very conversation between Urvaśī and him he [the sage] also related. (15) Thus [ends the section].

On this point, the Vājasaneyaka says: "The Apsaras Urvaśī desired Purūravas, the son of Ilā. Having found him, she said to him: 'Strike me three times a day with a cane; do not lie down with me when I am unwilling; do not look at me naked; for this, indeed, is the way of women.'"

She lived with him for a long time, and she became pregnant by him; she lived with him for so long. Then the Gandharvas said to one another, "For a long time indeed this Urvaśī has dwelt among humans; devise a means so that she may return. They bound one of her rams with a noose while she was lying on her bed. Then the Gandharvas released the other ram. She said, "Alas, they are carrying off my young man, as if my son! They released the second one; she spoke in the very same way.

Then he reflected: "How indeed could that [body] be without a hero (avīra) and without a person (ajana), so that I might not exist? He fell naked upon the earth. For a long time he thought it was better that he had not put on a garment. Then the Gandharvas produced lightning; they saw him as if naked even from a distance. Thereupon she (the Earth) disappeared, thinking, "Let me hide again. He wandered through Ādhyā, Jalpa, and Kurukṣetra. From there he went toward the Bimavatī mountain. She struck him here with her end. Then those Apsarases, having become birds, flew all around him.
Having recognized them, he said, "This indeed is that man in whom I dwelt. They said to him, "Let us appear to him. He said, "So be it," and they appeared to him.
Having recognized them, he addressed them with the words, "O wife, [come] to me with your mind" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.1), and so forth.

Come, O wife! Stay with me in thought, O terrible one; let us now exchange words together. These unspoken mantras of ours will bring us no joy even on the farthest day. Come, O wife! Stay with me in thought, O terrible one; let us now exchange words together. These unspoken mantras of ours will bring us no joy even on the farthest day.
The speech of Purūravas:
seeing his wife, he says, "O Hayī! O Ghore!"
Because she causes us suffering;
O wife who acts so terribly, remain for even a moment with a mind possessed of affection toward us, dwelling right in our presence.
[The word] "haye" [expresses] the absence of a breeze, which is a sign of approaching rain.
For what purpose is this arrangement? To that he says:
"Let us two quickly (nu) or today (adya) indeed (vā) compose (kṛṇavāvahai)—that is, let us perform—mixed utterances (vacāṃsi), namely sentences (vākyāni) consisting of speech and reply.
The root *kṛvi* means both to injure and to act.
The suffix *up* is applied according to the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyor acca*.
If it is asked for what purpose this verbal root is employed, it is said:

these mantras of ours—whose meanings are secret—are intended to be spoken; though not yet uttered, not being recited, yet being conversed between us and composed together, they exist even in the most distant days.
The word *caneti* is a collection of particles used in the sense of "even.
On many days, even on the final day, he experienced joy;
this is what is meant by the name "Sukha" (Happiness).
They do not perform what brings happiness;
therefore, let us two perform it.

"What shall I do with these words of yours? I have sent you away like a fire that has been kindled.
O Purūravas, go back to your own home; I am as difficult to capture as the wind."
What can I do for you with my speech? I have sent you forth like the first of the dawns. O Purūravas, go back to your home; difficult to attain am I, like a forest tree. 2.
With this [speech], Urvaśī replied to him:
"What indeed shall we do with this mere speech, which is devoid of further union?
Have I not now departed from your presence?"

Regarding the transgression, there is an illustration: "just like the foremost among many offerings. Just as those offerings made previously were foremost (*agryāgre*) among many offerings, so too am I.
Since this is so, therefore, O Purūravas, you should go back again from my presence to your home;
do not harbor desire for me.
She speaks of her own wretched state:
"I am like the wind; I am difficult to reach, difficult to attain, or indeed unattainable.
Thus says the Vājasaneyaka: "Or rather, 'I am difficult for you to obtain in this world,' with these words she spoke to him" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.1.7).

Like an arrow from a quiver for the sake of glory, like a guardian with a focused mind, like a swift rush winning a hundredfold; they have flashed forth in a rite devoid of heroes—like lowing cows, the roaring ones pondered their cry.

The arrow is not for glory; it is the discharge of the archer. Like one who wins cattle, like one who wins hundreds, his speed is not for a heroless purpose. It flashes forth in the rite; the roaring winds do not intend harm, like a bleating sheep.

By means of this [verse], Purūravas speaks to her regarding his own distress born of separation. Regarding *iṣudheḥ*: it is called *iṣudhi* because arrows (*iṣavaḥ*) are placed (*dhīyante*) therein; it is a quiver (*nipaṅga*).
From that [source], there is no discharge of arrows from the quiver for the sake of casting them toward the enemy for the glory of victory;
for even in thought, one does not fix an arrow upon the bowstring for the sake of battle.
Likewise, there is no speed.

I was not one who possessed speed in the presence of the enemy; nor did I become a *gopā*—a distributor of cattle—to those enemies; likewise, I was not a *śatasāḥ*—a distributor of hundreds, that is, of countless slayers of enemies.

Furthermore, when there is a sacrifice—a royal undertaking—devoid of heroes, lacking brave men, it does not flash forth; that is, its power does not manifest. Moreover, our soldiers are "shakers," those who cause trembling.
*Ūrā ūrau*: this is a substitution for the locative case according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
It means "in the broad battle. *Śmāyum*.
*Māyuḥ* is sound, so called because it is measured (*mīyate*) or cast forth (*prakṣipyate*).
According to the rule beginning with *kuvāpāji*, [the suffix *u* is applied].
They do not reflect upon, that is, they do not perceive, the lion’s roar.
The root *cit* is used in the sense of "perception" (*saṃjñāna*).
Because the rule is preceded by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), it is not mandatory; thus, there is no *guṇa* substitution for the vowel following the *ghu* class [of roots].
The elision (*luk*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Bestowing wealth upon her father-in-law, O Dawn, when she desires to go from her husband's house, she has reached the one for whom she cried out; by night she rests with him who is like a reed.

Bestowing wealth and vital strength upon her father-in-law, she goes forth at dawn; when she desires, from the nearby house she has reached her home, where she finds delight day and night, resting with her husband like a reed.
This is the speech of Urvaśī.
She reports what was done by the ancient self at the beginning:
"O Night, this Urvaśī, bestowing *vasu*—that is, clothing—and *vayas*—that is, food—upon the father-in-law, the father of her husband Purūravas, [remains] there in that house."
