3. In manuscript ta, there is elision (luk); in manuscript bha, there is elision (luk).
4. This is the northern [direction] of that moon.

5. In the speech of Urvaśī, "ta-mu. 6. Ga: "By this Supreme Self (paramātman), I approach what was performed"; Ta: "By the first, the son-self (putrātman), I approach what was performed"; Bha: "By the first, I approach what was performed in the past."
*Ṛgveda* 4.41:
"If she stays [there] and desires her husband, then [she should go] from *antigṛha*.
*Antigṛha* is the dining hall of the father-in-law located near the house where her own husband lives."
Therefore, Urvaśī reached her husband’s home;
she pervaded the house in which Urvaśī took delight.
And that Urvaśī, by day and by night—both during the day and at night—[remained] with the reed-staff.
"The penis is [called] *vaitasa*," according to the Nirukta (3.21).
By means of the male organ, she is both loosened and struck.
In this way, Urvaśī refers to herself indirectly.
Three times a day you unyoke my horses for the sake of Vetasena, and you satisfy my desire for wool.
O Purūravas, I have followed your will; O hero, you were then truly a king over my body.

Three times, indeed, you did not let the day slacken for me with your reed-staff; and you, O Purūravas, would satisfy my desire even when I was unfaithful. Following your will, O hero, you were like a king unto my body; that was how it was. 5.
Addressing Purūravas himself, she said:
"O Purūravas, you must not experience such intimacy with these women," thus spoke Urvaśī.
When this Purūravas was being born, the *bhrāḥ*—the celestial nymphs (*apsarases*) who are the wives of the gods—also gathered together;
or rather, while he was being born, that is, while he was growing for the sake of sacrifice, the wives of the gods likewise gathered and came together.
Moreover, the rivers, which move by themselves and serve as his refuge, strengthened him.
Furthermore, O Purūravas, because the gods slew you for the sake of a great and delightful battle, for the slaying of the Dasyus.

When she, leaving them behind, descended among the mortals, those who were there—like those intoxicated with pride, like those seeking enjoyment—were terrified; they were helpless, like those who have lost their way.

The husbands—when, while these [wives] were casting off their garment, a mortal man dwelt among those who were not human; then they, leaping away from me like a boat, were terrified like horses that have touched a chariot. 8.
These first three are *ṛc*-verses.
Therein, with the first two, he praises Urvaśī and others. When—*yat* meaning *yadā*, "when"—Purūravas was *sacā*, acting as a companion, [he beheld] *arkam*, his own form.
*Arka* is a name for form (*rūpa*).

While the non-human *apsarases*, who are divine beings, were abandoning or leaving [the scene], he, being human, approached them face-to-face; at that time, those *apsarases* retreated from me and were terrified. *Tras* is a verb meaning "to move away" or "to flee."
An illustration regarding flight:
"tarasann iva bhujyuḥ. Tarasan is the name of a deer.

His wife—meaning a woman who is the means for his enjoyment—is like a doe; she flees, terrified of the hunter. Furthermore, they are like the horses yoked to a chariot, which are the masters that touch the chariot.
"Just as they fled, so did he flee.
Having been told that Urvaśī had enjoyed pleasures with many of us together, he rejects this.
When the mortal man has touched the immortal one who is not to be grasped, through the worlds and by his own deeds—
he shall adorn those bodies like coursers, like playful horses biting their bits.

That which is attached to these mortal women who are themselves immortal—like nourishment provided by the fashioning worlds—let them adorn their own bodies like birds; like playful horses, let them bite with their teeth.

Whenever Purūravas, a mortal man, touches these immortal *apsarases* completely—meaning he comes into contact with them through his speech (*kṣoṇībhiḥ*), his actions as an agent, and his deeds—he establishes a close union with them.
The particle *na* here has a cumulative sense.
At that time, those *apsarases*, who have become his companions (*ātayaḥ*), do not adorn (*na śumbhate*) nor manifest their own bodies, their personal forms.
Like horses that are not [tame] horses, sporting like those at play, biting with their own tongues, devouring as if with garlands;
just as they, running about with restlessness, do not present their true form to the charioteer, so too is it difficult to perceive.
Like lightning falling and flashing, [the waters] have manifested my desirable longings.
The hero has been born from the waters; Urvaśī, the daughter of Manu, has extended her life for a long time.

Like a lightning flash falling with a brilliant gleam, she brought to me desirable waters from the depths. "O noble one, you have been born from the waters"—thus did the heroic Urvaśī arise; may she prolong my long life.

4. Ta3-na bhujyuḥ | 5. Ga-ta-te yathā | He praises the Varśī of these two.
She who is like a lightning flash, falling—that is, moving—shines intensely;
what is she doing?
She is providing water.
*Āpaḥ* is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
Bringing—that is, accomplishing—for me waters that are connected to it, which are pervasive (*vyāptāni*) or desirable (*kāmyāni*), or waters that are agreeable to us;

when from her who has arrived, the *vyāsaḥ*—one who is active in rites or possessed of ritual action—the *naryaḥ*—beneficial to men—the well-born son of the progenitor is born (*janiṣṭa*), then my *urvarśī* (fertile field) brings forth long life.
For the mantra says: "Thou art born again following after progeny; that indeed is thy immortality among mortals" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.5.5.6).

You were born indeed for the protection of the cattle, for you bestowed that strength upon me, O Purūravas. Knowing this, I spoke to you on that day; did you not hear me? Why do you speak as one who is indifferent?

You were born thus for the desire for cattle; indeed, you bestowed that power upon me in many places. Knowing you, I sought you on this very day; yet you did not listen to me. Why do you speak as one who has gained nothing? 11.
*Itthā ittham gopīdhyāya*:
*go* means the earth;
*pītham* means protection.
This is a secondary derivative (taddhita) used in its own sense.
You were indeed born (*jajñiṣe*)—that is, you have truly come into being—in the form of a son for the protection of the earth;
for according to the Vedic revelation, "the self is indeed called 'son'."
He says that very thing again: "O Purūravas, you have placed *ojas*—the power to procreate offspring—within me, in my womb;
may it be so."

Furthermore, if it is argued that one must remain there, he says: "I, being wise (*viduṣī*), knowing what was to be done, instructed (*aśāṃsam*) you—that which was to be performed by you on this entire day. You do not listen to my word."
Why do you, being *abhuka*—a non-eater or a non-protector who does not fulfill what was promised—utter such lamentations as "O wife" and so forth?
[In the word *vada*, the augment *āṭ* is applied before the present indicative suffix.]

"Restrain yourself three times a day; consider these two [days] as my sons; I shall go away when I see you naked"—such was the mutual agreement. Regarding this, the Vājasaneyaka has been cited: "The Apsaras Urvaśī desired Purūravas; having found him, she said: 'Three times a day, [strike me] with a cane' (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.1)," and so forth.
When did the sage, having known his father, desire to turn back that wheel while possessing discernment? Who separated the two spouses who were of one mind, now that Agni shines among the heroes?

When was it that the sage, having been born, desired his father? He shed tears like a turning wheel. Who has separated the husband and wife—those who possess triple knowledge and are of one mind—now that Agni shines among the heroes? 12.

11. From the first, second, third, sixth, and seventh [syllables] up to the production of a son;
this is the speech of Purūravas.
At what time, at which moment, would the son, having been born from your womb, desire me, his father?
[The root] *iṣ* means "to desire.
In the *leṭ* mood, with the suffix *śap*, there is the substitution of *cha* according to the rule "for *iṣ*, *gam*, and *mā*, *cha*."
By the rule "leṭo ’ḍāṭau," the augment *aṭ* is applied.
When, indeed, knowing [his father] and approaching me, did he cry out, weeping, and shed tears?
The particle *na* is used here in the sense of "not."
Furthermore, what son, being of what nature, could separate you and me—both husband and wife (*daṃpatī*), who are of one mind (*samanasau*, i.e., samanaskau)—if he were not of one mind?
[The root] *yu* means "to mix" or "to separate";
here, the Vedic suffix *śap* is replaced by *bhlu*.
Due to the rule regarding roots beginning with *tu*, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable.
Now (*adha*), at which time (*yat*), your embryo—situated within your heart and consisting of splendor—shone forth (*śuśreṣu*) among the hearers, blazing (*dīdyat*).
The root *dīdayati* is a Vedic form of the root *dīp* (to shine), according to the etymologists (*nairukta*).
I shall answer you who turns back your tears; do not weep for that which was for your own welfare. I shall send forth to you that which belongs to us; go home, for you, O fool, must not perish. 13.
This is the speech of Urvaśī:
"O Purūravas, I shall speak *to* you; I reply to you.
Your offspring shall shed tears—that is, it will cause tears to flow."
When a desired object is attained and when auspiciousness—meaning welfare—is present, one does not merely release the sound of weeping (*krandat*), but rather *rorayati* (roars/cries out);
the particle *na* here has the sense of "and" (*ca*).
Thus, the meaning is that he both weeps and roars.
That offspring of yours I send to you; that offspring belonging to you which has been placed among us—go to your home.
"Asta" is a name for the house.
Go back to your own home!
O fool (mūra), you do not reach me at all (mā... āpaḥ).

In the word *hinava*, from the root *hi* (to impel), the suffix *laṅ* is used in the sense of the future according to the rule "in Vedic [usage], the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [suffixes may be used for all tenses and moods]," and the substitution of *am* for the *mi* ending has occurred.
The suffix *guṇa* [is applied];
the elision of another [vowel] is Vedic;
and due to the rule of diversity (*bahulavacana*), there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*.

*Āpaḥ*: from the root *ā-plu* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāptau*). In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), by the rule "the substitutes for *tiṅ* endings take the place of *tiṅ* endings," the suffix *thal* is replaced by *ṇal*.

May Sudeva fly away today, never to return, having gone to the furthest distance; then may he lie in the lap of Destruction, and then may the impetuous wolves devour him. 14 Sudeva | today | may he fly forth | never to return | to the furthest distance | having gone | indeed | then | may he lie | in the lap of Destruction | then | him | the wolves | impetuous | may they devour || 14 ||
Then Purūravas, deeply distressed, said:
"May my husband Sudeva, who sports so joyfully with you, fall this very day;
let him fall right here."

Alternatively, being *anāvṛta* (unobstructed), he may go to the *paramāṃ parāvatam*, the furthest distance even beyond the distant, and perform the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*). Or else, if he is unable to go anywhere at all, he may lie down in the lap of *nirṛti*, that is, upon the earth.
Or again—
Nirṛti is the goddess of evil;
the meaning is that he should die in her lap, her bosom, or her presence.
Or else, let the wild wolves, the impetuous and swift dogs, devour him.
On this point, the Vājasaneyaka states: "A good deity has risen today; let him fly away, or let the wolves or dogs devour him"—this is indeed what he said there (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.1.8).

In *ga-ta-bha-mu*, the term "*asamanaskau*" (mindless) does not exist.
3. *dīdhīṅ* (from *ta4*) [is used] in the senses of "shining" and "divine play."
"Thinking it was a stone," he snatches it up, rolls it, weeps, and runs far away.
(Pāṇini 4.1.92–96). 8-bha: "That offspring"; ta4.5: "In the sense of offspring. 5. ta: "The impetuous ones are impetuous."

"O Purūravas, do not die; do not perish; let not the fierce wolves devour you. Indeed, there are no friendships with women; these are but the hearts of hyenas. Purūravas: "Do not die"—do not meet with death. In the *luṅ* tense of the root *mṛ*, after the suffix *thās*, the *sic* is elided by the rule "after a short stem. Likewise, "do not perish"—do not fall right here. In the *luṅ* of the root *pat*, because it belongs to the *pupādi* group, the suffix *cli* is replaced by *aṅ*; *pat* becomes *pum*. And "let not the fierce wolves devour you"—the word *u* has the sense of the particle *eva* (indeed). Let them not eat (*akṣan*). Why do you show such persistence toward me? Do not do so. This is the meaning. In the *luṅ* of the root *ad*, the substitute *ghasl* is used for *ad* by the rule "for *luṅ* and *san*, *ghasl*" (Pāṇini 2.4.37). By the rule "in a mantra, *ghas*" (Pāṇini 2.4.80), the *cli* is elided. By the rule "for *śas*, *vāsi*, etc.," the substitution of *ṣ* occurs. By the rule "also before a *khari*," the substitution of *c* occurs. Due to irregularity (*bāhulaka*), the augment *aṭ* is absent. Now she speaks of the worthlessness of her own affection: "Friendships made with women truly do not exist. They certainly do not exist. She states the reason for this absence: "These friendships are the hearts of hyenas. Just as the hearts of hyenas are murderous toward those who have placed their trust in them, such as calves and the like, so too are these [friendships]. On this point, the Vājasaneyaka says: "She said this: 'Indeed, there is no friendship with women; go back to your home,' and thus she spoke to him" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.5.1.9). 3.

When, having assumed a different form among mortals, I dwelt for four autumn nights—once a day I ate a drop of clarified butter; with that alone I now move about, fully satisfied. When, having become "virūpā"—having lost my innate divine form through contact with humans, or having taken various forms in accordance with the path—I moved among mortals, then I dwelt for four autumns, passing the nights in the houses of others. (The accusative case is used here to denote duration. At that time, once a day I ate a drop of clarified butter. With that very same [drop], I now move about, being completely satisfied.

I, Vasiṣṭha—the best among those who dwell together—seek to win over Urvaśī, who fills the mid-air with her own splendor and is the fashioner of the waters of the firmament. May the giver of good deeds, Purūravas, attend upon you; turn back, for my heart is burning. *antarikṣaprām* (filling the mid-air); *rajasaḥ* (of the firmament/waters); *vimānīm* (the fashioner); *upa* (near/for the sake of); *śikṣāmi* (I seek to win over); *urvaśīm* (Urvaśī); *vasiṣṭhaḥ* (the most excellent dweller); *upa* (near); *tvā* (you); *rātiḥ* (the giver); *sukṛtasya* (of good deeds); *tiṣṭhān* (may he attend upon); *ni* (down); *vartasva* (turn back); *hṛdayam* (heart); *tapyate* (is burning); *me* (my). She who fills the mid-air with her own brilliance and is the architect of the watery firmament—that Urvaśī—I, Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent abider among my peers, seek to bring under my influence. May Purūravas, the donor of noble actions, attend upon you. My heart is tormented; therefore, return. Thus spoke the king.
1. Then, regarding this affection of his;
2. Virūpā was supreme; 3. "...she was tormented... [The King said: "It does not exist"].

Thus do these gods say to you here, O son of Iḷā: "Since you have become one whose kinsman is Death, let your offspring worship the gods with oblations; and you, moreover, shall rejoice in heaven. 18. Thus to you, O son of Iḷā, these gods say: since you have thus become one whose kinship is with death, let your progeny worship the gods with sacrificial offerings; and you, indeed, shall revel in the heavenly world. 18.
"O Purūravas, come! These gods say this to you:

'You are a kinsman of death'—meaning one bound by death, or one who has become a relative of death, or one who has fallen under the power of death. Just as you are and shall be, being born preeminently among progeny (*prajā*), you worship with oblation those deities who are related to you and worthy of sacrifice.
And indeed, in heaven itself, you shall rejoice together with us."
The meaning is that they spoke thus:
"Since you act in this manner, therefore, having abandoned all verbal expression, become happy. This is what she said in reply to Purūravas.
Now follows the sixth hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "pra te mahe.
The seer is Varuṇa Āṅgirasa;
the deity is Indra’s son, named Sarvahari.
The twelfth and thirteenth verses are *triṣṭubh*s; the remaining eleven are *jagatī*s.
Indra’s two horses are the bay steeds (*harī*);
because these two are being praised here, this hymn has them as its deities.

And thus it is introduced in the Anukramaṇī: "pra te sasohnā bahuḥ sarvaharivendro harisutirdvitr̥ṣṭubantam" (The hymn beginning with 'pra te', addressed to Indra who possesses many bay horses and is the slayer of Vṛtra, consists of two Triṣṭubh verses at the end).
This hymn belongs to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin during the third round of the Atirātra sacrifice.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'pra te maha ūtī śacīvas tava vīryeṇa' is the Yājyā verse" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
At the performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice as well, the first [verse] of the *tvac* hymn is to be recited.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "I have praised for thee at the great assembly; 'the two bay steeds'—these three are in the *jagatī* meter" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.2).

I have proclaimed your two bay steeds at the great assembly; I win for you the desirable exhilaration from the one who presses. Like ghee, he who pours forth the beautiful [juice] with his bay steeds—may our songs enter you, whose form is golden-bay! I have proclaimed your two bay steeds at the great assembly; I win for you the desirable exhilaration from the one who presses. Like ghee, he who pours forth the beautiful [juice] with his bay steeds—may our songs enter you, whose form is golden-bay! 1.
O Indra, I have praised your two bay horses (*harā*) at the great, vast sacrificial assembly (*vidatha*); I have extolled them; I have sung their praise.
Thus [I have praised] the *vanuṣaḥ*, for the root *van* means "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*).
"O you who strike down [the enemy], that which is desirable (*haryata*) belongs to you; [the root] *harya* means 'to go' or 'to be beautiful.
The suffix *at* is added to it according to the *uṇādi* rules."
With a long delay, it is accented on the final syllable.
I solicit, I entreat, the desirable exhilaration that is directed toward us.
The root *van* means "to solicit."

O Indra, who, having gone to the *maghā* (liberal gifts), pours down—like clarified butter—the beautiful, flowing water that is like ghee; may our songs of praise enter you, who possess the form of the bay steeds (*harivapasa*), for your exhilaration.
"Varṣa" is a name for form;
[thus,] may our hymns enter you, whose form is the bay horse, for your intoxication.

For those who have sung together toward the seat of the two bay steeds, urging them on as they go to the celestial dwelling; him whom they fill with bay drops like milch-cows—sing the hymn of praise for Indra, the lord of the bay steeds, the one who possesses the bay. For those who have chanted together toward the womb [of the sacrifice], impelling the two bay horses as if to the divine assembly; him whom they satisfy with the golden [drops] as cows [fill the udders]—for Indra, sing the beautiful song to the one who possesses the bay steeds.

1. *bha-* "he... [there is] no death. 2. *ta-* "this comes to be. 3. *ta-* "those being born. 4. *ta-* "it becomes. 5. *ta1.2.3.6.8-bha1.2.4.7.8-* "The praise is in the Triṣṭubh meter. 6. *ga-ma1.4.5.8-* "clouds"; *ta1.2.3.7-* "of clouds"; *ta6.8-* "of clouds"; *bhara-* "of the Maghas.
Those former singers, the seers, intoned toward the "bay horse" (*hari*), which is the "womb"—the abode—of Indra.
The word *sva* means "one's own" or "water."
They offer praise.
What are they doing?
"Driving the two bay horses (harī) just as they drive Indra, they urge them forward toward the divine assembly (sadaḥ)—the sacrificial hall associated with the gods."
When the Soma has been pressed, Indra himself urges on the two horses in the chariot; therefore, the singers possess the power to impel the bay steeds.
Or rather, just as Indra may reach the divine assembly, so do they, through their hymns, urge on and impel the two bay steeds.
This Indra, whom the milch-cows—like cows that have recently calved—fill with milk and other products;
here, the particle *na*, though appearing before the word, serves the sense of comparison (*upamārthīya*).
[Indra] is filled and satisfied by the bay-colored, green-hued Soma-drops.
In the same way, you too, O singers, should worship with hymns Indra’s horse-drawn chariot and his heroic power.
Thus his thunderbolt is green, made of iron, and he, who desires the green, is green in his hands;
radiant, with a beautiful jaw, and green-hued in his arrows—green forms have been infused into Indra.

His is that golden thunderbolt, which is made of iron; it is golden, fulfilling desires, and golden. It rests in his two hands, O Indra—resplendent, with beautiful jaws, and possessing golden arrows. Golden forms have been infused into you.
This Indra’s ‘amaḥ’—his thunderbolt—is ‘haritaḥ’, greenish-yellow in color, and ‘āyasaḥ’, fashioned from the essence of iron.
And that ‘hariḥ’, the greenish-yellow thunderbolt, is ‘nikāmaḥ’, exceedingly desirable;
it is the slayer of enemies.
Such a vajra resides within his two arms—that is, in his hands;
this Indra is *dyumnī*. *Dyumna* means shining wealth.

He who possesses those [qualities] is "suśipraḥ," meaning one with beautiful jaws; he is "harimnyusāyakaḥ. His *manyu* (wrath) is his "sāyaka" (arrow), being either the slayer of enemies or the one who advances against them.
Or rather, he is one whose wrath is the slayer of enemies and whose arrow is likewise such.
What more need be said?
"In Indra, all forms have been infused with forms; the green ones have become infused with the green.
This is a form derived from the root *siñ* (to pour) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).
Like a beloved banner set upon the sky, the golden thunderbolt has spread itself out with speed;
the iron one, with its tawny mane, struck the dragon and became a bearer of a thousand flames, possessing a golden weight.

In heaven, the beloved banner has been set up; the thunderbolt, like a bay horse in its gallop, has spread itself out. Piercing the serpent, he whose jaws are golden and who is made of iron became one of a thousand flames, the bearer of the bay steeds. 4.

In heaven and in the intermediate space, he is like the sun, the signless indicator of everything through his light. Just as that [sun] is established above, so too this Indra has been "established above" (*adhi-dhāyi*), meaning he has been placed upon by the worshippers.
Furthermore, Indra’s "thunderbolt," being desirable and longed for, "pervades" (*vivyacat*)—that is, it encompasses—the host of enemies that is to be pervaded.
In this regard, there is an illustration.

The "green ones" (*haritaḥ*) are not green-colored; rather, they are the horses belonging to Āditya that traverse the paths. Just as they pervade whatever is to be pervaded by their speed (*raṃhyā*), so too his iron (*āyasaḥ*)—that is, made of iron—thunderbolt (*vajraḥ*) strikes (*tudat*) Ahi, Vṛtra, or the cloud.

This one of great majesty, Hariśipra—whose jaws are sprinkled with green [Soma] due to his zeal for drinking Soma, who bears the bay steeds (haribharaḥ), meaning Indra, the sustainer of the bay steeds—became possessed of a thousand flames (sahasraśokāḥ). [The root] *śuc* means "to shine";
thus, he possesses immeasurable radiance.

1. Or, as it were (yathā). 2. He would obtain (prāpnuyāt) in such a way (tathā). 3. Hari [is] for the chariot (rathāya). 4. Or he gratifies (āprīṇayati); variants include *vā* (in various manuscripts), while in some versions the word *ca* is absent. 5. The word *saḥ* is absent in certain manuscripts. 6. The word *hariḥ* is absent in certain manuscripts. 7. The word *manyuḥ* is absent in certain manuscripts. 8. The word *adhyadhāyi* is absent in certain manuscripts. 9. He pervades (vivyāpnoti). 10. Regarding the reading *asādhvāhatāraḥ*: some manuscripts read *asādhvāhatāraḥ*, others *asādhā vartate*, and yet others *asyādhvāhatāraḥ*. 11. This is he (*soyaṃ*). 12. By means of the essence (*rasena*). 13. Indra, the sustainer, is to be desired (*haryā bhartendraḥ*).

Thou indeed, O Indra, golden-haired, art honored by the ancient sacrificers; thou dost desire [the sacrifice], and all thy praiseworthy bounty is complete and desirable, O thou born of the golden ones. Thou indeed, thou indeed, hast been honored, O Indra, golden-haired, by the ancient sacrificers. Thou dost desire it; thine entire praiseworthy bounty is whole and desirable, O thou born of the golden ones.

O Indra, O you whose horses have green manes—that is, whose horses possess green hair—you alone, everywhere at the sacrifice, have been worthy of honor; you alone have desired the hymn or the oblation. Of what sort are you? You who are praised by the ancient ones—by those of former times, the sacrificers. O you born of green [horses] (harijāta)—you who have appeared as one of green color, or whose manifestation is golden; that is to say, you who have appeared for the purpose of slaying enemies. O such Indra, yours—[the word] "belonging to you" is to be supplied—is everything: the pervasive, consisting of Soma, sacrificial porridge, cake-offerings, and so forth; or else, whatever various oblations are offered there, all that; likewise, the hymn (ukthya).

He with the golden beard, he with the golden hair, the iron-strong one; at the drinking of the swift draught, he who is the drinker of the golden [Soma]; he who has prospered with the swift steeds, he whose wealth consists of horses; he who, with his two bay steeds, protects us across all difficulties. 8.

With a golden beard (*vharimaśruḥ*), golden-colored beard (*harivarṇaimaśruḥ*), golden hair (*vharikeśaḥ*), and golden-colored hair (*harivarṇakeśaḥ*), like a crow (*vāyasaḥ*) with an iron heart (*ayomayahṛdayaḥ*)—meaning he is the slayer of enemies—such is Indra, who at the *turaspeya* (the drinking of the swift-pressed Soma) is the drinker of the golden-hued Soma (*vharipāḥ*). He prospers (*vavadhat*) and increases; and he, the possessor of wealth (*vasuḥ*) and the prize-winner (*vājinīvasuḥ*), comes with his golden, speeding horses (*haribhiḥ aśvaiḥ*) that go forth.
*Vājina* is food characterized as an oblation;
that which possesses this is *vājinī*, namely the ritual action (*kriyā*).
He who has that very [action] as his wealth (*vasu*) is thus described.
The meaning is "possessing sacrificial wealth.
Alternatively,
"vājinī" is simply another form of "vājina."
He whose wealth is that very [wealth];
he, Indra, characterized as thus described, having yoked the two bay steeds (*vahī*) to his chariot, shall carry us across—*paripāt*—all, that is, every single one of our misfortunes (*duritā*).
From the root *pārayati*, the form is derived using the *leṭ* mood with the suffix *sip* and the augment *ḍāgama*.

Like two well-bred bays, his two bay steeds have sped forth at the peak for the sake of booty, as he vigorously shakes them; when, for the sake of the prepared cup, he has groomed the two bay horses after drinking of the exhilarating, desirable draught. Like two well-bred bays, his two bay steeds have sped forth at the peak for the sake of booty, as he vigorously shakes them; when, for the sake of the prepared cup, he has groomed the two bay horses after drinking of the exhilarating, desirable draught.
Having harnessed Indra’s two bay horses, which are bay-colored, they flew up to the chariot; having placed Indra upon it, they flew toward our sacrifice.
Or rather:
the two pupils of his bay horses, which are bay-colored, fly apart.
Praising toward the Soma;
therein is an illustration:
"like one who impels."
Just as those performing the oblation (*vipantaḥ*) [cleanse] a particular vessel filled with *suvā* oblation for the purpose of sacrifice, so too [the two horses cleanse themselves].

And likewise, when the two bay-colored (*hariṇī*) horses, whose manes (*śikhe*) are bay, shake (*vidhuvataḥ*)—that is, move about out of delight before the offered Soma for the sake of food characterized by Soma (*vājāya*). And when, having drunk the intoxicating, desirable food, the Soma, which is contained in the prepared (*kṛte*) and consecrated (*saṃskṛte*) cup (*camase*), the two bay horses (*harī*) thoroughly cleanse (*pra marmṛjat*) themselves.
The meaning is that he was praised at that time.

And indeed, the lord of the two beloved ones has bellowed like a prize-winning steed toward the booty; for even the great Dhiṣaṇā has been won over by his power. You, the beloved one, have established lofty vital strength within yourself. uta | sma | sabaṃ | haryatasya | pustyoḥ | atyaḥ | na | vājam | hari'vān | acikradat | mahī | cit | hi | dhiṣaṇā | aharyat | ojasā | bṛhat | vayaḥ | dadhiṣe | haryataḥ | cit | ā || 10 ||
Furthermore, there is the connection between the two nourishing worlds, Heaven and Earth, for the sake of Indra, who is to be invoked and is desirable.
Like a horse that brings forth strength (*vāja*), this one—possessing wealth (*harivān*) and possessing horses (*aśvavān*)—goes forth neighing.
For thus it is, O Indra, because the great *dhiṣaṇā* (hymn of praise) is directed toward you.
Bring Indra, who is endowed with seed and strength, for whatever one desires;
*v cit* is a filler particle;
therefore, he has roared for the prize of booty (*vāja*).
That being so, O Indra, you bestow— that is, you hold and offer— *vṛhat*, great *vayaḥ*, meaning food, for the *vharyataḥ*, the desirable sacrificer.
The particle *cit* is a filler.
1. In the manuscripts Ta₁, Ta₂, Ta₆, and Ta₇, the word *hṛdaya* is placed after *asya*.
2. In the manuscripts Ta, Bha, and Pā, [the text] reads *pārayati*.
3. In the manuscripts Ta₁, Ta₂, Ta₆, and Ta₇, [the text] reads *prayat* for *pratyasya*.

4. *ga*-priyāṃ calataḥ; *ta*-priyā calataḥ; *bha₁.₇*-priyabalajaḥ; *bha₂.₄*-priyabalataḥ; *bha₆*-priyāvalataḥ; *bha₈*-priyābalataḥ | 5. *ga*, *ta₁.₂.₃.₆.₇*, *bha₁.₂.₄.₇.₈*-yajamānāya | 6. *ga*, *ta₁₂₃₆₇*, *bha*, *mu*—the word "dhārayasi" is not present.

Desiring with your greatness the two worlds, O Asura, you desire the human hymn, even the beloved one; reveal the desirable nourishment of the cow for the golden Sun. Desiring with your greatness the two worlds, O Asura, you desire the human hymn, even the beloved one; reveal the desirable nourishment of the cow for the golden Sun.

O Indra, being desirous and longing, you fill the two worlds, heaven and earth, with your greatness— this is the ellipsis. Likewise, you quickly desire and long for a hymn that is new, straight, dear, and pleasing to the mind.
He is the powerful Asura;
*asu* means vital breath (*prāṇa*);
he possesses that.
The suffix *ra* occurs after [the word] *marut* when it means "wealth.
Such is the case with *indrago*.
The singular number is used because it refers to a genus (*jāti*).
Reveal, make manifest, and display to Hari—the Sun, the taker of water—the delightful and desirable dwelling-place of the cows, or the station of the water characterized by its qualities.

"Ā tvā... (RV 4.35.7) is indeed another mantra. Regarding that libation, O Indra, "madhumantam" means honeyed, i.e., endowed with intoxicating power; "mamaḍdhi" means drink—its sense is "taste," for the root *mad* has the meaning of tasting intoxicants. There is also the mantra: "pibantu madantu viyantu. "Satrā vṛṣan": the word *satrā* signifies "most abundantly. O Indra, most abundant showerer (*vṛṣan*), "ā vṛṣasva" means pour [the Soma] into your belly. || 7 ||
The seventh hymn consists of twenty-three verses beginning with "yā oṣadhīḥ. It is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Bhiṣaj, the son of Atharvan;
it is in the Anuṣṭubh meter and has the medicinal herbs as its deity.
And thus it is listed in the Anukramaṇī: "The hymn beginning with *yā oṣadhīḥ* [is addressed] to the Atharvanic physicians, [and] *adhisthirājuṣṭam*.

When a fever or similar affliction has arisen among those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*), one should perform purification (*mārjana*) with this hymn. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should sprinkle them with the *Oṣadhi-hymn* and then release them" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.9).
The herbs that were born first, three ages before the gods—
I now celebrate the hundred and seven abodes of those tawny ones.
Those herbs which were born in the beginning, three ages before the gods—I have now meditated upon them: the hundred and seven abodes of the brown ones. 1.
Those herbs which are the ancient, primordial herbs born and produced— from whom?
From the gods, the creators of the world.
Or alternatively:
the gods are the seasons (ṛtu) as they shine forth;
from them [is the offering].
At what time? "In three ages" (triyugam) means in the three ages;

specifically, with regard to his manifestations, he is associated with the three ages beginning with Kṛta, whereas in the Kali age, because of the scarcity of essential principles, he is required to be seen at the very beginning.
Alternatively, it means during the three seasons—spring, the rainy season, and autumn.

I think—I mean, I quickly recognize—that there are one hundred and seven abodes (dhāmāni) of the tawny ones, that is, of the Soma and other plants, which serve as their supports in the form of anointing, cleansing, consecration, and so forth.
The sense is: "I conceive of them."

Regarding this, the Vājasaneyaka states: "The herbs that were born first, three ages before the gods"—here, indeed, the gods [were born]; "from them these [herbs] are born in former times: in spring, in the rainy season, and in autumn. "'Now I [take] the brown ones'—Soma is indeed brown; the herbs belong to Soma; man is composed of herbs. "'A hundred abodes'—this refers to his being a hundred-year-lived, a hundred-fold worthy, and possessing a hundredfold vigor; these are his hundred abodes. "'And seven'—these are the seven vital breaths in the head; it is these he thereby mentions" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 7.2.4.26).

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: "The herbs that were born first, before the ages of the gods—I consider those brown ones to be the bearers and the carriers. And: "A hundred abodes, and seven. There are three kinds of abodes: places, names, and births; here, births are intended. "Seven hundred" means seven hundred vital points (*marman*) of a person; in these they place [the herbs]. (Nirukta 9.28).
A hundred, O mothers, are your abodes, and a thousand are your growths;
therefore, you who possess a hundred powers, make this one of mine free from disease.
A hundred, O Mother, are your abodes, and a thousand are your growths; therefore, you who possess a hundred powers, make this man of mine free from disease. 2.
O Mother Amba! Your medicinal herbs have a hundred—indeed, an unlimited—abodes, places, or births;
and moreover, your sprouts, your growths, your manifestations are a thousand—indeed, unlimited.
And furthermore, O you of a hundred powers, you whose deeds are a hundredfold, make this person of mine, or my people afflicted by disease, free from sickness.
*Gada* means disease;
make it free from that—do so!

1. *ta-bha* read *triyugeṣu*. 2. *ta-bhara* read *viśeṣa* at 4.6.8. 3. *ga-ta-mu* read *anulepa-saṃmārjana-abhiṣeka*. 4. In *bha*, the phrase "śatārhaḥ ... oṣadhayaḥ" is absent; in *ta-mu*, the word "tāni" is absent. 5. In *ta4.5*, read *sthānāny atra*. 6. *ga-ta-bha-mu* read *aparimitam*.

Rejoice in response, O plants—those that bear flowers and those that bring forth fruit; like victorious mares, may you, the climbing creepers, be those who carry us across to safety. (3) O plants! Rejoice in response to this sick man; be glad and joyful for him. Of what sort are you? You are flower-bearing (*puṣpavatīḥ*) and fruit-bearing (*prasūtavarīḥ*), for "fruit" (*prasava*) refers to that which is produced for the sake of enjoyment. Furthermore, like swift horses (*aśvā iva*) that reach their goal, you are victorious (*sajitvarīḥ*), overcoming disease. You are the "creepers" (*vīrudhaḥ*), growing upward, and the "carriers across" (*pārayiṣṇavaḥ*), delivering the afflicted person from illness. I address the plants as mothers; thus I speak to you, O goddesses. May I win back the horse, the cow, the garment, and my very self, O man. (4) The plants—thus I call upon you, the mothers; thus I speak to you, O goddesses. May I regain the horse, the cow... [and so on].
In whatever place the plants— meaning the various medicinal herbs— meet together, just as kings gather in an assembly or in battle, so too do they assemble;
in that place where there is such a gathering of those diverse herbs, the wise Brāhmaṇa is called a physician, a slayer of demons (rakṣohā).
It is the dispeller of disease. Disease (*amīvā*) means sickness;
at that time, it becomes the dispeller, the driver away, and the destroyer of that [disease].
Rich in horses, rich in Soma, invigorating, full of vigor—
may all these plants come to me for my safety and well-being.
The herb rich in horses, the herb rich in Soma, the herb that bestows vigor, the herb of supreme strength—may all these herbs come to us for our safety and well-being. 7.

The principal herbs, beginning with *aśvāvatī* and others, are from that [source]. All those herbs are manifest in the *ājāna*. The meaning is "belonging to Soma. "For his safety" (*ariṣṭatātaye*) means for the purpose of destroying that disease.
The Ucchuṣmā plants hasten toward us like cows from the cow-pen,
O Puruṣa, seeking to win wealth for you and their own selves.
The vital powers of the plants surge forth like cows from their stall, seeking to win wealth for you, O Puruṣa. 8.
The vital energies and strengths of the plants arise; they emerge,
meaning they cause their own vigor to flow forth from the broken [plant],
just as cows [emerge] from the cow-pen.
They arise from Nata just as [the rays do];
of what kind of plants?
It is said:
"Desiring to give wealth," meaning desiring to bestow that which is characterized by their own power;
"what is said in response?"—it is said: "O *pūruṣa*, O man afflicted by disease, [give] toward your own self, your body."

Alternatively, seeing the plants sprouting, he says: "O man, master of the priyaṅgu and other herbs, the vigor of the potent plants— desiring to win wealth in order to increase your own self— is rising up."
"Iskriti" is the name of your mother, and so you yourselves are the healers. You are winged furrows; whatever causes disease, you heal it away.
"Restoration" is your name; indeed, you are the makers of restoration. You are winged furrows; whatever is diseased, you heal away. 9.
O herbs, your mother is the progenitor named Niṣkṛti, who is renowned as the healer of all the sick, for she heals the diseased. Therefore, you too are Niṣkṛtis; you are healers.
Furthermore, you are ploughs—you are of the nature of moving and you possess wings, as it were.
[The substitution of *tan* for *tas* occurs in the word *tasanap*.
Moreover, if a person becomes ill—that is, if he falls sick—then you heal him; you restore him.
They have stepped over all obstacles as a thief over a pen; the plants have shaken off whatever blemish was upon their bodies.

1. *ga-ta-bha-mu*: medicinal herbs. 2. *gara-samagacchaṃta*: they came together [to the] poison. 3. *ta-bha-mu-‘nāśayitā’ nāsti*: there is no one who can destroy them. 4. *gata-bha-opadhyastatraḥ*: the medicinal herbs were there. 5. *ta-mu-ariṣṭatātaye asmai rogāya*: for this disease, for the sake of safety for him. 6. *ta4.5-darśayituṃ*: in order to show [it].

I have stepped over all encompassing plants as if a thief over a pen. The plants have shaken off whatever blemish there was upon my body. All-pervading and encompassing, the plants have stepped beyond their boundaries. Just as a thief steps over a pen, so have they acted; having done so, the plants have shaken off whatever blemish—characterized by disease—there was upon my broken body.

When I, seeking strength, take these herbs into my hand, the very self of the disease perishes, as if before the snatcher of life. (11) When—*yat*—I, *aham*, seeking strength (*vājayan*), take these (*imāḥ*) herbs (*oṣadhīḥ*) into my hand (*haste*), then the self (*ātmā*) of the disease (*yakṣmasya*) perishes (*naśyati*). How? "As if before the snatcher of life" (*purā jīvagṛbho yathā*). Just as the lives of living beings such as birds perish when caught by a predator, so it is here; or rather, just as the life-force (*jīva*) is taken away from the presence of Death (*mṛtyuḥ*) by the "snatcher of life" (*jīvagṛbh*), so it is with the disease.

O plants, you who spread through every limb and every joint of the one [afflicted], from that [limb] and from that joint you drive away the consumption, like a fierce king dwelling in the center [driving out his enemies]. O plants, you who spread through every limb and every joint of the one afflicted—meaning, you who take firm hold of each limb and each joint—from that limb and from that joint you drive away the disease, consumption. Just as a fierce king of formidable power, residing in the central region, drives out the immediate enemies who cause trouble at every step, so do you.

Fly away together with the disease, O Yakṣman, along with the blue jay, the *kikidīvi* bird; fly away together with the brilliance of the wind, perish together with the *nihākā* lizard. (13) O Yakṣman, the disease residing in the body of our man, fly forth quickly together with the blue jay (*cāṣa*), that bird which flies without ceasing; likewise, fly together with the *kikidīvi* bird. Furthermore, go forth together with the speed of the swiftly moving wind—the root *bhraj* meaning "to go"—that is, with its velocity. And perish together with the *nihākā*, the lizard. (13)
One of you is for the others, and the others are for this one;
may all of you, being in harmony, further this splendor of mine.
1. O plants that have gone forth! 2. O plants that have gone forth, there is no "as it was before" (yathā).
One [plant] has followed you; another has followed her; one has followed another. They have all come together; being in full agreement, bestow this splendor upon me. 14.
O herbs, among you, let one herb reach another herb;
here the root *ava* has the sense of "going.
Likewise, let one approach another, come near to it.

Thus, whatever medicinal herbs exist upon the earth, may they all, being in harmony with one another and having attained a single mind, truly favor this my speech, that is, my word characterized by prayer.
Those plants which bear fruit and those which are fruitless, those which flower and those which are flowerless—
impelled by Bṛhaspati, may they release us from sin.
Those plants which bear fruit, those which are fruitless, those which are flowerless, and those which are flowering—impelled by Bṛhaspati, may they release us from distress. 15.

Whether you are those that bear fruit, those that are fruitful, or those that are fruitless, devoid of fruit; whether you are those that are flowerless, devoid of flowers, or those that are flowering, possessed of flowers—you who have been sent forth by Bṛhaspati.
Bṛhaspati is the deity presiding over mantras;
[you are] authorized by him.
May they indeed deliver us, may they release us from distress.
May they release me from the curse of the oath, and also from that of Varuṇa;
and also from the fetter of Yama, and from every sin against the gods.
May they release me from the curse, and also from that which pertains to Varuṇa, and also from the fetter of Yama, and from every offense against the gods. 16.
May the plants release me from the curse—that is, from the sin arising from the act of cursing.
And furthermore, may they release me from that which pertains to Varuṇa (vāruṇya), originating from Varuṇa;
for Varuṇa binds a person with his noose as soon as he is born.
*Va* is a filler particle. *Atha u* means "also" or "moreover. May they release you from Yama’s *paḍvīśa*, that is, from the fetters and shackles that bind the feet.
Not only from the sin of Varuṇa and others, but from every single transgression (*kilbiṣa*), even from the sins committed by the gods, may they release you.
As they descended from heaven, the plants spoke:
"The living man whom we have chosen, that person shall not come to harm."

The eighth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "bṛhaspate prati," is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to all the deities, including Bṛhaspati and Mitra.
The seer is named Devāpi, the son of Ṛṣipena.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "In 'bṛhaspate' [etc.], there are twelve verses; Ṛṣipena’s son, the seer Devāpi, desiring rain, praised the gods."
The application of the hymn (*sūktaviniyoga*) has been concluded.
The author of the *Nighaṇṭuka* demonstrates the meaning of this hymn: "Devāpi, Śaṃtanu, and Śaṣṭipeṇa were two brothers, both Kauravas.
Of them, Śaṃtanu was the younger, yet he was consecrated; Devāpi, however, devoted himself to ascetic penance (*tapas*)."
Then, for twelve years during the reign of Śantanu, the god did not send rain.

In this context, one engaged in the office of the Brahman priest invokes Bṛhaspati. "O Bṛhaspati, come toward my deity"—that is, come toward the deities who are to be sacrificed to. Whether you are Mitra, or Varuṇa, or Pūṣan; or whether you are with the twelve Ādityas, such as Uṣas and others, or with the Vasus, the sustainers (such as Dhruva and others), or with the Maruts—the gods—being possessed of them; as such, send Parjanya, the satiating cloud, for King Śantanu, the bull-like ruler. The ninth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with “kaṃ naḥ,” is the seerly composition of Vatra Vaikhānasa; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and is dedicated to Indra.

What wondrous thing do you, O wise one, impel for us—that broad-named, roaring [weapon]—to increase? What gift shall there be from that giver at the breaking forth of his power? He fashioned the thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra; he made it swell. O Indra, what wondrous wealth (*citram*) do you, being wise (*cikitvān*), impel (*iṣaṇyasi*) toward us? Of what kind is it? It is "broad-named" (*pṛthumām*), attaining vastness, and "roaring" (*vāśram*), worthy of praise. For what purpose? To cause our increase (*vāvṛdhadhyai*). Furthermore, at the breaking forth (*vyuṣṭau*) of that Indra’s power (*śavasaḥ*), what gift (*kat*) shall there be for us? That thunderbolt (*vajram*), the slayer of Vṛtra (*vṛtra-turam*), which Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned (*takṣat*) well and perfected, he caused to swell (*apinvata*). This is to be connected with "at the breaking forth of his power. Or rather: O Indra, what is the gift of that thunderbolt? The construction is: "that thunderbolt which they fashioned for the sake of Indra. As another mantra says: "Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the great iron thunderbolt" (RV 10.48.3).

*Kutsāya*: for this named one, the wretched singer.

He overcame and shattered Śuṣṇa—the Asura named Śuṣṇa, who causes desiccation. There is another mantra: "For Kutsa, you struck down the non-drying Śuṣṇa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.16.12).
Furthermore, Indra subdued Uśanas Kavi—
the term *kavi* being used figuratively for the son by the name of his father—
who was praising [him], bringing that opponent under his control.
Or rather:
he brought the sage Bhārgava himself, who was being praised by the singers, under his own control;
for that sage becomes the winner and the distributor of Indra’s *varka*, his form.
The genitive case in "na lokāvyaya" is prohibited [by Pāṇini’s rule].
Furthermore, he led him who was the seer and winner for the *maruts*—the followers of Indra—who lead men by means of rain and other such gifts.
This one, a wonder-worker like Varuṇa, possessing magical power, shall bestow gifts upon the noble ones through these his divine deeds.
This youthful guardian of the seasons has recognized him who measured out the four-footed world.

This one, bestowing gifts with manly powers, this wondrous one, like the guileful Varuṇa among the gods; this youthful guardian of the seasons has been known—he who measured out the four-footed world. 10.
We are Indra, bestowing wealth upon our praisers;
"daśasyat" is a term for the act of giving.
Through these noble, beneficial, and great means, he extends [the gift] toward greater prosperity.
There is the elision of the *tip* suffix according to Vedic usage;
or else,
by transposition, there is the elision of the middle [person].

Likewise, he is *vdevebhiḥ*, shining with his own splendors; *vvasmaḥ*, beautiful to behold; like *vvaruṇaḥ*, that is, like Varuṇa—or Varuṇa himself, the Sun who wards off darkness (*tamovāraka*). Like him, he is *vmāyī*, possessed of creative power (*māyāvān*).
Likewise, he was known (*vavedi*) as the beloved (*vkanīnaḥ*, *kamanīyaḥ*) protector of the seasons (*vṛtupāḥ*, one who drinks at the proper time).
He measured out, that is, destroyed (*amināt*), the Asura named Varura.
He was the four-footed (*aruḥ*, *catuṣpāt*), endowed with a set of four feet.
The root *mī* is used in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*).
In the *laṅ* tense, the *bhū* substitute for the *vikaraṇa* suffix occurs by the rule "there is much [irregularity] in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Through his hymns, Auśija Ṛjiśvan, having filled the enclosure with his bull, won it;
when he had pressed the juice and sacrificed, his songs shone forth as he advanced toward the forts with his wondrous form.

With hymns of praise, Auśija Ṛjiśvan split open the enclosure; he prospered with his bull. When the presser had offered sacrifice, the song shone forth; moving toward the citadels, he overcame them with his wondrous form. 11.
1. From *prādhan* [the form] *prādhan*; 2. *ga*: *yaḥ kutsāya*; *ta*, *bha1.2.4.8*: *trayaḥ kutsāya*; 3. *ga4*:
*khaṇḍitavān* [is the form in the *leṭ* mood from the root *do* meaning "to break"].
4. Of the nature of one's own;
5. By these human beings (according to Ga₁, ₂, Ta, Bha₁, ₂, ₄, ₈, and Sa);
6. Illusory and wise (according to Ga, Ta₁, ₂, ₃, ₆, ₇, Su, and Māyāvān).

With hymns (*stomebhiḥ*)—that is, with praises (*stotraih*)—*Ṛjiśvan*, the son of *Uśij* (the name of this one being Ṛjiśvan), [attacked] the *vraja*—the cow-pen—belonging to the Asura named *Pipru*, which was guarded by him after having been seized [by force] with a *vṛṣabha*—meaning either with a bull or with the thunderbolt (*vajra*)—and he *darayat*, that is, he split it open.
*Yat* means "when"; [Ṛjiśvan was] a *sutvā*, a presser of Soma. [The suffix] *-vanip* is used here according to the rule *suyajo hanip*.
The *tuk* augment is applied by the rule "hasvasya piti.
[The text says: "yajataḥ" (sacrificing), "yaṣṭauśijaḥ" (the son of the sacrificer), "gīḥ" (songs) meaning words of praise, and "dīdayat" (he illuminated).
Likewise, whenever "iyānaḥ" (going) toward "puraḥ" (the cities) of the enemies.
Or rather:
he overcomes (*abhibhavati*) the sins that have gathered together as it were before him (*puraḥ-pura*).
"Abhi" means "overpowering."
By what means?
By splendor;
this is a name for form.
"With a form favored by Indra"—
the connection is that when he acted in this manner, he was "rending the cow-pen."
Thus, O great Asura, Vamraka approached Indra for protection; with his back he crawled near him.
Moving toward him, may he grant us well-being; may he bestow upon us food, vigor, a secure dwelling, and all splendor.

Thus, O great Asura, for the sake of protection, Vamraka has crept near Indra with his back. May he, being entreated, grant him well-being; he has brought all—food, strength, and a secure dwelling—to him. 12.

Having concluded the hymn with this praise, Vamraka makes his desired request: "O Asura, O powerful Indra, you have approached with your feet (pṛṣṭhibhiḥ) for the sake of carrying (vṛkṣathāya)—that is, for the transport of this great oblation or hymn, or for the attainment of the great heaven and other realms. Approaching thus, may he grant well-being—that is, freedom from destruction—to this Vamraka.
Likewise, may she bring hither nourishment, food, strength, sap, a good dwelling, a secure habitation, and everything entirely.
In the ninth Anuvāka, there are thirteen hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "indra dadhi," is addressed to the Viśvedevas; it belongs to Duvasyu, the son of Candana, or to Vāṣa.
The twelfth verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The remaining verses are in the Jagatī metre.
Thus it has been enumerated: "Indra duvasyu, Vāndana; the Vaiśvadeva [hymn], with the Svanayā as a Triṣṭubh.
The application [of these verses] has already been explained.
O Indra, Maghavan, grant us your aid; O you who are praised here, drinker of the pressed juice, be for our increase.
May Savitṛ, heard by all, protect us along with the gods. We choose for ourselves complete well-being.

O Indra, O Maghavan, come hither with your aid for our enjoyment; being praised here, be mindful of us as the drinker of the pressed juice for our prosperity. May Savitṛ, together with the gods, protect us; we choose for ourselves Aditi, the listener, and complete well-being. 1.
"O Indra, O Maghavan, O possessor of wealth—you, being such as you are, slay the enemy who is exactly like you!
For what purpose?
For our enjoyment (*bhuje*)."
For that purpose—being "unpraised" (*astutaḥ*) in this sacrifice (*iha asmin yajñe*)—"sutapāḥ," a drinker of the pressed (*suta*) and purified Soma, "bodhi," be awake;
that is, become present.
For what purpose?
"For our increase" (vṛdhe) means for our growth.

Furthermore, "with the gods" (devebhiḥ), together with the deities, may Savitṛ—the god who impels all beings toward their respective duties—"hear" (śrutam), that is, protect, our sacrifice which is well-known. Moreover, [may he grant] complete prosperity (sarvatātim).
The suffix *tal* is used in the sense of identity (*svārthika*). [Thus: "all" means "consisting of all.
Alternatively:
"Because all are protected in her, she is called *sarvatāti*";
the lengthening of the vowel is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
We choose such an *Aditi*, the inviolable Mother of the Gods.

1. By the bull (vṛṣabha) who has gone (ga-ta), for the sake of raining (varṣaṇe). 2. In Ga. 1.2, "iyānaḥ" is not present. 3. In Ta 1.2.3. 4.5.6 and Bha 1.2.4.7, it is "upagamyamānaḥ". 4. In Ta 4.5, it is "for the sake of obtaining a cow" (golābhāya).

Bring forth the timely portion for Bharas, the sustainer of all; offer it well to Vāyu, the pure-drinker, who seeks the sound [of the sacrifice]. He who has attained the drinking of the milk of the *gauḥ* (the radiant one)—we choose from Aditi complete protection. For Bharas, the bringer of battle or the nourisher of all—for Indra—bring forth well (*su bharata*) the portion (*bhāgam*) that is seasonal (*ṛtviyam*), produced at the proper time, O priests! Likewise, to Vāyu, the pure-drinker (*śucipe*), whose movement is accompanied by sound (*krandadiṣṭaye*)—for the swift motion of Vāyu is indeed perceptible through sound—bring forth the portion to such a god Vāyu. He, the god, who has attained (*ānaśe*) the drinking (*pītim*) of the milk (*payasaḥ*) of the *gauḥ* (the radiant, white-colored animal)—we choose from Aditi (*aditim*) complete well-being (*sarvatātim*). *Bharāya*: for the one who causes battle or for the supporter of all. *Sv*: well. *Bharata*: bring forth. *Bhāgam*: the portion. *Ṛtviyam*: timely, born at the proper season. *Pra*: forward. *Vāyave*: to Vāyu. *Śucipe*: to the pure-drinker. *Krandadiṣṭaye*: to him whose seeking is with sound. *Gaurasya*: of the radiant, white-colored. *Payasaḥ*: of the milk. *Pītim*: the drinking. *Ānaśe*: has attained. *Ā*: hither. *Sarvatātim*: complete well-being. *Aditim*: from Aditi. *Vṛṇīmahe*: we choose. **Note**: The commentary interprets *Bharas* as either the performer of battle or the nourisher of all, identifying him with Indra. *Krandadiṣṭaye* refers to Vāyu, whose rapid movement is characterized by sound. *Gaurasya payasaḥ* refers to the milk of the radiant, white-colored sacrificial animal. *Sarvatāti* signifies total protection or well-being. *Aditi* here is invoked as the source of this protection. The verse is a call to the priests to present the appropriate oblation to Indra and Vāyu.
This Indra, by means of the *uktha*—that is, by the power of praise—and by his strength, maintains (*dadhe*) the sacrificial waters, whether they belong to us or are divine.
O Bṛhaspati, you are the one who prolongs and increases my life; so be thus.
Likewise, may the Sacrifice—Manu, the thinker, whose wisdom is preeminent—acting as our father and protector, bestow upon us happiness (*kaṃ*).
Or rather:
may sacrifice, mantra, and intellect each bestow happiness.

Now, Indra’s well-performed divine power resides in Agni’s house; there the singer is wise and a seer, and the sacrifice has become beautiful in the assembly. We choose for ourselves complete prosperity and boundless freedom. indrasya | nu | su'kṛtam | daivyam | sahaḥ | agniḥ | gṛhe | jaritā | medhiraḥ | kaviḥ | yajñaḥ | ca | bhūt | vidathe | cāruḥ | antam | ā | sarva'tātim | aditim | vṛṇīmahe || 6 ||
That divine power (*sahas*) which is beneficial to the gods—that is Indra’s well-performed deed; indeed, it has been perfectly accomplished by Indra.
Or rather:
that divine power known as *marat* which exists is indeed related to Indra, belonging to Indra.
Alternatively:
"Now, Indra's well-performed divine power (*sukṛtaṃ daivyaṃ sahaḥ*), that is, his divine strength, exists in our own *agni-gṛha*, that is, in our sacrificial hall—this is the ellipsis.
The meaning is: belonging to Indra, perfectly accomplished, and being the strength of the gods, he exists as the lord of the *agni-gṛha*."

And that Agni is the "jaritā," the praiser of the gods; he is "medhiraḥ," possessing *medha*—which means either sacrifice (*yajña*) or the oblation (*havis*). He is also "kaviḥ," one of expansive wisdom, and he becomes "yajñaḥ," the one who is to be sacrificed to.
Where?
At the *vidatha*, that is, the sacrifice.
And what is this Agni like? He is *cāruḥ*, meaning he is to be approached with devotion, and *antamaḥ*, meaning he is the most intimate to us.

Not even your many misdeeds committed in secret, nor your open provocation of the gods, O Vasus, shall cause you harm. O Gods, let there be no trace of our falsehood for us; we choose from Aditi complete well-being. Not your many misdeeds committed in secret, nor your open provocation of the gods, O Vasus, shall cause you harm. O Gods, let there be no trace of our falsehood for us; we choose from Aditi complete well-being. (7)
O gods, we have not committed against you in secret— that is, in a hidden place— an abundance of evil deeds;
that is to say, acts of hostility.
Likewise, O Vasus—O gods who provide dwelling—may we not commit any manifest offense (*āviṣṭya*) against the gods, nor any provocation of their wrath (*devaheḷana*), nor any malice caused thereby.
Furthermore, O gods, may there be no attainment of the form (*varpasaḥ*) of falsehood (*anṛtasya*) for us;
that is to say, from now on, let there be no human form [bound by such falsehood].
The remainder has been stated.

May Savitṛ drive away disease; may the pressing-stones indeed drive it far away. Where the pressing-stone, the extractor of honey, is raised loudly, we choose from Aditi complete well-being. *apa amīvām savitā sāviṣat parvarīm id apa sedhantu adrayaḥ | grāvā yatra madhusut ucyate bṛhad ā sarvatātim aditim vṛṇīmahe || 8 ||*
May Savitṛ, the god who impels all, drive away (apa sāviṣat) our disease (amīvām);
that is to say, may he cause it to depart.
Likewise, may he cast down (nyak apa sedha) even further (varīyaḥ), that is, more remote, evil.
1. *ga-bha*: "That which exists... there is no strength.
*ga4-indrasya nu*. 2. *ga-ta8-bha7-mu-nu indrasya*; *ta1.2.3. 7-bha1.2.4.8- nu indrasya su*.
3. *Taṇḍya Brāhmaṇa* 1.2.3.7–*Bhāradvāja Śrautasūtra* 1.2.4.8: "The gods.
This refers either to the deities presiding over the mountains or those presiding over the pressing of the Soma.
If one asks where all of this takes place, it is said in reply:
In whatever region or in whatever sacrifice the presser of the sweet Soma—the pressing stone—is called or praised as "bṛhat," meaning greatly increased.
May the pressing-stone stand upright, O Vasus, as it presses; drive all enmities far away.
May that god Savitṛ, our praiseworthy protector, grant us complete well-being and freedom from distress; we choose this for ourselves.

May the pressing-stone stand upright; O Vasus, may it be the presser. Drive away all hostilities to a distance. May that god Savitṛ be our praiseworthy protector. We choose for ourselves complete well-being and freedom from distress. 9.
O Vasus, O gods, while I am performing the pressing of the Soma, let the pressing-stone be raised on high.
By means of that uplifted stone, drive away and separate all enemies and all those who hate us, hiding them far away.
May that god Savitṛ be our protector and guardian.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule "kṛvāpāj" etc.; it bears the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
He is also to be praised (*īḍya*) and worthy of hymns.
O cows, eat strength and fatness in the pasture, you who are anointed at the seat of Order in the reservoir.
Let your body be the healing medicine for our bodies; we choose complete well-being and freedom from distress.

O cows, eat strength, fatness, and fodder in the seat of Truth, where you are anointed in the reservoir. Let your very bodies be the medicine for our bodies; we choose complete well-being and freedom from affliction. 10.
O cows intended for the milk-mixture (*āśira*), you who are in the grassy place, eat—consume—the fat, the increased vigor, and the essence.
You who manifest yourselves in the seat of *ṛta*, in the house, in the stall, and in the milking-place—that is, you reveal yourselves in the body itself—eat that.
*Tanū-reva*.
The word *janaka* (begetter) is used for the *janya* (the one born).
May the body itself, or the milk itself, be the remedy for the essence of Soma.
Or else:
This is indeed a separate sentence:
"May it be a medicine for our bodies. Furthermore, "the body" (tanūḥ) refers specifically to the body of the sacrificial animal.
Because heaven can be accomplished when there is a sacrifice with an animal.
The singer is the one who clothes himself in the seasons; Indra is the protection for all who call upon him. Auspicious indeed is the providence of those who have pressed the soma.
He whose divine head is full when it is poured out—we choose from him complete well-being and freedom from distress.

The singer is the one who invokes at the proper season; Indra alone is the auspicious protector of those who offer libations. May his divine, upward-reaching power be fulfilled for our pouring; we choose from him complete well-being and freedom from distress.
*Ṛtuprāvā* is one who fulfills actions; [the root] *prā* means "to fill. The suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule beginning with "āto manin-."
The *jaritṛ* is the praiser;
he praises the sacrificer, saying, "Soma has been well-prepared.
Or else:
Indra alone is the destroyer of all eternal things; Indra alone is the protector (*avaḥ*) of the sacrificers who possess pressed Soma.
His providence (*pramati*) is auspicious through his auspicious praise.

For the sake of Indra’s pouring—that is, for his drinking—the udder, namely the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, becomes more elevated and filled with Soma; he alone is the protector, and he alone is the providence.

1. *ga-ta*: The gods who take pride in the mountains; *ta1.2.6.7.8-bha*: The deities who take pride in the mountains. 2. *ga*: "Madhusut" means the son of Madhu; *madhurasya*. 3. *ta3.7-mu-*: By this rule (*mu* etc.), the suffix *uṇ* is applied. 4. *ga-ta-bha*: By [the word] *yā*, [it refers to] you. 5. *ga-ta-bha*: He praises; or else, it has the sense of being worthy of praise (*stutyartha*). 6. *ta-bha*: Indeed, he is the horse.
His light is variegated; he reaches the seasons; he is the one to be invoked. There are rivals who are aged and seeking wealth.
With a straightening rope, he, the praiser of the cow, the worshipful one, encompasses the limit.

The variegated one; yours; the radiant one; the fulfiller of the seasons; the one who comes to our aid; there are rivals; those who reach the singer; those who seek the prize; moving through the air; with the cord; the drops of milk; he hastens around the summit; the one who offers worship. 12.
O Indra, that light of yours is brilliant, wonderful, and worthy of being sought after.
Likewise, that light fulfills our ritual acts and is to be approached with longing.
O Indra, for your praisers there exist riches that fulfill their desires, which are invincible by others and free from rivalry.

Since this is so, therefore, with a straightest cord, desiring to serve—that is, wishing to perform worship—the one named *goḥ*, *pṛṣaḥ*, and *paśoḥ* completely encircles and fastens it with these names.
The second hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "udbudhyadhvam," is the seerhood of Budha, the son of Soma.
Among these, the ninth verse beginning with "ā vo dhiyam" and another beginning with "kaṇvaratharaḥ" are two *jagatī*s;
the fourth and sixth are *gāyatrī*s; and the fifth, "nirāhāvān," is a *bṛhatī*.
The remaining verses are in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The Viśvedevas are the deity;
or alternatively, the deity is the meaning in the form of the expansion of the seasons.
And thus it has been enumerated: "O wise one, O gentle one, wake up! O priest, [the verses] are three, nine, and two Jagatīs; between the two Gāyatrīs, the fifth is a Bṛhatī.
The application of the hymn is concluded.
Awaken with one mind, O friends; kindle Agni together, you many who dwell in the same home.
I call upon you for protection—Dadhikrā, Agni, the goddess Dawn, and Indra—to aid us.
Awake! O friends, being of one mind, kindle Agni together—you many who dwell in the same home. I invoke for your protection Dadhikrā, Agni, the goddess Upas, and Indra, the two aids. 1.
The officiating priests (ṛtvij) speak while perceiving Agni:
"O friends, you who have become our companions—the ṛtvij—being of one mind (samanasaḥ), that is, having a common purpose and not being hostile toward one another;
in other words, being mutually cooperative in the performance of the ritual."
Being such as you are, awaken—that is, know—the supreme.
In what follows, he instructs exactly what must be done by you:
likewise, kindle the fire—that is, enkindle it perfectly.
The root *ji* is used in the sense of "shining" (*dīptau*).
It belongs to the *raudhādika* class.
In the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, the elision [of the penultimate vowel] occurs according to the rule "asoralopaḥ."

Many, numerous, and wise, dwelling together in a single hall, I repeatedly call upon you—for our protection—these three deities: the god Dadhikrā by name, Agni, and the goddess Uṣas, all accompanied by Indra. I invoke you most earnestly for our defense.
Make it resonant; spread out your prayers; make this [sacrifice] one that carries us across to the enemy-free shore.
Sharpen your weapons; prepare them; O friends, lead the horse-drawn sacrifice forward!
Sing forth! Prepare the prayers; spread out the vessel that carries across with oars. Make the weapons ready; prepare them well. O friends, lead the horse forward in the sacrifice. 2.
O friends, perform—make—the sweet, intoxicating hymns of praise.
[The root] *kṛvi* is used in the senses of "injuring" and "making. The suffix *u* is applied according to the rule *dhinvikṛṇyoraca*.
The letter *a* is a substitute for the final [letter].

Alternatively, there is the substitution of *śtu* for the root *kṛ* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Likewise, [the suffix] *dhiyaḥ* [is used] after the roots *tam* and *hiṃs* in the senses of doing and harming.
Perform, that is, extend the ritual acts such as the gathering of materials and the drawing of lines;
likewise, fashion—that is, construct—the boat called the *cayana*, which is to be crossed by means of the oar in the form of the drawing of lines and other rites;
and similarly, prepare—that is, make ready—the weapons, such as the plow and the yoke.
O friends, O officiating priests, lead forward—bring forth—the wise one, the bold one, and the sacrifice that is to be performed;
first, plow it so that it becomes wise. This is the meaning.
Yoke the ploughs, stretch out the yokes; sow the seed here in the prepared womb.
Through our song, may the harvest-yielding earth grant us a ready hearing; may the ripened grain come ever closer to us.
Yoke the plows; unfasten the yokes; scatter the seed here in the prepared womb. May our response through song be fruitful; may the ripened grain come even closer to us. 3.
"O friends, you must yoke the ploughs—the ploughs—with oxen.
In the imperative form of the root *yuj*, the suffix *ta* is replaced by *tha* according to the rule "tasanasanathanāśca";
for this very reason, because the suffix begins with *aś*, the elision of the penultimate vowel does not occur, in accordance with the rule "kṣasoralopaḥ."
For that purpose, extend the yokes one after another;
and when the furrow has been prepared, sow here in this furrow both the cultivated and the wild seed.

The meaning is that you should scatter the collection of cultivated seeds, such as sesame, beans, rice, and so forth, as well as the collection of wild seeds, such as millet, panicled millet, wild rice, and so forth, in both the ploughed and unploughed ground.
"Domestic animals are on the ploughed land; wild animals are on the unploughed land," so says Āpastamba.
Likewise, may our *śruṣṭiḥ*—our food—along with our *girā*, our praise and eulogy, become *sabharāḥ*, that is, abundant (*sabharas*) for us.
And likewise, may it be *nedīyaḥ*, indeed very near.
Suṇi-raṅkuśaḥ: one who is unrestrained like a goad;
aṅkuśavat-braka-lacitraḥ: one who is as variegated as a horse that has broken free from its goad; pakvaṃ stambaṃ eyāt: let him go toward the ripe stalk.

The word *śruṣṭiḥ* shall be [the subject] accompanied by the verb *asat*; and because of the recurrence of the particle *ca* in the phrase *sṛṇyaḥ paktvā iyāt*, there is no suppression (nighāta) of the first word according to the rule: "When joined with *ca* or *vā*, the first [word retains its accent]."

The seers yoke the ploughs; the wise ones stretch out the yokes separately, seeking favor among the gods with their devotion. 4. They yoke the ploughs; the seers stretch out the yokes separately, the wise ones, through their desire for favor toward the gods. 4.
The *kavayaḥ*—the wise officiating priests—yoke the *sīrāḥ sīrāṇi*, that is, the ploughs which are the means for tilling;
they also extend the *yugā yugāni*, the yokes, separately from one another, making them occupy distinct locations.
Of what kind are these *kavayaḥ*?
Among the gods, the wise ones— meaning those possessed of intelligence—
for what purpose? For the sake of favor.
*Sumnam* is a name for happiness (*sukha*).

It is [formed] from the word *sumna* with the suffix *kyac*, and then, in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), the suffix *ap* is added according to the rule *ap pratyayāt*. Thus, it means "by the desire for happiness."

The vowel *ā* is the substitution for the third case ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. Alternatively, it means "by the wise ones" (*dhīrāḥ*), that is, by those possessing intelligence, [acting] out of a desire for the well-being (*sumnayā*) of the gods;
that is, "may there be happiness among the gods."
By the rule “supāṃ suluk,” there is the substitution of *yāj* for the case ending.

Make the channels ready; fasten the straps together. Let us pour from the well that is full of water, easy to draw from, and inexhaustible. 5. Make the channels ready; fasten the straps together. Let us pour from the well that is full of water, easy to draw from, and inexhaustible. 5.
"O friends, the *āhāvas*!"— the *āhāvas* are watering places (*nipāna*) where cattle are called for the purpose of drinking.
Due to the context, they refer to drinking vessels made of wood, used as tools for the cowherds to drive the cattle to the site of the fire-piling (*abhicayana*).
"Make those *āhāvas* low; that is, dig them out. The word *āhāva* is derived from the root *hve* (to call), as established by the rule *nipānam āhāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.74).
It takes the accent of the *thāthādi* group.

Perform [the rite]! 1. *ta-bha*: substitution with *tanap*; 2. *ga-ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha-mu*: precisely in the vicinity; *ta4.5*: precisely in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). 3. *ga1.2-ta-bha-mu*: goes; *ga4*: go. 4. *ta-musīrāḥ*. 5. *ta-bha*: distinct locations.
The suffix *tanap* is applied by the rule beginning with "tasran" etc.
Furthermore, because [the root] is marked with *pi*,
there is the elision of the vowel *ā* by the rule "of the *ā* of an intensive (*abhyasta*) and [a root ending in] *ā*" (*bhābhyastayorātaḥ*).
For what purpose, then, are the making of the handle and the fixing of the leather thong?
To this it is replied:
we water the well.
What kind of well?
[The cloud] that pours forth water, that flows down [rain], that is well-fitted for pouring, and that is inexhaustible—never lacking in water.
I pour out the water-bearing, inexhaustible well, which has a well-formed basin, a good bucket, excellent straps, and is easy to draw from.
With its well-prepared opening, the pit, with its good rim, easy to pour from, full of water—pour it out, for it is inexhaustible. 6.
I pour [the water] into the well that has a manifest call, a refined call, a swift horse, and a wooden trough; I sprinkle it. Furthermore, of what sort is the well?

It is one with a beautiful rope, provided with a fine rope; one with a beautiful pouring, provided with a fine sprinkling of water; one possessing water, overflowing with water; and one that is inexhaustible.
Refresh the horses; you shall win what is beneficial. Prepare the chariot that brings well-being!
Pour out the drink for the heroes—the vessel with its trough, the stone-wheeled, the one whose cask is armor.

Refresh the horses! Having placed the oblation, may you conquer. Make ready the chariot that brings well-being. Pour out the well that has the trough as its mouth, the stone-wheeled, the armor-receptacle; pour forth the drink for the heroes! 7.
O officiating priests (ṛtvijas), you must satisfy these horses and oxen—those prone to exhaustion—by providing them with their accustomed fodder, water, and so forth;
that is to say, act in such a way that they are capable of plowing the field.
Having done so, perform the beneficial plowing suitable for the piling [of the altar] and accomplish it.
Likewise, make the chariot—whether it has a plough for its mouth or a furrow for its mouth—a bearer of well-being (*svastivāha*), that is, a carrier of happiness;
for that purpose, [make] it a *droṇāhāva*.
Here, an *āhāva* is a water-receptacle or a specific vessel, so called because oxen are summoned (*āhvayanti*) to it for the sake of drinking.

And pour out such a vat—whose basin is made of *droṇa* wood and whose nature is that of a pit—as a stone-wheel for traversing, or as a stone-wheel [itself], serving as a reservoir for water; a reservoir that, like armor (*aṃsatra*) or mail (*kavaca*) which protects one from harm, is fit for the drinking of men, the leaders of action, who are like kings. O priests, pour it out!
Such is the modification in this alternative view.
This is the application in the *vaiśvadeva* version of the hymn.
"Refresh them; refresh the horses.
The meaning is: "Make the horses fit for bathing and drinking, and ready for battle. "Attain victory."
"Hita" is an adverbial modifier.
How did you conquer? You conquered the battle in such a way that it was beneficial, as if it were composed of kinsmen and friends.
"Bring the chariot that brings well-being! 'Svasti' is a name for non-destruction; prepare the chariot that conveys non-destruction—the chariot of Indra."
The word *id* is used in the sense of "and.
Having made the chariot firm and having gone to the field of battle,
the words beginning with *droṇāhāvam*, ending in the accusative case, are qualifiers of the specific types of wells and battlefields that connect with the verb *siñcata*.
At Droṇa, he reached that very chariot made of wood; [he reached] that battle which had the *āhāva* (the wooden trough) as its place of standing.
He reached the *avata*, the well.
A well that is like a battlefield;
one possessing weapons such as stone wheels (*aśmacakra*) bound to the edge of the well,
or darts (*asanāni*), missiles (*kṣepaṇi*), or various types of circular weapons (*cakrātyāyudha*) within it.
Possessing the feet of Vyāsa, or possessing the strides of Vyāsa;
"Cakra is derived from the root *cak* (to move), or *car* (to move), or *kam* (to desire)," according to the Nirukta (4.27);
[and] a quiver for shoulder-armor.
Sprinkle that [battle] in which shields, bows, and armor are like water-jars;
sprinkle that battle in which the warriors of kings are drunk up—that is, slain—like water. O our warriors, sprinkle this well-like battle!
Because the *sūkta* is dedicated to the Viśvedevas, the meaning is that the soldiers, by the grace of various gods, perform all this.
In this way, in passages such as "nirāhāvān," one should understand that there is a description of battle under the guise of a metaphor for a well.

1. Because it has been praised by the four-footed [verse], once again: "In that manner, fasten the leather thongs (*varatrāṇi*). Place—that is, set down—the *pragrahas*, which are the means for binding. Or rather, the *āhāva* is the means for pouring out; in that *āhāva*, the leather thongs are called the means for restraining the water. Here too, the previous location [applies]. 2. *ta-bha*: the placing of the leather thongs. 3. *ta-bha*: "the bucket" (*kośa*) does not exist. 4. *ta-su*: thus, in the case of the variant reading regarding the side of praise. 5. *ga-ta*: the name for non-destruction. 6. *ga-ta*: *kṛṇudhvam* means "do ye. 7. *ta4.5*: *avaṭam* means "a pit. 8. *ga-ta-bha-mu*: "sprinkle, sprinkle copiously. 9. *ga-ta-bha-mu*: "of what kind?"
Prepare the cow-pen, for that is your protector; sew many wide cloths as armor.
Make forts with unassailable, noble walls; let not the cup of negligence destroy you.
Go forth! Prepare it; for he is your protector. Sew your armor; make many broad fortresses of iron, unassailable. Let not the cup of your joy be shattered. 8.
"O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), prepare the pen; construct a cow-pen (*goṣṭha*).
Build a stall for the cows for the purpose of milking the milk-mixture (*āśira*).
For that [milk] is indeed the drink for you, the leaders—the gods."
Regarding the phrase "the preparation of the drink for the gods": indeed, the gods drink the milk and other products of the cow in the form of *sāṃnāyya* or *vāśira*.
[The mantra says: "Sew on the armor, O you who possess armor."
