Because they cover the principal [sacrifice] on both sides like armor, the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and other such members are "armors" belonging to the eastern and western parts. "Sew them! Tear them apart! means: perform them.
Of what kind are the armors? "Many" means numerous;
and they are "broad," that is, extensive.

Likewise, "cities" refers to the dwellings such as the *dhiṣṇya* altars, or the bodies of the gods who are to be sacrificed; they are "iron"—meaning as solid as iron—and "unassailable," meaning unassailable by others.
Or, "cities" refers to the vessels (*grahas*) that are to be filled.
Make them according to those characteristics.
"Your cup"— meaning either the vessel called *yajña* (sacrifice) which is the means of consumption, or the actual *camasa* (cup);
in the case of the cup, the singular number is used in a general sense—
"may it not leak," that is, may it not flow out.
In the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *sravati*, the substitution of *ślu* for *śap* occurs by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. "Daṃhata" means "make firm";
act in such a way that he does not become impaired.
The root *hṛd* (to increase) belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*. From it, in the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, [the form] *hṛdiṣva* is derived.
Thus is the position regarding the praise of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Regarding the position of the *vaiśvadeva* [section]:
"You are our warriors."
"Men who are warriors drink the lives of their adversaries," so say kings;
such indeed is he of yours.
In the sense of a cow-pen (*goṣṭha*), however, he is surely the means for men's drinking.

The suffix *lyuṭ* [is applied] after the root *pā* in the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*) and locus (*adhikaraṇa*). "Sew on the armor"—that is, the coats of mail—so that they become abundant and broad.
"Make the cities"—the fortresses—of iron, and unassailable.
"May the swift one, the means for accomplishing the eating, not fail;
may he flow; let him strike it down"—thus speaks he who has obtained power through the favor of the deity.
I turn your divine prayer toward us for protection—O Gods, the holy and worshipful one—here, worthy of sacrifice.
May it yield for us like a great cow that has come for our aid, with a thousand streams of milk.

Turn hither your sacrificial thought for our protection, O Gods—divine, worthy of worship, and sacred. May she yield for us here, like a great cow who has gone to pasture, with her thousand streams of milk. 9.
"O gods, O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), I turn toward (*āvarte*)—that is, I direct—your worshipful (*yajñiyām*) thought (*dhīyam*), your intellect, for the sake of your protection (*ūtaye*).
Or rather:
O gods, O officiating priests, turn toward our worshipful thought, which is connected to you as that which is to be performed by you, for the sake of our protection."
Or rather, it is the gods themselves who are to be addressed:
"O gods, we turn your mind—your intellect—toward us.
For what purpose?"
For our protection— that is, for our preservation—
[we offer] what kind of prayer? A divine prayer, worthy of sacrifice, radiant, and venerable.

"In this sacrifice" (iha) means "in this place on earth. The word *yajñiyām* is used here as a filler (*pūraṇa*). "May our prayer" (*mā dhīḥ*)—that is, "our [prayer]" (*naḥ asmākam*)—"not fail" (*duhīyat*), meaning "may it not be milked dry."
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"as if having gone and returned to the cow-pen after grazing on grass, as it were,
[the word] *pīvī* [is used]."
Just as the great and vast cow yields milk with a thousand streams, so it is here.
1. "O distinguished gods, act with favor," says the seer of the hymn, the sacrificer:
"Make a pen; for *vraja* means a place that gathers together—that is, a battle—make that, or else make a host of enemies."
The meaning is: "Do not offer resistance.
"Vo" refers to you, O kings;
[or] belonging to those connected with "ta" and "bha."

Bring hither the tawny steed to the lap of the wooden block; fashion him with stone-edged axes. Embrace him on all sides with the ten reins; yoke the draft-horse to both poles. ā | tu | sinha | harim | īm | droḥ | upa'sthe | vāśībhiḥ | takṣata | aśman'mayībhiḥ | pari | svajadhvam | daśa | kaśyābhiḥ | ubhe iti | dhurau | prati | vahnim | yunakta || 10 ||
O Adhvaryu, place this Soma, which is golden-hued, upon the lap—that is, on top—of the wooden vessel (droṇakalaśa) made from a tree;
"tu" is a filler particle.
For that purpose, O makers of the vessels, fashion the vessels with axes made of stone or of the essence of iron.
The addition of the syllable *na* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Because the suffix *mayaṭ* is marked with the letter *ṭ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
You should embrace—that is, gather together—those ten vessels, each filled with Soma, in various ways (*kaśyābhiḥ*) by means of successive turns (*paryāyeṇa*).
Bring it here;
or else,
fashion a cart for the fire-chamber with stone axes.
And you two, embrace those ten [oxen] with ten cords made of *kaśā* grass. Yoke both draft-oxen, the carriers, to the two poles of the yoke.
Alternatively, this mantra may be explained as referring to the plow, the instrument for tilling the field where the couch is to be laid.

Pressing both poles together, the carrier moves like a bird within its nest; establish the lord of the forest in the wood, and set down the well for those who offer the sacrifice. 11 "Both poles"—the carrier, pressing them together, moves within like a bird in its nest. Establish the lord of the forest in the wood; set him down well for those offering the sacrifice at the spring. 11

The draft-ox, the carrier of the oblation, pressing against both poles of the *havirdhāna* cart and settling into its place, moves between those two like a bird (*dvijāni*) within its nest (*yoni*). That tree— the cart, which is a product of the forest (*vanaspati*)— stands as a central pillar (*methī*) within the wood,
that is, within the trees belonging to the forest.
Establish it there;
or rather,
establish it in the forest, in a desirable place.
Thereafter, place the *soma* found there very well; that is, establish it so that it may be comfortable.
And subsequently, at the place of pressing, "pouring forth the fountain"—meaning, produce its juice.
Alternatively, this mantra may also be explained as being concerned with the act of plowing.
The plow whose two poles the fire—though consuming and devouring—is not able to reach, like [the fire] within the womb; the rest is the same [as before].
Place such a plow, a product of the forest (*vanaspati*), upon the ground in the forest—that is, on the furrowed field intended for sowing.
Set that plow down well and properly everywhere.
Not digging up a spring that is the means of irrigation, nor a pit, nor a place already irrigated.
On the sixth day, in the recitation of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, this verse beginning with "kapṭharaḥ" is used;
for it is stated: "'kapṭharaḥ' and 'yadvā prācīrajaganta' [are the verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.3).

O you who strike down the necks, lift up the neck! Urge them on, dig them out for the winning of booty! Shake the son from those who stand firm, so that Indra, the great slayer, may come here for the drinking of the Soma for our protection. kapṭharaḥ | kaptham | ut | daghātana | codayata | khudata | vāje'sātaye | tiṣṭhibhyaḥ | putram | ā | cyavaya | ūtaye | indram | su'bārdhaḥ | iha | soma'pītaye || 12 ||

1. *ga*-*ta*-*bha*: *yunakta*, meaning "join" or "yoke. 2. *ga*-*ta*-*bha*: *teṣām antaḥ*, meaning "the end of those. 3. *ga*-*ta*-*su*: *āsthāpayata paścāt*, meaning "place them afterwards. 4. In *ta* and *bha*, the word *asu* does not exist. 5. In *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *mu*, the word *vā* (or) occurs. 6. In *ga*, *ta*, and *ā*, it is for the purpose of piling (*cayanārtham*). [Maṇḍala 10, Adhyāya 9, Sūtra 102] Eighth Aṣṭaka, 675.

That man is the leader; the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are [his] guides. This Indra is *kaprat*—the fulfiller of happiness for the sacrificers. *Kam* is a name for happiness; *kaprat* means the one who fulfills that happiness. Urge forth, impel, and delight Indra. The root *khurda* is used in the sense of "play" (*krīḍā*) and belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*. The suffix *śa* is used by transposition (*vyatyaya*), and the elision of the letter *r* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). *Saṃviṣṭa* means "prepared" or "adorned. For what purpose? For the winning of booty (*vājasātaye*), that is, for the acquisition of food. He says that very thing: O Hotṛ, [you are] the son of Niṣṭigri. Niṣṭigri is Diti, so called because she swallows (*girati*) her own co-wife. His son is Indra. The *sabādhaḥ* are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); they are called *sabādha* because they are oppressed (*bādhyante*) by evil, laborious, and difficult tasks. Being such, you [all], for the drinking of Soma—that is, for his drinking of Soma—and for our protection (*ūtaye*), bring him hither. The singular number is used by transposition (*vyatyaya*); the meaning is "bring him forth" (*ācyāvayata*). 19.

The third hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "pra te ratham," has Mudgala, the son of Bharmyaśva, as its seer (ṛṣi). The first, the third, and the last— these three verses— are in the Bṛhatī meter.
The remaining nine verses are Triṣṭubhs.
The mallet is named Dudhna;
it belongs to this [hymn], or rather, it has Indra as its deity.
And thus it has been introduced [in the Anukramaṇī]: "Pra te mudgalaḥ... jigāya"—this third verse is a Drāghaṇavādya, and the others are Bṛhatīs.
The application [of the hymn] has been explained.
Regarding this, they say: "Mudgala’s cows were stolen by thieves who left behind the old ox."
Having placed the remainder on the cart, he went alone to a straight path;
he yoked Durdhana elsewhere as a tracker of the thieves' trail.
Having stationed Durdhana at the front, he recovered his own cattle from the thieves. Thus it is said.
Likewise, this story is also indicated in the Nirukta: "Mudgala Bhārmyaśva, having yoked the bull-like seers Dudhaṇa and Ca, engaged in battle and won the contest" (Nirukta 9.23).
May Indra protect your chariot, fashioned for victory, with boldness;
O much-invoked one, protect us in this battle for glorious wealth among those who consume the spoils.
May Indra protect your chariot, which has been made ready, with boldness; O much-invoked one, favor us in this battle for glorious wealth and in the contests for booty. 1.

O Mudgala, Indra—whose nature is boldness—shall protect and guard your chariot, which has been made "mithu," that is, rendered defective or deprived of its companions such as horses; or alternatively, "mithu" is a name for falsehood, meaning it has been made empty of horses and the like. May he protect you.
Or alternatively:
with the *vajra* characterized by boldness (*dhṛṣṇu*), that is, by the nature of being daring;
in both cases, the case-ending (*sup*) is replaced by *yāj* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
Now, the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣakṛta*):
O *puruhūta*, you who are invoked by many, O Indra, in this battle— this conflict created by those who have carried off the cattle—
of what nature is it?
It means "famous" (*viśruta*) regarding what is to be heard. The suffix *ādyac* is applied according to the rule *śrudakṣi* (Uṇādi Sūtra 3.96).
While we are consumers of wealth— desiring to enjoy wealth in the form of cattle—
or alternatively,
while there are thieves who consume wealth in the form of cattle and must be conquered.
Do not [abandon us]; protect and guard us.
The wind blew fiercely from her as she won the prize-winning chariot-race;
Indrasenā, the daughter of Mudgala, became a charioteer and drove away the arrogant Bharekṛt.
The wind blew away her garment upon the chariot when she, the charioteer, won a thousand [cows] in the contest for cattle; Mudgalānī perceived the prize set in the battle, like Indra’s army.

Because it will be stated later, "The charioteer has become Mudgalānī," this refers to the garment (*aṃśuka*) of this Mudgala’s wife, who has become the charioteer. The wind (*vātaḥ*, *vāyuḥ*) carries it upward;
that is, it raises it up in order to remove the sweat produced by fatigue.
Alternatively, the meaning is that the wind generated by the rapid driving of the horses causes the garment to flutter.
When is it said? When—having mounted the *adhiratha* (the superior chariot)—he conquered a thousand, that is, a herd of cattle numbering one thousand;
or alternatively, it may be construed as "when he conquered a thousand cows belonging to her."
If there is no *gati* or *nipāta*,
it is not our [rule];
[therefore] there is *nighāta*.

Gaviṣṭhau [is so called] because of his seeking out the cows that had been carried away. Mudralānī, the wife of Mudrala, became a charioteer (rathīḥ), that is, she became the driver; the form with the long vowel -ā- is Vedic (chāndasa). Indrasenā is Indra’s army, which was pleased by her praise.
Alternatively:
Mudralānī, the commander-in-chief of Mudrala— the Indra who shatters his enemies—
sorted out (*vyacet*) the herd of cattle acquired (*kṛtam*) in battle (*bhare*).
She separated [them] from the enemies.
In the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *ci*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* suffix according to the rule "in the Vedic language (*chandas*), [the suffix is] frequently [elided]."
O Indra, restrain the thunderbolt of him who seeks to strike you down and would do you harm;
O Maghavan, drive away the weapon of the Dāsa or the Ārya to a distance.

Within! Restrain! The thunderbolt! Of him who seeks to kill, O Indra, of him who assails us—from the Dāsa or from the Ārya, O Maghavan—ward off the weapon to a distance! O Indra, restrain within [yourself] the thunderbolt of the enemy who seeks to kill and who assails us with malice. He says this very thing: O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, ward off—the word *vadha* here being a name for the thunderbolt—the weapon that is the means of slaying, whether it belongs to a Dāsa (one who is diminished or insignificant) or to an Ārya (one who is to be approached, i.e., a great one). *Sanutaḥ* is a term meaning "hidden"; keep the weapon hidden, concealed, and employed [against us] at a distance, and separate yourself from it.
The Udra drank from the lake with a leaping motion; he struck down the peak, warding off the attacker.
Bearing his testicles as a burden, seeking renown, he stretched out his swift arms and seized the enemy.

The bull drank the lake; drinking deeply, he was exceedingly exhilarated. He struck down the thief who had hidden his plunder on the mountain peak; having done so, he went forth to slay the adversary. Then, with heavy testicles—the testicles of a bull being large when it is in full vigor—that bull, desiring renown (for *śravaḥ* means "that which is heard," i.e., fame), longing for glory, seized the swift-moving enemy with his two forefeet (*bāhū*), or rather, he struck him. Or, *ajiram* may mean "quickly"; desiring to share [the spoil] quickly, he stretched out his forefeet. In this verse, the bull is praised: the bull, the *udra*, drank the lake, the deep reservoir of water, being intensely joyful (*jarhapāṇaḥ*). Likewise, he struck down (*tuṃhat*) the thief who had placed his booty on the mountain peak (*kūṭa*); that is to say, he tore him apart. Having done so, he went toward the enemy (*abhimātim eti*) to kill him. Afterwards, as one with heavy testicles (*muṣkabhāraḥ*), meaning one whose testicles have grown large—for the testicles of a bull do indeed swell when it is in rut—that great bull, desiring renown (*śravaḥ*), seeking fame, seized the swift-moving enemy with his two forefeet (*bāhū*), or by means of his two forefeet; he struck him. Alternatively, *ajiram* is a name for "quickly"; desiring to possess [the prize] swiftly, he stretched out his forefeet; that is to say, he extended them.
Roaring and bellowing as they approached, they urged the bull toward the center of the contest;
with him, Mudgala won the sun itself, along with a hundred and a thousand cattle, in the prize-fight.

They made him bellow, approaching him; they made the bull urinate in the midst of the battle. With him, Mudgala won a hundred and a thousand cows in the contest for the sun. Mudgala said: Because of the hearing of the word *tena* ("with him"), the word *yam* ("whom") is to be supplied. Whom? This bull (*vṛṣabha*), whom they made to bellow intensely (*nyakrandayan*)—who? Men (*naraḥ*) approaching (*upayantaḥ*), going near him. They did so by means of a fierce bellowing, such that the enemies, being terrified, fled. What [did they do]? They made the bull—the showerer (*varṣaka*), the dammer-up (*setṛ*)—urinate (*amehayat*) in the midst of the battle (*ājaḥ*).

1. [He] was in the form of a servant (ga4); [he was] in the form of an army (tā1.2.3.6.7.8-bhā1.2.4.8-seṇārūpī); [he was] in the form of an army (ta4.5-seṇārūpā); [he was] in the form of a general (bha7-senānīrūpī).
2. [He] struck with a mace (ta3.7-bha-mu-prahatavān);
they caused him to rest.
*Subharvam*.
The root *bharvati* has the sense of eating;
thus, it means one who eats excellent chickpeas and the like.
The meaning is that he acted in such a manner as it was;

or rather, this is a qualifying attribute of the thousand [cows]. By means of that bull of such a form, Mudgala—one who bears this name—I conquered (jigāya) a thousand cows, well-provided with fodder and the like, accompanied by a hundred, in the *pradhana*, that is, in battle. I have won them.
A bull was yoked to the ill-fated chariot, whose driver was Keśin;
as it sped along with its draft-animals, the footless ones reached the mud of the marshes.

At the sacrifice of Kukardai, the bull was yoked; he bellowed loudly. His charioteer was Keśin. As it sped along with the wagon, yoked with the draft-animals, the hoofprints sank into the soft mud. 6.

Indeed, for the destruction of enemies, the bull—the showerer of rain—was yoked; he was harnessed and bound to the chariot. Keśin, possessing long hair or reins, was the charioteer of this king’s chariot.
The meaning is "the female elephant.
The masculine gender in the word *keśī* is used with reference to the charioteer.
*Avāvacīt* means she uttered a cry that produced fear in the bull and fear in the enemy.
Alternatively:
*keśī* and *keśinī* are his charioteers;
the meaning is "this one."
He caused this bull to utter a sound.
This is the form in the *luṅ* tense of the root *vac*, meaning "to speak," which is used alone with an internal causative sense (*antarbhūta-ṇyartha*) and is in its *yaṅ*-lopped (*yaṅ-luk*) form.
Alternatively:
His charioteer, the bull Keśin—one with magnificent hair—acting as his companion, bellowed loudly (*avāvacīt*).

From the terrifying roar of that bull, who was difficult to restrain, who was rushing along with the cart, and who was galloping swiftly toward the midst of the enemy with the chariot, the warriors fleeing in terror approached their female companion, Mudgalānī, the charioteer; "approached" (*ṛcchanti*) here means they went toward her.
(The substitution *ṛccha* for *ṛ* occurs according to the rule *pāghrādhmādṛśyarti...*.)
And the wise one, knowing the felly of the head of the chariot, urged on the horse as he approached the assembly, providing skill here;
Indra, the lord of those who turn upward, made him worthy by means of his footsteps, bestowing wealth upon the prize-winners.

And indeed, knowing [the way], he struck out his fellies; there he yoked the bull, seeking to help. Indra, the lord of the prize-winning steeds, turned him back by means of his feet, making him worthy. 7.
Moreover, that wise Mudgala raised up the rim of this chariot— the *pradhi* being the wooden felloe with holes for the spokes and the outermost rim;
it serves as a representative term for all the parts of the chariot—
and having lifted it, he caused it to rise upward.
The meaning is "he harnessed the chariot.

Immediately thereafter, on this chariot, he—training (śikṣan), that is, instructing, the bull (vaṃsaga) whose movement is desirable—placed it upon the thongs (rajjuṣu) and yoked it (upāyunak) near the chariot to the pole (yuge).
[This is from] the root *yuj* in the imperfect (laṅ); the suffix *tip* is elided by the rule *halḍyādilopaḥ*.
This being so, Indra, the god, protected (āvrat) the most excellent lord of cattle that were not to be slain and were without a master.
Thereafter, the bull, performing his task, came with speed along the pathways (padyābhiḥ sarāṇibhiḥ).
The root *rāh* signifies motion.
The matted-haired one moved about seeking prey; hewing wood at the leather thong, performing manly deeds for the great folk, he beheld the cattle and bestowed the waters upon the parched earth.

Auspiciously, the one with matted hair moved along the leather thong, fastening the wooden yoke-pin; performing manly deeds for the great folk, he, observing the cattle, bestowed strength upon them. 8.

*Śunaṃ* is a name for happiness; [it means] "in such a way that there is happiness. *Aṣṭavī*: *aṣṭa* (eight) is the goad; he possesses it. The suffix *-vin-* is used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). *Kapardī*: possessing matted locks (*kaparda*); he moves about, he wanders. Doing what? While being bound—binding on all sides—the leather thong (*varatrā*) and the wooden block (*dāru*), which is a part of the chariot. (Note: 'sa' does not appear in manuscripts ga, ta, bha1, 2, 4, 8, mu. He is being fastened.
Furthermore, what was he doing?
Bestowing riches (*nṛmṇāni*)—whether wealth consisting of his own sons, servants, and so forth, or the pleasures belonging to his enemies—upon many people;
and touching the cows.
The root *sparś* means "to touch" or "to afflict.
Here, the suffix *kānac* is used in place of the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), according to Vedic usage.
Acting thus, he has taken up—or takes up—his *taviṣīḥ*, that is, his powers.
The meaning is that one attains victory.
Behold this mace, the companion of the bull, lying in the midst of the race-course;
with it Mudgala won a hundred thousand cattle in the contests for booty.
Look at this one, yoked as a bull, lying in the middle of the race-course while yielding milk—the one by whom Mudgala won hundreds and thousands of cattle in the contests for booty. 9.
He speaks to a certain friend who, due to the absence of an army and other allies, is deriding him regarding the matter of victory:
"The king won the battle with a club and a bull," thus speaking in response to those who say so.
Previously, the bull was described.
Here, the mallet (*dughaṇa*) is described. O friend, look at this very mallet.
To the question "Of what kind is it?", it is said:
The augment *num* is applied by the rule *yujerasamāse* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.71), resulting in *yujam*.
A friend (*sakhā*) is one who is joined (*yujyate*), hence he is called *yuk*.
It is the friend of the bull;
that is to say, it accomplishes exactly as much purpose as the bull accomplishes.
Furthermore, of what nature is it?
In the middle of the *kāṣṭhā*.
According to the *Nirukta* (2.15), "even *ājyanta* is called *kāṣṭhā*.
Thus, it means in the middle of *ājyanta*.

The meaning is "in battle. There, seeing him lying down— having slain all those he intended to kill, sleeping peacefully, and existing in a state of inactivity— one should look upon such a dense forest made of trees.
The construction is as follows: "Behold this very club with which I won a hundredfold, a hundredfold, even a thousand cattle in battles, in the contests for booty—I have conquered it.
This is the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *ji* (to conquer), according to the rule *saniṭojenaḥ*.
Thus, by virtue of this repetition, the *k* of the subsequent [suffix] becomes *kutva* (the substitution of *g*).
[The suffix] *mip* becomes *ṇal*.
Far away from evil—who has seen its end? That which they yoke, upon it they mount their chariots.
To him they bring neither grass nor water; he bears the yoke, commanding from above.
Far off are the evils! Who indeed has seen this? Him whom they yoke, him they cause to stand still. For him they bring neither grass nor water; he bears the burden further on, pointing the way. 10.

Who indeed among men now sees in this manner him who, even from afar or nearby, inflicts evils—sufferings in the form of enemies? Furthermore, they yoke that very mallet (*dughaṇa*) to the chariot and mount it upon it;
or alternatively:

They station that very person whom they yoke to the chariot as one unfit for combat; the meaning is that one performs the work of both [the driver and the warrior]. Furthermore, they do not bring, that is, they do not offer him even a blade of grass.
Likewise, they do not bring water;
[he utters] the roar "Haprahoraṃbhaḥ.

Such is the *dughaṇa* (mallet/hammer), which, being itself superior, carries the yoke—the burden of the chariot—of the southern bull. Being itself superior, it carries while pointing out [the way], either indicating victory to the master or indicating fear to the enemies.
This is the form [of the word] in the present participle (*śatṛ*) from the root *diś* with the suffix *alluk*, meaning "to grant" or "to bestow."
Turning as if toward the knowledge of her husband, swelling like one pouring with a ladle—may we conquer even with these chariot-paths; may there be auspiciousness and abundant wealth.

1. According to the Chāndasa (Vedic) rule [Pāṇini 6.1.109], the sandhi is applied. 2. *Vājin* (according to Ga, Bha 1.4.7–8). 3. Because it has been stated [in Ga, Ta 1.2.3.6.7; Mu]. 4. In the principal battle (according to Ga, Ta, Bha). 5. The meaning is "they ascend" (according to Ta, Bha). Like those who have turned back; like a husband's path; let there be a cry of joy (*ānṭ*). Swelling like a leather bag; achieving success as if with a winnowing basket; even by means of what is to come; may we conquer through skill; may there be a most auspicious gain; may the booty be full of nourishment. 11.
Here, Mudralānī, the charioteer, is being praised.
This Mudralānī is as if she were *vparivṛttā*.
[The root] *vṛjī* [is used] in the sense of "avoiding" (*varjane*).
Like a woman abandoned by her husband and separated from her husband, she is as one longing for her husband;
he is to be known, to be realized, and to be attained.
He is both a husband (*pati*) and a path (*vithya*);
thus he is *pativithyamānaḥ*. Likewise, *pativithyam* is a [Vedic] form. *Ānaṭ* is a verbal root meaning "to pervade" (*vyāpti*).

In the aorist (*luṅ*) [of the root *naś*], the suffix *cli* becomes *luṅ* by the rule "ghasla etc. in the mantra. By the rule "it is also seen in the Veda" (*chandasy api dṛśyate*, Pāṇini 6.4.73), the augment *āṭ* is applied even to roots beginning with non-vowels (*anajādīnām*). Alternatively, in the perfect (*liṭ*), the elision of the *t* of the root *akṣu* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Likewise, having come into the presence of her husband like a charioteer, she becomes swelling and increasing;
what is it like?
As if piercing with a goad.
*Ku* means the earth; *kūca* refers to its surface.
By that reason of being worthy of praise (*varṣaṇīyatva*), he is like a cloud raining water while accomplishing his purpose.

Just as even something of very small measure becomes great at the time of rain in the atmosphere, so too this [arrow] increases while raining down a stream of arrows in the midst of the enemy; such is the meaning.
Likewise, "epeṣyā":
that which is to be driven toward is this herd of cattle.
"She desires that"—this is the meaning of *tamicchati*.
By such a path, acting as our charioteer, may we win back the herd of cattle carried off by the enemies.
May its *sātam*—meaning given or enjoyed—be *sumaṅgala*, beautiful and auspicious, and *sinavat*, full of blessings.
May it be like sinānna; likewise, may the object be like the food consisting of cow-milk.

O Indra, you are the eye of the entire world, the bull of sight. When, as a bull, you desire to win the race with your bull-like companion, you urge it on with your ally, Vṛdhin. 12. You. Of the entire. World. Eye. O Indra. You are. Of sight. Bull. When. Race. Bulls. You desire to win. Urging. With Vṛdhin. Ally. 12.
Because Indra is the subject of choice in this hymn (*sūkta*), Indra is praised at the beginning and also at the end due to the praise of Indra.
O Indra, you are the eye of the entire moving world (*jagat*)—that is, the eye of all that possesses sight or perceives.
Even though each individual possesses a distinct eye produced by its own origin, you are the common eye of all.
The meaning is that by means of your vision, people perceive the objects of this world and the next;
for it is indeed by attaining you through sacrifices and other such means that they accomplish the goals of human life (puruṣārtha).
Or alternatively:
You are the eye of even that eye which is the innate eye of the entire world.

Since you are the showerer (*vṛṣan*), the one who rains down desired things, having yoked to the chariot the two powerful, raining steeds (*vṛṣaṇā*)—the prize-winners (*vājinau*)—with the bond of the snare (*vadhrinā pāśena*), and having urged them on, driving them against the enemies, you desire to win the race (*sipāsasi*); therefore, you are the eye.
The fourth hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ," is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Indraputra named Apratiratha.
The thirteenth verse is an Anuṣṭubh; the remaining verses are Bṛhatīs.
The deity of the verse "bṛhaspate pari dīya" is Bṛhaspati.
The deity of the verse beginning with "amīṣāṃ cittam" is the goddess Apvā;
the remaining verses belong to Indra;
the thirteenth may optionally be dedicated to the Maruts.

And thus it has been introduced: "The hymn beginning with *āśuḥ* [is addressed] to Saindra; the fourth [verse] is by Bṛhaspati; the others are addressed to Apām Napāt, to the Ādityas, or to the Maruts, and are in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
During the Sāmicitya sacrifice, when the altar-mounds (*cit*) are being prepared, this hymn is to be recited by the Brahman priest while moving to the south.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "And while moving to the south, having completed the hymn beginning with *āśuḥ śiśānaḥ*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.12).
And [it says]: "Having recited the *Apratiratha* [sūkta]... (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.8).
For the purpose of battle, when the king is preparing for combat, he should look upon himself with this hymn.
And it is stated in the *Sūtra*: "Then he should look at him with the *Apratiratha*, the *Śāsa*, and the *Sauparṇa* hymns" (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* 3.12.13).
Swift, sharpening his horns like a terrifying bull, the striker of the strikers,
the agitator of those who defy him, the roaring one, the unblinking, the sole hero— Indra conquered a hundred armies all at once.
1. There is no [reading] *ga-ta-'patyā*.
2. By the variant *ga-ta-bha*, [the reading is] *indravā*.
Swift, sharpening his weapons, like a terrible bull, the striker, the agitator of the peoples, bellowing, unblinking, the sole hero—Indra has conquered a hundred armies all at once. 1.
This Indra is swift—meaning he acts quickly—or pervasive; he is "sharpening," which means he is resolute, inspiring fear in his enemies. Like what?
"Like a bull, terrible. Terrible (*bhīma*) means that from which one fears;
he is like such a bull.
He is as formidable as one with two sharp horns;
or alternatively, "śiśānaḥ" means "sharpening his intellect," where the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used by way of grammatical anomaly.
"Like a bull, terrible"—just as a bull causes fear with its two horns, so too he causes fear to his enemies.

"Ghanāghanaḥ"—the slayer of enemies. According to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.12.7 (*hanteḥ dhaśca*), when the suffix *ac* follows the root *han* (in the sense of an agent), there is reduplication of the root, the augment *aṭ* is added to the reduplicated syllable, and the substitution of *gh* for both the root and the reduplicated syllable. Thus, from *han*, we derive *ghana*. The repetition [of the suffix] results in the form *ghana-ghana*.
"Of the *carṣaṇīs*:
*carṣaṇīs* are human beings;
he is the agitator, the one who causes agitation among those humans who are hostile."
*Saṃkrandanaḥ*: one who causes living beings to cry out intensely by means of drawing them near or by striking them;
*animiṣaḥ*: one devoid of blinking the eyes, always moving and fighting by himself.
The meaning is that he is untiring in his duties toward all directions.
"Ekavīra" (the sole hero):
he is called a *vīra* because he acts like a hero (*vīrayati*) against his enemies.
He is both one and a hero;
or rather, he alone is valiant—
the meaning is that he is capable of accomplishing the task without assistance.
Such is this Indra; he conquers, has conquered, a hundred armies simultaneously, with a single effort.
With Indra—the one who shatters, the unblinking, the victorious, the one who stirs up conflict, the one difficult to dislodge, the bold—conquer!
With that Indra, O men, fight and prevail in battle, with the bull whose hand holds arrows.

With the roaring one, the unblinking one, the victorious one, the one who makes the clash, the one difficult to dislodge, the bold one—with such an Indra, conquer that [battle]; overcome that [hostile force], O warriors, O leaders, with the arrow-handed bull. If it be asked: "Let Indra be as described; even so, what does it matter to us?", the text replies: With the one characterized as "roaring" (*saṃkrandana*) and "unblinking" (*animiṣa*), with the "victorious" (*jiṣṇu*) one who is habitually conquering, with the "one who makes the clash" (*yutkāra*)—*yut* meaning combat—he who brings about battle (the suffix *aṇ* is used in the sense of an action); with the "difficult to dislodge" (*duścyavana*) one who cannot be shaken by others (from the roots *cyuṅ* and *muṅ* meaning "to move," the suffix *yuc* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.129); with the "bold" (*dhṛṣṇu*) one who is daring—with such an Indra, conquer that battle. Overcome that enemy force, O warriors (*yudhaḥ*), O leaders (*naraḥ*). (The subsequent word is accented because, according to Pāṇini 8.1.74, the plural number is optionally treated as non-existent when a specific distinction is made. Furthermore, with what kind of Indra? With the one "having arrows in his hand" (*iṣuhasta*) and the "bull" (*vṛṣan*) who showers blessings.
He, the self-controlled one, is accompanied by those with arrows in hand and those bearing quivers; he is Indra, the uniter in battle by his excellence.
He is the victor over those who have united against him, the drinker of Soma, strong of arm, possessing a fierce bow, and a shooter with well-aimed arrows.

He [is] with those who have arrows in their hands; he with those who carry quivers; the controller; the one who comes together; he, Indra, through his quality, the conqueror of the joined; the Soma-drinker; strong of arm; possessing a formidable bow; a shooter with well-aimed [arrows]. In the previous mantra it was said, "Conquer with Indra. Here, the text shows Indra’s capacity as the means for victory. He—Indra—is *vaśī*: possessed of those who are under his control, such as the Maruts and others. Likewise, he is joined with *niṣaṅgibhiḥ* (those carrying quivers); *niṣaṅga* means a sword. He is the controller by means of those who possess such weapons. And that Indra, while *yudhaḥ* (fighting)—the suffix *ka* being added according to the rule for roots ending in *ig* or a short vowel—or alternatively, for the sake of battle (*yudhaḥ*), is *saṃsraṣṭā*: one whose nature is to come together with *guṇena*, the host of enemies. Because he is of such a nature, he is *saṃsṛṣṭajit*: the conqueror of those who come together in mutual conflict for the purpose of fighting. Likewise, he is *somapāḥ*: the drinker of Soma. *Bāhuśardhī*: *śardhaḥ* means strength; he possesses the strength of his arms (*bāhubalam*). The suffix *ini* is used here in the sense of possession. Or, from the root *śrudhu* meaning "to overpower": he overpowers or subdues with his two arms, thus he is *bāhuśardhī*. The suffix *ṇini* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.78 (*supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye*). *Ugradhanvā*: possessing a raised...
The archer, the slayer with arrows discharged against enemies—
meaning that where he desires to release them, they do not fail their purpose— with such an Indra, "conquer," is the connection.
O Bṛhaspati, fly around with your chariot, slaying the Rākṣasas and driving away our enemies; shattering the armies and crushing them in battle, be the victorious protector of our chariots.
O Bṛhaspati, fly around with your chariot, slayer of demons, driving away our enemies, shattering the armies, crushing them in battle, and conquering; be the protector of our chariots. 4.

O Bṛhaspati, protector of the great ones, fly around with your chariot— the root *dī* meaning "to go. Having arrived, as the slayer of demons (*rakṣohā*), destroying the enemies from all sides, likewise shattering the enemy armies and utterly crushing them.
The root *mṛṇ* is used in the sense of "to injure. The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u*. By what means does he injure?
"By means of *yudhā* (through battle)—
the vowel of the case-ending being acute according to the rule *sāvekācaḥ*—
you who are thus victorious, attaining victory in every respect, such as you, O protector (*avitā*) of our chariots (*rathānām*), be eager (*gṛdhi*) [to protect]."
O Indra, discoverer of strength, elder, preeminent hero, powerful, vigorous, victorious, fierce, superior hero, superior warrior, born of might, winner of cattle— mount your victorious chariot!

O Indra, you who are invincible in strength, ancient, preeminent hero, powerful, vigorous, triumphant, fierce, heroic, a warrior of the highest rank, born of power—ascend your victorious chariot, O protector of cattle! 5.
He is *Balavijñāya* because he knows the strength of every being;
or alternatively,
he is *Balavijñāya* because his strength is recognized by all as such, [thinking], "This is strength."
The meaning is that he is the strength of all.

He is *sthaviraḥ* (the steadfast), *mahān* (great), *pravīraḥ* (an eminent hero), *sahasvān* (possessing the power to overcome), *vājī* (swift, or possessing food), *sahamānaḥ* (conquering, the subduer of enemies), *ugraḥ* (of formidable strength), and *abhivīraḥ* (surrounded by heroes);
that is to say, one whose followers are heroic and full of valor.

O Indra, you who have overcome all beings (*abhisatvā*), who are born of power (*sahojāḥ*), and who are thus possessed of such greatness—you should mount your victorious chariot (*ratham ā tiṣṭha*), which is characterized by the habit of conquering, for the sake of assisting us. And you are the finder of cattle (*govit*), that is, either the obtainer or the knower of water (or of praise).
The breaker of the enclosure, the winner of cattle, with arms like thunderbolts—him who conquers, is unconquered, and crushes his foes by his might;
O kinsmen, follow after this Indra; O friends, rally together behind him!
Gotrabhid, Govid, Vajrabāhu, Jayanta, Aja, who crushes with his might—O kinsmen, follow him in valor; O friends, rally together after Indra! 6.
"Gotrabhidam": *gotra* refers to clouds, because they bring forth (*āyanti*) waters; or alternatively, *gauḥ* means the earth.
"Those who come toward her" refers to the mountains, the *gotras*.
He is the "breaker" (*bhettāram*) of them; "finder of the *go*" (*govidam*), that is, the obtainer of water; "thunderbolt-armed" (*vajrabāhum*), meaning one who holds the thunderbolt in his hand.
The reversal of word order [in *vajrabāhu*] follows Pāṇini 2.2.36.4, which prescribes the final position for words denoting weapons.

O kinsmen—those warriors born together—emulate this Indra! He is victorious, possessing the nature of victory; he is the Unborn (aja), ever-moving, who conquers the enemy force by his might (ojas), or rather, who wins the battle (āji) by his power; he is the crusher of enemies, overwhelming them. O you who are of equal origin, follow this great-souled one and act like heroes before him.
2. *ta-avitā* means "protector" or "guardian.
3. *ga-ta-bha- 'bhūtasya'* does not exist. Perform [your duty] hereafter; exert yourselves as heroes; perform heroic deeds; wage war.
The root *śūra* means "to be brave" or "heroic.
From the word *vīra*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied according to the rule *tat karoti tad ācaṣṭe* ("he does that" or "he describes that").
O friends—meaning you who have become mutual companions—exert yourselves together with this Indra as he exerts himself.

Plunging with force into the cow-pens, pitiless, heroic, possessing a hundredfold wrath, Indra—the unshakable, the conqueror of armies, the invincible—may he protect our armies in the battles. Plunging with force into the cow-pens (the clouds), the pitiless, heroic, one of a hundredfold wrath, Indra—the unshakable, the conqueror of armies, the invincible—may he protect our armies in the battles. This Indra, plunging with force into the cow-pens (the clouds/masses), entering them, being pitiless, heroic, valorous, possessing a hundredfold wrath (having performed many sacrifices or having great anger), unshakable by others, and himself the conqueror of armies...
Rouse up, O Maghavan, our weapons; rouse up the spirits of my warriors; rouse up the vigor of the steeds, O slayer of Vṛtra! Let the shouts of the conquering chariots go forth! 10.

O Maghavan Indra, cause our weapons to exult; cause them to rejoice exceedingly, meaning let them be prepared for striking. And cause the minds of my own *satvans*—my living beings, my soldiers—to exult as well.
O Vṛtra-slayer Indra, let the vigor—the speeds—of the prize-winning horses rise up;
likewise, let the shouts of the victorious chariots rise up.
May Indra be on our side; when the banners meet, may those arrows which are ours be victorious.
May our heroes be superior; O gods, protect us in our invocations.
Ours be Indra when the banners meet; ours be the arrows—let them conquer! May our heroes be superior; O gods, protect us in our invocations! 11.
May Indra be our protector when our own kinsmen have perished and the enemy army is in a state of panic; may our banners and the soldiers bearing those banners prevail.
Likewise, may our arrows alone conquer the enemies, and may our heroic warriors be superior and victorious.
O gods, protect us, even us; guard us in invocations and in battles.
Bewildering the minds of these men, seize their limbs and advance further! Press forward and consume them with grief; let the blind enemies be overtaken by darkness.
Alluring their minds, seize their limbs; go away, go further, go forward! Burn them up with sorrows in their hearts; let the enemies be possessed by blind darkness. 12.

O goddess who takes pride in evil, you who are deluding and bewildering the minds of these warriors and enemies, seize their limbs—their constituent parts such as the head and so forth—and take possession of them. Advance against them;
having gone into their presence, burn away their grief in their stolen hearts, utterly reducing them to ashes.
May those enemies, our adversaries, be possessed by and enter into blinding darkness.
May the lord of men, the conqueror of the departed, grant you protection;
may his arms be formidable so that you may be invincible.
Advance, O heroes, and conquer! May Indra grant you protection. May your arms be mighty, so that you shall be invincible. 13.
O men, you leaders, bearers of the burden of battle, and warriors, go forth with pre-eminence!
And having gone, conquer the copper-colored soldiers.
Because it follows a finite verb (tiṅ), there is no elision (nighāta) according to the rule "tiṅaṅatiṅaḥ."
May Indra grant you protection and happiness;
may your arms be fierce and possessed of formidable strength.
May your arms be so fierce that you shall become invincible, unassailable by others.
The fifth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "asāvi," is the seerly composition of Aṣṭaka Vaiśāmitra; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Asāvi consists of eleven [verses]; Aṣṭaka is a descendant of Viśvāmitra.
The application of this hymn has already been explained.
1. Of those [words] ending in -ga, -ta, -bha, or a śatṛ suffix.

The Soma has been pressed for you, O Much-invoked One; come quickly to the sacrifice with your two bay horses. For you, O Indra, the songs of the wise heroes, seeking you, have flowed forth; drink of the pressed juice! 1. *asāvi somaḥ* | *puruhūta* | *tubhyam* | *harībhyām* | *yajñam* | *upa* | *yāhi* | *tūyam* | *tubhyam* | *giraḥ* | *vipravīrāḥ* | *iyānāḥ* | *dadhanvire* | *indra* | *piba* | *sutasya* || 1 || O *puruhūta* (much-invoked), for *tubhyam* (you), the *somaḥ* (Soma) has been pressed (*asāvi*) for your sake. [From the root *puñ* "to press," in the passive sense, the form is *luṅ*. Therefore, with *harībhyām* (the two bay-colored horses), come *tūyam* (quickly) *upa yāhi* (to our sacrifice). For *tubhyam* (you), our *giraḥ* (songs)—which are *vipravīrāḥ* (possessing wise heroes as their inspirers, i.e., those whose heroes are inspired and impelled by the wise)—*iyānāḥ* (moving toward you) have *dadhanvire* (flowed forth); that is, they have been reached by us for your gratification. [From the root *iṅ* "to go," the suffix *śānac* is used in the sense of habit, with the Vedic elision of the conjugational suffix. The root *dhavi* means "to move"; the form *dadhanvire* is a Vedic perfect in the passive sense. Since this is so, *piba* (drink) the *sutasya* (pressed) portion, or the pressed Soma itself. In the first round, this verse, "apsu dhūtasya" (of that shaken in the waters), is the *yājyā* (offering prayer) for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* is 'apsu dhūtasya harivaḥ pibeha'. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).

Drink here, O Lord of the Bay Horses (*harivaḥ*), of that which has been shaken in the waters, pressed by the men; fill your belly! The stones have yearned for you, O Indra; with them, increase your exhilaration, O you who are borne by hymns (*ukthavāhaḥ*). O Lord of the Bay Horses—according to the Śruti, "The *Ṛc* and *Sāman* are indeed Indra’s two bay horses"—O Indra, who possesses those two bay horses consisting of the *Ṛc* and *Sāman* which serve as the support for the hymns and recitations, drink here at this sacrifice of that Soma which has been "shaken" (*dhūtasya*)—that is, stirred—in the waters, such as the *ekadhana* vessels; likewise, of that which has been "pressed" (*sutasya*) by the "men" (*nṛbhiḥ*), the leaders of the rite and performers of the action, such as the *adhvaryu*s. In both cases, because the rule "the mention of the action must be made" applies, the object receives the designation of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and thus the genitive is used in the sense of the dative according to the rule "frequently in the Veda. Drink such Soma here in this sacrifice; and having drunk, fill your own belly. The first verbal ending is not elided here according to the rule "optionally when the initial [element] is dropped. O Indra, those "stones" (*adrayaḥ*), the pressing-graves, have "yearned" (*mimikvaḥ*)—meaning they desired to form a continuous stream—for you; that is, they performed the pressing. This is a form of the root *miha* (to sprinkle) in the desiderative (*san*) with the *liṅ* suffix. O you who are borne by hymns, being praised by the *ukthas*, increase your exhilaration with those [stones]. In the second round (*paryāya*), this verse beginning with "progrām" is the *yājyā* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. It is stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* is 'aśvāvati prathamaḥ', 'progrām pītim vṛṣṇa iyarmi', and 'satyām'. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).

I offer a true draught for the bull to drink; O Indra, Lord of the Bay Horses, rejoice here in the pressed juice for your sake. Glorified by all our prayers and by our power, delight yourself here with our songs. I offer a mighty, true draught for the bull to drink; O Indra, Lord of the Bay Horses, rejoice here in the pressed juice for your sake. Glorified by all our prayers and by our power, delight yourself here with our songs. 1. *ta-bha-te* [variant reading]: for you.
O Indra, lord of bay horses, for you, the bull, the showerer of benefits, I urge forth—indeed, I impel—the fierce, uplifted, and true draught at the drinking of Soma.
For what purpose? For the sake of *prati*, that is, for the sake of advancing forward.
For whom?
For the one who has been pressed and has approached.

Therefore, O Indra, joined with *śacī*—whether by power or by action—and being praised (*gṛṇānaḥ*), do thou rejoice and be satisfied here at this sacrifice with all *dhenās*, that is, with all words of praise, and with all *dhīs*, that is, with all ritual acts.
In the sense of "intoxication" and "satisfaction," the *ātmanepada* [is used].
In the third sequence, for the recitation of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the verse "ūtī śacīvaḥ" serves as the *yājyā*.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* is 'ūtī śacīvastava vīryeṇa'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).

Through your aid, O Lord of Might, and by your heroic power, the seers who know the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and possess vitality have been established within the dwelling of man, O Indra; praising you, they stand there as companions at the shared feast, seeking progeny.

Through your aid, O Lord of power, by means of your heroic might, the yearning ones who know the Eternal Law, assuming vital strength, have stood in the dwelling of Manu, O Indra, praising you with offspring, as those who share in the communal feast. || 4 ||

O Indra, possessor of power and might, through your protection and through your assistance, we—the *uśijaḥ* (the yearning ones), knowing the *ṛta*, that is, knowing the sacrifice and the day—maintaining and upholding food accompanied by progeny, desiring you alone, the Aṅgirases, performing the sacrificial session (*sattra*), having mastered the ritual application on the sixth day, reached the end by means of the *Nābhānediṣṭha*; it is for this reason that they possess the knowledge of *ṛta*.

Such [are they], praising you and standing together as those who rejoice in the company of the Angirases, within the *duroṇa*—the sacrificial hall—of *manuṣ*, the human sacrificer. They stand as those who feast together (*sadhamādyāsas*).
[The word] *mādayate* [is derived] with the suffix *yat* in the sense of the agent (by the rule *aco yat*), according to the statement "the *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are used diversely";
the substitution of *sabhā* for *sadha-* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Therefore, the meaning is: "We too should remain."

O Indra, Lord of the bay horses, the people, through their hymns of praise, have well-fashioned the most bountiful form of the one who possesses good channels and wide radiance; thus do the worshippers, upholding it with their truthful songs, extend it to you.

O Indra, Lord of the tawny steeds, the people of Muṣṭi and Sumna, who shine with great luster, have increased their most abundant aid through their prayers; as your worshippers, O Indra, they sustain themselves with your truthful blessings. 5.

O Indra, O Lord of the bay horses (*haryaśva*), you who are endowed with green-colored steeds—of you, who are well-praised (*suṣṭuḥ*), whose aim is excellent (*supumnasya*), who are most blissful (*susukhasya*) or possess great wealth (*sudhanasya*), and who are many-shining (*pururucaḥ*)—by means of your leadings (*praṇītibhiḥ*), that is, your guidances consisting of the bestowal of wealth and other gifts, the people (*janāsaḥ*), namely the worshippers, [remain] with their *sūnṛtā*—words that are pleasant or truthful.

This is conjoined with the phrase "by these leadings. They remain, as the ellipsis implies, maintaining your protection (*ūtiṃ*)—which is most worthy of honor (*maṃhiṣṭhām*) and intended for bestowing upon other supplicants—while they themselves distribute it to others.
Come near, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, with your two bay horses, to drink of the pressed soma.
Indra, the sacrifice has reached you who are attentive; you are the mindful observer of this worshipper’s rite.

Come near, O you who possess the golden steeds, with your two bay horses; come to drink of the pressed Soma. O Indra, the sacrifice has reached you as you look on; you are the giver and the herald of the rite. 6.

1. *gatam* (already explained). O possessor of bay horses (*harivaḥ*), O Indra, come (*upa yāhi*) toward our prayers (*brahmāṇi*)—that is, toward our ritual acts or hymns of praise (*pariṣṭutāni*)—for the sake of drinking (*pītaye*), that is, for the consumption of the pressed Soma.
By what means? That is stated as follows: [the rest of the verse].
With two bay horses;
that is to say, by means of a chariot yoked with those two.
Or else:
The term *harivaḥ* is to be connected with *haribhyām*.
O Indra, the sacrifice—the Soma-sacrifice—reaches (*ānat*) you, who are patient (*kṣamāṇam*).
Regarding the verb *naśati*, in the *luṅ* tense, the suffix *cli* is elided by the rule *mantre ghasa*.
The augment *āṭ* is seen even in Vedic [usage], according to the rule "it is also seen in the Veda.
Alternatively, in the case of the root *aś*, there is the elision of the *tap-pratyaya* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), which is a Vedic phenomenon;
furthermore, the augment *nuṭ* is applied according to the rule "and after the root *aś*."
O you who clearly perceive the sacrifice, you are the giver of the fruit of ritual action.

The songs of the singer—invoking the one of a thousandfold strength, the overcomer of enemies, the bountiful lord who is easily won with well-fashioned hymns—wait upon him; they honor Indra, the unconquered, and celebrate him with reverent salutations.
A thousandfold strength,
the overcomer of hostility,
the delight in the pressed [soma].
The gift of Maghavan;
the well-prepared hymn; toward [him].
They adorn their words,
which are beyond compare.
To Indra,
let the praises of the singer pay homage.
The limitlessness of wisdom.

The hymns—words in the form of praises—adorn Indra, who possesses a thousandfold strength (*sahasravāja*), who has immeasurable power (*aparimitabala*), who overcomes adversaries (*abhimātipāha*), that is, the conqueror of enemies who harm from all sides; who delights in the pressed soma (*suteraṇa*); who is bountiful (*maghavān*); who is worthy of beautiful praise (*suvṛkti*); and who is unassailable (*apratīta*) by others in battle.
He says that very thing: the *jaritṛ*s (singers), the *namasyā*s (those worthy of homage)—that is, the praises—*pananta*, they praise.
The seven divine waters are invigorating and uninjured, by which you, O Indra, crossed the Sindhu through the fortresses;
you found a path for the gods and for man across the ninefold streams and the nine flowing rivers.
Seven are the divine waters.
Without conflict; uninjured;
by which.
O Indra, you crossed the Sindhu river.
The purifying waters: ninety rivers.
And nine flowing rivers.
For the gods;
a path for man.
And: Vinda.

O Indra, by your command, these seven—numbering seven—are the divine waters (*anvāpaḥ*), goddesses such as the Gaṅgā and others, who are *suraṇāḥ*, meaning either "well-rejoicing" or "possessing beautiful sounds.
The root *raṇ* signifies sound;
according to the rule *vaśiraṇyor upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 3.3.58), the suffix *ap* is added in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, the initial syllable of the final member is acute according to the rule "ādyudāttaṃ chandasi.
*Amṛktāḥ* means "unharmed"; the ellipsis is "flowing forth.
O *Indra*, you who are the destroyer of fortresses (*pūrbhid*), with those [rivers] such as the Gaṅgā and others, together with the flowing rivers, you crossed over the *sindhu*, the ocean.
The meaning is "you caused to increase.
Alternatively:
the seven divine waters, characterized by flowing and possessing the nature of waves, were created and flow forth—by means of which you crossed the river Sindhu.
Moreover, you have found— indeed, you obtained— the ninety-nine rivers, those flowing streams numbering ninety-nine,
which carry forth their currents;
you found these rivers for the sake of oblation for the gods and for the sake of enjoyment for man, as well as their *gātu*, their path to be traversed.

The waters, the great ones, have awakened for you against the one who curses; O God, you alone have prevailed over them. O Indra, with those [powers] which you exercised in the conquest of Vṛtra, may you, possessing all life, cause your body to flourish. 9 *apaḥ*, *mahīḥ*, *abhi*, *aśasteḥ*, *amu*, *atra*, *ajāgar*, *āsu*, *adhi*, *deva*, *ekaḥ*, *indra*, *yāḥ*, *tvam*, *vṛtratūrye*, *cakartha*, *tābhiḥ*, *viśvāyuḥ*, *tanvam*, *pupuṣyāḥ*. 9 1. *ga*: rivers; *ta1.2.3.7*: heaven; *ta4.5.8-bha1.2.4.8*: heaven. 2. *ga1.2-ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha*: "you" is not present.

O Indra, you, the great one, have struck down the vast waters from the assailant, the slayer, with your mighty arm. When the waters were released, O God, you alone—being truly solitary and without companion—stood watchful and vigilant.
Or rather: [the verse continues].
This is a restatement of the meaning along with its recitation:

O Indra, you performed (*vyakartha*), that is, you do perform (*karoṣi*), deeds for the sake of slaying Vṛtra—that is, for the destruction of the cloud. With all those waters (*adbhiḥ viśvābhiḥ*), you nourish (*pupuṣyāḥ*) your own body (*tanum*).
[The form *pupuṣyāḥ* is derived from the root *puṣ* "to nourish," where the *ślu* (reduplication) occurs by way of grammatical anomaly.]

Indra, the most heroic, the seasonal one, the well-praised—himself the voice, he seeks the one invoked by many. He pierced Vṛtra and made wide space; Śakra, the helper, overcame the armies in battle. vīreṇyaḥ (most heroic), ṛtuḥ (the seasonal one), indraḥ (Indra), su-śastiḥ (well-praised), uta (also), api (even), dhenā (the voice), puru-hūtam (the one invoked by many), īṭṭe (he seeks). ārdayat (he pierced), vṛtram (Vṛtra), akṛṇot (he made), ūm iti (wide), lokam (space). saṃsāhe (in the crushing battle), śakraḥ (Śakra), pratanāḥ (the armies), abhiṣṭiḥ (the helper). 10.
Indra is preeminent among heroes, a hero to be surpassed by heroes, or perhaps one who is exceedingly heroic; he is active in his deeds and possesses beautiful praise.
Furthermore, the word *vuta* is meaningless;
furthermore, there is *dhena*.
This is the name of the word *vāḍ*.
It is a pleasing word of praise; it invokes—that is, praises or honors—Indra, who is much-invoked (*puruhūta*).
Since he possesses the characteristics previously described, the meaning is "one who praises."
Furthermore, he slew Vṛtra—the Asura named Vṛtra, who is so called because he obstructs; the meaning is that he killed him.
Moreover, [he slew] Loka. One is called *loka* because one perceives (*lokayati*); thus, *loka* means light or manifestation.
He made it manifest; that is to say, having slain the obscuring Asura, he rendered it light.
Not only him alone, but furthermore, Śakra—the capable Indra, the overcomer of enemies—overcame the enemy armies in battle.

For prosperity, let us invoke the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty—the one who hears us, the fierce one for our protection in conflicts, the slayer of Vṛtras, and the winner of riches. For prosperity, let us invoke the bountiful Indra, the most heroic in this battle for the acquisition of booty—the one who hears us, the fierce one for our protection in conflicts, the slayer of Vṛtras, and the winner of riches.
This has been explained previously.
The sixth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "kadā," is dedicated to Indra.
Its seer is Nābhānediṣṭha, who was Durmitra by name but Sumitra by virtue; or alternatively, he was Sumitra by name but Durmitra by virtue.
The two verses beginning with "harī yasya suyujā" and "vajraṃ yaścakre" are *uṣṇih* meters, each having eleven feet with a pipīlikā-madhyama (middle-light) structure.
This [verse] is a *triṣṭubh*,
or alternatively a *gāyatrī*;
by the rearrangement of syllables (*akṣaravyūha*), it is also another view that it is an *uṣṇih*.
All the remaining [verses] are in the Uṣṇih meter.

Thus it has been enumerated: "When Kautsa Durmitra [addressed] Agni, or Sumitra by virtue of his qualities [addressed] Agni as Durmitra; the Uṣṇih [hymn] consists of the 'Horses,' the 'Thunderbolt,' and the 'Ant-like' [sections]; the last [verse] is a Triṣṭubh, while the first is a Gāyatrī.
The application (viniyoga) has been explained.
1. [He is] either one who possesses action or one who possesses wisdom.
2. This has been explained previously.
As for the meaning of the mantra: O Indra, "vājasātau" refers to that in which there is *sāti*, the acquisition, of "vāja," which is food.
In that *bhara*—wherein the warriors bear the fortune of victory—the word *bhara* signifies battle.

In that battle, we the Kuśikas invoke you for the sake of sacrifice: you, the auspicious one through your energy, the possessor of wealth (*maghavan*), and therefore Indra, endowed with unsurpassed sovereignty; the most excellent leader (*nṛtama*) of the entire world. We call upon you for the purpose of the sacrifice.

Thus, while we hear our own praise being performed, may we call upon you for protection—you who are fierce and terrifying to enemies, who slay all the *vṛtras* (demons) characterized by Vṛtra in every battle, who destroy them, and who are the conqueror of the wealth belonging to our foes. (3.
Ta-Mu-Nāmataḥ)

When, O Vasu, will you graciously accept this hymn? May you hold back these waters for the sake of the long-pressed juice and for Vātāpya. 1. When, O Vasu, will you graciously accept this hymn? May you hold back these waters for the sake of the long-pressed juice and for Vātāpya. 1.

O Indra, you who provide clothing, you desire the hymn composed by us; [we offer it] to you who desire it. Because of the rule "the mention of the action must be made," the object takes the dative case (saṃpradāna), hence the fourth case ending.
When—at what time—will you bestow it? You will grant it.
"And having obstructed [the waters], when will he hold them back?
When will such a time come for us?"—thus he hopes.
In the form *rudhet*, the *luṅ* (aorist) tense is used; by the rule "irito vā," the substitute *aṭ* is applied to the *cli* suffix.
The word *vāri* is derived from the root *vṛ* (to choose/cover) with the suffix *ali*; the absence of the *śap* augment is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Because of the rule “in the Veda, both ways” (*chandas y ubhayathā*), the suffix *ti* is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, which results in the elision of the *j* by the rule “*jer aniṭi*” (*jeraniṭi*), and subsequently the elision of the *ti* itself by the rule “*halṅyābbhyaḥ*” (*halṅyābhyaḥ*).
An illustration of this is provided therein.
"He attains the field"—this is the meaning of *rudhyā*.
This is a contraction of a simile (*luptopama*);
the sense is that just as one obstructs waters by means of a dam (*kulyā*) and, having obstructed them, holds them back, so it is here.
To the question "With reference to what is there this prohibition?", he says [the answer]:
"With reference to the Soma that has been pressed and poured out, extending through the form of the three long pressings.
To the question "For what purpose?", he then says:
For Vātāpya.
It is called *vātāpya* because it is made to swell by the wind (*vāta*) and is caused to fall downward; thus, it refers to water.
The meaning is "for the purpose of providing that [water]."

Whose two bay steeds, well-yoked, moving in different directions, swift and eager, follow after the tail; both are like two long-maned ones breaking down the obstacles—he is the lord of the gift. 2. *Harī iti*: the two bay steeds. *Yasya*: whose. *Suyujā*: well-yoked. *Vivratā*: moving in different directions. *Veḥ*: swift. *Arvantā*: eager. *Anu*: following after. *Śepā*: the tail. *Ubhā*: both. *Rujī iti*: like two breakers (or destroyers). *Na*: as it were. *Keśinā*: long-maned ones. *Patiḥ*: the lord. *Dana*: of the gift. 2.
Of that Indra, the two bay horses (*harī*) are well-yoked (*suyujā*),
meaning they are well-trained; they are *vivratā* [moving in different directions].

"Vrata" is a name for ritual action (*karman*). The two "arbantau" (the two who go) are those distinguished by their actions; "śepā" means possessing a penis (*śepa*). The possessive suffix (*matup*) is elided.
The meaning is "possessing praiseworthy manliness.
Both, both—like the two *rajīs*, that is, like heaven and earth;
or rather, like the two great protectors, the sun and the moon.

O Indra, you who are the lord and master of those two such horses—whether they are called *keśinau* because they possess hair (*keśa*), or because they shine with hair—belonging to you there; bestowing wealth (*dan*), you follow after and desire the hymns, recitations, and other rites (*anu veḥ*).

In the word *dann*, from the root *dā* (to give) in the present participle (*śatṛ*), the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule “*āto lopaḥ*” because it is treated as an ārdhadhātuka suffix according to the rule “*chandasyubhayathā*”;
for this very reason, the dental *t* remains.

Indra, who is free from evil, has come to our thought like one who is striving and fearing; for he, the powerful one, has harnessed himself for glory. apa | yoḥ | indraḥ | pāpaje | ā | matau | na | śaṃśamāṇaḥ | bibhīvān | śubhe | yat | yuyuje | tarvipīvān || 3 ||
Regarding "yaḥ indraḥ pāpaje": the particle *ā* is meaningless. "Pāpaja" refers to Vṛtra, who was born from evil (*pāpa*).

In that state of mind, he does not act like a human being who is praising [the enemy]; rather, while exerting himself in battle with him, he becomes both weary and afraid. The form *śaṃśamānaḥ* is the perfect (liṭ) of the root *śram*, used in the Vedic language; its suffix -kānac is applied by way of transposition (vyatyaya).
When— that is, whenever— that Indra, being full of vigor and powerful with the Maruts as his forces, has harnessed himself, is joined, and becomes ready for the sake of glory,
then he becomes the one who causes the waters of Vṛtra to flow away.
1. *ta*, *ta*, *ra*, *la*, *ga*, *na*, *bha*, *su*, *yu*, *ja* [are the syllables] in the *gilāpa* [meter].
2. *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, *su*, *yu*, *ja* [are the syllables in the second *gilāpa*].
3. *ta*, *bha*, *śa*, *va*, *bhā*, *va* [are the syllables in the third *gilāpa*].

Indra, the hero, attended to the two rivers of triple courses as they flowed toward the people, honoring them with his approach. 4. *sa* (he), *āyoḥ* (of the living man), *indraḥ* (Indra), *carṣe* (toward the people), *ā* (hither), *upānasaḥ* (with his footstep/approach), *saparyan* (honoring/attending), *nadayoḥ* (of the two rivers), *trivratayoḥ* (of those with threefold courses), *śūraḥ* (the hero), *indraḥ* (Indra). 4.

Of *vāyoḥ*: this is a name for a human being. For the sake of the human praiser, *carṣe* means for repeated marking, that is, for the purpose of bestowing wealth. *Sacā* means accompanied by the wealth to be given; or rather, *āyoḥ sacā* means having become an assistant to the living one. *Upānasaḥ*: he has approached the chariot (*anaḥ*). This is a *prādi*-compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.18.4 (*atyādayaḥ krāntādyarthe dvitīyayā*), with the compound-ending suffix *ṭac* added according to Pāṇini 5.4.103 (*anasantānnapuṃskāt*). The meaning is "one who has mounted the chariot. *Saparyan*: honoring the praiser with wealth; or alternatively, by a transposition of voices, the agentive suffix is used, meaning "being honored by praises and hymns. Such Indra, characterized by the aforementioned qualities, comes—supplying the appropriate verb due to the presence of the prefix (*upa-*). What kind of Indra? The controller of two horses that neigh (*nadayoḥ*) and possess distinct movements (*vivratayoḥ*), a hero (*śūraḥ*) who is valorous.

He who has mounted upon the two maned [horses], which are full of splendor as if for nourishment—he, the possessor of beautiful jaws, wins with his two jaws. 5. He who has mounted upon the two maned [horses], which are full of splendor as if for nourishment—he, the possessor of beautiful jaws, wins with his two jaws. 5.

Indra stands—meaning he mounts or occupies—for the sake of nourishment (*puṣṭyai*) two such horses: long-maned (*keśavantā*), tawny (*keśinau*), radiant (*vyr̥casvantā*), expansive (*vyacanavantau*), and pervasive (*vyāptimantau*). The particle *na* here is an expletive. Or rather, *na* has the sense of "and" (*ca*), whereby two qualities are conjoined: they have beautiful manes and are expansive; this is the meaning. That Indra, possessed of jaws (*śiprābhyām*) by virtue of his jaws (*śiprābhyām*), is called *śipriṇīvān* or *śiprāvān*. One part of the mantra’s meaning is a restatement (*anuvāda*). He desires or begs for Soma; [the root] *vanu* means "to beg. Or else, *vanu* is a verb whose action is striking; he strikes down his enemies. 26.1–3. O Indra, you stand for the sake of nourishment upon two such horses: long-maned, tawny, radiant, expansive, and pervasive. Or rather, the word *na* signifies "and"; thus two qualities are conjoined: they have beautiful manes and are expansive. That Indra, possessing jaws through his two jaws, is *śipriṇīvān*. [The root] *van* means to desire; or it means to strike. 26.1–3. O Indra, you stand for the sake of nourishment upon two such horses: long-maned, tawny, radiant, expansive, and pervasive. The commentary on the sixth mantra found in manuscripts Ga1 and Ga2: "Possessing lofty vigor (ṛṣvaujāḥ), possessing great vigor (mahaujāḥ)," Indra—endowed with might (śavasā) and strength (balena)—praises, or rather, extols, the battle together with the lofty ones (ṛṣvebhiḥ), that is, the great ones. The hero (śūraḥ) Indra fashions (takṣa), that is, he makes thin, his enemies; in this regard, there is an illustration.
The meaning is that he makes the body of the forest [the world] just as Mātariśvan Vāyu does by means of the seasons and ritual acts, appearing like the Ṛbhus.

(Ṛgveda 4.44) By the acts being performed; or alternatively, *kratu* is a name for wisdom. By means of strength and insights, he fashioned [the world], performing such deeds as the slaying of Vṛtra. Therein is the illustration: "like the Ṛbhus. The substitution of *su* for the nominative plural (*jasaḥ*) is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. The meaning is: just as the Ṛbhus, through their ritual acts and insights, fashioned the chariot, the cups, and other objects unique to themselves, so too did he.
He who wields the thunderbolt against the Dasyu for the sake of the good man— shameless himself yet full of shame—
is one whose jaw is unbroken, like the wondrous dust of heaven.
The Vajra—[that which] he fashioned for the easy slaying of the Dasyu—is golden-hued, golden, with unbroken jaws, like a wondrous expanse of space. 7.

Indra, who made the vajra—the weapon that is the means of striking—for the sake of slaying the dasyu, the enemy who is "suhanāya," meaning one easily to be slain or who causes destruction; he is connected with the phrase "you shall strike down the crooked ones" (*vṛjinā śiśahi*) later in the text.
What kind of Indra is he?
He is *hirīmaśaḥ*, meaning one with a golden beard.
It belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular formations].
"Hirīmān" means one who has green horses, or one who is green-colored; "arutahanuḥ" means one whose jaw is unimpaired.
Like what?
"Marvelous, not dust.
"Marvelous" is a name for the great;
"dust" refers to the coloring atmosphere (the intermediate space).
It is like the great intermediate space;
just as it cannot be obstructed by anything else, so too is it.
Cut away our crookedness; let the hymns find favor with you.
Without prayer, the sacrifice does not prosper; it thrives only through devotion to you.
O Aśvin, sharpen away our crookedness with your hymn; may we, through the hymn, conquer those who lack it. Without prayer, the sacrifice does not prosper apart from you.
O Indra, "ava-śiśīhi"— sharpen down excessively, that is, destroy— "our" (naḥ) "avṛjinā"— the crooked things, the sins that are to be avoided.
And may we, by means of "ṛcā"— the hymn as our instrument— "anu-ṛcaḥ"— those who do not praise, the non-sacrificing yajamānas— "vanema"— overcome or strike them down.
"He is no Brahman;

yet he is devoid of praise. As for the 'sacrifice'—a sacrifice that is performed separately and serves as the foundation for the ritual—he does not take pleasure in you, he does not serve you."
The meaning is "it does not please.
[The root] *jup* [is used] in the senses of "pleasure" and "service";
[here it is conjugated] with the substitution of the *śap* affix and the *parasmaipada* voice.
When the threefold [sacrificial fire] was established for thee, it supported the sacrifice; together with the people, it brought celestial glory to the one who possesses wealth.
That which was your triple-layered support when the sacrifice stood firm—may that be with us, bringing noble glory together with the living man, like a son to his father.

O Indra, this *aitinī*—that is, the triad (*tritaya*) of the three fires (*tretā*)—is yours; it belongs to you. The ritual action (*kriyā*) possessing that is the *traitigī*. When (*yadā*) it became (*abhūt*) elevated (*ūrdhvā*) and active, as there is no *anighāta* (non-stress) in the case of *yathogāt*, in what place? At the seat (*sadane*) of the sacrifice (*yajñasya*), that is, of the *yāga*; some say "in the *dhurṣu*, the functions of bearing the ritual acts. At that time, it was joined (*sañjūḥ*) with the sacrificer or with the Maruts.

Ashamed, with tawny beard, modest, possessing bay horses, with unbroken jaws, and one whose enemies are not even named—he, Indra, being such as this, attained a wondrous and great splendor; such is the meaning.

With the *ṛc* mantra, may we overcome—meaning slay—the *anṛcas*, those who are without mantras.
When the sacrifice is without *brahman* (i.e., without praise), it does not flourish separately while you take pleasure in it—that is, while you favor it.

That is to say, you make the sacrifice capable of carrying one across sin.

Being pleased, together with—alongside—the living man, the sacrificer, you mount the boat, the means of crossing, which possesses its own glory—that is, the glory that is the means of attaining [bliss] for yourself—and which is the instrument for crossing over.

The sacrificer mounts the very same chariot for the sake of his own crossing; you, as its accomplisher, mount that very chariot along with [the sacrificer].

Like two bamboo poles, like two ancient ones, like two pods; like two friends, like two observers of the cosmic order, like two givers of a hundred boons, like two seekers of truth; like two strengths, high with vigor, established in the heat; like two rams, moving together, worthy of worship, full of vital moisture. 5.

Like two bamboo poles, they are worthy of being approached; like two bulls, they are *pūṣryā*, meaning "belonging to Pūṣan," that is, those whose limbs are nourished. [The root] *puṣ* means "to nourish"; from this, the suffix *aran* is added in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) by the *auṇādika* rule. From that form, the suffix *yat* is applied by the rule "in Vedic [language], in the sense of 'being' (*bhave chandasi*)," which is circumflex-accented (*tisvaritam*). Likewise, *śimbātā*: this is a name for happiness (*sukha*). It means "attained" (*ātam*) or pervaded by the cause of *śimba*, which is the thinning away of sufferings. [The root] *śind* means "to sharpen. From this, the suffix *śimba* is formed by the rule of "excessiveness" (*bāhulakāt*), with the augment *muk* being irregularly inserted. From the root *at* (to extend), the suffix *ghan* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*); the case-ending is replaced by *āl*. Thus, you two are the bringers of happiness. Like two friends (*mitrāiva*): by the word "friend" (*mitra*), Varuṇa is also implied because of their constant association. Like Mitra and Varuṇa, you two are *vṛtā*, meaning "true" or "become reality" (*ṛtau satyabhūtau*), and thus possessors of the vision of ultimate truth. Likewise, *śatarā*: those who possess hundreds—that is, many—chariots and riches are so called. The case-endings are replaced by *ṅā*. Or else: *śatarā* is happiness, as it bestows (*rāti*) a hundred things such as clarity of the senses; you two possess that. *Śātapantā*: those who have sharp praise. *Śāta* means sharp; *panta* is derived from the root *pan* by the rule of "excessiveness" (*tan* by Uṇādi Sūtra 3.86). Or else, *śātapanta*: that which is praised (*panyate*) through *śāta*—the thinning away of sufferings—is *śātapanta*, meaning happiness. [The root] *śo* means "to thin"; the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used. From *pan*, the suffix *tan* is used. By that, you two are possessed of happiness. Although *śimbātā*, *śatarā*, and *śātapantā* are all names for happiness, there is no tautology because the intention is to express the bringing of happiness throughout the three periods of time, and thus the objects differ. Like two prize-winning horses (*vājaiva vājāviva*): just as two horses are full-limbed when urged on by fodder and the like, so too, by reason of *vayas*—that is, food in the form of oblations—you two exist *uccā*, meaning "highly" or "fully" nourished. *Uccā*: from the word *uccais*, the case-ending is replaced by *ṅā*; because it ends in *ṅ*, [the following vowel is strengthened].
