Or rather:
"Like a sṛṇi" means like a widow's sickle.
One [of these] shall remain as a tamed elephant;
the other shall be a source of affliction.
The suffix *nip* is applied by the Uṇādi rule *sarter niṣ kicca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.49; 104). Because the suffix is *kicca*, there is no *guṇa* strengthening.
The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule *kṛdikārād aktinaḥ*.
The form is *sup*. It is a circumflex (*svarita*) accent according to the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ."
They are not like two ears of corn; rather, they are like two *jarbhari*—those who support and establish [all things] in one place.
Likewise, they are *turpharitu*, the two who strike down and slay enemies.
*Jarbhari*.

The suffix *ip* is added to the root *bhṛ*, which has undergone *yaṅ*-luṅ (intensive) reduplication, according to the *uṇādi* rules. The substitution of *ja* for the reduplicated syllable is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) anomaly.
[The roots] *tuph* and *tumph* mean "to injure."

From this [root], the word *turpharītārau* is derived; the substitution of *ha* for *tha* occurs by virtue of its belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* group. Alternatively, by virtue of the general rule (*āhulaka*), the *auṇādika* suffix *arīta* is added and the vowel *u*-substitution (*utva*) takes place.

Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: “The *sṛṇi* is of two kinds: the supporter and the slayer; likewise, the Aśvins are also supporters. *Jarbharī* are the two supporters; *tarkarītū* are the two slayers” (*Nirukta* 13.5), and so forth.
[The word] *netośa* is like that; *nitośati* has the sense of killing.
He who satisfies is Nitośa;
his offspring is Naitośa.
Like those two, they are *turpharī*, slayers of enemies.
The root *tuph* has the meaning of "to injure.
From this root, the suffix *rip* is added according to the *uṇādi* rules, along with the change of the vowel to *u*.
Parpharikā, Parpharikā, you two who rend the enemies.

The root *ji* is used in the sense of "shattering" (*viśaraṇe*). From this root, the form [jiphala] is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātyate*) ending in the suffix *ik*, according to the rule *parpharīkādayaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.20).
Or rather,
they are the two who fulfill the desires of their worshippers by bestowing wealth and other gifts.
The root *pṛ* is used in the senses of "protecting" (*pālanā*) and "filling" (*pūraṇa*).
From this root, with the suffix *īkan*, everything is irregularly formed (*nipātyate*) as before;
or alternatively, it is derived from the root *karvati* in the sense of "filling."
Like one striving for water;
"udanya" means that which exists in water.
By the rule *padanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.63) and others, the substitution of *udañc-* occurs even in words such as *āśāprabhṛti*.
In that regard, they were as stainless as a jewel when it has been produced; the meaning is that they were endowed with splendor.
The two Germans were victorious.
The suffix *manin* is applied to the root *jan* according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well";
the absence of vowel lengthening is Vedic.
O you two who are intoxicated by an abundance of vigor, or rather, worthy of praise—

those two Aśvins endowed with the previously mentioned qualities— you two must make my *jarāyu*, that is, my body born from a womb and therefore subject to death (*marāyu*), free from decay (*ajara*) and devoid of the nature of mortality.
In the word *ajara-maram-itramṛtaḥ*, the initial syllable of the word *jara* following the negative particle *nañ* is udātta.
You worship the seer as a lover of the mortal; O fierce ones, you carry us across toward our goals.
O Rbhus, you have fashioned the donkey for the lord, and the swift-darting one has destroyed the obstacles to wealth.
1. Of him who stands between the two wives, you two are the fulfillers of his desire. 2. There is no "afterbirth" (ajarāyu) for him.

Like two sacrificial offerings, like a moving sound, like a lover, like a mortal, like flowing water—among our goals, you two, O fierce ones, cross over. Like the Rbhus, like the wind, like a sharp-edged weapon, like a sharp-edged weapon, he brings abundance; like the wind, he bestows and dwells among riches. 7.
Those two fierce ones, with their terrifying splendor aroused, are like two Aśvins; they are like two Pajñas, having acquired strength, standing like two heroes—
or rather, like two Pajñas.
‘O you two who overcome! Standing as if capable of overcoming with your two feet,

do you two drive away my body— which is subject to decay (*jāra*), which is characterized by aging (*jarā*), and for that very reason is mortal (*marāyu*)— from these things to be traversed, things to be crossed over, such as calamities and the like, just as one drives away a calf.
This is a name for water;
you cross over like water, meaning you cause others to cross over completely.
The root *tṛ* is used in the sense of crossing over (*plu-vandarataraṇayoḥ*).
From its *luṅ* form, in the present tense (*laṭ*), the augment *iṭ* is applied because the suffix *thas* is treated as *ārdhadhātuka* by the rule *chandasyubhayathā*.
The lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *vṛṇo vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.38).
Like the Ṛbhus—
here the dual number is used because of the similarity to the illustrative example—

the Ṛbhus, as it were, are those who, like a chariot fashioned by themselves that has arrived, are the two who will sharpen (khara-jrā), that is, the two who will purify the sharp (kharam) [intellect].
The meaning is that they possess exceedingly pure power.
The root *dum* means "to purify.
From this root, the suffix *rap* is added according to the rules of the *auṇādika* [section].
O you two, such as you are, swift as the wind and exceedingly rapid in movement, the chariot given by the Ṛbhus has reached you; it has arrived.
The root *ā-plu* means "to pervade.
In the *luṅ* tense, because it belongs to the *ludīc* class, *cli* is replaced by *aṅ*.
That chariot, like Vāyu—meaning like the wind—parpharat; that is, it filled [the space] everywhere.
The meaning is that it pervaded everywhere.
The root *pṛ* means "to fill.
From this, in the *leṭ* [subjunctive] mood, the *śap* [present tense marker] is elided by the rule "there is frequent elision (*bahulam*) in the Veda" (*chandasi*).
There is the augment *ruk* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) and the elision of the semivowel (*valopa*).
The augment *aṭ* is applied by the rule "leṭo 'ḍāṭau."
Then that chariot, ruling over riches—that is, wealth—brought treasures from the enemies.
The root *kṣi* is used in the senses of dwelling and going;
from this root, with the causative (*ṇic*) implied within it, the augment *āṭ* is applied in the *leṭ* mood.
Or rather:
the root *kṣi* has the sense of "envy";
he rules over riches.
The state of being unaccented (anudātta) is a Vedic peculiarity.
Like warm milk, she has won sweetness for her belly; like fortune, she is a winner of wealth, a destroyer of enemies.
Like two sons, she moves about with a glittering girdle; like a woman, she goes to meet her lover.

Like two heated cauldrons, honey is in his belly; like two winnowing baskets, they are the protectors in fortune. Like two wings, they move about, bright-shining, mind-swift, and human-like, as if hastening. 8.

Like two *gharma* vessels, like two great *mahāvīra* ladles, you are the possessors (*saneru*) of the honey within your own bellies—*madhunaḥ* [is used] with the genitive case-ending elided (*luk*). [The root] *vana-paṇa* means "to share"; from this, the *erup* suffix is added by the *auṇādika* rules. You are the protectors (*avitā*) of fortune (*bhaga*); *bhaga* means wealth; you are intent on its preservation. [The word *avatī* is derived from] the root *ava* with the suffix *ka* in the sense of state (*bhāve*). By the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, before a *kṛt* suffix, there is diversely (*bahulam*) [no elision]," there is no elision even in a *bahuvrīhi*. Alternatively, the *sup* case-ending of the form *avati* ending in *tṛc* is replaced by *ḍā*; the accent, however, is Vedic (*chāndasa*). You are *aram*, sufficient; *turpharī*, destroyers of enemies; therefore, you are *phārivā*. *Phāri* means a weapon; you are the possessors of them. [The root] *sphurati* has the meaning of killing; from this, the causative (*ṇic*) is applied, and by the rule "for *ci*, *sphur*, and *ṇau*" (Pāṇini 6.1.54), there is *ātva* (vowel lengthening). From that, the suffix *ip* is added, and the elision of the letter *s* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). By the rule "in the Veda, *ivanip* and *vanip*," the possessive suffix *vanip* is added. The *sup* case-ending is replaced by *ḍā*. Like two wings (*patra*) of a bird, you are *cacarā*, moving about; *candranirṇij*—*nirṇij* is a name for form. The *sup* case-ending is elided. You are those whose forms are like the moon (*candranirṇijau*), or rather, you are those whose form (*rūpa*) is moon-like (*candra*), i.e., pleasing (*āhlādaka*). You are *manaṛṅgā*, those whose adornment (*prasādhana*) is performed by the mind (*manas*); the root *ṛñjati* has the meaning of adorning; from this, the suffix *ghañ* is added in the sense of state. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. Like those who are *mananyā*, i.e., *mananyau*—those who are good (*sādhu*) at thinking, meaning they are worthy of praise. From the word *manana*, the suffix *yat* is added by the rule "good in that" (*tatra sādhuḥ*). It is circumflex-accented (*svarita*). Like such ones, you are *jagmī*, those whose nature is to come toward the sacrifice. From the root *gam*, the suffix *kin* is added by the rule "ā-gam-han... (Pāṇini 3.2.171).
Like two great ones, you find a firm footing in the depths; like those who know the way, you provide a ford for us to cross.
Like two ears, you surely heed our command; like two horses, O Maruts, grant us wondrous wealth.

Like two great ones in the depths, you find a firm footing like feet in shallow water; like ears following a command, you indeed remember; like two sharers, grant us a wondrous portion, even for the small child. 9.

"Like two great ones," "like two tall men," as it were—"in the depths," that is, in the unfathomable waters, you two find a firm foundation; likewise, in the deeps, the profound, and inaccessible places, you two "know," that is, you have attained a stable footing.
"Like two feet"—the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive—just as one crosses with two feet.

Just as the feet of a man crossing [the water] find a firm footing in shallow water, so may you two find and know a firm footing in these waters for us to cross. [The root] *vid* means "to know"; the suffix is *leṭ*, with the augment added.

"Just as the ears perceive the sound uttered [by others], so may you two remember—that is, recognize as favorable—the person who offers praise to you, O Āśus, the controllers. The suffix *leṭ* is used for the root *smṛ*, and there is an augment (*āgamah*).
Due to the presence of the particle *hi*, there is no suppression of the accent (*anighātaḥ*).
By the rule *adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.52), the word *śāsuḥ* takes the genitive case.

"Like two portions (*aṃśau*)"—that is, like two constituent parts—they partake of that sacrifice which possesses such parts; thus, O you two, "you partake of" (*bhajataḥ*), meaning you take refuge in, our "wonderful" (*citram*), that is, praiseworthy "labor" (*amaḥ*) or ritual action.
*Amas*:

from the root *ā-plu* in the sense of "pervasion" (*vyāptau*), the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of the object (*karma*) by the rule *hasvo nuḍ ca vā* (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.207); consequently, there is shortening of the vowel and the augment *nuṭ*.
That which is unaccented is acutely accented at its beginning.
Like two bees in a honeycomb, like two wasps in a nest with downward-opening openings;
like two miserly ones perspiring from toil, you two gather strength like a skin full of vigor from a field of good pasture.

Like two *ārañjaras*, like bees (*sāraghā*) [you] send forth honey; like two [bees] at a low-opening hive, like two laborers (*kīnārau*) sweating, you both cause sweat to flow; like two emaciated cows (*kṣāme*) with vigor, you come together at the place of good pasture. *Ārañjarā-iva*: From the root *gṛ* "to sound," in the sense of action, the suffix *ap* is added (by *ṛdorap*). *Aram* means sufficient, and *garaḥ* is a name for sound. Those related to that [sound]—the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *tasyedam* ("belonging to that")—are those possessing sound, like two intelligent ones. Just as [bees] send forth honey-water, so do you two "send forth" (*erayethe*), i.e., you impel. From the root *īra* "to impel," belonging to the cur-class (*caurādika*). *Sāraghā-iva*: Like two bees (*saraghā*). *Saraghā* is a honey-bee. *Sāraghā* is derived from *saraghā* with the suffix *aṇ* (by Pāṇini 5.4.38, because it belongs to the *prajñādi* group). Just as they send forth honey in a flower with a downward opening (*nīcīnabāre*), so do you two pour milk into the "cow"—that is, the udder—with its downward opening (*nīcīnabāre*). *Kīnārau-iva*: Like two wretched men (*kīnārau*), who are sweating (*svidamānau*), so do you two "causing sweat to flow" (*āsisvidānā*), i.e., causing the water of sweat to flow all around and sprinkling it. From the root *svid* "to ooze from the limbs," which is *anudātta*; in the Vedic *liṭ* tense, there is the substitution of *kānac*. *Kṣāme-iva*: From the roots *kṣai*, *jai*, or *pai* meaning "to perish," the suffix *manin* is added; the short vowel is a Vedic usage. A "wasted cow" (*kṣāmā*) is one that, while eating "good pasture" (*suyavasāt*)—from the root *ad* with the suffix *kvip*—eating excellent grass and fodder, comes together in the form of milk. Just as she does, so do you two "come together" (*saṃcayethe*) with "vigor" (*ūrjā*), i.e., with food in the form of oblation. From the root *vac* "to come together."

May we succeed; may we win the prize. O you two who are borne on a good chariot, come here with your sacred hymns! Like ripe honey within the cows, may the work of the Aśvins reach us. May they fulfill our desire.

May it prosper! May we win the hymn of praise; may we win the prize! O Aśvins, come hither with your beautiful chariot to our sacred words, like glory itself. Like ripe honey within the cows, Bhūtāṃśa has fulfilled the work of the Aśvins. 11.

1. The word *gambhareṣu* is absent in manuscripts *ta*, *bha*, and *a*. 2. The word *vidāthaḥ* is absent in manuscripts *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, and *a*. 3. In manuscripts *ga*, *ta*, *4*, *5*, and *yathā*, the two parts of the sacrifice [are mentioned]. 4. In manuscripts *ta*, *bha*, and *tathā*:
"O Aśvins, may we prosper—that is, may we cause to succeed and increase—the *stoma* consisting of the *trivṛt*, *pañcadaśa*, and other [forms]."
The root *ṛdh* means "to increase.
From this root, in the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*), the *yāsuṭ* suffix is marked as *kit* by the rule *kidāśiṣi*.
May we win—that is, may we offer—to you two the *vāja*, food characterized by the oblation.
‘paṇu dāne’:
beginning with *tāna*,
it is the optative (*vidhiliṅ*).
There is no loss of accent (anighāta) because it constitutes a different sentence.

Therefore, you two, being with your chariot— possessing a chariot and sharing the same chariot— having thus mounted the chariot, come here to this ritual and approach our mantra, that which is to be meditated upon, our hymn of praise. O Gopavantau, [come] like honeyed fame, [fame] that is situated in the udder of the cow, matured, and therefore sweet.
*Yaśas* is a name for food;
*naśa* has the sense of "destruction";
[and] *kṣīra-ājya*.
The connection is that food, being brought down upon the Great Hero who is characterized by the *dilakṣaṇa*, arrives.
In this manner, the portion of the elements—the seer named thus—fulfilled (*āprāḥ*) the desire (*kāma*) of the Aśvins with his own hymns;
that is to say, he made it complete.
The root *prā* means "to fill. It belongs to the second class (*adādika*). By way of transposition (*vyatyaya*), the middle voice form is used.
In this hymn to the Aśvins, we have merely indicated all the word-derivations;
in this manner, the intellect should be made to blossom through the specific meanings derived from the Nirukta, grammar, and other sciences.
‘Āviḥ’ is the eighth hymn, consisting of eleven verses.
The seer is Divya by name, an Aṅgiras;
or else Dakṣiṇā, the daughter of Prajāpati, is the female seer.
The fourth verse, “śatadhāram vāyum,” is in the Jagatī meter; the remaining ten are Triṣṭubh verses.
By means of this hymn, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) being given to the officiating priests, or the sacrificers who give them, are praised.
Therefore, that [sacrificial fee] itself is the deity.

Likewise, it is stated in the Cāturmāsya [Kalpa]: "The divine [sacrifice] is manifest; the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) belongs to Prajāpati; having given the sacrificial fee, the fourth [verse] is a Jagatī at Dāntavāstu.
Thus ends the application (viniyoga).

The great bounty of these [sacrificers] has become manifest; every living being has been released from darkness. The great light given by the Fathers has arrived; the broad path of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) has been seen. It has become manifest—great, the bounty of these [sacrificers]. Every living being has been released forth from darkness. The great light, given by the Fathers, has come hither. The broad path of the sacrificial fee has been seen.
This hymn is either a praise of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) or of those who give it.

The sacrificial fee, however, is an auxiliary element of the sacrifice; yet the sacrifice is not performed in the evening, as is heard in such passages as: “The gods do not favor what is offered in the evening” (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 5.77.2).
Therefore, the day alone must be observed. And since the day begins with the rising of the sun, the rising of the sun is mentioned at the beginning of the hymn. [This applies] to Māgha.
Maghavendra refers to Indra and Sūrya; for it is recorded in tradition that "in the month of Caitra, Indra [presides] over those two.
The term denotes a relationship with him.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule *tasyedam*.
Regarding the rule *saṃprasāraṇam abhihitam* (Pāṇini 6.1.133), which prescribes vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) before a suffix that is not a *taddhita*,
since all grammatical rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandas*), vocalization occurs here even before this *taddhita* suffix.
The great, innate majesty of Indra, whose essence is the sun, manifested for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice of these sacrificers;
it became clearly revealed and fully illuminated.
Therein, the entire universe—the whole world consisting of both the stationary and the moving—was liberated and released from darkness.
The form [of the verb] *muñcateḥ* is in the passive voice (*ciṇ*).

Immediately thereafter, that great light called the Sun—which was given by the Pitṛs, that is, by the divine ancestors, for our arrival at the oblations—has come, or is coming. Afterwards, the broad and great path belonging to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), which is an integral part of the sacrifice, has been seen by all the sacrificers.
The meaning is that they all, having performed the sacrifice, gave sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij).

High in heaven have those who give sacrificial fees taken their stand; those who give horses dwell together with the sun. Those who give gold partake in immortality; those who give garments shall prolong their life, O Soma.
1. In the manuscripts *ta* and *bha*, [the word] *maghonaḥ* is present; in *indraḥ*, it is absent. 2.
In manuscript *bha*, the phrase “*niramoci nirmuktam abhūt*” (it was released, it became liberated) is absent; in *ta* 4.5, it is stated that “by him it was liberated.
3. In manuscript *bha*, the phrase “*muñcateḥ ... tat*” (of the root *muc*, ... that) is absent.

"Those possessing sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇāvantaḥ*)—that is, those sacrificers who have given the sacrificial fee as a thing to be bestowed—stand high in the sky, the heavenly world, situated in lofty places.
Having spoken in general terms, he now states the specific fruit for specific types of givers:
"Those sacrificers who are givers of horses (*aśvadāḥ*) stand together with Sūrya, the Sun, the impeller of every individual's own action."
Those who are "givers of gold"—that is, givers of gold—“they partake of immortality,” meaning the state of being immortal or divinity;
for it is recorded in scripture: “Gold, indeed, is immortality” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.2.7.2).
Likewise, because of the scriptural statement, "The garment is indeed gentle" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.5), Soma himself is addressed.

O Soma, those who are the "givers of garments"—that is, givers of clothes belonging to you as their deity—stand together with you; this is the ellipsis. All these "extend," that is, they increase, "life," meaning the span of existence.
The root *tṛ* preceded by *pra* has the meaning of "increase."
The divine sacrificial gift is for the performers of meritorious works and the worship of the gods; for those who withhold their gifts do not bestow them.
But now, O men, those who possess great wealth bestow gifts upon all sides out of fear of blame.

The divine fulfillment is the sacrificial fee; it is the worship of the gods. Not at all from enemies—for they do not give—do men fulfill their purpose, being those who withhold the sacrificial fee out of fear of reproach; rather, the great ones give abundantly.
Divine means belonging to the gods.
The suffix *añ* is applied according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 4.1.85 (*devādyajñau*).
Such a *pūrtiḥ* (fulfillment) is protective; the *devayajyā* (sacrifice to the gods) is that which is accomplished by it.
The word *niṣṭakya* is derived as an irregular formation (*nipātita*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.123: "In the Vedic language, [the suffix -ya is added after the root tak with the prefix nis]."
The sacrifice to the gods;
its constituent part is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), which does not belong to those who obstruct the way.
From the root *ṛ* in the sense of "to go," the suffix *i* is applied according to *Uṇādi Sūtra* 4.138: *aca iḥ*.
It should not be offered to those who go in a contemptible manner;
it does not belong to these [deities].
Or rather:
The fulfillment belonging to the gods—that which fills [them] when mixed with hymns—such a sacrifice to the gods and the sacrificial fee do not belong to them. The reason for this is stated:
for indeed, because they are "goers in a base manner" (kutsita-gantāraḥ), they "do not satisfy" (na hi pṛṇanti) the gods by mixing [the offering] with hymns; they do not please them.
‘*Pṛṇa* means “to satisfy.
It belongs to the *tudādi* class. *Atha* (then) is used in the sense of a question.’
How does the performance of sacrifices to the gods and so forth come about for those who sacrifice?
It is said:

"The *naras* (leaders) are the leaders of rituals; therefore, they are *prayatadakṣiṇāsas*, those who have bestowed sacrificial fees (*dattadakṣiṇāḥ*). Many such sacrificers [act] out of fear of blame."
The word *gahya* is established as a nipātana (irregular formation) by means of the suffix *yat*, according to the rule *avadya-paṇya-varṇya-gahya-yāpyaṃ kutsite* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.101).
Out of fear of evil.
Indeed, misfortunes arise from the non-performance of prescribed duties;
therefore, out of fear of that, they "satisfy" (pṛṇanti), that is, they please the gods.
Therefore, the meaning is that for the sacrificers, it becomes the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sacrifice of protecting the gods.
They behold the oblation—the hundred-streamed wind, the sun, the light-finder, the one who watches over men.
Those who satisfy and bestow gifts at the assembly milk the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) that has seven mothers.

The hundred-streamed wind, the light-finding sun—those who behold men look toward the oblation; those who satisfy and bestow gifts in the assembly, they milk the sacrificial fee that has seven mothers. 4.

"Those sacrificers behold—that is, they perceive and know—the oblation (*havis*) for the sake of these two: the wind named *śatadhāra* (having a hundred streams) which is endowed with many streams, the *svarvid* (attainer of heaven or knower of all), and the *arka* (the sun, worthy of worship); as well as for the other gods such as Indra, who are *nṛcakṣas* (beholders of men).
[The form *caṣṭe* is the present indicative of the root *cakṣ*]."
Furthermore, [the word] "in the confluence" (*saṃgame*) is for the purpose of performing the ritual action. 1.
*ta-bha* lacks "givers of gold" (*hiraṇyadāḥ*). 2. *ta-bha-mu* reads *taddevatya*. 3. *ta-bha1.2.4.8* means "it comes into being. 4. *ta-bha* lacks "they know" (*jānanti*).
In this context, "saṃgama" refers to the gathering of the officiating priests (ṛtvij).

By the rule "grah-vraśca-bhrasj-a-sṛ-j-mṛ-j-yaja-rāja-bhrāja-ccha-śāṃ ṣaḥ," the letter *ṣ* is substituted [for the final consonant] when the suffix *ap* follows in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*).
Thus, the initial vowel [of the word becomes udātta].
In that sacrifice, those who are the sacrificers satisfy [the gods] with hymns of praise (*stuti*) and please them;
and those who present the oblations (*havis*) to those gods—
in both cases, there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*) due to their connection.
*V* te *v* saptamātaram:
she in whom there are seven sacrificial terminuses (*saṃsthā*), such as the Agniṣṭoma and others, which are like seven mothers; or alternatively: [she who has seven mothers].
There are seven mothers who are the fashioners and performers of rituals, namely the Hotṛ and the other priests;
they milk such a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the officiating priests.
The possessor of sacrificial fees comes first when summoned; the possessor of sacrificial fees goes at the head as the village leader.
Him alone I consider the lord of people who was the first to bestow the sacrificial fee.

The first one who is invited comes bringing sacrificial gifts; the leader of the village comes bringing sacrificial gifts. Him indeed I consider the lord of men among people, who was the first to bring forth the sacrificial gift. 5.

Summoned by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) who possesses the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇāvān*) goes as the first, being the foremost of all; he goes everywhere. Likewise, the village leader (*grāmaṇī*), the guide of the villages and their benefactor through his wealth, being one who possesses the sacrificial fee, goes at the head; he goes before everyone else.
I consider that very king to be a protector; I, a seer (*ṛṣi*), understand him as the first who has caused the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of people to come to him—that is, he causes it to arrive.
The root *vī* is used in the sense of motion and so forth;
this is its form in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*).
I consider him to be a king;
or rather,
"of the people" is the completion of the preceding sentence.
Among all people, I consider him alone to be the lord of men.

They call him alone the seer, him the Brahman, the sacrifice, the singer of Sāmans, and the reciter of hymns; he knows the three bodies of the pure one, he who was the first to succeed through the sacrificial fee.

They call that very seer "Om," they call him Brahmā, the one who knows the sacrifice, the singer of the Sāman, and the reciter of the Uktha; he knows the three bodies of the Radiant One, he who was the first to succeed through the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). 6.
They call him alone the giver of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the seer (*ṛṣi*) who perceives objects beyond the senses— or rather, they call him a seer because of his performance of virtuous deeds—
and likewise, they call him alone the Brahman; moreover, they call him alone the lord of sacrifice (*yajñanya*).
The root *ṇīñ* is used in the sense of "leading" (*prāpaṇe*).
[From this,] the suffix *kip* is applied;
then, by the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ*, the vowel *am* is substituted.
The state of being svarita.
They call him the leader of the sacrifice, the Adhvaryu; they call him the Sāman-singer, the singer of the Sāmans; likewise, the reciter of the Ukthas.
The root *śaṃs* means "to praise.
[The suffix] *kip* [is applied].
In the *saṃhitā*, the long vowel is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
They call him the Hotṛ, the reciter of the *uktha* hymns among the liturgical recitations (*śastra*).

Because he accepts that ritual action through the giving of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), he is the giver; he knows the three bodies—the three forms consisting of lightning, the sun, and the self—of the radiant, shining light.
Or rather:
He knows the three bodies of Śukra, which consist of the Āhavanīya fire and the others;
he is the first, the principal person who has propitiated [the gods] through the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), that is, who has honored the officiating priests and others.
The root *rādh* means "to succeed. This is the form in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). It takes the accent of the *liṭ* suffix.
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) gives the horse; the sacrificial fee gives the cow; the sacrificial fee gives the moon as well as the gold.
The sacrificial fee wins the food which is our very self; the wise man makes the sacrificial fee his armor.

The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is the horse; the sacrificial fee is the cow. He gives the sacrificial fee; the sacrificial fee is the silver and also the gold. The sacrificial fee wins food, which is our very self. Knowing [this], he makes the sacrificial fee his armor. //7//
1. The person [consists of] the *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *bha*, *ma*, *ya*, and *ra* phonemes.
2. The *rāhavanīya* fire-altars consist of the *ta*, *bha*, *ma*, and *ya* phonemes;
he gives a horse that has the nature of those [phonemes] as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Thus he gives a cow;
thus he gives the moon and the heavenly world;
and furthermore, whatever gold and silver there is.
Because of the scriptural tradition stating, "silver and gold" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.1,
2), she gives that;
moreover, she wins— that is, she gives— a horse.
The root *van* here has the sense of "giving.

Therefore, our own self (*ātman*), knowing it to be a *varman*—just as one knows armor (*kavaca*) to be that which wards off weapons by warding off arrows—performs the *dakṣiṇā*, being disposed toward the giving of horses and other gifts;
he bestows it upon the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
The liberal patrons do not perish for their sake; they do not come to ruin, nor do they suffer distress.
Whatever this entire world is, even unto heaven—all this he gives to the liberal patrons.

No; the Bhojas do not go to destruction; they do not perish, nor do they suffer distress. Indeed, the Bhojas—this entire world—unite for their own enjoyment and for the sake of the giver, bringing together the swift-moving horse;
the attendants prepare it perfectly.
The root *mṛj* means "purification" and "adornment. Likewise, the word *kanyā*:
here, by virtue of its proximity to the state of being a maiden (*kanyātva*), fresh youth is indicated.
A woman who is in the bloom of youth, beautiful, and radiant with the excellence of her bodily limbs as well as the splendor of her garments and ornaments, sits for that Bhoja, the giver;
likewise, the house or dwelling of Bhoja, the giver, becomes a source of delight to the heart.
Of what sort is it?

Like a lotus pond— a *puṣkariṇī* being a lake so called because it possesses *puṣkaras*, which are lotuses— just as such a pond is adorned with lotuses and the like, so too is this [place] "adorned," meaning embellished with canopies and other decorations.
In the case of the root *kṛ* preceded by *pari*, when it has the sense of "adornment" (*bhūṣaṇa*), there is the augment *suṭ* in a *saṃhitā* context.

By the rule "after *pari*, *ni*, and *vi*," there is the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in *suṭ*. By the rule "an immediate preceding *gati* [is unaccented]," the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the *gati* remains.
Likewise, in the case of *devamānā*,
the vowel *ā* is the substitute for the nominative singular ending according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
His dwelling becomes wonderful and captivating, like the celestial abode of the gods and like the path traveled by the gods.
Well-yoked horses carry the liberal patron; the well-rolling chariot of the Dakṣiṇā moves forward.
O gods, protect the liberal patron in battles; the liberal patron is the conqueror of enemies in the encounters.
The horses carry the Bhoja; the well-rolling chariot of Supvāhi moves along. O gods, protect the Bhoja in the battles; the Bhoja is the conqueror of enemies in the ranks of combat. 11.

*supvāhaḥ*. From the root *vah* (to carry), the suffix *pivap* is applied according to the rule *vahaśca*. [The word means] horses capable of carrying well. They carry the *bhoja*, the giver, to the destination; they cause him to reach the intended place. Then, the chariot of the *dakṣiṇā*-giver, the sacrificer—whose wheels and other parts turn excellently (*suvṛt*)—along with the horses and other equipment, rolls forward. Now, [the following is] in the direct address: O *devāsaḥ*, O gods, Indra and the others, protect the *bhoja*, the giver, in the *bhareṣu*. [The word *bhara*] refers to sacrifices (*yajña*), because they are "borne" (*bhriyante*) or "resorted to" (*āhriyante*) in the form of the Āhavanīya fire and so on. [Alternatively, from the root *bhṛ* in the sense of "battle"]: it is called *bhara* because warriors "bear" (*bhṛṇanti*) or "confront" (*bhartsayanti*) [the enemy] therein; thus, *bhara* refers to battles. In those [battles], protect the *bhoja*, the giver. Then, protected by you, the *bhoja*—being one who nourishes (*bhojayitā*) people through the giving of wealth and such—becomes a victor (*jetā*), one whose nature is victory, in the *samīkeṣu*, the battles. [From the root] *ji* (to conquer); the suffix *tṛn* is used here in the sense of habit (*tācchīlika*). For this very reason, by the rule *na lokāvyaya*, there is a prohibition of the genitive case for the word *śatru*. || 4 ||

The ninth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "kimicchantī," is in the Triṣṭubh meter. Bṛhaspati, the domestic priest of Indra, dispatched a divine dog named Saramā to search for the cattle that had been hidden in a cave by the soldiers of the Asura named Vala, who were known as the Paṇis. Having crossed a great river and reached the city of Vala, she found those cows led into a secret place.
Now, in the meantime, the Paṇis, learning of this occurrence, engaged in conversation with her in order to win her over as a friend.
Therein, the first, third, and so forth—the odd-numbered verses—are the words of the Paṇis;
here those seers are the Ṛṣis, and Saramā is the deity.
The second, fourth, and so on, up to the eleventh, which are the odd-numbered verses, are the six statements of Saramā.
Therefore, in these, the Paṇis are the deities.

Thus it has been enumerated: "Seeking what? Saramā, the divine dog sent by Indra, was searching for the cows hidden by the Asura Paṇis; the Paṇis, desiring friendship, spoke with the uneven [verses]; she, desiring those [cows], rejects them with the even [verses]."
The application has been explained.
Seeking what has Saramā come here, having traveled a long distance on the path far away? What was your mission for us, and what was your purpose? How did you cross the waters of the Rasā?

Seeking what has Saramā come hither? For the road is far and leads to distant realms. What is our mission? What was your purpose? How did you cross the waters of the Rasā? 1. What did you desire that Saramā came hither? For the path is far and leads to distant regions. What is our commission? What was your intent toward us? How did you cross the waters of the Rasā?
Seeing Saramā approaching, the Paṇis say:
"Saramā"—she who is so named because of her habit of wandering—this divine dog, desiring what, seeking what, has reached (pra ānaṭ) this place of ours?
The root *naś* preceded by the prefix *ā*:
1. ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bhara2.5-hiyata;
2. ta-bha-mu—“*kimicchantī*” is not present.
The root *vyas* takes the suffix *karma*.
In its *luṅ* (aorist) form, there is elision (*luk*) of *cli* by the rule "in a mantra, *ghas*" etc.;
furthermore, the augment *āṭ* is applied because [the rule] "it is seen even in the Veda" applies.

"By *parācaiḥ*—those goings which are turned away (*parāṅmukha*), devoid of return; by these, [the path] is 'difficult to traverse' (*jaguriḥ*), meaning it has a high pitch (*udvarṇa*). The sense is that it cannot be traversed even with great effort."
The root *gṛ* is used in the sense of "swallowing. The suffix *kin* is applied according to the rule beginning with *āhagamahana* (Pāṇini 3.2.171).
The substitution of *u* for *ṛ* occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.103).
Such is this path; for it is indeed not far away, though it is remote.
Or rather, she who goes with her eyes turned away—meaning she has gone far—having failed to look at the rear portion of the path, reaches this place.
"This path is far; it cannot be traveled at will.
Therefore, we ask her:
O Saramā, what is our destination like?"
What benefit is there for us?
What object desired by you has been placed within us?
Or rather:
What meaning has gone into us?
It is a form derived from the roots *dhā* (to place) or *hi* (to impel) with the suffix *ktin*.
"As you were coming, what kind of *paritakmyā*—a night—was it?"
Or rather,
*takit* means "having gone.
Of what nature was the *paritakana*— the going around or the moving about?

"And how did you cross the waters—the waters of the river Rasā, which resounds through the atmosphere and extends for a hundred *yojanas*? Tell this. In this regard, the *Nirukta* passage beginning with 'What desiring did Saramā reach here? (Nirukta 11.25) should be consulted."
Sent as Indra’s messenger, I wander about, seeking your great treasures, O Paṇis.
Out of fear, I leaped over that [obstacle]; I crossed the waters of the Rasā river.
As Indra’s messenger, sent forth, I wander about, seeking your great treasures, O Paṇis. With a leap over the danger, he protected us; thus did I cross the waters of the Rasā. 2.

With this [verse], Saramā replied to them: "O Paṇis"—the Asuras so named—"I am the messenger of Indra. The form *dūtīḥ* is the nominative singular; the *su* suffix is Vedic (according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*).
"I, being sent by him alone, wander about;
I come to your place. For what purpose?"
Desiring—that is, longing for—your great treasures (*mahaḥ nidhīn*), the treasures of Bṛhaspati's cow established upon your mountain, I wander.
Furthermore, [I am] "one who leaps over" (*atiṣkadaḥ*).
The root *skand* means "to go" and "to dry up."
The suffix *kip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
That river water was "our" (*naḥ*)— the plural being used for honor— due to the fear (*bhayasā*) born from the transgression (*atiṣkandanāt*) or overstepping [of the boundary].
He protected me;
in that manner, I crossed over the waters, the waters of the river Rasā.
What kind of man is he, O Saramā, what is his appearance, for whom you have come as a messenger from afar?
Come hither; let us speak together, and then he shall become the lord of our cattle.

What kind of Indra is he, O Saramā? What is his appearance, he for whose messenger you have come from afar? Let him also come here; we shall make him our friend. Then the Lord of Cattle will become ours. 3.

Their speech is as follows: "O Saramā, what is your master like? How great is his prowess? What is he like? What is his gaze like? How large is his army, which is the very embodiment of his gaze? You, who are his messenger, have come from afar—'parākāt' meaning from a very great distance—to this place of ours. Having spoken thus to her, they now say to one another: "Let this Saramā come here; let her arrive" (the augment *āṭ* is added to the root *gam*). "May he be the master"—let him indeed be the master. For he is not the master of a single cow, but rather the master of many cows. By the words *vṛtha* and *vṛtti*, both his lordship and his abundance are intended to be expressed.

1. *ga-ta-bha-mu-vā* | 2. *ga-saramā pra ūco*; *ta-bha-mu-sarametyūce*. "I do not know that deceiver who, as a messenger, has sped this far from afar. Deep-flowing rivers do not seize him; O Paṇis, you shall lie dead, abandoned by Indra. (4) I do not know that deceiver who, as a messenger, has sped this far from afar. Deep-flowing rivers do not seize him; O Paṇis, you shall lie dead, abandoned by Indra. (4)

Saramā speaks: "O Paṇis! I do not know—that is, I am not aware—of that Indra as one who is *dabhya*, meaning 'to be harmed. [The suffix] *yat* is used after the root *dabh*. How so? That Indra is *dabhat*; he harms, indeed he destroys all people. This is the form of the root *dabh* in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood; because there is a syntactic break (*vākya-bheda*), there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*). I am his messenger (*dūtī*); I have come from *parākāt*, from a very distant place, to this place of yours. He states the reason why Indra is not to be harmed: "The flowing ones. *Sravaḥ* means 'flowing'; they act like that, hence *sravataḥ*. [The suffix] *kvip* is used in the sense of habitual action; there is the augment *tug*; this is the form in the nominative plural (*jasi*). Those who are habitually flowing—the deep rivers—they do not seize him, they do not enclose him, they do not cover him, nor do they reveal him. By whose greatness we have crossed the ocean, therefore they make him manifest with the words "you are in our hands" (*aṃhisthaḥ*). [The root] *guh* is in the sense of 'concealing' (*saṃvaraṇe*); it belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*. Therefore, O Paṇis, you shall lie down, being abandoned by Indra of such prowess. [The root] *śīṅ* is in the sense of 'sleeping. Because of the rule 'in the Veda there is diversity,' there is no elision of the *śap* suffix."

These, O Saramā, are the cows which you sought, flying about to the ends of heaven, O fortunate one. Who, being unarmed, could release them to you? Moreover, our weapons are sharp. imāḥ | gāvaḥ | sarame | yāḥ | aicchaḥ | pari | divaḥ | antān | subhage | patantī | kaḥ | te | enāḥ | arbha | sṛjāt | ayudhvī | uta | asmākam | āyudhā | santi | tigmā ||5||
The enraged Paṇayas replied:

"O fortunate one, O Saramā, you who possess excellent good fortune, where are you going, flying about to the very ends—the boundaries—of heaven, the celestial world? What do you intend to do with these limbs of yours? Thus they spoke, as she was seen moving about with her own visible limbs. This is the meaning.
You desired those cows; you long for them. Those cows are yours by right. Who, being unopposed—being without a rival—would release them? He would release them from this mountain;
he would let them go forth.
The form *sṛje* is the present optative (*leṭ*).
*Ayudhvī*: from the root *yudh*, the suffix *kvap* is applied, and it is listed as an irregularly formed word (*nipātita*) by the rule "and *snātvā* etc. (Pāṇini 7.1.49).
Due to being a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), there is no substitution of *laya* for the final vowel;
the negative particle (*nañ*) retains its original accent (*prakṛti-svara*). Furthermore, we possess sharp weapons—indeed, our weapons are keen.
Therefore, who indeed can take away the cows without us engaging in battle?

O Paṇis, let your words be powerless; let your bodies be devoid of strength, O evil ones! Let your path be impassable for you to travel; may Bṛhaspati not show mercy to either of you. 6. O Paṇis, let your words be powerless; let your bodies be devoid of strength, O evil ones! Let your path be impassable for you to travel; may Bṛhaspati not show mercy to either of you. 6.
She spoke to them: "O Paṇis, your previously uttered words are *asenyāḥ*— that is,
they are not fit for an army (*asenya*)."
From the word *senā*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "one who deserves that" by the rule *chandasi ca*;
there is a compound with the negative particle *nañ*;
and the final syllable of the second member is acute-accented according to the rule *yayatoścātaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.156).
Likewise, O slender one, may your bodies not be emaciated—meaning, let them not be short through a lack of vigor.
(Note: 1. *ta-bha-mu* lacks "na"; 2. *bha-pa* means "unharmed"; 3. *ta-mu* means "O lady of auspicious fortune"; 4. *tara* means "let it take away").
May they not be deficient in prowess.
The suffixation is as previously stated.
By the rule "orguṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.146), a guṇa substitution occurs,
and the accent remains the same.
For indeed, "pāpīḥ" refers to those joined with evil.

The suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule "chandasī-vanipau. There is the substitution of *su* for *jas*. Furthermore, may your path, belonging to you (*vaḥ*), be *aṣṭaḥ*, meaning incapable of being traversed (*etavai*).

The suffix *tavai* is applied after the root *iṇ* (meaning "to go") in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*). According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.2.51, "And *tavai*, with the final [vowel] also, [are acute] simultaneously," both the root and the suffix are simultaneously acute.
He states the reason for this there.
May Bṛhaspati, impelled by Indra, not show mercy—that is, not grant happiness—to both kinds of your bodies mentioned previously;
rather, he shall afflict them.
The root *mṛḍ* means "to gladden";
this is derived from a written source.

And so you have come, O Saramā, having been suddenly driven away by divine power. We shall make you our sister; do not go back. O fortunate one, we shall share the herd of cows with you. (9) When she had spoken thus, the Paṇis spoke these words of conciliation: "O Saramā, since you have indeed come here—having been driven away by *sahasā* (force), meaning by the power belonging to the gods (*daivyena*), having reached the city of Vala, seen the cows situated there, and being tormented by him [to return]—if you have come in this manner, then we shall make you our *svasāram* (sister). The word *ca* is used in the sense of "and. [Grammatical note: There is no suppression of accent (*nighāta*) for the finite verb due to the rule *niśātairyadyadihanta*. The form is from the root *gam* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), third person singular (*thal*). The compound is formed by the separation of the rule *saha supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4). The suppression of accent (*nighāta*) for the motion (*gati*) occurs by the rule *tiṅi codāttavati*. The accent is that of the suffix *lit*. "In that case, we shall make you our *svasāram*, your sister. The singular number is used with reference to the group [of us]. But you, *punar mā gāḥ*—do not go back to Indra and the others. Rather, O fortunate Saramā, having caused the herd of your cows to depart from the mountain, we shall *bhajāma*—we shall divide them. That is to say, both you and we shall divide [them]; we shall effect a partition."

I do not know brotherhood, nor do I know sisterhood; Indra and the terrible Aṅgirases know them. Desiring my cows, they have covered [the place] where I went; depart, O Paṇis, to a wider space! (10) I do not know brotherhood (*bhrātṛtva*), nor do I know sisterhood (*svasṛtva*). Indra and the terrible Aṅgirases know [them]. Furthermore, when I went from this place toward Indra and the others—[the root] *aya* meaning "to go," this is the form in the imperfect (*laṅ*)—my [theirs], desiring the cows (*gokāmāḥ*) that were stolen by you, Indra and the others, have covered (*acchadyan*) your place; [the root] *chada* meaning "to cover. Therefore, O Paṇis, depart (*ita*) to a wider (*varīyaḥ*) space, leaving behind the vast herd of cows. Or rather, go to a more abundant and very distant region. [The root] *i* meaning "to go," this is the form in the imperative (*loṭ*). From the word *uru*, with the suffix *iyasun*, the substitution *vara-* occurs according to the rule "priyasthira... etc. I do not know brotherhood, nor do I know sisterhood; Indra and the terrible Aṅgirases know them. Desiring my cows, they have covered [the place] where I went; depart, O Paṇis, to a wider space! (10) I do not know brotherhood, nor do I know sisterhood. Indra and the terrible Aṅgirases know [them]. Furthermore, when I went from this place toward Indra and the others—[the root] *aya* meaning "to go," this is the form in the imperfect (*laṅ*)—my [theirs], desiring the cows (*gokāmāḥ*) that were stolen by you, Indra and the others, have covered (*acchadyan*) your place; [the root] *chada* meaning "to cover. Therefore, O Paṇis, depart (*ita*) to a wider (*varīyaḥ*) space, leaving behind the vast herd of cows. Or rather, go to a more abundant and very distant region. [The root] *i* meaning "to go," this is the form in the imperative (*loṭ*). From the word *uru*, with the suffix *iyasun*, the substitution *vara-* occurs according to the rule "priyasthira... etc.

Go far away, O Paṇis, to a more distant place! Let the cows go forth, breaking open the mountain that serves as the door-bolt by means of Truth (ṛta). Bṛhaspati, Soma, the pressing-stones, and the wise seers (ṛṣis) found those who were hidden. O Paṇis, you must go to a wider, more distant region. Let the cows—those which were seized by you—go forth, piercing and splitting the mountain that closes the door, by means of Truth. Bṛhaspati, Soma, the pressing-stones, and the inspired seers discovered those who had been concealed.
1. *gara* and *evā* likewise [are unaccented]. 2. The *nighāta* (elision of accent) applies to *ta*, *bha*, and *gam*. 3.

The *svara* (accent) is determined by the *ti* suffixes at positions 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8; by the *ma* suffixes at positions 1, 4, 5, and 7; by the *mu* suffixes at positions 4, 5, and 8; and the *tin* suffixes at position *bha* are *svarita*.
4. Those others—she those others; those others—he those others. 5. You are the *gara*, *ta*, and *paṇaya*s.
6. The region of *ta*, *bha*, *mu*, and *deśa*.
Therefore, let them rise up;
or rather,
let them move forward.
The present participle suffix *śat* is used here in the passive sense by way of transposition; those cows, being measured— that is, being driven— by you,
are "subdhyastyaḥ."
With the *ṛta*—the truth that must be followed—as their companion, Bṛhaspati and the others shall rise up from the mountain and emerge.

Bṛhaspati will find the cows that were hidden and deeply confined; likewise, Soma, the pressing stones (*grāvan*) that assist in his extraction, and the wise seers (*vipra*), the sages (*ṛṣi*) of the Aṅgiras lineage, shall also find them.
The root *vidalṛ* is used in the sense of "attaining" (*lābhe*).
It belongs to the Taudādi class.
From it, the suffix *laṭ* is applied in the sense of the future according to the rule: "In the Veda, *laṭ*, *liṭ*, and *luṭ* [are used for other tenses]."
The augment *num* is applied according to the rule “*śe sucādīnām*.”

"Te avadan" (They spoke)—thus ends the tenth hymn. The seer is the woman who expounds the Veda named Juhū, or perhaps the son of Brahmā named Urdhvanābha. The sixth and seventh verses are Anuṣṭubhs; the remaining five are Triṣṭubhs. The deity is the Viśve Devās. Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī:
"Having taken her by the hand, he led her away—he brought her; that is to say, he gave her."

*hastagṛha*: According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 1.4.77, "nityaṃ haste pāṇāv upayamane," the word *hasta* is designated as a *gati* when used with the sense of "taking in marriage. Consequently, in the compound with the root *grah*, the suffix *hyap* is applied;
furthermore, the elision of the vowel *e* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively:
after the word *hasta*, the suffixes *cha* and *yaP* are applied to the word *gṛha* in a compound according to Vedic usage.

"She must be taken by the hand alone; she is the wife of a Brahmin"—thus they said. She did not go as a messenger for him; thus is the kingdom of a Kṣatriya protected. 3. "She must be taken by the hand alone; she is the wife of a Brahmin"—thus they spoke. She stood there, not to be sent as a messenger; thus is the realm of a Kṣatriya guarded. 3.
The gods said to Bṛhaspati: "O Bṛhaspati, you are more excellent; you are our protector."
The body is called *ādhi* because ornaments (*ābharaṇa*) are placed (*ādhīyante*) upon it.
By the rule *upasargaṃ ghoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.92), the suffix *kvip* is applied.
Her body must indeed be grasped—that is, it must be taken hold of—by the hand alone.
Furthermore, those gods now spoke thus: "This is the wife of Brahmā. They said this.
The word *ca* has the sense of *cet* (if).
For this very reason, by the rule "nipātair yadyadihanta," there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent for the finite verb (*tiṅ*). The root *brūñ* means "in distinct speech."
In the *luṅ* [tense], the root is *vac*.
According to the rule "after the roots *as*, *vac*, and *khyāti*, there is *aṅ*," the suffix *cli* is replaced by *aṅ*.
Then, by the rule "for *vac*, there is *um*," the augment *um* is added.
The vowel of the augment (aṭ).
The prefix *vi-* is used in the sense of exclusion (*avadhāraṇa*). The root *veṣ* means "to go" or "to grow," as in the case of Brahmā’s wife (*brahmajāyā*).
The suffix *kir* is added to this root in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the *uṇādi* rules.
The form *tugabhāvaḥ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Because a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not invariably applied, there is an absence of *guṇa* substitution when the suffix is marked with *ṅ*.
By the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ," the case ending (*sup*) is circumflex (*svarita*).
The messenger sent by you for the sake of finding a wife did not remain true;
he did not reveal his own self.
The ātmanepada ending is applied to the root *sthā* in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) by the rule "prakāśanastheyākhyayośca" (Pāṇini 1.3.23).
Furthermore, by the rule "ślāghahuṅsthāśapāṃ" (Pāṇini 1.4.34), the messenger receives the designation of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
In this regard, there is an illustration:

just as one would not reveal to an enemy the well-guarded and protected kingdom (*rāṣṭra*) of a Kṣatriya king, so too she did not reveal herself to him because she was possessed by misfortune. But now, they said, "This [woman] is manifesting herself as one who is to be accepted by him," referring to her as *brahmajāyā*.

The gods spoke of her in the beginning, as did the seven seers who sat down for austerity. The wife of the Brahmin, brought near, is terrible; she establishes instability in the highest heaven. The gods spoke of her in the beginning, as did the seven seers who sat down for austerity. The wife of the Brahmin, brought near, is terrible; she establishes instability in the highest heaven.
The ancient gods of old, such as the Ādityas and others, spoke concerning this [earth];
they declared that she is free from evil.
Likewise did the seven ṛṣis.
The accent of the compound. Seven ṛṣis sat down—that is, they became seated—for the sake of *tapas*, for the practice of austerity.
This is the form of the root *sad* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The compound is formed with a prefix (*upasarga*);
thus, there is no *nighāta* (elision of accent) according to the rule *yathogāt*.
They also spoke as follows.
Then this wife of Bṛhaspati, who was virtuous and terrifying to wicked enemies,
was brought near and established by the gods in his presence.
The root *ṇīñ* means "to lead" (*prāpaṇe*).
The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*).
By the rule "the immediately preceding prefix [retains its] original accent" (*gatiranantaraḥ*), the prefix retains its natural accent.
For instance:
the power of asceticism indeed places even those difficult to restrain in the highest heaven, in the most excellent station.
Therefore, the greatness of asceticism, through the acceptance of these [sages] by the gods, establishes them in the presence of Bṛhaspati.

1. This is the measure (māna) of Ta-bha 1.2.4.8. 2. Ta 4.5 says: The student (*brahmacārī*) moves about, performing his various duties; he becomes a single limb of the gods. By him Bṛhaspati found his wife, as the gods [found] the *juhū* ladle led away by Soma. || 5 || The student moves about, performing his various duties; he becomes a single limb of the gods. By him Bṛhaspati found his wife, as the gods [found] the *juhū* ladle led away by Soma. || 5 ||
Thus the *juhū* speaks indirectly: "In this way my own husband has obtained me.
O gods, formerly that *brahmacārī* moved as a celibate student because of his state of being without a wife;
therefore, as a *vipaḥ*, he pervaded all sacrifices, and by serving the gods with praises and services, he became a single limb of the gods.
The husband and wife are indeed two limbs of the sacrifice.
*veviṣad*: from the root *vi-plu*, meaning "to pervade";
it belongs to the *juhoty-ādika* (third) class.

By the rule *nijāṃ trayāṇāṃ guṇaḥ ślau* (Pāṇini 7.4.75), there is guṇa substitution for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). By the rule *nābhyastācchatuḥ*, the addition of the augment *num* after the suffix *śatṛ* is prohibited. By the rule *abhyastānām ādiḥ*, the first syllable receives the udātta accent.
By means of that service to the gods, Bṛhaspati found me, his wife named Juhū;
that is, having followed her, he obtained her.
The word *na* is used here in the sense of comparison (*upamārtha*).

Just as in the past he obtained the *juhū* ladle—which had been led away by Soma according to the sequence beginning with "Soma gave [her] to the Gandharva" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.85.41)—so too has he obtained it now.
We offer oblations (*juhūma*). [The root] *hu* means "to give" or "to eat.
The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule: "It is also seen after other roots."
By the rule "juhoterdve ca," there is reduplication and lengthening.

When the acute accent on the case-ending would have applied by the rule "udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt," it is prohibited by the rule "noddhātvoḥ. Consequently, by the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ," the resulting *yaṇ* vowel becomes circumflex (*svarita*).

The gods indeed gave her back; men, too, gave her back. The kings, making their word true, gave back the wife of the Brahmin. 6. Indeed, the gods gave her back; indeed, men also [gave her back]. The kings, making their word true, gave back the wife of the Brahmin. 6.
He states the reason for the gain:
the gods gave back the sacrificial ladle *juhū*, which was the wife of Brahmā, to Bṛhaspati.
The word *vai* expresses well-known tradition.
The word *uta* has the sense of "also.
Humans (*manuṣyāḥ*) also gave again.
Thus, making the gift performed by gods and humans true—that is, making it accord with reality—the kings also gave to him again.
The sense is that he thus destroyed even the sin which was the cause of his being beyond conventional discourse.
Having restored the wife of Brahmā and been cleansed of all sin by the gods, they enjoyed the vigor of the earth and worship the Wide-striding One (Viṣṇu). || 7 ||
The gods [say]: "By the rule 'supām supo bhavanti,' there is a replacement of the nominative plural suffix *jas* by the third case [instrumental] ending."
O gods, [be] free from sin!
When there is an absence of meaning [of the constituent parts], it is an *avyayībhāva* compound;
its accent is that of the compound itself.
Having rendered her free from sin.
The word *brahmajāyā* is established [as a valid form] by this rule: "and *adya*."
Having taken the wife of Brahmā—the consort of Bṛhaspati—and having given her back again, having given her back once more.

Furthermore, by the rule "In the Vedic language, *canaḥ* should be stated as having the designation of a *gati*" (Pāṇini 1.4.60.2), the word *punar* receives the designation of a *gati*; consequently, there is a compound (*samāsa*) and the suffix *lyap*. [This is subject to] the rule "Not before *lyap*" (Pāṇini 6.1.39). [The resulting forms are: *abhavat* (ta7-bha1.2.4.8); *abhavat* (bha7-avyayavat);
and [the variant] *evam devamanuṣyā anyava* (2. ga).
4. 69) Thus ends the prohibition regarding the word *īśvara*. [The rule for] the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member following a *ku-* prefix applies.
Having partaken of the sevenfold strength of the earth—the essence of sap, food in the form of oblation.
The augment *yag* is applied by the rule *kvau yak* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.47).
Having broken and divided the sacrifice of Bṛhaspati—which has wide-reaching power, great fame, and is to be praised by many—they worship and serve it.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "samiddhaḥ," is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Its seer is Jamadagni of the Bhṛgu lineage,
or his son Rāma, who is renowned as Paraśurāma.
This is the Āprī-sūkta.
Therefore, the deities for each verse begin with *samidh* and end with *tanūnapāt*, excluding *narāśaṃsa*.
Accordingly, it has been enumerated: "In the *samiddha* [sūkta] there are eleven verses; they are the Āprīs composed by Jamadagni or by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni."
In the animal sacrifice of the Jāmadagnyas, this is the *āgnisūkta*; or rather, it applies to all without distinction.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The verse beginning with *samiddho adha* belongs to all, or according to the respective ṛṣi" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.2).
In the Prājāpatya animal sacrifice, which is an ancillary part of Vedic study (*adhyayana*), this *āgnisūkta* is obligatory for everyone.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "But in the Prājāpatya [rite], the son of Jamadagni [is the officiant] for all. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.2)
Kindled today in the house of man, O Jātavedas, you, a god, sacrifice to the gods.
Bring them hither, O you who are rich in friends; you are the wise messenger, the seer, and the one of keen insight.

Kindled today within the dwelling of man, O Jātavedas, you, a god, sacrifice to the gods. Bring them hither, O you of Mitra-like luster, you who are observant; for you are the messenger, the seer, and the wise one. 1.

O Jātavedas, you whose wisdom is born, O God shining by your own splendor, you who are kindled today in this rite within the *durona*— a term for the house, meaning a dwelling that must be protected with effort— of the human sacrificer, you worship the gods, Indra and the others.
Worship with oblations.
*Samiddhaḥ*: from the root *indhī*, meaning "to kindle" or "to shine," with the suffix *ka* in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*).

There is a prohibition of the *it*-augment by the rule "śrīdito niṣṭhāyām" (Pāṇini 7.2.14). By the rule "gatiranantaraḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.49), the preceding prefix retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).

O you who are great for your friends (*mitramahas*), worthy of praise, and the honor-giver (*māna*) to those who are like friends—the singers—being honored by them; O you who are observant (*cikitvān*), knowing the praises offered by them, or being conscious, bring the gods here to our sacrifice and cause them to partake [of the offerings].

The root *prā* is used in the sense of "attaining. This is a form in the imperative (*loṭ*). There is no suppression of accent (*nighāta*) because of the rule: "When joined with *ca* or *vā*, the first [verb retains its accent]."

Likewise, you are a seer (kavi) of far-reaching wisdom; for that very reason, you are highly perceptive (pracetāḥ), possessing excellent knowledge. As such, you act as the messenger of the gods, performing a beneficial service by conveying the oblations.
O Tanūnapāt, fair-tongued one, anointing with honey the paths that lead along the way of Ṛta,
do thou, prospering our prayers through our insights and our sacrifice, bring our ritual to the gods.

O Tanūnapāt, anointing with honey the paths of Truth and the ways of travel, O fair-tongued one, make them savory; prosper our thoughts through inspired visions and the sacrifice, and perform our ritual service among the gods.

He is *tanūnapāt*. *Napāt* is a name for a descendant; here, the body (*tanū*) is carried (*ūhyate*). Because enjoyments such as milk and the like are extended (*tatāḥ*) within it, [it is called *tanūnapāt*].
From that, milk is produced; from milk comes food, and from that, fire.
Or alternatively:
the waters are spread across the intermediate space; from them come plants and so forth, and from those, fire.

O you of such form, O seven-tongued one, O you of beautiful flame— or rather, since *jihvā* is a name for speech, O you of beautiful speech, O Agni— sprinkling with honey, that is, with intoxicating sap, or alternatively, with the sap produced by speech, the paths of *ṛta*, that is, of sacrifice— the paths which are the means for attaining the fruits of the journey and the stations for the oblation— illumining them perfectly, make them savory; cause them to be tasted.
Make it sweet!
The root *svad* means "to taste. The absence of vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) in the penultimate syllable before the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

Furthermore: "My hymns" (*manmāni*). [This is derived] from the root *man*, meaning "to praise. They are hymns intended by us, worthy of being meditated upon, [offered] with prayers (*dhībhiḥ*), that is, with insights or ritual acts. And furthermore: "the sacrifice" (*yajñam*)—that which is worthy of worship—with oblations (*haviṣvā*), accomplishing it.

From the word *deva*, the suffix *ā* is applied in the sense of the locative case by the rule “*deva-manuṣya-*” and so forth.
Being invoked, worthy of praise and adoration, come, O Agni, well-pleased with the Vasus!
You are the mighty Hotṛ-priest of the gods; as such, may you, the most skilled sacrificer, worship them here.

Being invoked, worthy of praise, and worthy of adoration, come hither, O Agni, in harmony with the Vasus. You are the mighty Hotṛ-priest of the gods; as such, being the most excellent sacrificer, worship them according to our desire.

O Agni, come (*ā yāhi*) to our ritual act (*asmat karmaṇi*). Of what nature? Being invoked (*ājuhvānaḥ*), that is, calling the gods; from the root *hu* (in the sense of giving or eating), belonging to the *juhotyādi* class, with the accent on the reduplicated syllable. Worthy of praise (*īḍyaḥ*)—the root *īḍ* has the sense of requesting; one who is to be requested or entreated. Worthy of homage (*vandyaḥ*), meaning to be lauded. Together with the Vasus, the gods, rejoicing in their company (*sajoṣāḥ*). And having arrived, O Great One (*yahva*)—this is a name for the great—O Great One, you are the invoker (*hotā*) of the gods. Therefore, being more skilled in sacrifice (*yajīyān*)—from the word *yaṣṭṛ* with the suffix *īyasun*, where the *tṛ* is elided by the rule "turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu"—you are the greater sacrificer. Being thus impelled and entreated by us through our worship (*iṣṭitaḥ*), do you sacrifice (*yakṣi*) to these gods; honor them with the oblation (*havis*).

The sacrificial grass is strewn toward the east according to the direction of the earth; for this dawn, O Agni, it is prepared as is fitting. It spreads itself out further and wider, a pleasant seat for the gods and for Aditi.

The sacrificial grass is strewn toward the east, according to the direction of the earth; it is spread upon her surface. O Agni, worthy of honor, it extends further and wider, a pleasant seat for the gods and for Aditi.
That which is this sacrificial grass (*barhis*)—ancient, directed eastward, and facing the east—is the *vastu* (site) of the earth characterized as the altar (*vedi*).
[The root] *vas* means "to cover";
the suffix *tun* is applied.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of the dative, according to the rule “*caturthy-arthe bahulam chandasi*” (Pāṇini 2.3.62).
Alternatively,
the suffix *tosun* should be understood as being used in the sense of indicating a state (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
For the purpose of clothing and covering, at the beginning of the days—in the forenoon—it is selected, praised, and brought from this eastern direction by means of a mantra that is clearly visible.
Thus says the Vedic scripture: "Those sages bring [the sacrificial grass] from the front," and so forth.
And that unwashed *barhis* (sacrificial grass) spreads itself out widely, becoming more extensive and more vast.
Only three things are presented upon the altar:
thus, it becomes *syona*, providing comfort, for the gods, for Aditi, and for the earth characterized as the altar;
for upon the wide sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the gods sit down in comfort.
Let the radiant doors open wide, like women adorning themselves for their husbands;
O divine, lofty, all-impelling doors, be easy of access for the gods.
Radiant, wide, let them open wide like wives adorning themselves for their husbands; O divine, lofty doors, all-enlivening, become easy passages for the gods. 5.
*Vyarcasvatīḥ*:
*vyacas* means pervasiveness; that which possesses this is *vyarcas*.
The long vowel resulting from the substitution of the preceding homogeneous sound (pūrvasavarṇadīrgha) is applied according to the rule "vā chandasi" [Pāṇini 6.1.106].
Those door-deities [shine] far and wide.

From the word *uru* in the third case singular, there is the addition [of the suffixes] *hy*, *āḍ*, *iy*, *āj*, *īkār*, and *āṇ* (Pāṇini 7.1.1, Gaṇapāṭha). [Examples: *tvam hy asmi karmaṇi*; *tvam āḍ asmi karmaṇi*; *tvam iy asmi karmaṇi*; *tvam āj asmi karmaṇi*; *tvam ī asmi karmaṇi*; *tvam āṇ asmi karmaṇi*. 2. *pūjyamānaḥ* (Ta4.5); 3.
*aditaye adīnāyai* (Ga1.2).
39. 1) "iti" is a substitute.
"Let them spread out widely; let them be distinguished and take their places.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

"Just as wives, adorning themselves and beautifying themselves for the sake of their husbands at the time of union, spread out—that is, take their positions—so too let them spread out in this ritual act."
O you two vast ones, O you two who impel all!
The oblation (*haviḥ*) is for the purpose of gratification.
Therefore, when *karman* is the upapada, the suffix *aṇ* is applied; thus, [the word] *aiṣṭra* is formed by virtue of the *idit* designation.
In the rule "tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam," because of the word "bahulam" (variously), there is also the non-elision (aluk) of the second case ending.
O all you divine doors, you who preside over the gates, for the sake of the gods—meaning for the supreme benefit of the deities—be easy of access, well-traversed, and wide open.
Let the two swelling ones, the worshipful Night and Dawn, sit down together in their place;
let the two celestial maidens, the lofty and gold-adorned, assume their radiant and brilliant splendor.

"Coming forth," "she sacrifices," "I worship," "Dawn and Night," "let them sit down," "in their place," "the two celestial maidens," "the lofty ones," "the well-adorned ones," "bestowing splendor," "brightly colored. || 6 ||
*Susvayantī*: [from] the root *sū* meaning "to go," with the prefix *śata-*. The dual ending *-au* for the root-final *s-* is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage.
"Suṣṭhu ayantyau" means going well; or alternatively,
it is a corruption of "svaperyantyau," with the elision of a syllable.
Causing [all] to sleep; she sacrifices to the two worthy of sacrifice, the two who have approached close at hand—Uṣas and Night, both Dawn and Night.
In a *dvandva* compound, there is the substitution of *uṣāsā* for *uṣas-* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.31.
Furthermore, by the rule "in a *devatā-dvandva*," both the preceding and following members simultaneously retain their original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
May the two deities, Day and Night, sit down—meaning they should settle or take their seats—in this womb, this place of sacrifice, most firmly or according to rule.
From the root *sad* (to sit), the form is derived using the *luṅ* suffix; because it belongs to the *ludita* class, the substitution of *aṅ* for *śli* occurs.
Of what nature are they?
The two celestial ones, those who exist in heaven, are like two women who ought to be gratified;
or alternatively,
the two women are joined together and indistinguishable from one another.
The two *bṛhatī*s are great by virtue of their qualities; they possess beautiful golden ornaments and are splendidly radiant.
*Rukmam*:
this form is derived from the root *ruc* with the suffix *man*, and the substitution of *ku* for *k* having been applied.
They both bestow and sustain supreme prosperity, which is white-hued and shining in form.
The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first, eloquent ones, measuring out the sacrifice for man to perform;
the two poets who impel [the rites] at the assemblies, pointing toward the ancient light by their direction.

The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first, eloquent ones, measuring out the sacrifice for Manu to worship; the two poets who impel [the rites] at the assemblies, pointing toward the eastern light by their direction. 7.
Divine.
In the phrase “devādyajñau,” the suffix *yañ* is applied.
May the two Hotṛ priests associated with the gods—the two named Hotṛ who accomplish the oblation, namely Agni and Āditya—sit down at this sacrifice. Of what nature are they?
The two first [priests], who existed before the benefactor of men, possessing fair speech and beautiful hymns, [are present] for the sake of performing the sacrifice for every human sacrificer.
The suffix *śadhyai* is used in the sense of the infinitive of purpose after the root *yaj*.

Measuring out the sacrifice, fashioning it, and bringing it forth at the *vidathas*—wherein the *vidathas* are the sacrifices, as the officiating priests (*ṛtvijas*) perform their respective duties—they impel and urge forward the sacrificers; they are the two poets (*kārū*), the makers of hymns of praise, who by the excellent path of instruction, or rather by the mantra being entered, direct and carry out the light known as the Āhavanīya fire, which stands in the eastern direction as the object of worship.

1. In the sacrificial rite (yajñakarmaṇi). 2. The word *deśaḥ* is the substitute *ḍā* for the case-ending *sup*. 3. The word *ni* does not exist in the Ta and Bha recensions. 4. In the Ta and Bha recensions, it is *samite*. 5. In the Ta4.5 recension, it is *śobhamānarūpām*. 6. The suffix (*pratyayaḥ*) is present in the Ta and Bha recensions.

May Bhāratī, Tūryā, and Ilā—like Manu, perceiving [us] here—these three goddesses, skillful in their work, sit upon this pleasant sacred grass (*barhis*) at our sacrifice. May Sarasvatī also sit there.
May Bhāratī come swiftly to our sacrifice; may Iḷā, mindful like Manu, be present here. May the three goddesses—Sarasvatī and the others—skilled in holy works, sit upon this pleasant sacred grass.
1. Bhāratī: Bharata is the sun; [Bhāratī] is the radiance inherent to him.
In the sense of "belonging to him" (*tasyedam*), [the suffix *cha* is applied] because of the rule *utsādita-tvāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.86).
By the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
[The word *tūryā* thus means] "our" (*naḥ*) sacrifice; may she "quickly" (*tūrya*) "come" (*ā etu*), that is, arrive.

Likewise, just as a human being knows, "This must be done by me," so too, O Goddess Iḷā, being conscious and knowing, making the *majman* and the other oblations clearly manifest, do thou approach and bestow them.
By the rule *gatir gatau* (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.70), there is the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) of the preceding *gati*.

Furthermore, let the *vanaspati*— this sacrificial post (*yūpa*)— and the deity named *śamitṛ*, or alternatively the god *agni* (the blazing fire called *āhavanīya*), together with *madhu*— that is, sweet *ghṛta* (clarified butter)—
or else with water (*madhu*) used for sprinkling and *ghṛta* used for bringing forward the offering—
make the *havya*, the oblation fit for sacrifice, savory (*svādu*). Let them make it delicious.
Born immediately, Agni measured out the sacrifice; he became the leader of the gods.
May the gods eat the oblation consecrated with "svāhā" upon the speech of this Hotṛ priest, who has been appointed.

As soon as he was born, Agni measured out the sacrifice; he became the leader of the gods. May the gods eat the oblation consecrated with *svāhā*, offered according to the direction of this Hotṛ-priest and within the speech of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*). 11.
This Agni, having been born— that is, even as he is being born— immediately at that very moment, has specially fashioned,
that is, produced, the sacrifice.
The root *māh* occurs in the senses of measuring and sound;
it belongs to the *juhotyādi* class.
For this very reason, this Agni became the *purogā*—the one who goes before, the leader, the chief—of the gods.
When the suffix *dhiṭ* is applied to the root *gam*, and the substitution of *āśva* has been made, this is the resulting form.
Then, in the *pradiś*—the pre-eminent direction, the east—in the speech of this *hotṛ*, Agni, who has arrived in the form of the Āhavanīya fire and who establishes the oblation;

here, by the mention of "speech," the mouth is indicated as the locus. May all the gods consume—that is, eat—the *havis* offered with the exclamation *svāhā* in that speech, which is to say, in the mouth.
This hymn was correctly explained by Yāska (Nirukta 8.5–21);
let it be investigated here accordingly.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “manīṣiṇaḥ,” is the seerly composition of Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra Vairūpa; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra.
Thus it is enumerated: “Manīṣiṇaḥ, ten [verses]; Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra. The application [of the hymn] has been explained.
O wise ones, bring forth your inspired hymn, according as the thoughts of men arise;
for Indra is the noble lord through his true deeds—he is the hero who loves songs of praise and is well-known.
O wise ones, bring forth your inspired hymn, according as the thoughts of men arise. Let us impel Indra with truthful deeds; for he is the hero, the lover of songs, who is well-known. 1.

O wise ones, you who are singers, bring forth—that is, perform—for Indra a hymn that is the "lord of the mind" (manīṣā), which governs the intellect. Offer praise according to your own thoughts, in whatever manner your minds are inclined.
And we, by means of these "made" (kṛtebhiḥ)—that is, composed and true (satyaiḥ) hymns that correspond to reality—shall cause Indra to come toward the sacrifice; we shall summon him.
The root *īr* means "to move";
this is the imperative (*loṭ*) of its causative form (*ṇyanta*).
For since he, Indra, is *vidānaḥ*— knowing, capable— and *girvaṇasyuḥ*—
desiring those who are *girvaṇasaḥ*, namely the singers, so called because they "enjoy" (*vananti*) or partake of him through their songs (*gīrbhiḥ*).
The form is *vanat-sun-i*.
The lengthening of the vowel in the prefix (*upapada*) is a Vedic (archaic) feature.
The suffix *kyap* is added after that [base].
The suffix *up* is applied [in the sense of] "in what Vedic meter? (*kyāc chandasi*).
Indeed, desiring his praisers,
he was therefore praised by him.

For from the seat of Truth the inspired thought has shone forth; the bull, seeking the kine, has attained the cows with the kine. He has arisen with the flight of the seer and with a roar; he has encompassed even the vast regions.

For from the seat of Truth, the inspired thought has shone forth; the bull, the gatherer of the herd, has met with the kine. He has arisen with the roar of a seer; he has encompassed even the vast regions.
1. *ta* 1.2.3.6.7.8-bha—just as; 2. *ga*—*ta* 1.2.3.6.7.8-bha—*prakudadhve*; 3. *ga*—the hero (*vīraḥ*) is capable (*samarthaḥ*); 4. *ga*—they worship (*saṃbhajanti*).

Indra, the sustainer (*dhīti*) of *ṛta* (truth), of water, of the seat (*sadas*), and of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), has shone forth; he illuminates and manifests himself.
