For [the particle] *hi* indicates what is well-known. [The root] *dyut* means "to shine. In the *luṅ* tense, by the rule "*dyudbhyo luṅi*" (Pāṇini 1.3.91), the *parasmaipada* ending is used. The suffix *kleluc* is Vedic; there is also the *vṛddhi* strengthening according to the rule for stems ending in consonants (*halanta*). Alternatively, *adhaud*: such an Indra approaches the sacrifice. [The root] *dyu* means "to approach," belonging to the *adādi* class. This is the *laṅ* tense; the *vṛddhi* is applied by the rule "*uto vṛddhiluki hali*" (Pāṇini 7.3.89). Gārgya says: A cow (*gauḥ*) is a female that has calved once. Its offspring is the bull (*vṛṣabha*). He reaches (*sam-ānaṭ*) and counts together with the cows (*gobhiḥ*). In the same way, he too pervades everything by his own greatness. Likewise, with *taviṣeṇa*—this is a name for "great"—with a great roar or sound, he has risen up; he has become exalted and lofty. Therefore, even the great (*mahanti cit*) waters or worlds (*rajāṃsi*) he reaches and counts together.

Indra, it is said, knows this for the sake of hearing, for he is victorious and the maker of paths for the Sun. The unshakable Lord of the firmament has made her his own; he is the conqueror of heaven, never overcome.
Indra indeed knows this for the sake of hearing; for he is victorious, the maker of space. Then, making the cow his mate, the unshakable one became the lord of heaven, well-born and irresistible. 3.
Indra indeed knows—verily Indra alone knows—for the sake of hearing this our hymn;
for he alone is victorious, the conqueror of enemies, and the maker of paths for the sun. Moreover, Indra, being unshakable and making himself the beloved wife of Vṛṣaṇaśva, [attains] his goal.
"He comes to our sacrifice.
"He became the friend of Vṛṣaṇaśva, the doer of good deeds" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.51.13)—this is another mantra.
The root *as* is used in the senses of going, shining, and taking; it belongs to the Bhū class. He became the lord (*pati*) of the sky (*divaḥ*), that is, of the heavenly world (*dyuloka*).
The suffix *laṅ* [is applied] to the root *bhū*.
Due to the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*), there is no *anighāta* (lack of accentuation).
Indra, being praised by the Aṅgirases, has shattered the laws of the great ocean;
he who, through his devotion to truth, has established many extended realms and upheld the yoke.
Indra, being praised by the Aṅgirases, shattered the laws of the great ocean; he spread out the many realms and sustained the cosmic order through his truthfulness. 4.
Indra, being praised and extolled by the Aṅgiras ṛṣis, [came] from the great ocean.
The suffix *vap* is applied according to the rule "arṇasaḥ salopaśca" (Kātantra 5.2.109.3).
He destroyed—that is, he struck down—by his own greatness alone, every single vow, that is, every action, of the water-bearing cloud.
The root *mī* is used in the sense of "to injure.
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, the short vowel [is substituted] by the rule "in the Vedic canon (*nigama*), [the long ī of] *mīnāti* [becomes short]."
Then he spread out many indeed, even numerous waters;
he made them flow downwards—that Indra who, in the pursuit of truth, extends the divine order.
Or rather: [he spread out] the many waters.
The suffix *tān* should also be understood here as having its own inherent meaning (*svārthika*) following the word *satya*.
[He] maintained, that is, sustained, the power that supports— that which holds up— the *satya*, the heavenly world.
Indra is the counterpart of heaven and earth; he knows all things and slays the demon Śuṣṇa.
He has spread out even the vast sky with the sun, and as a more steadfast pillar than the pillar itself, he has propped it up with his support.

1. *abhigamane* (in approaching); 2. *ta-bha-luṅ* (the *luṅ* [aorist] suffix after *ta* and *bha*); 3. *ga-ta4.5-patiḥ svāmī* (the word *patiḥ* [lord] follows *ga* and *ta4.5*); 4. *ta-bha-' vratā* does not exist; 5. *ta-bha-dādhārayat* (he established).

Indra is the counterpart of heaven and of earth. He knows all names; he slays Śuṣṇa. Even the great sky he has overspread with the sun; he has propped it up with a pillar more firmly than a pillar itself. ||5||
Indra, the counterpart and representative of heaven and earth by virtue of his greatness, knows all the *savanas*—the soma-pressings—for the purpose of drinking the soma;
he slays *Śuṣṇa*, the asura of that name who withers everything.
(The lack of *nighāta* [accentual suppression] occurs due to the division of the sentence.)
Moreover, he overspread even the great earth and the vast sky with the sun;
he made them endowed with light everywhere.
As the most excellent among those who support (skabhīyān), he supported (cāskambha) by means of his very power, which is the instrument of restraint (skambhena).
He brought the heavenly world under his control.
The root *skambh* belongs to the Sautra roots.
In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), there is lengthening according to the rule “*tujādīnām*.
In the case of *cit-kambhanena*, there is the elision of *s* in the *saṃhitā* [due to the rule *saṃhitāyām*].

Regarding the root *stambh* preceded by the prefix *ud*, the elision of *s* is prescribed by the rule "udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.61). This same elision also occurs for the root *skambh* preceded by *vi*, because it falls within the domain of Vedic usage (*chandoviṣayatvāt*).

For with the thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra struck down Vṛtra; you shattered the magic powers of the godless, arrogant one. O bold one, there you struck him down with boldness. Then, O Maghavan, you became mighty through the strength of your arms.

With the thunderbolt, indeed, the slayer of Vṛtra struck down Vṛtra; he shattered the magic powers of the godless, arrogant one. There, O bold one, you struck him down with courage; then, O Maghavan, you became possessed of the strength of arms.
O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, you who are the killer of Vṛtra, with your thunderbolt you have struck down Vṛtra; you have slain him.
In the *laṅ* [aorist] of the root *stṛ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* suffix by the rule "there is frequent elision in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
There is *guṇa* [substitution] before the *sip* ending.
Due to its connection with *hi*, it does not undergo *anighāta* (lack of accentuation).

Immediately thereafter, O bold one—O you whose nature is to be daring—you, with your powerful thunderbolt, boldly destroyed the magical illusions of that non-god, who was unshining and swelling with his own strength, at this very moment.
In the case of *han* in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, when [the suffix] *thali* follows, [the reduplication is formed] according to the rule "and from the reduplicated syllable" (*abhyāsācca*).
Then, O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, you became one whose strength lies in your arms, possessing the power of your forearms.
They sing together when the dawns [appear] with the sun; his bright rays find the light. When the star of heaven is seen, no one truly knows it as it returns again. || 7 ||
When the Dawns, together with the Sun, have shone forth—that brilliant wealth his rays have found—then that star of heaven is seen; yet no one truly knows from whence it comes again. 7.
Whenever the dawns— the times of dawn— unite with the sun, that is, with Indra who is of the nature of the sun;
the root *sac* means "to join," and belongs to the *bhū* class.
At that time, his own rays—his banners that illuminate everything—attained and obtained *rām*, meaning various-colored splendor and wealth.
Furthermore, immediately after his rising, when no star of heaven was seen, he alone shone forth.
The *liṭ* [perfect] occurs after the root *dṛś* when it has an object;
because of this [application], there is no suppression of accent (*anighāta*).
At that time, because—
In the case of *iṇ* ending in a present participle (*śatṛ*), the case-ending is acute according to the rule “*śaturanumo nadyajādī*” [Pāṇini 6.1.173].
No one at all knows—indeed, no one knows—the rays as they go everywhere;
this is truly so.

Far indeed have the first of these gone, the waters that flowed forth at the impulse of Indra. Where now are they today? Where is their source? And where is your middle now? Where is your dwelling? 8.
1. Even to the great earth (mahīm api). 2. [The reading] *ta-bha-mu* does not exist; [the word] *iṇaḥ* is absent.

Far away, indeed, they went. Of these [waters], those which flowed forth at the impulse (*pra-save*) of Indra—what is their source (*arpam*), what is their foundation (*budhnaḥ*), what is their middle (*madhyamam*), and what is their end (*antaḥ*)? 8.

Of these waters, those which are "first," meaning those that go first, have indeed gone far; they have truly gone to a distance. Just as the waters flow at the "impulse" (*prasave*)—that is, the impelling—of Indra; [the root] *pū* means "to impel. According to the rule *pā. sū. 3.3.56.4*, "and after *java* and *sava*," there is the acute accent on the final syllable of the compound. At his command, they "flowed"—that is, they move; they indeed go. Now, the following is spoken in the direct mode of address: O Waters, where indeed is "your front"? Where does it abide? And where is your "bottom," your root? Likewise, where now is your "middle"? And where is your "end," your limit? The meaning is that because they pervade all things, their course is not perceived. [Grammatical notes: From the interrogative pronoun *kim*, the suffix *ap* is added in the sense of the locative case according to *kimo't*; the substitution of *kā* occurs by the rule *kāti*, and it is circumflexly accented (*svarita*). For the root *am* in the sense of "going," the suffix *tan* is applied according to the rule beginning with *asihasi*.
When the streams have been swallowed by the swift-moving [wind], these [waters] then rush forth with speed;
those seeking release and those already released—once set in motion, they do not rest.
The swift rivers, swallowed by the Dragon, were then released with speed; those that sought liberation and those that were already liberated—half of them do not rest, rushing on with impetuous flow.
O Indra, [those] who have seized the serpent Vṛtra, who is not to be slain, or the sacrifice with their mouths.
The root *gras* (meaning "to eat") is anudātta;
in the Vedic language, the *liṭ* (perfect) tense takes the suffix *kānac*.
You set in motion the flowing waters of the rivers; you released them and caused them to flow forth.
"Ādit" is used here for emphasis.
Immediately thereafter, these waters surged forth with speed and force;
they became utterly agitated everywhere.
The root *ovijī* is used in the senses of fear and trembling;
it is anudātta (unaccented).
In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), by Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.4.76, *irayo re*, the substitute *re* is applied for *ira*.
Moreover, those waters which were seeking liberation—desiring to be released by Indra—were indeed liberated (mumuce) by Indra.
The *liṭ* [perfect] affix occurs after the root *muc-* when it expresses the object.
Furthermore, immediately thereafter, the waters—meaning those that are exceedingly pure—do not "rest";
they do not sport in one place.
Rather, the meaning is that they are by nature inclined to move everywhere.
Moving together like women longing for the river, they have approached their lover from of old; he has been honored by the many Dāsas.
May your earthly treasures come to us, O Indra, and may your many true blessings reach us.

Moving together like longing women toward the Sindhu, they have come from of old; the lover has been welcomed into their stronghold. O Indra, may your earthly treasures come to us, and may your many blessings reach our home.
United.
In the word *sahasya sadhiḥ*, there is the substitution of *sadhrīc* [for *saha*]. By the rule "the addition of *ṅīp* after the root *añj*," the suffix *ṅīp* is applied.
This results in the elision of the final vowel and the lengthening of the preceding vowel.
The long vowel of the same quality as the preceding (pūrvasavarṇadīrgha) is applied by the rule "or in the Vedic language" (vā chandasi).
The waters, moving together and flowing together, went toward the Sindhu, the ocean, their supporter; they came to it.
Therein is an illustration:
just as longing women approach their own husbands out of desire, so it was.
The destroyer of enemies, Indra, from of old has been the master of these waters by virtue of being their impeller.
O Indra, our own earthly riches— the oblations that satisfy like wealth— and your many pleasant words consisting of hymns of praise have reached your dwelling.
2. The suffix *ta* (past participle). 3. The form *tadbhava-asujaḥ* does not exist.
They went to the house; let them come.
Or rather, let our praises go to your house;
let your earthly riches come to our house.
The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the Vedic sense to denote all three times (*sārvakālika*).
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “indra piba,” is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Indra.
The seer (ṛṣi) is Virūpa of the Gotra Nabhaḥprabhedana. Thus it is enumerated: “indra piba; [the seer is] Nabhaḥprabhedana.”
The application has been explained.
O Indra, drink of the pressed juice according to your desire; for here at the morning pressing is the first draught.
Rejoice, O Hero, to slay the enemies! We shall proclaim your heroic deeds through our hymns of praise.

O Indra, drink of the pressed juice according to your desire; for the morning pressing is indeed your first draught. Rejoice, O Hero, to slay the enemies! We shall proclaim your heroic deeds with hymns of praise. 1.
O Indra, those various desires which people desire according to their wish—
this is an *avyayībhāva* compound; its accent is as follows.
Drink that portion of the pressed-out juice which is to be given to you, according to your desire.
Because the one being addressed is not present [in the context], there is an anudātta (low-pitched) accent due to its status as beginning with a *pāda*.

The Soma being pressed at the morning pressing during the *prātaḥsavana*—for it is there [that you drink]; the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental. By you alone is the *pūrvapītiḥ*, that which is to be drunk first of all, to be consumed.
Or alternatively: *prātaḥsāvaḥ* [is derived from] *prātaḥsavanam*,
with the locative case ending changed to *su*.
At that very place during the morning libation, the first drinking indeed belongs to Indra; for in the draughts dedicated to Indra-Agni and others, it is known that Indra drinks alone.
In the case of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the acute accent falls on the end of the first member due to its inclusion in the *dāsībhārādi* group;
alternatively, it may be a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
Therefore, O hero, O capable one, rejoice—be glad—to slay the enemies.
And let us proclaim with hymns, with praises, your heroic deeds characterized by the slaying of Vṛtra and other such exploits.
O Indra, come with that chariot of yours which is swifter than thought, for the drinking of Soma.
Let your bay steeds hasten quickly, those bulls with whom you come, rejoicing.

O Indra, let that chariot of yours which is swifter than thought come hither for the drinking of Soma; come quickly! Let your bay steeds, those stallions with which you go while rejoicing, hasten forward.
O Indra, with that chariot of yours which is swifter than thought and moves with exceeding speed, come hither—to our Soma-drinking—to drink our Soma.
The root *pā* means "to drink. By the rule *aco yat*, the suffix *yat* is applied; by the rule *īyati*, the substitution of *ī* occurs.
The guna substitution is conditioned by the fact that [the suffix] is an *ārdhadhātuka* affix;
the word-accent is that of the original form of the final member of the compound.
Likewise, let those *haris*—your horses yoked to the chariot—run forth quickly (*tūyam*) toward us;
let them proceed. With those stallions (*vṛṣabhaiḥ*), being exhilarated (*mandamānaḥ*) and rejoicing, you go.

One should not object that Indra has only two horses based on the statement "Indra’s two *haris*" (Nirukta 1.15.1), for this is seen in other Vedic citations such as "A thousand, a hundred [horses] toward you" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.1.24).
With green-hued splendor and with the most excellent forms of the sun, cause your body to be radiant.
O Indra, being invoked by us, your friends, sit down and rejoice together with us in harmony.

With the splendor of the sun, which is possessed of tawny steeds, and with the most excellent forms, make thy body radiant; O Indra, being invoked by us who are thy friends, sit down and rejoice in our company. 3.
1. The word *ta-bha-*, meaning "excessively," is not present.
O Indra, [you who are] possessed of the Maruts (*harivat*).
The substitution of *v* [for *s*] occurs by the rule "jhayaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.10), following the suffix *amtu* of the word *hariścchada*.

With a golden-yellow hue like that of the sun’s brilliance and splendor, and with forms as excellent, most praiseworthy, and refined as those of the Ashmīyas, he expands his own body— or my own; or else,
"tanūyam" refers to a portion of the body.
Touch that; make it endowed with splendor. Furthermore, may it be auspicious.
The suffix *kha* is applied [to the root *śvi*] optionally in the sense of "speediness," according to the rule *vibhāṣā śver ādikṣiprayām*.
Being invoked—that is, being summoned—by us, your friends who have become companions with great friends, do you, having descended and seated yourself at the sacrifice, rejoice;
be gladdened by the drinking of Soma.
Whose greatness, in the exhilarations of the soma-juice, these two great worlds, heaven and earth, have not been able to contain like a ship—
come to that dwelling-place, O Indra, with your beloved, harnessed bay horses, toward our dear friend.

O Indra, those two great worlds, heaven and earth, could not fully express that greatness of yours in your states of exhilaration. Come to that dwelling with your harnessed, beloved bay horses, toward the beloved food.

O Indra, those two great worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), do not separate—that is, do not distinguish—that greatness of yours which arises during the exhilarations produced by the drinking of Soma;
rather, they both abide within your very majesty.
The root *vi-cir* means "to separate.
It belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class.
In the *laṅ* [tense], [the rule] "a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical designation is not mandatory" applies.
Thus ends the section on the absence of accentual qualities due to repetition (*abhyāsa*); as in the case of *ugādanighāta*.
Come with your beloved, most dear, harnessed bay horses toward our pleasing, gratifying food characterized by Soma; come toward that dwelling, our sacrificial feast.

O Indra, for him whose enemies you have perpetually made powerless through your irresistible and delightful deeds—O Indra, he stirs up for you abundant wisdom and power; this Soma is pressed for your exhilaration.

O Indra, that Soma which you have ever drunk, for which you have performed deeds against the enemies that cannot be imitated and which are worthy of delight—that very Soma stirs up your overflowing power; it has been pressed for your exhilaration, O Indra. 5.
He, Indra, having drunk; for the root *pibati*, the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule "after a monosyllabic root ending in a vowel, the augment *iṭ* is added."

"You have drunk the Soma with a weapon that is *raṇyā*—meaning, by virtue of its capacity to slay the enemy in a single stroke, being devoid of imitation (*anānukṛtyā*), and suited for battle (*sāṃyugīna*)";
from the word *raṇa*, the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of "excellent" according to Pāṇini 5.1.97.
For whichever sacrificer you have repeatedly, many times, struck down his enemies.

The root *kṛñ* is used in the sense of "injury. In the *liṭ* (perfect) tense, in the case of *thala*, because it is not subject to the rule of non-udātta (*anighāta*), it retains the accent of the *liṭ* suffix.
Or rather, he impels—that is, sends forth—for your sake great power and abundant praise.
The root *ṛ* means "to go.
It belongs to the *jauhotyādi* (third) class.
By the rule "*atipiipavyoḥ*" [Pāṇini 7.4.75], the vowel of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is changed to *i*.
The substitution *iyaṅ* occurs by the rule "abhyāsasyāsavarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.4.78).
That Soma, pressed for Indra, is sufficient for your exhilaration;
or rather,
that Soma is pressed by the sacrificer.
There is a transposition of words. He impels the pressed Soma for its own exhilaration.
This is your cup, O Indra, filled with the finest wealth; drink the Soma from it, O Lord of a hundred powers! It is full, a vessel of intoxicating liquor, which all these gods together offer to you.
This is your vessel, found by the seers; O Indra, drink the Soma from it, O Śatakratu! The ladle is full of the exhilarating, intoxicating juice, which all the gods indeed desire. 6.

1. *gara-indrasya*; ta1.2.3.607.8-bha1.2.4.8-mu-kiṃtu tasya; bha7-kiṃtu | 2. ga-ta1.2.3.6 7.8-bha-mu-pāte | 3. ta-bha-mu-sayuṅginenāyudhena | 4. ta-bha-prāgavahatiyo | 5. ga-ta-bha-yathā | O Indra, for you (*te*)—for your sake—the vessel, such as the *camasa* cup and so forth, has been found (*sanavittam*).
It has been obtained by us from long ago.
In the sense of acquisition; the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used in the sense of the object.
O Śatakratu, you of many deeds, Indra, drink this Soma with this vessel.
For the vessel for drinking—a specific type of cup serving as a drinking place—of the intoxicating wine, the honey, and the soma, has become full, that is, filled.
The root *heñ* is used in the sense of competition (*spardhā*).
The word *āhāva* is derived as an irregular form (*nipātita*) according to Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.74: "A water-trough is called *āhāva*."
"The gods, being summoned by hymns of praise, drink the Soma here"—
this is the rule for [the suffixes] *tha*, *thā*, and so forth.
Whomever all the gods— the Viśvedevas— honor (abhi-yarhanti), that is, desire intensely;
[the root] *harya* means "to move" or "to desire," and belongs to the Bhūvādigaṇa.
Just as, when there is an absence of *nighāta* for the finite verb (*tiṅ*), there is *nighāta* of the movement (*gati*) by the rule "when a *tik* [element] is accented."

For indeed, O Indra, bull, many people with prepared offerings yearn for you in many ways. May these most honey-sweet [offerings] of ours be yours; hear them all, and take pleasure in them. 7. vi | hi | tvām | indra | purudhā | janāsaḥ | hita-prayasaḥ | vṛṣabha | haryante | asmākam | te | madhumat-tamāni | imā | bhuvan | sarvāṇi | te | teṣu | harya || 7 ||
O Indra, O bull, showerer of desires, [we],
the people who have prepared the oblation— people who offer the *prayas* (sacrificial food), so called because it causes satisfaction— and who have gathered the offerings, [pray to you] in many ways.
The word *hi* is used for emphasis;
they *vi-haryante*, that is, they invoke you in various ways.
The root *hañ* is used in the sense of competition (*spardhā*). The *ātmanepada* ending is applied according to the rule *nisamupavibhyo haḥ*.
These libations here, which are our own, have become exceedingly rich in sweetness and abundant in soma for your sake;
therefore, take pleasure in those libations and desire the soma.

O Indra, I shall proclaim those former deeds, and now indeed the first heroic exploits you performed. With true wrath, you loosened the mountain; you made the cow easy to find for the one who offers prayer. 8. O Indra, I shall proclaim those ancient deeds, and now indeed the first heroic exploits you performed. With true wrath, you loosened the mountain; you made the cow easy to find for the one who offers prayer. 8.
O Indra, I shall now—this very day—proclaim in detail your heroic deeds (*vīryā*), those which were first performed by you from the beginning, and those ancient ones from of old.
The word *ekaḥ* is used as a filler.
I have spoken.
In the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, *bhuvaḥ* becomes *vaciḥ*; [and] in the *clī* (subjunctive) tense, there is *aṅ*.
Which are they? "Satīnamanyu. *Satīna* is a name for water.
Possessing the intent to rain down water, you loosened the mountain-cloud and struck the serpent with your thunderbolt.
"For Brahmā and Bṛhaspati, you made the cow—stolen by the Paṇis, yet easily known (*suvedanā*, i.e., easily to be identified)—[your own]," and so forth.

Sit down well among the hosts, O Lord of the Hosts; they call you the wisest of seers. Nothing whatsoever is done without you in this world; O Maghavan, praise the great hymn of praise! 9. Sit down well among the hosts, O Lord of the Hosts; they call you the wisest of seers. Nothing whatsoever is done without you in this world; O Maghavan, praise the great hymn of praise! 9.
O Gaṇapati, sit down well— be seated— for the purpose of hearing our hymns among the hosts of worshippers;
for they call you the wisest among poets, those of transcendent insight.
Furthermore, in the competition between you and Ta-bha, there is no speech [or] vigor in Ga-ta4.5-ma, except for Ṛte.
The ablative case ending is used according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 2.3.29: *anyārāditarartebhyaḥ*.
Except for one's own [self], no action whatsoever—whether far away, near, or in between—is left undone;
therefore, O Nīpāt.

Then, O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, having fashioned our hymn (*arka*)—which is great, worthy of worship, characterized by the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* stomas, and manifold in form—into something wonderful, do you honor it with praise.
Dhidhehi. The root *arc*, meaning "to worship," belongs to the Bhvādi class.
O Maghavan, be mindful of us;
O Lord of Wealth, among our friends, be the one who awakens us.
O maker of joy, grant us delight; O you of true vigor, break even those who hold back, and lead us toward wealth.

O Maghavan, O friend, take note of us as we approach you; O Lord of Wealth, O creator of joy, grant joy to your friends. O you of true strength, even if we have not shared in it, grant us a portion of wealth. 10.
O Maghavan, O possessor of wealth, [help] us who are crying out for you, O Moon-like one.
The root *yāc* (to beg), belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*,
is *anudātta-ita*.

Make us, who are entreating you, endowed with *abhikhyā*— that is, with manifest splendor— or indeed, make us renowned. O friend, O giver of wealth, O Lord of treasures (*vasupate*), you who are our friend through our state as singers, take heed of (*bodhi*) our hymns that are being sung.
The root *budh* is used in the sense of "understanding.
It belongs to the Bhvādi class.
In the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*, which is a Vedic usage.
By the rule *chandasyubhayathā*, because the suffix *hi* is treated as non-ārdhadhātuka, it is *ṅit*; consequently, by the rule *aditaśca*, *hi* is replaced by *dhi*.
For this very reason, there is *guṇa* substitution.
Because it is *sārvadhātuka*, it is *ṅit*, and thus [the root] has an udātta accent on its final syllable.
The elision of the vowel is a Vedic archaism (chāndasa).
O you who have made war with enemies, O you whose vigor is true to its name, perform the battle;
slay the foes!
In the imperative (loṭ) of the root *kṛ*, there is the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* according to the rule "śru-śṛṇu-pṛ-kṛ-bhyaś chandasi."
Furthermore, even though this place is unworthy of worship, bestow upon us a share; grant us wealth and make us partakers.
In the *saṃhitā* [text], there is a long vowel [substitution] by the rule "aco 'stiṅaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.127).
In the tenth section (anuvāka), there are sixteen hymns (sūkta).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "tam asya," is dedicated to Indra;
its seer (ṛṣi) is Vairūpa, named Śataprabhedana.
The other [verse] is a *triṣṭubh*, and the remaining ones are *jagatīs*.
Thus it has been enumerated: "In this [hymn], the breaker of a hundred [fortresses] ends with a *triṣṭubh*.
This hymn is the *mahattvatīya* at the eighth day of the ten-day sacrifice (*daśarātra*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The verse beginning with 'tamasya dyāvāpṛthivī mahī' and 'indro nṛvad' is the Marutvatīya [śastra]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.7).
May Heaven and Earth, being of one mind with all the gods, favor his impetuous strength;
when he went forth displaying his Indra-like greatness, having drunk of the Soma, he grew mighty in wisdom.

Heaven and Earth accompanied him; with all the gods they aided his impetuous strength when he went forth, performing his great Indra-power. Having drunk of the Soma, the wise one increased in might. ||1||
Together with the conscious one, the two conscious ones; heaven and earth, the pair heaven-and-earth; together with all the gods—of this [one].
The substitute *aś* for the pronoun *enad* in subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) is unaccented. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.32)
May they protect—that is, guard—this *śuṣma*, the power that withers enemies, of this Indra.
The sense is: "May his power first protect us, and afterwards may these [others] also protect us. This is the *laṅ* (imperfect) form of the root *ava*.
Performing the slaying of Vṛtra and other deeds, he attained his own greatness, Indra-like power, and sufficient heroic vigor whenever it occurred.
The root *iṇ* means "to go. It belongs to the *ad-ādi* (second) class. By the rule "of *āṅ* and so forth," the augment *āṭ* is applied.
Then, being in his season and possessing the power of action, having drunk of the Soma, he grew strong.
The technical designation *saṃpradāna* is applied to the object [of the action] by the rule "the mention of *kriyā* must be made.
The genitive case is used by the rule "frequently in the sense of the dative.
[The form is] *pītvī*.
It is established as an indeclinable by the rule "svāryādayaśca."
1. In the *ta-bha* [meter], "abhikhyā" does not exist.
2. Another *triṣṭubh* [verse] has an additional hundredfold division; Ṛgveda 4.46.

Viṣṇu, having impelled the stalk of the intoxicating Soma with his might, proclaims aloud the greatness of this Indra through his own power. Having slain Vṛtra together with the gods—the Maruts—who were his companions, Indra, the bounteous one, became the most desirable of all. *Viṣṇu*: the one named Viṣṇu; Vyāsa, or the sacrifice. *Madhunaḥ*: of the intoxicating Soma. *Aṃśum*: the stalk, a portion of the plant. *Dadhanvān*: impelling, setting in motion. (In this context, after the root *dhā*, the augment *iṭ* is added by rule, and the vowel is elided before the suffix *kan*). *Ojasā*: with his own vigor. *Asya*: of this [Indra]. *Tam mahimānam*: that greatness. *Vi rapsate*: he proclaims aloud in various ways; he praises. *Maghavā*: the bounteous one, the possessor of wealth. *Sayāvabhiḥ*: with those who go along with him. (From the root *yā*, the suffix *kanip* is applied according to the rule "āto maninkvanibvanipaśca"). *Devebhiḥ*: with the gods, the Maruts. *Vṛtram jaghanvān*: having slain Vṛtra. *Indraḥ*: Indra. *Abhavat vareṇyaḥ*: he became the one to be chosen, the one to be honored by all.

When, bearing weapons, you stood together with the serpent Vṛtra for battle, so that praise might be found; then all the Maruts, together with their own selves, increased your fierce majesty and Indra-power. When, bearing weapons—such as the thunderbolt and others—for the sake of combat, you, O Indra, stood together with the serpent Vṛtra, who was to be slain; [then] praise was found. "Praise" (*śaṃsam*) refers to the act of praising with words; I offer hymns to declare your heroic deeds, such as the slaying of Vṛtra. Furthermore, O fierce one of exalted strength, at this very moment, all the Maruts, together with their own selves, increased your majesty and Indra-power. The elision of the vowel is a Vedic archaism. Indeed, the Maruts are the source of Indra’s heroism.

As soon as he was born, he drove away his rivals; the hero looked out toward manly valor and the battle. He split the mountain, released the flowing waters, and by his skillful work propped up the broad firmament. As soon as he was born (*jajñāna eva*), he drove away (*vyabādhata*) his rivals (*spṛdhaḥ*). The hero (*vīraḥ*) looked forth (*prāpaśyat*) toward his own manly power (*pauṃsyam*) and the fray (*raṇam*). He split (*avṛścat*) the mountain (*adrim*); he released (*avasṛjat*) the flowing waters (*susyadaḥ*); and by his skillful action (*svapastyayā*), he propped up (*astabhnāt*) the vast sky (*nākam pṛthum*). The word *jajñāna* is from the root *jan*, meaning "to appear"; it is the *kānac* suffix used for the Vedic perfect tense. As soon as he was being born, he intensely oppressed (*atyartham apīḍayat*) his rivals—the enemies. *Spṛdhaḥ* is derived from the root *spṛdh* (meaning "to contend"); the suffix *kvip* is applied, and the form is established here just as in the Vedic irregularity *apaspṛdhethām*, where vocalization is seen. Thus, being a capable hero, he looked toward the battle and beheld his own strength. He perceived with excellence: "Such is the extent of his power. Furthermore, he split the mountain—the cloud—for the sake of raining; thereafter, he released the flowing waters—those that flow down—and sent them forth downward. Likewise, he [propped up] the broad...
1. Ta1.2.3: They stood firm against Vṛtra;
2. Ta1.2.3.6.7.8-Bha1.2.4.8: for the sake of raining down and so forth, [they reached] the great *nāka*, the heavenly world, through their skillful action (*svapastayā*).
The suffix *kyac* is applied after the word *sup* [meaning "desire for"] when used reflexively. By the rule *a-pratyayāt* (Pāṇini 3.3.102), the feminine form is derived by adding the suffix *ap*.
Out of a desire for auspicious action, he *astamnāt*—
he brought it to a standstill.
The root *stambh* is a verbal root listed in the Sūtra.
Then Indra, the good protector, exerted his powers; he pushed heaven and earth far apart.
He hurled the iron thunderbolt at the enemy, bringing auspiciousness to Mitra, Varuṇa, and the donor.
Indra truly brought forth his powers; he forced asunder heaven and earth. Boldly he hurled the iron thunderbolt, bringing welfare to Mitra, Varuṇa, and the donor. 5.

Moreover, that Indra *overcame* (approached) the great powers, the vast armies, all at once (*satrā*). [The root] *pad* means "to go"; it belongs to the *divādi* class, with a metathesis of the vowels. Alternatively, it has the sense of "to rule" (*pathati*). He rules over the armies; the meaning is that he became their lord. He, by his even greater majesty, *oppressed* heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*)—the word *varīyaḥ* being the form of the instrumental case. He crushed the enemies situated between them. Being *bold* (*dhṛṣitaḥ*), confident in slaying the foe, he *wielded* (*avābharat*) the iron (*āyasa*) thunderbolt (*vajra*). For what purpose? To bring *bliss* (*śevaṃ*)—that is, happiness—to Mitra, Varuṇa, and the donor who has offered oblations, the sacrificer. 14.
Then, for the sake of Indra’s powers, the swelling ones rushed forth to satisfy his wrathful intent;
when the fierce one, with his might, cut Vṛtra asunder—he who bore the waters and was encompassed by darkness.

Of Indra, here, for the sake of his powers, the three-fold swelling ones hastened forth for his wrath, as he, the fierce one, cut Vṛtra asunder with his might—he who bore the waters and was encompassed by darkness. ||6||

At this very moment, they hastened forth for the sake of the majesty—the power—for the wrathful manifestation of Indra, who is vast, roaring aloud in various ways, and increasing [in strength] by harming his enemies. (The dative case here functions in the sense of the ablative. For the purpose of terrifying [his foes], they rushed forward.
The waters went out;
this is the meaning of *rahigartya*.
He, the fierce one (*ugra*), the uplifted one, [beheld] the waters (*apaḥ*)—the waters (*udakāni*)—bearing [them], holding [them], enveloped on all sides by darkness (*tamasā parīvṛtam*).
The suffix *kta* is applied to the root *vṛṇoti* in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The accent is determined by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*.
In the *saṃhitā*, there is lengthening according to *upasargasya ghañi* (Pāṇini 6.3.122).
When he, by means of his might—that is, by his own heroic power—cut him asunder, he then slew Vṛtra.
Having performed their first heroic deeds, the two who abide in greatness have come together;
the thick darkness was cast away, for Indra, the great one, was struck down in the first invocation.

Having performed the first heroic deeds with their great powers, the two moving together encountered the thick darkness; it was cast down when Indra, having slain [Vṛtra], prevailed at the great morning invocation.

Striving with their great and glorious inherent powers, Indra and Vṛtra exerted themselves for battle; those various heroic deeds (*vīryāṇi*) which were to be performed—actions that had previously occurred—they both joined together and accomplished. (Note: The suffix *tvan* is used here in the sense of the verbal root *kṛ*, meaning "to do" or "to perform.")
The root *iṇ* means "to go.
In the perfect tense (*liṭ*), there is lengthening by the rule *dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.4.69).

Between those two, [he] rules over the army (senā); he rules over the army of the burden (bhara-senām īṣṭe). 2. He supported (ādhārayat). 3. For the purpose of causing them to flee (apahlāpanāya). 4. "Indra and Vṛtra" does not exist [in this version].
When Vṛtra was slain by Indra, the darkness—an exceedingly dense gloom—was cast down.
It became utterly destroyed and ruined.
The *liṭ* [perfect] suffix follows the root *dhvaṃs*.
There is elision of the *kvi* suffix and so forth, as well as the elision of the *an* augment.
But Indra, by his own great majesty, arrived at the first oblation during the initial invocation;
the meaning is that he alone was the very first among the heroes to be summoned.

All the gods indeed increased your manly powers with speech accompanied by Soma. With the blow of Indra, [he struck] Rudra, Vṛtra, and the serpent; like Agni with his jaws, he caused the food to satisfy [the hunger]. 8. viśve | devāsaḥ | artha | vṛṣṇyāni | te | avardhayan | soma-vatayā | vacasyayā | rudram | vṛtram | ahim | indrasya | hanmanā | agniḥ | na | jambhaiḥ | tṛpṇum | annam | āvayat || 8 ||

O Indra, immediately after the slaying of Vṛtra, all the gods—the officiating priests—by means of a speech-filled desire for praise (*vacasyā*), that is, a hymn accompanied by Soma, have strengthened and continue to strengthen your manly powers (*vṛṣṇyāni*).
The word *hanman* refers to Indra’s act of slaying; *han* is a root meaning "to strike" or "to kill.
*Arcati* is a verb meaning "to praise."
"I shall worship the gods; give them [those things].

In *mamyatelaṃṭi*, there is elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* suffix by the rule "the *vikaraṇa* is frequently elided in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), and the augment *aṭ* is added to the suffix *sip*.
Because *sipaḥ* is unaccented due to its being a suffix (*pi-stveṇa*), the accent falls on the verbal root (*dhātu-svara*).
With those *sugebhiḥ*—meaning "by easy paths" or "by means of wealth" or "by means of hymns" that are well-traversed—we may cross over *viśvā duritā*, all difficulties or sins.
O Indra, in this rite, graciously (*su*) recognize with great extent (*urviyā*) and high honor our hymn (*stotra*) which is being composed and performed for us.
Vidūṣaka: You surely know.

The second hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “gharmā,” is dedicated to the Viśvedevas. The seer (ṛṣi) is Sadhri by name, a descendant of Virūpa; or it is Dharma, the son of Tapas. The fourth verse is in the Jagatī meter; the remaining verses are in the Triṣṭubh meter. Thus it has been declared: “gharmā: [the seer is] Sadhri or Tāpasa, [the deity is] Vaiśvadeva; the fourth [verse] is in Jagatī. The application (viniyoga) [of this hymn] has been explained.
The heat pervaded the threefold world on all sides; from those two, the mother came forth as the age of the horses.
Desiring to obtain the milk of heaven, she trembled like one who has turned away; the gods [attained] the hymn of a thousand powers.

The two Gharma oblations, having equal ends, have spread out through the threefold [sacrifice]. Mātariśvan has gone to the pleasure of those two. Desiring to obtain the milk from heaven, they trembled; the gods knew the hymn of the one who is victorious. 1.
On all sides, on every side, reaching to the limits of the directions, are the *gharmas*.
[The root] *ghṛ* means "to flow" and "to shine.
The two shining *gharmas* are the two other suns; they are threefold.
Because of the traditional teaching: "These three worlds are indeed threefold" (Ai.
Ā. 1.1.2), they have pervaded the three worlds;
they have pervaded them with their own splendors.
Mātariśvan is the wind moving in the intermediate space;
he attained the favor— that is, the affection— of those two, Agni and Āditya,
when [he was] "possessing a thousand melodies."
The word *sāman* is indicative [of all the Vedas];
it is accompanied by the splendor of the three Vedas, because of the scriptural tradition: "All splendor is indeed eternally of the nature of the *sāman*" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.2).
The radiant gods, consisting of light, knew—that is, they found and obtained—such a sun, worthy of worship.
Then, desiring to support—that is, having the nature of sustaining—the worlds, they pervaded the waters of the path belonging to heaven; that is to say, they clothed themselves in them.

In the word *divaspayaḥ*, the substitution of *s* for the genitive case ending occurs by the rule *ṣaṣṭhyāḥ patiputrau*. [The form] *didhiṣāṇāḥ* [is derived from the root] *dhip* in the sense of "holding."
The suffix *cānaś*; the elision (*ślū*) of the root *śap*;
or alternatively:
The root *dhṛ* means "to hold.
The suffix *ānaś* is used for the desiderative (*sananta*) form.
The absence of lengthening (as in *añjanagamāṃ sani*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively:

The two *gharmas*, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who are equal, united, and self-luminous, pervade the triple *māyā* consisting of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Mātariśvan, the Supreme Self, as the controller, attained *jṛṣṭi*—the joy arising from the objects of enjoyment—for those two in their relationship as the controller and the controlled.
He has gone;
the gods know him as this Sūrya, who consists of the Veda.
Three Nirṛtis wait upon the one worthy of praise, for they, far-famed, truly know the means of conveyance.
The sages have discerned their foundation, they who abide in distant and secret ordinances.
Three Niyut-steeds wait upon the Ordainer; far-famed indeed are those bearers, for the sages have discerned their foundation, they who abide in distant and secret ordinances. 2.

The Nirṛtis have taken hold of the earth; by this, the other two worlds are also indicated. Therein, the three deities beginning with Agni abide, and for the sake of instruction—that is, for the offering of oblations—they wait upon [the sacrificers]. The sacrificers perform their worship. Consequently, those deities, who are far-famed (*dīrghaśrutaḥ*)—possessing abundant renown—and who are the bearers (*vahyaḥ*) that convey the world, distinguish them; they indeed recognize the worship performed by these [sacrificers]. Or else:
1. *ga-ta-bha-mu-’su* does not exist. 2. *tā.1.2.3.6.7.8-bha-vavarṣuḥ*. 3. *ga-ta2. 3.6.7.8-bha-dhipu*. 4. *ga-ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha1.2.4.8-gamitavān*.
Regarding *nirṛtīḥ*: they are called *nirṛtayaḥ* because they go (*ṛcchanti*) or proceed (*gacchanti*) without remainder (*niḥśeṣeṇa*).

Those three—creation, maintenance, and dissolution—they worship for the sake of the Self’s presiding over the granting of the fruits of karma; they are "long-hearers" (*dīrghaśrutaḥ*), meaning they have heard long within the long cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) and know the objects of thought and perception, yet do not know the true nature of those objects of mantra and perception.
For this very reason, they are "bearers" (*vahyaḥ*), the carriers of transmigration, and they do not know [the Truth].

But the seers of all-pervading vision have thoroughly discerned—that is, they know—the cause, the fundamental source, which is the Supreme Self, of those [activities] such as creation and so forth, or of those [beings] such as the one consisting of food (annamaya) and so forth.

Or, they have discerned the cause of those activities that exist regarding other superior or secret matters, such as the duties of cows and others, or the observances (vrata) consisting of restraints (yama), regulations (niyama), and so on; they know them.
The root *ciñ* means "to pile.
In the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*), by the rule "optionally for *añj*" (*vibhāṣāñjeḥ*), there is a substitution of a guttural (*ka-varṇa*) for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*). Alternatively:
In the case of the root *cāy* in the *liṭ* [perfect] tense, the substitute *kī* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.35, "cāyaḥ kī," which applies specifically to the Vedic language (*chandasi*).
The young woman with four braids, well-adorned, clothed in wisdom, wears clarified butter as her face;
upon her two strong-winged males have settled, where the gods have established their portion.

The four-crested maiden, well-formed and beautiful of face with ghee, clothes herself in sacred ordinances. Upon her two strong-winged bulls have settled, where the gods have established their allotted portion.

The altar is four-cornered, having four hair-knots; it is a young woman, beautiful in form, well-adorned with fine ornaments, and having ghee as its face—that is, having ghee as the primary oblation. It clothes itself in *vayunāni*—the things to be known, whether they be categories of objects, ritual acts, or hymns of praise.

Upon that altar, the two "bulls"—the two who rain down through the oblation—the two "fair-winged" ones (*suparṇau*) who fly beautifully, namely the wife and husband, or the sacrificer and the Brahman priest, have sat down.
There, upon that altar, the gods, Agni and the others, [receive] their allotted portion.
The suffix -dheya is used in its own sense (svārthika).
They have offered—that is, they maintain—their own respective portions as the oblation;
or alternatively:

She who has four braids—namely, the four classes of words, nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles, which stand in the place of her braids—is that youthful maiden, eternal, whose limbs (or aspects) shine like clarified butter; she, the Vedic Speech (*vāg upaniṣad*), clothes herself in *vayunāni*, that is, in knowledges.
Upon that Speech, two fair-winged birds (*suparṇau*)—the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—are seated. Where...
In the rule "itarābhyo 'pi dṛśyante," the suffix *na* is used in the sense of the third case;
for example: *vācā devā bhāgaṃ dhārayanti*.
The single Suparṇa has entered the ocean; he gazes upon this entire world.
With a simple mind, I beheld him from nearby: the Mother licks him, and he licks the Mother.

The single one, the fair-winged bird, has entered the ocean; he gazes upon this entire world. With a simple mind, I have beheld him who is near at hand. The Mother licks him, and he, in turn, licks the Mother.
Alone, without companion in all his undertakings, the fair-winged, well-flying god who dwells in the intermediate space has entered the ocean, the atmosphere; and having entered it,
he beholds this entire universe, the whole world— the totality of beings—
looking upon it with favor.
I saw—that is, I beheld—such a god from nearby, that is, in close proximity, with a mind that was matured and fully ripened.
Furthermore, the mother—the creative source of waters, namely the intermediate speech (mādhyamikī vāk)—licks it, that is, she tastes it;
here, only mere subsistence is indicated.
He indeed licks and lolls his mother’s speech;
he subsists on that very thing.
[The root] *lih* means "to taste."
Alternatively:
the "fair-winged one" (*suparṇaḥ*)—meaning the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which possesses wings and moves without support, or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—[enters] the ocean;
that is, it enters into the ocean.

1. *ta-ma* 1.2.4.8: long vowel (*dīrgham*). 2. *ga-ta-ma*: the word "aprateṣu" is absent. 3. *ta-bha-mu*: the substitution of the *ka*-class (*kavargādeśaḥ*). 4. *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bhara.4.8*: *dadhaṃta*.
"The ocean" (*samudram*) is the intermediate space (*antarikṣam*), because the waters (*āpaḥ*) arise from it.
Or else: [the rest of the passage].

Flowing toward the ocean means moving everywhere; he entered into that which is characterized by such a nature, born of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), according to the Vedic scripture: "Having created that, he entered into it" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.6).
In the case of Vāyu, he entered [the world] in the form of air and so forth.
He beholds—meaning he specifically pervades—this entire universe, all the worlds.
For when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) or the Supreme Self exists, living persons cause the world to become renowned.
I, an upāsaka, [worship] that God from all sides with a mind matured by ripened knowledge (pāka).

The suffix *tasi* is added after the word *antika*. According to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 6.4.149, "In place of *antika*, when *tasi* follows, there is elision of the *kādi* portion and the word becomes ādyudātta," there occurs the elision of the *kādi* portion.
I saw it nearby, in my own heart.
The mother, Speech, swallowed that breath;
the meaning is that Speech is contained within Breath.
For during sleep, the activity of speech is not observed, whereas the activity of breath is indeed observed.
The wise poets, with their hymns, fashion the single Suparṇa in many ways;
establishing the meters at the sacrifices, they measure out twelve cups of Soma.
The wise poets, with their hymns, fashion the one Suparṇa in many ways; establishing the meters at the sacrifices, they measure out twelve cups of Soma.

The wise, intelligent, and poetic men of lovely insight fashion—that is, they construct—in many ways through words characterized by praise, the Supreme Self who is the single, well-winged (suparṇa) one.

Furthermore, those same poets, maintaining the seven meters such as Gāyatrī and others during the sacrificial rites (*adhvara*), measure out—that is, they fashion—the twelve cups (*graha*) of Soma, such as the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma, which are the vessels used for the extraction of the juice.
The *grahas*.
They are called *grahas* because things are seized (*gṛhyate*) by means of them; the suffix *ap* is applied in the sense of an instrument according to the rule "graha-vṛ-ni-bhṛ-gam-śra."
In the word *somasya*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
In the word *dvādaśa*, the original accent of the first member of the compound is applied by the rule *saṃkhyā* (Pāṇini 6.2.35).
Arranging thirty-six and four, and establishing the meters up to twelve,
the seers, having measured out the sacrifice with their wisdom, set the chariot in motion by means of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*.

Thirty-six; four; fashioning; the meters; and establishing them up to twelve; having measured out the sacrifice with their wisdom, the sages set the chariot in motion by means of the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman*. 6.
Previously, the sacrificial cups (*yajñagraha*) were mentioned in general; now, the sacrifice consisting of all the cups and other elements is described.
There are thirty-six [cups]:
two are the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma*.
There are eight two-deity cups beginning with the Aindravāyava;
two [cups] for the Śukra and Manthin;
and three [cups], namely the Āgrayaṇa, the Ukthya, and the Dhruva.
There are twelve Ṛtugraha cups;
two for Indra and Agni and for the Viśvedevas;
and three Marutvatīya cups.
There is one Māhendra cup; two Āditya and Sādhin cups;
and three cups consisting of the Vaiśvadeva, the Pātnīvata, and the Hāriyojana.
Thus, there are thirty-six.
In the Atyagniṣṭoma, there are the previous thirty-six cups, plus four more: the two Aṃśu and Ābhya cups, the Dadhigraha, and the Ṣoḍaśin;
thus, they prepare these forty cups, filling them with Soma.
Furthermore, regarding "ādvādaśam":
by the rule *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.13), this is an avyayībhāva compound; its accent is as follows.
Up until the conclusion of the twelve-fold *prauga* and other *śastra*s:
1. *ga*-samudaṃnaṃ; tā1.2.3.6.7.8-samaṃdanaṃ; ta4.5-samudajaṃ; bhara4.4-sumadaṃtaṃ; bha7-samudranaṃ | 2.
tā1.2.3.6.7.8-bha- sarvato ...... [this is] not present in the *vāyupakṣa*.
3. Ga in the form of external wind; Tā1.2.3.6.7.8-Bha in the form of wind. 4. Tā1.2.3.6.7.8-Bhara4.8-Sadevamu. 5. Ta4.5-Relha.
The activity of speech is observed at the time of study; for the vital breath indeed devours the mother, speech. 6. *Ga*: twelve, meaning those numbered as twelve.
7. Then, thirty-six [grahas] in number; thereafter, the four grahas.

These are recited in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "By means of the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (apāna) alone are the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [grahas]. 8. In the manuscripts Ta and Bha, the word "three" (trayaḥ) is not present.

The seers (*kavayaḥ*), upholding the *gāyatrī* and other meters in the form of the *stṛta*, *śākhā*, and so forth— by means of their inspired thought (*manīṣā*) [the instrumental case ending *-ā* being substituted for the third case ending *-ābhiḥ*]— having thus measured out and constructed the sacrifice as a chariot.
"Delightful is this place"—here, "chariot" refers to the sacrifice.
They set forth that chariot, the sacrifice, by means of the *Ṛg* and *Sāman* [Vedas], that is, they bring it to completion in an excellent manner.
In the word *caturaḥ*, there is an udātta accent on the final syllable according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.167: *caturaḥ śasi*.
Fourteen other powers belong to him; the seven sages lead them forth with their speech.
Who here can declare the ford, the path by which they drink of the pressed soma?
Fourteen others are his majesties; the wise lead him forward with their speech. Who here has proclaimed the sevenfold ford, the path by which they drink of the pressed juice?
Of this Supreme Self in the form of sacrifice, there are fourteen other glories, that is, manifestations numbering fourteen.

Wise and intelligent priests, such as the Hotṛ and others, seven in number, lead forth that sacrifice with their speech in the form of ritual recitations (śastra). They lead it forward to its full realization. It is the Self (Ātman).
The root *ā-plu* means "to pervade.

In the formation of this word, the suffix *ānaś* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchilika*), and there is an interchange of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) by way of grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).

Who has proclaimed, who speaks here at this sacrifice of that ford which is characterized by knowledge, capable of delivering one from sin, and situated between the sacrificial pit (*cātvāla*) and the mound (*utkara*)—by which path, by which sacrificial route, the gods drink, indeed drink excessively, the pressed Soma? None at all; such is the meaning.
In the sense of "drinking" (*pāna*), the substitute *piba* is applied according to the rule beginning with *pāghrā*;
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
This is a compound with a prefix (*upasarga*).

Because there is no suppression of accent (*anighāta*) due to the presence of *yad*, the prefix undergoes suppression of accent (*nighāta*) by the rule "and [a word] before a non-verbal form that possesses an udātta accent."
In a thousand ways there are fifteen hymns; as vast as heaven and earth are, so great is this.
A thousandfold are the greatnesses, a thousand; as far as Brahman extends, so far extends speech.
A thousandfold are the fifteen hymns; as vast as heaven and earth are, so great is that [Vāk]. A thousandfold are its greatnesses, a thousandfold as far as Brahman extends, so great is Vāk. 8.
In the thousands—that is, in the thousands of bodies ranging from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—there are fifteen [components]:
the five, namely eye, ear, mind, speech, and breath;
and the ten elements in the form of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, which have come from the mother and father as their substrata and are combined therein.
Thus, fifteen-fold hymns (ukthas), which are constituent parts, exist within the bodies of living beings that have been born;
[so too do] heaven and earth.
In the case of the genitive dual ending, there is a long vowel homogeneous with the preceding one by the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39).

Whatever the extent—that is, whatever the measure—of heaven and earth, to that very same extent does the body of a living being, presided over by the Self, come to be. In the words *yāvat* and *tāvat*, the long vowel [ā] is applied according to the rules: *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatuṣ* (Pāṇini 5.2.39) and *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.91).
Furthermore, "in a thousand ways" means that there are a thousand greatnesses— that is, thousands of great specific modes of activity—
because the accomplishment of activities such as seeing and hearing occurs for every object and at every moment.
In the word *sahasradhā*, the suffix *dhā* is used in the sense of "manner" or "way."

To whatever extent the Brahman—the reality that is the cause of the world—exists, having assumed the form of the bodies of various kinds of living beings and being established (*viṣṭhita*) as such, to that same extent speech exists, possessing that same measure.
This is because each individual object to be denoted requires its own name.
1. *ga2-rametetreti*.
2. *ga*-ta-bha: fourteen worlds; *mu*: worlds numbering fourteen. 3. *ga*-ta-bha-*mu*: “seven” is absent. 4. *ga*-śrā; *ta*1.2.3.6.7.8 *bha*-ca; *ta*4.5 *jñā*.

5. *ga*–*ta4.5*: "Thus, in the bodies of living beings"; *ta1.2.3.6.7-bha*: "In the bodies of living beings [mentioned] in the *uktha*. 6. *ga*–*ta4.5*: "Of the words *yat* and *tat*. 7. *ta-bha1.4.8*:
"Because of the accomplishment of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*); *bhara*: because of the non-accomplishment of worldly convention."
It is also heard elsewhere: "Having reflected upon all forms and having created names, the Wise One abides calling them forth" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7).
Passages from the Āraṇyaka such as "The fifteen-fold hymns are a thousandfold, for there are five decades" (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 1.3.8) should be considered here as well.

What wise man knows the application of the meters? Who has mastered the inspired speech that resides in the mind? Whom do they call the eighth hero among the officiating priests? And who indeed has truly discerned the secret power of Indra?

Who is the wise one who knows the application of the meters? Who has mastered the inspired speech? Whom do they call the eighth hero among the officiating priests? And who indeed has discerned Indra’s two bay steeds? 9.

Who is the wise and intelligent man among mortals who, like a young child, has clearly understood the purpose of the meters—Gāyatrī and the rest—who, though following his mothers for nourishment, does not approach them? If he has brought them forth, he has indeed grown great, performing his mighty office as a messenger.
The purpose is for the chest of the infant, who has become like an infant and is therefore a young and newly kindled fire.
Now, the suffix *atha* is [added] to the root *vakṣ* according to the *Uṇādi* rules. 1.

He who is born as the wonderful carrier of the oblation, indeed a marvel itself, does not fail to approach the two Mothers—the makers of all, who are like mother and father, namely Heaven and Earth—or the two lower ones, for the sake of bestowing nourishment.
‘Dhet pāne’:
the suffix taven is used in the sense of the infinitive (tumun).
He does not even go to suckle at the breast.
The root *i* means "to go.
There is a compound with the prefix *laṭ*. By the rule "tiṣṭha codāttavati," there is the suppression (*nighāta*) of the accent of the verb of motion.
The followers.
This is a negative (*nañ*) *bahuvrīhi* compound.

Since the suffix *anaṅ* is desired [only] at the end of a compound in the feminine gender (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.131), there is no application of *anaṅ* here. The singular number is used because each [member] is intended to be expressed individually.
If this world and that world had produced this Agni— who is situated above—
then it would be logical that he does not go to suckle at the breast;
yet such is not the case.
However, Heaven and Earth are indeed the fulfillers of the desires of all;
nevertheless, he does not go [to them].
Therefore, his carrying of the oblation is marvelous.
And indeed, immediately after being dispatched, on this very day, at that very moment, swiftly [perform] the great mission.
In the rule "dūtasya bhāgakarmaṇī" (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.4.120), the suffix *yat* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Performing the work of a messenger, he has grown strong;
he carries the oblations toward the gods.
Agni has indeed been established as the most skillful worker, he who gathers the forests together with his ash as if with a tool;
with his tongue that crushes all things, he performs the perfect sacrifice, like a bull snorting toward the pasture.

Agni has indeed been established as the most active one, he who gathers the forests together with his ash as if with a broom; the skillful sacrificer, with his consuming tongue, is like a mighty bull snorting as he rushes toward the pasture.
The most excellent of waters.
From the fact that the word *āpaḥ* has its final syllable accented (*antodātta*), it is understood that the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) has been elided;
otherwise, if the suffix *asun* were applied according to the rule "āpaḥ karmākhyāyām," the word would necessarily have its initial syllable accented (*ādyudātta*).
He is the most excellent of waters and the most excellent of ritual actions.
The name is Agni.
There is elision (luk) of the third case ending.
By means of the oblation consisting of our names, or by means of praise, he is indeed established and maintained by the sacrificers;
for he is the giver of wealth to those who offer sacrifice.
In the word *dadāna* [from the root] *dān*,
by the rule *hetau chandasy ubhayathā*, the suffix *śatṛ* is treated as if it were a verbal root (*dhātu*), resulting in the elision of the long vowel *ā*.
For this very reason, the addition of the suffix *śap* is impossible.
That Agni who, by means of his ash— that is, his illuminating, radiant, and burning brilliance— and by his teeth, joins together (*saṃ yuvate*), that is, unites or consumes, the forests, the woods;
for the root *yu* signifies "mixing and not mixing."
By metathesis, *ś* [is substituted],
and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) also [applies]. Thus, *dutā*.
In the word *danta*, the substitution of *dan* occurs by the rule beginning with *‘pann’*;
in *‘asidam’*, the first member of the compound is udātta due to the accentuation of the case ending.
Furthermore, they are exceedingly malleable.
The root *mūrch* is used in the senses of fainting (*moha*) and rising up (*samucchrāya*).
From this, by adding the suffix *kvip*, there is the elision of the letter *ch* according to the rule “*rālopaḥ*.
Alternatively, it may be derived from the root *mur* in the sense of enveloping (*saṃveṣṭana*), with the suffix *kvip*.
The original accent of the final member of a compound ending in a *kṛt* suffix [is retained].

The fire, whose sacrifice is beautiful (*svadhvara*), moves among the edible oblations with the *amitra*—that is, the raised and uplifted ladle, or rather, the specific vessel named *juhū* which is surrounded on all sides by the offerings; this is the sense.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
he is a capable lord (*inaḥ*).
Panting, fully developed, and with well-nourished limbs, he moves about like a bull among fodder, as a stallion does in a pasture.
Do not obstruct that god of yours, the exhilarating drop, who snorts and scatters the ocean;
he is a bearer like a horse with his flame, exuberant, possessing great ordinances, and a well-kindled one upon his path.
1. *ga* reads *gatamuvahe rauṇādikaḥ*; *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha* read *gatamuvahe rauṇādikaḥ*.
2. *ga* reads *dyāvāpṛthivyau hi*; *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha1.4.7* read *dyāvāpṛthivyau tu*; *bha2.8* read *dyāvāpṛthivyau nu*. 3. *ta-bha* do not have the word "citraṃ".
4. *ga* and *caraṇa* are not present; 5. *ga* is present when the suffix *śatṛ* follows the causal (*hetu*); 6. *ta*, *bha*, and ‘*bhavanā*’ do not exist.
7. [In the verses] beginning with *ga-ta* (1.2.3.7.8) and *bha* (1.2.4.7), [the words] *khādanīye*; *ta* (1) and *bha* (8) [occur in the context of] *svādanīye*.

Him, like a horse difficult to restrain, the divine one, the drop (*indu*) of the soma-juice, snorting and gliding forward like a surging ocean, like a draft-horse with his mouth, the drinker of flame, overflowing, of great vows, not letting the paths grow old. (3)
O you praisers, worship him. Of what sort?
Like a bird, [worship] him who dwells in the rain-cloud.

The "bad tree" (durvṛkṣaḥ) refers to a tree characterized by its lack of fruit; [the poet] addresses the one seated within that tree—the "shining god" (devam dyotamānam), the "drop" (indum) of the "soma-juice" (andhasaḥ), which moistens and brings to the singers their food.
The suffix *up* is applied by the rule *undericādeḥ* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.13).
Due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *nit*, the word is accented on its first syllable.
"Snorting and bellowing, cutting down the forests like Atharvan, [he is] an ocean."
The suffix *va* is applied in the sense of possession [matvarthīya] according to the rule "arṇasaḥ salopaśca."
"An oblation cast into the fire," and so forth, in this sequence, [he] "reaches" that which possesses water.
The substitution of *asanna* for the word *āsya* occurs by the rule beginning with "apahnū0," and the elision of the vowel is due to Vedic usage.
With the mouth, [he praises] the bearer of oblations;
or rather,
with the mouth.
This is a name for that which is near; it brings the oblations into the presence of the gods. There is an illustration regarding its carrying.

Like a draft-animal, for it is heard [in scripture]: "The ox is indeed the carrier" (Tai. Brā. 1.8.2.5). Thus, he is like an ox capable of carrying; by means of his "flame"—that is, by his own brilliance—he is "virapśin.
This is a name for greatness.
He who is great, whose vows are vast, whose deeds are mighty like the sun,
and who simultaneously illumines the paths—
thus he has been praised.
*Sa-rajantam*:
[This form is derived from] the root *rañj* in the sense of "coloring" (*rāge*).
In the present participle (*śatari*) of the root *rañj*, by the rule *rañjeśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.26), the nasal (*n*) is elided, and after the substitution of *sa* for *saha*, the form is established.
Alternatively:
that which moves is a *saras*;
[he is] the progenitor of the water of the lake.

Or, it may be that the form [of the word] arises when the suffix *tap* is applied to the root *jan*; thus, this failure to grasp [the meaning] stems from a lack of discernment regarding its etymological derivation.

O undecaying one, whose winds, as you conquer and burn, cannot obstruct on all sides—those unshakable, roaring, and warlike flames reach Trita like warriors seeking a champion, urging him forward for his sacrifice.
O Agni, you who are ageless and free from decay, [this is] for the one who is victorious.
The meaning of the word *jayati* is "he goes."
By virtue of the rule of diversity (bāhulaka), the suffix *asāna* is also applied after this [root].
Of one who is habitually wandering and burning with desire.
The suffix *san* is applied after the root *dah*.
According to the rule "In the section concerning reduplication (*dvirvacana*), it should be stated that in the Veda [reduplication] is optional" (Kāśikā 6.1.8.1), there is no reduplication.
The suffix *u* is then added to that which ends in that [root].
For you, who desire to burn the forest, those powers of yours which are your own—indestructible, meaning they cannot be shaken by enemies—surround and move everywhere like the winds.
The *astaleṭ* [suffix] occurs where, due to its connection, there is the striking of fire.
The word *yuyudhi* is derived from the root *yudh* with the suffix *kin*.

Like a warrior dwelling in the field of battle, or like the swift-moving Gaṅgā, or like the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) shouting for the sake of the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*), desiring to perform it, pouring forth [oblations], or wishing to partake—[they have reached] you, the powerful *Satvan*, the *Trita* spread out across the three places, namely the Āhavanīya and the other sacrificial fires;
they pervade you with hymns or with their various powers.

With *sahobhiḥ*, meaning by your own powers;

O Indra, these various oblations have been set forth toward the high altar; you have taken them up. *Adrīt* means "to hold" or "to take"; consume them indeed. *Canas* is a name for food; take that up, sustain it, and place it within your belly.

With hymns, I shall win fair speech from Agni and Soma, like a ship being driven upon the river.

"For the two gods Indra and Agni, [I offer] eloquence. By the rule "and in the Veda," the suffix *yat* is applied.
I "impel" or send forth this praise worthy of being well-spoken.
The root *ṛ* means "to go"; it belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class.

"Just as they propel a boat upon a river in the midst of the Sindhu, so too have I uttered this praise, accompanied by hymns (*arkaiḥ*)—that is, by mantras worthy of worship—as something to be impelled."
The root *īr* means "to move.
This is the first person singular present indicative (*laṭ*) of its causative form (*ṇyanta*), with the substitution of *ām* for the personal ending.

Those "non-gods" (adevāḥ) have been praised; they are called *ayāḥ* because they go (*ayanti*) to perform their duties, that is, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) or the ritual workers. Like them, they move about (*pari-caranti*).
They honor us with gifts of wealth and other such things—
those gods who are givers of wealth to us, and those who are destroyers of our enemies.

The seer is Bhikṣu, a descendant of Aṅgiras.
The first and second verses are Jagatīs; the remaining seven are Triṣṭubhs.
Here, the giving of wealth and of a command is praised;
therefore, this [verse] is appropriate for that purpose.
And thus it has been cited: "Or rather, two Jagatī verses [are used] by a mendicant for the praise of the gift of wealth."
The application [of the mantra] has been explained.
Indeed, O gods, deaths do not approach one who is consumed by hunger or who eats voraciously;
yet the wealth of the liberal giver does not fail him, and he finds no one to show him mercy when he has given away his all.

No, indeed; O gods, you have given hunger as our weapon of death. Even those who have eaten are overtaken by deaths. Furthermore, the wealth of the liberal giver does not fail him; yet he finds no one to comfort him in his distress.
The Bhikṣu first praises the gift of food by way of contrast:
"The gods—indeed, all the gods—did not give hunger; that is, they did not bestow it.
Rather, they gave only death."
He who pacifies such hunger, which takes the form of death, by the gift of food—he is indeed a true giver.
The particle *u* is for filling the meter.
Even unto that man who eats while having already eaten—that is, one who eats after being satiated—the "deaths," meaning deaths themselves, approach; they draw near.
The initial syllable [of *āśita*] is acute-accented by virtue of Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.207: *āśitaḥ kartā*.
"For those afflicted by hunger and for those who eat, death is the same; what is the use of giving which takes the form of the destruction of wealth? To this, he says:
"Uto"—
the word *uta* has the sense of "also. "The wealth (*rayiḥ*), that is, the riches, of the person who gives (*pṛṇataḥ*) or bestows, does not fail (*nopadasyati*), that is, it does not diminish."

The root *das* (in the sense of "destruction") belongs to the *div-ādi* class; *pṛṇa* (in the sense of "giving") belongs to the *tud-ādi* class. Because it ends in the present participle suffix *-śatṛ*, the accent falls on the first syllable of the case-ending according to the rule: *śatṛ-ñ-jo nady-aj-ādī*. In connection with the topic of giving, he censures the non-giver: "A person who does not give (*apṛṇan*), that is, one who does not bestow gifts, finds no one to comfort him (*marḍitāram*), no one to bring him happiness. He finds no such person anywhere. In this world, even kinsmen do not provide comfort due to his failure to give, and even the gods [do not help] because of the absence of offerings."
He who comes to the needy man who longs for food, to the one who is emaciated and has approached him—
though he may make his mind firm and serve [the gods] before him, he finds no comforter for his heart.

He who, though possessing food, hardens his heart toward the needy man who longs for nourishment and has come to him in distress—even before he can serve him—that thoughtless man finds no one to comfort him. 2.
The man who, though himself "possessed of food" (*annavān*),
is "distressed"— one who is distressed is called *ādhra*, meaning weak— to him,
desiring "pits," that is, desiring food.
*cakamānaḥ* has the sense of "shining" (*kānti*). *Raphitāya*: the root *raph* has the meaning of "harming" (*hiṃsā*).
He makes his own mind unsteady—that is, he causes it to waver—toward a guest who has come to his house, returned from afar, and is afflicted by poverty;

The root *kṛ* is used in the sense of "to injure" and "to do. By the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyor acca*, the suffix *up* is applied [with the substitution of *a* for the final vowel].

Not only does he cause suffering, but even before that, he enjoys pleasures.
