One should rather seek another who gives, even if he be a stranger.
He states a censure by way of contrast:

"That person is not a friend" who, toward a "friend"—one who is "ever-present," whose nature is to be constantly together, who is "attending" or serving as a subordinate, and who is a companion—"does not give food," that is, does not offer nourishing foods. The meaning is that he is not a true well-wisher.
"From this non-giving friend, let him depart;
let him go away, leaving him behind."
The root *iṇ* means "to go.
In the potential mood (*liṅ*), the augment *yāsuṭ* is applied.
In that case, "that home" (tadokaḥ)—meaning the dwelling or residence—does not exist, it does not come to be;
for a residence is indeed surrounded by kinsmen.
That man who has departed would desire, or long for, even another mortal, namely a master, who bestows food and other gifts.

One should purify oneself; one who is seeking wealth should look along the path that is most worthy and farthest-reaching. For riches roll hither like chariot wheels, approaching now this man, now another. puṇīyāt | it | nārthamānāya | tavyān | drāghīyāṃsam | anu | paśyet | panthām | o iti | hi | vartante | rathyā'iva | cakrā | anyam'anyam | upa | tiṣṭhanta | rāyaḥ || 5 ||
Wealth impels a man toward giving.
A man who is more powerful, stronger, and pre-eminently increased by riches would surely give wealth to a supplicant—a guest who is begging—for he ought to give.
The root *pṛ* is used in the senses of protecting and filling.
It belongs to the *ṛthādi* group.
By the rule "the short vowel is substituted for the roots beginning with *pvā*," [the long vowel is shortened].
If he should give, [he should give] for a longer period.
From the word *dīrgha*, when the suffix *īyasun* is added, the substitution *drāghīya-* occurs according to the rule beginning with "priyasthira."
One should behold—that is, one should look upon—the "longest path," meaning the well-trodden path of righteous conduct.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used here by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).
He states the reason for this:
"Riches, that is, wealth— oh!— they indeed surely return."
The meaning is that they do not remain in one place.
Therein is the illustration:
"just as the paths [do not stay] on the road."
The suffix *yat* is applied [to *ratha*] by Pāṇini’s rule 4.3.121, *rathādyat*, in the sense of "belonging to this" (*tasyedam*).

The wheels belonging to the chariot revolve in an upward and downward manner; he thus demonstrates that very process of revolution. They stand near one another, person after person, toward the riches; they come together and become assembled.
The *ātmanepada* ending is used [in the rule] "upādhve pūjāsaṃgatikaraṇa" (Pāṇini 1.3.25.1).
Therefore, the sense is that wealth should be given away.

The thoughtless man gains food in vain; I speak the truth: for him there is only destruction. He nourishes neither Aryaman nor his friend; he who eats alone becomes solely a vessel of sin. He gains food in vain, the one lacking wisdom. I speak the truth: for him there is indeed death. He does not nourish Aryaman, nor does he nourish his friend. He becomes possessed of only evil, the one who eats alone.
It censures the non-giver:
"The one who is *apracetāḥ*—one whose mind (*cetaḥ*) or thought is not directed toward giving—obtains food that is *moghama*, that is, entirely in vain."
The root *vidl* means "to obtain.
It belongs to the *taudādika* (the tenth class).
By the rule *śe mucādīnām*, the augment *num* is added.

1. For the sake of those people; 2. Friendship with Ga, Ta, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8; residence in Ta, 4, and 5; 3. "hi" does not exist in Ta and Bha; 4. when [the sage] had spoken, it becomes so; 5. "ceto" does not exist in Ga, Ta, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8.
I declare that this is the truth, exactly as it is in the hermitage;
I, a seer, speak this.
Not only is it useless, but for that man who grasps the dice, that very act of grasping is his own death.
The masculine gender of the word *tat* [in the rule] is due to its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "killing" (*vadha*);
just as in the case of Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.4.52, *jīryater aṇ niḥ*, where that which is the object is itself the agent.

Alternatively, that killing is indeed useless by which a man does not nourish— this is an elliptical expression meaning he does not sustain— all the gods, beginning with Aryaman, by the offering of oblations; nor does he nourish his friends, nor a guest who has arrived at his dwelling, nor the circle of his kinsmen.
The root *puṣ* (in the sense of nourishing) belongs to the *divādi* class.
Due to the ellipsis of the word *yat*, there is no *anighāta*.
For this very reason, [the rule applies] even to those who eat alone.
The suffix *ṇini* is applied by the rule *adeḥ supyajātau* (Pāṇini 3.2.78); consequently, there is vṛddhi substitution of the vowel in the penultimate position.
Eating food without a witness, he becomes solely sinful;
he becomes a possessor of nothing but evil;
only evil remains for him.
"Neither for this world nor for the next"—
therefore, their intention is that [the result] may be attained in some way or other.
Plowing with the plowshare, he makes food for himself; as he speeds along the path with his footsteps, the speaking priest is a better winner than the one who does not speak.
May the liberal kinsman surpass the one who gives nothing.

The plowshare makes the miser eat; when he clears the path with his feet, the speaking Brahmin is more successful than the one who speaks not. The liberal kinsman should prevail over the one who gives nothing. 7.
While plowing—that is, performing the act of cultivation—the plow makes the farmer who is hungry into one who is fed;
likewise, the traveler proceeds upon the path.
The augment *num* is added to the root *iṇ* before the suffix *śatṛ*.
A man walking away reveals himself by his own conduct and gait;
he wins over the wealth of his master.
The root *vṛjī* means "to avoid" or "to exclude. It belongs to the first class (*adādika*) and is anudātta (unaccented).

One who speaks the meaning of the scriptures, one who declares it, that Brahmin, by speaking the meaning of the scriptures, becomes more worthy of being honored, more deserving of support, and more affectionate than one who does not speak it.
In the word *tyajantaḥ*, the suffix *tṛc* is elided by the rule *turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu*.

Just as those [who do not give] proceed in their own actions to cause harm to others, so too a man who gives (*pṛṇan*), directed toward a person who does not give (*apṛṇantam*), should become a friend (*āpiḥ*)—that is, he should become a kinsman.
The one-footed has stepped out from the two-footed; the two-footed overtakes the three-footed from behind.
The four-footed comes to the call of the two-footed, looking upon them as he stands at the fifth row.
The one-footed strode forth further; the two-footed follows behind the three-footed. The four-footed comes to the call of the two-footed, standing near and beholding the fivefold rows. ||8||
In this context, the word *pāda* signifies a "portion.
A person possessing one *pāda*—that is, one portion of wealth—is on the path of one who possesses two *padas*, meaning double the wealth.
[The suffix] *su* is used for the third case.
After a long time, he strode forth; he went in various ways.
The Ātmanepada ending is used [here] because of the Pāṇinian rule (1.3.41): *veḥ pādaviharaṇe* ("after the root *vi*, [the Ātmanepada is used] when meaning the moving of the feet").
Likewise, the two-footed man subsequently approaches—that is, goes toward—the three-footed man who possesses three parts of wealth.
The four-footed [animals] have four parts of wealth, while bipeds have one part;
by the use of the plural, those with one foot and so forth are indicated.

Perceiving—that is, correctly observing—the rows of those possessing the wealth of one foot and so on, as they approach during the *abhisvara* (the chanting toward the sun), he goes—that is, he proceeds—while remaining present.
All things are superior or inferior only in relation to one another;
therefore, you should not think, "I alone am wealthy," for what is the point of giving wealth to guests? This is the meaning.

1. In manuscripts ga, ta1, 2, 3, 6, 8, and bha, 'na' is not present. 2. In manuscripts ga, ta1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, and bha-ya, it is 'āśitam'. 3. In manuscripts ga, ta4, 5, and bha-na, it is 'bhavati'. 4. In manuscript ga and bha, it is 'manyasva'. 5. In manuscripts ta4 and 5, it is 'kiṃvatithibhyo'.

Even two hands that are alike do not perform their work equally; even two mothers who are alike do not yield milk in equal measure. Even twins do not possess equal powers; even though they are kinsmen, they do not bestow gifts equally. 9. Even two hands that are alike do not perform their work equally; even two mothers who are alike do not yield milk in equal measure. Even twins do not possess equal powers; even though they are kinsmen, they do not bestow gifts equally. 9.
If it is argued that even though my brother does not give wealth to guests, he will do so [later], the reason for this is stated:
"His two hands are indeed equal and likewise identical, yet they do not perform the same task; they do not pervade [the work].
The root *vi-plu* means "to pervade."
*Jauhotyādika*:
Due to the non-universality (*anityatva*) of a rule conditioned by a specific technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), there is an absence of *guṇa* in the reduplication (*abhyāsa*).
Likewise, two cows that are both mothers of the same calf do not yield milk equally—that is, in the same measure—from the path.
Even among twins born together, the strengths of two sons are not equal.
Therefore, even though they are kinsmen born in the same family, they do not give equally; they do not bestow [gifts] alike.
Therefore...

Offered with oblations, Agni shines forth, worthy of praise through our song; his face is anointed by the ladle. (3) He, being offered oblations (*āhutaḥ*), shines forth (*vi rocate*). Agni is worthy of praise (*īḍenyaḥ*) through our song (*girā*). His face (*pratīkam*) is anointed (*ajyate*) by the ladle (*sruca*) containing clarified butter. *Āhutaḥ*: "Offered toward [the deity]. The original accent of the prefix *ā-* is retained according to the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*. *Girā*: Through speech characterized by hymns of praise. *Īḍenyaḥ*: Worthy of being praised. That Agni shines forth intensely; he blazes brilliantly. Likewise, his face—the foremost among all the gods—is anointed, that is, sprinkled, by the ladle filled with clarified butter.

Agni, whose face is honey, being offered oblations, is anointed with clarified butter; he is radiant, the possessor of light. With clarified butter, Agni is thoroughly anointed; he, whose face is honey, being offered oblations, is shining, the possessor of light. Agni is thoroughly anointed—that is, well-sprinkled—with clarified butter as his sacrificial offering. Of what nature is he? He is "honey-faced," meaning his limbs are permeated by the clarified butter; he is "offered," being praised with hymns or fed with oblations; he is "radiant," blazing brightly; he is the "possessor of light" (*vibhāvasu*), covering everything with his own splendor. Alternatively, he is one for whom radiance itself is wealth.

In the *ukthya* sacrifice that is not a *soma*-pressing (*asoḍyāma*), the *anurūpa* triplet is "O you who are awakened by praise, know this; being praised, you are kindled" (*jarābodha tad vividdhi jaramāṇaḥ samidhyase*). And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "‘O you who are awakened by praise,’ ‘know that,’ ‘being praised, you are kindled’" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 9.11). Being praised, you are kindled, O bearer of oblations for the gods; may mortals invoke you. (5) **Being praised** (*jaramāṇaḥ*): You are **kindled** (*sam-idhyase*). **For the gods** (*devebhyaḥ*). **O bearer of oblations** (*havyavāhana*). **Him**, you, **may mortals** (*martyāḥ*) **invoke** (*havantu*). (5) O **bearer of oblations** (*havyavāhana*), you who cause the offerings to reach [the gods]—[the suffix] *ṇyuṭ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.66, "in the word *havya*, when it does not occur within a *pāda*. **Being praised** (*jaramāṇaḥ*): being lauded by the singers of hymns; the root *jarati* has the sense of praising. As such, you are **kindled** (*samidhyase*) for the sake of the gods; you shine forth perfectly with the sacrificial offerings. **Him**, such as you are, **mortals** (*martyāḥ*)—that is, virtuous human sacrificers—**invoke** (*havante*). The change to *havante* is due to the substitution of *saṃprasāraṇa* in the *laṅ* tense, according to the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). (24)

O mortals, worship with clarified butter that immortal Agni, the inviolable lord of the house. O mortals—O officiating priests—worship with clarified butter as an oblation that immortal Agni, who is free from human attributes; serve him. The root *sapar* belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class. Of what nature is he? "Inviolable" (*adābhya*), meaning incapable of being harmed by anyone. The suffix *ṇyat* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.124.3 (*dabheścit vaktavyam*). He is the "lord of the house" (*gṛhapati*), the master of the home in the form of the sacrificer. In the compound, the accent of the first member remains as it is, according to the rule *patyāvaiśvarye*.

O Agni, burn the *rakṣas* with your invincible flame; shine as the guardian of the cosmic order (*ṛta*). O Agni, you—burn all *rakṣas* (the word is used here in the singular for the class) with your invincible, unassailable radiance. Furthermore, as the protector of the *ṛta*, that is, of the sacrifice, shine forth resplendently.
As such, O Agni, with your face, burn against the sorceresses; shine far among the wide dwellings. 8. He. You. O Agni. With your face. Against. Burn. The sorceresses. In the wide dwellings. Shine. 8.
1. The phrase "ta-bha- 'yajñasya gopāḥ'" is not present.
O Agni, you—by means of your "pratīkena," that is, by the splendor (tejas) which constitutes a part of you—"pratyoṣa," burn against the "yātudhānyaḥ," the female sorceresses, the Rākṣasīs.
[The root] "upa" is used in the sense of burning.
It belongs to the *bhū* class (*bhauvādika*).

In the *loṭ* [imperative] mood, there is elision of the suffix *hi*. By the rule "from a genus-name that refers exclusively to females" (*jāter-astri-viṣayāt*, Pāṇini Sūtra 4.1.63), the suffix *ḍīṣ* is applied to the word *yātudhāna*.
The term "svarita" [is applied] by the rule "udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ.
What is he doing?
He is "shining," that is, blazing forth, "in the wide dwellings," namely, in the extensive abodes such as the Āhavanīya fire-altar and others.

"The *uru-kṣayāḥ* (those with wide dwellings) have kindled you, the bearer of oblations (*havyavāham*), with songs (*gīrbhiḥ*)—you, the most worthy of sacrifice (*yajiṣṭham*) among the human race (*mānuṣe jane*). That [song], being performed by the praisers (*stotṛbhiḥ*), as a hymn of praise (*matī*), stands near me (*upa vasthita*) and unites me with you."
The Ātmanepada ending is used because of the rule *upādyamaḥ svakarmanya* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.56).

How so? Just as a lowing cow (*vāśvā*) approaches her dear calf (*putraṃ*), so too [does she approach him]. Just as a lowing cow, making a sound, comes together with her beloved calf, in that same way.

I, as it were, seek out that chariot-seat for the crossing; with my heart, I direct my thought: "Have I perhaps drunk of Soma? (5) I. tadaiva. vandhuram. pārye. acchāmi. hṛdā. matim. kuvit. somasya. apām. iti. (5)
Just as a carpenter today prepares the seat— that is, the place where the charioteer dwells—
or rather,
he fashions the chariot itself so that it possesses such a seat; even so, with my own heart— that is, with my mind— I direct my speech, my thought, and my praise toward you.
I go forth for the sake of performing what is right.

"Even the cattle and the lepers did not satisfy my eye; perhaps it was from drinking the Soma," so [he thought]. 6. Not even; me; has fallen upon; indeed; have satisfied; the cattle; the lepers; perhaps; of the Soma; having drunk; thus. 6.

The compound particle *vacaṇa* is used in the sense of "also. Thus, *vpañca vkuṣṭyaḥ* means "also the five tribes," namely the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth, who are the five peoples (*pañca janāḥ*).
Or else:

Gods, humans, and others—[in this] world, they do not cast their own eyes—that is, the falling of the eyes or the movement of the gaze—toward me; indeed, they do not look [upon me]. For it is stated in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (14.7.1.23): “For there is no loss of sight.”

In the case of *chardir apavāraṇe*, because it belongs to the *cur*-class, it takes the causative suffix (*ṇic*); thus, even in the absence of the suffix here, there is the *vṛddhi* substitution [of the vowel] by virtue of its ending in a consonant (*hal*) in the *luṅ* tense (Pāṇini 7.2.3).
Because one offers the omentum of the Soma daily.

Neither both heaven and earth together are equal to even one of my wings; have I not indeed drunk of the Soma? (7) Neither both heaven and earth are equal to even one of my wings; have I not indeed drunk of the Soma? (7)
Both worlds, heaven and earth, do not even equal one of my two wings, much less both wings together.

I have surpassed the sky in greatness; I have surpassed this vast earth. Have I not drunk of Soma? (8) abhi dyām mahinā bhuvaṃ abhīmāṃ pṛthivīṃ mahīm | kuvit somasyāpām iti || 8 || I have surpassed the sky by my greatness; I have surpassed this vast earth. Have I not drunk of Soma? (8)
He establishes the meaning already stated:
by my own greatness (mahimnā), I pervade (abhivavāmi) the sky (dyām), that is, the celestial world;
likewise, by my own greatness, I pervade this great earth (pṛthivīm).
In the case of the root *bhū*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) according to Vedic usage;
when the *guṇa* substitution is prohibited by the rule “*bhūsuvostiḥ*” (Pāṇini 7.3.88), the substitute *uvaṅ* is applied.

"Come now, I shall lay down this earth either here or there; perhaps I shall drink of the Soma. || 9 || Come now! I! This earth! Shall lay down! Either here! Or there! Perhaps! Of the Soma! I shall drink! Thus. || 9 ||

*vahanta* means "in the sense of possibility" or "in the sense of permission"; that is, "I consider this possible" or "I permit it. What is that? "Shall I place *vahaṃ* [the wind] upon this earth, or in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), or in the world of heaven (*dyuloka*)?"—thus he points with his hand. In the imperative (*loṭ*) of the root *dhā*, *meḥ* becomes *niḥ*.
1. Like a son (ta8.5-putramiva). 2. They open [the door] (ta1.2.3.6.7.8-ma2.4.8-hāpāvṛṇvaṃti); ta8.5 reads hāpivṛṇvaṃti. 3. From which (ga-ta1.2.3.4.5.6.8-ma-yasmāddhu).
4. Regarding *ta-bha*, it does not exist [as a substitute] for the root *dhā* in the imperative (*loṭ*).

"Swiftly indeed may I strike down the earth here or there; have I not drunk of Soma? (10) "Swiftly indeed," "the earth," "I," "may I strike down," "here," "or," "there," "have I not," "of Soma," "drunk"—thus [the verse]. I, aiming at the earth, shall swiftly strike down—that is, drive away intensely—the Sun, the burner by his own splendor, either here in the intermediate space or there in the heavenly world. The particle *hat* is a filler (*pūraṇa*). [Grammatical note: This is the imperative of the root *han* in its *yaṅ-luk* (intensive) form, meaning "to go" or "to move"; the absence of the elision of the *jhaP* suffix is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

"One wing of mine is in heaven; the other I have drawn down below. Have I not drunk of Soma? (RV 10.112.11). One wing of mine is established in heaven, in the world of light (*dyuloka*). "Below" (*adhas*): the suffix *asip* is added according to Pāṇini 5.3.39, *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ*, and there is a substitution for the root. Below, on the earth, I have drawn down—that is, I have fixed—the other wing. The root *kṛṣ* means "to scratch" or "to produce. In the *luṅ* tense of the causative form, the vowel *u* is substituted according to Pāṇini 7.4.8, *niśya chandasi*. "Scratching" here means "producing"; that is, I have brought it forth, I have established it.

"I am the great festival, risen toward the center of the sky; have I not drunk of Soma? (12) I am. The "great festival" (mahāmahaḥ). Risen toward the "center of the sky" (abhinabhyam). Have I not? Of Soma. Drunk? Thus. (12) Regarding *abhinabhyam*: that which exists at the navel, the central place, is *nabhya*; it refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). The suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 5.1.2 (*ugavādibhyo yat*), and the substitution of *bha* for *na* occurs because that word is included in the *ugavādi* group. The compound takes the form *abhi-nabhyam* according to Pāṇini’s rule 2.1.14 (*lakṣaṇenābhipratī ābhimukhye*), which prescribes the indeclinable nature of the preposition. It bears the accent of the compound. I, whose self is the Sun, having risen upward toward the intermediate space, am the "great festival. I am the greatest even among the great. Or else: I am one whose splendor (*mahaḥ*) is "great," meaning abundant; I possess abundant splendor. The substitution of *āt* for the final vowel occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.46 (*ātmahataḥ*).

"I have gone as one made ready for the gods, O bearer of oblations; perhaps I have drunk of the Soma," [he says]. (13) *Gṛhaḥ*, *yāmi*, *aram-kṛtaḥ*, *devebhyaḥ*, *havyavāhanaḥ*, *kuvit*, *somasya*, *apām*, *iti*. (13) I am the *gṛhaḥ*—the receiver of the oblations (*haviṣām*). Made ready (*aram-kṛtaḥ*) by the sacrificers, I, being the very self of Agni, go (*yāmi*) as the *havyavāhanaḥ*—the carrier and deliverer of the oblations—to the gods, Indra and the others. [The root] *yā* means "to reach"; here it is in the present tense (*laṭ*). In the word *havya-vāhanaḥ*, the suffix *yuṇ* is applied after *vah* when preceded by *havya*; because it has the *ji* augment, it is udātta on the first syllable. In the compound, the accent remains on the original form of the second member (*kṛd-uttara-pada-prakṛti-svaraḥ*). Thus, because I have indeed (*kuvit*) many times drunk (*apām*) the Soma, Indra praised his own self, saying, "Therefore, I have performed this [act]. (27)

May Vidyātīrthamaheśvara, dispelling the darkness by illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, bestow the four aims of human existence. Thus ends the sixth chapter of the eighth book in the *Mādhavīya Vedārthaprakāśa*, a commentary on the *Ṛgvedasaṃhitā* composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the chief minister of the empire of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the supreme sovereign of kings, the highest lord, and the promoter of the Vedic path.
1. *ga*-ta4.5 cause [it] to reach;
2. *ga*-anyebhyaḥ; *ta*1.2.3.6.7.8-*bha*-ajñebhyaḥ.
|| Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the seventh [section] is explained.
In the tenth anuvāka of the tenth maṇḍala, the collection of hymns has been explained.
The eighth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "tad it," is the seer's work of Gṛhadi, the son of Atharvan; it is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to Indra.
And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: "That, indeed, [is] Bṛhadiva, the Atharvaṇa.
This hymn is recited during the Niṣkevalya litany on the twenty-fourth day.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "And one should recite 'tad id āsa' before the hymn" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.3).
In the *Vyomaviśvadeva* [sacrifice] and subsequently in the one-day (*ekāha*) sacrifice called *Āradīya*, this very [stotra] serves as the *niṣkevalya-nivid-vāna*.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "For these three, the midday [pressing] consists of 'kayā śubhā' and 'tad id āsa'. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.8).
This same *niṣkevalya-nivid-vāna* also applies to the two one-day sacrifices known as *Rāśimarāya* and *Asya*.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "In the *rāśi* and *marāya* [sections], [the hymns] *kayāśubhīya* and *tadidāsīya*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 9.8).
This same hymn is also used in the *niṣkevalya* [laud] of the *mahāvrata*.
Likewise, in the fifth *Āraṇyaka*, Śaunaka has prescribed: "'Tadidāsa bhuvaneṣu jyeṣṭham', 'Tāṃ su te kīrtiṃ maghavan mahiṣvā'" (*Aitareya Āraṇyaka* 5.1.6).
That indeed was the most excellent among all beings, from which was born the fierce one of impetuous valor;
as soon as he was born, he overthrew his enemies—he in whom all the waves of strength rejoice.
That indeed was the eldest among the worlds, from which the fierce one of brilliant valor was born; as soon as he was born, he overcomes his enemies—he in whom all the waves of power rejoice. || 1 ||

"That" refers to that which is well-known in all the Vedāntas as the cause of the universe. The word "iti" is used for emphasis. Regarding "in the worlds" (*bhuvaneṣu*): the root *bhū* means "to exist."
Among the six worlds beginning with earth, Brahman alone was the cause of the universe and was "the eldest," meaning the most excellent;
for it possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*), whereas all things other than it are merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).
Alternatively:
He became the eldest, the most ancient, and the primordial source of all things by virtue of being the cause of the universe.

In the periphrastic perfect (*asterliṭ*), because it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix by the rule "in the Veda, both ways" (*chandasyubhayathā*), there is no substitution of *bhū* for *as* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.52 (*asterbhūḥ*).
Alternatively, that very Brahman, being ancient, *āsa*— that is, it shone forth by virtue of its self-luminosity.
The root *as* is used in the senses of "going," "shining," and "taking. This is the form [of the verb] in the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

From that Brahman, who is the source of taking (*upādāna*), Indra—who is "fierce" (*ugra*) meaning exalted, and whose "valor is brilliant" (*tveṣanṛmṇa*) meaning possessing blazing strength—was born; he came into being as the Sun.
For it is heard in scripture: "From the eye the sun was born" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.90.13), and also:
"The Ordainer fashioned the sun and moon as they were before" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.190.3).

By the rule *'janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ'* (Pāṇini 1.4.30), the material cause (*prakṛti*) receives the technical designation of "source" (*ādāna*), whereby the ablative case ending (*pañcamī*) is applied in the word *yataḥ*.
Regarding the root *jan* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*), there is elision of the penultimate vowel according to the rule *'gamahana-'* etc.
Then, by the rule *'dvirvacane'ci'*, that [elision] is treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), resulting in reduplication and so forth.
The prohibition of the *nighāta* accent applies by the rule "yadvṛttānnityam."
And he, "being born"—that is, at the very moment of his birth—"immediately," that is, swiftly, "destroys" or slays the "enemies," such as the Mandehas and other Rākṣasas who seek to cause harm;
or rather, he destroys the enemies in the form of sins for those who worship him.
And thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "For as soon as he was born, he struck away evil" (Ai. Ā. 1.3.4).
*Jajñānaḥ* is a form derived from the root *jan* (to be born) in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *kānac*.
*Riṇāti*: [from] the root *rī*, meaning "to go" or "to impel."
The root begins with *ru*.
The shortening occurs according to the rule "the roots beginning with *pvā* undergo shortening."
"Viśve" means all. "Ūmāḥ" refers to living beings (prāṇinaḥ), because they protect (avanti) or guard; the suffix *man* is added to the root *ava* according to the Uṇādi rules.
By the rule "jvaratvara" and so forth, *ūṭh* is substituted in place of the vowel *va* and its penultimate vowel.
All living beings rejoice and exult, thinking, "The Sun, who is Indra, has risen for my sake; he has risen for my sake."
The root *mad* is used in the sense of "joy";
the suffix *śap* is applied by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).

And thus: 1. Because *ta*, *bha*, and *asat* [are absent]; 2. Because *ga*, *ta*, and *bha* signify the ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*); 3. Because *ga* and *bha* signify the conventional (*vyāvahārikatva*), and because *ta* signifies the non-conventional (*avyāvahārikatva*); 4. Because *ga*, *ta*, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, and 8, as well as *bha* and *mu*, indicate birth (*janer liṭ*).
As it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "The Viśve Devas and the Umās are indeed all beings; they rejoice after him, saying, 'He has risen, he has risen! (Ai. Ā. 1.2.4).
And the Taittirīyaka says: "Therefore, everyone thinks, 'It has risen toward me'" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.5.4.2).
Or else:
after [the sun] has honored him with hymns of praise and so forth, all living beings rejoice because they have obtained their desired objects.
Because of the rule *anurlakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 1.4.84), *anu* has the status of a *karmapravacanīya*; consequently, by the rule *karmapravacanīyayukte dvitīyā*, the second case ending is employed.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "That Indra was born."

Increasing in strength and possessing even greater vigor, he, as an enemy, strikes fear into the Dāsa. Both the unswallowing and the swallowing [sacrificial food] have been offered; they cry out together in the exhilaration of the soma-drinks.

Growing strong with power, possessing even greater vigor, he, as an adversary, strikes fear into the Dāsa. Both the one who does not eat and the one who eats three times [a day] lie prostrate. They have cried out together to you when the offerings were presented during the exhilarations of the soma.

Increasing by his might (*śavasā*) and growing ever stronger, Indra—the destroyer (*śatruḥ*) who possesses abundant power (*bhūyaujāḥ*)—bestows fear (*bhiyam*) upon the Dāsa, the destructive enemy; he causes it; he brings it about. He has overcome him.
The various things that "breathe" (vyanat) are like the vital breath, consisting of the conscious;
that which is the opposite of that, not breathing (avyanat), is the stationary.
Both of these, when thoroughly cleansed by Indra, become perfectly established (saṃsthitam).
In the case of the root *snā*, the suffix *kin* is applied in the sense of the object by way of transposition (vyatyaya), according to the rule "āda-gam-hana."
Alternatively, the suffix *kin* is used here in the sense of the agent itself, with the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it;
thus, he becomes one who thoroughly bathes—that is, purifies—by means of rain and so forth.
In the rule "na lokāvyaya," there is a prohibition of the genitive case in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The remaining quarter-verse is based on direct perception:

O Indra, when your exhilarations have arisen through the oblation and hymns of praise, all created beings—held forth or nourished with excellence (*prabhṛtā prabhṛtāni*)—*saṃ nacanta*, they come together.
The meaning is that they gather together to offer praise and to present the oblations.
He is the one whose karma has nine and ninety destinies.
*Prabhṛtā*:
This is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *bhṛ* (to bear) used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The elision of the suffix *śa* occurs according to the rule "In the Vedic language, the remaining [suffixes] are frequently elided" (*śeṣacchandasi bahulam*).
In the phrase "gatiranantaraḥ," the word *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
All turn their will toward you; these helpers become threefold when doubled.
Mix the sweeter with the sweet; fight well for us with honey against honey.
All indeed turn their will toward you, when these helpers become twice or thrice [in number]. Mix that which is sweeter than the sweet with sweetness; win that honey well with honey! 3.
O Indra, [it is] in you, in you.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is the substitution of "śe" for the locative singular ending.
"All" (viśve) means all the sacrificers (*yajamānāḥ*) "accomplish" (*vṛñjanti*)—that is, they complete—the "sacrificial rite" (*kratu*), the action to be performed.
The word "api" is intended to include all beings and all minds as mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa.
The meaning is that all elements, such as the earth and so forth, the minds of all living beings, and all sacrificial rites are completed by the sacrificers in you alone, O Vyāsa.
And thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "In you all these beings, all minds, and even all sacrifices are contained"—this is what that [passage] declares (Ai. Ā. 1.3.4).
Because these [beings] are *ūmaḥ*, i.e., satiating.
The suffix *man* is added to the root *bhū* in the sense of "satisfying" and so forth, according to the *uṇādi* rules;
by the rule beginning with "jvarasvara," there is the substitution of *ūṭ* for the vowel *u* and the following semivowel *v*.
Such sacrificers, having initially been alone, later become twice-born through the female form and the male form; then, together with him, they become thrice-partakers of the jaw [of the sacrifice].
Thus, the single Self is born in the form of both woman and man, according to the Vedic revelation:
"The wife is indeed half of this self" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.3.3).
The son is also indeed the self; for it is said:
"The self, verily, is the name of the son" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.8.3.6). He [the father] breathed out.
2. [The suffix] *ghan* occurs after roots ending in *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, *ja*, *nya*, *i*, *pu*, and *ṛ*; 3.
after roots ending in *ta*, *ma*, *pra*, and *sr*; and after roots ending in *ta*, *bha*, *pra*, and *pū* (according to Śruti 14.9.4.26).
Since these [progeny] thus come to increase, it is understood from this that all ritual action performed by you reaches its completion in them.
And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "Two indeed, being a couple, procreate for the sake of progeny" (Ai. Ā. 1.3.4).
O Indra, unite and join together with a sweet, most delicious, and more beloved offspring than even the pleasant home and such things—with a sweet couple consisting of mother and father.
Or rather:
unite even that offspring which has been produced by a pleasant disposition.
He says this very thing:

O Aditi, do thou thoroughly combat—that honey-like, sweet offspring—with honey, that is, with the cause of intoxication, namely with the other pair or with the grandson; fight it on all sides; sport with it everywhere.
Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *yudh* here functions in the sense of "playing."
The Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "A couple indeed is sweet; offspring is sweet" (Ai. Ā. 1.3.4) should be consulted here.
Thus indeed do the inspired singers rejoice after you as you win riches at every exhilaration;
O bold one, extend your more powerful and steadfast strength—let not the evil-doing sorcerers harm you.

For indeed, O wise one, the inspired singers rejoice after you at every exhilaration as you win the riches. O bold one, extend your might more powerfully and firmly; let not the sorcerers of evil deeds harm you. 4.

Thus, O Indra, indeed, at every exhilaration born of drinking the soma, the wise—the intelligent singers—rejoice after you, following you as you conquer and obtain through victory the riches of the enemies.
(The particle *anu* functions as a *karmapravacanīya* in the sense of a characteristic mark.
They, the sages, exult and take delight.
Or rather, they "rejoice" (anumadanti) in you, that is, they praise you in succession;
*madati* is a verb meaning "to praise. The prohibition of the *nighāta* accent applies here by the rule "hi ca."
O bold Indra, subduer of enemies!
[The suffix] *knu* is applied after the roots *gras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*. [Thus:
*ojīyas*.
From the word *ojasvin* with the suffix *-īyasun*, there is the elision of *vin* by the rule "elision of *vin* and *matup*" (*vinmator luk*).
There is the elision of the final *ṭi* by the rule "elision of *ṭi*" (*ṭeḥ*).
Therefore, [the form is] *balavattara*. Spread forth—that is, extend on all sides for our sake—wealth that is thus more powerful, stable, and firm.
May the evil-doers—the ill-fated *yātudhānas* and *rākṣasas*—not deceive you, nor may they harm you.
Through you we have prevailed in battles, beholding many things worthy of combat;
with my words I urge on your weapons, and with sacred prayer (*brahman*) I train your vital powers.
By you, we, beholding many things worthy of battle in the contests for dominion, urge on your weapons with our words; I perfect your vital powers through sacred prayer. 5.
O Indra, favored by you, we utterly strike down our enemies in battles and conflicts.
The root *śad* is used in the sense of "cutting" (*śātane*).

From this final [root], by the rule "in the Veda, both ways," it is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix; consequently, there is the elision of the *tal* (the *a* of the present stem marker) and the elision of the *yal* (the *ya* of the class marker).
Doing what?
Engaging in battles worthy of combat.
In the sense of "what is to be done," the suffix *kenya* is applied after the root *yudh* (to fight), as in *tavaikenyam*.
Bhūri means many strengths.
The elision (*luk*) of the case-ending *śas* occurs by the rule "supām suluk.
"Prapaśyantaḥ" means perceiving clearly or knowing thoroughly. Furthermore, "te āyudhā" refers to your weapons—the instruments for combat such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and others.
The elision of the *śi* suffix is according to the rule "śeṣchandasi bahulam.
With words—that is, with hymns of praise—I impel [the arrows] toward the enemies.
For your sake, these arrows are accompanied by *brahman*, that is, by mantras in the form of hymns.
In this regard,
it is not so: "I thoroughly prepare" means I properly instruct, that is, I thoroughly refine.
The root *śo* means "to thin.

The *bhū* suffix [for the present tense] is applied by Vedic license (*chāndasa*). The vowel *i* is substituted for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) according to the rule "in the Veda, diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

1. In Ga and Ta, "bhara" is present; in Bha, it is absent. 2. In Ga, Ta, Bha, and Ma, "apautreṇa" is absent. 3. In Ta and Bha, "su" is absent. 4. In Ga, Ta, Bha, and Ma, "ojīyaḥ" means "ojasvitaram. 5. In Ta and Bha, there is the suffix "ken."

Let us praise this one, who possesses many forms, the skillful, the most powerful, the kinsman among kinsmen. With his might, he rends the seven Dānus; he overcomes many adversaries. 6. Let us praise this one... who possesses many forms... the skillful... the most powerful... the kinsman among kinsmen... with his might... he rends... the seven Dānus... he overcomes... many adversaries. 6.

"I praise this one who is to be praised (*stuṣeyam*). The suffix *-kṣeyya* is an *uṇādi* formation according to Uṇādisūtra 3.99: *stuvaḥ kṣeyyaś chandasi*. [I praise him who is] *puruvapasaṃ*: possessing many forms; *ṛbhvam*: wide-shining or vast-become; *vinatamam*: preeminent as a lord; and among those who are to be attained (*āpyānām*), [the one who is] *āpyam*: the very one to be attained. "I praise Indra," is the ellipsis.

Now Indra, by his own power and strength, [the seer] Bṛhaddiva recites these prayers for Indra so that they may bring him joy; he speaks them in such a way that they become a source of happiness (*śūpam*).
The use of the third person (*prabravīti*) is an indirect reference to himself.
The root *vac* is used in the sense of speaking;
it belongs to the *ad-ādi* class.
The *śap* affix is elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," the *it* augment is applied to the reduplicated syllable. The seer (*ṛṣi*) is thus distinguished. *Adhriyaḥ* means "born before" (*agre-bhavaḥ*).

The foremost among the seers (*ṛṣi*); that is to say, the best. The suffix *ghac* is applied after the word *agra* in the sense of "foremost" according to Pāṇini’s rule 4.4.117 (*ghacchau ca*). *Svarpāḥ* means those who share in heaven (*svarga*).
Or else,
Indra is the sun:
for another scriptural passage states, "That sun, indeed, is Indra" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.7.1.3).
The meaning is that he is a partaker or a servant of that [forest]. [The root] *vana-paṇ* is used in the sense of "partaking" (*saṃbhakti*).
According to the rule "jana-sana-khana-krama-gamaḥ viṭ," the suffix *viṭ* is applied.
The substitution of *ā* [for the vowel *i*] is according to the rule “viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt,” and the substitution of *pa* [for the final *t*] is according to the rule “sanoteranaḥ.

Indra, by his power, [opened] the great mountain-cave (*gotra*) which had been placed there by the demon Vṛtra for the purpose of concealing the cows; [the cave] which was self-ruling (*svarāja*), shining by itself.

The phrase “the inclusion of the word *kriyā* must be made” [is used] because the object (*karman*) functions as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and thus the genitive case is employed in the sense of the dative.
He causes such a mountain to *kṣayati*, that is, to disappear;
for the root *kṣi* means "to perish."
It belongs to the *bhū* class (*bhauvādika*).
Alternatively, from the word *go*, the suffix *ap* is added in the sense of a collection according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 4.2.51: *initrakavyacaśca*.

Of the *gotra*—that is, the great herd of cattle (*gosamūha*)—there is a lord (*indra*), who rules (*kṣayati*) over the great self-ruling one (*svarāja*), shining by his own power (*svayameva rājamāna*). The root *kṣi* denotes the act of exercising sovereignty.
Because the word *sva* is used as a prefix (*upapada*), the suffix *kvip* is applied to the root *rāj* according to the rule *satsṛdviṣa*.
The word retains the original accent of the final member of the compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*).

He opened—meaning he made free from obstruction—all the *duras* (caves) and *biladvārāṇi* (entrances to the caverns), which were all the *svāḥ* (belongings) belonging to the demon Vala. He rendered them accessible.
Or rather:
he opened the distant [caves] and found all the cows that were his own, existing within the interior of the mountain-caves; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
To such an Indra, for that Indra—this is the syntactical connection (*vākya-śeṣa*).
Thus the great Atharvan of the lofty heaven drew Indra to himself by his own body;
his sisters, dwelling in the mother-womb, impel him with their power and cause him to grow strong.
Thus has the great Atharvan Bṛhaddiva spoken here: the sisters dwelling in the mother, the stainless ones, impel Indra with their own bodies and strengthen him with their power. 9.

Atharvan was great and preeminent in virtues; the terms "son" and "father" are used here figuratively. The seer named Bṛhaddiva, the son of Atharvan, spoke thus—uttered this extensive praise directed toward Indra himself—among the gods regarding his own body.

In *vaceluṃḍi*, the substitution of *aḍ* for *cli* occurs according to the rule “*asyativaktītyādinā*”; the augment *um* is added by the rule “*vaca um*”; and because it occurs at the beginning of a word (*pādāditvāt*), it is not elided.
Moreover, these very rivers, *mātaribvarīḥ*—existing (*bhavantyaḥ*) upon the earth (*mātari*), the ground that brings forth (*bhava*) the entire multitude of living beings—[serve him].
The suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule "also seen after other [roots]" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyam*);
and by the rule "after *van*, *r* and *ī*" (*vano ra ca*), the feminine suffixes *ṅīp* and *repha* are added.
In the word *jasi*, the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) is applied by the rule "vā chandasi.
The elision of the nasal (*ṇalopa*) occurs because it belongs to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

The rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others—called *ariprāḥ*, meaning "sinless," and *svasāraḥ*, meaning "those who move by themselves" or "sisters to one another"—*hinvaṃti*, that is, they please [the sacrificer] by serving as the means for the sacrifice.
The root *hvi* means "to please";
it belongs to the *bhūvādi* class;
the suffix *śa* is applied by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
From the root *id*, with the suffix *num* and the prefix *gad-vā*; [the root] *hi* means "to go" and "to increase."
The suffix *inu* is applied after roots beginning with *svṛ*.
They approach that Indra for the sake of rain;
and having approached, they strengthen him with *śavas*, the power generated by sacrifice.
The ninth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “hiraṇyagarbhaḥ,” has Hiraṇyagarbha, the son of Prajāpati, as its seer (ṛṣi) and is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Its deity is Prajāpati, who is denoted by the word "Ka. Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “Hiraṇyagarbha; [the hymn] of ten verses; Hiraṇyagarbha is the son of Prajāpati; [it is addressed to] Ka.”
The application of the hymns (*sūktaviniyoga*) has been explained.

For the animal sacrifice to Prajāpati, the first three verses of each set are respectively the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum, the cake, and the oblation; the subsequent three are the offering verses (*yājyā*).
As it is stated in the Sūtra: "The six verses beginning with *hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre* belong to Prajāpati."
(Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
At the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices, this verse beginning with "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ" is the *yājyā* for the oblation to Ka.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Pratiprasthātṛ [recites] 'kayā naścitra ā bhuvat' and 'hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre' as the third [offering] at the Vājina."
(Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.17).
1. *ga* and *ta4.5*: "The *brahmāṇi* are the hymns (*stotrāṇi*). 2. *ta* and *bha*: "The *bṛhadivā*."

3. Thus indeed: In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists. He supported this earth and this heaven. To which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists. He supported this earth and the sky. To what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? 1.

Hiraṇyagarbha: Prajāpati, who is the embryo within the golden egg, is Hiraṇyagarbha. Thus says the Taittirīyaka: “Prajāpati indeed is Hiraṇyagarbha, because he exists within the womb of Prajāpati” (Tait. Saṃ. 5.5.1.2).
Alternatively, that Sūtrātman in whose belly the golden egg resides as an embryo is called Hiraṇyagarbha.
In the beginning, prior to the emergence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), he existed;
he was born from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who, presiding over *māyā*, desires to create.

Although Hiraṇyagarbha is indeed the Supreme Self itself, nevertheless, because the ether and other elements that constitute his limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are produced from Brahman, he too—who is conditioned by them—is said to have been "born."

And as soon as he was born, being alone and without a second, he became the lord and master of all that has come into being—the entire world consisting of the manifold transformations of the cosmic egg and so forth.
Not only was he the lord, but then that Hiraṇyagarbha [ruled] over the vast earth, the sky (dyu), and moreover this very earth visible before us, which we perceive;
or alternatively, "earth" (pṛthivī) here is a name for the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
He has supported, that is, he sustains, the intermediate space, the heavens, and the earth.

By the rule "In the Veda, the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [tenses may be used for all times]," the *liṭ* (perfect tense) is employed here to denote any time. Because it belongs to the *tuji*-class, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable.
To whom? Here, because its specific nature is not yet known, the word *kim* refers to Prajāpati.
Or alternatively:
The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of "one who desires for the sake of purification" (*mṛṣṭi*),
according to the rule *kamer ṇyaḥ*.
Alternatively:
"Ka" means happiness;
because it has that nature, it is called "ka.
Alternatively, when Prajāpati was questioned by Indra, he said, "Having bestowed this greatness upon you, what shall I be? Of what kind shall I be? (and thus became "ka").
That Indra replied, "If this belongs to you, then who shall I be? [Prajāpati said,] "Become that very thing.
For this reason, Prajāpati is called *Ka*.
One should consult the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with, "Indra, having slain Vṛtra, having conquered all victories, said... (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 3.21).

When that word is the pronoun *kim*, then the substitution of *me* is established by virtue of its being a pronoun (*sarvanāman*). However, when it is used etymologically (*yaugika*), it should be understood as occurring by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). Regarding the [proposed] elision (*pragṛhya*) by the rule *sāvekācaḥ*, there is a prohibition by the rule *na gośvan-sāvavarṇam*.
The word "action" (*kriyā*) must be supplied [to complete the sense]. Because the object (*karman*) functions as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the fourth case ending is used.

Whom? Prajāpati, the divine one endowed with qualities such as generosity. With what? With an oblation (*havis*)—either in the form of a sacrificial animal dedicated to Prajāpati or with a cake (*puroḍāśa*) prepared on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*). We, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), shall worship him; that is, we shall serve him.
The root *vidhati* has the meaning of service (*paricaraṇa*).
He who is the giver of self, the giver of strength, whose command all the worlds and the gods revere;
he whose shadow is immortality and whose shadow is death—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

He who is the giver of the self, the giver of strength, whose command all wait upon, whose command the gods obey; he whose shadow is immortality and whose shadow is death—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? 2.
He who is Prajāpati;
the giver of self,
for all selves indeed arise from that Supreme Self.
Just as sparks arise from a fire, so it is [in this case].
Or else, he is the purifier of the selves;
[from] the root *daip*, meaning "to purify."
By the rule *āto manin*, the suffix *vic* is applied.
*Baladāḥ*: one who gives or purifies strength (*bala*).
And whose excellent command—that is, supreme instruction or order—all living beings (*viśve prāṇinaḥ*) worship, seek, or serve.

The root *śās* is used in the sense of "instruction. By Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.4.34, *śāsa it*, the vowel *i* is substituted for the penultimate vowel when followed by a suffix beginning with a consonant other than *y*.
Furthermore, by the rule *śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca*, the substitution of the cerebral *ṣ* occurs.
The word *kruddha* has its original accent on the final syllable due to the rule regarding the accent of the base of a compound whose final member is a past passive participle.
Because the root *ās* is marked with an indicatory vowel *u* (anudāttet), the suffixes of the present system (*sārvadhātuka*) are unaccented, and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
Furthermore, by the rule “*tiṅi codāttavati*,” the prefix (*gati*) is unaccented when followed by a finite verb (*tiṅ*) that possesses an acute accent.
Likewise, even the gods wait upon his command;
moreover, "immortality" (amṛtam) refers to the state of immortality (amṛtatvam),
the expression being one where the abstract quality is predominant.
1. By that which is called the *ta4.5-kapāla*; 2. In the versions *ta1.2.3.6.7.8*, the word ‘*ātmadāḥ*’ is absent;
or alternatively:

*Amṛtam*: that in which there is no death (*maraṇa*) is *amṛta*, i.e., nectar (*sudhā*). In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, the words *jara*, *mara*, *mitra*, and *amṛta* [are udātta when preceded by *nañ*]," the final syllable of the subsequent member is accented acute (*udātta*).
Furthermore, he for whom the shadow of Prajāpati exists as if it were his own shadow,
and for whom Death and Yama, the snatcher of life-breaths, exist like a shadow—
to that deity [is this offering]; the rest is the same as with the previous oblation, but the specific difference is "with the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśāgman*).
He who by his greatness alone became the sole king of the breathing and blinking world;
he who rules over these bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?
He who by his greatness became the sole king of all that breathes and blinks, who rules over this world of bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? 3.

He who is Hiraṇyagarbha, of the breathing (*prāṇataḥ*) and of the perishing (*pradhvasataḥ*); [the root] *ana* means "to breathe," belonging to the *Adādi* class; the accentuation of the case-ending is due to the rule "śataranumaḥ. Of the blinking (*nimiṣataḥ*), i.e., performing the movement of the eyelashes; here too, as before, the case-ending is accented. Of the moving (*jagataḥ*), i.e., that which is mobile.

By whom the fierce heaven and the earth were made firm; by whom the sky was propped up, and by whom the firmament was established; he who is the measurer of the space within the mid-region—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? (5) By whom Prajāpati [the Lord of Creatures], the fierce *dyauḥ* (heaven/mid-region), and the *pṛthivī* (earth) were made firm—by whom they were rendered stable; and by whom the *svaḥ* (the celestial world/heaven) was *stabhitam* (propped up/established)—meaning it was placed above so that it would not fall down; [the form *stabhitam* is a Vedic irregularity for *stambhitam*]. Likewise, the *nākaḥ* (the sun/firmament) was propped up by him within the *antarikṣe* (mid-region). And he who is the *vimānaḥ* (measurer/architect) of the *rajaḥ* (water/space) within the *antarikṣe*—to that *kasmai* (to whom), etc., as explained previously. (5)

To whom, when the two crying ones, supported by his power and trembling in their minds, looked upon [him]—wherein the risen sun shines forth—to what god shall we offer worship with oblation? (6) *Yam*: whom; *krandasī*: the two crying ones, namely Heaven and Earth (dyāvāpṛthivyau)—for it is heard in scripture: "Because he wept (*arodat*), therefore these two are called *rodasī*" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.9.4); *avasā*: by means of protection, for the sake of protecting the world; *tastabhāne*: being established and having attained stability after being created by Prajāpati; *abhyaikṣetām*: they both gazed upon that Prajāpati with their mind—that is, with their intellect—perceiving, "By him our greatness is manifested"; from the root *īkṣ* (to see), in the *laṅ* tense, it is accented on the first syllable because it belongs to the *adādi* class. Of what nature are Heaven and Earth? *Rejamāne*: shining, gleaming; the change of *ā* to *e* is by metrical license (*vyatyaya*); due to the rule regarding the unaccented nature of the suffixes following the root, the accent falls on the root itself. Alternatively, it is the *kānac* suffix of the perfect tense (*liṭ*); according to Pāṇini 6.4.125, there is the change of *ā* to *e* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable; since it is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix in the Veda (*chandasyubhayathā*), the *śap* suffix is applied; hence, by the rule "the beginning of reduplicated forms is accented" (*abhyastānāmādiḥ*), it is accented on the first syllable. *Yatrādhi*: in whom, upon that Prajāpati who serves as the support; *sūraḥ*: the sun; *uditaḥ*: having reached its rising; *vibhāti*: shines forth, becomes manifest. The past participle (*niṣṭhā*) is derived from the root *i* preceded by *ut*; the preceding prefix retains its original accent according to the rule "a preceding prefix retains its accent" (*gatiranantaraḥ*). *Kasmai devāya haviṣā vidhema*: this is easily understood.

When the vast waters entered all things, bearing the embryo and generating Agni, from that the one life-force (asus) of the gods arose. To which god shall we offer worship with our oblation? *bṛhatīḥ*: "Vast," meaning great; in the *jas* case, the long vowel is substituted by the rule *vā chandasi*. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is accented according to the rule *brahmamahatopasaṃkhyānam*. This [mention of] Agni is illustrative; it refers to everything beginning with the ether, characterized by Agni.

1. [The word] *ga-ta* is *mu-stambhita* (stiffened by *mu*). 2. [The root] *stambhe* belongs to the *ga-bha* group. 3. [The word *stambha*] has the acute accent on the first syllable because it begins with *a* (i.e., it belongs to the *ajādi* class). 4. [This applies] to the letter *a* in *ta-bha*.

Generating the elements that have come into being, and holding within themselves as their embryo Prajāpati—who is the embryo of the golden egg—the Waters indeed pervaded the entire universe; for that reason, from that cause, Prajāpati, the one life-breath of all beings including the gods, came into existence. (Padyā).
From that embryo which the waters, abiding as the self of all, held within them, from that Prajāpati who had become the embryo, Vāyu—the vital breath of the gods and others—was born.
Or alternatively: *yat* (which).
There is an exchange of gender and number:

from those waters, which possess the aforementioned characteristics and stand enveloping the universe, there emerged—from them as a source—another, the one, non-dual *asu*, Prajāpati whose nature is breath (*prāṇa*).
Regarding him, the phrase "to whom" (*kasmai*) and so forth has already been explained.
He who by his greatness surveyed the waters as they brought forth skill and the sacrifice—
he who was the one God above all gods— to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

He who by his greatness surveyed the waters as they held within them creative power and generated the sacrifice—he who was the sole God above all gods—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? (8)

Generating—that is, producing—the sacrifice, which is characterized by the sacrifice and consists of the entire range of manifested effects; for that purpose, sustaining within themselves Prajāpati, who is capable (dakṣa) and expanding in the form of the phenomenal world; [the word] *dadhānāḥ* is the present participle (*śānac*) used in a causal sense from the root *dhā*;
its initial vowel is acute according to the rule "the first syllable of reduplicated forms."
"Such are the waters"—the nominative case is used by way of transposition; "the waters" refers to those existing at the time of universal dissolution; "with greatness" means with majesty.
The elision of the *m* is Vedic.
He who—namely Prajāpati—beheld [this] all around by his own majesty, and he who, being a god among the gods (*adhideveṣu*), was the sole, peerless lord even over them—he exists.
The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here in a Vedic sense for the root *as*.
The augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *asti-sico-'pṛkte* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.96).
The forms *tasmai*, *kasmai*, and so forth, have already been explained.
May he who is the progenitor of the earth, or he who, possessing true laws,
generated heaven, and he who generated the great, shining waters— him, the God, we shall worship with an oblation.

May he not harm us—he who is the progenitor of the earth, or he who, possessing true laws, propped up the heavens, and he who propped up the great, shining waters. To which god shall we offer worship with our oblation? 9.
May that Prajāpati not harm us, may he not oppress us—
he who is the progenitor, the creator, and the generator of the earth.
(In the word "janitā" used in the mantra, the elision of the suffix *ṇi* is prescribed by rule.)
By the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*, the case-ending following the word *pṛthivī* is acute.

And he who is the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*), whose nature is truth—that is, whose law (*dharma*) is true and unerring, and who is the sustainer of the world—generated all the worlds, including heaven as represented by the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
[The root] *janī* is used in the sense of manifestation.
In the case of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), there is *vṛddhi* [of the root vowel].
Because [the roots] *jan*, *jṛṣ*, *kas*, *sur*, and *rañj* take the *ṇiṅ* suffix according to the rule "janījṛṣkasurañaḥ...",
there is shortening of the vowel by the rule "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ".

Then, because of the prohibition "in the case of a suffix marked with *li*" (Pāṇini 3.1.35), the *ām* suffix does not occur; thus, after the *ṇi* suffix, there is *vṛddhi* [of the root vowel] for the *tip* ending.
By the rule "*liti*", the syllable preceding the suffix receives the acute accent (*udātta*).
And he who generated—that is, brought forth—the great, shining, and gladdening waters.
By the rule beginning with "uḍiḍam," the *śas* following the word *ap* is acute-accented.
The forms such as *tasmai kasmai* have already been explained.
For the oblation to Prajāpati at the sacrifice of the one who supports the *iḍā*, "O Prajāpati" (*prajāpate*) is the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*).

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "At the sacrifice of the one who supports the *iḍā* for Prajāpati: 'O Prajāpati, none other than you... (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 2.14). Offerings defiled by hair, nails, insects, and the like, should be cast into water by someone else.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "They should descend into the waters [with the mantra]: 'O Prajāpati, none other than you [has created] these things... (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.4.7). [The variants] "yat...yadvā" do not exist;
[the variant] "sthitāstāḥ" is found in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra (3.10).
This same [procedure] applies to the *caula* and other rites for the purpose of oblations;

and it is stated in the Sūtra: "Before those [rites], one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the verses beginning with 'Thee, O Child,' and then with the three verses beginning with 'Thou purifiest our lives,' and with 'O Prajāpati, none other than thou... (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.4.4).
O Prajāpati, no one other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
Whatever desire we have as we offer this oblation to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches.
O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
Whatever desire we have as we offer this oblation to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches.
O Prajāpati, other than you, there is no one else who [created] all these existing arrangements (vidhāni) at present.
The elision of the *śi* suffix occurs by the rule "śeṣchandasi bahulam" (Pāṇini 6.1.70).
All those various classes of beings that have been born, possessing their first modifications— you did not encompass them, nor do you grasp them,
nor do you pervade them;
the sense is that you alone are able to create them by grasping them.
The root *bhū* preceded by *pari* has the sense of "accepting" or "taking possession.
And whatever desires we have—whatever fruits we are longing for—we offer oblations (*havīṃṣi*) to you; may that fruit be ours.
Likewise, may we become masters, lords of riches and wealth.
By the rule "nāmyanyatarasyām," the name [of the word] is acute-accented.
The tenth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "vasuṃ na," is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Citramahas, the son of Vasiṣṭha; it is addressed to Agni.
The first and fifth verses are Triṣṭubhs, while the remaining ones are Jagatīs.
Thus it has been declared: "Vasuṃ na—aṣṭau [verses]; by Citramahas, the son of Vasiṣṭha; addressed to Agni; in the Jagatī meter; the first and the fifth are in the Triṣṭubh."
This hymn belongs to the Āgneya sacrifice, during the Prātaranuvāka and the subsequent Śastra, and is composed in the Jāgata metre.
As it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘vasuṃ na citramahasam’ is in the Jāgata [metre]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
I praise him who is like a treasure of wondrous luster—the lovely, gracious guest who is to be sought by the pious.
May he, Agni, the invoker and lord of the household, bestow upon us all-sustaining riches and heroic strength.

I praise Agni, who possesses wondrous luster, like a treasure—desirable, auspicious, a guest to be sought by the pious; may he, the invoker and lord of the household, bestow upon us all-sustaining wealth and heroic strength.

I praise Vasu, the one of wondrous luster, the lovely and gracious guest who is not to be assailed by the stones. May he, Agni—the Hotṛ-priest and lord of the house—bestow upon us all-sustaining riches and heroic strength.
Like a dwelling that provides shelter, like the sun of variegated splendor, and like Agni of venerable luster, I praise you—extolling you for your virtues.
The root *gṛ* in the sense of "sound" belongs to the *krayādi* class;
there is a change of person (from passive to active).
In words such as *pū* and others, [the substitution] of *āt* occurs in place of *avas*.
Alternatively,
*citramahasam* is in the accusative case used in the sense of the nominative; *na* is used in the sense of "now."
Now I praise the dwelling, the beloved, the wondrous day.
Of what sort is it?

It is lovely (vāma), desirable, auspicious (śeva), and bringing happiness; it is worthy of being honored like a guest (atithi), or else, for the purpose of carrying the oblation, it is ever-moving; and it is not to be hated (adviṣeṇya), being free from enmity.
The suffix *ken* is applied [to the root] *dviṣ* by the rule "kṛyārthe tavaikena" (Pāṇini 3.4.19).
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound with the negative particle *nañ*, the final syllable of the second member is udātta according to the rule "nañsubhyām" (Pāṇini 6.2.172).

That Agni bestows upon the sacrificers *śurudhaḥ*—cows who obstruct and ward off distress—and who sustain the entire world through the provision of milk and other nourishments; he also grants them excellent heroic power (*suvīrya*).
In the root *rā* meaning "to give," the suffix *leṭ* is applied;
by the rule *sibbahulam*, the suffix *sip* is added.

The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). From the root [√vah] with the word *viśva* as its prefix, the suffix *asun* is applied according to the rule "from √vah, √hā, √dhā, and √mā.
Because the term *ṇit* is understood from the previous context, the augment *yuk* is applied by the rule "āto yuk ciṇ" (Pāṇini 7.3.33).
Because it begins with "marut" and so forth, the final syllable of the preceding member bears the udātta accent.
What kind of fire is it?
It is the Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods, or the performer of the oblation; it is the Gṛhapati, the master of the house of the sacrificer. (Note:
The word "dviṣeḥ" does not exist in the Ta and Bha recensions.)
2. Ga-ta-bha: Pure from sorrow;
the Lord.

The suffix *kap* is applied to the root *grah* by Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.1.144 (*gehe kaḥ*). The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs according to the rule beginning with Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.16 (*grahijyā*).
By the rule “*pathāvaiśvarye*,” the original accent of the first member of the compound is retained.
In the bahuvrīhi compound *śobhanavīrya*, meaning "one whose vigor is beautiful," the final syllable of the second member is unaccented according to the rule *vīravīryaṃ ca*.

O Agni, graciously accepting my word, take pleasure in it—you who know all ways, O wise one, whose garment is clarified butter. Send forth the path for our prayer; the gods brought you forth according to your sacred law.

Taking pleasure in it, O Agni, graciously accept my splendor; you who know all ways, O most skillful one, whose garment is clarified butter, open a path for our prayer. According to your ordinance, the gods have brought this forth.
O Agni, being pleased and delighted, do thou graciously accept (*prati-harya*) my speech, that is, my hymn of praise;
[the root *harya* means "to move" or "to desire"].
Likewise, O *sukrato*—one of beautiful deeds or beautiful wisdom—do thou [accept] all *vayunāni*, that is, all [paths of knowledge].
This is the name "jñāna," which occurs here in the sense of that which is to be known (*jñātavya*). A wise person exists while knowing the various objects that are to be known;
the suffix *śatṛ* is used here in the sense of cause (*hetu*).
The meaning is: "From whatever cause you know [it], from that very cause, desire my word. O *ghṛtanirṇik*, you whose body is cleansed—that is, nourished—by clarified butter (*ghṛta*);
for the root *ṇijira* signifies both purification and nourishment.
Or alternatively:
*nirṇik* is a name for form.
O you of radiant form, bring (*erya*)—that is, cause to come—the sacrifice, which is to be traversed (*gātu*) or known, to the Brahman, that is, to the Brāhmaṇa sacrificer.
Following after your ghee—your own sacrificial act—all the gods, Indra and the rest, have generated [it];
that is, they produce fruits for the sacrificer.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Bring your sacrifice to the sacrificer."

The term *anu* has the status of a *karmapravacanīya* when used in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Because it is joined with a *karmapravacanīya*, the word *vratam* takes the second case ending.
The verb *jan* is in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense, used in the Vedic style after the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
Because [the root] belongs to the *mi* class according to the rule “*janījṛṣmasuśruo'mantāśca*,” there is shortening by the rule “*mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*.”
Pervading the seven stations, O mortal, bestow gifts upon the liberal donor who performs good deeds;
O Agni, favor him who has approached you with fuel, with wealth consisting of brave sons and self-sustaining power.

Seven are the stations; the immortal one goes around them. Bestow gifts upon the donor who performs good deeds. O Agni, honor him with wealth consisting of brave sons and with prosperity that is ever-present. Welcome with favor him who has reached you with kindled fuel. 3.

O Agni, you who are immortal and free from the nature of death, moving all around the seven stations—the worlds consisting of the earth and so forth—grant great wealth to that performer of good deeds, the sacrificer who offers oblations such as the *puroḍāśa* cake; that is, to the one who has given and performed the sacrifice well. *Mahatiḥ* is a verb meaning "to give."
By the rule *sukarmapāpa* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.89) and others, the suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *kṛ* following the word *suparvan*, in the sense of the past tense.
And whatever sacrificer, O Agni, reaches you—that is, attains you—by means of the fuel (*samidh*), which is the instrument for kindling (*samindhana*) through the act of increasing (*edhana*).
The root *naś* has the sense of "going. From this root, the *laṅ* suffix is used according to Vedic usage;
by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
The augment *āṭ* is seen even in the Veda;
or, by means of transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is *śam* from the root *aś*.
That sacrificer [is blessed] with *suvīra*;
that is, one whose sons are excellent heroes.
In the compound *vīravīrya*, the final syllable of the second member (*vīrya*) is unaccented.
Enjoy yourself together with such self-existent wealth—riches that are well-established on all sides, increasing, and worthy of being bestowed.

1. In manuscripts ga, ta4.5, and bhara, the word *iha* (here) is present; in manuscript ta, however, it is absent. 2. In manuscripts ga, ta, bha, and ma, the word *jñātavyam* (should be known) is absent. 3. In manuscripts ga, ta4.5, and bhara, the words *caru-puroḍāśādīni* (the sacrificial oblations of cooked rice, cake-offerings, and so forth) are present. 4. In manuscripts ta1.2.3.6.7.8 and ma, the word *vardhiṣṇunā* (by the increasing one) is absent. 5. In manuscripts ga, ta4.5, and bhara, the instruction is *juṣasva sevasva* (enjoy and serve).

Those possessing oblations praise him, the banner of sacrifice, the first domestic priest, the vigorous one, Agni who hears us, whose back is anointed with ghee, the sprinkler, the god who bestows excellent heroic strength upon the giver. 4. Of the sacrifice. The banner. The first. The domestic priest. Those possessing oblations. Praise. Seven. The vigorous one. Hearing. Agni. Whose back is anointed with ghee. The sprinkler. Bestowing. The god. Upon the giver. Excellent heroic strength. 4.

The banner of the sacrifice—the indicator of the ritual, the foremost among all the gods, or the one occupying the primary position; or rather, the domestic priest (purohita) who acts for the benefit of those before him;
or else, he who is established in the eastern direction in the form of the Āhavanīya fire.
By the rule *pūrvādharā* (Pāṇini 5.3.39), the suffix *asi* is added to the word *pūrva*;
by virtue of that same rule, the base *pūrva* undergoes the substitution *pura*.

Since the resulting form is a *taddhita* suffix that does not function as all case-endings, it receives the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by the rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.38). Consequently, by the rule *puro'vyayam* (Pāṇini 1.4.67), it receives the designation of a *gati*.
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied to the root *dhāñ* in the sense of the object;
for the root *dadhāti*, it is replaced by *hi*.
Subsequently, in the compound, by the rule "the prefix immediately preceding [a member] retains its original accent," the prefix retains its *prakṛtisvara* (original accent).

[We praise] the one who possesses vigor (*vājin*), who is powerful, or who possesses horses; who hears our hymns, knowing them through his hearing; whose back is glistening with clarified butter (*ghṛtapṛṣṭha*), whose limbs are radiant; the bull (*ukṣan*)—that is, the distributor of rain by means of sacrifice, or rather, the one capable of pouring it forth; the youth; for the sacrificer who bestows oblations (*pṛṇate*), that is, who gratifies him.
[The root] *pṛṇ* [in the sense of] "to gratify" belongs to the Taudādika class.
In the word *śatarūnāmāḥ*, the accentuation belongs to the case-ending (*vibhakti*).
According to the rule “the mention of an action must be included,” the object is treated as a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and thus the fourth case is employed.
[The term refers to] those who gratify the sacrificer with oblations (*havirbhiḥ*) and gratify the one who bestows wealth with riches (*pṛṇantam*).
Or alternatively: *pṛṇati* means "to give," as it refers to the act of giving. [The word refers to] one who gives the oblations to the sacrificer, bestowing wealth upon him.

Those possessing oblations (*haviṣmantaḥ*)—namely, the seven principal *hotṛ* priests and others who utter the *vaṣaṭ* call—praise and extol Agni, who is endowed with excellent vigor (*suvīrya*), who is radiant (*deva*), and who is possessed of qualities such as generosity (*dāna*); that is, they praise him who is distinguished by such attributes. [The root] *īḍ* means "to praise";
it belongs to the *ad-ādi* class.

You are the first messenger, the most excellent; being invoked for the sake of immortality, you take delight. The Maruts purified you in the house of the donor; the Bhr̥gus caused you to shine forth with their hymns of praise. 5. You are the messenger, the first, the most excellent; being invoked for the sake of immortality, you take delight. The Maruts purified you in the house of the donor; the Bhr̥gus caused you to shine forth with their hymns of praise. 5.

O Agni, you are the messenger of the gods, appointed to the task of a messenger; you are the foremost, the principal, the celebrated, or the renowned, and you are the most excellent, worthy of being honored.
As such, for the sake of immortality—that is, for the purpose of [our] freedom from death—being invoked by us or being gratified by our oblation, do you rejoice;
"mad" means to be exhilarated.
The elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Moreover, the Maruts—the hosts of gods dwelling there—purify (*marjayan*, i.e., adorn) you as you abide in your middle station with your manifold forms (*vaiśvarūpeṇa*).

Likewise, in the house of the donor (*dāśuṣaḥ*), the sacrificer who has offered oblations, the Bhṛgus—the seers of the Bhṛgu lineage—have illuminated (*virurucuḥ*) you preeminently with hymns (*stomaiḥ*).
After the word *bhṛgu*, the suffix [denoting descent] is elided when applied to a plural number by the rule *atribhṛgukutsa* (Pāṇini 2.4.65). Thus, *rurucuḥ*.
[The root] *ruc* means "to shine."

From this [root], the *liṭ* (perfect tense) suffix is used according to Vedic usage. 5. Milking for nourishment the well-milking cow who provides all sustenance, O Agni of good wisdom, for the sacrificer who loves the sacrifice; you who drip with clarified butter, having circumambulated the three times the long-extending ritual acts, you proceed for the sake of the one of good wisdom. 6. *iṣam* (nourishment); *duhan* (milking); *sudughām* (well-milking); *viśvadhāyasam* (all-sustaining); *yajñapriye* (for the one who loves the sacrifice); *yajamānāya* (for the sacrificer); *sukrato* (O you of good wisdom); *agne* (O Agni); *ghṛtasnuḥ* (dripping with clarified butter); *triḥ* (three times); *ṛtāni* (the ritual acts); *dīrgha* (long); *vṛtiḥ* (enclosure/extent); *yajñam* (the sacrifice); *pariyan* (circumambulating); *sukratūyase* (for the sake of the one of good wisdom).
