[The root] *ruca* in the sense of "shining" is not present [here].

O Agni, O performer of good deeds (*sukṛt*), O doer of auspicious actions (*sukarman*), or O you of beautiful wisdom (*śobhanaprajña*), for the sake of the sacrificer who delights the gods with sacrifices and oblations (*yajñapriya*), you—milking (*duhan*) and pouring forth (*kṣārayan*) the milk that is the fruit of sacrifice, which is the desired food (*iṣam*) consisting of the sacrificial reward, a cow that sustains all (*viśvadhāyasam*), one that is easy to milk (*sudughām*), and whose form is the sacrifice; likewise, you are one who bathes in clarified butter (*ghṛtasnuḥ*), being anointed with the sacrificial oil (*ājya*).
The suffix *ku* is added to the root *snā* according to the *Uṇādi* rules;
or alternatively, he is so called because his lofty ridge (*snuḥ*, i.e., *sānuḥ*)— meaning a mass of flames— is glowing (*ghṛtaḥ*) or blazing.
By the rule "An addition is made for *māṃsapṛṣṭha* and others" (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.63.1), the word *sānu* undergoes the change to *snū*.
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.
Such as you are, [you have entered] the three places—earth and the rest—which are true (*ṛtāni*), meaning real, and which are repeated three times (*triḥ*).

Or rather: illuminating the sacrificial stations such as the *gārhapatya* and others, and moving around—reaching each respective sacrificial hall and each respective sacrifice—while encompassing the entire sacrificial hall and the entire sacrifice being performed, you perform your good work (*sukṛtyase*).
You desire for yourself a beautiful ritual (*kratu*) or sacrifice.
Or else:
One whose sacrifice (*kratu*) is beautiful is a "well-performer" (*sukṛt*), namely a sacrificer (*yajamāna*). You act like him;
that is to say, just as he proceeds with the correct performance [of the rite], so too do you yourself proceed for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of the sacrifice—this is the meaning.
At the break of dawn, human beings, making you their messenger, have sacrificed to you.
The gods have magnified you for your great glory, O Agni, as they prepared your sovereignty at the sacrifice.

Making you their messenger at the break of this dawn, human beings have performed sacrifice; the gods have magnified you for your great glory, O Agni, as they purified the clarified butter at the ritual. 7.
Now, during the dawning, the brightenings, and the breakings of this very dawn that is seen here, O Agni, human beings—making you alone their messenger of the gods—have sacrificed and sacrifice;
the meaning is that they sacrifice to you alone, who are the self of all the gods.
Likewise, even the gods [sacrifice] to you for the sake of magnifying and honoring you.

In the word *mahāpūjāyām*, the suffix *āya* is added in the sense of an abstract noun (*bhāva*) according to the *auṇādika* rules. They have increased, or they cause to increase, for the sake of their own worship.
What are they doing? In the *adhvara*—wherein *dhvara* refers to the transgression caused by violence—they offer clarified butter (*ājya*) in a sacrifice free from that [violence].
This is an elliptical expression (an *upalakṣaṇa*).
Wiping away— that is, casting into— you all the oblation characterized by clarified butter,
the Vasiṣṭhas, the wise ones, have invoked you, the powerful one, O Agni, while praising you in the sacrificial assemblies.
Bestow upon the sacrificers an increase of wealth; do you all protect us always with your blessings. 8.

The Vasiṣṭhas, the wise ones, have invoked you, the vigorous one, O Agni, chanting praises at the assemblies. Bestow upon the sacrificers an increase of wealth; do you all protect us always with your blessings. 8.
"O Agni, they find the gods who are to be worshipped in this *vidatha*"; here, *vidatha* means sacrifice.

In those [sacrifices], the *vasiṣṭhas*—the sons of Vasiṣṭha or the sages—are the ordainers (*vedhasaḥ*) of rites; praising and extolling you, the one rich in food or strength, they have summoned you down most intensely. They have offered praise.
The ātmanepada suffix is applied by the rule *hvejo luṅi 'nisamupavibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.30).
The substitution of *ṇl* for the suffix is prescribed by *ātmanepadeṣvanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.54).
Regarding the suffix *arthan* prescribed after the word *vasiṣṭha*, its elision (*luk*) occurs when referring to many individuals, according to the rule *atribhṛgukutsa...* (Pāṇini 2.4.65).
As such, O Agni, bestow and establish among us, who are performing the sacrifice, the nourishment—that is, the increase—of *rāyaḥ*, meaning wealth.
The sixth case ending after the word *rai* is acute by virtue of the rule beginning with "udittvāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.171).
Furthermore, the *s* sound replaces the *visarjanīya* by the rule "ṣaṣṭhyāḥ patiputro" (Pāṇini 8.3.53).
The rest has been explained. Even for a single object, the plural number may be used.

The eleventh hymn, beginning with “This Vena,” consists of eleven verses; its seer is Vena Bhārgava, its meter is Triṣṭubh, and its deity is Vena.
Thus it is indicated in the Anukramaṇī: “This Vena [is the seer]; [the deity] is Vainya.”
In the Pravargya rite, during the pressing of the Soma, this [verse] is to be recited first.
It is stated in the Sūtra: “In the Ṛc, ‘This Vena impels the drops from the womb of the speckled one’” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.6).
This same verse is also to be used as the Dhāyyā in the Vaiśvadeva Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Vena, the first carpenter, impelled those whose womb is the speckled one" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.18).

Vena is the beloved; this deity, known by that name, resides in the middle station. Jyotirjarāyu means that the cloud, which possesses light, has light as its amnion.
The *jarāyu* is that by which the embryo, being enveloped, remains in the womb;
he who has such an envelope is so described. The meaning is that he stands like an embryo in the midst of the clouds.
In the *vimāna*: that in which the waters are measured (*vimīyante*) or fashioned (*nirmīyante*) is the *vimāna*, namely the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
Of the dust (*rajasas*).
Remaining in the intermediate space, this Vena creates waters;
"pṛśni" refers to the sun,
and these are its offspring.
Or alternatively:

the *pṛśni* rays are the sunbeams of brilliant color; he impels the waters situated in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), which have become the embryos of those rays, and sends them forth toward the earth.
At the meeting, at the gathering of the waters, of the intermediate spaces, and of the sun—in the atmosphere—the wise, the inspired singers lick this Vena with their prayers and hymns.
*Rihatī* is a verb meaning "to lick";
they praise him.
They worship;
that is to say, they praise.
Like a child.
Just as parents and other relatives fondle their young child with words of praise, so too [is he treated].
In that very same hymn of praise, there is this verse: "From the ocean, the wave...
For it is stated: "Vena raises the wave from the ocean; the drop goes toward the ocean" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.7).

From the ocean Vena raises up the wave; born of the mist, the back of the beloved one has become visible. He has moved upon the ridge of the ridge of Truth; they have sung toward the common womb, the protectors. From the ocean, Vena raises up the wave; born of the mist, the back of the beloved one has become visible. He has moved upon the ridge of the ridge of Truth; they have sung toward the common womb, the protectors. 2. From the ocean, the wave rises up; Vena, born from the mist, has made visible the back of the beloved one. Upon the ridge, on the summit of Truth, he has moved; they have cried out toward the common womb, the protectors. 2.

Because waters flow from it, the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is called "samudra. From that, this Vena raises up—causes to emerge—the wave, which is a mass of water; the meaning is that he causes half [of it] to fall. Of what nature is he? He is "nabhoja," born in the sky (nabhas). They call out toward this Vena. [The root] *nu* is used in the sense of praise (*stuti*); it belongs to the *kuṭādi* group, and the elision [of the suffix] is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

The many mothers of the calf, standing together and lowing toward their common goal, dwelling in the same nest, moving upon the ridge of *ṛta*, the voices lick the honey of immortality. samānam | pūrvīḥ | abhi | vāvaśānāḥ | tiṣṭhan | vṛṣṇaḥ | mātaraḥ | sa-nīḍāḥ | ṛtasya | sānau | adhi | cakramāṇāḥ | rihanti | madhvaḥ | amṛtasya | vāṇīḥ || 3 ||
1. It is fashioned (*vimāyate*) or created (*nirmīyate*).
Having reached many former common places shared by Vena and oneself, they lowed toward [it], crying out on all sides;
or else:

Desiring that very *vena*, the waters of the atmosphere—acting as mothers (*mātaraḥ*) to the lightning-fire which occupies the place of a calf (*vatsasya vatsasthānīyasya*), being of the same nest (*sanīḷāḥ*) and sharing a common abode (*samānanilayāḥ*)—remain there. Furthermore, moving about (*cakramāṇāḥ*) upon the high ridge (*sānau*) of the ridge of *ṛta* (water), they lick (*rihanti*) the sounds (*vāṇīḥ*) of the sweet nectar-like water; that is, they praise this *vena*.
The meaning is that they adorn themselves.
Knowing [the way], they have adorned their forms; the Brahmin has followed the sound of the wild buffalo as it moves.
Going by the Truth (ṛta), they stand upon the river; the Gandharvas are the names of the immortals.

The sages, possessing infinite wisdom, longed for the form; they went toward the cry of the wild buffalo. Moving according to the Eternal Law, they stood over the river; the Gandharva discovered the immortal names.
The wise, the intelligent singers of this Vena, knowing his form, have yearned for him—they praise him;
for the root *kṛp* has the meaning of "to praise.
To the question "How do they know his form?", he says:

Of the deer that is to be sought after, [and] of the buffalo—this is a name for the great. Because they go toward, that is, they approach, the roar, characterized by thundering, which is the sound residing in the cloud of the Great Ones (mahatām) and the Desired One (venasya), therefore they know its form; such is the meaning.
In the Vedic *laṅ* tense of the root *gam*, there is elision of the *śap* suffix according to the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*” (Pāṇini 2.4.73).

There is elision of the penultimate vowel according to the rule “*gamahana*” (Pāṇini 6.4.98). And there is the absence of the augment *aṭ* even when joined with *māṅ* according to the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge ’pi*” (Pāṇini 6.4.75).
Moreover, people who go toward—that is, reach—that *vena*, doing so through a hymn or sacrifice that is *ṛta* (cosmic order) and *satya* (truth), stand upon the *sindhu*, the flowing mass of water.
The meaning is that for them, that *vena* brings about rain.

If one asks what the reason for this is: it is because this *gandharva*—the sustainer (*dhartā*) of the *gāḥ* (waters)—is the *vena* whose name is the *amṛtāni* (immortalities), which are the causes of immortality.
This is a name for water (*udaka*). Water is so called because its nature is to flow (*namanaśīla*). "He who knows" (*vidat*) means he who knows;
the meaning is that they abide under his control.
Therefore, for those devoted to Him, rain is easily obtained.
An Apsaras, smiling toward her lover, the woman supports him in the highest heaven. Moving among the wombs of his beloved, being the Beloved himself, that Vena sits upon the golden wing.
The Apsaras, the woman smiling toward her lover, bears him in the highest heaven. Moving within the wombs of the beloved, he, being beloved, sits upon the golden wing; he is Vena. 5.

*Apsarā*: one who is the charioteer of the waters, or one who moves (*sarantī*) within the waters for the sake of sport; *upasiṣmiyāṇā*: having approached the vicinity of her beloved, smiling; from the root *smi*, meaning "to smile" or "to laugh. The form is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) perfect (*liṭ*).
From that [perfect tense suffix] *liṭ*, the suffix *kānac* is applied by the rule "liṭaḥ kānaj vā.
Such a woman—a female in the form of lightning—is the "lover" (*jāra*), that is, the one who causes the waters to age;
or alternatively:
Like a lover or a paramour, he cherishes this beloved one;
he sustains and nourishes this Vena in the highest, most excellent sky— the intermediate space.
Or he sustains [them].
Just as some pregnant woman, having approached her lover, laughing aloud nourishes him in a secluded place, even so, by means of this Vena, lightning flashes; such is the meaning.
Move within the *yonis*—the places—of this beloved Vena.
She who has the form of lightning (*vidyut*) moves and goes;

she goes by herself in the manner of a woman going to meet her lover (*abhisārikā*). And he, her beloved, being most favorable to her, sits—sits down—upon the wing, that is, upon the cloud which is his own wing, which is golden (*hiraṇyaya*), made of gold, possessing the sound of a golden thunderbolt, or rather, possessing a form that is exceedingly delightful.
He sits down together with her.
At the consecration (*abhiṣava*), the verse is "Upon the vault of heaven, the fair-winged bird" (*abhiṣave ‘nāke suparṇam*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the words 'Upon the vault of heaven, as he flies toward,' when [the rite] is completed, one should sit down with the *praṇava*" (*āśva. śrau. 4. 7*). [Note:
In version 1, ga, ta4, ta5, and bhara, the word 'sānau' does not appear.]

When they beheld you with longing in their hearts as you flew down to the firmament—the golden-winged messenger of Varuṇa, the bird hurrying to the seat of Yama—6. When they beheld you with longing in their hearts as you flew down to the firmament—the golden-winged messenger of Varuṇa, the bird hurrying to the seat of Yama—6.

When the singers, longing for you with their hearts—that is, with their inner selves and minds—behold you in the *nāka*, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), then you approach; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Of what nature [are you]?

The one of beautiful flight (*suparṇam*), moving through the atmosphere as he flies; the one with golden wings (*hiraṇyapakṣam*), endowed with two golden pinions; the messenger (*dūtam*) and scout of Varuṇa, the deity presiding over the waters; the bird (*śakunam*) existing in the form of a winged creature within the womb—the place of the atmosphere—at the forefront of Yama, the restrainer, the son of Vivasvat;
the sustainer (*bhuraṇyam*), or alternatively, the nourisher of the entire world by means of bestowing rain and other such acts.
The root *bhuraṇa* belongs to the class beginning with *kaṇḍū* (the *kaṇḍvādi* group), meaning "to support" and "to nourish.
From this root, the *uṇ* suffix is applied according to the rules of the *auṇādika* [section].

The Gandharva has stood upright upon the firmament, facing us, bearing his brilliant weapons. Clothed in a fragrant garment, fair to behold, he has generated his own dear names like the light of heaven. ūrdhvaḥ | gandharvaḥ | adhi | nāke | asthāt | pratyaṅ | citrā | bibhrat | asya | āyudhāni | vasānaḥ | atkam | surabhim | dṛśe | kam | svaḥ | na | nāma | janata | priyāṇi || 7 ||
The Gandharva, existing in the upper region, is the sustainer of the waters (gavaḥ).
In the word *gavīghan*, the suffix *vap* is added to the root *dhṛñ* (meaning "to hold") with *go-* as its prefix; furthermore, the prefix *go-* undergoes the change to *ghan*.
Such is Vena; facing us, with his face turned toward us, he stands upon the *nāka* in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
What is he doing?
Bearing and holding the wondrous, marvelous, and admirable weapons that belong to his own self.

In the case of *bibharti* with the suffix *śatṛ*, the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable occurs by the rule *bhṛjāmit*. There is a prohibition of the *num* augment by the rule *nāmyastāt ṛcchatuḥ*.
The acute accent on the first syllable is established by the rule *abhyastānām ādiḥ*.
Likewise, wearing a beautiful, fragrant garment—his own expansive form—he covers himself everywhere;
for what purpose? For the sake of being seen.
The form *dṛśe viśve* is an irregularly formed (nipātita) word ending in the suffix *ke*.
*Kam* is a filler word. In this regard, there is an illustration: gold.
*Svaḥ* refers to the Sun, the Āditya who is beautiful to behold;
just as he covers his own form everywhere so that it may be seen, in that same manner [he acts].
Immediately thereafter, he *janata*, i.e., generates—brings forth—the *nāma*, meaning waters which have the nature of bowing (*namanaśīla*), which are dear and favorable to all.
The meaning is that it causes rain to fall.

This verse, "The drop goes toward the ocean," is for the *pravargya* rite; and it is stated in the Sūtra: "The drop goes toward the ocean... O friend, turn toward your friend" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.7). 8. The drop goes toward the ocean, O Vidharman, beholding with the eye of a vulture. O Upholder of Law (*vidharman*), situated in the intermediate space (*antarikṣe*) which is the upholder (*vidharmaṇi*) and the sole supporter (*vidhāreke*), [is] the *drapsa*, that which is by nature mobile (*dravaṇaśīla*).
Or alternatively:
*drapsa* means water-drops; [the word] *drapsin* means "possessing those."
The suffix *ac* is applied because [the word] belongs to the *arśas-ādi* group.

When the Sun (*gṛdhra*), who longs for the essences (*rasa*), beholding with his eye—that is, his splendor—shines forth as the *vena*, he approaches the ocean, the cloud that has the nature of overflowing. At that time, the Sun (*bhānu*), shining with his bright (*śukra*) flame (*śocis*) or splendor, desiring (*cakāna*) in the third realm or world, performs (*cakre*) those dear things which are desired by all.

The twelfth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "imaṃ no agne," was composed by the Aṅgirases while they were preparing for the consecration; having become the very forms of the deities, they praised their own selves as those deities. Therefore, they themselves are both the seers and the deities of these verses.
The remaining [verses] were praised by Varuṇa and Soma;
therefore, those six [verses] have them as their seers (ṛṣis). The first [verse] is addressed to Agni.
The ninth [verse] has Indra as its deity;
in the remaining four, the deities are those indicated by their respective marks.
The seventh is in the Jagatī meter; the rest are in the Triṣṭubh meter.

And thus it has been indexed: "This for us, O Agni... (RV 10.2), "The highest... (RV 10.3), "The Nihnavas... (RV 10.4), "Varuṇa, Soma... (RV 10.5), "Of the Ādityas... (RV 10.6), "The first is addressed to Agni" (RV 10.7), "Three [verses] are praises of Agni" (RV 10.8–10), and the remaining [verses] are according to their respective deities; the seventh is a Jagatī. The application [of these verses] has been explained. We approach this sacrifice for us, O Agni—the five-pathed, threefold, seven-threaded.
This one has been our leader, a winner of cattle; like the dawn, he has lain long in deep darkness.

1. O Agni, we approach this sacrifice of ours; come hither! To the five-pathed, threefold, seven-threaded [sacrifice]. This one has been our leader, a winner of cattle; for a very long time indeed, he has lain in deep darkness. 1.
When the horses carrying the oblation had died and Agni, having fled out of fear of death, was hidden in a cave, you placed him [the fire] within it.
The seers invoked him through this hymn:
"O Agni, come (*upa ihi*) to this sacrifice (*imaṃ yajñam*) of ours (*naḥ*)."
Attain it! Do not flee!
Of what sort is it?
It is "fivefold" (*pañcayāma*) because it is performed by the sacrificer and the five officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
or alternatively, because it is attained through the five oblations (*havis*), such as parched grain (*dhānā*) and ground meal (*karambha*), or through the five fore-offerings (*prayāja*).

"Trivṛtam" means threefold, either by way of the distinction between *pākayajña*, *haviyajña*, and *somayajña*, or by way of the three *savanas*. "Saptatantum" means having seven threads; that is, one whose extenders of the ritual acts (*tantr*)—the *hotṛ* and other priests—are seven, or whose utterers of the *vaṣaṭ* call are seven. Alternatively, it refers to that which is expanded sevenfold as: Agniṣṭoma, Atyagniṣṭoma, Ukthya, Ṣoḍaśī, Vājapeya, Atirātra, and Aptoryāma.

Having approached such a sacrifice, immediately thereafter, be "havyavāṭ"—the carrier of our "havyāni," the oblations. (The augment *ḍ* is added by rule). Furthermore, be our "purogāḥ," the one who goes before us.
The word *viṭ* is derived from the verbal root *viś* (to enter),
with the substitution of *ā* for the nasal according to the rule *viṅvanorunāsikasyāt*.
[O Agni,] having abandoned us for a long time (*jyok*), you have lain for a long duration (*dīrgham*) in the cave (*guhāyām*) within the great darkness (*tamaḥ*).
Having taken your seat, you made your bed;
the meaning is that from this point forward, do not come to us from that place.
"On this very day, being wise and dwelling in the cave, perceiving [the truth], I attain immortality."
I praise the auspicious one who is auspicious; from my own source of happiness, I do not flee from the fire-drill, the navel [of the sacrifice].

From the godless, I become a god; as one of great wisdom, while perceiving that which is hidden, I attain immortality. I praise the auspicious one who is auspicious; being inauspicious myself, I do not flee from my own source of happiness, the fire-drill, the navel. 2. From the godless, I become a god; as one of great wisdom, while perceiving that which is hidden, I attain immortality. I praise the auspicious one who is auspicious; being inauspicious myself, I do not flee from my own source of happiness, the fire-drill, the navel.
From one who is *adaiva*—that is, devoid of the habit of gambling—and from *guhā*, meaning existing within the cave (the heart);

here the locative case ending is elided according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. *Pracetāḥ*, by means of the solicitation of the gods, *yat* when going forth, *devaḥ*—I, whose nature is to play—I, being *prapaśyamānaḥ*, that is, beholding and observing the portions of oblation consisting of the *prayāja*, *anuyāja*, and so forth, which have been prepared for my sake by the gods, attain *amṛtatvam*, immortality.
I attain the state of divinity, which is the absence of the nature of death.
By the transposition of the locative case (*dṛśoḥ*), the *ātmanepada* ending is used.
Having fled from the one who carries the oblation (*havirvāhana*), he took refuge in places such as water and so forth.
1. *ga-ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha1.2.4.8-vistāryamāṇam* | 2. *ta1.2.3.7-bha1.2.4.8-āsthāpaya*.

The hidden meaning is: when he was again entreated by the gods for the sake of being carried forth, he then said, "By means of this oblation (*havis*), I have attained the state of divinity. This is the sense.

Although I, having emerged from the cave and being manifest, perform a beautiful sacrifice, yet when—being inauspicious, of an unlovely form, and unmanifest—I abandon and relinquish you, the auspicious and beautiful one, at that time of union, I go to and reach the *nābhi* (the navel-like binding place) and the *araṇi* (the friction-stick), which are by nature binding; for I, who have long resided there in the form of a horse, approach them out of affection due to my own friendship with them.
I have measured out many abodes of the guest of Paryanya, the offspring of Vayā, and the foundations of Ṛta.
I proclaim auspiciousness to the Father, the Asura; from that which is unworthy of sacrifice, I come to the portion worthy of sacrifice.

The other [is] the guest of another; of the lineage [I am] the guest. I have measured out many abodes of the cosmic order (*ṛta*). I proclaim what is auspicious to the Father, the Asura. From that which is unfit for sacrifice, I go toward the portion that is fit for sacrifice. 3.

Beholding the Sun—the guest who constantly moves from my own abode, the earth, toward another place, the heaven—and knowing his course, I follow the path of the Sun and, during the seasons such as spring, fashion and bring forth the many, manifold bodies (*dhāma*) of *ṛta*, that is, the sacrifice.

Then, having become the *hotṛ* priest for the sake of the Father—the divine host dwelling in the heavenly world, the *asura* skilled in casting away enemies—I recite the hymns (*ukthāni*) directed toward auspicious happiness.

Since this is so, for that reason, having departed from the *ayajñiya*—the place unworthy of sacrifice—I go to and reach the *yajñiya*, the portion of earth characterized as the altar or characterized by the oblation (*havis*), which is worthy of sacrifice.
In the word *yajña*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 5.1.71 (*yajñavigbhyāṃ ghañjau*) to denote fitness for the purpose.
"For many years I have acted; choosing Indra within this [sacrifice], I abandon my father."
Agni, Soma, and Varuṇa—these shift; that which has turned away, I drive back hither.
Outside, I have made them equal; within this [space], choosing Indra, I abandon the father. Agni, Soma, and Varuṇa—they move away. O Ārvat, that kingdom has come back to me. 4.
In this place characterized by the altar, I have performed [the rite] for many years (*bahīḥ samāḥ*), that is, for many years;
I have dwelt there for a long time.
There, choosing and honoring Indra, I abandon—that is, I relinquish—the father who consists of the forest (*araṇya*).
But when I had emerged from among the gods and was hidden in the cave, then those gods—Agni, Soma, and Varuṇa—fell away;
they were displaced from the kingdom.
Even though each one had become an oblation for a day, there is a distinct and direct designation of them as separate deities.

"O Āyana, let us return! That kingdom which was seized by the Asuras—turning back, turning around, and returning toward me—I protect that kingdom, that sovereignty, and the sacrificial ground from the Asuras.
[The word] *paryāvart* is derived from the root *vṛt* with the prefix *upa-sṛṣṭa*, according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.75: "It is seen after other roots as well."

By the restrictive rule *rātsyasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24), there is no elision [of the final *m*] according to *saṃyogāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.23). Having created [this], the Asuras became [my] enemies; and you, O Varuṇa, desire me.
O King, entering into truth by means of truth, come to the sovereignty over my kingdom.

1. Having come together from all sides, 2. having approached from the ancient path—those Asuras were devoid of *māyā*. Om! They were indeed [the ones]. And you, O Varuṇa, do not desire me; O King, by means of Truth (*ṛta*), you have utterly cast out untruth (*anṛta*). Come to the sovereignty over my kingdom! 5.
When you had reached the middle region, O Asura, those seven [beings] became free from *māyā*; that is to say, all the *māyās* belonging to the Asuras were burnt away by me. And you too, O Varuṇa.

And this word *ca*, occurring in the sense of *cet* ("if"), is another indeclinable (*nipāta*). Because it is joined with this [particle], the prohibition of the loss of accent (*nighāta*) for the verbal ending in *kāmayāse* applies by the rule "In the presence of particles such as *yat*, *yadi*, *hanta*, etc. (Pāṇini 8.1.30).

O Varuṇa, if you should desire me, then, O King, O Lord, by means of our *ṛta*—that is, by our truthful action—separating and removing the *anṛta*, the unreal, illusory conduct of the Asuras, take possession of the sovereignty, the lordship, and the mastery over my kingdom—that realm which has been established by me.
This is for you two, O Svardr̥ś; this is the lovely, radiant, and wide mid-air.
Having slain Vṛtra, come forth, O Soma! Being present as the oblation, let us worship with the oblation.
This is yours; this indeed was the lovely thing for you both. This is the light, the wide mid-air. Let us slay Vṛtra. Come hither, O Soma! We worship thee, the wise one, with an oblation. 6.
This is either a statement of Ṛgveda 10.124.5 or of Varuṇa.
O Soma, this heaven (svaḥ)—or alternatively, this beautiful red sun—this very thing has become desirable (vāma) for you.
By the word "this" (idam), the previously mentioned heaven (svaḥ) is referred to.
And this light is the support of light; O Soma, behold this vast and wide intermediate space (antarikṣa).
Therefore, at this very moment, let us two slay Vṛtra;
for that purpose, come forth, having gone out.
O you who are the oblation, becoming the essence of the deity in the form of a creeper—may we worship you with the oblation, such as the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa*.
The poet: Having assumed his form in heaven at the beginning of time, Varuṇa released the waters.
Like women seeking security, the rivers carry his bright color upon them.

The poet: Through his poetic power, he assumed form in heaven. Varuṇa, acting without rival, released the waters. Like women, the rivers created security; they, bright and radiant, bear his color upon themselves. 7.
A poet is one who has transcendent vision; he is a friend by virtue of his poetic nature.
By the rule "supām suluk," the third case ending is replaced by the vowel 'ā'.
With his all-pervading vision, he fixes his own form—his radiance—upon the sky, in the celestial world.
In *pañja saṃge*,
there is the elision of the nasal (*n*) by the rule *daṃśasañjasvañjāṃ śapi* (Pāṇini 6.1.25), following the addition of the suffix *śap* in the present indicative (*laṭ*).
7. Non-existence through non-existence.
By the rule "supām suluk," there is a long vowel of the same quality as the preceding one for the third case ending.
With very little effort, Varuṇa released the waters from the cloud; he caused them to flow forth.

Released by Varuṇa, those waters became rivers—streams characterized by their constant flowing—and like wives who bring security to their husband, they provide security for the world, protecting it. Pure, bright, or radiant, they bear, that is, they intensely uphold and maintain, the white and luminous color of this Varuṇa.

In the rule *dādhryādi* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.65), because of the inclusion of *bharibhrat* as an irregular form (*nipāta*), there is an absence of *jaśtva* substitution for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) when the suffix *yaṅ* is elided (*yaṅluk*).

1. *ta-bha* 1.2.4.8—*etatsomam*; 2. *ga-ta-bha* 1.2.8—*etasmin samaye bhava etatsamaya*; 3. *ta* 1.2.3.6.7.8—*bha* 1.4.7.8—*hināvāva*; 4. *ta-bha*—*aprabhūṇā*; 5. *ga-ta* 1.2.3.6.7.8—*bha* 1.4.7.8—*jaśtvādeśaḥ*. [Maṇḍala 10, Adhyāya 10, Sūtra 125]. The Eighth Aṣṭaka, 765.

They gather unto him his supreme power; he dwells within them, rejoicing in their own nature. Like subjects choosing a king, they, shrinking back in fear, stood apart from Vṛtra. They gather unto him his supreme power; he dwells within them, rejoicing in their own nature. Like subjects choosing a king, they, shrinking back in fear, stood apart from Vṛtra. 8.

Those aforementioned waters, having been rained down, gather together—that is, they come together with and partake of—the most excellent, that is, the greatest, *indriya*, or heroic power of this Varuṇa;
the meaning is that they sustain it.
This is according to the Vedic revelation: "The waters were the wives of Varuṇa" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.5.4.1).
By *svadhā*—
this is a name for food— meaning "rejoicing," that is, becoming exhilarated by the food characterized as the oblation.
Or rather:
"Varuṇa goes toward (ā kṣeti) those very waters (tāḥ apaḥ), which gladden him through the oblation produced by means of rice and other grains."
The root √*kṣi* means "to dwell" and "to go. Here, there is the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) according to Vedic usage.

And those *tāḥ*—namely, *enam* (him)—*varuṇa*, just as *viśaḥ na viśaḥ* (subjects, like subjects) serve a king, their master, so too do they *vṛṇānāḥ* (choosing, serving him), being *bībhatsuvaḥ* (trembling with fear).
Or alternatively:
"bound" means being obstructed by Vṛtra.
When he was slain, they stood apart from that Vṛtra;
having retreated, they remained here and there.
From the root *badh* in the sense of "binding," the suffix *san* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.6 (*mān-bhr̥-dān-śāntyaḥ*), and there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable.
The suffix *u* is applied by Pāṇini’s rule *sanāśaṃsabhikṣuḥ* (3.2.168).
The substitution of *uvaṅ* occurs in the *jas* case-ending as a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

They call him the swan, the companion of those who loathe [impurity], moving in the dwelling place of the divine waters. The seers have discerned Indra through their inspired thought as he moves along with the *anuṣṭubh* being recited. bībhatsūnām | sayujam | haṃsam | āhuḥ | apām | divyānām | sukhye | carantam | anuṣṭubham | anu | carcyamānam | indram | ni | cikyuḥ | kavayaḥ | manīṣā || 9 ||
Of those who are loathsome, whose limbs are trembling— or alternatively,
of those bound by *medha*—
the *haṃsa* is the sun, so called because it goes (*han*) or moves.
They call him the "yoked companion" (sayuj);
the exponents of the Veda (brahmavādinaḥ) declare this very thing. Indeed, it is so.
Moving within the friendship—that is, the state of being a friend—of the divine waters, those belonging to heaven and those belonging to the intermediate space;
[moving toward] the Anuṣṭubh, that which is to be praised as such.
Or alternatively:
By the word *anuṣṭubh*, the sacrifice or the hymn connected with it is indicated— namely,

the sacrifice associated with the *anuṣṭubh* meter, or a specific hymn joined with the *anuṣṭubh* meter. [The term *anucaryamāṇam* means] being repeatedly consumed or moving toward that which is aimed at (*anu*).

In the case of *caryaṅ* [from the root *car* with the suffix *yaṅ*], by the rule *utparasyātaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.88), there is the substitution of *u* for the vowel *a* following the reduplicated syllable.

Although the elision (*luk*) of the suffix would have been applicable by the rule *caraphalaukṣa* (Pāṇini 7.4.87), the augment *ruk* is applied to the reduplicated syllable instead because the suffix is not *liṭ*.
Thus, the *kavayas*— the seers of far-reaching vision— have discerned and honored with their *manīṣā*, that is, through their hymns of praise, Indra who is distinguished by such qualities;
or rather, they have discerned him— that is, they know him— through their *manīṣā*, their intellect.
From the word *manīṣā*, there is elision (*luk*) of the third case ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
From the root *cāy* in the sense of "worship" or "perception," in the Vedic *liṭ* [perfect tense], the substitution of *kī* for the root occurs by the rule *cāyaḥ kī* (Pāṇini 6.1.35).
Then, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs by the rule *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82).
The hymn beginning with "I am" (*aham*) is the thirteenth *sūkta*. The daughter of the great seer Abhraṇasa, named Vāc, who was a knower of Brahman, praised her own self.
Therefore, [the word] "clarified butter" (*sarpiḥ*).
The Supreme Self (Paramātman), whose nature consists of consciousness and bliss, who is all-pervading, is the deity.
Therefore, experiencing identity with Him, she praises her own self, saying, "I alone am everything," by appearing in the form of the entire universe and as the substratum of all.
The remaining [verses] are in the Jagatī meter.

1. From this [verse] beginning with *ga-ta-bha*. 2. The *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha* [meter] is friendship (*sakhitva*). 3. The *ga-ta-bha-mu* [meter] is to be recited as *anuṣṭubh*. 4. The *ga-ta-4.5-bha* [meter] does not exist at all; it consists of *triṣṭubh*s.
And thus it has been stated in the index (*anukramaṇī*): "In 'I am eight,' the speech of Ambhṛṇī [consists of *triṣṭubh*s], while the second verse, which speaks of the self, is a *jagatī*."
The application is concluded.

I move with the Rudras and with the Vasus; I [move] with the Ādityas and also with the Viśvedevas. I support both Mitra and Varuṇa; I [support] Indra and Agni; I [support] both the Aśvins. 1. I. With the Rudras. With the Vasus. I move. I. With the Ādityas. And. With the Viśvedevas. I. Mitra and Varuṇa. Both. I support. I. Indra and Agni. I. The two Aśvins. Both. 1.

I am Vāg-Āmbhṛṇī, the seer of the well-spoken hymn; becoming of the nature of that Brahman which is the cause of the universe, I move about in the company of the Rudras—the eleven Rudras—the instrumental case here expressing identity. Thus, in the form of that [Brahman], I move.
In this way, in passages such as "with the Vasus," one should construe it as "I move in that respective form.
Similarly, regarding "Mitrāvaruṇā," meaning Mitra and Varuṇa,
the vowel *ā* is the substitute for the accusative dual ending according to the rule "supāṃ suluk."
Both and both—I alone, having become Brahman, sustain and maintain them;
even Indra and Agni, I alone maintain;
both and both—the two Aśvins, I alone maintain.
For the entire world is superimposed upon me, like silver on a white shell, and thus appears as real;
and Māyā undergoes a transformation (vivarta) into the form of the world.
Through such Māyā acting as its substrate, there is the production of everything—even of that Brahman which is described as unattached—described in such a manner.

I bear the mighty Soma; I [bear] Tvaṣṭṛ, as well as Pūṣan and Bhaga. I bestow wealth upon the sacrificer who offers oblations, who is skillful in his work, and who presses the juice. 2. I. Soma. Āhanasam (mighty). Bibharmi (I bear). Aham (I). Tvaṣṭāram (Tvaṣṭṛ). Uta (as well as). Pūṣaṇam (Pūṣan). Bhagam (Bhaga). Aham (I). Dadhāmi (I bestow). Draviṇam (wealth). Haviṣmate (upon the one possessing oblations). Suprāvye (who is skillful in his work). Yajamānāya (upon the sacrificer). Sunvate (who presses the juice). 2.

I myself sustain Soma—the one who strikes down [the enemy], who is to be struck down, and who is to be drunk; or rather, Soma, the slayer of enemies, who dwells in heaven and is the very self of the gods.
Likewise, I myself sustain Tvaṣṭṛ, as well as Pūṣan and Bhaga.
And likewise, for the one possessing oblations, for the one joined with oblations, for the one who is well-pleasing, the bringer of beautiful oblations to the gods, and the satisfier.
From the root *avan* with the sense of "satisfying" (*tarpaṇa*), the suffix *haṅ* is applied according to *Uṇādi-sūtra* 3.158 (*avitṛstṛtamantrabhya haṃ:*), resulting in the suffix *ikāra*.

In the singular dative case, after the *yaṇ*-substitution, the case-ending (*sup*) becomes *svarita* according to the rule: "The *anudātta* vowel following a *yaṇ* that results from an *udātta* or *svarita* vowel becomes *svarita*."
To the one who presses the Soma, performing the extraction of the juice.
The word "śatrunumaḥ" has its acute accent (udātta) on the fourth syllable.

To such a sacrificer, I myself bestow—that is, I maintain—*draviṇam*, wealth, which consists of the fruit of the sacrifice. Furthermore, this Brahman’s status as the giver of fruits has been established by the venerable Commentator in the section beginning with the aphorism: "The fruit [comes] from Him, because that is logical" (Brahma-sūtra 3.2.38).

I am the sovereign ruler, the gatherer of treasures, the conscious one, the first among those worthy of sacrifice. The gods have established me in many places, me who have many stations and who cause many things to enter [into being]. 3. I am the sovereign ruler, the gatherer of treasures, the conscious one, the first among those worthy of sacrifice. The gods have established me in many places, me who have many stations and who cause many things to enter [into being]. 3.
I am the sovereign ruler (*rāṣṭrī*).
This is a name for the Lord;
I am the mistress of the entire world.
Likewise, she is the bringer together (*saṃgamanī*), the one who causes the meeting and leads the worshippers to the *vasus*, which are riches;
she is *cikituṣī*, having realized through her own nature that Supreme Brahman which is to be directly perceived. Furthermore, she moves together with the Ādityas.
And furthermore, she has directly perceived [it] together with the Viśvedevas. (Maṇḍala 10, Anuvāka 10, Sūkta 125) Eighth Aṣṭaka, 767.

Indeed, those gods have established me— who am the first and foremost of these sacrifices, distinguished by such qualities, who abide as the manifold expansion (*prapañca*) through many modes (*bhūristhātrā*), and who cause many classes of beings (*bhūri bhūriṇi bhūtajātāni*) to enter [the world] by manifesting myself in the form of the individual soul (*jīvabhāva*)— in many places (*puhatrā*). This is because I exist in the aforementioned manner through my universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*).
The meaning is that whatever they do, they do it all unto Me alone.
He who perceives, he who breathes, and he who hears what is spoken—by me they are fed.
Those who do not understand dwell near me; hear, O you who have heard! I speak to you with faith.

He eats the food by me—that one who sees, who breathes, and who hears what is spoken. Those who lack understanding dwell near me. Hear, O you who are heard! I speak that which is worthy of faith to you. 4.
He who eats food eats it through me alone, in the form of the power of the enjoyer;
and he who sees— that is, perceives—
and he who breathes— that is, performs the activity consisting of inhalation and exhalation— he too does so through me alone.
And whoever hears what has been spoken.
The root *śru* means "hearing. According to the rule *śruvaḥ śra ca*, the suffix *śra* is applied;
the root *śru* undergoes the substitution of *śra*.
Those who do not know me as I exist in such a form as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin)—being thoughtless, meaning they do not reflect upon or recognize me—dwell in proximity [to suffering];
that is, being exhausted by saṃsāra, they become fallen.
The suffix *tṛc* is applied after roots such as *man* and *raṇ*.
In a compound with *na*, there is an acute accent on the final syllable by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Alternatively:
The suffix *tṛ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
Consequently, in the *bahuvrīhi* compound, by the rule “*nañ-subhyām*,” there is udātta accent on the final syllable of the latter member.
Thus, *māma-mantaḥ* means those who are devoid of pride and sacrificial knowledge.
O friend Śrutaviśruta, listen!
Hear what I am about to say.
In Vedic usage, there is elision (luk) of the verbal suffix (vikaraṇa).
By the rule “śru-śṛṇu-pṛ-kṛ-vṛ-bhyaḥ,” the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs.
What is that which is to be heard?
It is faith.
Faith is [produced] by the faithful.
This is appropriate;
the meaning is that it is obtained by means of faith (*śraddhā*).

1. The house of poison (gara-gṛha).
2. The funeral pyre (cita) of Gauryā, who was burdened by the syllables *ga* and *ta*.
3. Coming (*āgacchantī*), she was moving about (*vāyatī*).
From the root *eti* preceded by the prefix *ā*, when the suffix *śatṛ* is applied, there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of *śap*; [thus we have] *āyat*.
By the rule *iṇo yaṇ* (Pāṇini 6.4.81), the substitution *yaṇ* occurs;
and by the rule *ugitaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.6), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is added.
In the word *śataranumaḥ*, there is likewise an acute accent (*udātta*).

[The form] *vakṣabhiḥ* [is derived from] the stars appearing as if they were dice (*akṣa*). The substitution of *ha* for the place of *kṣa* in the word *akṣa* occurs because [the rule] "it is also seen in the Vedic language" (*chandasy api dṛśyate*) applies.
Or alternatively:
by means of the *akṣas*, i.e., the marks or splendors;
she is the goddess (*devī*), whose nature is to shine (*devanaśīlā*), in many places (*purutrā*).

By the rule "devamanuṣyapuruṣapurumadhyebhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.2.39), the suffix *a* is applied to the word *puruṣa* when it denotes excellence; thus [we have] *pauruṣeya*. This Night-deity (*rātrī*) indeed sees (*paśyati*) this entire world (*viśvam*) in its particularity (*viśeṣeṇa*). The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule "rātrennājasau" (Pāṇini 4.1.31).
In the form *syāteḥ*, the *liṅ* suffix is replaced by *cleḥ* (the *aṅ* augment) in the *luṅ* tense according to the rule *asyativaktyūṣibhyaḥ* and so forth.
Furthermore, this [goddess] supports (*dadhāti*) all these glories (*viśvāḥ śriyaḥ*).
In the *luṅ* tense of the root *dadhāti*, the substitution of *it* occurs according to the rule *sthādhvorica*.
The *sica* [suffix] is marked with the *kit* designation. By the rule "after a short vowel, from a stem," there is the elision of the *sica*.

With her broad tip, the immortal goddess, descending from the heights, drives away the darkness with her light. ā | uru | agrāḥ | amartyā | nivataḥ | devī | udvataḥ | jyotiṣā | bādhate | tamaḥ || 2 || With her broad tip, the immortal goddess, from the depths and from the heights, drives away the darkness with her light. || 2 ||
The immortal, deathless goddess—the night, characterized by shining—is the vast, wide intermediate space (antarikṣa). First, the winds (vātaḥ) fill it with darkness;
[the root] *prā* is used in the sense of "filling."
It belongs to the *ad-ādi* class.
In the *laṅ* tense, the middle person is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Likewise, it covers with its own brilliance those things that grow downward, such as creepers and shrubs, and those that rise upward, such as trees.

Immediately thereafter, that darkness—the gloom—is overcome and suppressed by light in the form of planets, lunar mansions, and so forth. As the goddess Dawn approaches, she has driven away her sister, the Night; indeed, the darkness now departs. ni | om iti | svasāram | akṛta | uṣasam | devī | ā'yatī | apa | ita | om iti | hāsate | tamaḥ || 3 ||

The goddess Night, whose nature is to shine, as she approaches, has made her sister Dawn appear; that is, she adorns her with light, or rather, she causes her to turn away. When that Dawn has arisen, the darkness of night departs—it goes away. [From the root] *ohāṅ* "to go," the augment *iṭ* is added in the imperative (*leṭ*), and the suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule *sibbahulam*.

May she [protect] us today, at whose coming we have settled down, as birds settle for their dwelling in a tree. 4. She—[protect] us today! At whose [coming] we have settled down; at your coming, as birds [settle] their dwelling in a tree. 4.
May that goddess Night be gracious to us at this time; when her course has been reached—upon her arrival—we shall enter, we shall settle down comfortably in our homes.
The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to Pāṇini 1.3.17 (*nerviśaḥ*), and there is the Vedic elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix.
In this regard, there is an illustration:

just as birds (*vayas*) dwell upon a tree—that is, they take up their residence at night by resorting to nests in a tree—so too do we dwell. The villages have settled down; those with feet have settled down; the winged ones have settled down; even the falcons seeking their prey have settled down. (5) The villages have settled down; those with feet have settled down; the winged ones have settled down; even the falcons, though seeking their prey, have settled down. (5)

*vgrāmāsaḥ* means *grāmāḥ*. Here, the word *grāma* refers to a multitude of people, as in the expression "he has come to the village" (*grāma āgataḥ*). All the people *vni vavikṣata*: they settled down when that night had arrived; they lay down. This is derived from the root *viś* preceded by the prefix *ni*, in the Vedic *luṅ* (aorist) tense, with the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) as previously explained.
1. *ta1.2.3.6.8-bha-akṣabhiḥ* | 2. *ga-tamobhiḥ* | 3. *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha-tathā dadhāter luṅi* | 4. *ga-tamasāvṛṇoti*.

[In the case of *dadhāti* in the *luṅ* tense: by the rules "after a root ending in *śal*, having a penultimate *i*, and being *aniṭ*, there is *ksa*" (Pāṇini 3.1.45) and "the elision of *k* of *ksa* before a vowel" (Pāṇini 7.3.72), there is the elision of the letter *a*.
Likewise, those with feet—such as cattle, horses, and so forth—settle down;
likewise, birds and those endowed with wings settle down; as do those who have a purpose.

The meaning of *ater* is "going. They are endowed with swift movement. Even the hawks (*śyenāsaḥ*) settle down during this night; the meaning is that this night, having come of its own accord, brings comfort to all classes of beings who have become exhausted by their wandering during the day.

Drive away the she-wolf and the wolf; drive away the thief from our dwelling. Then, become easy for us to cross. 6. Drive away! She-wolf! Wolf! Drive away! Thief! From our dwelling! Then! For us! Easy to cross! Be! 6.

He says, "O Night! This is a name for the night. O Night, keep away from us the she-wolf—the female of the wolf—and the wolf that seeks to harm us; separate them from us, so that they may not reach us to oppress us. Keep away the thief and the robber; sever them from us. And thereafter, become easy for us to cross with comfort, bringing us security.

The most brilliant darkness has settled upon me, clearly manifesting its blackness. Drive it away, O Lord, as one settles a debt. 7. upa | mā | pepiśat | tamaḥ | kṛṣṇam | vi-aktam | asthita | uṣaḥ | ṛṇā-iva | yātaya || 7 ||
The darkness—thickly painting, clinging to all things, black and black-colored, clearly manifesting its own nature as it pervades everything—such a terrifying darkness approached me.
This is the means for bringing about union with the Self.
O Uṣas, O goddess, drive away that darkness as one drives off debts;
just as you discharge the debts of your worshippers by bestowing wealth, so too do you dispel the darkness—this is the meaning.

I have brought [this] to you like cattle; O Night, daughter of Heaven, accept the hymn as one accepts [the prize] from a victor. 8. I have brought it to you like cattle; O Night, daughter of Heaven, accept the hymn as one accepts [the prize] from a victor. 8.
O Night, O goddess of night, I approach you as one approaches a milch-cow or a cow that yields milk, and I turn you toward me with hymns of praise.
In the Vedic *luṅ* tense, the root *kṛ* takes the substitute *aṭ* for *cli* according to the rule *kṛmṛdruhibhyaścleraṅ*.
O daughter of Heaven, daughter of the shining Sun, or rather, O daughter of that very Heaven.

Furthermore, by the rule *param api chandasi* (Pāṇini 2.1.2.6), because the subsequent word ending in the genitive case behaves like the preceding vocative member, the entire compound of two words undergoes the eighth-case [rule] of being entirely unaccented (*sarvānudātta*).
By your grace, may I conquer my enemies; accept my hymn of praise as if it were an oblation, and partake of your own portion.
From the root *ji* (to conquer), the *liṭ* suffix takes the form *kasu*.
By the rule "sanaliṭojeḥ," the *j* following the reduplication undergoes *kutva* (change to *g*).
The dative case is employed in the sense of the genitive, according to the rule "the dative should be stated in the sense of the genitive."
The semivowel substitution (saṃprasāraṇa) occurs by the rule "vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam."
The sixteenth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “*mama agne*,” is the seerly composition of Vihavya Āṅgirasa; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas.
Of this hymn, the first verse is in the Jagatī meter, while the remaining verses are in Triṣṭubh.
For it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “*Mama agne*: nine verses; [the seer is] Vihavya; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas; it ends in Jagatī.”
When the *saṃsava* has become the occasion, this [hymn] is to be recited before the *vaiśvadeva* hymn.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "One should place the *nivid* for the *vaiśvadeva* hymn either with the verse ‘*mām agne varcaḥ*’ or with this very same one" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.6).
During the *samāvartana*, one who desires success should offer fuel-sticks while reciting this hymn, verse by verse.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “With the mantra ‘O Agni, may splendor be mine,’ one should add fuel-sticks, verse by verse” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.9.2).
O Agni, may splendor be mine in the invocations; may we, kindling thee, nourish our bodies.
May the four quarters bow down to me; with thee as our overseer, may we conquer the hostile armies.
1. Hawks and vultures have gone to the sky. 2. On this day, all beings have become [as follows]. 3. Of one who has conquered.

O Agni, let there be splendor at the three libations; kindling you, may we nourish our bodies. Let the four quarters bow down before the great one; with you as our ally, may we conquer the hostile armies. 1.
O Agni! *vihavāḥ* are battles, so called because heroes are summoned in various ways (*vividham āhūyante*) therein;
or alternatively:
The *vihavas* are sacrifices (*yajñas*) because the gods are invoked in them for various sacrificial purposes.
By the rule *‘haḥ saṃprasāraṇaṃ ca nyabhyupavibhu’* (Pāṇini 3.3.72), there is the suffix *ap* in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇe*) and *saṃprasāraṇa*.
By the rule *thāthādi*, the final syllable of the compound is udātta.
May *varcas*—that is, luster—be mine through your grace, whether in battles or in sacrifices.
And we, kindling you and causing you to be fully ignited, may we nourish—meaning, increase through oblations—the body of you, your physical form.

In the case of *handhi* with the suffix *śānac*, although the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) of *śānac* would otherwise apply by the rule "the acute accent [of the suffix] by virtue of the removal of the acute [of the preceding element]" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*), the initial acute accent is instead optionally applied by the rule “*avibhāṣā vaṇivandhānayoḥ*” (Pāṇini 6.1.215).
May we nourish our bodies.
After the root *puṣ*, the suffix *aṅ* is applied in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*) when the optative (*liṅ*) follows.
Moreover, in *mama* and *madartha*,
by the rule "ṅi ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.212), the word *asmad* takes the udātta accent on its first syllable.
The four quarters are the excellent directions;
the meaning is that the people living therein should bow down,
becoming humble of their own accord.
In the case of the root *nam* used in the sense of the agent as the object (*karmakartṛ*) in the imperative (*loṭ*), there is a prohibition of the suffix *yak* by the rule "na duhasnunamām."
With you as our leader and protector, may we, together with you, conquer and overcome the hosts—the armies of the enemy.
May all the gods be present at my invocation—the Maruts accompanied by Indra, Viṣṇu, and Agni.
May the atmosphere be a vast space for me; may the wind blow favorably for me in this desire.

At my vital point, may all the gods be present at the three libations; may the Maruts be accompanied by Indra, and may Agni be swift. May my vital point and the mid-air be a wide space; may the wind blow favorably for this desire of mine. 2.
May all the gods be present for me in the invocation, in battle, or in sacrifice; may they be my very achievers.
Who, then, are they? The Maruts accompanied by Indra, as well as Viṣṇu and Agni.
Likewise, may the intermediate space be my vast world, possessing expansive illumination.
The root *lokṛ* means "to see.
The suffix *ghañ* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). Thus, *loka* means "light" or "illumination" (*āloka*, *prakāśa*).
In the bahuvrīhi compound *uruloka*, there is the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member.
Moreover, while this desire remains to be fulfilled and its fruit serves as the causal sign, let the wind—the air—blow favorably.
The root *pūṅ* means "to purify" (*pavane*).
It belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*.
By the rule beginning with *uḍidam*, the syllable following *sa* in *idam* becomes udātta.

May the gods bestow wealth upon me through sacrifice; may the blessing be in me, and in me the invocation of the gods. May the two divine Hotṛ-priests first accept [the offering]; may we, with our bodies, be masters of heroes and free from enemies. 3. In me—may the gods—wealth—bestow—through sacrifice. In me—may the blessing—be. In me—the invocation of the gods. The two divine Hotṛs—may they accept. First—free from enemies—may we be—with our bodies—possessing good heroes. 3.

May all the gods bestow—cause to come to me, their worshipper—wealth and riches; that is to say, may they grant me great bounty. Likewise, may the blessing—the fruit of the sacrifice which is to be desired—be mine alone.
The *devahūti* is the sacrifice (*yajña*), so called because it is the invocation (*hūti*) of the gods (*deva*) within it;
may that be in me.
Furthermore, these [oblations] belong to the gods, thus they are divine (*daivya*).

The suffix *yañ* is applied according to the rule ‘*devādy-acaḥ*’. May such Hotṛ-priests—my own officiating priests who accomplish the perfect oblation—being the first to appear before the priests of others, worship and serve the gods.
In the Vedic *laṅ* of the root *vanati*, by the rule "there is extensive transposition," there are three modifications:
the *upratyaya* suffix, the *sip* ending, and the absence of the augment *aṭ*, which is a Vedic feature.
And may we ourselves be unharmed and uninjured in our bodies, possessing excellent heroes and excellent sons.
In the compound "vīravīryau," the acute accent (udātta) falls on the first syllable of the final member of the compound.
1. [Ta-bha-prāpta] Maṇḍala 10, Adhyāya 10, Sūkta 128. [Aṣṭaka 8, Anuvāka 7, Sūkta 75] Let them offer sacrifices for me; let my intention be true in my mind.
Do not lead us astray in anything whatsoever; O All-Gods, speak in our favor!
Let them sacrifice for me; let my offerings be accepted. May the intention of my mind be true. Let me not fall into any sin whatsoever. O All-Gods, speak in our favor. 4.
"Let the officiating priests sacrifice for me; let them worship the gods with oblations on my behalf.
Or else, the dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
The meaning is: "my own," that is, my officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
"My own oblations" refers to those oblations which exist, such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*; the meaning is "by means of those offerings.
Likewise, may the intention (*ākūti*) of my mind—the mental resolve, the prayer for what is desired—be true, that is, in accordance with reality.
Moreover, may I not go toward any sin whatsoever—neither toward that which is committed nor toward that which is intended, nor even toward that which is merely contemplated;
that is to say, may I not commit any evil.
In the aorist (*luṅ*) of the root *iṇ*, there is the substitution of *gā* according to the rule "in the aorist, *iṇ* becomes *gā*. [The mantra:
"O Agni, driving away their fury, as an undeceived guardian, protect us on every side! Let those who revile return again toward their own homes; let their awakening consciousness perish. (6)
O Agni, driving back—that is, propelling toward and repelling—the *manyu*, the anger, of those enemies; being *abādhyah*, unassailable by anyone; you are the *agopāḥ*, the protector.

From the root *gup* in the sense of "to protect," with the suffix *āya*, followed by the *kvip* suffix, this form arises after the elision of *v* (as per *ver apṛktasya*) and the subsequent elision of the semivowel (*valopa*).
O such as you, protect us—guard us on every side from all directions. Those enemies, turning back against us, shall be hidden away.
The root *guhū* means "unmanifest sound";
from this, with the suffix *kip*, there is the augment *tuk*.
Uttering sounds that are extremely indistinct and faltering due to fear, let them go back to their own place; let them return.
Furthermore, let the *citta*—the mind which is the instrument of cognition—of these enemies who are waking up, perish simultaneously and utterly.
The singular number is used in the sense of each individual.
[The form] *aśat* is derived from the root *aś* in the sense of "not seeing," with the Vedic elision (*luk*) of the suffix;
due to its inclusion in the *pupādi* group, there is the substitution of *ah* for the suffix *cli*.
According to the rule *naśimanyor aliṅgatvaṃ vaktavyam* (Pāṇini 6.4.120, vārttika 5), the substitution of *ai* for the vowel *a* does not apply here.
May Dhātṛ, the ordainer of ordainers, the lord of the world, the divine protector who wards off assailants,
and both Aśvins— may Bṛhaspati and the gods protect this sacrifice and preserve the sacrificer from distress.
May Dhātṛ [the Ordainer], the lord of the worlds, the gods, Bṛhaspati, and both Aśvins—[and] the god Trātṛ, the overcomer of adversaries—protect this sacrifice and the sacrificer from misfortune. 7.

The meaning is: "I praise that Indra—or Savitṛ—who is the creator (dhātṛ) even of the creators of the elements (dhātūn), the creator of the entire world and of all living beings; who is the Lord (pati), the protector (pālayitṛ); that God (deva) whose nature is to shine; the Savior (trātṛ), the protector from all fears; the subduer of adversaries (abhimātipāham), the overcomer of enemies (abhimātīnām); [I praise] Indra or Savitṛ distinguished by such qualities. This is the remainder of the sense.
‘pāha abhabhave’: the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *chandasi sahaḥ*;
the acute accent on the case-ending is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
"Both Aśvins, Bṛhaspati, and all the gods headed by Citra— may they [protect] this sacrifice being performed and the sacrificer from *nyartha*, that is, from misfortune or sin; or rather,
*nyartha* is the absence (*abhāva*) of *artha*, meaning purpose."
Therefore, "may they protect" means "may they guard and make [this] fruitful."
By the rule *neranidhāne* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.192), the final syllable of the compound is udātta.
May the far-reaching bull, invoked by many, rich in food, grant us protection at this sacrifice.
O Indra, lord of bay horses, be gracious to our progeny; do not harm us, nor abandon us.

May the wide-striding buffalo grant us great protection; may he, invoked by many, rich in cattle, at this invocation—O Indra, Lord of tawny horses, be gracious to our progeny; do not harm us, nor abandon us. 8.
*Uruvyacas* means "widely pervading"; *mahis* means "great" or "worthy of worship"; *puruhūta* means "invoked by many sacrificers"; and *purukṣu* means "having many dwellings."
The suffix *ḍa* is applied by the rule "an addition [should be made] for *mitadrū* and others" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.180.1) to the root *kṣi*.
Or alternatively:
being praised—that is, extolled—by many (puru) people.
The suffix *ḍa* is applied as before.

In the case of the root *kṛ* with the suffix *kvip* denoting the object according to the *auṇādika* rules, there is an absence of the *tuk* augment, based on the principle that "the teaching regarding augments is not always obligatory."
Such is Indra at this *hava*, that is, this sacrifice (*yajña*).
It is called *hava* because offerings (*havi*) are poured into it; the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of the locus of the action of pouring (*juhoti*).
Or rather:
in this *hava*, that is, in this joyful encounter concerning you.
For, by the rule "bhāve 'nupasargasya," there is the suffix ap after the root *hā* when it is without a prefix, as well as vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*).
"May he grant (yaṃsat)—that is, bestow or give—'śarma,' meaning happiness, unto us (naḥ), that is, unto ourselves."

1. Of these who are ignorant, [they are] gurus; of these who know, [they are] enemies. 2. Being praised (*śaṃsyamānaḥ*). The augment *aṭ* is added by the rule *yama-ram-nama-ātām*. The suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule *srivahulam*. O Haryaśva—O Indra, you whose horses are bay (*harī aśvau yasya*)—[addressed as] "he" (*he*), may you (*vaḥ*) for us (*naḥ*), that is, for our progeny (*prajāyai*); the dative case is used in the sense of the accusative. Make our progeny—sons, grandsons, and so forth—happy (*mṛḷaya*). Do not harm (*mā rīriṣaḥ*) us (*naḥ*). And do not abandon us (*mā ca parā dāḥ*). "Abandonment" (*parādānam*) means casting off. The meaning is: do not cast us away.
May those who are our rivals be driven away; may we subdue them with the help of Indra and Agni.
The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas have made him—the one who reaches upward—the perceiver of our well-being and our sovereign lord.

Those who are our rivals—let them be driven away! By means of Indra and Agni, may we repel them. May the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas place me above them all, making me a fierce observer and sovereign ruler. 9.

May those enemies who are our rivals depart from us; let them go away, let them be displaced from their own places and driven out. Having been favored by Indra and Agni—who are pleased by our oblations and hymns—we shall utterly repel those rivals and destroy them completely.
Moreover, may the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas make me—me, who touch the heights, the one who has attained the exalted station, the most excellent among all—[so];
likewise, [may they make me] fierce, of formidable strength, and a perceiver, a perceiver.
The absence of the augment *iṭ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
May they all make me the knower of all, the sovereign ruler, and the supreme lord of all.
In the Vedic *luṅ* tense of the root *kṛ*, the suffix *śluk* is applied by the rule "in mantras, [the substitution of] *ghas* etc. and so forth.
In the eleventh section (anuvāka), there are twenty-three hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "nāsad āsīt," is in the Triṣṭubh meter;
its seer (ṛṣi) is Prajāpati named Parameṣṭhin.
Since the creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth of entities such as space (viyat) are the subjects to be expounded here, their agent, the Supreme Self (paramātman), is the deity.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: “The non-existent, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, and the activity of beings.
The application (viniyoga) has been explained.
Neither non-existence nor existence existed then; there was no atmosphere, nor the sky beyond it.
What was concealed? Where? In whose protection? Was there water, unfathomable and deep?
Neither non-existence nor existence existed then; there was no air, nor the sky that is beyond it. What was concealed? Where? In whose protection? Was there deep, bottomless abyss? || 1 ||
The creation will be explained later in passages such as "From the pillar of austerity, one was born.
For now, that prior state—prior to that [creation]—which is the state of dissolution (pralaya) wherein the entire phenomenal world (prapañca) has been cast out, is being described.
At that time, during the state of dissolution, that which is the root cause of this world did not exist as a non-entity (asat), like the horn of a hare, which is indefinable.
For the origin of this existing world from such a cause is not possible.
Likewise, it was not non-existent (*asat*), nor was it definable as having the nature of existence (*sat*) like that which possesses the essence of being.
Although "existent" and "non-existent" are each distinct by nature, nevertheless, even the coexistence of both presence and absence is possible.
"How can there be identity between those two?"—the meaning is that something entirely distinct from both must have been the expressible reality.
Now, one might object: "The phrase 'not existent' (na sat) is a negation of ultimate existence;
therefore, it follows that even the Self (ātman) would be indeterminable (anirvācya)."

Now, it might be argued: "No; the existence of that [Brahman] will be stated later in the verse 'It breathed without wind' (Ṛg Veda 10.129.2); therefore, it is only by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣanyāya*) that existence is denied here."
Even so, the qualification "at that time" is for the purpose of [distinguishing it from] the state of conventional usage; for even then,
there is the persistence of their existence.

3. [The letter] *ga* does not exist in the first, second, third, sixth, seventh, or eighth [position] of the *bha*-group, because it lacks ultimate existence (*pāramārthikasattā*). Now, since conventional entities such as earth and so forth do exist, how can there be a negation stating "it is not existent"?
Regarding this, he says:
"There was no dust," and so forth.
Yāska states: "The worlds are called *rajas*" (Nirukta 4.19).
And here, the singular number is used with reference to the class [of things].
Since space (*vyoman*) will be mentioned later, the meaning is that the regions below it, beginning with the netherworlds (*pātāla*) and ending with the earth, did not exist.
Likewise, *vyoma*—the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)—that too did not exist.
The word *paraḥ*, ending in the letter *s*, functions in the sense of "beyond" (*parastāt*). From the word *para*, the suffix *asi* is applied according to Vedic usage (Pāṇini 5.3.27).
The meaning is: even that which exists beyond the sky—in the region above, from the heavenly world down to the earthly world—that too did not exist.
By this, the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which contains fourteen worlds within its interior, is negated in its own form.

Now, by way of refutation, he proceeds to negate in sequence—both by implication and directly—the regions where those elements such as space (*viyat*) and the rest, well-known in the Purāṇas as the envelopers of that [egg], reside, as well as the cause for their enveloping, with the words "kim āvarīvar" (What would it cover?). "What is to be covered? refers to that very [egg]. "What would it cover? refers to the collection of elemental substances acting as the coverer.
It would have completely veiled [it].

The meaning is that because there was no object to be veiled, the veiler itself did not exist. This is a form derived from the root *vṛ* (to cover) in its yaṅ-luk (intensive without suffix) form, in the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense, with the *tip* ending, according to Vedic usage.
Or rather:
why [is it] the first [case] alone?
What reality could conceal that which is itself the concealer?
The meaning is that even that [act of veiling], while being resorted to, did not exist by its own nature.
"Like one who veils" (āvṛvat): in what place (kuha), in what location, does it remain and veil?
The meaning is that such a supporting location also did not exist.
Furthermore, the suffix *ha* is used here in the sense of the locative case according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
By the rule "ku tihoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.104), the base is replaced by *kā*. [The meaning is:

upon what protection (*śarman*)—that is, upon the experience (*bhoga*) characterized by the direct perception of pleasure and pain belonging to which enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), namely the individual soul (*jīva*)—acting as the instrumental cause, would that reality which veils it conceal [the object]?

For creation is indeed for the sake of the enjoyment of living beings (*jīva*). Since that [creation] exists, there is the envelopment of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) by the elements; yet, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the enjoying beings—the *jīvas*—are dissolved due to the dissolution of their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Thus, because no enjoyer whatsoever is possible, the [envelopment] does not occur even due to the absence of a cause for such envelopment.
By this, it is stated that at that time, just like the world of objects of enjoyment (*bhogya-prapañca*), the world of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ-prapañca*) also did not exist.
Regarding the word *kiṃcchā*: for the suffix *ḍas*, the acute accent (*udātta*) which would otherwise apply by the rule "sāvekācaḥ" is prohibited by the rule "na goṣpadamasūtraṇa.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending of *śarmaṇi*.

Although the negation of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) along with its covering necessarily excludes the water (*ap*) contained within it, nevertheless, based on the Vedic scripture, "In the beginning, this was indeed water, a vast expanse" (*āpo vā idam agre salilam āsīt*), someone might suspect the presence of water.

The text refutes that [view] with the word "ambu" (water): "Was there such water—dense (*gahana*), difficult to enter (*duṣpraveśa*), deep (*gabhīra*), and difficult to stand in (*duravasthāna*) as well as bottomless (*agādha*)?
The meaning is that even that did not exist at all.
This [scriptural statement] refers to the dissolution (*pralaya*) occurring between two intermediate cycles of creation (*sṛṣṭi*).
There was neither death nor immortality then; there was no sign of night or day.
That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power (*svadhā*); other than that, indeed, nothing else existed beyond it.
There was neither death nor immortality then; there was no sign of night or day. That One breathed, windless, by its own inherent power (*svadhā*). Beyond that, nothing else whatsoever existed.

But surely, since there is only one agent of dissolution (*pratisaṃhāra*) and he is dependent upon that which is to be dissolved, that very agent—Death—must exist; therefore, [the author] says: "There was no death.

But if he did not exist, then by his absence, there would be "immortality" (*amṛta*), meaning the non-death and persistence of living beings even at that time. To this [the author replies]: No, because the description must pertain specifically to the state of dissolution (*pralaya-dashā*), and thus it is appropriate to mention that [absence]; for even then, [death] is absent in its true nature (*tattvena*).
2. tā. 1.3—of phenomena; ta7—also of phenomena. 3.
ga—ta1.2.3.6.7.8—bha—as being an obscuration to that; ta4.5—as being an obstruction to that.
4. ta2.7—ma2.4.8—also its protector; ta3.8—bha5—also its protector; ta6—also its protector.
