8. [The suffix] *udātta* is applied when it has reached (*prāpta*) *ga*, *ta*, *bha*, *pra*, *ta*, *ma*, *mu*; 9. [The suffix] *anudātta* is also applied when it has not reached (*aprāpta*) *ta*, *bha*, *ma*, *pa*, *ta*, *ma*, *ha*, *tā*, *sa*, or *tva*. Regarding this, he says:
"It was not nectar, then. "Then" means at that time of the *pratihāra* [chanting].
This is the intended meaning.

When all the karma of every living being—which had ripened and served as the cause for experience—had been fully exhausted through enjoyment, then, due to the absence of further objects of experience, the desire to withdraw the universe arises in the mind of the Supreme Lord, thinking, "This world has now reached its end.
Likewise, [the question arises]: "Since Death destroys the entire world, what is the purpose of this Death? In the absence of such a destroyer, how could there be immortality?
It is with this very intention that the Kaṭha Upaniṣad declares: "He for whom both the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya are merely food..."
"Death was its condiment; who knows where it is? (KaU 2.25).
Now, one might object that time exists as the substratum for all this; therefore, he says, "Not by night.
"Of the night"—and of the day—there was no perception, that is, no cognition.
Because of the absence of the sun and moon, which are the causes thereof.
By this negation of day and night, all time consisting of them—beginning with months, seasons, and years—is rejected.
How then is there a temporal designation such as "at that time, neither being nor non-being existed"?
We say it is by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

Just as the present time is the delimiting factor for the present negation, so too *māyā* is the cause of its delimitation; thus, due to this similarity in being a delimiting factor, the cognition of "time" occurs even with respect to what is not time.
Or rather, we stated previously that the ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*) of Brahman will be explained later; we shall now demonstrate that very point.
He has brought—that reality of Brahman well-known throughout all the Vedāntas—into being; that is, He has breathed it forth.

Now, one might object: "In this way, the existence of Brahman would belong only to Him who has become the agent of breathing, and not to the intended Brahman which is free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), since it is said, 'For He is without breath, without mind, pure,' and thus lacks any connection with breath. To this, he replies: "It breathed, or rather, It breathed not."
This is the intended meaning:
in the word *ānīt*, three meanings are perceived—the action denoted by the verbal root, its agent, and its connection with the past tense.
Among these, the aggregate is not being enjoined—as in the case of "the sacrificial cake on eight potsherds" (*śreyaḥ-aṣṭakapāla*)—such that the existence of Brahman would not be established.

What, then, is the case? Having restated the agency (*kartṛtva*), a quality characterized by existence in the past time is enjoined. This is like the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) in the statement "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), which is an restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Agnihotra sacrifice enjoined by another sentence. Even there, it is not the existence in prior time of that [sacrifice] as qualified by this agency that is enjoined, for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of the impossibility of its negation. Therefore, by means of this agency, the existence in past time is enjoined of that very Supreme Brahman which is now indicated (*upalakṣita*) by it and is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*); thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

Now, since such a Brahman cannot have a connection with *māyā*, it must be that the *mūlaprakṛti*—independent, of the nature of existence (*sat*), and composed of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* as accepted by the Sāṅkhyas—is what is intended. How then can there be the negation "not existent" (*no sat*)? To this he replies: "by its own power" (*svadhayā*).
*Māyā* is called *svadhā* because it is placed (*dhīyate*), supported (*dhriyate*), or exists depending upon itself (*svasmin*).
Likewise, that which delimits it had become undivided.

The instrumental case ending [in *saha*] occurs even in the absence of the word *saha*, provided there is a connection with the sense of "together," according to the rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Pāṇini 2.3.19); this is indicated by the evidence of the exceptional usage (*nipātana*) in *vṛddho yūnā* (Pāṇini 1.2.65).
Here, by means of both the base and the suffix, its independence is precluded.

Although no connection with Māyā is possible for Brahman, which is by nature unattached (*asaṅga*), nevertheless, through ignorance (*avidyā*), a connection is superimposed upon it just as its own essential nature is, like silver upon mother-of-pearl. By this, its status as being real (*sadrūpatva*) is also refuted. Now, if Māyā has attained non-differentiation from Brahman, then because Māyā is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), would it not follow that Brahman is also so? How then can its reality be asserted in the passage, "It breathed, the windless breath" (*ānīd avātam*)?
[Objection: "If Brahman exists, it follows that this [world] must also exist; therefore, how can there be a negation of its existence in the statement 'Was it not non-existent?
[Reply: Not so.

Even though there is an appearance of identity with an irrational view, when analyzed through reasoning, it has been established that the existence of Brahman remains while the appearance of *māyā* is unavoidable."

Now, if it is admitted that there are only two categories of entities—namely, "the two were invisible" (RV 10.129.2) and "breathless it breathed by its own nature" (RV 10.129.2)—then what else remains that could be negated by the words "there was no darkness" and so forth? To this, he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt).

Therefore, indeed, from the previously mentioned Brahman accompanied by Māyā, there was not, nor did exist, anything else whatsoever—a reality consisting of the elements and their derivatives, namely the world. Because of the rule "chandasyubhayathā," the *liṭ* [perfect tense] is treated as a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; thus, by the substitution of *bhū* for *as*, there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.

Now, one might object: "At that time, the negation of another [entity] is not to be suspected; for if it were non-existent, there would be no point in its negation because it was never even presented as a possibility. To this, he says: "The other" (*para*). The meaning is: "This world, which exists subsequent to creation—that is, after [the initial moment]—did not exist at that time."
The meaning is that, otherwise, according to the aforementioned method, there would be no negation whatsoever.

4. ta-bha—is prescribed; 5. ta2.3.6.7.8-bha 4.5.7.8—what?

6. Even though there is an appearance of unity from the perspective of experience (*anubhavadṛṣṭyā*) according to *ta17-bha2.5-mu*; even though there is an appearance of unity from the perspective of experience according to *ta2.3.6.8-bha*; even though there is an appearance of unity from the perspective of reasoning (*ayuktitas*) according to *ta4.5*; and even though there is an appearance of unity from the perspective of experience according to *bha7*. 7. Precisely because of its impelling nature (*prerakatva*), according to *ta4.5*. 8. According to the method stated [in the respective texts], according to *ta-bha*.
In the beginning, there was darkness hidden by darkness; all this was an indistinguishable ocean.
That which existed, enveloped by the void, was one, and it was born through the power of heat (tapas).
Darkness existed; in the beginning, all this was hidden by darkness, indistinguishable, a mere ocean. That which was, enveloped by the void, that One was born through the power of heat (tapas). 3.

Now, if this world existed previously in such a manner, how then can there be its birth? For that which is being born must be a causal factor (*kāraka*) by virtue of being the agent (*kartṛ*) in the act of birth; and since a causal factor is a specific type of cause, it necessarily exists in the moment immediately preceding [the effect]. If, however, one wishes to avoid this difficulty and asserts that the world exists even prior to the act of birth, [then...]

How was its birth? To this he says: "Enveloped by darkness in the beginning. That is to say, *agre*, before creation, during the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), the entire world consisting of the elements and their derivatives was *tamasā gūḍham*, enveloped by darkness.

Just as nocturnal darkness veils the entire multitude of objects, so did desire arise in the beginning, covering the essence of the Self. That which was the first seed of mind, the bond of the existent within the non-existent—having sought it within their hearts through inspired thought, the seers discovered it by means of wisdom. 4. Desire. That. In the beginning. Fully arose. Over. Of the mind. The seed. First. Which. Was. Of the existent. The bond. In the non-existent. Out. They found. In the heart. Having sought. The seers. By wisdom. 4.

If it is asked what the basis for that very reflection of the Lord—which, according to the principle of *nanuphara*, is the cause for the re-creation of the world—is, he says: "Desire arose in the beginning.
In the beginning—that is, in the state prior to the creation of this multitude of modifications—desire arose perfectly within the mind of the Supreme Lord;
the meaning is that the impulse to create (*sisṛkṣā*) was born.
To the question, "What is the cause of the Lord's desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*)? he says: "Of the mind.

[This refers to] that which belongs to the mind—that is, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—and which is inherent in the internal organ when it has dissolved into *māyā* by means of the residue of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The singular number is used with reference to the genus.
The meaning is that it is inherent within the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of all living beings. By this, the notion of the Self being a substratum for qualities (*guṇa*) is refuted.

Such *retas*—the seed of the future world-manifestation (*prapañca*), consisting of the meritorious karma performed by living beings in a past aeon (*kalpa*)—existed, that is, came into being, at the time of creation from which cause [it arose].
The meaning is that it was born as something growing and flourishing, and having reached full maturity, it became ready to manifest its fruit.
For that reason—from that cause—the desire to create arose in the mind of the Supreme Lord, the witness of all, the presiding deity over karma, who bestows the fruits of action.
And once that desire had arisen, He reflected upon what was to be created and then brought forth the entire universe.

And thus it is recorded in scripture: "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate. He performed austerity. Having performed austerity, he created all this, whatever exists here" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.6).
This Śruti passage establishes the meaning as understood from the Self, corroborating it with the experience of the wise by stating, "He [did so]."

The poets—seers who have transcended [ordinary perception] and possess knowledge of the past, future, and present—having reflected with their minds restrained within the heart by means of their all-encompassing intellect (*manīṣā*), [perceive] the collection of karmas performed by living beings in other kalpas, which is the *bandhu*—the bond, the cause—of this world that now exists as a reality being experienced and is destined to continue. (Note: The *luk* elision of the third-case ending in *hṛdi* is according to Pāṇini’s rule *supāṃ suluk...*.)
The lengthening [of the vowel] in *anyeṣām api* is according to the rule of the *Māṇḍūka*.
7. When there was no cause that was characterized as real (*sat*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*), they 7 *niravindan*: they extracted and obtained;
the meaning is that they discerned and understood.

A transverse ray was stretched across them; was it below, or was it above? There were seed-bearers, there were powers, self-sustenance was below, and impulsion was in front. tiraścīnaḥ | vitataḥ | raśmiḥ | eṣām | adhaḥ | svid | āsīt | upari | svid | āsīt | retaḥdhāḥ | āsan | mahimānaḥ | āsan | svadhā | avastāt | prayatiḥ | purastāt || 5 || A transverse ray was stretched across them; was it situated below, or was it situated above? There were the depositors of seed, there were the greatnesses; self-sustenance was from below, and impulsion was from the front. || 5 ||
Thus, ignorance, desire, and action have been stated as the causes of creation.
Now, their swiftness in producing their own effects is being demonstrated.

That which was established by the verse "Non-being did not exist" (nāsad āsīt), and that desire which was at its beginning—namely, "desire, which was the first seed of the mind," and that which was action—of these [three], ignorance, desire, and action, as they were creating the collection of elements beginning with space: there was a "ray," meaning like a ray; just as the sun's ray, immediately after rising, pervades the entire world simultaneously in a mere moment, so too there was that aggregate of effects which pervaded everywhere very swiftly and was "extended," that is, spread out.
The word "was it? (svid āsīt), which is to be mentioned later, is also connected here.
The protracted vowel (*pluta*) is applied according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.2.97, *vicāryamāṇānām*;
since the term "acute" (*udātta*) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvṛtti*) there, that [protracted vowel] is also acute.
The particle *svit* is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarke*).
Was that mass of effects initially situated horizontally, standing across in the middle; or was it below, down below? Or was it above, on high?
Regarding the phrase "upari svidāsīt," there is a protracted (pluta) vowel which is unaccented (anudātta), according to Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.102.

Although the sequence is established by the ablative case in such scriptural passages as "From the Self, space was produced; from space, air; from air, fire" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.1)—just as in the expressions "from that, the Udgātṛ" and "from that, the Hotṛ"—[nevertheless, the soul's departure occurs] like a flash of lightning.
1. ta-bha-tadeva vā | 2. bhara-puṇyāpuṇyātmakaṃ |
Because that process of creation was so rapid and its sequence difficult to discern, it is now considered which of these three stages holds primacy;
the meaning is that in this very manner, creation was completed swiftly in all directions.
He analyzes this very point.

Among the created effects, some entities were "retodhāḥ"—individual souls (*jīvas*) who are the ordainers, performers, and enjoyers of *retaḥ*, that is, action which serves as the seed; other entities were "mahimānaḥ"—the great objects of enjoyment, such as space and so forth (the suffix *iman* being used in its own sense). Thus, beginning with the passage, "The Supreme Lord, accompanied by Māyā, is the creator of the entire world; He entered into that very [creation]" (*Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 8.6), this is established.
And there, between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, was *asvadhā*—
this is a name for ignorance (*ajñāna*).
The manifold world of the enjoyed (*bhogyaprapañca*) was "below," meaning inferior and base.

"Prayatiḥ" means the one who strives; "prayatitā" means the striver. "Aparastāt" means "afterwards," while "paraḥ" means "supreme" or "excellent. The meaning is that he made the manifold world of objects of enjoyment (*bhogya-prapañca*) subordinate to the manifold world of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ-prapañca*). The suffix *astāti* is used here in the sense of the first case ending according to Pāṇini’s rule: *vibhāṣā parāvarābhyām* (Pā. Sū. 5.3.29).
By the rule *astāti ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.40), the word *avara* undergoes the substitution *ava*.
In the form *avastāt*, there is preservation of the original stem (*prakṛtibhāva*) in the *saṃhitā* due to its inclusion in the *īpāakṣa* group.
Who truly knows? Who here can declare it—from where was this creation born?
The gods came later than its manifestation; who then knows from whence it first came into being?
Who truly knows? Who here can declare it? Whence was it born, whence came this creation? The gods are later than this world’s creation; who then knows from whence it first came into being? 6.

Thus, creation has been presented in brief by way of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, just as it is said: "This much indeed is this: food and the eater of food; Soma is the food and Agni is the eater of food" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.4.2.13). Now, lest this creation be considered difficult to understand, he says "Who indeed... so that it may not be left unexplained in detail.
"Who is the person who knows truly—that is, in the ultimate sense?
Or who here in this world has declared it?
From what—that is, from what material cause—has this manifest creation come forth, this manifold creation consisting of various kinds of beings, elements, enjoyers, and objects of enjoyment?"
"From where, and for what causal reason, was she born—meaning, manifested and appeared from all sides?
Who truly knows both of these, or who would be able to explain them in detail? [The opponent objects:
"But surely the gods do not know."
Since all these [beings] teach and are capable of speaking, he says "arvāk" (subsequent).

"And the gods," by means of the emission of this world—that is, after the production of the elements such as ether (*viyat*) and so forth—were made "arvāk," meaning subsequent, through the various acts of creation;
the sense is that they were born after the creation of the elements.
How could such beings as those know the creation that preceded their own birth?
Or, not knowing it, how could they have spoken of it?
He concludes the statement regarding its difficulty to discern.
"Now, this being the case, it is said that even the gods do not know [it].
Apart from them, what human or other being indeed knows—that is, understands—that cause from which the entire world was brought forth, i.e., born?"
This creation came into being, whether it was fashioned by a maker or not;
he who is its overseer in the highest heaven—he truly knows it, or perhaps even he does not know.
This creation—whence it came into being, whether he fashioned it or whether he did not—he who is its overseer in the highest heaven, he indeed knows, or perhaps even he does not know. (7)
Just as this creation of the world is difficult to comprehend in the manner described, so too is the created world difficult to sustain; thus he says, "This" (iyam).
From the Supreme Self, who is the material cause (*upādāna*), "this"—that is, this manifold creation (*visṛṣṭi*) consisting of various forms such as mountains, rivers, and oceans—has come forth.

1. *ta8.5-bhava* means "to spread quickly. 2. *ga-bha* reads "it is possible" (*śakyate*). 3. *ga-ta1.2.3.6.7.8* reads "the state of being difficult to know" (*durjñānatvam*). 4. *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha* does not contain the word "indeed" (*kila*). 5. *ga-ta2.3.6.7.8* reads "was born" (*ājāyata*). 6. *ta-bha* does not contain the word "from which" (*yataḥ*).
He indeed became manifest; he, moreover, either supports them or does not support them.
And if that is so, who else indeed could possibly sustain them?
If he were to sustain them, it means that God alone would sustain them.
By this demonstration that Brahman is the sustainer of the effect, its status as the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) is stated.
Accordingly, the *Pāramārthasūtra* states: "And [Brahman] is the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples" (Ve.
Sū. 1.4.23). Or else:
In this sense, it should be understood that what was stated previously—that creation is indeed knowledge—is correct.
The phrase "who knows? (ko veda) carries over from the previous verse.
Who knows from whence this manifold creation has arisen—that is, from whom it was born on all sides?
No one at all.
There is no birth of this world at all, and there have been many thinkers who maintain that the world has never been otherwise than it is now. For:
By the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.30), the term *prakṛti* receives the designation of "material cause" (*upādāna*), and thus the ablative suffix *-tasil* is applied.
Who knows that Supreme Self from whom [the world] originated—that material cause which is the Supreme Self?
No one at all.
Indeed, many are deluded by the notion that the world's origin arises either from primordial matter (*prakṛti*) or from atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Likewise, [the text asks]: "If that very Supreme Self, being both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*), himself established, created, or produced this world—or if he did not produce it?
This statement regarding what is beyond doubt is made with a sense of doubt, provided that the scriptures are authoritative; for example: [as in the following verse].
He alone ordained it;
no one knows.
Yet many, though ignorant, have held the contrary view that this world arose spontaneously from the inert *pradhāna* as something entirely without an agent.
Even though they do not know the process of creation as it is being performed,
who indeed knows that this very [Self] is the material cause?
No one at all.
Indeed, many maintain that God, being entirely separate from the material cause (*upādāna*), is a detached bystander who fashions the world.
The meaning is: "If even the gods do not know this, what need is there to speak of those of inferior luster knowing it?

Having raised the doubt that if the creation of the world is thus so difficult to comprehend, it cannot then be established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he establishes the existence of that [God] by means of God himself in the verse beginning with *yo asya*.

The Lord, who is the supervisor and sovereign of this world consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives, resides in the supreme, most excellent, and truly existent *vyoman*— the space that is like the sky,
pure and luminous. Alternatively, [it may be derived] from the root *av*, meaning "to satisfy," with the suffix *manin* according to the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante*.
By the rule *nedvaśi kṛti*, the substitution of *it* is prohibited.
By the rule *jvaratvara* etc., *ūṭ* is substituted for the vowel *u* and the following semivowel *v*.
There is elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending.
The elision of the *n* [in *viśvan-tṛpta*] is prohibited by the rule "na ḍisaṃbuddhayoḥ.
"Specially satisfied in the sky" means having the nature of unsurpassed bliss.
Alternatively,
the root *ava* has the sense of "going";
thus, it means "having gone specifically" or "pervaded" in the sky (*vyomani*).
The meaning is that it is not delimited by place, time, or substance.
Alternatively,
the root *ava* has the sense of "knowing."
In the sky—that is, specifically in the Knower, whose nature is distinguished knowledge—He is thus established in His own self.
For it is heard in the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Nārada: “Venerable sir, on what is He established? On His own majesty” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
Such is the Supreme Lord; "vaṅga" and "aṅga" are used here as particles of emphasis.
Even she, indeed, knows him—this is the meaning.
Whether he knows it or does not know it— who else indeed could know it?
The meaning is that only the omniscient Lord (Īśvara) would know that creation, and no one else.
The second hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "yo yajñaḥ," is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Yājñasya, the son of Prajāpati.
The first verse is in the Jagatī meter; the remaining verses are in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Here too, the creation of certain things such as sacrifices and so forth is set forth.
Therefore, that very deity is the primary meaning which constitutes the act of creation;
Prajāpati himself, as its creator, is the deity.
And thus it has been introduced: "The sacrifice which is the sacrifice belonging to Prajāpati, beginning with the Jagatī [meter]. The application [of the mantra] has been explained.
That sacrifice which is stretched out on all sides with threads, extended by one hundred and one divine acts;
These fathers weave; they sit upon that which has been stretched out, saying, "May he extend our life."

5. *ga-bha2.4.8*: "In you, O Eternal One" (*nityatute*). 6. *ga-ta1.2.3.6.8-bha2.4.8*: "In the same way, the agent" (*tadvat kartā*).
By the threads—the expanding elements such as space (ākāśa) and the rest—which extend [the world], the sacrifice consisting of emanation is stretched out on all sides, everywhere extended.
Likewise, "one hundred and one":
one and one hundred make one hundred and one.
In the word "saṃkhyā," there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound.
The meaning is "one hundred plus one.
The number "hundred" is used here with the intention that [the sage] lives for those hundred years which constitute a *brahman*.
It is said that there are one hundred and one [deities] together with that living Prajāpati, as in the passage:
"Man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred powers; the self is the one hundred and first" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.7.6.4).
The accusative case is used here to denote immediate conjunction (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
The lifespan of Brahmā extends for a hundred years, measured by the deeds performed by the enjoyers (the gods) directed toward the gods.
He remains for that duration of time.

Thus, the gods—the creators of the universe who constitute the vital breaths of Prajāpati and act as his protectors—weave or construct that sacrifice which consists of the aforementioned creation, possessing such length and breadth.

The gods, having pervaded the entire world through their creative act, came together. Furthermore: what was the covering? What was the womb? What was the supporting measure? What was the counterpart? What was the cause? What was the clarified butter? And what was the enclosing-stick?
What was the *chandas*, what was the *prauga*, and what was the *uktha* when all the gods sacrificed to the god?

What was the measure? What was the model? What was the cause? What was the clarified butter? What was the enclosing-stick? What was the metre? What was the *prauga*? What was the hymn (*uktha*), when all the gods sacrificed to the god? (3)

When the sacrifice was created by Prajāpati as the means for the creation of the universe, the gods—the creators of the universe—undertook that sacrifice for the purpose of universal creation. At that time, since the world had not yet come into being, this question is raised: how could there have been those objects that serve as the implements of sacrifice, which sustain the world? When all the Sādhyas, the gods, sacrificed to the god Prajāpati, what was the measure, the extent, and the nature of that sacrifice at that moment?
Likewise, the image (*pratimā*):
it is measured (*mīyate*) or fashioned (*nirmīyate*) as a counterpart to the oblation (*havis*), thus it is the deity's image (*pratimā*).
And that [image] was his for that sacrifice.

Likewise, what was the *nidāna*—the primary cause—that impelled one who had not previously engaged in sacrifice? What was the fruit [of that action]? Likewise, what was the *ājya* (clarified butter)—this being illustrative of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*)—for that sacrifice? And likewise, what was the *paridhi* (enclosing stick)?

They are called *paridhi*s because they are placed all around (*parito dhīyante*). There are three such enclosures, measuring the length of an arm, made from sacrificial wood such as *palāśa* and others.
The suffix *ki* is applied [to the root *dhā*] by the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.92), resulting in the form *paridhi*.
The singular number is used with reference to the class [of objects].
The meaning is: "Who were the enclosing-sticks (paridhi)?
Likewise: "What was the meter (chandas) of that sacrifice, such as the Gāyatrī and so forth? And likewise, what was the Prauga-uktha?"
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
What were the *ukthas* or *śastras*, such as the *ājya* and *prauga*?
To these questions, he states the answer for three of them.
Through the Gāyatrī, Agni became possessed of good yoking; Savitṛ was united with the Uṣṇih;

The Gāyatrī became the companion of Agni; Savitṛ was united with the Uṣṇih; Soma, exalted by hymns, [was joined] with the Anuṣṭubh; Bṛhaspati protected speech with the Bṛhatī. 4.
The *sayugvā*, meaning "yoked together" or "acting as a companion," was the *gāyatrī* that became the companion of Agni. She was born from the mouth of Prajāpati, who is to be worshipped;

And likewise, the Taittirīyaka states: "Prajāpati desired, 'May I procreate. He fashioned the Trivṛt from his mouth; after it, he created Agni as the deity and the Gāyatrī as the metre" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.1.4).
The god Savitṛ became united with the Uṣṇih and the Uṣṇih-metre at that sacrifice of Prajāpati.
The form *uṣṇihā* is derived from the word *uṣṇih* by the addition of the suffix *ṭāp*, according to the rule "the suffixes *ṭāp* and *cāp* also [occur] after words ending in a consonant."

Likewise, the glorious and radiant Soma was born from that very Prajāpati together with the *ukthas* (recited hymns), the *stotra-śastras* (chants and liturgical recitations), and the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
Similarly, the speech—the utterance—of the god Bṛhaspati, as well as the *bṛhatī* meter, protected him or went toward him;
the meaning is that Bṛhaspati also was born from that Prajāpati together with the *bṛhatī*.
Virāj entered into the two coverings; Abhiśrī entered Indra with the Triṣṭubh, for that was his due portion here.
Viśve Devās entered with the Jagatī; by means of that, the seers and human beings were fashioned.

The meaning is that Indra and Prajāpati were both born from the presence of [the Creator].

And so says the Taittirīyaka: "From the chest and from the two arms he fashioned the fifteenfold [stoma]; Indra was released as its deity, and the Triṣṭubh meter and the Bṛhat Sāman [were produced]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 7.1.1.4).

And so says the Taittirīyaka: "All the gods as deities followed after him in creation; the *jagatī* metre, the *vairūpa* sāman" (TS 7.1.1.5).
In the manner described, the answers to the three questions—"What was the image? What was the metre? What was the *praḍaṅga* and what the *ukatha*?"—have been produced.
The answer to the questions "What was the clarified butter? What was the enclosing-stick? is to be found in the *Puruṣasūkta*.

Therein it is thus recorded: "The gods performed the sacrifice; spring was its clarified butter, summer the fuel, and autumn the oblation. The seasons were its enclosing-sticks; thrice seven were made the kindling-sticks" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.90.6; 15). This is the meaning.

The non-existent, the generator of all, had the clarified butter (*ājya*) as the sacrificial oblation for that sacrifice which was the means of creating the world; the meaning is that such a spring (*vasanta*) was born together with the juices beginning with the clarified butter. The summer season (*grīṣma*), the dryer of all things, was the fuel (*idhma*).
The meaning is that summer arose together with parrots and wooden sticks.
Autumn, joined with ripening rice, was the sacrificial oblation for this sacrifice.
The meters, becoming three times seven and twenty-one-fold, became eighteen fuel-sticks and as many enclosing-sticks.

Regarding the two questions—"What is the measure? and "What is the cause?"—the answer to both is likewise given in the Taittirīyaka: "In former times, the immortal creators of the universe (viśvasṛjaḥ) remained consecrated for a sacrificial session (satram) for a hundred thousand years," and "By this [sacrifice], indeed, the creators of the universe created this entire universe" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.2;
8). Therefore, the duration of that sacrifice is measured by a thousand years.
The meaning is that the creation of the entire world is its purpose, its motive, and its fruit.
This is what is meant:
when the gods, the creators of the universe, worshipped the god Prajāpati with the sacrifice called Viśvasṛjāmayana, then all the implements of sacrifice were born from the presence of Prajāpati.
Since the six meters, beginning with the Gāyatrī, were born together with the deities beginning with Agni, for that reason those deities are called the "meters" (chandas).
And it is stated in the Chandovicitih: "Agni, Savitṛ, Soma, Bṛhaspati, Mitra and Varuṇa, Indra, and the Viśve Devās are the deities" (Piṅgala Sūtra 3.63).
Thus was the sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati performed.
By that sacrifice, the ṛṣis and humans fashioned the meters.
They were fashioned; they were created.
In the case of the root *kṛp* with the *liṭ* suffix in the sense of the object (*karmani*), there is the substitution of *ra* by the rule "irayoḥ.
Then, by the rule "kṛpo ro laḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.18), there is the substitution of *la* for *ra*.
Due to its inclusion in the *tujādigaṇa*, there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
The meaning is that by means of that very sacrifice, he created the entire world.

When this ancient sacrifice was born and performed by the creators of the universe, through that sacrifice the seers, human beings, and our ancestors fashioned [the world]; I behold them with the eye of my mind—those who performed this sacrifice in former times. When this ancient, long-standing sacrifice was born and properly performed by the creators of the universe, through that sacrifice the seers, human beings, and our ancestors—our forefathers—fashioned it; they were created. I behold them with the eye of my mind—those who performed this sacrifice in former times.
1. By means of herbs and so forth. 2. *Bhara*: the meaning is that the summer season was born. 3. *Ta-Bha*: or else. 4. *Ta1.3.1.7.8-Bha*: in that [place].

I think—I perceive with my chest, that is, by means of the mind which is the cause of vision—that those ancient Sādhyas, the gods who were the very breaths of Prajāpati and performed sacrifice (*ayajanta*), meaning they stood firm;
I praise those very same all-accomplishing (*viśva-ṛdh*) gods.
The root *man* has the sense of praising.
The seven divine seers, accompanied by hymns, meters, ritual turnings, and measures,
beholding the path of the ancients, have followed it like charioteers following their reins.

Together with their hymns, together with their meters, together with their ritual turns, together with their measurements—the seven divine seers, having beheld the path of the ancients, the wise ones have followed it, just as charioteers follow the reins.

Accompanied by *stomas* such as the *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa*; accompanied by *chandases* such as the *gāyatrī* and other meters; revolving (*āvṛtaḥ*) and recurring; together with *pramā*, where *pramā* means the measurement or the thorough knowledge of the sacrifice; belonging to the divine (*daivyāḥ*), that is, related to the god Prajāpati—or alternatively, having their natural accent (*prakṛtisvaratvam*).
O wise one, drive away all such enemies and adversaries from us;
likewise, O Indra, the overcomer of foes, drive away all those who stand behind us, facing away from our front;
and furthermore, drive away those who stand above us, facing upward.
From the root *an* preceded by the prefix *ut*, the suffix *kin* is applied as before; in accordance with the rule *ud īt*, the vowel *i* is substituted for the letter *i*;
the accentuation is as before.
Thus, "drive away even such enemies."

Likewise, O hero, like valor itself, O Śakra, drive away those who are below—in the lower region or the space beneath—and also those enemies who are from below. The formation of *anvataḥ* with the word *adhara-* as an upapada and the suffix *śas* follows the same process as before.
By the rule "cau," the final syllable of the preceding member (*adhara-*) is udātta.

Thus, in this and that place, in every location, make these riches—the means for attaining their portions—the food of these sacrificers; "dhananāmaitat" (this is a name for wealth) refers to riches that serve as the instruments for obtaining a share. Make them so.

The absence of the *laṅ* suffix [for the past tense] is due to the rule: "In the Vedic language, there is optionally no substitution for the suffix *utaśca*" (Pāṇini 6.4.106).

Seeking cattle (*gūyyantaḥ*), desiring cows, we—the wise ones (*viprāḥ*)—invoke that Indra, the showerer (*vṛṣaṇam*), for the sake of exhilaration (*surayāya*) and for the performance of friendship; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Of what nature are they? Desiring horses for themselves (*aśvayantaḥ*), desiring food (*vājaryantaḥ*), and desiring strength (*balakāmāḥ*).
In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the verse beginning with “yuvam” is the invitatory formula (puronuvākyā) for the cups of *surā* liquor.

the two auspicious lords.

O Aśvins, O Lords of Splendor (or of beautiful ornaments), O protectors of the waters, having drunk deeply of this oblation which is a source of great delight, you two, being together and united, protected Indra in his deeds—namely, the acts of battle—when the Asura named Namuci, the son of an Asura, was to be slain.
*vipipānā*:
from the root *pā* (to drink), the suffix *kānac* is applied after the perfect tense (*liṭ*);
the vowel *i* is substituted for the reduplication by the rule "in the Veda, diversely" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

In the case of *śubhaspatī*, by the rule *subāmantrite* (Pāṇini 2.1.2), the genitive-ending word behaves as if it were part of the subsequent member; consequently, the entire group consisting of the genitive and the vocative is subject to the universal low-pitch (*sarvānudātta*) prescribed by the eighth chapter [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī].
The *yājyā* for the very same planets mentioned previously is "putramiva. This is also stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* is 'putramiva pitarāvaśvinobhe' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.9)."

Like two parents [protecting] their son, O Indra, both Aśvins protected you with their poetic wisdom and wondrous deeds. When you drank the *surāma* [offering] with your powers, O Maghavan, Sarasvatī attended upon you. Like two parents, O Indra, both Aśvins protected you with their poetic wisdom (*kāvyaiḥ*) and wondrous deeds (*daṃsanābhiḥ*). When you drank the *surāma*—the sacrificial oblation that is a source of bliss—with your powers (*śacībhiḥ*), then, O Maghavan, the goddess Sarasvatī attended upon (*abhiṣṇak*) you. The root *bhiṣṇak* means "to attend upon. It belongs to the *kaṇṇvādi* group. There is an absence of the suffix *ya* due to Vedic usage. In the *laṅ* tense, there is the elision of *śap* by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," and the elision of the feminine suffix by the rule "halaṅyābhyaḥ. *Note:* Regarding the form *putramiva*, the rule "pitā mātrā" (Pāṇini 1.2.70) dictates that when a dual compound of "father and mother" is used with another word, the term for "father" remains as the remainder; thus, *pitarau* becomes *putramiva*. The word *ubhā* is a Vedic form for *ubhau* (both). The middle voice (*āvathuḥ*) is used here by metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*). The term *surāma* refers to the oblation that is a means of pleasant delight. The verb *abhiṣṇak* is derived from the root *bhiṣaj* (to heal/attend), with the suffix *kvip* dropped in the Vedic form. The *laṅ* ending results in the form *abhiṣṇak*. The final vowel is elided according to the rule "halaṅyābhyaḥ."

May Indra, the good protector, the possessor of wealth, with his aids, be gracious to us—he who possesses all knowledge. May he drive away our enemies and grant us fearlessness; may we be masters of heroic vigor. 6. Indra. The good protector. Possessor of wealth. With his aids. Gracious. May he be. All-knowing. May he drive away. The enemy. May he create. Fearlessness. May we be. Masters of heroic vigor. 6.

May we abide in the good favor of that worshipful one, and also in his auspicious goodwill. May that Indra, the excellent protector and possessor of wealth, drive our enemies far away from us. May we abide in the good favor of that worshipful one; may we also be in his auspicious goodwill. That Indra, the excellent protector and possessor of wealth, shall drive our enemies far away from us.
This has been explained in the commentary on the verse beginning with “trātāram indram” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.47.12–13). As for the literal meaning:
may Indra—the excellent protector, the possessor of wealth, the knower of all—be a source of great happiness through his protections; may he destroy our enemies and grant us freedom from fear.
Therefore, may we become the owners of wealth that has been well-acquired through effort.
But regarding the seventh [verse]:
"May we become the objects of that Indra, who is worthy of sacrifice, when he possesses a mind intent on favoring us and a disposition of goodwill;
may that Indra, the excellent protector and possessor of wealth, establish the concealment of our enemies at a great distance from us."
The fourth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "ījānam," belongs to Śakapūta, the son of Nṛmedha, and has Mitra and Varuṇa as its deities.
However, the first verse has the Earth and the Aśvins as its deities, indicated by its internal marks; it is composed in the Nyaṅkusāriṇī meter and possesses two sets of twelve syllables.
The second and sixth verses are Prastārapaṅkti meters, each possessing two sets of twelve syllables.

this is for the purpose of the phrase "having kindled" (samidhya) and "having gone away" (apetya). The particle *u* is a filler.

Or else: [the verse continues].
"Vana" is a name for water;
for Varuṇa dwells in the midst of the ocean.
[I see him] seated in the forest, that is, in the waters of the ocean.
In both cases, the suffix *kvip* is applied as before.
In the word *vanasat*, the letter *r* is elided according to Vedic phonetic rules (*chāndasaḥ sāṃsthitikaḥ*).
O Mitra and Varuṇa, by you two, Nṛmedha—my father—was saved; that is, he was protected from distress, which is to say, from sin.
The word is derived from the root *trai* (to protect) in the sense of the object (*karman*) with the perfect tense (*liṭ*).

Alternatively, by figurative usage (*upacāra*), the word "father" (*janaka*) is applied to those who produce [protection]. I, Śakapūta, the son of Nṛmedhas, have been protected from sin by you two in that place.
Another, Sumedha, and Suyajña the sacrificer, were also protected from distress—that is, saved from sin—by you two alone.
According to Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.4.25, *bhītrārthānām*, the word *aṃhas* is designated as the *apādāna* (ablative).
The fifth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "pro ṣu," is the seer-hymn (ārṣam) of Sudās, the son of Pijavana; it is dedicated to Indra.
The first triplet is in the Śakkarī meter;
the Śakkarī consists of fifty-six syllables.
The second triplet is a mahāpaṅkti;
the [verse] of fifty syllables is a mahāpaṅkti;
the seventh is a triṣṭubh.
And thus it has been introduced: "Pro ṣu sudāḥ Paijavana [performed] the Śākvara and Mahāpāṅkta [sāmans]; the first two triplets are [in the Gāyatrī meter], the others are Triṣṭubh.
At the Ṣoḍaśin-śastra, the first triplet is to be recited.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'Trikadrukeṣu mahiṣo yathāśiram' and 'Pro ṣvasmai puroratham'—these two triplets are in the Āticchandas meters" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.2).
In the *mahāvrata* sacrifice, during the midday pressing (*mādhyandinasavana*), within the *brahmakhaṇḍa*, there is one verse for the *anurūpa* triplet: "pro vvasmai.
Likewise, it is prescribed in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: "The *anurūpa* is 'pro vvasmai puroratham'" (AiĀ 5.1.1).
Sing forth this powerful hymn for this Indra, whose chariot is foremost;
he is the maker of room even in close combat, the slayer of Vṛtra in the clash of battles. Be our inspirer; let the bowstrings of our enemies snap upon their bows.

Proclaim it! Sing forth a powerful hymn to this Indra, whose chariot is foremost. Even in close combat, he is the maker of space; the slayer of Vṛtra in the clash of battles, be thou our inspirer. Let the bowstrings of our adversaries snap upon their bows. 1.
For this Indra— the dative case used in the sense of the genitive—
before the chariot of this Indra, that is, in front of his chariot.
In the compound *puro’vyayam*, the word *puraḥ* is treated as a *gati* (preverb) due to the rule [Pāṇini 1.4.67], resulting in an *atya-samāsa*.
O singers, worship well—thoroughly praise—the form and power that stands before the chariot. O chanters, honor it excellently.
The combination of particles *pra* and *u* forms *pro*.
By the rule *ot*, this receives the designation *pragṛhya*.
Indra is thus specified.
*Samatsu*:
because it is equal (*samānam*) in the middle and at the end, it is *samada*, meaning "battle";
the suffix *kvip* is added in the sense of a locus according to the *Uṇādi* rules.
The form *samānasya* is a Vedic usage [of the genitive].

In the phrase *samatsu*, meaning "in battles" (*saṃgrāmeṣu*), it refers to the enemy force that is to be encountered (*saṃge saṃgamanīye*). The suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *gam* according to Pāṇini’s rule *ṅo’nyatrāpi dṛśyate* (3.2.48).

Even in the face of immediate danger, even when the enemy has drawn near—even in a situation of hair-to-hair combat—the world-maker, the sustainer of the universe, the slayer of Vṛtra (the destroyer of those who obstruct), such as that Indra, being the impeller of wealth for us his worshippers, take heed!
May he be aware of the services rendered by us.
(Note: Variants *ta1.2.3.6.7.8* and *ma1.4.5.7.8* do not contain the phrase "vanyadaṃ...niṣīdantaṃ".)
2. The two *anurūpa* verses are *triṣṭubh*, while the others are different.
3. The *anurūpa* verse is "ta1.2.3.7-ma1.2.8-'mi". 4. [The reading] is "pālayitā" according to Ga1, Ta4.5, Bha7.8.
In the Vedic *luṅ* tense, by the rule "adīpanabudha" etc., there is the substitution of *ciṇ* for *cli* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge 'pi," there is the absence of the augment *aṭ*.

Furthermore, upon the bows (*vadhi*)—that is, the weapons—of these contemptible enemies (*vaanya*), may the wretched bowstrings (*vajyākāḥ*)—the lowly cords—be destroyed; that is, may they strike them down or perish.
From the word *jyā*, the suffix *aska* is added in the sense of censure, according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 5.3.70 and 74 (*prāgivāt kaḥ*). The root *nabha* is used in the sense of "to injure" (*hiṃsāyām*);
it belongs to the *kaiyādika* class.
One should curse by means of transgression.
You released the rivers to flow downward;
you slew the dragon, O Indra. You were born without a rival; you nourish every desirable thing. We embrace you; let the bowstrings of others snap upon their bows.

You released the rivers to flow downward; you slew the dragon, O Indra, for you were born without a rival. You nourish every desirable thing; as such, we embrace you. Let the bowstrings of others snap upon their bows. 2.
O Lord, you caused the rivers—which are by nature flowing with floods of water—to flow downwards; that is, you made them go toward the lower regions with their mouths turned downward.
You sent forth the clouds with their waters because you slew Ahi, the cloud that had gone into the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
Or alternatively:

Having come against Ahi, you slew Vṛtra, the Asura who obstructs the entire world; therefore, O Indra, you are born as *vajraśrī*, one whose enemies have been destroyed by the thunderbolt. In the Bahuvrīhi compound *vajraśrī*—meaning "one for whom no enemies exist"—the final syllable of the second member is acute by the rule *nañsubhyām*.
In *janer liṭi gamahanādibhyaḥ*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*).
Due to the rule *dvirvacane 'ci*, the reduplication (*dvirvacana*) occurs by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*).
Likewise, you cause to increase (*vapuṣyasi* = *vardhayasi*) all wealth (*viśvam* = *sarvam*) that is to be chosen (*vavāryam* = *varaṇīyam*) and worthy of being honored (*saṃbhajanīyam*).
The root *vṛh* means ‘to gather together. [The suffix] *ṇyat* is applied according to the rule *ṛhalorṇyat*.
The acute accent on the first syllable is established by the rule *iḍvandvavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ ṇyataḥ*.
Having spoken such a vow, we embrace you with oblations and hymns;
that is to say, we bring you under our control.
[The root] *dhvañj* means "to embrace."
By the rule *daṃśasañjasvañjāṃ śapi* (Pāṇini 1.4.25), there is the elision of the nasal; the rest has been explained.
May all hostilities be scattered; may the prayers of the noble one reach us.
O Indra, you are the hurler of the weapon at the enemy who seeks to slay us; may the bowstrings of others snap upon their bows.

May all hostilities, even those of the noble, be utterly dispersed; may our prayers reach you. O Indra, you are the hurler of the weapon against the enemy who seeks to slay us. That delight of yours which dwells in heaven—may the bowstrings of others snap upon their bows. 3.

*Vaviśvāḥ*: all; *vārātayaḥ*: those who should not be given [gifts], those who are to be avoided, those who are to be approached [only for harm]—our enemy-like subjects; *vasu*: wealth; *vavi vanasanta*: let them perish.
O Indra, for your sake, let *vadhiyaḥ*—deeds or hymns of praise—proceed.
O Vaindra, *vayaḥ*: he who desires to strike us, who wishes to kill us.
In *hanteḥ sani*, there is lengthening according to the rule *añj-āgamāṃ sani*. There is also the substitution of *k* for *h* according to the rule *abhyāsācca*.
To that *vaśatru* (the one who strikes down by will), you (*tasmai*) shall become the *vadhastā*—the hurler of the *vadha*, the weapon which is the instrument of striking.

The root *asu* is used in the sense of "throwing. The suffix *tṛn* here expresses a habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*). In the word *vate*, *vayāḥ* refers to the hand, which is the cause for bestowing wealth.

May that *rātiḥ*—the giver of *vasu*, wealth—be a bestower of riches unto us. The suffix *kip* is applied to the root *dadāti* by the rule *ā-dā-g-maha-na*. The absence of the genitive case after the word *vasu* is due to the rule *na lokādhyaya*. The rest is established. 4. O Indra, whoever among our people, acting like a wolf (*vṛkāyu*), seeks to harm us from all sides and hurls weapons at us—cast him beneath our feet! You are the oppressor; you are the conqueror. Let the bowstrings of our enemies bend upon their bows. 5. O Indra, whoever seeks to harm us—whether he be a kinsman (*sanābhi*) or one of low birth (*niṣṭya*)—subdue his strength here, even as the great heaven [subdues the earth]. Let the bowstrings of our enemies bend upon their bows. 6. O Indra, we, desiring you, take hold of friendship. Lead us along the path of Truth (*ṛta*) beyond all difficulties. Let the bowstrings of our enemies bend upon their bows. *** **Notes on the Translation:** * **Mantra 4**: The term *vṛkāyuḥ* means "one who acts like a wolf," where *vṛka* refers to a harmful wild dog or a thief. The verb *ā-dideśati* is derived from the root *diś* ("to hurl/point") with the *lyap* augment and the Vedic substitution of *ślu* for *śap*. The accentuation follows the rule *abhyastānām ādiḥ*. The phrase *adhaspadam* means "under the foot. The term *vibādhaḥ* means "the oppressor" of enemies, and *sasahiḥ* means "the conqueror. * **Mantra 5**: The distinction is made between a *sanābhi* (a relative born of the same lineage) and a *niṣṭya* (one of inferior birth). The suffix *yat* is added to the word *niṣṭya* in the sense of "born from" (*jātārthe*) according to Pāṇini 4.2.104. The sandhi *padavam* (becoming a word) occurs because of the rule *hrasvāttādau taddhite* (Pāṇini 8.3.101). The phrase *tira* is used in the sense of "destroy" or "overcome" (*vadhakarmā*). * **Mantra 6**: The term *tvāyavaḥ* means "desiring you" (*svātmānam icchantaḥ*). The word *ṛtasya* refers to the path of Truth or the sacrificial path (*yajñasya*). The elision of the suffix *ṭā* is noted, and the instrumental case takes its accent according to the rule *udāttanivṛtti-svara*. The phrase *ā rabhāmahe* means "we undertake" or "we embrace" the state of friendship (*sakhitvam*). The sacrifice itself is characterized as the essence of friendship. The state of being accented.
Lead us across—carry us beyond—all difficulties, that is, all hardships, evil paths, and the fruits of sin.
The last word has been explained.
O Indra, bestow upon us that which yields according to the singer’s desire;
may the great cow, whose milk-streams are unbroken, overflow for us with a thousand streams of nourishing fluid.
O Indra, bestow upon us that [cow] which yields according to the singer's desire, with an unbroken udder, so that the great cow may nourish us with milk in a thousand streams. 7.
O Indra, do thou bestow that cow well upon us, thy praisers;
for "śikṣ" means to give. That cow which yields the desirable milk day after day in unceasing succession for the singer who praises thee.

The absence of the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix is due to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in Vedic usage, [the rules] are manifold). Since it follows a root taught with a short *a* (*adupadeśāt*), the *śap* suffix is unaccented (*anudātta*) because it belongs to the *lasārvadhātuka* category; furthermore, it is unaccented because it is marked with the *pi* indicator.
The radical vowel remains.
It is better [to derive it] from the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*), with the suffix *ap* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) according to the rule *grahavṛdṛniśrigamaśca*.

That bestowed cow—unpierced, striking, and possessing thick udders, and therefore having a thousand streams, being abundant with many streams of milk, and being great (mahī)—may she nourish us with milk; let her cause us to increase. This is the remainder of the sense.
The root *pyai* means "to grow.
The suffix *ṇi* has been elided according to Vedic usage;
by transposition (*vyatyaya*), the verbal root undergoes the change to *pī*.
The absence of *a* is a Vedic archaism.
The sixth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "ubhā yat," has Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva, as its seer (ārṣa).
The seventh verse, together with the half-verse beginning with "pūrveṇa," has as its seer the woman named Godhā, a knower of Brahman (brahmavādinī).
The seventh [verse] is in the Paṅkti meter.
The remaining verses are *paḷaṣṭakas*, which are *mahāpaṅktis*.

Indra is the deity. Thus it has been enumerated: "In the two [verses] beginning with 'yanmāndhātā', [the seer was] Yauvanāśva; they are *mahāpaṅktis*; the last one is a *paṅkti*; regarding that, Godhā saw."
The application of the hymns (*sūktaviniyoga*) has been concluded.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, the triplet beginning with "ubhe yad indra rodasī" is an optional *stotriya* for the Acchāvāka.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "ubhe yad indra rodasī bhava yacca śatakrato" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).

Since you, O Indra, have filled both worlds as the dawn fills them, the divine mother has brought you forth—the great sovereign of the great ones, the ruler of the peoples; the auspicious mother has brought you forth.

Both [worlds], O Indra—when you have filled the two worlds like the Dawn—you, the great one among the great, the sovereign lord of the peoples, the goddess Mother has brought you forth; the auspicious Mother has brought you forth. 1.
O Indra, you who have filled both *rodasī*, heaven and earth, with your splendor— you fill them completely; [the root] *ā-prā* means "to fill," belonging to the *ad-ādi* class.

The *liṭ* (perfect tense) ending is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Just as the Dawn (*uṣāḥ*) fills the entire world with her own light, so too did Aditi—the divine (*devī*), playful (*devanaśīlā*), and excellent progenitor (*janitrī*)—give birth to you, O Indra, who are the greatest (*mahantam*) among the great (*mahīnām*) gods and the sovereign ruler (*samrājam*) over all people (*carṣaṇīnām*). She brought you forth.

This is the form [of the verb] in the *luṅ* tense with the *caṅ* suffix from the root √*jan*. Because this mother (*janitrī*) gave birth (*ajījanat*) to such a son, for that reason she became (*jātā*) auspicious (*bhadrā*), beautiful, and praiseworthy.
The suffix *tṛn* is used here in the sense of "one who performs an action well" (*sādhukārī*) derived from the root √*jan*.
In the word *janitrī*, the elision of the suffix *ṇi* is applied by irregular rule (*nipātana*) before *iḍ* and other such suffixes, according to the rule "in *mantra*.
The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to the rule "after roots ending in *ṛt* and *ej*."
1. In the versions of Ga and Bha 1.7, it is *ṛtasya*; in Ta and Bha 2.4.8, it is *na ṛtasya*. 2. In Bha 7, it is *asau*.
3. In Ta and Bha, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the *ṇi* suffix.
Relax the firm strength of that mortal who seeks to harm us;
cast him beneath our feet, he who points against us. The divine Mother has brought us forth; the auspicious Mother has brought us forth.
O Arvan, loosen the firm foot of the mortal who seeks to strike us; cast him down who aims his shafts at us. The Goddess Mother has brought you forth; the Auspicious Mother has brought you forth.
Of the mortal, the human enemy who acts with a cruel intent and inflicts painful slaughter, loosen his firm and steadfast strength; let it hang down, let it be cast low.
(The particle *sma* is a filler.
Make that very enemy lie beneath your feet, positioned below your two feet.
The enemy who commands against us, who desires to kill us— the rest is the same.

O slayer of enemies, O Śakra, with all your powers and all your aids, shake down those vast, all-glittering showers of rain here, O Indra. The divine mother gave birth [to you], the auspicious mother gave birth.

These great ones, all-glittering, O slayer of enemies, O Śakra, shake them down with your powers; O Indra, with all your aids. The divine Mother brought them forth; the auspicious Mother brought them forth.

O *amitrahan*, slayer of enemies—that is, O *śakra*, Indra—by means of your own powers (*śacībhiḥ*), or by your own deeds, [bring] those well-known, vast (*bṛhatīḥ*) and all-delighting (*viśvaścandrāḥ*) [waters]. [The feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is applied [to *bṛhat*] according to the rule "the addition of *ṅīp* for *brahman* and *mahat*," and it bears the acute accent (*udātta*). [The waters are called] *viśvaścandrāḥ*.
"Those whose [ornaments] are all (viśvāni) golden (candrāṇi) moons (hiraṇyāni). The augment *suṭ* is applied by the rule "In a mantra, when *candra* follows a short vowel in a compound.
The acute accent on the final syllable of the first member (*viśva*) is applied by the rule "In a *bahuvrīhi*, *viśva* is accented on the final syllable when it is a proper name."
Shake down such arrows along with all your protections and aids;
cause them to fall headlong upon us—meaning, bring them toward us.
The rest has been explained.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, the verse "ava yadhvam" serves as an optional *anurūpa* for the *acchāvāka*.
However, the rule regarding this has already been cited at the beginning of the *sūkta*.

O Indra of a hundred powers, descend; you shake off all [obstacles] for the one who presses the soma, as if shaking down wealth, along with thousandfold aids. The divine mother has brought you forth; the auspicious mother has brought you forth.

O Indra, O Śatakratu, since you shake all wealth together with the one who presses the soma, along with your thousandfold aids—O Goddess, the Mother has brought you forth; the auspicious Mother has brought you forth. 4.
1. *ta-bha-āvarta*.
O Śatakratu—O Indra, who possesses many deeds or great wisdom—to the one pressing the Soma (the performer of the *sunoti* [pressing] action), [be present].

By the rule "hunujoḥ sārvadhātuke," the *yaṇ* substitution occurs.

For such a sacrificer, whenever (*yat* = *yadā*) you shake down (*ava dhunuṣe*) all pervasive riches—that is, you cause them to come toward him, you give them—this is the meaning.
Then, grant us wealth—both wealth in the form of sons and material riches—along with thousandfold protections, that is, safeguards numbering in the thousands.
The rest has been explained.
Here, let the two worlds weave [the sacrifice] on all sides from the sweat;
like threads of dūrvā grass, let them extend. May the evil-minded goddess depart; the mother has given birth to the radiant one; the mother has given birth to the radiant one.

Let sweat fall on all sides from every direction like drops; let the fibers of the *dūrvā* grass fall away from us like threads. Let ill-will depart from us. The divine Mother has brought [the child] forth; the auspicious Mother has brought [the child] forth. 5.
Like drops of sweat from the body, let the weapons of Indra—or his splendors—shine forth on all sides from the two mountains; let them fall here from every direction, facing in all ways.
Like threads of *dūrvā* grass, they are seen to be spread out extensively, just as the stalks of *dūrvā* grow forth in many places.
May the evil-minded one, the one with wicked intent, the enemy—may he go away from us, may he depart and be separated from us.

O such Indra, you bear—that is, you maintain—[it].
[The root] *ḍubhṛñ* means "to support" and "to nourish."
The root *hu* belongs to the *juhotyādi* class.
By the rule *ścau bhṛñām it*, there is the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable.

O Maghavan, O Indra, possessor of wealth, just as a goat (*ajaḥ*) pulls at a branch (*vayām*) with its foot (*padā*) while standing on the front part of the body, so too, having drawn [them] by the aforementioned power, you, Yama, restrain the enemies.
Namely, there is the augment yaṅ;
by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the elision of the śap suffix. The rest has been explained.
We do not diminish the gods; we do not neglect them. We act in accordance with the hearing of the sacred hymns.
With our wings, even with our very feathers, we clasp them closely.
We do not diminish [the gods]; we do not cause them to fade away. We move according to the hearing of the sacred hymns. With wings and with outspread wings, here we cling together.

O gods, Indra and the others: in your domain, *nakiḥ*—we do not harm (*minīmasi*) anything at all. [The root] *mīhū* means "to injure"; it belongs to the *krayādi* class. According to the rule *mīnāter nigame*, there is a shortening [of the vowel]. The suffix *masi* ends in *i*. The vowel *ā* is used for conjunction. *Nakiḥ* means "not at all" (*na kiṃca*). 1. From the *ga* manuscript: *vaktrāt*. 2. *tara*. 3. 7-bha1.2.4.8: *mantumaḥ* does not exist.
3. *nakir āva*; 7. *nakir ā*.

We shake off; we cause to be shaken off. We cause [you] to be deluded by non-performance. [The root] *yu* means "to delude. What then? This mantra—having made that ritual action pertaining to you, which is to be established by the mantra and set forth in the injunctive statement (*vidhi-vākya*) of the Śruti, our own—we perform it; we carry it out; we practice it. Furthermore, with the *pakṣas*, that is, with the *stotra* chants which stand in the place of wings; [or] with the *apikṣas*. The *apikṣa* is the middle part of the arm. By means of the injunctions that constitute the armpits (*apikakṣa*) of the sacrifice, here in this sacrifice, on all sides, we firmly grasp you; we properly take hold of you. 22.
The seventh hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "yasmin," is the seerhood of Kumāra of the Yama lineage; it is in the Anuṣṭubh meter and has Yama as its deity.
Thus it is enumerated: "yasmin; Kumāra, son of Yama, [composed] the Yāma [hymn], which is in the Anuṣṭubh meter."

On that tree with beautiful foliage where Yama drinks together with the gods—there our Father, the Lord of All, looks with favor upon the ancients. 1. On that tree with beautiful foliage where Yama drinks together with the gods—there our Father, the Lord of All, looks with favor upon the ancients. 1.
On the tree: this is a simile for "lusopa" (emaciated).
Like a tree that has beautiful foliage—meaning it is endowed with excellent leaves and possesses a magnificent garden.
Alternatively:
on a tree possessing beautiful leaves;

just as the root of such a tree provides comfort by dispelling the fatigue born of heat, so too, in that place which provides comfort, Yama—the son of Vivasvat, the ruler—is "drinking together," that is, he enjoys [his meal] with the gods who have become his attendants.
The meaning is "he drinks.
Viśvapati is the lord (adhipati) and father of us all, that is, of all creatures; the plural number is used by way of grammatical transposition (vyatyaya).

My father Vājaśravasa, the progenitor of Naciketas, desires me here in this abode of Yama—that I might dwell near his ancient, long-residing ancestors, following after them. A youth named Naciketas, having been sent to the realm of Yama by his father Vājaśravasa, beheld Yama, propitiated him, and returned once more to this world.
This matter is set forth by these initial mantras.
Alternatively,
"Kumāra" refers to some other seer than Naciketas;
and "Yama," because he restrains (yacchati), refers to the Sun (Āditya).
He praised with this hymn:
"In that beautiful place, like a tree with fine foliage, Yama—the Āditya—is [present] with the gods;
for 'gods' (devāḥ) are those who shine, namely the rays."

He drinks together with them, that is, he associates with them. Due to the influence of the prefix (*upa*), the root *pā* here has the sense of "associating. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).

Abiding here in this place, the Lord of the Universe— the Sun, who protects all creatures by illuminating and raining upon them, and who is the progenitor of all through his nature as the vital breath (prāṇa)— desires us, his ancient worshippers, as those to be favored. Or rather, he desires our ancient ancestors, who abide in this place, according to their succession.

Beholding him who follows the ancient ways, yet wandering with that evil course, I looked upon him with resentment; therefore, I desired him no more. *purāṇān* (of the ancients), *anuvenantam* (following after), *carantam* (wandering), *pāpayā* (with evil), *amuyā* (by that), *asūyan* (resenting), *abhi* (towards), *acākaśam* (I looked), *tasmai* (for him), *aspṛhayam* (I desired), *punar* (again). 2.

I first beheld with mental anguish my father Vājaśravas—who was longing for the ancient, primordial ancestors, who followed after them, and who lived with this wretched, base intellect—displeased with him, thinking, "He lives in comfort; go to the presence of Death! "Look at me! he said. 1. anu-hi.
2. In the versions designated as ta1.2.3.6.7.8 and bha, the phrase "eats... of Naciketas" is absent. 3. In the version designated as ta and bha, the word "by the gods" is absent.
4. In the versions designated as ga, ta1.2.3.6.7.8, and bha, the passage from "the root *pibati* here... up to "protector" is absent.
This is the path.
[The root] *asū* [is used] in the sense of mental affliction (*upatāpa*);
it belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* group.
Furthermore, later on, [he said]: "Therefore, out of a desire for my father's recognition, I wished to obtain that clay.
The root *spṛh* means "desire";
it belongs to the curādi class and ends in *d*.
By the rule *spṛher īpsataḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.36), the designation of recipient (*saṃpradāna*) applies, and thus the dative case is used after the word *tat*.
Alternatively:

he was envious—by means of a base, evil intellect incapable of praising—of him who moves through the sky by rising and setting, desiring in succession his ancient, long-standing praisers, his ancestors, or his forefathers.
Envy (*asūyā*) is the manifestation of faults in virtues.
While looking on with disdain, I manifested faults in another's virtues;
I perceived him merely as "some person" by way of his general form.
But now, once again perceiving the majesty of that Sun, I no longer longed for him;
rather, I desired to attain that very Sun through hymns of praise and through actions consisting of service.
The new chariot-wheel, O youth, which you fashioned with your mind— having a single felly yet biting into everything on all sides— you stand upon it, unseen.
O Youth, that new chariot which you fashioned with your mind—having no wheels, with a single pole, and facing in every direction—standing upon it, you look out from above. 3.
With the following verse, Yama attempts to entice the youth named Naciketas:
"O youth, [this is] new—never before seen by you here.
He clarifies that it is indeed something brand-new.

"Though that chariot is wheelless, devoid of wheels, and belongs to those who are alone among the many, yet you have fashioned with your mind that chariot which moves forward, reaching out everywhere; having made it, you see it and mount it, discerning what is to be done and what is not to be done.
Or rather, the Sun, appearing directly before the singer—the seer named Kumāra—awakens him to the discrimination between the body and the Self."

O Sage, you fashioned with the mind—that is, with the internal organ—that new chariot which consists of the body, which moves everywhere, and which has a single life-breath (*prāṇa*) as its pole and a single wheel. It is beneficial for some; it is one whose pole is the vital breath. Such was the chariot, consisting of the body, that you created with the mind.
For desire arises from the mind, which consists of volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*).
When desire exists, action consisting of merit and demerit is performed.
And by that [action], this body is commenced for the sake of providing experience; thus, it is through this causal sequence that the mind is the producer of the body.
Perceiving—that is, knowing—that chariot which consists of the body;
the present participle suffix *śatṛ* is used here in the sense of a cause according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.2.126 (*lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*).
You preside [over it] because of your thorough knowledge of my true nature.
You accept [them] as the basis for enjoyment.
The chariot which you, O youth, caused to roll forth from the sages—
that the Sāman followed after it, like a boat launched upon the waters.
O youth, that chariot which the swift horses brought forth for the inspired singers—that *sāman* followed after it, placed together here upon the ship. 4.

"O Kumāra Naciketas, you have set in motion this aforementioned chariot; you have brought it even unto me, from above the wise ones—meaning from above the relatives of the intelligent who dwell on the earth, that is, from the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
[The change of the visarga to *s* occurs according to the rule: *pañcamyāḥ parāvadhyarthe*."
That chariot—the consolation fashioned by his father—followed him, instructing him in the means for his return: "Even having gone to the presence of Yama, you must speak exactly thus";
it followed him from this world.
Of what nature was it?
"In the boat"—that is, in the intellect which is the means for crossing over—"well-placed" (samāhitam), meaning properly fixed.

Alternatively: 1. *ta4.5*—knowing; 2. *ga*—desired to attain; 3. *ta4.5*—impels; 4. *ta-bha*—the phrase "tamekaṃ" is absent; 5. *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha1.2.4.8*—or having made; 6. *ta-bha*—division of duties; 7. *ta-bha*—is produced; 8. *ta-bha*—the phrase "karma... śarīrātmakam" is absent.
O wise sage, you who have set out upon the journey through saṃsāra, that chariot consisting of the body which you have mounted—after that chariot, the *sāman* has followed.
This is an elliptical expression;

[it means] the hymn accomplished by the *ṛc*, *sāman*, and so forth, and the ritual action (*karman*) which is well-established as the object to be properly performed, have both been set in motion from this world within the speech consisting of the Vedas, which is like a boat to be made to cross over.
Thus, by means of the thorough knowledge of the nature of the self, the bondage of the body and the various activities of worldly conduct have been described.

However, the intention is that if one directly realizes the Supreme Self—the agent whose nature consists of truth, knowledge, and so forth—as one's own self, then what has been stated [regarding bondage and activity] is no longer possible.
Who gave birth to the prince Ratha? Who brought him back?
And who could tell us how she became his bride-price?
Who begot the prince? Who turned the chariot back? Who was the woman? Tell us that, O Anudeyī, exactly as it happened. || 5 ||
"Who is this man who begot this boy?"—
the word "who" (*ka*) is used here in a sense of reproach.
How could such a father be considered proper, sending such a child to the presence of Yama?
Let that be for now. Who indeed was the man who turned back that chariot for this boy to go to the presence of Yama?
He too was a fool; such is the meaning.

In whatever manner this youth was to be followed—that is, to be pursued—accordingly, one should speak words suited to that purpose as an expedient. Otherwise, at this time, who among us would say, or indeed express, such a thing?
The meaning is that even if one were to go first to the presence of Yama and afterwards speak of the means for departure from there, one would not be wise.
Or alternatively:
The Seer, perceiving his own self-nature as the Youth (Kumāra) and showing that no other exists apart from himself by means of the interrogative particle *kaḥ*, says:
"Who begot me, the Youth?
No one at all."
"I am of the nature described in the Śruti: 'Unborn, eternal, and everlasting' (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.18).
And who has fashioned—or fashions—the chariot consisting of the body?
Since there is no creator other than myself, and since no other object to be created is possible."

Now, at this time, in the state of experiencing one's own essential nature (sāvātmyānubhava), who indeed could tell us what specific manner [of manifestation] exists—by which manner the existence of other objects distinct from "I" was or is to be inferred?
The meaning is that even that manner is difficult to express.
Just as the Anudeyī was born from him, so too was Agramajā born;
first Budha was stretched out, and afterwards Trayaṇa was made.
For example: "It was. "A gift was given. "From that. "The foremost. "Was born. "In front. "The wise one. "Extending. "Behind. "The most excellent. "Was done. (6)

*Anudeyī* means that which is to be given subsequently. Just as in whatever manner this boy was given by Yama with reference to his father, so from that father Ājaśravas, [the instruction] arose—that is, it became manifest—consisting of the words "Go forth to the presence of Yama," which Naciketas was to speak in the presence of Yama, as stated in another Brāhmaṇa: "He said, 'You shall go to him when he has departed on a journey'" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.11.8.2), and so forth.
The meaning is that the father instructed him.
Previously, before that, the wise one had heard the exceedingly extensive statement: "Go to Yama’s abode, which is the very root.
Therefore, realizing that it was impossible to avoid, he later abandoned his anger and adopted the path of departure—that means of emerging from there—which had been practiced by his father.
Or rather:

*Anudeyī*: that which is to be given after oneself, existing as other entities distinct from the nature of the self, according to how they actually exist. 1. *gata*—in this world; 2. *ta-bha-ca*—by that; 3. *ga-ta1.2.3.5.6.7.8-ma*—in her; *ta4*—of that; 4. *ta-bha*—of what kind; 5. *ta-bha*—he turned back.

(Rig Veda 4.51) Then, from that Self characterized by *māyā*, the first principle of mind (*manastattva*), the cause of the desire to create, was born—that is, it arose—as the very beginning of the entire collection of evolved effects.

Before creation, in the prior state, the foundation— the root, the unmanifest cause consisting of *māyā*— was spread out (*ātataḥ*), extended on all sides. Afterwards, following the emergence from darkness, there occurred the "going forth" (*nirayaṇa*), the departure of the effects belonging to that cause from that cause, which took the form of assuming individual identities through distinctions such as jars, cloths, and so forth.
It was created by Brahmā.

Likewise, a modification of clay, such as a jar and so forth, does not become something other than the clay. By the grace of Āditya, for me who has attained the state of non-existence as Brahmā, this phenomenal world (prapañca), which is my modification, does not become something other than myself. Thus, the previously mentioned objection regarding distinct entities such as the lump of clay and so forth is supported.
