Intoxicated by the state of a sage, we have ascended upon the winds. You mortals behold only our bodies; you do not see us. Intoxicated (*unmaditāḥ*)—by the state of a sage (*mauneyena*), through the abandonment of all worldly activity, acting like those who are mad, or rather, having attained an exalted intoxication of joy (*mada*). We have *ascended* (*ā tasthima*) upon the *winds* (*vātān*), the very breaths that blow through us. O *mortals* (*martāsaḥ*), humans, you behold only our *bodies* (*śarīret*); you do not see us, because we have attained union with the formless wind.

He flies through the intermediate space, beholding all forms; the sage, the well-disposed friend of every god for the sake of their good deeds. (4) The *muni*—the seer of this Ṛgvedic hymn, the sage Vṛṣāṇaka, who has attained the state of the Wind or the Sun through various forms of worship—flies, that is, moves, through the *antarikṣa*, the intermediate space or atmosphere. What is he doing? Beholding (*avacākaśat*), looking upon, and revealing by his own splendor all (*viśvā*) forms (*rūpā*), that is, the entire multitude of manifest objects. Likewise, he is the friend (*sakhā*) of every (*devasya-devasya*) god—the repetition being used in the sense of totality—and thus he is the *hitaḥ*, the well-disposed or established one, for the sake of *saukṛtyāya*: for the sake of the good deed (*sukṛta*), namely the sacrificial rite performed excellently for the gods, so that it may be properly accomplished.

The horse of Vāta, the friend of Vāyu, and moreover the sage impelled by the gods—he dwells in both oceans, that which is eastern and that which is western. 5. The horse of Vāta; the friend of Vāyu; and moreover; impelled by the gods; the sage; in both; oceans; he dwells; that which; and; is eastern; or; the western. 5.
1. For the worldly [state], everything is *ta-bha-la*.
2. For *ta-bha-mu*, it is *nosmān*.
Like the movement of the wind, the horse is pervasive.
Alternatively,
"aśitā" means the eater of air;
the meaning is that air itself is his food.

For this very reason, the *sakhā* (friend) of *vāyoḥ* (the wind)—that is, one who has become a friend to the wind—and furthermore, *deveṣitaḥ*, impelled by or reached by the shining *deva*, whether the wind or the sun; [in this compound, the accent of the first member remains as it was, according to the rule] “*tṛtīyā karmaṇi*” (Pāṇini 6.2.48). Such a *muniḥ* (sage), the seer named Karika, being of the nature of the wind or the nature of the sun in the manner described, *ākṣeti* (dwells in/attains) both *samudrau* (oceans), that is, the two seas.
The roots *kṣi* [meaning] "dwelling" and "going" [take this form]; there is the elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Which two are those oceans?
And that which is the eastern ocean—
the word "uta" has the sense of "and"— and that which is the western ocean.

Moving in the path of the Apsarases, Gandharvas, and wild beasts, Keśin—knowing the intention, a friend, sweet and most intoxicating. 6. [In the path] of the Apsarases, [of] the Gandharvas, [of] the wild beasts; moving; Keśin; knowing the intention; a friend; sweet; most intoxicating. 6.

Moving upon—the apsaras, the celestial women, and the gandharvas—in the divine atmosphere which is their place of movement, and likewise moving upon the earth, the domain of wandering for wild beasts such as lions; pervading and traversing all this, Keśin—whether Vāyu or Sūrya—is the knower of *ketas*, that is, of every category of object to be known; or rather, he is the wise friend of this knowable world impelled by him. Being thus the knower of everything without distinction, he is *svāduḥ*, the one who tastes, the fashioner, and the producer of all that is delightful; therefore, he is *madintamaḥ*, the most exhilarating.
In the word ‘nādasya’, the augment *nuṭ* is applied.

since it is heard in scripture that "this Agni is indeed Rudra" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.3.1), Rudra here refers to the fire of lightning.
That which exists together with that [poison] is "aviṣa";
this is a name for water.
Because the action is expressed by the rule "kriyāgrahaṇaṃ kartavyam," the sixth case is used in the sense of the fourth case, since the object (karman) functions as the recipient (saṃpradāna).
Whenever he drank poison and water with his vessel—that is, by means of the rays of light—he then caused Vāyu to churn for this Keśin;
he consumes every existing essence.
Or rather:
When he drank—that is, when he had drunk—he consumed that water which had become solidified within the solar orb and had taken the form of wind.
By means of churning, he stirred it with the fire of lightning.
Likewise, the intermediate speech (*mādhyamikā vāk*), which is "pinat"—meaning it bends even that which is base (*ku*) intensely, yet is itself unbendable and independent—used to crush it.

Just as it flows downward, so it pulverizes; this is a well-known fact. The root *añj* preceded by the prefix *ku-* [forms *kvañj*]; with the suffix *ac* (of the *pacādi* class), there is the elision of *yaṅ* by the rule “*yaṅo 'ci ca*” (*Pāṇini* 6.1.45).
The final syllable of the word following *sthā* and others is acute-accented.

The ninth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “uta devāḥ,” is in the Anuṣṭubh meter and is addressed to the Viśvedevas. The seers (ṛṣis) for each verse, in order, are Bharadvāja, Kaśyapa, Gotama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “uta devāḥ: seven seers; one verse each; addressed to the Viśvedevas. The ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.
O gods, you raise up again that which has been cast down;
O gods, you restore again the life of one who has gone to the other world.

Two winds blow: from the ocean and from the far distance. May one of them bring you strength; may the other blow away whatever is evil. These two visible winds—the wind from the front and the wind from behind—blow from the ocean (taking *ā* as a marker of limit) or even from beyond the ocean, making that distant region their boundary. [The root] *vā* means "to go" or "to move"; it belongs to the *adādi* class. Of these two winds, O singer, may one bring (*ā-vātu*) your strength (*dakṣa*) to you; and may the other blow away (*parā-vātu*) whatever evil (*rapas*) belongs to you.

O Vāta, blow hither the medicine; O Vāta, blow away whatever is disease. For you, possessing all medicines, move as the messenger of the gods. O Vāta, blow hither the medicine—the bliss that pacifies disease, or the healing herb—bring it near. O Vāta, blow away whatever is our sin; remove it from us, separate it from us. For you indeed are the messenger of the gods, the possessor of all medicines (*viśvabheṣaja*); in this *bahuvrīhi* compound, the first member is accented on its final syllable according to the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, *viśva* [is so] when it is a name. You go constantly, you move about. [The root is] *iṅ* "to go," belonging to the *divādi* class. Because the suffix *iyana* has the marker *mit*, the word is accented on its initial syllable by the rule "that which begins with *mit* is always [accented on the first]. By the rule "also after *hi*," there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (elision of accent).

I have come to you with healing remedies and with means for safety. I have brought you auspicious strength; I drive away your consumption. I have come to you with healing remedies and with means for safety. I have brought you auspicious strength; I drive away your consumption. And furthermore, O gods, you lift up again him who was cast down, afflicted by poverty and struck by misfortune. O gods, having seen me, lift me up once more—rescue me and lead me to an exalted state. And furthermore, O gods, [you lift up] the one who was cast down.

O singer, I have come to you with *śantāti*s—protections that bring happiness—and also with *ariṣṭatāti*s—protections that cause non-injury. In both cases, the suffix *-tāti* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 4.4.143 (*śiva-śama-ariṣṭasya karaḥ*).
By the rule *liti*, the vowel preceding the suffix is acute-accented.
Moreover, may your auspicious and beautiful strength (*dakṣa*), which is to be brought or carried from the presence of Vāyu, come to you;
likewise, I drive away and destroy your disease (*yakṣma*).
May the gods protect him here; may the host of Maruts protect him;
may all beings protect him, so that he may become free from disease.
May the gods protect him here; may the host of Maruts protect him; may all beings protect him, so that he may be free from harm. 5.
May all the gods protect us here in this place;
likewise, may the host, the assembly of the Maruts, protect us;
and may all other beings, every class of living creatures, protect us and guard us.
The meaning is: "so that this body and so forth of ours may be *arapāḥ*, i.e., free from evil (*rapas*).
*Rapas* is a name for sin.
In the *bahuvrīhi* compound with the negative particle *nañ*, the final syllable of the second member is accented according to the rule *nañsubhyām*.
There is the addition of the augment *aṭ* due to the particle *asterleṭ*. There is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) by virtue of the rule *yāvadyathābhyām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.36).
The waters indeed are healers, the waters are the drivers away of disease;
the waters are the healers of everything—may they provide healing for you.
The waters indeed are healing; the waters drive away disease. The waters are the healers of everything; may they provide a remedy for you. 6.
The waters indeed—verily the waters themselves—are healing; they are the means of medicine, being the causes of well-being through bathing, drinking, and so forth.
Or alternatively:
Having transformed into the form of medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*), they become the causes for the alleviation of disease.
By the rule *kevalamāmaka°* (Pāṇini 4.1.30), the suffix *ṅīp* is applied after the word *bheṣaja*. Due to the accent known as *udāttanivṛtti-svara*, the *ṅīp* becomes accented (*udātta*).

In the word *jasi*, the long vowel of the same class as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghatvam*) is applied according to the rule "or in the Vedic language" (*vā chandasi*). For this reason, the waters (*āpaḥ*) are *amīvacātanīḥ*—that is, they are the destroyers of diseases (*amīva-cātanyaḥ*).
The root *cānayati* has the sense of killing (*vadhakarmā*).
Furthermore, the waters are the healers—acting as medicine—for the entire class of living beings, not for only a few;
may those such waters act as medicine for you.
With our two hands, which have ten fingers, and with the tongue, the forerunner of speech—
[which are] free from disease— with those two we touch you.
With both hands, with the ten fingers; with the tongue, the leader of speech; with the two that cause no harm—we touch you with them, we touch you closely. 7.

Created by the two hands of Prajāpati— those hands which possess ten branches, meaning ten fingers that serve as their branches— the tongue, the organ of taste, became the "leader" (*purogavī*), that which goes before, of speech, i.e., sound;
wherever there is sound, there it is always present.

The meaning is that [the hands] are active before one for the purpose of uttering sound. O singer, with those two hands which cause the forest to bend and which are the causes of perfect health, we touch you closely;
*masi* here ends in *-id*.
The repetition of "vavṛdhāna" is for the purpose of completing the meter.
The tenth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "tava tya," is in the Jagatī meter and is dedicated to Indra; it was composed by Urugava, the son of Ajāśva.
And thus it has been listed: “tava tya ṣaḍ ṛcaḥ aurvaḥ jāgatam.
The application [of the hymn] has been explained.
O Indra, in your friendships, many [sages], considering it as the Truth (ṛta), have opened up Vala.
In which [battle], showing favor, you sent forth the waters for Kutsa, and you shattered Vala while honoring the prayer and the sacred word;
where, showing favor, you released the waters for Kutsa, [shattering] the dawns and the days with your thunderous roar.

These many [deeds] of yours, O Indra, were performed in friendship; mindful of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), you rent asunder Vala—where, showing favor, you released the waters for Kutsa, [shattering] the dawns and the days with your thunderous roar.

O Indra, while your friendship and companionships exist, your well-known, powerful carriers (*vahvayaḥ*)—whether of oblations or hymns—being thus aware of the chosen sacrifice (*vṛtaṃ yajñaṃ*), the Aṅgirases utterly tore apart (*vyadadir*) Vala, the asura known by that name who had carried off the cattle.
The root *dṛ* means "to tear apart.
From this root, in the *yaṅ*-lopped form (*yaṅluganta*), the *luṅ* (aorist) ending is to be understood according to the rule *sijabhyasta*.
The *guṇa* [substitution] occurs in the word *juṣi ca*.
This is due to a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*).

Furthermore, at that time when there was hymn after hymn (*manman*) of praise, you, O Indra, acting for the sake of the great seer Kutsa—bestowing favor (*daśasyan*) by removing the waters that had been mostly non-existent because they were obstructed by Vṛtra, and likewise choosing the waters (*vapaḥ*) which were waterless due to being covered by Vṛtra, and making them flow from that place—you thus prevail.
The root *rī* is used in the sense of "going" (*gati*) and "seeking" (*eṣaṇa*).
It belongs to the *kryādi* (fourth) class.
By the rule "pvādīnāṃ hrasvatvam," its vowel is shortened.
At that time, the deeds of Vahni and the serpent Vṛtra became futile—this is the meaning.
You released the plants; you caused the mountains to tremble; you drove forth the waterless cows, the sweet and beloved honey.
By his wondrous power, he struck down the two trees; the sun blazed forth through the hymn born of Truth (Ṛta).
2. You released the waters;

you made the mountains flow; you drove out the cows; you drank the beloved honey. By his wondrous power, you struck down the two Vṛtras; the sun shone forth through the hymn born of Eternal Order (Ṛta). 2.
O Indra, that which is the impelling force, the procreation, and the birth of the waters— you have released those waters, which are the cause of that [birth],
having caused them to fall down from the cloud that envelops them.
Likewise, you caused the mountains—the peaks—which had been placed by force to cover the cave of Gomati, to go away; that is to say, you terrified them. [The root] *śri* means "to go."
In the form *asmān*, the absence of the augment *aṭ* in the *luṅ* tense occurs by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge’pi*” (Pāṇini 6.4.75).

According to the statement “*samānavākye nighātayuṣmadasmadādeśā vaktavyāḥ*” (Vārttika on Pāṇini 8.1.18), the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* must occur within the same sentence; since the preceding word does not belong to the same sentence, there is no loss of accent (*nighāta*) for this [verb] according to the rule “*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*” (Pāṇini 8.1.28).
Likewise, after splitting the mountain, you brought out (*udājaḥ*), that is, you caused to emerge, the cows that had been placed in the cave by the demon Vala.
Then you drank the milk, curd, clarified butter, and so forth—what is dear and agreeable—as well as the sweet oblation (madhu-havis).
Or rather:
when those cows, which are the means for preparing the mixture, have arrived, you drink—the sacrificers drink—the desired and beloved honey consisting of Soma.
Likewise, "vṛkṣān" refers to trees connected with a forest; or alternatively,
"vana" is a name for water.
You cause the oceans joined with those [waters] to swell by means of the bestowing of rain;
O you who are born from the chosen [oblation].
By the *ṛta* sacrifice;
by the *girā*—that is, by the speech consisting of the Vedas—which praises the Bull, Indra, who was born for that purpose; by the *dasasā*, the deed, of him;
with the two [hands] that bring nourishment (*bhara*) and are free from disease (*anāmayitṛ*), being the causes of freedom from disease.
2. ta1.2.3.17.7.8–ma1.4.7.5– The rule "in a single sentence... there is no absence of *nighāta*" does not apply here.
Even for Vṛtra and others who were obstructing [the light], the sun blazed in the sky as if illuminated by its impelling nature;
or alternatively:
The phrase "by the speech born of Truth" (*ṛtajātayā gire*) is a qualification of Sūrya alone; the meaning is that he is illuminated by speech in the form of the three Vedas (*trayī*).
Here, one should refer to the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa passage: "In the forenoon, the god moves in heaven with the *ṛc*s" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.1).

In the phrase *śuśoca*, even though it stands after another word (*ityasya*), there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) because the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "or [the rule applies] from the beginning of a quarter [of a verse]" (*vāpadādau*) continues to apply.
Sūrya has unyoked his chariot in the midst of heaven; the Ārya, having established his counterpart, has spread it out.
Indra, acting as the creator, has shattered the firm fortresses of Pipru, the deceitful Asura, for the sake of Ṛjiśvan.

In the midst of heaven, Sūrya released his chariot; he found a means of retaliation for the Dāsa through his deeds. Indra, having performed [these acts], shattered the strongholds of the wily Asura Pipru by means of Ṛjiśvan. In the midst of heaven, the sun, Āditya, unyoked his chariot for its departure.
Even though his army was thus pierced—by a widespread and pervasive force that tore it apart—he remained with an unassailed host.
Or rather:
With his vast and pervasive form, piercing and rending the forces of the enemy with his thunderbolt, Indra—the slayer of Vṛtra who has indeed slain Vṛtra—such as he is, bestows;
he gives; he grants wealth to those who praise him.
The root *dāś* means "to give. The augment *ḍa* is added [by Pāṇini 6.1.45].
Likewise, he sharpens—that is, attenuates or diminishes—the enemy forces that are to be urged on (*tujyāni*).
The root *tij* means "to sharpen.
Alternatively, he sharpens— that is, whets and makes keen— the weapons that are to be hurled against the enemies.
Before such an Indra, from his all-surpassing and destructive thunderbolt, the entire host of enemies is struck with fear and attains terror.
Thus, when the Asuras had been driven away by Indra, Śundhyū—the Sun, so called because he purifies—set forth, having begun to move for the purpose of illuminating the world;
and Uṣas, the goddess Dawn, abandoned her own chariot, leaving it behind as she departed.
The root *ohāk* means "to abandon.
These are your deeds as heard in the revelation (*śruti*): that you alone made the one [world] devoid of sacrifice;
then, by means of the moon, the ordinance was established in heaven, and by you it was divided, while the Father bears the rim of the wheel.

These are your own glorious deeds: that you alone made one [of the two] devoid of sacrifice; that you established the threefold division of the months in the sky; and that the father bears the chariot-felly split apart by you. 6.
O Indra, these—these alone—are your heroic deeds; they are exclusively yours, worthy of being heard by the sacred revelation (śruti) and deserving of praise.
They do not belong to anyone else.
But what, then, are they?
Alone, without companion, you made the Asura—the preeminent one who was devoid of sacrifice—into one who is without sacrifice; that is, you destroyed him. This is the singular deed.
[The root] *kṛv* [is used] in the senses of "injury" and "making";
here it has the sense of injury.
The suffix *ap* is applied after the roots *dhā*,
*ni*, *vṛ*, and *kṛṇvi*, and there is the substitution of the vowel *a* for the final letter [of the root].
When that [suffix] is elided, due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present), there is an absence of the *guṇa* strengthening of the penultimate vowel (*ghu*-penultimate).

Likewise, for *māsān* [the form] *māsām*. By the rule beginning with "pada-n" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 7.1.59), the word *māsa* undergoes the substitution of *mās* [before the genitive plural ending]. (*Uṇādi-sūtra* 8).
By the rule beginning with "159," the case ending (*vibhakti*) is udātta.
You placed (*adhāḥ*), that is, you established, the ordainer (*vidhātāram*), the maker (*kartāram*), the Sun, above the sky (*adhi dyavi*), in the celestial realm (*dyuloka*).
In the word *vipūvān*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to the rule "the kṛtya and lyuṭ suffixes are applied diversely."
This is another function [of the thunderbolt]:
likewise, the father Pālaka, the heavenly world (*dyuloka*), split apart—that is, rent asunder or separated from Vṛtra—the *pradhi*, which is the side of the chariot wheel.
The side-boards are called *pradhī*.
He himself bears—that is, supports—the rim of such a chariot belonging to the Sun, which otherwise would be impossible to sustain;
this is another of his deeds.
The meaning is that these and other deeds performed by you are unique to you and are always worthy of praise.
26. The eleventh hymn, consisting of six verses, beginning with "sūrya raśmiḥ," is in the Triṣṭubh meter;
its seer is the Gandharva named Viśvāvasu.
He praised Savitṛ with the first verse and himself with the second;
therefore, Savitṛ is the deity of the first verse and Gandharva of the second.
Thus it has been recorded: "Sūryaraśmi, the divine Gandharva Viśvāvasu, praised himself in the first half."
The application has been explained.
Savitṛ, the golden-haired sun-ray, rises as the light in the east with straightforward power.
At his impulse, the wise Pūṣan goes forth, the guardian who beholds all beings.
The sun’s ray, golden-haired, Savitar has risen from the east as the light, straight and vigorous. At his impulsion, Pūṣan goes forth, the wise one, the guardian who beholds all beings. 1.
1. *ta-bha*: worthy of praise. 2.
*ta-bha-1.2.4.8*: thus. 3. *ga-ta4.5*: of that, after the elision of *ataḥ*; *ta1.2.3.6.7.4-bha2.8*: in connection with that; *bha1*: in the absence of *aya*; *bha4*: in the absence of *aca*.
4. Anupūrvārdha:
Sūryaraśmi. The deity presiding over that period of time which follows the manifestation of the dawn and precedes the rising of the sun is called Savitṛ.

He whose rays are like those of the Sun—the Sun being the impeller of all—is thus called *sūryaraśmiḥ*. He whose hair (*keśaḥ*)—meaning either the rays that have the nature of seizing (*harayaḥ*), or those that are green-colored (*harita-varṇāḥ*), or the shining lights (*dīptayaḥ*) standing in place of hair—is thus called *harikeśaḥ*. Such is *Savitṛ*, the god who impels all; he causes the light (*jyotiḥ*), the splendor (*tejaḥ*), to rise (*udayāt*) incessantly (*ajasram*) in the east (*purastāt*), in the eastern direction.
The root *yā* here contains an implied causative sense; the present tense (*laṭ*) is used according to Vedic usage, and the plural number is by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
In the *saṃhitā*, the *n* is shortened by the rule "after a long vowel, before a vowel [beginning with] *aṭ*, within the same *pāda*."
By the rule "āto 'ṭi nityam," the vowel *ā* is nasalized.
At the impulse, the impulsion, or the permission of that Savitṛ, the wise one—the protector, the guardian, the nourisher, the divine Āditya—travels through the sky.
What does he do?
Illuminating clearly, he beholds all beings, all the various classes of living creatures.
This far-seeing one sits in the midst of heaven; he has filled the two worlds and the intermediate space.
He beholds those that turn toward all and those that drip with ghee, between the eastern and the western sign.

The far-seeing one; he sits in the midst of heaven, having filled both worlds and the intermediate space. He gazes upon all the ghee-dripping ones that extend in every direction, between the eastern and the western beacon.
Beholding men now, or rather shining with men—that is, with his rays—this Savitṛ sits in the midst of heaven.
What is he doing?
Filling both worlds, heaven and earth, as well as the intermediate space, with his own splendor.
The root *prā* means "to fill. From this root, the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) is formed according to Vedic usage; by the rule "and *kasu*," its substitute is *kasu*.
In the case of *vastrakājādasām*, there is the augment *iṭ*.
That god beholds—that is, illuminates—the all-reaching, all-moving, and all-pervading great directions such as the East;
likewise, he illuminates the ghee-reaching directions, such as the Southeast, which possess radiant forms.
From the root *añc* with the suffix *kvip*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule “*añcater upasaṃkhyānam*”.
Then, when the designation *bha* applies, the vowel *a* is elided by the rule “*acaḥ*”, and the lengthening occurs by the rule “*cau*”.

When the acute accent of the suffix *ṅīp* would otherwise be obtained by the rule for the accentuation of the disappearance of an acute vowel (*udāttanivṛttisvara*), the preceding vowel becomes acute by the rule “*cau*”.
Likewise, he beholds—that is, he illuminates—the front part, the rear part which is to be made known as the banner, and the space between them.
The foundation of wealth, the gatherer of treasures, he gazes upon all forms with his powers;
like the god Savitṛ whose laws are true, he stands like Indra in the encounter for the winning of riches.
The foundation of wealth, the gathering place of treasures, he beholds all forms with his powers. Like the god Savitṛ whose laws are true, like Indra, he stands at the encounter of riches. 3.
The foundation of wealth—that is, the bond or the root-source of riches.
By the rule beginning with “‘uḍidam,” the vowel following the word *rai* is acute (*udātta*).

Likewise, Savitṛ— the gatherer, the one who brings together and bestows the *vasūni*, the riches— beholds, that is, perceives and illuminates, all forms (*viśvā rūpā*), meaning all categories of objects to be discerned, by means of his powers (*śacībhiḥ*), that is, his splendors. Moreover, this divine Savitṛ, the impeller, is one whose nature is true (*satyadharmā*), meaning he possesses a true, unerring law (*dharma*) or the action that is the cause for upholding it.
Likewise, like Indra— just as Indra stands in the encounter, in the battle for the attainment of riches—
this Savitṛ stands ready and firm.

1. ta-bha1.2.4.8—The eternal people; 2. ta1.2.2.6.7—the god. Having seen Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva, the waters went forth according to the Truth (ṛta). Indra, hastening after them, perceived the enclosures of the sun around them. viśvāvasum | soma | gandharvam | āpaḥ | dadṛśuṣīḥ | tat | ṛtena | vi | āyan | tat | anu'avait | indraḥ | rarahāṇaḥ | āsām | pari | sūryasya | paridhīn | apaśyat || 4 ||
"O Soma, [bring] me, who am known by the name Etasa, together with you, [to] Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva, who maintains sound as his form and song as his voice.
In the subsequent portion, because the word "that" (tat) is heard, the word "which" (yat) is to be supplied.
"[Which] waters," known as the *vasatīvarī*s, "have seen" (*dadṛśuṣīḥ*) [him].
The suffix *kasu* follows the root *dṛś*. The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule “*ugitaśca*”.
The semivowel substitution (*saṃprasāraṇa*) occurs by the rule “*vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam*”.
In the case of *jasi*, the long vowel of the same class as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*) applies by the rule "or [it is so] in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*).
"At that time, by means of the *ṛta*—that is, by means of the sacrifice as the cause—the sacrificers went forth (*avyāyan*), moving in various directions.
Indra, the swift mover (*rarahāṇaḥ*) who causes them to go, became aware of (*anvavait*) that movement.

Having become aware of it, he looked all around (*pari apaśyat*) at the enclosures (*paridhīn*) of the sun—the regions of the quarters such as the east and so forth—to see where the sacrifice had commenced."

May Viśvāvasu, the divine Gandharva, the measurer of the mid-air, proclaim that for us—whatever is true, or even what we do not know; may he, impelling our thoughts, protect our prayers here. (5) Viśvāvasu shall proclaim that for us; the divine Gandharva, the measurer of the mid-air, whatever is indeed the truth, or even what we do not know—impelling our thoughts, may he truly protect our prayers. (5)
May Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva, favorably proclaim that to us; may he speak it toward us.
The root *gṛ* meaning "to sound" belongs to the *kaiyādika* group; it takes a short vowel because it belongs to the *pvādi* subgroup.
Of what nature is he? "Divine" (divya) means existing in heaven; likewise, he is the "architect" (vimāna), that is, the creator, of the "rajas-less" (arajasaḥ), which is water.
What, then, is that?
"Or rather: whatever collection of actions is indeed true, non-false, and possesses results according to reality;
and whatever we do not know—that is, we are unaware of—may both of these be for our well-being (*avīt*). This is the meaning."
In the passage beginning with "ṛci tunugha," the vowel *gha* is lengthened according to the rules of *saṃhitā*.
The remaining quarter-verse is established by direct perception:
"O Viśvāvasu, impelling our mental works and causing them to prosper through Soma."
The root *hi* means "to go" and "to increase.
Alternatively:
"impelling," that is, reaching, our prayers (*dhiyaḥ*)—meaning either our ritual acts or our thoughts—O [Agni], protect (*avyāḥ*) our prayers, that is, our actions or our intellects.

In that very course of the rivers he found [the way]; he threw open the doors of those whose prisons were of stone. Of these, the Gandharva proclaimed the nectar-like waters; Indra fully understood the skill of the dragons. 6. In that very course of the rivers he found [the way]; he threw open the doors of those whose prisons were of stone. Of these, the Gandharva proclaimed the nectar-like waters; Indra fully understood the skill of the dragons. 6.

"In this [place], the *añji*—the cloud that thoroughly bathes the entire world—[is present]. [The root] *ṇvi* is used in the sense of purification. By the rule *ā-dama-hana*, the suffix *kin* is applied. Due to a change in gender, the dual number is used. He found [it] "in the movement," that is, in the place of circulation, the atmosphere, of the "rivers," the waters that produce sound. Indra obtained it. And having obtained it, [he found] the "stone-pens. A stone (*aśman*) is a pervasive cloud; [he found them] moving therein. Or rather, those whose "pen" (*vraja*)—that is, their dwelling place—is the cloud, such are the waters."
1. Of the rivers (*nadīnām*), that is, of those roaring (*nadatām*); [variant *bha7*: of the rivers, of those sounding (*nadamānānām*)].
He opened (*apāvṛṇot*), that is, he threw open (*apāvṛtavān*), the gates (*duraḥ*), namely the passages for the clouds and fire to pass through.
Or else:

When the rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and Yamunā—whether moving along, going forth, or having their courses pervaded—encountered the rugged rocks as an obstacle to their passage, Indra found a cloud for that purpose;
and having found it, he opened the doors of the cloud, which are the means for the outflow of the waters contained within.

Likewise, Indra—the Gandharva existing in the form of Viśvāvasu, the holder of the thunderbolt (*gorvajra*)—proclaims, that is, he declares, these immortal waters of the rivers which effect immortality;
he gives permission for them to be carried forth.
So he shall speak.
"He bestows the water of skill" (*dakṣyudakaṃ prayacchati*): *dakṣa* refers to a cloud capable of scattering [rain].
He "knows around" (*pari jānāti*) such a cloud among the clouds (*ahīnām*), that is, he knows it completely on all sides.
The root *jñā* means "to understand."
The source [of ownership] is from a document; the substitution of *jā* for the roots *jñā* and *jan* is according to the rule "jñājanorjā."
The twelfth hymn, consisting of six verses, begins with "agne tava.
Its deity is Agni as characterized by the quality of purity (pāvaka).
The first verse is a *viṣṭārapaṅkti* containing eight, twelve, two, and eight syllables respectively.
Then there are three *satobṛhatīs*, characterized by the rule "the odd [feet] are *jagatī*.
The fifth is an *upariṣṭājjyotis*;
the sixth is a *triṣṭubh*.
And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: "O Agni, [the hymn] 'Agni tavāgniḥ pāvaka'; the deity is Agni; the metre is Viṣṭārapaṅkti; there are three Satobṛhatīs, followed by an Upariṣṭājjyotis.
In the Mahāvrata, this hymn is used for the purpose of the Stotriya and Anurūpa verses in the Āgnimāruta Śastra. It has been sūtra-ed in the same way in the Pañcama Āraṇyaka (Ai. Ā. 5.3.2).
O Agni, your fame and vital strength are great; your rays blaze forth, O Lord of Radiance. Bestowing abundant gifts through your power, O Sage, you grant praiseworthy nourishment to the donor.
O Agni, yours is glory and vital power; great are your flames, O Lord of Light. O Bṛhaddāna, O Bṛhadbhānu, through your might you bestow praiseworthy booty upon the donor, O Sage.

O Agni, yours is vital strength, food, and fame worthy of being heard— fame that is praiseworthy because it consists of the oblation (*havis*) and is rendered excellent through its consecration by mantras.
The meaning is that among all fires, yours alone is the most excellent food.
O *vibhāvaso*! *Vibhā* means distinguished radiance;
*vasu* is wealth, and you are such that you possess it. Your *arcayaḥ*, meaning flames or radiances, *ājante*, meaning they shine or blaze, *mahi*, meaning greatly or abundantly.
The root *dīp* (to shine) is anudātta-it and belongs to the bhūvādigaṇa.

O Bṛhaddāna (of vast bounty), Prauḍhadīpta (of intense luster), Kavi (O Seer), Krāntadarśin (O Far-seeing) Agni! You, who possess such great majesty, [bestow] that which is endowed with śavas (strength/power)—the Ukthya (praiseworthy one);
or rather, the Ukthya sacrifice.
You bestow—that is, you give and present—to the donor, the sacrificer who has offered oblations, that appropriate *vāja*, which is food.

Possessing purifying luster, possessing bright luster, possessing undiminished luster, rising up with your radiance, O seer, as a son wandering with his mother you protect us; you fill both heaven and earth.
Of purifying luster, of bright luster, of undiminished luster, you rise upward with your radiance. Moving about as a son among his mothers, you protect and fill both heaven and earth. 2.

"Pāvakavarcāḥ" means having purifying brilliance; "śukravarcāḥ" means possessing stainless luster; "anūnavarcāḥ" means having complete splendor. O Agni, such as you are, you "udiyarṣi"—you rise up—with "bhānunā," that is, with your radiance.
[The root] *ṛ* (in *ṛ sṛ gatau*) means "to go."
It belongs to the *jauhotyādika* class;
by the rule "ati-piptyośca," there is the substitution of *i* for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).

As such, being the Son (*putra*), moving about within the two mothers—the two kindling woods (*araṇī*)—and reaching them especially at the end of the run, you protect the sacrificers who have approached you.

Likewise, you fill both *rodasī*, heaven and earth; that is to say, you join them together, filling the celestial realm with oblation and the earthly realm with rain. [The root] *pṛcī* means "to unite."
It belongs to the *raudhādi* class.
1. The means of accomplishing the burden of the earth. 2. Moving between heaven and earth, you protect them;
you fill both worlds, heaven and earth, with your splendor.
"By means of smoke he fills this world for the sake of rain," so says the Vājasaneyaka.

O Son of Strength, Jātavedas, rejoice with fair praises and with our prayers, being well-disposed toward us. In you they have gathered the offerings—those of many forms, with wondrous aids, born of what is desirable. O Son of Strength, Jātavedas, rejoice with fair praises and with our prayers, being well-disposed toward us. In you they have gathered the offerings—those of many forms, with wondrous aids, born of what is desirable.

O Son of Strength (ūrjaḥ napāt), O Agni Jātavedas, knower of all that is born—O son of the terrestrial and forest food (anna)—rejoice and be glad through our excellent praises (suśastibhiḥ) being offered by us;
likewise, being well-disposed and satisfied by our ritual acts (dhītibhiḥ), such as the Agnihotra and other rites, be fully gratified.
Moreover, [be so] for those of manifold forms (bhūrivarpasaḥ).
*Varpaḥ* is a name for form.

*Bahurvidharūpāḥ* means those possessing many kinds of forms; *citrotayaḥ* means those whose aids (*ūtayaḥ*) are wonderful and diverse; *vāmajātāḥ* means those whose birth (*jātam*) is desirable (*vāmam*, i.e., worthy of being sought). Such *iṣaḥ*—that is, foods characterized by oblations—they place together in you alone;
that is, the sacrificers offer them correctly into you.
Alternatively,
the phrase "of many years" (*bhūrivarpasaḥ*) and so forth may be a qualification of the agent;
in that case, *citrotayaḥ* should be construed as "possessing manifold protection."

Ruling, O Agni, spread yourself out with living beings; bestow wealth upon us, O Immortal One! As such, you shine forth with a visible form; you fulfill our winning power of will. 4. Ruling, O Agni, spread yourself out with living beings; bestow wealth upon us, O Immortal One! As such, you shine forth with a visible form; you fulfill our winning power of will. 4.
O Agni, ruling over (*irajyan*), being envious (*īrṣyan*), and competing (*spardhāṃ kurvan*) with the born beings, that is, with the enemies;
[the root] *iraj* is used in the sense of envy (*īrṣyāyām*);
it belongs to the *kaṇḍvādi* class.
Or rather:

the root *irajyati* itself has "purposeful action" as its meaning; thus, *irajyan* means "being sovereign," ruling by means of his own splendors (*tejobhiḥ*) which are produced (*janyamānaiḥ*) by living beings (*jantubhiḥ*).
O immortal Agni, free from death,
spread forth— make vast— our *rāyaḥ*, that is, our riches; [here, the genitive case ending is replaced by *śe* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.]
In place of the suffix *śas* after the word *rayi*, there is *jas* by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
Alternatively, by the same transposition, the rule "the third case ending is udātta" (*uḍiḍam*) is not applied.
Thus, you shine forth with that body (*vapuḥ*) which has been shown—that is, the visible, radiant body.
Or, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental:
"You shine especially with this body.
Or alternatively: [the construction may be understood as such].
"Sovereignty" (*rājatir*) is indeed the act of ruling;
"body" (*vapuḥ*) is a name for form.
You shine forth—that is, you rule preeminently—with a beautiful form.
Therefore, you fulfill—that is, you cause us to attain—the praiseworthy *kratu*, meaning the ritual action worthy of being honored;
or rather, you endow it with its fruit.

The wise ordainer of the sacrifice, who rules over great wealth—you bestow upon him a fortunate and abundant gift of lovely things, great nourishment, and winning riches. (5) Ordainer of the sacrifice; the wise one; ruling over; great wealth; the gift; of lovely things; fortunate; abundant; nourishment; you bestow; winning; riches. (5)
The fashioner and the refashioner—
here there is a Vedic elision of a syllable—

he is the one who prepares and perfects the *adhvara*, the sacrifice; he is the far-sighted one (*pracetasaṃ*) of exalted knowledge, the lord (*kṣayantam*) and master of great wealth (*maho rādhasaḥ*).
*Kṣabhati* alone means "one who performs the action for the sake of wealth.
*Vāmasya* means "of desirable wealth"; *rāti* means "the giver. The suffix *kip* is used here in the sense of the agent of the root *rāti*.

The ellipsis is "we praise you who are such. As such, you bestow—meaning you give—to the worshippers a fortunate (or, rather, one freed from misfortune), great earth, abundant food, and wealth that is to be shared.

The people have placed before them for their welfare Agni, the observer of cosmic order (*ṛtāvān*), the mighty one, visible to all; you, the divine one with ears that hear, most far-reaching, through song—throughout the ages of mankind. ṛtāvānam | mahiṣam | viśvadarśatam | agnim | sumnāya | dadhire | puraḥ | janāḥ | śrutkarṇam | saprathastamam | tvā | girā | daivyam | mānuṣā | yugā || 6 ||

[We praise] the one who possesses the cosmic order (*ṛta*), who possesses truth, or who possesses sacrifice; [the suffix] *vanip* is used here in the sense of possession according to the rule "in Vedic meters, *vanip* and *ini*" (*chandasīvanipau*). [We praise] the mighty one (*mahiṣam*), meaning great or worthy of worship, who is visible to all (*viśvadarśatam*), that is, to be beheld by everyone.
Alternatively, it means "he whose vision is universal.
According to the rule *bahuvrīhau viśvaṃ saṃjñāyām*, the final syllable of the first member (*viśva*) is udātta.

Such an Agni, people—consisting of both officiating priests and sacrificers—place before them (*puraḥ dadhire*) for the sake of bliss (*sumnāya*), that is, for the sake of happiness. They place him in front.
They maintain it before all ritual acts;
or rather, they maintain it "in front" (puraḥ), that is, in the eastern direction in the form of the Āhavanīya fire.
It is made manifest by the subsequent half-verses.

Moreover, O Agni, you whose ear is keen—meaning you who hear our hymns perfectly with that organ of hearing—you are the most renowned (*saprathastama*), or rather, you are the one who is extended everywhere; such as you are, a divine being connected to the gods by virtue of being the bearer of their oblations, you are praised with song—that is, with hymns—by human generations, by the successive ages consisting of wives and sacrificers, according to the desires of men. This is the sense.

The hymn beginning with “agne,” consisting of six verses and the thirteenth [verse], is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Agni distinguished by the qualities of an ascetic; it is addressed to the Viśvedevas (vaiśvadeva) and is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “‘agne’—[the hymn] of Acchāvāka and Tāpasa, addressed to the Viśvedevas, in the Anuṣṭubh meter, indeed.
The application (viniyoga) has been explained.

O Agni, speak here to us; turn toward us with a gracious mind. Bestow upon us, O Lord of the People, for you are the giver of wealth to us. 1. O Agni, speak to us here; turn toward us with a well-disposed mind. Grant us [your favor], O Lord of the People, for you are the giver of riches to us. 1.
O Agni, speak here in this place to us, addressing us with what is dear;
likewise, turn toward us and be well-disposed, with a gracious mind.
O Lord of the People, protector of the subjects characterized by the sacrificer, bestow wealth upon us, grant it to us, since you are the giver of wealth to us, the one who provides riches.

May Aryaman grant us [wealth]; may Bhaga grant it; may Bṛhaspati grant it. May the gods grant it, and may Sūnṛtā, the goddess, grant us riches. 2. May Aryaman grant us [wealth]; may Bhaga grant it; may Bṛhaspati grant it. May the gods grant it, and may Sūnṛtā, the goddess, grant us riches. 2.

May Aryaman— the restrainer of enemies and the creator of noble ones, the deity known as Vaitara— bestow wealth upon us. Likewise, may the deity known as Bhaga bestow it, and may Bṛhaspati also bestow it.
May all the gods grant [their blessings],
and may Sarasvatī— the goddess who delights in play, whose speech is full of pleasant truth— bestow upon us, her devotees, riches and wealth.
By the rule beginning with "udittam," the case-ending of the word *rāyaḥ* is udātta.
1. There is no *ta-bha-mu-‘naḥ* here.

We invoke King Soma for protection, Agni with songs of praise, the Ādityas, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, and Bṛhaspati the priest. || 3 || Soma | King | For protection | Agni | With songs | We invoke | Ādityas | Viṣṇu | Sūrya | And | Priest | Bṛhaspati || 3 ||
We invoke with hymns of praise—songs of laudation—the King, the Resplendent One, or the Lord, as well as Soma and Agni, for the sake of protection.
Likewise, we invoke for the sake of protection the Ādityas, the sons of Aditi such as Mitra and others, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Brahmaṇaspati (Prajāpati), and Bṛhaspati.

We invoke Indra and Vāyu, Bṛhaspati, who are easy to call upon, so that every person may be well-disposed toward us in our assembly. (4) Indra and Vāyu, Bṛhaspati, those who are easy to invoke—we call them hither, so that every single person may be well-disposed toward us in the gathering. (4)
*Indra* and *Vāyu* together form *indravāyū*.
According to Pāṇini’s rule 6.3.26.1, "the prohibition [of the *ānaṅ* substitute] must be stated for *vāyu* in both cases," there is a prohibition of *ānaṅ*.

Furthermore, by the rule "not when the second member begins with an unaccented vowel" (*nottarapade'nudāttādau*), there is a prohibition of the original accentuation of both members (*ubhayapadaprakṛtisvara*) which would otherwise apply by the rule "in a *devatā-dvandva*" (*devatādvandve ca*).
The word *samāsasya* indicates that the final syllable is udātta.
Regarding *bṛhaspatim*: he is the protector (*pati*) of the great gods (*bṛhatām*).
According to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.157, *tadbṛhatoḥ karapatyoḥ*, the augment *suṭ* and the elision of the *t* suffix are applied.
[The accentuation] follows the rule for *vanaspati* and similar compounds, whereby the original accent of both members of the compound is retained.
We invoke Indra-Vāyu and Bṛhaspati—those who are easily invoked, the pair who are easily invoked—at this rite here.
Just so that every single person among us may be well-disposed (*sumanāḥ*) at the gathering, that is, upon the acquisition of wealth; such is the meaning of our invocation.
There is this scriptural authority: "It must be so."

Urge Aryaman, Bṛhaspati, and Indra to bestow gifts; urge Vāta, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and the vigorous Savitṛ. (5) Aryaman, Bṛhaspati, Indra—urge them to give. Vāta, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and the powerful Savitṛ. (5)
O singer, impel—the gods beginning with Aryaman—to give, that is, to bestow wealth; urge them forward with your hymn.
Likewise, impel Vāta (the Wind), Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, Vājin (the one rich in food or strength), and Savitṛ, to give.

O Agni, do thou increase our sacred word (*brahman*) and our sacrifice with thy fires; do thou impel us toward the assembly of the gods for the granting of wealth. 6. O Agni, do thou increase our *brahman* and our sacrifice with thy fires; do thou impel us toward the assembly of the gods for the granting of wealth. 6.
O Agni, you, together with other fires that are your own manifestations, increase our *brahma*— that is, our hymn of praise—
and our sacrifice. Likewise, for our sake, for the sake of the gods (*devatātaye*), impel the givers to bestow wealth (*rāyaḥ*) for the purpose of the sacrifice.
The fourteenth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "ayam agne," is dedicated to Agni.
*Śāṅga* is the name of a particular species of bird.
Jaritṛ and the others—four in total—are the seers (draṣṭāraḥ) of the *ṛca*s, belonging respectively to the various lineages of the Śāṅgas.
The first two are *jagatī*s;
then four *triṣṭubh*s;
and then two *anuṣṭubh*s.

And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: "This [hymn] beginning with 'ayam agne' consists of two ṛcs; Śāṅga Jaritā Droṇa Sārisukta and Stambamitra [are the seers]; it is addressed to Agni; there are two Āgneyī Jagatīs and four Triṣṭubhs.
The application (viniyoga) has been explained.
O Agni, this singer has come to you, O son of strength; for he has no other kinship than yours.
For your auspicious protection is threefold; keep harm far away and drive off the adversary.

This singer, O Agni, has become dependent upon you, O son of strength; for there is no other kinship to be found. For your auspicious protection is threefold; keep those who cause harm far away and drive them off.
"O Agni, in thee"— here,
by the rule *supāṃ suluk*, the locative case ending is replaced by *śe*.
This seer has also become a singer, a praiser.
The word *api* (even/also) expresses possibility;
he is now considered possible [to be] a praiser.
He states the reason for this:
O Son of Strength, O Son of Power! There is indeed nothing else to be attained (*āpyam*) from you; it simply does not exist.
Therefore, I attain you alone, who are to be attained, through this hymn of praise.
For from you comes *bhadram*—auspiciousness—and *śarma*—bliss—which is threefold in form and the remover of the three types of suffering. It is yours; it exists within you.

Alternatively: "Since you indeed possess a beautiful house with three forms and three stories, therefore, drive away—push back and ward off—from afar (āre), far from us, the blazing flame (didyum) belonging to us, which is the burning of those who injure and those being injured. [Drive it] away; remove it; restrain it.
[The *luk* elision of the verbal suffix occurs by Vedic license.]
The substitution of *dhi* for the imperative suffix *hi* occurs by the rule "śruśruṇupṛkṛbhyaḥ."
O Agni, you have come forth from the birthplace of the father; like a companion, you anoint all beings.
May our prayers, having flowed forth, win the prize; they go forward of their own accord like a herdsman.

Downward, O Agni, are your births; you proceed from your father. Like a companion, you anoint all beings. May our prayers, having flowed forth, win the prize; they move forward of their own accord like a herdsman.
O Agni, you who provide nourishment, desiring food for yourself, your birth—your manifestation—is pre-eminent and excellent.
The suffix *vati* is used here in the sense of "becoming" according to the rule *upasargāc chandasi dhātvarthe*.
Like a companion (*sācīva saciva iva*), you, O Agni, direct and govern all the expanded worlds, that is, all created beings.
The meaning is "you bring under your control.
Our *dhiyaḥ*—our hymns of praise, which are *sasruṣaḥ*, having the nature of flowing forth—*pra saniṣanta*: they thoroughly and intensely worship you, who are such.
The single word *pra* serves as a filler.

Regarding *araṇyānī*: the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*) maintain that *araṇyānī* is a certain presiding deity who protects the forest. Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇāḥ*), however, prescribe the suffix *ṅīṣ* for the word *araṇya* when denoting its greatness, according to the rule "for *hima* and *araṇya*, when [denoting] greatness" (Pāṇini 4.1.49).
O deity presiding over the forest, O Forest, you who flee away toward the deserts and wildernesses—
here "preva" has the sense of "from here";
the verb "naśyati" means "to reach."
Here, by way of transposition, there is this [suffix] *iy*.
Now, even a village is for the sake of protection;
or rather:
Since you are staying in a desolate place, you are indeed perceived as such;
why then do you not ask for the way to the village? How can you find delight in a lonely forest?
Surely fear does not find you—that is, it does not reach you?
The protracted vowel (*pluta*) indicates deliberation (*vitarka*).
The particle *iva* is used here in the sense of "now" or "indeed," or perhaps in the sense of "as if."

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: “*Araṇyānī* is that which belongs to the forest, being further within the forest; or it is so called because it is a place of non-delight (*aramaṇa*) compared to the village.

They recite her as *araṇyānī*: ‘O *araṇyānī*, you who enter the forests as if going away, why do you not ask for the village? Does fear not find you? Here, *iva* is used in the sense of ‘as if’ or for the purpose of expressing apprehension” (Nirukta 9.29–30).
When the cicada chirps near the one who speaks with a bull-like roar,
the forest exults as if it were being pursued by drummers.
When the cicada sings nearby like one playing upon musical instruments, Araṇyānī exults at the lowing of the bull. || 2 ||
*Vṛṣāravāya*:
that particular minute insect named *jhilli* whose sound or cry at the time of mating is like a bull's roar; that is what is meant by the term.
The meaning is "possessing a harsh sound."
To that king, who is like a bull and who utters the sound "cī-cī," the *ciccika*— the creature that makes the sound "cī-cī"—
approaches by making the sound "cī-cī" as a response to the word spoken by the bull,
or having approached, it protects him.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like lute-players. *Āghāṭayaḥ* refers to lute-players (*ghāṭikāḥ*), that is, those who play the *kāṇḍavīṇā*.
Like a singer, she causes those [sounds] to flow forth, purifying the excellent notes beginning with *nipāda*;
at that time, that *araṇyānī*—the great forest—is greatly honored.
The suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied by the rule *indravaruṇau* (Pāṇini 4.1.49) and others; by its co-occurrence (*tatsaṃniyogena*), the augment *an* is added,
and the short vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
For this very reason, there is no elision of the *su* suffix according to the rule beginning with *halṅyābbhyaḥ*.
Now it appears like grazing cattle, now like a dwelling;
at evening, the forest seems to discharge its carts.
And indeed, they eat like cattle; and it appears like a dwelling house. And the forest, at evening, lets out [its sounds] like carts. 3.
Moreover, even the *gavaya* and other wild beasts eat—that is, consume—grass and the like in this forest;
furthermore, creepers, shrubs, and so forth appear just like a dwelling or a house;
and moreover, this forest (*araṇyāni*) [is so called] because of its state as a forest at evening (*sāyam*), that is, during the evening time.
The word *ivaḥ* is used in the sense of "now.
Now he releases—that is, dismisses—the carts that have arrived for the purpose of carrying away the wood;
or alternatively:
"It appears as if they are unloading carts.

This statement refers to the following: during the day, having reached the great forest by means of carts, all the people load the required wood and other materials onto the carts and depart from there in the evening. It is with this intention that these words were spoken.
"The cow-robber is calling out; the wood-robber has struck down [the tree];
he thinks, 'The wild beast has howled in the evening.'"
1. The forest (araṇyāniḥ). 2. Like carts (śakaṭāniva).

O friend (aṅga), this one calls the cow (gām) hither (ā hvayati). O friend (aṅga), this one has struck down wood (dāru). Dwelling in the forest (vasan araṇyānyām), he thinks at evening (sāyam): "I have cried out" (arkukṣat iti manyate). 4.
O Araṇyānī, this man dwelling here in the great forest presided over by you now calls out to his kinsmen.
And this other person strikes down a piece of wood with his foot.

Likewise, at evening time, while dwelling in the great forest, a man hearing various sounds such as those of birds and wild beasts thinks, in fear, that someone is shouting at him with a sword or similar weapon.
The forest does not kill [the deer] unless another approaches it;
having eaten the sweet fruit, the noble one lies down at his pleasure.
No, indeed; the forest goddess does not strike down anyone else who does not approach her. Having eaten of the sweet fruit, he lies down at his pleasure. || 5 ||
Indeed, the forest does not truly strike down or harm one who dwells within it;
however, if another— such as a tiger or a thief— should approach, then [one suffers] from the fruit, which is like the delicious taste of meat.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Having eaten—that is, having consumed—the fruit, the person dwelling there reaches, enters, or exists therein according to his desire, that is, as he wishes.

In the case of the *ktvā* suffix, the substitution of *jagdhi* [for the root *ad*] occurs by the rule "In place of *ad*, *jagdhi* is substituted before a *kit* suffix" (Pāṇini 2.4.36). Then, the suffix *yak* is added by the rule "The suffix *yak* is added after a root ending in *kvip*" (Pāṇini 7.1.47).
I have praised the forest, fragrant as ointment, abounding in food without the toil of agriculture— the mother of wild beasts.
Fragrant as ointment, sweet-smelling, abounding in food, requiring no tillage—I have praised Araṇyānī, the mother of wild beasts. 6.
*Paāñjanagandhim*: *Añjana* refers to collyrium, such as musk and the like; she whose fragrance is like the fragrance of that is *paāñjanagandhi*.

By the rule *upamānācca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.137), the suffix *yat* is replaced by the substitute *ya*. Therefore, [the word] *surabhīm* means "endowed with fragrance. *Bahvannām* means "possessing abundant food," that is, endowed with many edible things such as fruits and roots. *Akṛṣīvalām* refers to those who do not practice agriculture; for *kṛṣīvalāḥ* are those for whom agriculture (*kṛṣi*) exists—namely, cultivators.
By the rule *rajaḥkṛṣi* (Pāṇini 5.2.112), the suffix *valac* is applied;
by the rule *vale* (Pāṇini 6.3.118), the vowel is lengthened.
Deprived of those [trappings], I have praised—that is, I have extolled in the manner described—such a one, the mother (*janitrī*) of wild beasts, the forest-dweller (*araṇyānīm*).
The twenty-fifth hymn, consisting of nineteen verses beginning with "śrat te," is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Suveda, the son of Śirīṣa.
The fifth verse is a Triṣṭubh; the remaining verses are Jagatīs.
Indra is the deity.
For it is recited in sequence: "śrat te pañca suvedāḥ śairīṣikhiṣṭubantam.
This hymn belongs to the Praśāstṛ priest during the third round of the night sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'śrat te dadhāmīdaṃ vyapātram indrapānam' is the Yājyā [verse]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.4).

1. *ga-ta* 1.2.3.6.7.8: "Having gone (*gatvā*), he calls (*hvayati*) the lost cow; and seeking the cow, he says, 'O you who have found it (*anvidvan*), call out for him who is yours (*tvadīyam*),' so it is said. *ta* 8.5: He calls; having found the cow, he says, 'O you who have found it, call out for him who is yours. *bha*: He calls while seeking the lost cow; he says, 'Call out for him who is yours. 3. *ta* 1.2.3.6.7.8-*bha*: "'This... strikes away (*apahanti*),' [this phrase] does not exist."
4. In the *ta-bha* recension, "asāyam" is not present.
5. In the *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha8* recensions, it is in the forest (*araṇye*).
I place [this] first in my mind; I recall that on this day, while leading Vṛtra away, he released the waters.
And both the worlds, heaven and earth, tremble before your might, even the earth and the sky.

I place faith in you, O first-born, as I remember when you struck down Vṛtra and set the manly waters free. When both worlds, heaven and earth, submit themselves to you, even the earth trembles at your might, O mountain-shaker.
O Indra, I place my *śraddhā*— that is, an excess of reverence— toward your *manyu*, which may mean anger or splendor, as its primary and foremost object. I direct it toward that [object].

With that fury (*manyu*) by which you slew Vṛtra—the obstructing Asura or cloud—O Leader of men (*narya*), and having slain him, with which you released the waters (*apaḥ*) that were blocked by him and brought them back to this world;
to that fury [be glory].
When both the worlds (*rodasī*), heaven and earth... [were encompassed by it].
He has taken pleasure in the well-sustained wealth of the arrow, he who understands his impetuous speed;
O Maghavan, strengthened by you and winning the prize of horses, he swiftly brings booty and riches with his men.

He indeed shall now take pleasure in well-sustained wealth—he who understands his impetuous course. O Maghavan, the worshipper of the sacrifice who is strengthened by you quickly brings forth booty and riches with his men.
He, that very same praiser, now quickly desires such wealth— wealth well-accomplished— as the object of his longing; here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
The meaning is "he obtains. *Raṃhaḥ* means speed or velocity.
He who is the praiser (*yaḥ stotā*) recognizes—that is, knows through words of praise—the exhilaration (*madam*), the joy born from drinking Soma, of this Indra.

O Maghavan, the sacrificer—strengthened by you, increased by you, and having offered the sacrifice—quickly brings together, accomplishes, and wins through his leaders or officiating priests both riches and food.
O Maghavan, being praised, by your greatness grant wide space to our host; bestow wealth upon us.
You are Mitra and Varuṇa to us, the master of wondrous power; like a dispenser of food, O Wondrous One, you deal out riches.

Praised for your greatness, O Maghavan, grant wide space to our host; hear us and bestow wealth upon us. You are Mitra and Varuṇa, the master of wondrous power; like a father, O Wondrous One, you distribute food as its dispenser.
O Indra, being praised with great majesty through this hymn, bestow wide and abundant strength upon our host.
O Maghavan, grant us riches;
O wondrous Indra, you who are the distributor of wealth, like Mitra and Varuṇa, being possessed of creative wisdom (*māyī*), grant these things to us.
*Naḥ* is used in the sense of "now. Now, you take pity upon us and bestow knowledge.
The hymn beginning with “supvāṇāsaḥ” consists of twenty-five verses; it belongs to Pṛthu, the son of Vena, and is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, dedicated to Indra.
It is thus enumerated: “supvāṇāsaḥ pṛthur vainvaḥ.
Its ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.
O Indra, we praise you as we press the soma; O you of many heroic deeds, we praise you as we hasten for the prize.
Bring us a well-fashioned [gift], for which we long; with our whole being, may we, protected by you, win it.

O Indra, we praise you with well-formed hymns; O you of many heroic deeds, we who are victorious in battle pray for booty. Bring us excellent wealth, for which you yourself take pleasure! May we, protected by you, win it for ourselves and our descendants. 1.
O Indra, we, having pressed the Soma and purified it for you, praise you—we praise you.

O you of many heroic powers (*tuvinṛmṇa*), whether meaning great strength or great wealth, we, having partaken together of the sacrificial food (*vāja*) characterized by the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings, praise you.
For this reason, bring to us—that is, bestow upon us—well-attained, excellent wealth.

The meaning is: "I shall bring that wealth which you desire (*cākan*) as being exceedingly dear to you. And furthermore, "protected by you" (*tvotāḥ*), meaning guarded by you, [we shall obtain] *tanā*—this is a synonym for wealth (*dhana*).
May we obtain, through your grace, vast riches—attained by ourselves, by our own selves, and indeed independently of any other.
1. [The syllables] ta, ta, ra, la, va, bha, ya, vyāptavyaṃ;
2. in the manuscript *bha*, the phrase "dhanaṃ...tanā" is absent.
O Heroic Indra, you were born great; may you overcome the Dāsa women along with Sūrya.
You bear the secret one placed in the cave, hidden within the secret place, like Soma in a spring.

Lofty one, O Indra, hero, as soon as you were born, you were to conquer the Dāsa tribes by means of the Sun. You brought forth from the waters that which was hidden in secret, concealed and kept within them, like Soma at its pressing.

O *śūra*, heroic Indra, you, the great and worthy of being seen, as soon as you were born (*jāta*), you overcame with the Sun— the very soul of the Sun— the *dāsīḥ* peoples, that is, the subjects belonging to the Dāsas, the Asuras who cause destruction. You conquered them.

Likewise, O Indra, Hero, hear our call as we invoke you against the demon named Vala, who is hidden in the secret cave, placed within the cave, and thus concealed and invisible in the waters; and against the one called Kuyava. You are praised by the hymns of Vena;
let the Vakas hasten toward your ghee-filled womb like waves flowing downward through valleys.

Hear the call, O hero Indra, from the broad earth; you are praised by the hymns of the seer. He who has approached your butter-rich womb—like a wave flowing down slopes, let the birds hasten toward it.
O heroic Indra, hear—listen to this wide-reaching invocation from the earth.
And furthermore, you are praised with hymns by me, the son of Vena, through these *arkas*, that is, sacred mantras;
[the suffix] *śap* is used here by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*).

The one who is a praiser, having approached (*ā astvāt*)—that is, he has praised (*abhyasvāpīt*)—your womb (*yoni*), your dwelling place, which is rich in clarified butter (*ghṛtavat*) and rich in water (*udakavat*). [Grammatical note: From the root *svṛ* (meaning "to heat" or "to cause pain"), in the *luṅ* tense with the suffix *tip*, there is an absence of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*bahulam chandasi*), followed by the elision of the *hal* and *ḍi* sounds; then, by the rule "the *s* of *rās*" (*rāstasya*), there is the elision of the *s*.
Or alternatively:
"The womb rich in clarified butter" and so forth; this refers to the sacrificial oblation. "I take hold of it."
The construction is: "Having reached the sacrificial hall, he who praises you—of that Vena, by means of his hymns (arkaiḥ). Furthermore, "vakāḥ" means "those who speak."
From the root *vac*, the suffix *vanip* is applied according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well.
The substitution of *va* for *va* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
In the nominative plural (*jasi*), the elision of *ū* occurs due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group.
All other worshippers as well cause you to flow like a mass of water with its waves through downward and excellent paths;
by means of their hymns of praise, they hasten toward you and approach you alone.
"Savitā yantraiḥ"—this twenty-first hymn consisting of five verses is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Arcan, the son of Hiraṇyastūpa; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and has Savitṛ as its deity.
It is recorded thus: "Savitārcana̭ hairaṇyastūpaḥ sā tritram."
The application has been explained.
With his supports, Savitar has firmly fixed the earth; in that which is without a pillar, Savitar has established the heat.
Like a stone, he has milked out the atmosphere; Savitar has bound the ocean with the immortal.

With his supports, Savitṛ has fixed the earth; in the supportless space, Savitṛ has struck out the sky. Like a stone, he milked the roaring atmosphere, which was bound by falsehoods; Savitṛ [fixed] the ocean. 1.

Savitṛ, the impeller and instigator of all, the deity residing in the intermediate region—he, by means of *yantras* (restraints), that is, instruments for controlling [the waters] or methods such as the bestowing of rain through the power of the wind, has caused the broad earth, the expansive ground, to rest (*aramṇāt*);
he establishes it in comfort.
Likewise, that same Savitṛ [acts] in the supportless space (*askambhane*).
"Support" (skambhana) is that which prevents falling;
even upon ground devoid of such support, he "struck" (ahat)—that is, he made firm—the sky, the celestial world.
The meaning is that he established it by his own means so that it would not fall downward.

Like a roaring stone, he causes that which is to be shaken to shake; he is the shaker of the atmosphere, dwelling within it, situated in the intermediate space, unassailable by anyone, and ruling over the sky or the firmament bound by the cords of wind; Savitṛ has milked the ocean consisting of clouds—he milks the waters.
Or rather, the word "antarikṣam" (atmosphere) is used in the nominative case with the sense of the locative.
In the unbounded mid-air, Savitṛ has milked—as if from a stone—the cloud that is bound, surging, and trembling;
he causes it to suffer.
[The root] *dhukṣ* [is used] in the senses of inflaming, causing distress, and living.
The meaning is that just as a rider distresses a horse through training, so too does Savitṛ distress the cloud for the sake of raining.

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: “Savitṛ made the earth tremble with his restraints; in the supportless mid-air, Savitṛ milked the cloud like a stone; he milked the cloud bound in the mid-air, ‘bound in the untruth’ or ‘wishing for water’; Savitṛ is the one who has opened the ocean” (Nirukta 10.32).
1. [In the variants] ta1.2.3.6.7.8–, there is elision of the *sa* (salopa); in *venasya*, it does not exist. 2. In *ga-ta8-bha*, it reads *savitārcato*; in *ta4-5*, it reads *savitārcato*.
3. In *ta4*, it reads *samuditāram*.

Savitṛ knows that ocean where the waters' son (Apām Napāt) has been established.
From this, O Earth, the dust arose; from this, heaven and earth were spread out.

Where the ocean was held back and surged forth—the Son of the Waters, Savitṛ, knows that; from there the earth arose, from there the mid-air emerged, and from there heaven and earth were spread out. 2.

In whatever intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) the ocean—the cloud, characterized by its nature to flow together—is supported or held fast, bound by the cords of wind, it specifically moistens the earth, drenching it with waters.
[The root] *undī* means "to moisten";
this is the form of the verb in the Vedic *laṅ* tense.
O Apāṃ Napāt, Savitṛ—the impelling god who belongs to you, who dwells in the middle [region]—knows and understands his station.
From him alone, Savitṛ, the earth (bhūḥ) came into being;
from him alone the atmosphere (rajaḥ), which stands aloft, arose and was born.

1. This is the hymn *ga* 1:2.

It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "He should insert [the verses] beginning with *īṅkhayantīr apsu yuvaḥ* as the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin's portion" (*AiĀ* 5.1.1); it is also prescribed in *ta* 1.2.3.6.7.8 and *ma* 1.4.5.8; and this hymn is prescribed in *ta* 4.5 and *bha* 2.
O Indra, you are the overcomer of all born beings—that is, all living creatures—by means of your might, that is, your strength.
Likewise, as such, you have reached all worlds—having attained all places on earth—you have pervaded them from every side.
(The root *bhū* is used here in the sense of "attaining.")
The third hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "Somaḥ," is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
Its seer is Yamī, the daughter of Vivasvat.
Herein, the conduct of those being sacrificed, such as the sacrificers and others, is expounded.
Therefore, this [hymn] has that deity. Thus it is enumerated: "Soma, Yamī, Bhāvavṛtta; it is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
This hymn is for the worship of the deceased.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "For some, [the sacrificial post] is made of Soma-wood; for others, of Uruṇasa-wood; for others, of Udumbara-wood, which satisfies those who have not drunk [Soma]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.10).

Soma purifies himself for some; others sit near him for clarified butter; for those for whom the honey flows forth—to them indeed may he go. 1. Soma purifies himself for some; others sit near him for clarified butter; for those for whom the honey flows forth—to them indeed may he go. 1.
Soma flows clear for certain ancestors;
it flows as a stream for their enjoyment.
Their lineage-descendants recite the Sāmans during the Brahmayajña.
For it is heard [in scripture]: "That Soma purifies for these [ancestors] through the Sāman chants" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.10).
Some other ancestors worship—that is, they approach or partake of—clarified butter (ghṛta), which is sacrificial ghee (ājya). This is the meaning.

The sons and others of these [sages] recite the *yajus* formulas at the time of the *brahmayajña*. There is also a scriptural passage (*śruti*) stating: "The *yajus* formulas are streams of clarified butter.
[This refers to those] from whom [the offerings are made] for the ancestors.
The dative case is used here in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*).

Honey (*madhu*)—meaning *kṣaudra*—flows, meaning it moves swiftly in the form of a stream, for the purpose of enjoyment. For those who study the *Atharvaṇa* mantras for the sake of knowing Brahman, a stream of honey flows for their ancestors.
And thus it is handed down in scripture: “When the Atharvaṇas and Aṅgirasas are streams of honey.
O deceased one, you too should go to—indeed, enter and attain—all those very ones previously mentioned.

Those who are invincible through austerity, those who have won the heavenly light through austerity, and those who have performed great austerity—unto them alone may he go. 2. Through austerity, those who are unassailable; through austerity, those who have seized the heavenly realm; and those who have performed great austerity—unto them indeed may he go. 2.
Those people who, being engaged in austerity such as the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances, become invincible—that is, unassailable by sins;
and those who, through austerity in the form of sacrifices and other means, go to or attain heaven (svarga);

and those who have performed or perform great (mahaḥ) austerity—difficult for others to accomplish—such as the Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, and other rites, or the worship of Hiraṇyagarbha; [they dwell] in those worlds.
O preta, go even to those very same ascetics.

Those who fight in great battles, those heroes who lay down their bodies, or those who give away thousands as sacrificial fees—go even unto them alone. 3. *ye* (those who) | *yudhyante* (fight) | *pradhaneṣu* (in great battles) | *śūrāsaḥ* (the heroes) | *ye* (those who) | *tanutyajaḥ* (lay down their bodies) | *ye* (or those who) | *vā* (or) | *sahasradakṣiṇāḥ* (give thousands as sacrificial fees) | *tān* (them) | *cit* (even) | *eva* (alone) | *api* (unto) | *gacchatāt* (go). 3.
1. With respect to *ga*, there is the "stream of many" (*bahukulyā*); with respect to *bha*, there is the "stream of honey" (*madhukulyā*).
2. By way of its form as *taya-niyama* and so forth.
3. It exists among the worlds of *taya*; it proceeds among the worlds of *bha*.
In battles (*pradhana*). Because wealth (*dhana*) is scattered (*prakīrṇa*) therein, they are called *pradhana*, meaning battles.
In those [battles], the heroic ones (*śūra*) are those possessing valor; they are those who fight the enemies and strike them down.

And those who have cast off their bodies, having abandoned their physical forms there; or those who are givers of a thousand-fold sacrificial fees, having performed sacrifices accompanied by a thousand fees—
enter into yourself along with all of them.
The meaning is: "Attain that world in which those [sages] dwell in the highest worlds."
Even those who were formerly followers of the *ṛta*, performers of deeds, and increasers of the *ṛta*—those fathers who are full of fervor—to them indeed let him go. 4.
To those very ancestors who were ancient observers of *ṛta*, possessors of *ṛta*, increasers of *ṛta*, and full of fervor—let him go even unto them. 4.

O Yama, go forth to those very ancestors who were performers of *ṛta*—those men of old who touched *ṛta*, that is, truth or sacrifice; who for that very reason were possessors of *ṛta*, joined with *ṛta*, and increasers of *ṛta*; and who were endowed with austerity (*tapas*). To them, O self-controlled one, do you go.
O Yama, may those seers who possess a thousand paths and who protect the sun,
and who are rich in austerity— may you go to them, for you are born of austerity.
The poets with their thousandfold songs who protect the sun—the seers born of fervor—may he go even unto them who are rich in ascetic heat. 5.

O Yama, go to those seers who possess a thousand songs, a thousand eyes, who are poets of far-reaching vision, who protect and guard that Sun, the Āditya—those who are ascetic, endowed with austerity, born from austerity itself; O self-controlled one, enter into them.
The fourth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "arāyi," is the seer-poem of Śirimbiṭha, the son of Bharadvāja; it is composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
Through recitation, burnt offerings, and other rites, this hymn brings about the destruction of snakes.
In this hymn, the deity of the first and last verses is indeed the rat.
The second and third [verses] belong to Bṛhaspati;
the fifth belongs to the Viśvedevas.

For it is recited in sequence: “*Arāyi*, *Śirimbiṭha*; the descendant of Bharadvāja [composed] the destroyer of misfortune (*alakṣmīghna*); the second and third [verses] belong to Bṛhaspati, and the last belongs to the Viśvedevas.”
The application is concluded.
O one-eyed, deformed Arāyī, you who ever pursue us, go to the mountain!
With the powers of Śirimbiṭha, we strike you down and drive you away.
O Arāyī, one-eyed, hideous, ever-seeking Sadānvā! Go to the mountain! We drive you away with the powerful, leaping dogs of Śirimbiṭha. 1.

O Arāyi, you who do not give, you who oppose giving; O one-eyed one, you who make contemptible sounds or have a contemptible appearance; O Vikaṭā, you of deformed gait or deformed limbs; O Sadānvā, you who always follow after, you who constantly revile—the deity of famine and such—you go to the mountain, to a desolate region!
Do not afflict us!
[This is] of Śirimbiṭha.
The *biṭha* is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). It perishes.
Those gods and ancestors.
"Viṭe antarikṣe": Śirimbiṭha is the cloud.
With its *sattvas*—the waters existing within it—with those various [waters], we drive you away; we cause you to perish.
Or alternatively:
"O Alakṣmī, by means of those various virtuous deeds performed by this son of Bharadvāja known as Śirimbaṭha, we destroy you.
Depart from here at once and go to the mountain!"
Driven away from here, driven away from there, you have fled from all the embryos; O Brahmaṇaspati, with your sharp sting, strike down the Arāyī!
Driven away from here! Driven away! The immortal one! All embryos! The Aruṣī! The Arāyī! O Brahmanaspati, with your sharp horns, go forth, driving them out! 2.
May that ill fortune (*alakṣmī*), having been driven away from this world, be utterly destroyed by us; may she also be driven away and harmed from yonder world.

That ill fortune which destroys all embryos born from the womb and all the sprouts of every herb—she who is *āruṣī*, the slayer, the goddess presiding over famine, the stingy one who gives nothing and opposes the giving of gifts—O *Brahmaṇaspati*, O Lord of the sacred word, O deity of sharp horns and sharp splendor, drive her out from this place, cast her forth, and go!
O you of evil intent, seize that raft which floats upon the far shore of the river, devoid of men; by means of it, go to the further bank.
That wood which floats on the far shore of the river, devoid of men—that do thou seize, O Durhaṇo! O Durhaṇo! Go with it to the furthermost distance. 3.

That wooden [image] of Puruṣottama, a divine body made of wood, which exists in a distant place—devoid of a person (*apūruṣa*), meaning lacking a creator-man—and which floats upon the water on the far shore of the ocean (*sindhoḥ pāre*), O you who are difficult to strike (*durhaṇo*), O invincible one, O singer, take hold of it! Grasp it; that is to say, worship it. By means of that wooden deity being worshipped, go to the most excellent, transcendent (*parastaram*), and supreme Vaiṣṇava world.
Another says:

O Durhaṇo—O you who are difficult to strike, or O you who are possessed of a wicked blow—O Alakṣmi! On the far shore of the ocean, at the edge of the sea-coast, there is a wooden vessel (*āru*) made of wood that floats, devoid of men (*apūruṣa*), situated in a region far from us. Grasp that wood;
having grasped it, impelled by Brahmaṇaspati, go to another island by means of that wood, which is *parastaram*—exceedingly easy to cross.
On the sixth day, at the third pressing during the recitation of the Brahman-śastra, this verse "yad vā prācīḥ" is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The [verses] beginning with 'kapṛn', 'aro', 'yad vā prācīḥ', and 'jagant' are these [to be used]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.3).
Or rather, the ancient enemies of the moving world have been cast into the cauldron of molten iron;
all the foes of Indra have been offered as oblations, their very essence reduced to ashes.
