When they rushed forward toward the chest, those foul-smelling ones, the enemies of Indra, were all offered as oblations, their speed like that of bubbles. 4.

He [sees] those women who, like *maṇḍūra* (rust), produce contemptible sounds; or rather, those who hold (*dhāraṇī*) the wealth of the dull-witted (*mandana*), being themselves unperceivable (*alabhya*). The root *ur* has the sense of "to injure.
From this, by the rule *kip ca*, the suffix *kip* is applied, followed by the elision of *r* according to the rule *rāl lopaḥ*.
Thus, this form [is derived] in the nominative plural (*jasi*).
*Hiṃsiyaḥ*:
1. *ta* 1.2.3.6.7.8-bha 1.4.8—also from this;
2. *ta* 5—like a frog (*maṇḍūka*).
You, being *prācīḥ*—that is, having gone forth pre-eminently (*prakarṣeṇa*) and having proceeded excellently (*prakṛṣṭa-gamanāḥ*)—indeed (*yaddha*), when you went (*ajaganta*).
In the middle plural form *gameḷanti*, there is the Vedic substitution of *śap* for *ślu*.
By the rule "tasanasanatanāśca," there is the replacement of *ta* for that [suffix]. Precisely because of this, due to the absence of a short vowel, the elision of the *anusvāra* does not occur.
At that very moment, all the enemies of Indra became as swift as bubbles;
"yāḥ" means those which go (yānti),
and "āśavaḥ" means those which move swiftly (aśuvataḥ).
And those who were swift and impetuous,
being of a ruinous disposition, were sacrificed and perished.

These have encompassed the earth; they have encompassed Agni; they have established glory among the gods. Who shall dare to attack them? 5. These have encompassed the earth; they have encompassed Agni; they have established glory among the gods. Who shall dare to attack these? 5.
These gods, all of them, led around the cow— the singular number being used with reference to the species— all the cows of the gods that had been carried off by the Paṇis. They led her about.
The sacrificing Aṅgirases brought him to completion;
then they "honored" (pari-ahaṣata) Agni, meaning they distributed him all around,
establishing him in various places for the sake of sacrifice in the form of the Gārhapatya and other fires.
Having acted thus, they produced—that is, they fashioned—the food (*śravaḥ*) for the gods Indra and others who are to be worshipped.
What enemy, such as an Asura, can dare to overcome—that is, is able to conquer—all these gods? The meaning is: no one at all.
The fifth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “agnim hinvantu naḥ,” is the seerly work of Abhipūtra named Ketu; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and is dedicated to Agni.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “Agni Ketu [is the seer]; it is addressed to Agni, in the Gāyatrī meter.
This hymn is to be recited in the Gāyatrī meter during both the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The hymn 'agnir hinvantu naḥ' and 'pra agnaye vācam' [are used] for Agni" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).

May our prayers impel Agni, the swift courser in the races; through him may we win prize after prize. 1. May our prayers impel Agni, the swift courser in the races; through him may we win prize after prize. 1.
O Agni, may our *dhiyaḥ*—whether they be ritual acts or hymns of praise—*hinvantu*, that is, impel you;
may they incite you toward the sacrifice or cause you to increase. [The root] *hi* [is used] in the senses of "going" and "increasing."
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as warriors urge on a swift horse—one that is fast-moving and characterized by its habit of running—in battles, that is, in combats;
likewise, through that Agni, may we conquer *dhanadhanaṃ*, that is, all wealth.
O Agni, by that aid of yours through which we bring hither the cattle with our army—that, do you impel for us, for the winning of wealth. || 2 ||
O Agni, by that protection (*ūti*) of yours which is accompanied by this army— or which takes the form of an army— with which we bring the cattle before us (i.e.,
obtain them), lead that very protection toward us. Send it to us.
For what purpose? "Maghattaye," for the sake of giving wealth;
that is to say, for our acquisition of wealth.
In the Ābhilāvika Ukthya, for the Śastra, the triplet beginning with "āgne sthūram" is an optional *anurūpa* verse.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ā te vatsaḥ... agne sthūraṃ rathi bhara" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.8).
O Agni, bring us a sturdy chariot, broad, rich in cattle and horses; turn hither the swift, full, and well-filled one.
1. Those whose intellects are [fixed] on the Truth;
2. for the sake of gain. O Agni! Bring us solid wealth—vast, consisting of cattle and horses. Eat [the oblation]; turn the wheel; make it full. 3.

O Agni, bring to us— that is, bestow upon us— wealth that is solid, massive, grown great, broad and extensive, rich in cattle, endowed with horses, and consisting of chariots. Fill the firmament— that is, the intermediate space— with the waters of rain.
Or rather:
"With your own splendors, uphold [us]—that is, illuminate us.
Drive away the Paṇi, the merchant, the Atātāra, or the Asura; cast them out from here."
Or rather:
"Engage in giving!

O Agni, you have caused the sun, the unaging constellation, to ascend in the sky, bestowing light upon the people. 4 O Agni, the unaging constellation; you have caused the sun to ascend in the sky, bestowing light upon the people. 4.
O Agni, [this is] starless.
It is called a *nakṣatra* because it constantly approaches (*nakṣati*) or moves;
[from the root] *nakṣ*, "to go. [From the root] *am*.

May Indra, together with the Ādityas, fashion for us the sacrifice, our body, and our offspring. (2) And may Indra, together with the Ādityas—the sons of Aditi—fashion for us (*naḥ*) the sacrifice (*yajñam*), such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others; our body (*tanvam*); and our offspring (*prajām*), such as sons and so forth. May he ordain (*cīklṛpāti*) that the sacrifice and the rest become capable of their own respective functions.

May Indra, together with his host of Maruts and the Ādityas, be the protector of our bodies (or offspring). With the Ādityas—the sons of Aditi, such as Mitra and others—and with the Maruts, may Indra, accompanied by his host, be the protector and guardian of our bodies or of our children.

Having slain the Asuras, when the gods went forth, the gods, guarding their godhood. (4) "Having slain"—the gods, Indra and the others, having slain—that is, having destroyed—the Asuras, such as Vṛtra and others who were their oppressors; "when they went forth," that is, when they arrived at their own place, then those gods were "guarding their godhood," meaning they were protecting their own immortality on all sides. The sense is that, due to the absence of any obstructors, they established themselves everywhere.

With their powers, they brought the hymn toward them; then indeed, they beheld the vigorous *svadhā* all around. (5) With their powers—that is, with their ritual acts consisting of service—they brought the *arka*, the means of praise, directed toward [the gods] such as Indra; the singers caused it to reach them. As soon as this was done, immediately thereafter, all people beheld all around the vigorous (*iṣirām*), ever-moving *svadhā*, which is the water of rain. Or alternatively: [the gods] behold all around the desirable (*iṣirām*) *svadhā*. This is a term for the ignorant; all the gods behold the food characterized by the oblation. (5)
The seventh hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “sūryo naḥ,” is the seerly composition of Cakṣus, the son of Sūrya; it has Sūrya as its deity and is in the Gāyatrī meter.
Thus it is enumerated: “sūryo naḥ... Cakṣus, [the seer] of Sūrya; [the hymn] belongs to Sūrya, in Gāyatrī. This hymn belongs to the Sauriya-kāṇḍa in the Āśvina-śastra, to be recited after sunrise.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The nine [verses] beginning with 'May the Sun protect us from heaven' and 'Up that Jātavedas'... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.5).
Among the recitations preceding the *śugādāpana* (the taking up of the ladle) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices, this verse 'sūryo naḥ' is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'May the Sun protect us from heaven; salutations to the great ones, salutations to the small ones'... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.4).

May Sūrya protect us from heaven; may Vāta [protect us] from the intermediate space; may Agni [protect us] from earthly beings. (1) Sūrya—the god who impels all or who is beautiful—may he protect *naḥ* (us) from *divaḥ* (heaven), that is, from the celestial world or from those residing in the celestial world. May Vāta, the wind, protect us from the *antarikṣa* (intermediate space), that is, from harm situated in the middle region. Likewise, may Agni, who dwells on the earth, protect *naḥ* (us) from *pārthivebhyaḥ* (earthly beings), that is, from enemies existing upon the earth.
1. [The word] beginning with *gatamaputrādikaṃ*;
2. *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-ma1.2.4.8* read *pratyañcatam*; *ta4-bha7* read *pratyañcatam*; *ta5* reads *pratyañcam*; 3.
*ta-bha-mu* read *gamanaśīlām*.
4. *ga-ma1.2.4.5.8-mu* occurs at a later time; *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha7* occurs at a later time.
5. *ga-ta4-bha-*—this is to be recited:

*joṣā savitur yasya te haraḥ śataṃ sūnṛtārhati | pāhi no dyutaḥ patantyāḥ || 2 ||* *joṣa* (be pleased), *savitur* (O Savitṛ), *yasya* (of whom), *te* (your), *haraḥ* (flaming bolt), *śatam* (a hundredfold), *sūnṛtā* (truthful speech), *arhati* (deserves). *pāhi* (protect), *naḥ* (us), *dyutaḥ* (from the falling lightning). || 2 ||
O Savitṛ, the impeller of all, O Sun, graciously accept this hymn and other offerings from us.
Your *haraḥ*—your radiant energy, which has the nature of seizing [the essence]—is worthy of, or is appropriate for, a hundred *savān*, that is, many sacrifices.
Or alternatively:
He worships by means of illumination and other such acts.
As such, you [protect] us from *dyut*, which is a name for the thunderbolt (*vajra*), as it falls— that is, as it is restrained— being hurled at us by our enemies.
Protect and guard Śakrā as she shines from her weapon.

May the god Savitṛ grant us sight; may Parvata also grant us sight; may Dhātṛ bestow sight upon us. 3. Sight. For us. The god. Savitṛ. Sight. For us. Also. Parvata. Sight. Dhātṛ. May he bestow. Upon us. 3.
May Savitṛ, the impelling deity, [grant] us sight—the illuminating faculty—and the senses.

Yonder sun has risen; this fortune of mine has risen. Knowing that, I, the unconquerable one, have overcome my husband, O Brahmins. (1) Yonder sun has risen; this fortune of mine has risen. Knowing that, I, the unconquerable one, have overcome my husband. Yonder sun, situated in the heavenly world, has risen—that is, attained its rising. My own fortune (*bhaga*), which is to be honored, or Indra himself in the form of the sun, has risen. Or rather, my own good fortune has risen. Knowing that—the splendor of the rising sun—or having obtained my husband, I, being especially victorious (*vipāsahiḥ*), have overcome [my rivals]; "rivals" is the word understood. This is a form of the aorist of the root *sah*, meaning to overcome. Or rather, being the conqueror of my rivals (*viprāsahiḥ*), I have overcome my husband. I have acted so that he remains long under my control alone.

By means of that oblation (*havis*), Indra became my sustainer (*bhartā*); having performed his deeds, he became the doer of actions and likewise possessed of splendor (*yumnī*). *Yumna* refers to shining glory or a radiant limb.

That by which one becomes possessed of the highest and most excellent oblation— O gods, O praisers, O officiating priests, this very oblation has been prepared; let it be performed by you who seek victory.
Alternatively:
O gods who are to be sacrificed to, this oblation is yours, and I too am [present].
[The form is derived from] the root *kṛ* with the suffix *luṅ*; after the augment *iṭ*, by the rule *mantra ghasa...* (Pāṇini 2.4.80), there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *cli*.
For this very reason, I indeed became, or was, *asapatnā*—that is, truly free from enemies (*śatru*);
the short vowel is used here according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Without rivals, slayer of rivals, victorious, all-surpassing—
may I seize the splendor of others, just as one takes the wealth of those who are weaker.
Without rivals, slayer of rivals, victorious, all-surpassing—may I seize the splendor of others, like the wealth of those who have settled elsewhere. 5.
"I shall be without rivals, without those who seek to devour me.
From where [does this come]? To this he says: "Without rivals..."
Of this intense, most exhilarating [Soma], drink! Unyoke your two bay horses here from all enemies, O Indra! Let not other sacrificers detain you; these pressed juices are for you alone. 1.
Of this Soma, which is intense, sharp, quickly intoxicating, and capable of being consumed— *vayaḥ* being a name for food— of him whose food consists of such things as the *caru* and the *puroḍāśa*.
The rule "the mention of *kriyā* (action) must be made" applies here; because the object (*karman*) functions as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.
O Indra, drink—drink the Soma here.
The absence of the *śap* suffix after the root *pibati* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
For that purpose, unyoke here in this sacrificial hall the two bay horses, the steeds of the chariot whose nature is to move everywhere; release them from the chariot.
O Indra, let other sacrificers—not us—never cause you to rest;
the meaning is that we alone shall cause you to rest.
Therefore, for you and for your sake alone, these pressed juices—these *soma*s being directly perceived—are present.
For you the pressed juices, for you the songs—having been pressed and having been drunk—are brought to you as things to be heard.
O Indra, enjoying everything today, you who know all, drink the soma here.

For you are the pressed juices; for you indeed are those yet to be pressed. To you the resonant songs, worthy of being heard, cry out, O Indra. Taking pleasure in all this today, knowing everything, drink the Soma here. O Indra, for you alone are all the Somas that have been pressed, and for you indeed are those yet to be pressed—[the suffix *tvat* is used here in the sense of the future passive participle (*kṛtyārthe*)]. And the resonant songs, the words in the form of hymns, flowing swiftly and continuously, cry out toward you alone. O Indra, taking pleasure in this pressing—the morning pressing and so forth—at this time, you who know all things, drink the Soma here in this sacrifice.
Whosoever, desiring the gods, presses the Soma for him with a longing mind and with his whole heart—for him Indra does not give up his cattle; he makes that [Soma-presser] famous and dear.

He who, with a longing and desiring heart—meaning one whose entire heart is undivided—or rather, with the heart of all the officiating priests (the possessive sense being implied by the context), with a mind full of devotion, the sacrificer, desiring the god Indra, presses out and extracts the Soma for this Indra. Indra does not give away the cattle of that sacrificer; "giving away" here means destruction, and he does not destroy them. For this sacrificer, he makes the wealth truly beautiful, and therefore praiseworthy; the word *itaḥ* is used for emphasis, meaning he makes it only praiseworthy wealth.
Among these, he remains unperceived by him who, though wealthy, does not press Soma for him;
Maghavan casts that man down into the pit and slays his haters of sacred knowledge without being entreated.
He becomes unperceived. This is his [nature]: he who, though wealthy, does not press Soma for him—Maghavan places that man in his aratni; he slays the haters of prayer without being directed. 4.

For that sacrificer whose *vepas* (inspired fervor) becomes visible to Indra—that is, comes within the range of his sight—Indra, who is possessed of wealth (*vrevān*), presses the *soma* for that Indra.

Maghavan, endowed with riches, takes that sacrificer by the hand and places him in his own lap; being his protector, he draws him near and holds him fast. And having heard [the call], even though unbidden and unsolicited by him, he slays and destroys the enemies who hate the *brahman* (the haters of the sacred word).
At the Śunāsīrīya festival, for the offering "a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra Śunāsīra," the verse "aśvāyantaḥ" serves as the *yājyā*.
Alternatively, even for an offering made with a deficient mantra such as "Indro vā śunaḥ," this same *yājyā* is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Desiring horses, desiring cattle, desiring booty, let us invoke the auspicious Maghavan Indra" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.20).
Desiring horses, desiring cattle, and desiring booty, we call upon you to come to us.
May they be present in your new favor; O Indra, may we invoke you for our welfare.
Desiring horses, desiring cattle, desiring booty, we call upon you to come hither; O Indra, adorning ourselves for your new and gracious favor, may we invoke you for our prosperity. 5.
*vaśvāyantaḥ*: desiring horses for themselves; in some places, [the form] *aśvāghasyāt* occurs according to Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.37. *gavyantaḥ*: desiring cows for themselves.
The substitution of *ava* [for *ava-ja*] is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.79: *vānto yi pratyaye*.
*Vvājayantaḥ* means "kindling the fires with fuel (*vāja*) such as winnowing baskets (*śūrpa*) and so forth.
[The root] *vā* is used in the sense of "motion" and "perfuming."
In the case of the causative (*ṇic*), the augment *jug* is added by Pāṇini’s rule 7.3.38, "vo vidhūnane.

From this [root], when the suffix *śatṛ* is applied, the vowel becomes unaccented (*anudātta*) due to the accent of the upadeśa and the *sārvadhātuka* affix; furthermore, because the *śap* is also unaccented due to being *pit*, the accent of the *ṇic* itself remains as the final residue.
Another teacher says:
"Desiring *vāja*, that is, food, for ourselves"— in this case,
the absence of the avagraha and the accentuation should be understood as Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Being such as we are, O Indra, we call upon you, we invoke you, in order to approach you, to reach you.
In the word *game*, the suffix *tave* is applied according to the rule *tum-arthe seseṇa*.

In the compound with a *gati* particle, by the rule *tave cāntaś ca yugapat*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the *gati* is retained and the final syllable of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is acute-accented (*antodātta*).
The syllable *vu* is a filler (*pūraka*).

O Indra, in your new, praiseworthy, and auspicious favor— or in your beautiful wisdom— we abide, honoring you on all sides; or rather, performing worship on every side while remaining within your benevolent thought, may we invoke you, the bringer of happiness, for our well-being.
The fifteenth hymn, "Muñcāmi," is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Yakṣmanāśana, the son of Prajāpati.
The first verse is an *anuṣṭubh*, while the remaining verses are *triṣṭubhs*.
Since no specific deity is indicated, Indra is the presiding deity.
And so it has been handed down: "I release [thee]; [this is] a *prājāpatya* [verse], a destroyer of consumption (*yakṣman*), [addressed to] *rājyakṣma*, in the *antyānuṣṭubh* meter.
For the purpose of pacifying the multitude of diseases, headed by heart disease, one should offer oblations with this hymn (*sūkta*).

For it is prescribed: "For one who is diseased, afflicted, or seized by consumption, an offering of *palā* [wood] is made with the verse 'I release thee' (*muñcāmi*) and the oblation (*svāhā*) for the sake of life" (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* 3.6.4–5).
I release you by means of this oblation so that you may live, from *karmayakṣma* and from *rājayakṣma*.
If *grāhi* has seized him, O Indra and Agni, release him from her.
I release you with an oblation so that you may live—both from the unknown wasting disease and from the royal consumption. If the seizer has seized him, O Indra and Agni, release him from her! 1.

1. ta1.2.3.6.7-8-°anudātte; ta4.5-°anudāttaṃ | 2. ta-bha-mu-°danudāttatvaṃ | 3. ta-bha-īrānīm | 4. ga-bhara-śobhanabuddhau anugrahabuddhau | 5. ga-ta4.5-ayarogapramukhasya | 6. tara2.3.4.5.6.8-bha-vyādhi- tasyādhitasya | ka.:4-54 O you who are overcome by *yakṣma*, [I address] you with this oblation (*havis*), by means of this *caru* and the sacrificial offering (*homana*), from *ajñātayakṣmāt*. Now, *ajñātayakṣmā* is an unknown disease located in the body, being unrecognizable as to its specific name.
I release—that is, I separate—him from such a disease.
For what purpose? For the sake of life; that is, for the purpose of living.
The meaning is: for the sake of remaining in this world for a long time. "Ka" is a filler [particle]. "Uta" means "and also," [referring to] from consumption (rājayakṣman).
*Rājayakṣmā* is the king of wasting diseases (*yakṣmaroga*), meaning *yakṣmāṇāṃ rājā*.
The inversion of the subordinate member [of the compound] occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule 2.2.31, beginning with *rājadanta*.
From that [disease] as well, I release myself.

Or if, at this very moment, some deity—seizing by nature, possessing the form of a *graha*, and having seized him—has taken hold of this sick man, then from that deity, O Indra and Agni, release him completely.

Whether his life-span has been exhausted, or whether he has departed, or even if he has been brought into the very presence of Death—I bring him back from the lap of Destruction, that he may be uninjured for a hundred autumns. yadi kṣitāyuḥ | yadi vā parāitaḥ | yadi mṛtyoḥ antikaṃ nīta eva | tam ā harāmi nirṛter upasthāt | aspārṣam enaṃ śataśāradāya || 2 ||

If he is seized by disease, if his life-span is exhausted or his vitality has waned, if he has departed from this world and gone to the hereafter, and if he has indeed been led—utterly brought—into the presence of Death, the son of Vivasvat; even such a person as this, I bring back from the presence, from the vicinity of Nirṛti, the goddess of evil who causes the decay of life. Having brought him back, I make him strong and robust for a life of a hundred autumns, for the sake of living a hundred years.
(The root *sṛp* signifies both "to please" and "to strengthen.")

With an oblation that has lasted for a hundred autumns, providing a hundredfold life-span, I have brought this thousand-eyed one hither, so that Indra may lead him for a hundred autumns to the further shore of all misfortune. sahasrākṣam | śataśāradena | śatāyuṣā | haviṣā | ā | ahārṣam | enam | śatam | yathā | imam | śaradaḥ | nayāti | indraḥ | viśvasya | duritasya | pāram || 3 ||
"Sahasrākṣam" (the thousand-eyed).
"Sahasra" is a name for "many. That which has a thousand eyes—that is, eyes as the fruit of the oblation—is "sahasrākṣam."
In the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the suffix *pac* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 5.4.113 (*bahuvrīhau savathyakṣṇoḥ*).
A year related to autumn is *śārada*. That which possesses a hundred autumns is thus described [as *śataśārada*].
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member [is maintained].

For this very reason, it means "by such an oblation" (*haviṣā*) as that which has as its fruit a lifespan (*āyuḥ*) consisting of a hundred years, or a life-measure of one hundred years. Alternatively:
Indra is the thousand-eyed one.

By means of that [oblation] which pertains to a hundred autumns— that is, by means of its being the giver of a hundred years, and by means of the oblation (*havis*) characterized by a lifespan of a hundred years as the instrument—
[the priest] has drawn this [victim] out from the seizure of the *yakṣma* disease.

In whatever manner, by which means, Indra may lead this person for a hundred autumns— that is, for a hundred years (the accusative case is used here to denote duration)— to the further shore, the end, the freedom from suffering of all, of every misfortune (*durita*), that [means] must be sought; such is the meaning.
Live for a hundred autumns, increasing in strength; live for a hundred winters and a hundred springs.
May Indra, Agni, Savitṛ, and Bṛhaspati restore this man to life with a hundred-year oblation.
1. By means of the *sādhana-homa* (the oblation for accomplishment) [ta-bha1.2.4.8].
2. By this [means], it receives that name [ta-bha1.2.4.8].
3. Human (*mānuṣa*: ta1.2.3.7, ma1.2.4.8; *manuṣya*: bha7).
4. From the attendance upon the burden of Ga-ta4.5, there is the attainment of peace (sarmāpāt).
5. By this [person] who is like Ga-ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha; by Ta4.5, it is "by this one who is like that" (tādṛśamanena). 6.
From Ga-na4.5-bhara, there is indeed no taking up of disease (rogādanaiva); from Ta1.2.3.6.7, it is "only the taking up of disease" (rogādānaiva).

Released from consumption and increasing—attaining growth day by day—may you live for a hundred autumns; that is, maintain your life-breaths for a period numbering one hundred autumn seasons. As before, the accusative case is used here to denote duration.
Live for a hundred winters and for a hundred springs.

The word *u* signifies a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Furthermore, may Indra and Agni, Savitṛ the impelling god, and Bṛhaspati—the protector of the great gods—being gratified by the oblation which is the cause of a hundred-year lifespan, grant this person back to us again and again.
I have called you; I have found you. You have returned, O ever-new one!
O you who possess all limbs, I have found for you your entire sight and your full span of life.
I have called you back; I have found you. You have come back again, renewed. O you who are whole in every limb, I have found for you your entire sight and your entire lifespan. (5)

"Seized by disease, I have brought you here; I have rescued you from the presence of Death. Therefore, I have found you; I have obtained you. O *punarnava*, ever-renewed one, come back again; come once more into our presence."
With all my limbs and every part of my body restored, I have perceived everything of yours; this is a figurative expression meaning that I have regained the entire collection of my sense faculties.
I have found all of your life and existence in its entirety.
"Brahmāgni": this consists of six hymns, eleven verses in total, in the Anuṣṭubh meter. The seer is named Rakṣohā, the son of Brahmā.
Since it teaches the protection of the embryo in the form of the pacification of miscarriages, this is a hymn for that purpose.
And it has been recited: “With six [verses] by Brahmā, the Brāhma [sūkta]; the Rakṣohā [is used] for the expiation of miscarriage; it is indeed Ānuṣṭubha.
The application [of these verses] is to be understood from their indicative power (*liṅga*).
May Agni, acting in concert with Brahmā, the slayer of demons,
drive away from here whatever disease is in your womb or whatever ill-formed thing lies within your birth-place.
May Agni, acting in concert with Brahmā, the slayer of demons, drive away from here the disease that, bearing an evil name, lies within your womb and your embryo. 1.
In harmony with the *brahman* mantra—that is, having attained unanimity—may Agni, the slayer of *rakṣases*, drive away and destroy the *rakṣasas* and other obstructors from this place.
As for that *rakṣasa* who, being in the form of disease (*amīvā*), lies within your womb (*āśaye*):
[the *t* is elided by the rule *lopasta ātmanepadeṣu*].
He attains the power to destroy.
*Durmāmā* is a disease known as *arśas* (hemorrhoids).
Being of that nature, may he afflict him who dwells within your *yoni*—the receptacle for semen, the place of the embryo; such is the syntactical connection.
Whatever disease, whatever evil spirit has settled upon your embryo or your womb—
Agni, together with the sacred prayer (brahman), has driven that flesh-eater away.
The disease that has settled upon your embryo, the foul-named one who dwells in the womb—Agni, together with the sacred prayer (brahman), has driven that flesh-eater away.

1. ga-ta1.6-punarabhinavamutpanna; tara.3-punarabhivamutpanna; ta7-punarabhimamutpanna; bha1.4.8-punar-abhivamutpanna; bhara-punarabhivamutpanna | 2. ta4.5-of the characteristic of the embryo (garbhalakṣaṇa); 3. ta4.5-the embryo seeks a locus (āyatana).

The first half-verse has been explained. May Agni, accompanied by the Brahman, utterly destroy that flesh-eating, meat-consuming being, such as a Rākṣasa. 3. "He who strikes the embryo as it falls, he who [strikes] the one lying within the womb, he who strikes the crawling one, and he who seeks to kill the one already born—him we cause to perish from here. O woman, he who strikes your embryo as it falls (patayantam)—moving in the form of semen into the womb—and thereafter as it lies within the womb (nipastanum); he who strikes the crawling one (sarīsṛpam), meaning the embryo that has reached all its limbs after three months; and he who seeks to kill (jighāṃsati) the infant born after ten months—him we cause to perish from this place. 4. "He who separates your thighs, he who lies between the husband and wife, and he who licks the interior of the womb—him we cause to perish from here. O woman, he who separates your thighs (ūrū), the bases of your feet, for the sake of destroying the embryo; he who lies between the couple (dampatī) for the purpose of killing the fetus; and he who, having entered within, licks the interior of the womb (āreliha), meaning he tastes with his tongue the emitted semen—he we cause to perish from here. (The root *lih* means 'to taste'; it belongs to the Adādi class. The variation in form is according to the *kapilakādi* group. 5. "He who approaches you as a brother, or as a husband, or as a lover; he who seeks to kill your offspring—him we cause to perish from here. O woman, he who—a Rākṣasa or similar being—approaches you (nipadyate) having taken the form of a brother, or the form of a husband (pati), or else taking the form of a lover (jāra), an illicit paramour; and he who seeks to kill your progeny—him we cause to perish from here. The rest is clear. 6. "He who approaches you after deluding you with sleep-inducing darkness; he who seeks to kill your offspring—him we cause to perish from here. He who approaches you after bewildering you with a slumbering darkness (svapnena tamasā); and he who seeks to kill your offspring—him we cause to perish from here. 1. *ta-bha-anīnaśat nāśayat* | 2. *ta4.5-yonijātam* | 3. *ta-bha-nāśayāma* |

That woman, or that demon and so forth, having deluded you—having caused you to fall into a state of confusion—by means of sleep, which is one's own natural state, or by means of darkness, which is slumber, goes to lie down for the purpose of destroying the embryo.
The rest is as before.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "akṣmībhyām," is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
The seer is named Vivaha, born of the Kaśyapa lineage.
Since it treats the destruction of consumption (yakṣman), the entire hymn has that as its deity.
And it has been recited: “With the two eyes, [the sage] Kāyapa [performs] the wedding, [the hymn] that destroys consumption.
This is the application based on indicative marks (*laiṅgika-viniyoga*).
From your two eyes, from your two nostrils, from your two ears, and from your chin— out of your head,
from the brain and from the tongue, I root out the consumption (yakṣman) from you.
From the two eyes, from the two nostrils, from the two ears, from the chin—out from the head, from the brain, from the tongue, I pull away the disease from you. 1.
I root out—that is, I extract—the disease of consumption from your two eyes, which are seized by consumption; the meaning is that I separate it [from you].
By the rule *ī ca dvivacane* (Pāṇini 7.1.77), the word *akṣi* undergoes the substitution of the vowel *ī* at the end;
and that [substituted vowel] is acute.
Likewise, from the two nostrils and from the sense of smell, from the two ears and from the two organs of hearing, and from the chin—that is, from the region below the jaw;
the prefix *adhi* here is meaningless.
Moreover, [he took it] from the head.
A disease occurring in the head is *śīrṣaṇya*.
[The suffix] *yat* is applied by the rule *bhave chandasi*;
furthermore, the substitution of *śīrṣan* for *śiras* occurs by the rule *ye ca taddhite*.
The original form of the word is maintained by the rule *ye cābāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.168).

Such a disease (*yakṣma*) as this, I extract and pull out from your *mastiṣka*— the *mastiṣka* being a specific kind of flesh situated within the head— and from your tongue (*jihvā*), that is, the organ of taste.
The meaning is "I separate.
The verbal root is *vṛh*, meaning "to tear out" or "to extract."
From the neck, from the shoulders, from the vertebrae, and from the spine;
from the forearms and from the upper arms, I drive away the consumption and the disease from you.
From the neck-joints, from the shoulders, from the collarbones, from the spine, from the disease of the forearms, from the upper arms, and from the hands—I drive away your consumption. 2.

From the diseased parts, from the hot, upward-facing, oily, and heated sinews (*snāyu*), from the neck-regions (*grīvā*) and the vessels (*dhamani*) located in the throat—your consumption (*yakṣma*) I root out.
Likewise, from the bones (*kīkasā*) and from the joints of the bones (*anūkyā*), I root out the consumption.
[The root *uc* is used] in the sense of gathering together.
The joint of the bones is called *anukya* because it is joined together (*samaveyate*). [This is derived from the root] *añc* with the suffix *ṇyat* according to the rule *ṛhaloṇyat*;
and by the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* for the *c*.
The svarita accent is elided.
Furthermore, that which pertains to the arms (*doṣas*) is *doṣaṇyam*.
As before, by the rule beginning with “*pada*” and so forth, the word *doḥ* undergoes the substitution of *dops* at its beginning.
The original form remains as before.
I also tear away that very disease (*yakṣma*) from your shoulders (*aṃsau*) and from your arms (*bāhū*).
The hands are the upper parts of the shoulders, and the arms are the lower parts.
From your intestines, from your rectum, from the large intestine, and from the heart;
from your kidneys and from your stomach, I root out consumption for you.
1. In the state of sleep; in the state of sleep. 2. By means of sleep. 3. Non-productive. 4. Of the head. 5. Or. 6. That action also. From the intestines:
from them; from the rectum; from the large intestine; from the heart; from above; the consumption; from the kidneys; from the liver; from the spleen; I pull it away from you. 3.
O you who are overcome by consumption, from your entrails—
from the intestines which serve as the receptacle for food and drink—

from the sinews connected to them, from the rectum, and from those channels through which the essence of food is led to the bodily tissues by the *samāna* wind: from all these, I root out the consumption.
Likewise, from the rectum, from the large intestine, from the heart, and from the lotus of the heart, I tear away the *yakṣman* (consumption/disease).
And also from your two *matasna*s—
*matasna*s are the two kidneys located at the sides, shaped like raw meat.
From those two comes the liver (*yakṛt*).
The liver is a specific type of black flesh located near the heart;
and from that [liver].
By the rule beginning with ‘padanū0’, the substitution of *yaka* for the word *yakṛt* is applied.

From the spleen (*plīhan*), from others as well—namely from those designated as *kloman*, *plīha*, and so forth—and from the flesh, I drive away (*va vṛhāmi*), that is, I expel, the disease *yakṣman*.

From your two thighs, from your two kneecaps, from your two heels, and from your two foreparts; from your two hips and from the pubic region—I root out the disease (yakṣma) from you. 4. From your two thighs, from your two kneecaps, from your two heels, from your two foreparts, from your two hips, and from the pubic region—I root out the disease from you. 4.
O you who are afflicted, I tear away the *yakṣma* from your two thighs, from your two knee-caps, and from your two knees.
Likewise, I tear away the *yakṣma* from your two heels—the rear parts of the feet—and from your two foreparts of the feet;
moreover, I tear away the *yakṣma* from your two hips and from your two buttocks.

Likewise from the buttocks: "buttocks" (bhasat) refers to the region of the hips; because of its connection with that, from the shining buttocks—that is, from the anus—I pull apart your consumption (yakṣma).

From the organ of generation, from the making of wounds, from your body hairs, from your nails—from your entire self—I pull this consumption away from you. 5. From the organ of generation; from the making of wounds; from your body hairs; from your nails; consumption; from the entire self; that; this; away; I pull; from you. 5.
Or because it is the instrument for producing water (*vana*). Water (*vana*) refers to the bodily fluid;
that by which it is produced—that is, emitted—is the "instrument for producing water" (*vanakaraṇa*).
Therefore, from your urine, from your excrement, from your body hair, and even from your nails, I tear away the *yakṣma* disease.
What more need be said?
Now, this very *yakṣma* disease, I tear away from you, from your entire self—that is, from your whole body.

From every limb, from every hair, from every joint, from the entire self—whatever consumption (*yakṣma*) has arisen, that I now pull out from you. (6) From limb after limb, from hair after hair, born at every joint—from the whole body, that [consumption], this I pluck away from you. (6)
From every limb, from all the members, from every hair, and from every joint—the very connection of the members—I pull apart the consumption that has arisen and been produced therein.
This is another [incantation].
1. *ta* 1.2.3.7–*ma* 1.2.8: *tava tvam*. 2. *ta* 1.2.3.1.7: *°rādhārabhūtam*. 3. *ta-bha-mu*: *śarīram*. 4. *bhara*: *saṃdhau saṃdhī*.
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "apehi," has Aṅgirasa Pracetas as its seer (*ārṣam*).
The third verse is a *triṣṭubh*, and the fifth is a *paṅkti*.
The deity is the destroyer of bad dreams.
Thus it is enumerated: "Apehi pañca pracetāḥ; [this hymn] ends with a Paṅkti verse and has a Triṣṭubh in the middle.
The application is based on indicative marks (liṅga).
Depart, O Manasāptī; go away and move forward!
Proclaim far and wide to Nirṛti that the mind of the living man is manifold.
Depart, O Lord of the mind; go away, move forward, proceed ahead for the sake of deliverance from death. Look upon the mind of the living in many ways. 1.

O Lord of the mind, O master of the mind abiding in the state of dreaming, depart from this evil dream; go away, O presiding deity! Depart from me who am in the state of dreaming, and having departed, vanish.
"Cast your feet to go to another land"—
the meaning is, "go to a distant country.
And having departed, "move elsewhere"— that is, dwell as you wish in a remote region beyond.
Moreover, speak to Nirṛti, the goddess of evil, who stands far beyond, saying:
"Do not harm me in vain. For the mind of one who lives becomes manifold, in many ways.
The meaning is: while one is still desirous of many objects to be enjoyed, lead him away from that vision of an evil dream which causes its destruction.
They choose indeed what is auspicious as their boon; they yoke what is auspicious on the right.
Auspicious is the eye in the realm of Vaivasvata, and manifold is the mind of one who lives.
They choose what is auspicious as their boon; they harness the auspicious right hand. Auspicious is the eye in the realm of Vaivasvata; the mind of the living wanders in many places. 2.

All people choose—that is, they pray for—the auspicious (*bhadram*), which is indeed beautiful (*śobhanam*) and the most excellent (*varam*), the desirable fruit consisting of the destruction of evil dreams.
They employ and attain that auspicious and beautiful fruit which has increased through the right path.
In the realm of Vaivasvata—of Yama, the son of Vivasvat—I pray for the auspicious and beautiful eye, that is, for vision.
May Vaivasvata, the presiding deity of bad dreams, not afflict us.
The meaning is: may he grant me only auspicious visions here in this world, characterized by stability.
For my mind dwells upon many things—indeed, upon many objects—as I live.
Whatever desire we have harbored while awake or while sleeping— whether it be harmful,
destructive, or malicious— may Agni cast all those unwelcome misdeeds far away from us.
Whatever curse, lack of hope, imprecation, or offense we have committed while awake or while sleeping—may Agni place all those unpleasant misdeeds far away from us. 3.

Whatever evil we have committed while awake—by means of longing, by expectation, or by desire—while remaining in the state of wakefulness; and whatever we have approached while sleeping—having attained it during the state of sleep;
likewise, whatever evil we might have incurred in these two states through "out-breathing" (the absence of desire) or "in-breathing" (the presence of desire).
May Agni cast all those things—whether they be agreeable or disagreeable, or evil deeds and wicked actions—far away from us; may he remove them and place them in a distant land.

1. ta1.2.3.7-bha1.2.8-vm May we approach the Lord; bha7-may we approach the Lord. O Indra, O Brahmaṇaspati, whatever offense we commit against others, may the wise Aṅgirasa protect us from the enmity and from distress. ||4|| O Indra, O Brahmaṇaspati, whatever offense we commit, may the wise Aṅgirasa protect us from our enemies and from sin. ||4||

O Indra, O Brahmaṇaspati, regarding that which we practice—namely, hostility (*abhidroha*), that is, harmfulness, evil, or a bad dream without cause—within the domain of you two, protect us from this hostility; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Furthermore, may Varuṇa—the descendant of Aṅgiras, accompanied by his kinsmen, the Angirases who are the singers of praise, and the wise one (*pracetāḥ*)—protect us from the sin (*aṃhas*) of our enemies, that is, from the evil committed by those who hate us against us.
Or else: [the same].
A change of case:
"The descendant of Aṅgiras, belonging to the lineage of Aṅgiras, our seer Pracetas.
A change of number.
May he protect me from the sin of those who hate me;
by virtue of the context, it is understood that "he" refers to Indra.

We have conquered; we have sat [in the seat of victory]; we have become free from sin. May that evil intention which we harbor while waking or sleeping reach him whom we hate; may it reach him who hates us. (5) We have conquered; today we have sat; we have become free from sin. We are sinless. The evil intention during waking or sleep—may it reach him whom we hate; may it reach him who hates us. (5)
Then at this time we have conquered;
we have become victors over all that was to be conquered because the evil dream has been destroyed.
Immediately thereafter, we have eaten and we have shared out what was to be shared.
Thus we have been innocent and without fault.

May that evil intention—which pertains to both the waking and dreaming states, which is of the nature of sin and the fruit of sin, and which is the determination of a bad dream—reach and seize that enemy whom we hate;
and may it reach and seize him who hates us.
"O Gods" (*devāḥ*): this is the fourteenth hymn, consisting of five verses; it is the seer's work of Kapota, the son of Nirṛti, composed in the Triṣṭubh metre, and addressed to the Viśvedevas.
Thus it is enumerated: "The son of Nirṛti, Kapota [is the seer]; [it is used] as an expiation when a pigeon enters [the house], and it is addressed to the Viśvedevas.
If a pigeon should enter the house, then one should offer oblations with this hymn.

For it is stated in the Sūtra: "If a dove should enter the house and alight upon it, one should offer a sacrifice or recite the mantra 'O gods, the dove... (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.7.7) according to the specific occasion."

O gods, since the dove, sent as a messenger by Nirṛti, has come here seeking [us], let us offer worship to him, making amends; may there be well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds. O gods, since the dove, sent as a messenger by Nirṛti, has come here seeking [us], let us offer worship to him, making amends; may there be well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds. (1)

O gods, this dove has arrived, sent as a messenger and follower of Nirṛti, the goddess of evil; since it has come to and reached this house of ours, uttering cries of distress and seeking to cause harm, we offer worship to that source of affliction for the sake of averting that harm.
We honor you with an oblation.
Then, providing atonement—that is, effecting the removal of the fault arising from the dove's entry—may you grant us deliverance.
By this offering of oblations, let us perform [this rite].
Therefore, may there be well-being and happiness for our two-footed children, and may there be well-being and happiness for our four-footed [animals], such as cows, horses, and so forth.
1. [The reading] *saṃbandhaḥ* (in manuscripts ta1.2.3.7) and *saṃbandhavaḥ* (in manuscript bha1.2.4.8); [the reading] *anu-* (in manuscript bha7). 2. This is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). 3.
[The reading] *putrādye* (in manuscripts ga, ta4.5).
May the dove sent by Śiva be auspicious for us; O gods, may this bird be harmless in our homes.
May the wise Agni accept our oblation, and may the destructive weapon of the woodpecker spare us.

May Śiva be auspicious; may the dove be harmless to us, O gods. May the bird in our house be innocent. Let Agni, the inspired sage, accept our oblation. May the destructive weapon with its sharp beak avoid us. 2.

O gods, that bird known as a pigeon (*kapota*), which has entered our houses, is auspicious (*śiva*), a source of happiness, a forest-dweller, and a bringer of sinlessness. For since the wise Agni accepts the oblation (*havis*) prepared for you by us, may he—being pleased—cause this winged missile (*heti*), the cause of slaughter, to avoid us; let it leave us alone.
May it not afflict us.
The weapon of the pigeon does not harm; it makes its station in the fire-chamber as if in a nest.
May there be well-being for our cattle and for our men; O gods, let the pigeon not injure us here.

The missile, the winged one—let it not harm us. It makes its footprint in the dwelling place, in the fire-chamber. May there be peace for our cattle and for our men; let the dove not injure us here, O gods. 3.
May the pigeon, which possesses wings like a bird of prey and is the cause of destruction, not strike us nor harm us.
In the vast forest, in a place fit for the maintenance of the sacred fire—where fire is brought and established—it makes its dwelling;
that is, it intends to dwell in that very spot.
Alternatively, "aśvatthasmin" refers to the *āṣṭrī*, that is, the kitchen;
[it means] in that [kitchen].
In the place where the cooking fire is brought—that is, in that location where he places his foot—he sets down his step.
May there be no harm caused by that for us; such is the meaning.
Moreover, may there be well-being (*śam*) for our cattle and for our men—well-being being either happiness or the pacification of censurable defects.
O gods, this dove has entered this house; may it not harm us. By your grace, may it not cause us distress.
That which the owl speaks is in vain, as is that which the pigeon places its foot in the fire;
to him whose messenger this has been sent—to that Yama, to Death, let there be homage!

That which the owl utters is in vain; that which the pigeon makes its footprint in the fire is likewise vain. He who has sent forth this as his messenger—to that Yama, to Death, let there be homage. 4.

Let the owl—the bird known as *ghūka*—that speaks or utters inauspicious things, indicating them by its own cry, be fruitless and ineffective. And let the dove (*kapota*) that makes its footprint (*pada*) within the fire-chamber (*agni*), that is, inside the house, also be fruitless and devoid of power. Let the dispatched messenger, the dove, who becomes the servant and attendant of this master, be an offering of salutation (*namaḥ*) unto Death (*mṛtyu*), the slayer, for his destruction.

1. *Ta* and *Bha* do not have *yadvā*. 2. *Ta* and *Bha* read *padā nidhānam*. 3. *Ta* and *Bha* read *tasya*. 4. *Ga₂* reads *yamāya*. 5. *Ga*, *Ta₄*, *Ta₅* do not have *yamāya*. 6. *Ta₁*, *Ta₂*, *Ta₃*, *Ta₆*, *Ta₇*, *Ta₈* read *etannāmakāya*;

*Ta₄*, *Ta₅* read *evam*. With a verse, drive away the dove; gladdening yourselves with food, drive it out. Enclosing it on all sides, ward off all misfortunes. Having left us strength, let it fly away, flying farthest away.

With a verse: Drive away the dove, drive it far away! Rejoicing in the food, lead the cow around us. Warding off all misfortunes, let the most swift bird fly away from us, leaving behind our nourishment. 5.
O gods, being praised with *ṛc* verses and mantras, do you drive away—the one to be driven forth, to be cast out—the dove, that bird, from this house; expel it.
Likewise, rejoicing (*madantaḥ*), exhilarated by the oblations given by us, bring to us food (*iṣam*) and a cow;
may I be the slayer of rivals (*sapatnahā*), the destroyer of enemies.
Just as Indra is indeed inviolable by anyone, so may I also be most excellent, inviolable, powerful, and foremost.
May all these visible rivals be placed beneath my feet, trampled under my two feet.
Right here I bind you both like the two bowstrings of a bow; O Lord of Splendor, restrain these [words] so that I may speak what is lower than myself.
Right here I bind both of you, like two bowstrings. O Lord of Speech, restrain these [words] so that they shall speak lower than me.

In whatever region you dwell, O rivals, right there— in this very place— I bind you fast with fetters, like two bow-ends joined by two cords. Thus ends the sixteenth hymn, consisting of four verses, beginning with "This for you," composed by Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni, in the Jagatī meter, addressed to Indra.

The verse beginning with “somasya rājñaḥ” is the third [verse] of this group; its deities are those mentioned by their indicative marks (liṅga), namely Varuṇa, Vidhātṛ, Anumati, Dhātṛ, Soma, Bṛhaspati, and Iti.

Thus it has been enumerated: “This group of four, beginning with ‘tubhyedam,’ belongs to Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni; it is in the Jāgata meter, and the third verse has as its deity those mentioned by their indicative marks.
The meaning of the word “vā” (or) is that, according to another view, Indra alone is the deity and the others are merely recipients of the oblation (nipātabhāj).
The application has been explained.
For you, O Indra, this honey is poured out; you are the lord of the pressed vessel.
Bestow upon us wealth consisting of many heroes; as the scorcher, you have conquered and won the light of heaven.

For you, O Indra, this honeyed mead is poured out; you are the lord of the pressed soma in the beaker. Bestow upon us wealth with many heroes; you, having scorched the scorcher, have won the light of heaven. 1.
O Indra, this honey characterized by Soma is for you; for your sake,
I have now commenced this praise and hymn today.

O Dhātṛ, O god named Dhātṛ; O Vidhātṛ, O god named Vidhātṛ—permitted by you both, I have consumed the *kalaśas*, that is, the portions of Soma remaining after the oblation which were situated in the *kalaśa* vessels.

At the birth [of your son], you made me your food even as I was cutting; and now, O Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni, since I have come before you with this gift at the sacrifice, I first release this hymn for you both. May I be free from harm through this favor toward you.

Impelled, I have performed the consumption [of the Soma]; I have offered this hymn as the first patron in the sacrifice. When I came to you both at the pressing with a gift, O Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni, I released [the Soma] in your dwelling. 4.

O Indra, impelled by you, I have prepared the *bhakṣa*—the portion to be consumed or the oblation—at this sacrifice characterized by the two movements (*cara*) or the two feet; I have performed this for your sake. As the foremost, the excellent singer (*sūri*), I cleanse and prepare this hymn (*stoma*) for you;
that is to say, I utter it.
Now Indra, being in an intermediate form (*antarāmarūpa*), addresses even the two seers of the hymn, saying:

"O Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni, when I come at the time when the Soma has been pressed in your house—the sacrificial hall—then you two should perform the praise, together with the wealth that is to be shared. This is the meaning.
The hymn beginning with “vātasya,” consisting of four verses, is the seventeenth hymn; it is composed by Anila of the Vāta lineage, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and has Vāyu as its deity.
Thus it is enumerated: “vātasya; [the seer] Anila, [born of] Vātāyana, [addresses] the Vāyavya [hymn]. Its ritual application (viniyoga) has been explained.
Now, the greatness of the wind’s chariot: its thundering sound goes forth, shattering [the world].
Reaching to the sky, it makes the young plants sprout; scattering the dust of the earth, it moves onward.
Now, the greatness of Vāta’s chariot—crushing [the earth], it goes; its thundering sound touches the sky. It moves, making the regions ruddy, and it goes scattering the dust of the earth. 1.
I now quickly proclaim the greatness—the majesty—of Vāta’s chariot, which is by nature swift-moving.
The roar of this Vāta, producing a threefold sound within mountain caves and other places, goes forth, shattering and pervading the entire world of both the stationary and the moving.
And that Vāta, touching and pervading the sky, proceeds while making the intermediate quarters of the directions assume their various forms and turn ruddy.
Moreover, casting up—that is, seizing and scattering everywhere—the dust, the soil of the earth, he goes;
for this very reason, it is said that "he makes [the paths] ruddy."
They are impelled along the paths of the wind; they go toward him as women go to a festival.
With them, the god travels on a single chariot, he who is the king of this entire world.
The manifestations of the wind rush forth; they go toward him like women to a festival. Yoked with them on the same chariot, the god speeds along, the king of this entire world.
The mountains and other things situated specifically (*viṣṭhāḥ*) move together toward the quality of the wind (*vātasya guṇam saṃ prerate*);
that is to say, they tremble in the direction toward which the wind blows. Just as in a battle (*samanam na*), so do the mares (*yoṣāḥ*), the female horses, go toward the wind.
With those mares, Vāyu— the shining one— goes forth, mounting his own chariot, which is yoked by himself alone and is a single common vehicle for all. (The root *iṅ* means "to go.")
He becomes the king, the master, of all this entire world—that is, of the multitude of beings who partake in the second transformation [of matter].
Or rather:
just as passionate women approach a man created for union, so do women in the form of trees, shrubs, and the like, approach Vāyu.
"With them, the god goes along with his chariot, together with his chariot."
Holding the earth in the intermediate space, he does not settle down; what indeed has he said?
The first-born friend of the waters, the observer of *ṛta*—who was he born from, and from where did he come into being?

Moving through the mid-air and over the earth, he does not settle down anywhere; none at all know him, O Ahura. Who is the first-born friend of the waters, the observer of cosmic order (*ṛtá*)? Where was he born, and from whence did he come into being? (3)
Moving along various paths existing in the intermediate space and the sky, the wind does not rest or sit down even for a single day;
rather, it moves at all times.
The reflexive voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to Pāṇini’s rule 1.3.17, *ner viśaḥ*.
Moreover, Vāyu is the friend of the waters;
for the Śruti states: "Vāyu indeed rules over the rains" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.4.9.1).

Being the first-born—having arisen before all living beings—and being one who abides in truth (*vṛtāvā*) or possesses the sacrifice (*yajñavān*), from what region indeed was such a Vāyu born? From which place did he emerge and become this entire world, pervading it?
The meaning is that because this exists at all times and in all places, its origination and the manner of its pervasion cannot be known by anyone.
The self of the gods, the embryo of the world, this god moves according to his will;
his sounds alone are heard here, not his form. To that Vāta, let us pay worship with an oblation.
The Self, the germ of the gods and of the world—this god moves according to his own will; his roars alone are heard, not his form. To that Vāta we shall offer worship with an oblation. 4.

This wind is the self (*ātman*) even of the gods, Indra and the others, because it abides within them in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*); it is also the "womb" (*garbha*)—that is, existing as the internal essence—of the entire world, the aggregate of all beings. Such a god moves according to his own power, according to his will, and according to his desire. Having unobstructed movement, he goes swiftly in some places and slowly in others; he exits from one body and enters another body. The meaning is that he exists and acts according to his own pleasure.

As that wind approaches, its *ghoṣas*—that is, its sounds alone—are heard; however, its form (*rūpa*) or essential nature is not seen, because it is formless. The meaning is that it is inferred solely by means of sound, as it is beyond the reach of the senses.
To that Vāta, to Vāyu, let us offer worship with an oblation consisting of cooked rice, sacrificial cakes, and other such offerings; let us serve him.
The eighteenth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with “mayobhūḥ,” is the Ṛṣi Śabara Kakṣīvata’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and has the Cow as its deity.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī: “Mayobhūḥ; Śabara [is the seer]; [it is] for the Cow, belonging to Kakṣīvata.
When cows are setting out toward the pasture, they should be consecrated with the first two verses.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “One should address the cows as they are setting out with these two verses: ‘May the wind blow pleasantly upon you,’ and so forth” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.10.5).
May the wind blow upon you with healing; may the plants full of vigor reach you.
May they drink from the fatness of the earth, providing sustenance for your life. O Rudra, be gracious to our footsteps.

I have become the earth; I am the wind. Blow upon thee! Let the vigorous plants, rich in sap and fatness, reach thee. Let them drink from the flowing streams; let them flow down. O Rudra, be gracious to our footprints. 1.
May the wind, the purifier,
being the bringer of happiness, blow toward the cows.
And may those cows, full of vigor and rich in sap, graze upon the herbs and strong grasses on every side.
Likewise, let the swelling, abundant waters—those that bring prosperity to living beings and delight the living—drink [the poison].
O Rudra, O God who destroys by the mere glance of diseases such as fever, be gracious (mṛḷa) toward this Agni, who is intent on his task and is in the form of a bull;
do not afflict him. This is the meaning.

Those who are alike, those who are diverse, those who are of one form—whose names Agni knows thus; those whom the Aṅgirases have gratified here with nourishment—to them, O Parjanya, grant great protection. 2. Those who are alike, those who are diverse, those who are of one form—whose names Agni knows thus; those whom the Aṅgirases have gratified here with nourishment—to them, O Parjanya, grant great protection. 2.

O Parjanya, grant great protection and happiness to all these cows—those of uniform appearance, those of similar form, those of diverse forms, and those of a single color; for Agni knows their names, such as "Īḍā," "Rantī," and "Aditi," by means of the Viṣṭi sacrifice; and the Aṅgiras seers, through austerity characterized by the Citrā sacrifice and other rites which serve as the means for attaining cattle, have produced them here in this world. To all these cows, O Parjanya, bestow great and abundant well-being.

With the two verses beginning “yā deveṣu,” he should consecrate the cows as they return home in the evening. For it is stated in the Sūtra: “He recites the remainder of the hymn beginning with ‘yā deveṣu tanvam airayanta,’ and some [recite] the Āgāvīya” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.10.6–7).

Those who sent forth their bodies among the gods, whose every form Soma knows—those, swelling with milk and rich in offspring, O Indra, bestow upon us in our cow-pen. 3. Those who sent forth their bodies among the gods, whose every form Soma knows—those, swelling with milk and rich in offspring, O Indra, bestow upon us in our cow-pen. 3.

The cows manifest their own bodies among the gods at the sacrifices; they send forth their forms in the shape of oblations. And Soma knows all the forms of these cows—the milk and other substances used for mixing that are being prepared. For our sake, those cows which swell with milk and thus increase, and which are therefore rich in offspring—that is, accompanied by their calves—O Indra, drive them to our own cow-pen.
‘Ri’ is the root for the act of going;
the absence of the verbal suffix (vikaraṇa) is according to Vedic usage (chāndasa).

For Prajāpati, bestowing these upon me, in harmony with all the gods and the ancestors, has made them auspicious and true; let them enter our cow-pen, and may we dwell together with them and our offspring. (4) Prajāpati, bestowing these upon me, in harmony with all the gods and the ancestors, has made them auspicious and true; let them enter our cow-pen, and may we dwell together with them and our offspring. (4)
1. The phrase *ta-bha- ‘balavanti’* does not exist.
2. *ta1.2.3.6.7.8-ma-* are endowed with only a single form; *ta4.5-* are endowed with multiple forms. 3.
*ta1.2.3.6.7.8-ma-su-* are to be consecrated (*anumaṃtrayitavyāḥ*); *ta4.5-* should consecrate (*anumaṃtrayīta*).
4. ta4.5-bhara- In our cow-pen, Prajāpati, the Ordainer, having granted these cows to me who praises him—giving them—[is present].
The suffix *śānac* is used here by the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.128] regarding the root *rāti*.
The suffix *śap* is elided by Vedic license (*chāndasa*).
By the rule "the first syllable of reduplicated forms [is acute]," there is an acute accent on the initial syllable.

Having attained unanimity—that is, having reached a state of agreement—with all the gods and the ancestors, may he make our cows auspicious, virtuous, and well-being-bringing; that is, may he bring them to our cow-pen, or to the vicinity of the cow-pen.
Through the offspring of those cows, may we be united and gathered together.
The affix *liṅ* is used in the sense of benediction when it denotes a command; in the case of benediction, the affix *aṅ* is substituted for *liṅ*.
The nineteenth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with "vibhrāṭ," is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of one named Vibhrāj, the son of Sūrya; its deity is Sūrya.
The first three verses are in the Jagatī meter;
the fourth is a Vyāstārapaṅkti consisting of two octosyllabic and two dodecasyllabic pādas.
And thus it has been introduced: “*Vibhrāṭ*, *vibhrāṭ*; [this is] the Saurya [hymn], in the Jāgata [meter], ending with an Āsapaṅkti.
At the Viṣuvat [sacrifice], the first triplet in the Niṣkevalya [śastra] is the *stotriya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Vibhrāḍ bṛhat pipītu somyaṃ madhu*, *namo mitrasya varuṇasya cakṣase*—these are the *stotriya* and the *anurūpa*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.6).
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, the *yājyā* for the additional *uktha* is the verse beginning with "vibhrāṭ.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* for that [additional *uktha*] is 'vibhrāḍ bṛhat pipītu somyaṃ madhu'; [it is performed] with hundreds of cows" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.9).

May the radiant, great Soma-drink swell with honeyed sweetness; may it bestow undiminished life upon the lord of the sacrifice. He who, impelled by the wind, protects by his own power, has nourished all creatures and shines forth in many ways. vibhrāḍ bṛhat pipātu somyaṃ madhu; āyur dadhad yajñapatau avihutam. vātajūto yo abhirakṣati tmanā; prajāḥ pupoṣa purudhā virājati. (1) May the radiant, great [Soma] cause the honey-sweet Soma-juice to swell; bestowing unimpaired life upon the lord of the sacrifice—He who, impelled by the wind, protects by his own self, has nourished all creatures and shines forth in many ways. (1)
May Sūrya—the radiant, shining, and pre-eminently blazing one—drink the great, exalted, and abundant honey-like nectar consisting of Soma.
What is he doing?
Bestowing, that is, bestowing upon the lord of the sacrifice, the patron, an unimpaired and straight path of life.
That Sun, impelled by the wind—that is, being driven by the great wind—protects by himself, that is, by his own self, as he gazes upon and preserves the entire world.
Since the circle of the zodiac is impelled by the wind, the Sun likewise moves in that manner.
That Sun nourishes all creatures by providing rain and other benefits; he shines forth preeminently in many ways, that is, in manifold ways.

Radiant, great, well-sustained, most effective in winning booty, the upholder of the law, established upon the support of heaven as truth—light has been born, the slayer of enemies, the slayer of Vṛtra, the greatest slayer of Dasyus, the slayer of Asuras, and the slayer of rivals. vibhrāḍ bṛhat subhṛtaṃ vājasātamaṃ dharman divo dharuṇe satyam arpitam | amitrahā vṛtrahā dasyuhantamam jyotirjajñe asurahā sapatnahā || 2 || Radiant, great, well-sustained, most effective in winning booty, the upholder of the law, established upon the support of heaven as truth—light has been born, the slayer of enemies, the slayer of Vṛtra, the greatest slayer of Dasyus, the slayer of Asuras, and the slayer of rivals.

The radiant, shining, vast, mature, well-sustained, and well-nourished light—most excellent at winning strength (vāja), the best giver of strength or power, established by Vāyu within the sustaining sphere of heaven, fixed upon the supporting mandala of the sun—that eternal, indestructible light has been born; it is the slayer of enemies (the destroyer of those who are hostile), the slayer of Vṛtra (the destroyer of obstructors), the greatest slayer of Dasyus (the most effective destroyer of those who cause affliction), the slayer of Asuras (the destroyer of those who cast down), and the slayer of rivals (the destroyer even of co-born enemies). Such is the solar splendor that has manifested.
This is the best of lights, the supreme light; it is called the all-conquering, the wealth-winning, the vast.
All-shining, a great radiance, Sūrya has spread wide for us to see, along with unfailing, steadfast power.

This is called the Great One, the best among lights, the supreme light, the conqueror of all, the winner of wealth, the vast, the all-pervading, the radiant, the mighty sun. For all to see, he has spread wide his enduring power and invincible strength. ||3||

The solar radiance produced is the most excellent—that is, the most highly praised—of all lights, including other luminaries such as the planets and constellations; it is illuminating, and for that very reason it is called supreme and preeminent. It is the conqueror of the universe, the victor over all things, and the winner of wealth; it is said to be vast and abundant.
Thus, it is designated by all as being distinguished by these qualities.

Moreover, the all-pervading, the illuminator of the universe, the impelling, the impelled, the great Sūrya has spread forth for all to see his vast, conquering power—overcoming darkness, immovable, indestructible, and his vital energy in the form of splendor.
Shining with light, go to the heavenly realm, to the radiant sphere of heaven,
by which all these worlds were supported— by Viśvakarman, who is accompanied by all the gods.
Shining brightly with light, you have ascended to the sun, the luminous realm of heaven, by which all these worlds were brought forth by Viśvakarman, who possesses all divine power.
O Sūrya, shining with your light and splendor, illuminating the entire world, you have gone to—attained—the radiant station belonging to heaven.
You are accompanied by Viśvakarman, the cause of all activities;
*viśvadevya* means that which is beneficial for all the gods, such as sacrifice and other rites.
Or rather, by that solar splendor, all these visible worlds— the waters on earth— are brought together during the summer season;
or else,
all the classes of beings are brought together, held from all sides, and nourished.
The syntactical connection is with the words "by that light."
The hymn consisting of four verses beginning with “tvaṃ tyam” is the twentieth; it is composed in the Gāyatrī meter by Iṣṭa, the son of Bhṛgu, and is dedicated to Indra.
It is cataloged thus: “tvaṃ tyam... [is] the descendant of Bhṛgu, in Gāyatrī.
Its ritual application has been explained.
O Indra, you protected that chariot from here for the one who had pressed the Soma; you protected the wave of the flowing juice.
O Indra, you indeed protected that chariot from here; come quickly to the one who has pressed the juice, to the one with the flowing wave, the possessor of Soma. 1.

O Indra, with the pressed Soma of the one who has performed the libation—the well-pressed juice offered here according to the rite—you, by means of those [hymns] bearing this name, protected that celebrated chariot. (Note: The form *sutenābhiputena* is explained as a compound where the suffix *ṅasi* [genitive singular] is replaced by *su* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. The word *etatsaṃjñyaiḥ* refers to those hymns designated by this name.)
Hear my invocation, O Soma, you who are joined with Soma, as I call upon you from the ocean.
You struck off the head of the snorting beast from its skin; you went to the house of Soma.
You [O Indra], from the head of the wildly shaking [foe], you stripped away the skin; you went to the house of the Soma-presser. 2.

O Indra, you brought down—that is, having torn away and separated from—the head in the form of the Pravargya from the skin, meaning from the body characterized by its skin, of the trembling and fleeing sacrifice for the sake of the gods;
you struck it off.
In ancient times, Indra, by means of his thunderbolt in the form of the bowstring’s impact, severed the head of the Person-shaped sacrifice as it emerged from the gods.
With this intention, it was said:
for it is heard in scripture—“Indra, by means of his thunderbolt, cut the bowstring of that Dhanu; he [the bow] shattered the head of Ugra, and he became the Pravargya” (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.5.2).
Therefore, you have come, or rather, come to my house, which possesses Soma.
1. The state of being a womb for one who has sons.

O Indra, you [subdued] that mortal, the son of Vena, for Āstrabudha—for Manasyu—easily and repeatedly. O Indra, you subdued that mortal, the son of Vena, namely Pṛthu, for Āstrabudha—Āstrabudha being the name of a certain person—for his son Manasyu, who desired a meditative hymn; you easily and repeatedly struck him down; that is to say, you brought him under control.

O Indra, you place that very sun, which was in the west, in the east—even beyond the will of the gods. O Indra, you place that very sun, which was in the west at the time of evening, in the east at the time of dawn on the following day. (Note: there is an interchange of verbal suffixes. Of what nature is it? Even beyond the will (*vaśam*) of the gods—that is, hidden from them, so difficult to discern as to where it has gone—and yet desirable.
The fourth hymn, consisting of twenty-one verses beginning with "ā yāhi," belongs to Saṃvarta Āṅgirasa; its deity is also [the same].
All four [verses] consist of twenty syllables each and are *dvipadā virāj* meters.
Thus it has been enumerated: "ā yāhi: Saṃvarta; the first two are *dvipada*."
In the first *Chandoma* day, this hymn precedes the *vaiśvadeva* hymn.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Ā yāhi vana’, ‘imā nu kam’, ‘babhruḥ’, and ‘kaḥ’—these are the two-footed hymns" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 8.7).
This [hymn] is also used in the *Niṣkevalya* section of the *Mahāvrata*.
Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "The nine [verses] beginning with 'Come hither with the wood' are recited" (AiĀ 5.2.2).

Come hither with thy lovely splendor or wealth; let the cows follow upon thy path as they rise upward. (1) Come hither with thy lovely splendor or wealth! Let the cows, which serve as the draft-animals for the Dawn, follow upon thy path—that is, attend to the chariot. Come hither by means of that chariot. "Which" refers to the cows characterized by their rising upward—meaning they are full; those are the cows [that follow]. Such is the connection.

Come hither with a wealth-bestowing thought, O most bountiful one, you whose sacrifice is ever-praised, together with those who give good gifts. (2) Come hither with a wealth-bestowing thought—whether it be a gracious intention, a ritual act, or a hymn of praise. Come, O Dawn! And may that time of dawn be most bountiful through men who provide excellent food and gifts; for this reason, it becomes a sacrifice that exhausts my wealth.

Like those who support their fathers, we, the givers of good gifts, maintain the thread; we bite into it and we sacrifice. (3) Like those who support their fathers—like sustainers of food—we, the givers of good gifts (*sudānavaḥ*), meaning those who give beautiful gifts, maintain the thread (*tantum*) as it were, that is, the extended [sacrificial thread]. We hold it fast by way of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). And through that sacrifice, we worship her.

1. *ta-bha* read *ahiṃsīt*. 2. *ta¹.².³.⁶.⁸-bhara* read *taṃ taṃ te*. 3. *ta⁷* reads *tyaṃ taṃ*. 4. *ga-ta-bha¹.⁴.⁸* read *taṃ taṃ*; *bhara* reads *taṃ taṃ*. 5. *ga* reads "the sacrifice itself, which is extensive. On the tenth day, during the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) at the *upastha* ritual, in place of the verse beginning with "upo bhadebhiḥ," this verse "upā apa svasuḥ" is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'upā apa svasutama'—reciting the two-footed verse in three parts at the *upastha*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.12).
The Dawn, well-born, rolls up the darkness of her sister and opens the path. 4. Dawn; away; of the sister; the darkness; together; she rolls up; the path; well-born. 4.
This Dawn drives away— the very darkness belonging to her sister, the Night—
and dispels it by means of her own splendor;
being well-born, she brings the chariot to its path because of her own noble birth and the excellence of her offspring.
"Ā tvā"—this twenty-second hymn consisting of six verses belongs to Dhruva, the son of Aṅgiras; it is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
Its deity is the subject matter in the form of a praise of the consecrated king.
Thus it has been enumerated: "Ā tvā—six [verses]; Dhruva [composed] a praise of the king; it is indeed Anuṣṭubh."

When the king prepares for battle, the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) must be performed by the domestic priest (*purodhā*) with this hymn (*sūkta*). This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Having stationed [the chariot] behind with the verse 'Come to you... within the two worlds' (*ā tvāhāryam antareṇa dhīḥ*), etc. (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.12.2).

I have brought you hither; abide within, be firm and immovable. May all the subjects desire you; let not the kingdom fall away from you. I have brought you hither; abide within, be firm and immovable. May all the subjects desire you; let not the kingdom fall away from you. 1.
O King, I have brought you hither; I have led you to the sovereignty over our kingdom. Therefore, abide among us as our lord;
being firm and eternal, remaining utterly motionless, stand firm—stand over the kingdom.
And may all the subjects and progeny desire you;
may they wish, "Let this very one be our king.
[The root] *vāñchi* is used in the sense of "desiring."
From you—from your presence—may the kingdom, the sovereignty, not fall away; may it not be lost;
may it not become separated.
(The root *andh* means "to fall downward.")

Be right here; do not fall away, as immovable as a mountain. Stand firm here like Indra; uphold the kingdom here. 2. Be right here; do not fall away, as immovable as a mountain. Stand firm here like Indra; uphold the kingdom here. 2.
O King, prosper here in this very kingdom, remaining forever as its sovereign; do not fall away— do not be deprived of it, do not depart from it.
Just as a mountain remains immovable, so may you be unwavering and free from agitation.
Just as Indra remains in heaven, so may you stand firm and stable in this world.
And may you uphold the kingdom in this world.
Establish each person in their respective duty.
2. ga-tā.1.2.3.6.7.8-bha—also free from movement. 3. gara—entirely for us; tā.1.2.3.6.7.8-ma1.2.4.5.8—for all of us.
4. In the kingdom of existence; 5. remove that darkness. Indra has established this [pillar] as firm with a firm oblation.
For him Soma shall speak favorably, and for him Brahmanaspati.
Indra has established this [earth] as firm with a firm oblation; for him may Soma speak favorably, and for him may Brahmaṇaspati likewise. || 3 ||
Being gratified by this constant and firm oblation, may Indra maintain him firmly and steadfastly;
and may Soma speak in his favor, declaring,
"This one is mine," and thus utter words of partiality for this king.
Therefore, for him and for him alone, Brahmaṇaspati, the god who is the protector of the mantra, shall speak in favor.
Firm is the sky, firm is the earth, firm are these mountains;
firm is this entire world, and firm is this king of the people.
Firm is the sky; firm is the earth; firm are these mountains; firm is this entire moving world; firm is this king of the people. 4.
The sky becomes firm and stable;
the earth also becomes firm and stable;
these visible mountains and great bearers of the earth are firm and stable.
This entire universe, this whole world, becomes firm and stable;
even so, may this king, being the lord of the people (viśām), remain firm and stable.
Firm is your kingdom, O King Varuṇa; firm is it, O god Bṛhaspati.
May Indra and Agni maintain your kingdom as something firm.
Firm be thy kingdom; may King Varuṇa, firm may the god Bṛhaspati, and firm may both Indra and Agni uphold thy sovereignty. 5.
O King, may Varuṇa, the shining sovereign, maintain your kingdom firmly and steadily;
may the divine Bṛhaspati, endowed with qualities such as generosity, maintain it firmly;
and may both Indra and Agni together maintain your kingdom firmly and steadily.
The word *dhruva* is used twice with reference to both Indra and Agni.
With the firm oblation, we take hold of Soma with that which is firm;
and so may Indra make the clans bring tribute to you alone.
With the firm oblation we touch Soma firmly; and so may Indra make those clans subject to you alone, paying tribute. 6.
With the firm and stable oblation, such as the *puroḍāśa* cake and so forth, we touch—the firm and stable Soma.
We, the officiating priests, touch it while aiming toward the deities for the sake of the sacrifice.
Moreover, Indra shall make the subjects (*viśaḥ*), who are yours alone and exclusive, the givers of tribute (*balihṛtaḥ*)—that is, the providers of taxes.
1. *ta* 1.2.3.6.7–*cadapuroḍāśādi*; *ta* 4.5.8–*bha* 1.2.4.8–*puroḍāśādi*. 2. *ta* 1.2.3.7–*bha* 1.2.4.8–of the *kāra*.
The twenty-third hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “*abhīvartena*,” belongs to Āṅgirasa Abhīvarta and is in the *ānuṣṭubha* meter.
