As before, the deity is the praise of the king. Thus it has been enumerated: “With the *abhīvarta*, there are five *abhīvarta* hymns. The domestic priest should cause the king, who has donned his armor for battle, to recite this hymn.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "Then, as he is being sent away, he causes him to recite the Abhīvarta hymn addressed to Upāra" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.12.12).
With the all-encompassing oblation by which Indra was encompassed,
with that, O Brahmaṇaspati, do thou encompass us for the sake of sovereignty.
With the *abhīvarta* oblation, by which Indra was turned toward victory—with that, O Brahmaṇaspati, turn us toward sovereignty. 1.
By means of the *abhīvarta*.
It is called *abhīvarta* because one approaches (*abhigacchati*) by means of it.
The suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*).
By the rule regarding the accentuation of *thā-thādi* compounds, the final syllable of the second member bears the udātta accent.
Furthermore, by the rule “*upasargasya ghañy amanuṣye bahulam*” (Pāṇini 6.3.122), there is lengthening of the vowel [of the prefix].
O Brahmanaspati, with that very oblation by which Indra has turned toward us and attained everything, turn us—purified by that oblation—toward the kingdom so that we may obtain sovereign rule.
Overpowering our rivals, overpower those who are hostile to us; stand over him who attacks us, over him who seeks to harm us.
Turning against our rivals, against those who are hostile to us, stand against him who attacks us, and against him who seeks to harm us! 2.

O King, having surrounded and driven away our rivals and enemies, do thou also overcome those who are our adversaries—those offspring who are stingy by nature. Overcome him who seeks battle, who desires his own armies, and who is eager for combat.
From the word *pṛtanā*, by some means, there is an elision of the final syllable in the form *kadhyadhvarapṛtanasya*.
And whoever plots against us or is envious of us—
*iras* and *tiras* belong to the class beginning with *kaṇva* in the sense of envy—
overpower even him.
Or alternatively,
Brahmanaspati himself, who is the subject under discussion, is to be addressed here as well.
Thee may the god Savitar encompass, thee may Soma encompass;
may all beings encompass thee, so that thou mayest be victorious.
The god Savitṛ has encompassed you; Soma has encompassed you; all beings have encompassed you, so that you may be victorious. 3.
O King, may the divine Savitṛ, endowed with qualities such as generosity, turn you toward it;
may he cause you to attain the kingdom.
And may Soma also cause you to turn toward it.
May all beings, including the earth and all others, turn toward you;
in whatever manner you are the *abhīvarta*, existing as one who turns everywhere.
The absence of the elision of *śap* after the root *ās* is Vedic.
By means of that oblation with which Indra became preeminent in glory—this very thing, O gods, I have now performed; indeed, I have become free from rivals.
1. *vācayīta*; 4.8 *vācayīta*.
With that oblation by which Indra became a doer, most resplendent—this have I performed, O gods: "May I indeed become one who has no rivals. 4.
By means of this oblation offered by us, O Indra, you became a performer of deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra;

you became resplendent—*dyumnī*, either shining with light or possessing speech—and for that very reason, you became supreme (*uttama*) and most excellent. This very oblation, O gods, has been prepared (*akri*).
Or rather:
"I have done what ought not to be done; for that very reason, indeed, I have become one who has no rival."
Indeed, I was even free from enemies.

Without rivals, slayer of rivals, possessing a sovereign realm, invincible—just as I have become the sovereign ruler over these beings and over the people. (5) Without rivals, slayer of rivals, possessing a sovereign realm, invincible—just as the pressing-stones, established in their places, acting in unison, rejoicing together, or having come together, [stand] upon the *upara* stone.
The *upara* is the broad stone placed in the midst of the four pressing-stones, serving as a support for them.
The plural number is used in consideration of the various regions.
They are magnified and shine forth at the borders of the upper realm.
The suffix *ā* is for the purpose of filling out the meter.
Doing what?
Bestowing—that is, granting—manly vigor (*vṛṣṇyam vīryam*) to Soma, the showerer (*vṛṣṇe varṣitre*).
May the pressing-stones and the god Savitṛ now press you out according to the sacred law for the sake of the sacrificer who pours the libation.
O pressing-stones, may the god Savitṛ now press you forth according to the sacred law for the sake of the sacrificer who presses the soma. 4.
O stones, let the god Savitṛ, endowed with qualities such as generosity, impel you— by means of his own sustaining power— to press [the Soma] quickly; that is,
for the sake of the sacrificer who performs the pressing of the Soma.
The meaning is that of the accomplishment of that Tathāgata.

The hymn consisting of twenty-five verses beginning with "pra sūnavaḥ" has the Ṛbhus' son as its seer; he is also the seer for the verses addressed to the Sūnus. The second verse is in the Gāyatrī meter, and the remaining three are in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
The remaining verses belong to the primordial deity (Ādideva), while [the first] belongs to Agni.
Thus it has been enumerated: "O sons, the son, the Ābhūvas; [these] are addressed to Agni in the Anuṣṭubh meter, and the second is a Gāyatrī addressed to Ābhūvi.
The application [of these verses] has already been explained.
The sons of the Ṛbhus have raised their loud voices at the sacrifice—
those who, all-sustaining, have fed upon the earth as they would on a mother cow.
The sons of the Ṛbhus have raised a loud shout in their great battle, they who, all-sustaining, have fed upon the earth as a calf feeds upon its mother-cow.

The sons known as the *Ṛbhus*—namely Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja—are designated by their first name even when referring to all three. Their sons, with great (*bṛhat*) abundance (*prabhūtam*), went forth (*pra...navanta*) into battle (*vṛtanā*); for *vṛtanā* is a name for combat. The root *navati* means "to go"; they go forward, they proceed with excellence. By this excellent progress, victory is indicated; the meaning is that they conquer their enemies therein. Even though the word *sūnavaḥ* (sons) refers to a single group, it is expressed in the plural for the sake of honor. Those *Ṛbhus*, who are *viśvadhāyasaḥ*—the sustainers of all—enjoyed (*aśnan*) the earth (*kṣām*). The root *aś* here means "to pervade" (*vyāptau*); there is a grammatical substitution (*vyatyayena*) for *kṣā*. They were like a milch-cow (*dhenum na*); *dhenu* is a cow that provides satisfaction. This is the connection: [they were] like those *Ṛbhus*. Alternatively, the rays of the sun are also called *Ṛbhus*. Those rays of the sun which shine widely (*uru bhāsamānāḥ*), drinking (*dhayantaḥ*) or sucking up (*pibantaḥ*) the *viśvadhāyasam*—all the essence—or rather, being the sustainers of all through the bestowing of rain and so forth, they enjoyed (*aśnan*) the earth (*kṣām*); they drank all its essence. Therein lies the illustration: just as calves drink from their mother, the milk-giving cow, so do these *Ṛbhus* who enjoy [it]. This is the connection: of those *Ṛbhus* who eat.
At the time of carrying forward the fire, the triplet beginning with "pra devam" should be recited.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "Being prompted, he begins the verses for the carrying forward of the fire: 'pra devam devyā dhiyā'—these three" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.17).
Bring forth the god Jātavedas with divine thought;
may he carry our oblations hither.
Bring forth the god Jātavedas with divine prayer; may he carry our oblations to him without fail.

O priests and sacrificers, bring forth—bring forward with great care—or lead hither this Agni Jātavedas, the knower of all that is born, the one possessed of born wisdom or born wealth, a god endowed with qualities such as generosity. By what means? He says: by divine luster, by devotion, or by wisdom (dhiyā), or by ritual action (karman). Alternatively, this instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment: "joined with divine devotion. What is the purpose? [The verse continues: ... [the gods] spoke... [he is] the one who possesses milk... [end of fragment].
3. *taḍ-pibantyaḥ*; *bha*-pibanti.
Regarding "the people" (*janam*):
[it means] "our" (*naḥ*) "oblations" (*havyā*), that is, the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*), he shall "carry" (*vakṣat*) "successively" (*ānupak*), that is, in due order (*ānupūrvyāt*).
This Agni shall carry;
he shall cause the gods to arrive.
In *vahelanti*, the suffix *sip* is applied according to the rule *sidbahulam*.

This very one, seeking the gods, the Hotṛ-priest, is led forth for the sacrifice; like a chariot that brings what is desired, enveloped in flames and glowing with heat, he takes heed by his own power. 3. Om! This one, seeking the gods, the Hotṛ-priest, is led forth for the sacrifice; like a chariot that brings what is desired, enveloped in flames and glowing with heat, he takes heed by his own power. 3.
This very one is that Agni; he is "devayu," meaning he becomes one who desires to go toward the gods.
Because of the word *deva*, there is a prohibition of the substitution of *i* and lengthening by the rule "and not in the Veda for [the word] *aputra*."
He alone is the *hotṛ*, the invoker of the gods;
he alone is led forth (*pra ṇīyate*) for the sake of the sacrifice (*yajñāya*), being brought forward toward the place of the *āhavanīya* fire.
Moreover, he is the chariot (*ratha*), characterized by swift motion, or the Sun who possesses a chariot.
In Vedic usage, there is the elision of the possessive suffix denoting "possessing."

He is like one who is compassionate and radiant; he is the one who has offered that [oblation], the mixer of the two [worlds], and the one who causes [the sacrificer] to meet with the gods through the oblation.
Thus: by the rule "they are seen after other [roots] as well," the suffix *vic* is applied.
He was surrounded and encircled by the officiating priests and the sacrificer.
In the word *vṛṇoti*, the lengthening of the first member of the compound occurs by the rule *anyebhyo 'pi*;
the original accent (*prakṛtisvaratva*) of the prefix *pra* is maintained by the rule *gatir anantaraḥ*.
Agni, being thus constituted, perceives by himself, through his own self; he knows how to worship the gods correctly.
In the case of mantras, there is the elision of the letter *ā* according to the rule "of the self [the suffix] beginning with *adhi*."

This one protects [us] as if from immortality; this god, more powerful than even the powerful, has been made for the sake of life. 4. This Agni protects [us], as if from immortality, from birth; he is the god more powerful than even the powerful, made for the sake of living. 4.

This Agni protects—that is, he guards—from that which is born from the immortal, meaning from the gods; and likewise, he protects even from that which is born from the mortal, meaning from human beings.
Yāska [states] that the root *uruṣyati* has the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣākarmā*) (Nirukta 5.23).

In the case of the word *amṛta*, which expresses a state (*bhāvavācin*), when it forms a negative *bahuvrīhi* compound with the particle *nañ*, the rule "the first syllable of *jara*, *mara*, *mitra*, and *mṛta* becomes udātta" applies, resulting in the acute accent on the initial syllable of the final member. Furthermore, by the rule "of those expressing fear or protection" (Pāṇini 1.4.25), it receives the designation of the *apādāna* (ablative).
Moreover, this [word] *sahas* is a name for strength (*bala*), as in *sahasāśrita*.
Therefore, there is elision (*luk*) of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) following it, according to the rule "frequently in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).
Even in the case of the word *cic-chanda*, it has the sense of "also.
[The phrase] *sahasvataḥ* means "of the powerful," and *sahīyān* means "more powerful."
From the word *sahasin* with the suffix *īyasun*, there is the elision of *vin* by the rule "vinmatoḥ," and the elision of the final vowel (*ṭi*) by the rule "ṭeḥ."
The god, being thus, was created—meaning brought forth by Brahmā—for the sake of sacrifice, that is, for the purpose of sustaining life.
The hymn beginning with "pataṅga," consisting of three verses, is the twenty-sixth hymn; it is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Pataṅga, the son of Prajāpati.
The first verse is in the Jagatī meter, and the following two are in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Since the differentiation of *māyā* is its subject matter, this hymn has that [differentiation] as its deity.
And it has been listed [in the Anukramaṇī]: "The triplet beginning with 'pataṅga' is by Pataṅga, the son of Prajāpati; it is a variety of *māyā*, beginning with a *jagatī*.
These two verses are recited in the *abhiṣṭava* section of the *pravargya* rite.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'pataṅgamaktam asurasya māyayā yo naḥ sanutyaḥ' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.6)."

The wise behold the Bird, anointed by the magic power of the Asura, with their heart and mind; within the ocean the seers discern him, and the ordainers seek the station of the rays. pataṅgam | aktam | asurasya | māyayā | hṛdā | paśyanti | manasā | vipaścitaḥ | samudre | antaḥ | kavayaḥ | vi | cakṣate | marīcīnām | padam | icchanti | vedhasaḥ || 1 ||
1. *ta* 1.2.3.6.7.8-*bha-mu-yo devayuḥ*. 2. *ta-bha-°dyādeva*.

By means of *māyā*—which is connected to the Supreme Brahman, who is the Asura (the one beyond the senses), skilled in non-existence (*asanakuśala*), and devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*sarvopādhivihīna*)—that which was unmanifest (*avyakta*) has become manifest (*vyakta*), that is, fully revealed. It consists of the three *guṇas*.
Or rather:
"Māyā" is a name for wisdom (*prajñā*);
[he is] the all-pervading *patanga* connected with wisdom.
The sun is called *pataṅga* because it flies (*patati*) or goes (*gacchati*). The wise ones, the learned, [perceive] him with the heart—that is, with the organ of the heart;
such is the etymological derivation.
With their minds restrained within the heart,
the seers (*kavayaḥ*)— those of far-reaching vision— behold and know [the Truth] in the ocean;
for it is called "ocean" (*samudra*) because the rays of light emerge (*samudravanti*) from it, namely the solar orb.
Within that, in its center, they behold—that is, they perceive clearly;
the meaning is that they also know the golden Person who dwells within the orb.

Those who are thus *vedhasaḥ*, ordainers—performers of the worship of the Sun in the manner described—they desire, that is, long for, the *padaṃ* or station of the *marīcīnām*, the rays, namely the solar orb.
The meaning is that they attain [the Self] through its worship.
Or alternatively:

the wise ones, by means of the Vedānta teachings, perceive with their inward-turned minds situated in the heart the Self—which is enveloped by *māyā* and manifested in the form of the individual soul—as the *pataṅga*.
The Supreme Self is called *pataṅga* because it "falls" (descends) or "pervades.
They "behold" It;
the meaning is that, by abandoning all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), they directly realize the identity of the individual self (*jīvātman*) with the Supreme Self.

Moreover, those seers, who possess far-reaching vision and are conversant with the Vedānta, perceive—that is, they clearly behold—all that is visible as being within, in the midst of the "ocean" (samudra). It is called the ocean because from it all limbs (aṅga) flow forth; it is the Supreme Self (paramātman), which serves as the foundational substratum. Within that, they discern the entire aggregate of the perceptible as having the nature of the Self.

Therefore, because everything other than Brahman is false, those who possess fear desire that very Supreme Brahman—which is the ground (*pada*), the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the functioning cognitions (*vṛttijñāna*) of the rays [of consciousness], and which consists of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss;
indeed, they long for the attainment of That alone.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāc, "pataṅgo vācam" is the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "yadvā vadantyavicetanāni... pataṅgo vācaṃ manasā bibharti" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
The bird bears speech within his mind; the Gandharva uttered it within the womb.
At the station of Eternal Order (Ṛta), the seers guard that radiant, celestial, and inspired thought.
The bird bears speech within his mind; the Gandharva spoke it within the womb. At the station of Cosmic Order (Ṛta), the seers guard that radiant, celestial, and inspired thought. || 2 ||
The Sun, the "flying one" (*pataṅga*), sustains—that is, holds fast—the Speech consisting of the three Vedas by means of his mind and wisdom.

For it is heard in scripture: "In the forenoon the divine Sun moves in heaven with the Ṛgveda; he stands at midday with the Yajurveda; at sunset he is glorified with the Sāmaveda; thus the Sun is never devoid of these three Vedas" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.1).
That very same Speech, while existing within the womb, that is, in the midst of the body, is the Gandharva.

The *gandharva* is the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), so called because it "bears" (*dhārayati*) sounds (*gāḥ śabdān*). It "speaks within," that is, it speaks or impels from within; for according to the traditional teaching: "The wind, moving through the *tūrṇi*, produces the deep (*mandra*) tone" (*Pāśupata-śikṣā* 7).

The wise seers, the poets (*kavayaḥ*), guard—that is, they preserve through teaching—the *manīṣā*, which is shining, celestial, leading to heaven, or beneficial for heaven; which is the mistress of the mind, or which consists of the three Vedas; [they guard it] at the *pada*, the station of *ṛta*—the sacrifice, or the sun which has become reality. The Sun (Pataṅga) is the Supreme Self, pervasive and devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
At the beginning of creation, He sustains speech by means of the mind;
the meaning is that through mental deliberation as to what things were to be created, He mentally grasped the Veda, which expresses all objects of knowledge.
For it is recorded: "In the beginning, that Great Lord fashioned [the world] from the very words of the Veda.
The Gandharva, dwelling within the golden embryo—the cosmic egg—uttered that speech first;
that speech, characterized by qualities such as luminosity, the seers—the gods who possess far-reaching vision—guard closely at the station of Ṛta, the Truth, which is Brahman.
At the Pravargya and Abhiṣava rites, the verse "I saw the herdsman" (apaśyaṃ gopām) is used;
and it is stated in the Sūtra: "I saw the herdsman, never resting, in his own vigor" (āpaśyaṃ gopāmanipadyamānaṃ svake dapsasya, Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.6).
1. *tai.1.2.3-bha*: of Asuranakula; *ta7*: of Asurakula. 2. *tai.1.2.3.6–8*: "He" is not present.
"I beheld the herdsman, following no fixed path, moving hither and thither along his ways."
Clothing himself in converging and diverging rays, he moves repeatedly within the worlds.
I have seen the blameless Guardian, moving hither and thither by his paths; clothed in converging and diverging rays, he revolves repeatedly within the worlds.
This has been explained in the hymn *Asyavāmīya* (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.164.31): "I have seen the guardian"— that is, I have perceived the Sun, the protector—
because he protects all classes of living beings through his actions of rising, setting, and so forth.
Of what kind?
Not sitting down, but moving upward;
for it never falls downward.

By the paths, the paths of the sky, he who moves toward us in the forenoon and moves away from us at evening— those two *ca* words serve to conjoin the two modes [of movement]. That Sun [traverses] the converging rays (*sadhrīcīḥ*) and the diverging rays (*viṣūcīḥ*).

These worlds are the chariots; [he is] one who will swiftly cross over them at the time of seizing the Soma. For it is heard [in scripture]: “For he indeed crosses these worlds immediately” (AiB 4.20). Regarding the root *tṛ*, the augment *vṛ* is prescribed by the rule “*prasitastambhitavṛta...*” (Pāṇini 7.2.34). *Ariṣṭanemi*: one whose chariot is unharmed. Or alternatively, *nemi* is a weapon characterized by its bending (*namanaśīla*); thus, one whose weapon is unharmed. Or again, by metaphorical usage, the word for the product (*janya*) is applied to the progenitor (*janaka*). Thus, [the meaning is] my progenitor, Ariṣṭanemi. *Pṛtanām*: the driver, the one who drives forward, or the conqueror of *pṛtanās*, that is, enemy armies. From the root *aj* [meaning] “to go” and “to throw,” the suffix *kvip* is applied. By the statement “an option is desired before an affix beginning with a consonant (*valādi*) when it is an *adhātuka* suffix” (Kātyāyana on Pāṇini 2.4.56), there is the optional absence of the *guṇa* strengthening. Alternatively, the suffix *ḍa* is applied to the root *ji*. *Āśu*: moving swiftly.
Invoking your favor as if that of Indra, may we ascend you for our well-being like a ship.
O wide, broad, vast, and deep ones, may we not suffer harm from you whether we approach or depart.

Invoking your favor like that of Indra, may we mount you for our well-being as if upon a ship. O wide ones, broad ones, vast ones, deep ones—may we not come to harm in your approach, nor in your departure. 2.

Invoking the gift of Tārkṣya, who is like Indra, and calling out again and again for our well-being—that is, for non-destruction—we would ascend her, as one ascends a boat that carries one across the difficult-to-navigate ocean, so that we may cross over suffering; may we have ascended her.
The affix *liṅ* is used for the benedictive; *liṅ* is used in the sense of benediction.
O you two, the vast and wide, O you two, the broad and renowned, O you two, the manifold and infinite, O you two, the deep and endowed with profundity—such are you, O Heaven and Earth!
The word *na* is used here in the sense of "now.
Now, at the arrival and departure of Tārkṣya, may we, belonging to you two, not suffer harm.

The suffix *kin* is applied after the root *iṇ* preceded by the prefixes *āṅ* and *upa* when denoting an abstract state (*bhāva*). By the rule “*tādau ca niti*,” the root vowel retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) due to the following *n*-suffixed suffix.

Swift with his arrow, Śarva has overspread the five peoples as the sun with its light overspreads the waters. Winning thousands, winning hundreds is his impetus; they do not hold him back, as one would not ward off a young woman’s arrow.

He who by his might instantly [subdues] the five peoples, like the sun with its light [overcomes] the waters—he, the winner of thousands, the winner of hundreds, his impetuous rush cannot be checked, any more than a young woman or an arrow.

Even he who is Tārkṣya has swiftly, by his own power, spread out the waters characterized as nectar; just as Sūrya, the Aditya who impels all, spreads out the waters during the rainy season with his own light, so too [Tārkṣya]. Toward the *kṛṣṭīs*, the people—toward the fivefold classes of people.
The meaning is that he hears the five classes of people, including the Niṣādas.
The *raṃhiḥ*—the speed or course—of this Tākṣya becomes a winner of thousands, a giver or a gatherer of wealth numbering in the thousands;
likewise, it becomes a winner of hundreds, a giver or a gatherer of wealth numbering in the hundreds.
From the roots *sanati* or *sanoti*, the suffix *viṭ* is applied according to the rule “*janasanakhanakramagamaviśibhyaḥ viṭ*” (*Pāṇini 3.2.67*).
Then, by the rule “*viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*” (*Pāṇini 6.4.41*), the vowel is lengthened.
Indeed, no one at all can obstruct such a course as this of the son of Tarkshya.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a *śaryā*—an arrow made of reeds—released from a bow, which seems as if it were not to mingle with its target;
just as that [arrow] is difficult to ward off, so too is she impossible for anyone to restrain. This is the meaning.

Regarding this, the Nirukta states: “He who, even instantly, spreads the waters by his might, like the sun with its light over the five classes of men; he is the winner of thousands, the winner of hundreds—his course they do not obstruct, for he is like a swift arrow released from the bow” (Nirukta 10.29).
1. *gara-taya.5-sa1.4.7-taritāraṃ*; *ta1.2.3.6.7-netāraṃ* | 2. *ta-bha-mu-saṃbandhi*.
The hymn consisting of the triplet beginning with "uttiṣṭhata" is the twenty-eighth hymn dedicated to Indra.
The first is an *anuṣṭubh*, and the remaining two are *triṣṭubhs*.
The seer (*ṛṣi*) of the first is King Śibi, the son of Uśīnara;
that of the second is Pratardana, the lord of the Kāśīs.
Vasumān, the son of Rohidaśva, is the [author] of the third [verse].
Thus it is enumerated: “The *ṛc*s beginning with ‘uttiṣṭhatā’ [are by] Śibi Auśīnara, Pratardana Kāśirāja, Rohidaśva, and Vasumān; the first is an *anuṣṭubh*.
The Dadhigharma [hymn] should be recited first.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "When [the Adhvaryu] says, 'O Hotṛ, look at the Vedas,' he replies, 'Rise up, look here. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.13)
Arise now and behold Indra’s seasonal portion!
If it is cooked, offer it; if it is not yet cooked, wait.
Arise! Look here at Indra’s seasonal portion. If it is cooked, offer it; if it is not cooked, wait. 1.
O officiating priests!
Arise;
rise up from your seats.
Do not sit down;
because the action is directed upward, the *ātmanepada* ending is not applied (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.24).
Having stood up, look down—that is, gaze upon—the *dadhigharma*, which is being cooked, the portion belonging to Indra that is to be enjoyed during the *ṛtu*, the season such as spring.
From the word *ṛtu* with the suffix *ghas* in the sense of *jha*, there is [the form] *ṛtviya* in the Veda;
by the rule "before *si* and *ca*" (Pāṇini 1.4.16), the designation of *pada* applies, which subverts the designation of *asaṃjñā*, and thus there is an absence of *guṇa*.
The word *bhāga* is derived from the root *bhaj* with the suffix *ghan* in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The word ‘karṣātvataḥ’ has its final syllable accented.
If that portion has been cooked—that is, if it is ready—then offer it as an oblation;
offer it into the fire for the sake of Indra. In the word *juhotana*, the substitution of *tanap* occurs according to the rule "na-sa-na-ya-ta-nā-śra."
By the rule *bhīhrī* (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.192), etc., the vowel preceding the suffix ending in *pit* becomes udātta.
If he is uncooked— that is, raw— then gladden him, intoxicate him;
or rather,
exhilarate him with hymns of praise.
In this case, by that very rule, there is the substitution of *ta* for *na*.
For that very *dadhigharma* offering, "The oblation is cooked" (*śrātaṃ haviḥ*) serves as the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "When [the Adhvaryu] has said 'The oblation is cooked,' [the Hotṛ] recites 'The oblation is cooked'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 5.13).
The oblation is cooked; come forward, O Indra! The sun has reached the middle of his path.
Your friends surround you with offerings, like householders attending a lord of wealth as he moves abroad.

The oblation is cooked; come well forward, O Indra! The Sun has traversed the middle of his paths. Your friends sit around you with their offerings, like guardians of a household waiting for the lord of booty as he moves abroad.
O Indra, this oblation called *dadhigharma* (the curd-heat offering), which is yours, has been *śrātam*—cooked or prepared.
The root *śrīñ* (in the sense of cooking) takes the suffix *niṣṭhā*, and the form *śrā* is prescribed as a Vedic irregularity (*nipātana*) in such instances as *apastṛdhethām*.
O Āu! Come forth well; come quickly with excellence.
The Sun, the illuminator, has reached the midpoint—the central portion free from the distress of unevenness—of the path, the way that is to be traversed;
the meaning is that midday has arrived for your sacrifice.
Your friends, the officiating priests who share the same station, sit around you, surrounding you together with the Soma juices that have been set down and placed within the vessels.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as sons who are protectors of their family and lineage [bring] the *vājapati* (lord of the prize).
The *vāja*s are the houses that are to be reached.
The meaning is that they wait upon their lord as he moves and goes about, saying "So be it."

The root *vraj* means "to go. From this, the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). By the rule *ajivrajyośca* (Pāṇini 7.3.60), there is a prohibition of the substitution of *ku* for *ra*.

In the case of *karṣātvataḥ*, the final syllable is udātta by the rule [Pāṇini 6.2.172]; however, in the case of *patyau vaidharye*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) applies.
For that very *dadhigharma* offering, the verse beginning with “I consider it cooked” (*śrātaṃ manye*) is the *yājyā*.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: “He offers with the words, ‘I consider it cooked in the udder; it is cooked, O so-and-so’” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.13).
1. *tabhamu tardāyam*. 2. With those accompanied by the hymn of praise:

"Cooked in the udder, cooked on the fire—well-cooked, I deem that newest truth. Drink, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, much-invoked one, enjoying all the curd of the midday [sacrifice]. (3) Cooked in the udder, I deem it cooked on the fire; well-cooked, I deem that newest truth. Drink, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, much-invoked one, enjoying all the curd of the midday [sacrifice]. (3)
I believe—that is, I know—that this oblation called *dadhi-dharma*, which has been milked from the cow's udder, is cooked (*śrātam*) and ripened in the form of milk;
furthermore, the milk that has been milked is also cooked and ripened in the fire. Now, even while it exists in the state of curds, it is cooked in the fire.
Therefore, I consider and know it to be well-cooked and well-prepared.

Thus, this oblation becomes *ṛta*, that is, true, and *navīyaḥ*, meaning newer, more recent. O *vajrin*, wielder of the thunderbolt; O *puruhūta*, much-invoked *indra*, being pleased (*juṣāṇaḥ*), do thou [accept] the curds belonging to the midday libation (*savana*) of the midday.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the object:
"Drink the oblation called Dadhidharma."
The twenty-ninth hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with "pra sasāhiṣe," is addressed to Indra; its seer is Jaya, the son of Indra, and it is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "pra sasāhiṣe; [the seer] Jaya; addressed to Indra. The application of this hymn has already been explained.
For the *darśa* offering of Indra's oblation, "pra sasāhiṣe" is the *yājyā*.
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "pra sasāhiṣe puruhūta śatrūn mahā indro ya ojasā" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.6).
This same verse serves as the *yājyā* for the cake (*puroḍāśa*) in the eleven-animal sacrifice dedicated to Indra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O much-invoked one, leader with [your] steeds, you have utterly overcome the enemies for our well-being" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7).
Among the oblations of the Devasū sacrifice, this very verse is the invitatory formula (anuvākyā) for Indra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O much-invoked one, you have utterly overcome the enemies; you have become great, O Indra, through the sacred word (brahman)" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.11).

O much-invoked one, you have utterly overcome the enemies; may your supreme power be our gift here. O Indra, bring [wealth] by the right path; you are the lord of the wealthy rivers. *pra sasāhiṣe puruhūta śatrūn jyeṣṭhas te śuṣma iha rātiras tu | indrā bhara dakṣiṇena varmani patis sindhūnām asi revatīnām || 1 ||*
O Puruhūta, O Indra invoked by many, you have utterly subdued—meaning you completely overcome—the enemies, the adversaries.
Your *śuṣma*, your drying power or strength, is the most excellent, the most praiseworthy, or the greatest.
In this rite, let there be *rāti*, your gift, for us.
For that purpose, O Indra, bring, fetch, and lead hither with your right hand the *vasūni*, the riches.
You are the lord, the master, of the *revatīnām sindhūnām*—the flowing rivers possessed of abundant wealth.

From the word *rayi*, when the suffix *matup* is added, there is vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) according to the rule "vocalization occurs abundantly before *matup* when it denotes possession" (*Pāṇini 6.1.34*). The substitution of *va* for *matup* occurs by the rule "in the Vedic language, *va* is substituted for *matup* after *ira*" (*Pāṇini 8.2.9*). And its [the *va*'] acute accent (*udātta*) is established by the rule "and after the word *re*" (*Kāśikā 6.1.176.1*).
For the oblation of Vaimṛdha, the verse beginning with "amṛgo na" is the *yājyā*.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "vi na indra mṛdho jahi mṛgo na bhīmaḥ kucaro giriṣṭhāḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.10).

Like a terrifying wild beast, roaming and dwelling in the mountains, you have come hither from the furthest distance. And having approached, O Indra, having sharpened— that is, thoroughly whetted— the sharp and pointed thunderbolt (vajra) which is of the nature of death (sṛka), strike those three times— meaning, specifically strike and destroy— our enemies, our adversaries, with that thunderbolt.
The root *taḍ* means "to strike";

Likewise, "drive away" (vi nudasva)—that is, specifically overcome—those "enemies" (mṛdhaḥ), meaning those engaged in battle and desiring to fight, as well as others.

The hymn consisting of thirty verses beginning with "prathaḥ" is addressed to the Viśvedevas and is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The seer of the first verse is Pratha, a descendant of Vasiṣṭha;

The *ṛṣi* Dharma, the son of Sūrya, is the seer of the third [hymn]. Thus it is enumerated: "Then the *carca*s; Prathas, Vāmiṣṭha, Sapratha Bhāradvāja, Dharma Maurya [are the seers] of the Vaiśvadeva [hymn].
This hymn is recited in the *pravargya* ritual during the *abhiṣṭava*.

And then, from the Anuṣṭubh hymn whose names are Prathas and Saprathas,

The far-extending and the widely-spread name of the one whose oblation is in the Anuṣṭubh meter—whatever oblation of the radiant Dhātar, of Savitṛ, and of Viṣṇu there was—that Rathantara hymn Vasiṣṭha has brought forth. ||1||

Of that Vasiṣṭha whose son was Pratha, and of that Bharadvāja whose son was Sapratha—between those two, Vasiṣṭha brought forth from the radiant Savitṛ and Viṣṇu the *rathaṃtara*, which is the oblation-producing Sāman of the *anuṣṭubh* meter, belonging to the sacrifice characterized by the *anuṣṭubh* meter; it is called *rathaṃtara* because it is the means for attaining the chariot (*ratha*). Of what sort? Cekitānam: one who intensely knows [the fruits of] ritual actions; born from *tapas*—that is, produced anew from the consecration (*dīkṣā*) or else arisen from the merit performed in previous births; and from the cause of the *tapas* being currently practiced and known, you are *vibhūtam*: pervading, renowned everywhere.

O you who desire sons, longing for sons, do you here in this world, delighting in offspring in the form of sons, grandsons, and so forth, and delighting in wealth (rayi) here in this world, be propagated through progeny; that is, be born in the form of sons and the like—the meaning is that you shall produce offspring.

The meaning is that since everything originates through sacrifice performed for a month, I am the cause of the birth of all people.
The hymn beginning with "viṣṇuḥ" consists of three verses (a *ṛc*) and twenty-three syllables; it is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Tvaṣṭṛ, the creator of embryos, or Viṣṇu, the son of Prajāpati.
The deities, as indicated by their names, are Viṣṇu, Tvaṣṭṛ, Prajāpati, Sinīvālī, Sarasvatī, and the Aśvins.
And thus it has been introduced: "Viṣṇu, Tvaṣṭṛ, the maker of the embryo; or Viṣṇu, the son of Prajāpati; the prayer for the embryo; having the deity indicated by its marks; in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
The application is based on the indicative marks.
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms;

The root *piś* means "to divide" (*avayave*). The suffix *num* is applied because it belongs to the *sūc*-class.

May Vāta, the wind, blow toward our heart as a medicine—be it an herb or water. Of what nature? One that brings about well-being (śambhu), the promoter of the alleviation of disease, and one that brings about joy (mayobhu), the promoter of happiness. Furthermore, may he extend our lifespans.

O Vāta, O Vāyu, from that which is your treasure—the storehouse of immortality (amṛta) deposited and established within your abode or place—grant us, for our very life, that immortality which lies beyond the body. Give it to us! Grant it to us!
The thirty-sixth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “prāgne,” is the seerage of Vatsya, the son of Agni; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and is dedicated to Agni.

Thus it has been enumerated: “‘prāgne’: five [verses]; [the seer] Vatsa is [the son] of Agni, but [the hymn] is addressed to Agni. These two hymns, beginning with this one, are in the Gāyatrī meter and are employed in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.
For it is prescribed: “*prāgne vācam*, *iti ma sūkta*, *imāṃ me agne samidham*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).
On the ninth day of the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*), this hymn to Jātavedas is the locus for the insertion of the *Nivid*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*maruto yasya hi*, *prāgne vācam*—this is the *āgnimāruta* [section]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.11).

Send forth your speech toward Agni, the bull among the peoples; may he carry us across our enemies. 1 Send forth your speech toward Agni, the bull among the peoples; may he carry us across our enemies. 1
O singer, send forth—utter—the hymn of praise for Agni. For what kind of one?
For the bull of the *kṣitis*, that is, of men, the sacrificers; for him who rains down desires.
If it is asked what the purpose is:
may that Agni carry us across, beyond our enemies, those who hate us.

He who shines forth from the farthest distance, across the desert, may he carry us beyond our enemies. 2. He; from; the farthest; distance; across; the desert; shines forth; he; us; may he carry; beyond; enemies. 2.
That Agni who, from the furthest distance— from an exceedingly remote region— shines forth, blazing across the desert, the waterless land; or alternatively,
across the firmament (*dhanva*).
In the expanse of the sky, it shines intensely, radiating both horizontally and vertically;
the rest is understood.

He who, as a bull, utterly consumes the Rākṣasas with his bright flame—may he carry us across our enemies. 3. He; the Rākṣasas; utterly consumes; the bull; with bright; flame; he; us; may he carry across; beyond; the enemies. 3.
The bull, the showerer, Agni, with his bright, stainless, or radiant-colored luster—that is, his splendor—consumes and utterly destroys the *rakṣas* who are the slayers of the sacrifice.
The root *jūrvī* is used in the sense of harming.
The rest has been explained.

He who looks out upon all beings and beholds them together—may he carry us across our enemies. 4. He; all; toward; looks out; beings; and; together; beholds; he; us; may he carry across; beyond; enemies. 4.
1. You are that Agni who, in the form of the sun, looks upon (*abhi-vipaśyati*)—that is, gazes with particular brilliance toward—all (*viśvā*) created beings (*bhūtajātāni*).
The meaning is that he illuminates them.
He beholds and correctly knows all worlds and all classes of beings;
this is established by others as well.

That bright Agni who was born on the far shore of this world, may he carry us across beyond our enemies. (5) He who, on the far shore of this world, of the mid-region (antarikṣa), that bright Agni who was born—manifesting himself in the form of lightning or in the form of the sun—may he carry us across beyond those who hate us. (45)
The thirty-seventh hymn, consisting of three verses beginning with “pra nūnam,” is the seerly work of Śyena Abhipatra; it is in the Gāyatrī meter.
Its deity is Agni, characterized by the quality of Jātavedas.
Thus it has been cataloged: “pra nūnam: three verses; [the seer] Abhīya Śyena [composed this] Jātavedasya [hymn].”
The application [of the verses] for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra has been stated.

Now, indeed, urge forth Jātavedas, the vigorous steed; let him sit upon this sacred grass of ours. (1) Now, indeed, urge forth Jātavedas—the knower of all that is born, or the possessor of wealth already born—the vigorous steed who pervades [all things] through his deeds, the one rich in food. O officiating priests and sacrificers, urge him forth, certainly; or rather, impel him with praises like a horse. [The root *hi* means "to go" and "to increase. Here, in the imperative (*loṭ*), the suffix *ta* is replaced by *ta* according to the rule *tasanasanathanāśca*. For what purpose? So that he may sit upon this sacred grass (*barhis*) spread out for us, having reached it. The meaning is: "Let him sit upon the sacred grass. The suffix *-ken* is used in the sense of the gerundive (*kṛtyārthe*) according to the rule *tavaiken*.

I offer forth a great and beautiful hymn of praise to this Jātavedas, the hero among sages, the bounteous one. (2) To this Jātavedas—the knower of all that is born; to him whose heroic sons are wise sages (*vipra*); to such a bounteous one (*mīḷahuṣ*), the showerer—I send forth a great, excellent hymn of praise. The root *ṛ* means "to go"; it belongs to the *jauhotyādi* class. By the rule *artipiparyośca*, the vowel of the reduplicated syllable becomes *i*.

May those splendors of Jātavedas which carry the oblations to the gods—may they promote our sacrifice. (3) Those splendors (*rucaḥ*) of Jātavedas (*jātavedasaḥ*), which are the carriers of oblations (*havyavāhanīḥ*) unto the gods (*devatrā*); with them (*tābhiḥ*), may he promote (*invatu*) our (*naḥ*) sacrifice (*yajñam*). The splendors of Jātavedas—that is, of Agni—are the seven tongues, such as Kālī, Karālī, and so forth, which are radiant (*rocamānāḥ*). "Unto the gods" (*devatrā*): the suffix *trā* is used here in the sense of the accusative case according to Pāṇini 5.4.56 (*devamanuṣyapuruṣāpuruṣamartyebhyaḥ*). They are the "carriers of oblations" (*havyavāhanīḥ*), meaning they are the ones by whom the offerings (*havyāni*) are to be carried or delivered. The long vowel in the nominative plural (*jasi*) is due to the rule *vā chandasi*. With those tongues (*jihvābhiḥ*), may he promote our sacrifice—that is, the oblation which is the means of the rite—by delivering it to the gods. The root *ivi* means "to pervade" or "to extend"; the form *invatu* is derived from this root with the addition of the *idit* marker, which causes the elision of the *num* augment. (46)
The hymn beginning with “āyaṃ gauḥ,” consisting of three verses, is the thirty-first; it is in the Gāyatrī meter.
It belongs to the one named Sārparājñī, or its deity is she herself, or else it is Sūrya.
And thus it has been introduced [in the Anukramaṇī]: “The hymn beginning with ‘āyaṃ gauḥ’ belongs to Sārparājñī; its deity is either the All-gods (daivata) or the Sun (saurya).
On the day when no [other] recitation is permitted (avivākya), there is the taking of meat.

4. In Ta1.2.3.6.7.8-bha, [it is] by way of the nature of lightning.
5. In manuscripts ta1.2.3.7 and bha1.2.4.8, “mahī” is absent; in manuscript bha7, it is “pahi. 6. In manuscripts ta and bha, “havyavāhanī” is absent.

The *gauḥ*—meaning one whose nature is to move, the speckled (*pṛśni*), having attained color, that is, having attained splendor—is the Sun; he has stepped forth (*ākramīt*), meaning he has reached the mountain of sunrise. And having stepped forth, he has sat down (*asadat*) upon the Mother—the Earth, the creator of all classes of beings—in the front, that is, in the eastern direction.
There is elision of the suffix *cha* due to the rule regarding *sadeś*. Because of the presence of the vowel *ṝ*, there is the substitution of *aḍ* for *ślu*.

Moving forward—that is, proceeding with great speed—toward the father, the protector, and by implication the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), he becomes *svaḥ*, meaning "one who sounds well" or one whose movement is beautiful.
Or rather,
he proceeds toward his father, who is departing for the heavenly world.

Moving within his luminous realm, breathing out from his breath, the Great One has illumined the sky. 2. *antaścarati rocanā asya prāṇād apānatī | vyakhyad mahiṣo divam || 2 ||* He moves within his radiant sphere, exhaling from his inhalation; the Mighty One has looked out across the heavens. 2.
The shining radiance of this sun, its luminous splendor, moves and exists within the body in the form of the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa). What does it do?
It flows from the prāṇa as the apāna.
The chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) has five functions, beginning with prāṇa.
Among these, *prāṇana* is the upward movement of the wind through the channels (*nāḍīs*).
Immediately after that *prāṇa* comes *apāna*.
Exhalation is the downward movement of the wind through the channels;
they perform that [function].
From the root *an* preceded by *apa*, the suffix *śatṛ* is applied in the *leṭ* mood;
due to its belonging to the *adādi* class, there is elision (*luk*) of the *śap* augment;
and by the rule "and [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* after an *ugit* stem," the suffix *ṅīp* is added.
The word "śataranumaḥ" has an udātta accent on the vowel of the first syllable because it is the name of a river.
Or rather: between the inner wind and the earth, the *rocanā*—the shining, radiant light—of this sun moves, that is, it travels.
The root *ruc* means "to shine.
According to Pāṇini's Sūtra 3.2.149, *anudāttettvaśca*, the suffix *yuc* is applied [to form the noun *rocana*].
What is she doing?
Moving from the out-breath (prāṇa) to the in-breath (apāna) immediately thereafter, she goes to her setting at the time of evening;
he is joined with such a meditation (dīdhī).
For this very reason, the great buffalo, the sun, has looked upon— indeed, gazes upon and illuminates— the sky and the intermediate space between sunrise and sunset.
In *maheḥ*, the suffix *ṭiṣac* is applied according to the Uṇādi Sūtra 1.46 (*avi-mahoṣṭiṣac*).
For the root *cakṣiṅ*, there is the substitution of *khyāñ*.
In the Vedic *luṅ* tense, the suffix *cli* is replaced by *aṅ* according to the rule beginning with *asyativakti*.

He shines forth through thirty domains; speech is bestowed upon the Bird. Day by day, at every dawn, [he is perceived] through the days. 3. Thirty. Domains. Forth. He shines. Speech. To the Bird. Is bestowed. At each. Dawn. Truly. By the days. 3.

"Thirty abodes" (*triṃśaddhāma*) refers to thirty places; there is a change in grammatical number (from singular to plural). They belong to "the dwelling" (*vastoḥ*), meaning they are constituent parts of the day-and-night period. The word *ahaḥ* is used here for emphasis. "By the days" (*dyubhiḥ*) means by the very rays of the sun; [the sun] shines forth, that is, it shines brightly or illuminates intensely. [The plural form] is used because of the multiplicity of moments (*muhūrta*). Here, the "abodes" refer to the moments: fifteen of the night and fifteen of the day. For the "flying one" (*pataṅgāya*)—he is called *pataṅga* because he flies or moves; this refers to the Sun. To him, speech in the form of praise is "placed," that is, directed toward him. Alternatively: during the day, there are thirty abodes. This refers to the *ghaṭikās* (hours); there are thirty *ghaṭikās*. The accusative case is used here to denote continuous duration. For such a length of time, that Sun shines forth by his rays—that is, he illuminates intensely. And at that time, speech in the form of a song is "placed" before him, held toward him, who is the Sun in the form of the flying one (*pataṅga*). The meaning is that she serves the Sun. For it is heard [in scripture]: "Agni... [and so on].

1. [The syllables] *tā* 1.2.3.6.7.8 and *bha* 1.2.7.8 [constitute] the world of mortals (*bhūrloka*). 2. [The syllables] *tā* 1.2.3.6.7.8 bestow [it]; *bha* 1.2.4.8 bestowing [it]. 3. [The syllables] *tā* 1.2.3.7 and *bha* 2.4.8 [constitute] thirty.
4. To that Sūrya; 5. Regarding *tā-bha*, the phrase "pratimukhaṃ stotṛbhyaḥ" is absent; 6.
According to *ta4.5*, it is designated as such.
7. [The word] "to the one whose form is the sun" (*sūrya-rūpāya*) does not exist [in the text].
[For it says: "In the forenoon the god moves in the sky; he stands in the midst of the day in the Yajurveda" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.1), and so forth.
When this hymn is a self-praise by Sārvarājñī, then it should be understood that she is praised as being of the nature of the Sun.
The thirty-ninth hymn, beginning with "Ṛtam," belongs to Aghamarṣaṇa, the son of Madhucchandas; it is half-Anuṣṭubh.

Since it sets forth the creation and other processes of entities such as Night and so forth, its deity is the very nature of those entities. Thus it has been cataloged: "Ṛtam: [the seer] Mādhucchandasa Aghamarṣaṇa; it concerns the activity of entities and is in the Anuṣṭubh meter."
The application [of a mantra] is to be understood from its indicative mark (liṅga).
From the heated tapas, Ṛta and Satya were born;
from that, night was born; from that, the ocean and the sea arose.
From the heated tapas, Ṛta and Satya were born;
from that, night was born; from that, the billowing ocean arose.
*Ṛta* is a name for truth. *Ṛta* is mental, consisting of a thought-conception that accords with reality; *satya* is verbal, consisting of speech that accords with reality.
By the two particles (*ca*), other categories of duty prescribed by the scriptures are also included.
All that arose from the blazing one on every side, born from the Brahman who had previously performed ascetic penance for the sake of creation;
it arose above, in the sense of being superior.
It arose;
for the Śruti says, "Having performed austerity, he created all this" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.6).
And here, "tapaḥ" (torture/austerity) is characterized as the contemplation of what is to be seen.
For another scriptural passage states: "He whose austerity consists of knowledge" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9).
The suffix *niṣṭhā* is applied after the root *indh-* preceded by the prefix *abhi* in the sense of the object (*karman*).
There is a prohibition [of the substitution of *i* for *it*] by the rule *śrīdito niṣṭhāyām* (Pāṇini 7.2.14).
According to the rule *gatiranantaraḥ*, the preceding prefix retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*).
By the rule "svarito vānudātte padādau," the single-substitute (ekādeśa) is accented with the svarita tone.
Or rather:
from the *abhīddha*—the Paramātman shining forth on all sides, who is the substratum of *māyā* and serves as the material cause—the *ṛta* (the eternal order) and the *satya* (truth) were born.
By the rule "janituḥ prakṛtiḥ" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.30), the term *prakṛti* receives the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *apādāna*.
From that very Lord, night was born;
this is also an elliptical expression for day—
both day and night were born.
The suffix *ṅīp* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule *rātreścājjasau* (4.1.31).
From that very Lord, therefore, comes the ocean (*arṇavaḥ*), which is endowed with *arṇas*, meaning water.

Since the word "ocean" (*samudra*) is intended to apply commonly to both the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and the sky (*dyu*), it is specified here by the word *arṇa* in order to clarify the intended meaning.
According to the rule *arṇasaḥ salopaśca* (Kāśikā 5.2.109.3), the suffix *v* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), and there is the elision of the *s* of *arṇas*.
From the ocean, the vast sea, the year was born,
ordaining days and nights, the ruler over all that gazes upon it.
From the ocean, the vast sea, the year was born,
ordaining days and nights, the ruler over all that gazes upon it.
After the ocean-clad earth was created, the year arose; from that year, all time was manifested.
For it is heard in scripture: "All moments, the divisions of time, the kalās, muhūrtas, and kāṣṭhas were born from the Puruṣa" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 10.1.2).
That Lord, ordaining—that is, fashioning and creating—all classes of beings characterized by days and nights, brought them forth.
The word *abhyastānām* has an acute accent on its first syllable by the rule "the first [syllable] of reduplicated forms" (*abhyastānām ādiḥ*).
Then, in the compound, the original accent of the final member (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvaratvam*) applies.
Having become the controller and master of the entire universe—the totality of living beings endowed with eyes that do not blink and other such faculties—he exists.
The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before;
he fashioned heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and the sky.
The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before;
he fashioned the heaven and the earth, the intermediate space, and likewise the sky.
1. For whom there is no [other] (ta1.2.3.7-bha2.4.8-'yasya' nāsti).
2. From that which is manifest, from self-luminous [consciousness] (ta4.5-prakāśamānāt svaprakāśāt).
3. And Truth was born (ta4.5- ca satyaṃ vājāyata).

[The reading] *miṣato ... vartate* does not exist in Ta3, 4, 5, 8, Bha4, 5, 7, 8; in Bha2 it is *viśvasya trailokyasya miṣataḥ*, meaning "while the entire threefold world is looking on, he who is being born is the controller and the master. In Ta1, 2, 6, 7, it is: "That such Creator, the Supreme Lord, having transcended the respective forms of the gods beginning with Sūrya and the worlds beginning with the Earth exactly as they were in a previous creation, fashioned them;
he brought them into existence by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*).
Because 'heaven' (*div*) is included [in the compound], the word *svaḥ* is intended to signify a specific enjoyment (*bhoga*)."
Having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite,
he then shows three verses for the purpose of immersion (*avagāhana*).

According to the sequence of Mādhava’s commentary on the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, there is no commentary on the third mantra in the editions of the text found in [the libraries of] Ta, trī, upaniṣad, bṛhadāraṇyake, and mādhavīyavyākhyāpakti (specifically in the manuscripts designated as 3.4.5.8).
The sun and the moon serve as the banners of Time; heaven, earth, and the intermediate space—thus [constitutes] the triple world, *svaḥ*.
The word *svaḥ* denotes happiness (*sukha*). It is an adjective qualifying heaven (*div*).

The meaning is that the Creator (dhātā), the Ordainer (vidhātā), has fashioned all this—just as He fashioned it in the past, in a previous kalpa—so too will He fashion it in the coming kalpa.

Thus far, the Śākala Saṃhitā of the Ṛgveda has been printed; now the *Khilas* (supplementary hymns) are being compiled.
According to the *Caraṇavyūha*, there are five recensions (*śākhās*) of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā: the Śākala, Vāṣkala, Āśvalāyana, Śāṅkhāyana, and Māṇḍūkāyana.
According to some authorities, however, there are twenty-one, twenty-five, or even twenty-seven recensions of the Ṛgveda.
It had been determined up to this point that the Śāṅkhāyana-śākhā and the Kauṣītaki-śākhā were merely two names for one and the same branch.
However, it has now been established that the Kauṣītaki-śākhā is distinct from the Śāṅkhāyana-śākhā;
indeed, Dr. T.R. Cintāmaṇi in Madras has published the Kauṣītaki-gṛhyasūtra as being entirely different from the Śāṅkhāyana-gṛhyasūtra.

They have also introduced in their preface that the two texts, the *Kauṣītaki-Śrautasūtra* and the *Kauṣītaki-Brāhmaṇa*, will be published separately from the *Śāṅkhāyana-Śrautasūtra* and *Brāhmaṇa*. Following the printing of those two, it will be easy to understand what specific characteristics existed within the *Kauṣītaki* recension of the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā. (Preface, p. 909)
Wherever a *khila* (supplementary hymn) is to be inserted or recited within the *saṃhitā*, there is an indicator for it.
If several *khilas* occur in one place, then at the end of the other *khilas*, a representative verse (*pratīka*) from a *ṛc* mantra is extracted.

In this book, both the *saṃhitā* and the *khilas* are provided with accent marks;
however, its system of writing accents is entirely different.
Generally, in written manuscripts, the *svarita* is marked with a sign above and the *anudātta* with a sign below.
In this book, only two types of accents have been shown—namely, the udātta and the jātyasvarita—while the anudātta and the other kind of svarita have been excluded.
The udātta is indicated by a line placed above, and the jātyasvarita is indicated by this particular mark. This mark appears twice in the khila sections (at 1.11.4 and 12.7).
If the final syllable is udātta or begins with a svarita, it is indicated by the very sign of the *jātyasvara*.
Even when the svarita is short, it is written with three bends (*trikampa*);
beneath it, the mark for the *anudātta* is made, or above it, the mark for the *svarita*.

According to the opinion of the venerable Professor Śephṭelovits, this system of accents bears a resemblance to the accentuation systems of the Maitrāyaṇī and Kāṭhaka Saṃhitās and serves as their basis;
he adopted that very system of accent notation for his two volumes.
I have likewise adopted it here.
Among those additional *khila* sections that were printed in their own edition from the Kashmirian *khilas*, this *vaidyudātta* accent is shown in some of the *sūktas*.
I have, however, printed the additional *khilas* entirely without accents, because there is no agreement between the printed editions and the manuscript copies regarding their accents.
Professor Max Müller also printed the *khilas* in his own edition for the most part without accents.

Among all the works I have consulted regarding the recitation and determination of the *khila* passages, the two copies of the *Ṛgveda* belonging to the Śāṅkhāyana school, written in the Nāgarī script and provided by Paṇḍita Sātavalekar of the city of Aūdha, deserve first mention.
One of these was copied in the year Saṃvat 1754 at Jīrṇadurga (the city of Junāgaḍh) in the Gujarāt region, and the other was copied in the city of Natrā in the year Saṃvat 1849.
Therefore, in the sixth chapters of both [works], the *saṃhitā* is divided;
however, the *aṣṭakas* are not enumerated. Rather, the beginning and end of the *maṇḍalas* are shown.
The vowels are marked with red ink.
In the Nāgarī manuscript, the anudātta and svarita accents are shown according to the current convention.
In the Junāgaḍh manuscript, the anudātta is shown as before, but the svarita is likewise treated as anudātta; however, it is shown by splitting the middle of the syllable.
Mr. Peter Peterson, having examined manuscripts of the Śāṅkhāyana Saṃhitā of the Ṛgveda and its Padapāṭha located in Alwar, described them in his catalogue.

Since the readings in the Junāgaḍh and Nahrānagar manuscripts are identical, I have utilized only the more ancient of the two—the Junāgaḍh manuscript—in this work, referring to it here and there by the designation "Junā."

There is no written evidence for this manuscript being a descendant of the Śākhāyana recension. Furthermore, according to the opinion of Mr. Peterson, the manuscripts located in Alwar city also follow the Śākhāyana recension;
however, even in those cases, there is no written evidence for their belonging to the Śākhāyana recension.

However, since it is well known in the world that the Brāhmaṇas of the Gurjara country belong to the Śāṅkhāyana school, it is appropriate to accept that their manuscripts belong to the Śāṅkhāyana recension.

It is difficult to say whether these *khila* (supplementary) texts were included within the *saṃhitā* of the Śāṅkhāyana school as *khilas*, or whether they were incorporated there for some other reason.
For it is clear from the manuscripts that the *khilas* are contained within each chapter, arranged in sections (*vargas*).

In the *Caraṇavyūhabhāṣya*, the distinctive feature of the Śākala branch is demonstrated as follows: "The tenth Vālakhilya hymn, *yam ṛtvijaḥ* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.54), should not be recited; instead, the two mantras located therein, *eka evāgniḥ* and *yam ṛtvijaḥ* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.88.18), should be recited as a *khila* immediately after the mantra *kati prayajaḥ kati sūktavācaḥ*."

In accordance with this, two mantras have been written in the Junagadh manuscript—excluding the tenth Vālakhilya hymn—immediately after the mantra beginning with "kati prayāḥ. It is not known whether this constitutes a specific feature of the Śākala branch in the Alwar manuscript; however, this has been indicated in the catalogue compiled by the venerable Mr. Peterson.
By comparing the Ṛgveda manuscript sealed by the nobleman Āuphraṣṭa with that of the nobleman Pīṭarsan, the *khilas* found in the Alwar manuscript were identified and described by [the latter].
There are ninety-one *khilas* present in the Alwar manuscript that do not exist in the Āuphraṣṭa manuscript.
Alternatively, if they do exist, the question of what their readings are remains a subject of inquiry.

I had intended to examine the Alwar manuscripts myself; however, due to the regulations of the library authorities, which prohibit taking manuscript books out of the library, I was unable to view them.
Consequently, my work had to be carried out solely by following the descriptions of those manuscripts provided by Mr. Pīṭhāsaṃnama.

By comparing the Alwar and Junagadh manuscripts, the following specific differences regarding the *khila* section come into view: (1) The *khila* titled "yastunairadhyayanam" occurs after Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.49 in the Alwar manuscript, but after Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.48 in the Junagadh manuscript.
(2) The Śrīsūkta (2.6) is absent from the Alwar manuscript.
It is found in the Junāgaḍ manuscript.
(3) The Śivasaṃkalpasūkta (4.11) is not present in the Alwar manuscript;
it is found in the Junāgaḍ manuscript.

(4) The three *khilas* numbered 3.19, 3.20, and 4.12 are found in the Junāgaḍ manuscript, whereas their absence is observed in the Alwar manuscript. (5) The *khila* numbered 2.12 is fragmentary in the Junāgaḍ manuscript, while it is complete in the Alwar manuscript.

Excluding these specific differences, everything else in the Alwar and Junāgaḍa manuscripts is identical.

From this difference it is inferred that although these *khilas* are generally included within the enumeration of the sections (*vargas*), they were nevertheless not counted among them in the Śāṅkhāyana Saṃhitā of the Ṛgveda. Another matter for consideration is which specific *khilas* were included as such in the Śāṅkhāyana recension. In both manuscripts, the *khila* beginning with "vidā maghavan vidā" is found.
Immediately following that, even the portion beginning with "agnirdeveddho vidā maghavan vidā" is identical in both.
The *khila* readings in both manuscripts are also for the most part the same;
those variant readings which are found in the Junāgaḍ manuscript have all been indicated by me in their respective places.
The specific characteristics of the Jūnāgaḍh manuscript among the aforementioned *khilas* have already been demonstrated in the various footnotes.

In this collection of *khilas*, the *Śivasamkalpopaniṣad* consisting of thirteen mantras is found (*khila* 4.11). However, in the manuscript of the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā* held in the British Museum in London (catalogue number Add. 5351), that same text consists of twenty-eight mantras. In the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā printed by Paṇḍit Sātavalekar Mahodaya, the Śivasamkalpopaniṣad, consisting of twenty-six verses, has been printed in some places with different readings and in a different order. The well-known Śrīsūkta appears in this supplementary collection (khila-grantha) as the sixth khila.
Since ancient times, this Śrīsūkta has been recited by followers of the Vedic dharma in Bhāratavarṣa.
Certain mantras dedicated to it have been cited in the Śruti, Smṛti, and other scriptures.
Manuscripts of this Śrīsūkta, in both complete and incomplete forms, are available throughout Bhāratavarṣa.

Although I made great efforts to acquire those two volumes, I was unable to obtain them because they were sent abroad due to the fear of destruction during the Great War.

In the *Saṃhitā* manuscript, the seventh *Aṣṭaka* is written in the Nāgarī script, dated to the year 1850.
In it, the *khila* "pāvamānīḥ svastyayanīḥ" is recorded according to the reading of Max Müller.

(*yenedaṃ bhūtam*), must have been written there, since the nineteenth mantra, "Favored by cows, by wealth... (*gobhirjuṣṭo dhanena*), is indicated as being contained therein in the index leaf.
In the same manner, the *khilas* (supplementary hymns) such as "asaṃjñānamuśanā," "narhaṃsya senādaraṇaṃ," "prādhvarāṇāṃ pate," and "vidā maghavan vidā" are also written therein.
The word-text (*padapāṭha*) of the sixth book (*aṣṭaka*) in this manuscript was written during the year 1653.
The compilers of the catalogue have noted that in the fourth chapter, there is one additional *sūkta* in the Max Müller manuscript compared to this one.
It appears that someone—surely the author of the tenth *Vālakhilya* hymn—intended to include an additional portion among them.
In the Aundh manuscript, a certain section of the *Khila* is present that exceeds that found in other manuscripts;
its specific textual characteristics have already been demonstrated by me in the footnotes.
Regarding the two *khila* sections (4.5 and 4.11), the missing portions existing in the Kashmir manuscript were found in the Aundh manuscript and have been inserted there.
At 3.20, the lacuna in the *khila* section as it exists in the Kashmir manuscript has been filled on the basis of the Junāgaḍh manuscript.
Furthermore, although there are many other lacunae in the Kashmir manuscript, their restoration is impossible due to the lack of available manuscripts and the absence of printed editions.

Although the eleven Vālakhilya hymns have been printed in the eighth Maṇḍala according to the traditional sequence, they are nevertheless included here at their proper places (1.4; 6; 3.1–8; 18) because they are contained within the *Khila* section of the Kashmiri manuscript.
Variant readings are found in the Vālakhilya hymns of the Kashmiri manuscript and should be consulted therein.
Furthermore, some incorrect readings are also encountered in the *Khila* section of the Kashmiri manuscript.

In such instances, the esteemed Śeṣṭeloviṅga Mahāśayas have adopted correct readings based on parallel Vedic recensions or through conjecture; furthermore, the incorrect readings found in the manuscripts have been recorded in the footnotes.
They have also indicated the previously mentioned printed *khila* manuscripts and their respective variant readings (912).
The *khilas* (supplementary hymns) have also been specified;
those passages where there is a similarity of composition between the *khilas* and the *saṃhitā* and other texts, as well as the related variant readings, have been recorded by them.

Following them, I too have provided a commentary for each *khila* (supplementary hymn); however, that commentary has not been cited verbatim. Regarding matters of stylistic similarity, I have consulted the original texts and performed necessary corrections and additions as required.
Furthermore, those additional *khila* mantras or variant readings (*pāṭhabheda*) found in printed editions and manuscripts have been collected in the commentary.
The *khilapāṭha* (supplementary readings) contained in the Kashmir manuscript was accepted by me almost exactly as it was printed by the noble Śephṭelovitz;
however, wherever there was some doubt regarding the reading, I also consulted the Kashmir manuscript.

In those instances where they had rejected the reading found in the Kashmir manuscript in favor of a correct one—while noting the incorrect reading in a footnote—I have not recorded that same incorrect reading.
In certain places, they have retained the incorrect readings as they were in the *khila* sections while indicating the correct readings in their footnotes.
Some of these indicated readings, particularly those occurring in the *Sauparṇasūkta*, have been incorporated by me into the main text.
Apart from the determination of the readings, other matters concerning them that appear in the footnotes should likewise be consulted there.

In some instances, having discarded an incorrect reading found in a manuscript, I have adopted a correct reading based on either a printed edition or another manuscript. During the critical study of the *Khila* texts by the venerable E. B. Keith, three correct readings were pointed out; these have been accepted here.
The notes on the *Khilas* have been written by me in the Sanskrit language itself.
Certain symbols have been employed for the purpose of achieving brevity in writing; these are demonstrated in the "Explanatory Notes" (*saṃkṣepavivaraṇa*).
Regarding the writing of annotations (*ṭippaṇī*), this procedure has been adopted: (1) A table of contents for each chapter is provided at the beginning of that chapter.
Variants in the readings of the table of contents are also indicated in this very place.

(2) An indication of the location in the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā* where the *khila* is to be recited. (3) A listing of the names of those works in which the *khila* has been printed, either in its entirety or in part.

(4) A listing of the names and other details of those Vedic and non-Vedic texts in which the *khila* appears, whether in full or in part, with variations in the sequence of mantras or differences in the readings.
(5) A demonstration of variant readings according to the sequence of the mantra-texts.
The accepted reading is first set forth in bold typeface,
together with the titles of the source texts upon which it is based.

Subsequently, the various textual variants have been provided with references to their respective sources. Where the basis for the adopted reading was not explicitly shown and the basis for a variant was minimal, it should be understood that no mention was made because the superiority of the basis for the adopted reading was self-evident. (6) Additional mantras found in printed *khila* manuscripts and other texts.
(7) Variants of the readings of the additional mantras;

the time of composition of the *khila-sūktas* and their relationship with the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā* and the *Bāṣkala* and other recensions have been discussed at great length by the venerable Professor Max Müller in his own book and various papers written in the German language.
The essence of that work has been extracted here in the Introduction written in the English language.
I have previously stated that I have collected the *khilas* here following the *Khilakāṇḍa* printed by the venerable Śepṭelovijha;
therefore, I consider it appropriate to offer my first thanks to them.
Other printed editions of the *khilas* and other Sanskrit texts that I utilized for determining the readings of the *khilas*, as well as their authors, also deserve my gratitude.

I am especially worthy of thanks to Professor Sātavalekar Mahodaya, who resides in Aundh Nagar, for having assisted me by providing two volumes of the Ṛgveda Śākala Saṃhitā edited by himself for my use.
Likewise, I have examined many manuscript copies of the Khila texts found in the libraries located in cities such as Tanjore, Tiruvanantapuram, and Adyar;
I extend my gratitude to those institutions as well.
I have consulted several books and articles written in the English and German languages for the composition of this work; their authors also deserve my thanks.

Finally, the author Ciṃ. Ga. Kāśīkara, who is devoted to the learned, offers his gratitude to those scholars who have provided assistance in the matter of printing the supplements (*khila*)—whether through suggestions, by providing printed copies of books, or in other ways.
